title: No agreed parameterization or format for unanchored PAIC sensitivity
text: QBA-29 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising

title: No agreed parameterization or format for unanchored PAIC sensitivity
text:
Statement
Unanchored PAICs depend on cross-study exchangeability and transportability assumptions that are strong and partly untestable: Phillippo et al. 2017 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740), the peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18, state that unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions, which are widely regarded as infeasible. The report’s rule, that no unanchored PAIC receives a strong causal interpretation without a formal QBA or partial-identification analysis or an explicit exploratory label, is a reporting safeguard rather than a condition for identification: QBA is neither mathematically necessary when the identifying assumptions hold nor sufficient to justify a causal claim, and it never establishes the absence of bias outside the specified model or range. Residual bias is unestimable from the usual observed data law without auxiliary information, so negative controls, proxies, validation data or additional structural restrictions are what would change that, and there is still no agreed parameterization, threshold or reporting format for the sensitivity analysis the rule would require.

title: No agreed parameterization or format for unanchored PAIC sensitivity
text:
Why it is open
Residual bias in an unanchored comparison is a function of unmeasured prognostic structure, so within the usual data law it can only be bounded by assumption, and there is no agreed parameterization, prior or reporting format for that bias in the ITC setting, so even a willing analyst has no standard instrument. Enforcement depends on journals and appraisal bodies while unanchored PAICs continue to be submitted as primary comparative evidence with no quantification of residual bias, often where no alternative exists, so the pressure is toward a point estimate rather than a bias range. There is no agreed threshold for what counts as a formal QBA, so a token one-parameter analysis could satisfy the letter of the rule. Labeling a result exploratory also removes the basis for a reimbursement decision that still has to be made, which creates pressure against applying the rule exactly where it matters most.

title: No agreed parameterization or format for unanchored PAIC sensitivity
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




NICE Decision Support Unit, Technical Support Document 18: Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Submissions to NICE
Long-standing guidance treating the unanchored population-adjustment assumption set as unusually demanding. The entry cited it with no locator; this is the document it referred to.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18)
States that unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions, which are widely regarded as infeasible, and that the accuracy of unanchored estimates is unknown because residual bias from unobserved factors cannot be quantified. Supplies the real citation for the entry’s unsourced NICE claims.


Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Motivated by the observation that robustness of unanchored results with regard to model assumptions is often only qualitatively discussed, corroborating the absence of a routine residual-bias sensitivity analysis.


Leahy et al. 2023, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
HTA workshop recommendations whose ninth item is that QBA should generally be considered a sensitivity analysis, supporting the claim that no standard residual-bias analysis routinely accompanies unanchored PAIC.

title: No agreed parameterization or format for unanchored PAIC sensitivity
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Adopt the rule as a reporting safeguard rather than as an identification criterion: require unanchored submissions to state the exchangeability and transportability assumptions explicitly and, for decision-grade use, to accompany the estimate with QBA or partial identification over substantively justified departures, qualifying the causal interpretation as exploratory where adequate sensitivity analysis is unavailable. Define a minimum standard for what qualifies, so a token one-parameter analysis does not satisfy it, and state in the output that the analysis characterizes robustness under its own assumptions rather than establishing the absence of bias. Pair the exploratory label with decision procedures that can act on bounds, and where auxiliary information exists, whether negative controls, proxies, validation data or defensible structural restrictions, use it rather than treating residual bias as unaddressable in principle.

title: No agreed parameterization or format for unanchored PAIC sensitivity
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “No strong causal claim from an unanchored PAIC without QBA” The title states a rule the audit found too categorical, since quantitative bias analysis is neither necessary when the identifying assumptions hold nor sufficient to justify a causal claim.
The source said. “The report proposes reclassifying unanchored comparisons as transportability analyses and applying a strict rule: no strong causal interpretation of an unanchored PAIC without either a formal QBA or a partial-identification analysis, or a transparent statement that residual bias cannot be usefully quantified and the result is therefore exploratory.”
What was wrong with it. The entry was flagged unattributed in the source and its only reference was a bare NICE DSU technical support document with no locator; it is now sourced to Phillippo et al. 2017 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740), with Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) and Leahy et al. 2023 (doi:10.1017/S0266462323002702) supporting the absence of a routine residual-bias sensitivity analysis. GPT-5.6 Sol found the rule too categorical as a technical claim and narrowed the never-estimable premise to the usual observed data law without auxiliary information; the literature auditor noted the rule is weaker than TSD 18’s own position, which treats unanchored results lacking such evidence as not worthy of consideration.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Flagged source_unsourced; I can convert the two load-bearing assertions into sourced ones. Claims 2 and 3 are directly supported by the NICE DSU authors’ own published account of TSD 18: ‘Unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions, which are widely regarded as infeasible’, and the accuracy of unanchored estimates described as entirely unknown because residual bias from unobserved factors cannot be quantified. That is the real reference the entry’s bare ‘NICE DSU technical support document’ placeholder should carry (Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams, Welton). Claim 5 is corroborated by Ren et al. 2025, whose entire motivation is that ‘the robustness of the results with regard to model assumptions is often only qualitatively discussed’, and by Leahy et al. 2023, whose ninth recommendation is that ‘QBA should generally be considered a sensitivity analysis’. Claims 4, 6, 7, 8 are normative and defensible. Note that claim 7’s rule is in tension with TSD 18’s stronger position that unanchored results without such evidence are not worthy of consideration at all.

open / overstated. The underlying concern remains open, but the central rule is too categorical as a technical claim. An unanchored cross-trial contrast generally requires conditional exchangeability or transportability of potential-outcome levels across studies, plus consistency, positivity, estimand alignment, and valid estimation. This makes C2 and the technical content of C3 directionally correct when comparing otherwise sound anchored and unanchored ITCs, although no design is universally the least credible. C4 and C8 are correct: sensitivity methods characterize robustness only under their specified assumptions and cannot exclude bias outside the modeled mechanisms or parameter ranges. C7 confuses a prudent reporting safeguard with a condition for causal identification. QBA or partial identification is neither mathematically necessary when the identifying assumptions hold nor sufficient to justify a strong causal interpretation. The claim that residual bias can never be estimated from the data is valid only for the usual observed IPD-plus-aggregate-data law without auxiliary information, negative controls, proxies, validation data, or additional structural restrictions. C5 and C6 are empirical practice claims that cannot be established from statistical theory alone. At cpaic@9d150e9, NAMESPACE exposes no general residual-bias QBA for unanchored MAIC or STC: prior_sensitivity varies cML-NMR priors, while bridge_fragility addresses bounded component main-effect drift. This supports the package-level gap but cannot establish field-wide absence or routine practice. C1 is a provenance flag rather than a methodological claim. The issue is genuinely high severity when an unanchored estimate drives a decision, but not automatically for explicitly exploratory work.

title: Prespecification and outcome-driven choice of sensitivity ranges
text:
Statement
Sensitivity parameters, their scales, ranges, distributions and dependence assumptions should be prespecified where feasible, and this is already published HTA guidance rather than a new proposal: Leahy et al. 2023 (doi:10.1017/S0266462323002702) recommend that input parameters be identified through a systematic and transparent approach and specified a priori in a protocol or analysis plan, with code and data shared with HTA bodies and early engagement on the nature of the QBA. Ranges tuned after seeing which values preserve statistical significance or cost-effectiveness must not be presented as prespecified, although a disclosed post hoc tipping search is a legitimate exploratory analysis. What is missing is enforcement rather than the principle: no dedicated registration or auditable tooling makes a post hoc range change visible in the record, and no QBA-specific correction repairs undisclosed data-dependent selection over models and ranges, even though a specification can already be time-stamped in an ordinary protocol or registry and general selective-inference, multiverse and worst-case methods exist.

title: Prespecification and outcome-driven choice of sensitivity ranges
text:
Why it is open
QBA multiplies analyst degrees of freedom because every bias parameter has a scale, a range, a distribution and a dependence structure that are chosen rather than estimated, and the analysis is typically performed by the sponsor after the primary result is known. A reviewer reading the submission cannot distinguish a prespecified range from one tuned until the conclusion survived, because the tuning leaves no trace in the output and nothing in the record time-stamps the specification unless the analyst volunteers it. No statistical correction can repair an undisclosed choice of bias model and range, so the guarantee has to come from governance and auditable tooling rather than from inference, and transparency currently depends entirely on voluntary disclosure.

title: Prespecification and outcome-driven choice of sensitivity ranges
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Leahy et al. 2023, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
HTA workshop recommendations requiring that input parameters be identified through a systematic and transparent approach and specified a priori in a protocol or analysis plan, that evidence be collected transparently, that all code and data be shared with HTA bodies, and that decision makers be engaged early. Already covers the prespecification principle; supplies no registration mechanism or correction for selection over ranges.

title: Prespecification and outcome-driven choice of sensitivity ranges
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Operationalize the guidance that already exists rather than restate it: time-stamp the sensitivity specification, including scales, ranges, distributions and dependence assumptions, in the protocol or analysis plan lodged with the decision maker before results are known, and engage the appraisal body early as the workshop recommends. Build auditable tooling that records the specification and any later change so a post hoc range change is visible in the record alongside reproducible code, seeds and elicitation materials. Label a post hoc tipping search as exploratory and disclose the full search rather than presenting it as confirmatory, using existing selective-inference or multiverse reporting where a disclosed search has to be summarized.

title: Decision QBA: net benefit, tipping surfaces and extrapolation
text:
Statement
For an HTA governed by cost-effectiveness the decision-relevant QBA output is the economic model evaluated over the plausible bias region, reported as incremental net benefit surfaces, decision-reversal proportions and expected regret against clinical and cost-effectiveness thresholds, and because HTA needs lifetime survival the bias region must be carried through the extrapolation model as well. A p = 0.05 tipping boundary is a valid answer to an inferential question and merely insufficient for the decision, though the entry’s exemplar analysis does read its result off exactly that boundary. The claim that nothing links the ITC sensitivity region to the economic model is wrong: Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) explicitly recommend incorporating sensitivity results into economic scenario analyses and judging robustness by whether all scenarios yield ICERs below the threshold; what does not exist is a link to the model’s probabilistic sensitivity analysis through a shared parameter space, or any framework indexing the survival extrapolation model jointly with the bias parameters.

title: Decision QBA: net benefit, tipping surfaces and extrapolation
text:
Why it is open
The map from a bias parameter to a decision runs through survival extrapolation, costs and QALYs and is strongly nonlinear, so a modest change in a hazard ratio can move the decision quantity far more than it moves the effect estimate, and propagating a single corrected point estimate cannot reproduce that. Economic models are usually built by a different team in different software from the ITC, so evaluating the model at every point of the bias surface is organizationally and computationally expensive, and nothing shares draws or parameters between the ITC sensitivity region and the model’s probabilistic sensitivity analysis even though nesting or conditioning over bias scenarios is statistically possible. Bias parameters are naturally specified for the observed follow-up while the decision depends mostly on a period in which no data exist, and no framework indexes the extrapolation model choice by the bias parameters, so the two are explored separately and their interaction is never displayed. With several bias parameters the tipping point is a surface with no accepted summary, and judging whether the tipping region is attainable still requires the elicitation the method was often adopted to avoid.

title: Decision QBA: net benefit, tipping surfaces and extrapolation
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Recommends that sensitivity analysis results be incorporated into scenario analyses within economic models, explicitly assessing their impact on the ICER, with robustness judged by whether all scenarios fall below the threshold. Counter-evidence to the claim that no link to the economic model exists; it does not link to the model’s probabilistic sensitivity analysis or share a parameter space. Its case study also reads a significance-crossing point off a deterministic sensitivity curve.

title: Decision QBA: net benefit, tipping surfaces and extrapolation
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Move from the scenario analysis published guidance already recommends to a shared parameter space: nest or condition the economic model’s probabilistic sensitivity analysis over bias scenarios using shared draws, and report incremental net benefit surfaces, decision-reversal proportions and expected regret against noninferiority margins and cost-effectiveness thresholds alongside the feasibility and support map. Index the extrapolation model jointly with the bias parameters so the sensitivity surface reports lifetime survival and net benefit rather than in-trial effects only. Build interfaces so a PAIC QBA object can be consumed directly by the health-economic model, and pass a single effect parameter only where it demonstrably carries the whole modeled bias.

title: Decision QBA: net benefit, tipping surfaces and extrapolation
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 2 findings from 2 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “The decision-relevant QBA quantity is incremental net benefit as a function of the bias parameters, together with the probability of recommendation reversal and expected regret, not whether a 95% interval for a log hazard ratio excludes zero. Tipping points should be surfaces computed against clinical and cost-effectiveness thresholds rather than a p = 0.05 boundary, and because HTA needs lifetime survival the bias region has to be carried through the extrapolation model as well.”
What was wrong with it. The literature auditor found the claim that nothing links the ITC sensitivity region to the economic model contradicted by Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13), which recommends precisely that link as scenario analysis against the ICER threshold, leaving only the probabilistic-sensitivity-analysis link and the shared parameter space missing. GPT-5.6 Sol softened two absolutes: a p = 0.05 tipping boundary is legitimate when the prespecified conclusion is statistical significance, and passing one effect parameter into the economic model is adequate when that parameter is a sufficient conduit for the modeled biases and its full scenario or uncertainty distribution is propagated, rather than a misuse in every case.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 2 surviving findings from: Accounting for Heterogeneity in Relative Treatment Effects f; Quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in una. New citations: 10.1017/rsm.2025.13, 10.1177/0272989X15570113

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Claim 2 is corroborated by the very method the agenda holds up as the state of the art: Ren et al. 2025’s case study reads its sensitivity result off a significance boundary, ‘If the proportion is greater than 28%, then the treatment effect becomes statistically significant’, which is exactly the p=0.05 anchoring claim 2 calls a misuse. The caveat is claim 9. Ren et al. 2025 do explicitly link the sensitivity region to the economic model, recommending that ‘These sensitivity analysis results can be incorporated into scenario analyses within economic models, explicitly assessing their impact on the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER)’, with decision rules based on whether all scenarios fall below or above the threshold. So a link to the economic model exists in published guidance; what does not exist is a link to the model’s probabilistic sensitivity analysis or a shared parameter space, and no published work indexes the survival extrapolation model jointly with the bias parameters (claims 7, 8). Claims 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 are normative and correct in substance. Tipping-point machinery for evidence synthesis exists but only for arm-based network meta-analysis correlation parameters, not for unanchored PAIC bias surfaces.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 is correct only after defining the reference point, feasible set, direction, or metric: with several parameters the tipping set is a boundary or hypersurface, but ‘smallest departure’ is otherwise undefined. C2 is too categorical. A p=0.05 tipping boundary is valid when the prespecified conclusion is statistical significance; it is merely insufficient for an HTA decision. C3 is appropriate for a conventional cost-effectiveness decision rule, but incremental net benefit is not the only possible HTA decision quantity and cannot replace clinical, budget, equity, or other constraints. C4, C5, C7, and C8 are valid possibility statements. C6 is false as a universal rule: if bias acts only through one treatment-effect parameter and the full scenario or uncertainty distribution for that parameter is passed to the economic model, it can be sufficient; a single corrected point estimate is inadequate only for a question about the whole bias region. C9 is an absolute practice claim outside a technical audit and is not a statistical impossibility: probabilistic sensitivity analysis can be nested or conditioned over bias scenarios using shared draws. The remaining open work is integration, extrapolation specification, and software workflow, not a new identification result, so the asserted very-high severity is inflated.

title: Propagating every uncertainty layer without prohibitive cost
text: QBA-23 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging

title: Propagating every uncertainty layer without prohibitive cost
text:
Statement
A decision-grade unanchored PAIC QBA should inventory and propagate the material data and model uncertainties, state which sensitivity assumptions are held fixed and which are probabilistic, and separately quantify numerical integration and Monte Carlo error rather than folding them into inferential uncertainty as if they were random scientific parameters. The source’s count of eleven layers is not defensible: read literally the list names thirteen entities and about ten categories when paired items are grouped, and it conflates sampling uncertainty, model uncertainty, nonidentified sensitivity assumptions, deterministic numerical error, Monte Carlo estimation error and downstream decision-model uncertainty. Nested resampling and a fully joint Bayesian model are two important options but not the only credible ones, since sandwich or estimating-equation variance, the delta method, multiple imputation, modular Monte Carlo schemes, parametric bootstrap and hybrids also apply, and only the resampling route has a failed-replicate problem at all.

title: Propagating every uncertainty layer without prohibitive cost
text:
Why it is open
Several uncertainty sources are produced by different teams in different software and delivered only as summary numbers, so there is no object in which they can be combined and completeness is determined by what the software happens to support. Pseudo-IPD reconstruction error, and integration and Monte Carlo error for the fits that do not report them, are conventionally treated as negligible without ever being quantified. Nested bootstrap cost is multiplicative in replicates, grid points and model fits wherever every outer replicate must re-solve the calibration or refit outcome models at each bias-grid point, though it depends on which quantities must be refitted and which computations can be reused or approximated. Where failed replicates are dropped the reported interval is conditional on the weighting having succeeded, which understates exactly the positivity problem the sensitivity analysis was meant to expose, and there is no accepted way to represent failures inside an interval.

title: Propagating every uncertainty layer without prohibitive cost
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9, cmaic() and plot_integration_error()
The stratified bootstrap in cmaic() re-estimates weights and refits the outcome model, propagating weighting and outcome-model uncertainty jointly, and fails closed below a minimum successful-replicate fraction rather than silently keeping an arbitrary subset. plot_integration_error() reports quasi-Monte-Carlo integration convergence for non-survival cML-NMR fits but not for survival fits. It propagates only part of the list.

title: Propagating every uncertainty layer without prohibitive cost
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Specify one propagation scheme appropriate to the estimator, whether nested resampling, a joint Bayesian model, sandwich or delta-method variance, multiple imputation or a hybrid, and require the analysis to state which layers were propagated and which were held fixed. Report numerical integration and Monte Carlo error as computational diagnostics next to the statistical uncertainty rather than inside it, extending the integration-convergence diagnostic that already exists for non-survival fits to survival fits. Report the failure map alongside the effect surface and develop resampling schemes that bound the contribution of failed replicates or return an identified set instead of an interval when a nonnegligible fraction fail, reducing cost with warm starts, surrogate models over the bias grid or analytic approximations validated against the full nested computation.

title: Propagating every uncertainty layer without prohibitive cost
text:
Our study

Bootstrap intervals over a bias grid when resamples fail
The question put to it. When a bootstrap sensitivity analysis drops resamples whose weights fail near the edge of support, how does the interval behave, and is conditioning on success immaterial?
What it found. No. Near the edge of the source’s support, up to 67% of bootstrap resamples failed to produce MAIC weights, and the percentile interval from the survivors covered only 0.29 to 0.65 (0.14 to 0.56 counting failed original fits as giving no interval). The surviving resamples are those that contain the few patients who make the weights possible, so their spread understates the estimate’s. The failure share should be reported as a result and the interval withheld where it is material.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: coverage given success 0.288 to 0.645 where more than 10% of resamples failed.
Where failures were rare, coverage 0.87 to 0.93, already below nominal at low effective sample size.
Effective sample size fell to about 3 of 100 or 5 of 300 at the most extreme assumed target mean.

Design.

Estimand

A’s target mean outcome at each assumed target covariate mean

Methods compared

MAIC with percentile bootstrap over successful resamples

Data-generating mechanism

Unanchored MAIC with a sweep of the assumed target mean toward the source’s support boundary; percentile bootstrap intervals from successful resamples; coverage conditional on success and unconditional. 2 cells, 500 replicates each, 200 resamples.

Replicates

500 per scenario, 1,000 in total, 200 resamples each at 4 grid points


What this does not answer. One covariate, continuous outcome; cost and surrogate approaches and identified sets not studied. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Propagating every uncertainty layer without prohibitive cost
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “A complete unanchored PAIC QBA may need to propagate eleven distinct uncertainty layers, from IPD outcome-model and aggregate-outcome uncertainty through estimated weights, target moments, sensitivity parameters, measurement-error validation data, censoring models, pseudo-IPD reconstruction, numerical integration and Monte Carlo error, component and bridge drift, to economic-model uncertainty. The two credible implementations, nested resampling and a fully joint Bayesian model, are respectively prohibitively expensive and prone to conditioning on the replicates that happened to succeed.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol found the eleven-layer count incoherent and the two-implementation dichotomy false, and noted that a fully joint Bayesian fit has no bootstrap replicates, so the entry’s paired criticism was category-confused. It also read cpaic at commit 9d150e9 and found that cmaic() already re-estimates weights and refits the outcome model in one stratified bootstrap, propagating both sources together, that plot_integration_error() reports quasi-Monte-Carlo integration convergence for non-survival fits, and that failed resamples are not silently accepted, because the package rejects an edge below an 80% success threshold, although above that threshold the standard deviation is still conditional on success.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1’s exact count is not coherent: read literally, the list names 13 entities; with the paired items grouped, it names about 10 categories. More importantly, it conflates sampling uncertainty, model uncertainty, nonidentified sensitivity assumptions, deterministic numerical error, Monte Carlo estimation error, and downstream decision-model uncertainty. For C2, numerical integration error and Monte Carlo standard error should be checked, reduced, and reported, but ordinarily should not be folded into inferential uncertainty as if they were random scientific parameters. C3 applies only when the economic model is part of the target decision analysis. C4 is an unverified universal absence claim; cpaic already propagates weight-estimation and outcome-model uncertainty together in cmaic(), but not the full list. C5 is possible, not inherent: cost depends on which quantities must be refitted and which grid calculations can be reused or approximated. C6 is correct if failed replicates are silently omitted. cpaic does omit failed resamples when computing the successful-replicate SD, but rejects the entire edge below an 80% success threshold, so it does not silently accept an arbitrarily selected subset; above the threshold, the SD is still conditional on success. C7 is false: estimating-equation or sandwich methods, the delta method, multiple-imputation or modular Monte Carlo schemes, parametric bootstrap, and hybrids are credible alternatives. A fully joint Bayesian fit also has no bootstrap replicates, so the statement’s ‘respectively prone to conditioning on successful replicates’ is category-confused.

Literature and prior-art check

open / unverifiable. No prior_work, and the load-bearing claims are enumerations internal to the source report (claim 1’s eleven layers) or no-implementation-exists assertions (claim 4). Claims 5 and 6 are the substantive and checkable part, and both are consistent with what I retrieved: Ren et al. 2025 use a non-parametric bootstrap with 10,000 replications for a single deterministic grid, which makes the multiplicative cost of nesting that inside a probabilistic bias-parameter layer immediately apparent, and they note MAIC extensions ‘may even fail to produce feasible weights’, which is exactly the failed-replicate selection problem in claim 6. But neither the eleven-layer enumeration nor claim 4 can be adjudicated against literature, and I found no PAIC paper that quantifies pseudo-IPD reconstruction, numerical integration or Monte Carlo error as propagated layers. Claim 7 (nested resampling and fully joint Bayesian modelling are the two broad credible implementations) is a taxonomy statement rather than a finding. I vote unverifiable on support.

title: Unreleased cpaic has no QBA interface beyond box-bounded drift
text:
Statement
cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9); it is not on CRAN and a reader cannot install it. Its bridge_fragility() is stronger than the entry described: for each posterior draw it computes the absolute distance between the contrast and the decision threshold divided by the sum of the absolute component loadings, which is the smallest common absolute bound under which some component-specific drift vector could push a link-scale contrast to the decision boundary, so it is an adversarial worst case over an L-infinity box rather than a same-sign uniform scalar drift or a one-dimensional slice, and no correlated same-bound main-effect vector can reverse a draw it labels robust. What it does not cover is unequal component-specific bounds, a stochastic dependence model, component-by-modifier drift, omitted target variables, outcome measurement and censoring bias, joint bias interactions and marginal natural-scale standardization, and the package exports no qba() interface.

title: Unreleased cpaic has no QBA interface beyond box-bounded drift
text:
Why it is open
The fragility number is a single common bound on absolute component main-effect drift, so it says nothing about drift that is unequal across components, about component-by-modifier drift, or about omitted variables and measurement and censoring bias, any of which can reverse a decision the diagnostic reports as robust. It is computed on the link scale, so under non-collapsibility it does not translate into the marginal natural-scale effects that drive decisions. Extending it requires specifying a drift dependence structure and integrating over the target distribution, which multiplies both the elicitation burden and the computation. The result object it would need involves design decisions nobody has fixed, such as what counts as a feasible scenario, how to summarize a decision-reversal surface and what attribution rule assigns dominance to a bias layer, so QBA remains bespoke scripting whose assumptions are invisible to reviewers.

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text: QBA-19 Unverifiable Very high priority Emerging

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text:
Statement
A Bayesian latent-U or fully joint QBA can conceal nonidentification: if the likelihood is flat in a sensitivity parameter and the prior factorizes, that parameter’s posterior equals its prior while the causal contrast derived from it stays prior-driven and looks fully probabilistic, and convergence diagnostics assess computation rather than identification. Soutar et al. 2025 (doi:10.1186/s12874-025-02551-z) avoid the fully joint construction for this reason, using a two-step data-augmentation design with user-specified sensitivity parameters and warning that fully Bayesian approaches, if not correctly performed, may result in estimation issues such as non-identifiability. Part of the diagnostic infrastructure the entry asks for already exists: cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) plots priors against posteriors and refits under tighter and looser priors to show which contrasts move, but these are generic cML-NMR diagnostics rather than a latent-U QBA module, and it offers no cut feedback or formal prior classes.

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text:
Why it is open
A nonidentified sensitivity parameter under a proper prior produces a finite, smooth, apparently well-behaved posterior that standard output cannot distinguish from an identified quantity, and no amount of sampler diagnostics changes that. Feedback from the outcome likelihood can update a clinically elicited sensitivity distribution that was never meant to be learned from the data, and where an external module is deliberately insulated or thought misspecified there is no modular fitting route in the ML-NMR software stack to prevent it. The diagnostics that do exist are generic parameter-level displays rather than a sensitivity module that labels parameters as identified, partially identified or nonidentified and shows how the causal conclusion depends on the prior class, and latent-U augmentation is computationally demanding on top of that.

Confirms the one-stage gap: QBA could be adapted for ML-UMR by incorporating bias parameters or simulated unmeasured covariates into the outcome regression and standardization steps, which means it has not yet been done.

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build a prior-transparent sensitivity module on top of the prior-movement diagnostics that already exist, labeling parameters as identified, partially identified or nonidentified and reporting how far the causal contrast moves across a class of defensible priors rather than under one arbitrary choice. Offer modular or cut-feedback fitting as an option justified by an explicit modular argument rather than as a default, since a fully coherent joint fit is legitimate when the joint likelihood is what the analyst intends. Report deterministic parameter grids alongside the posterior mixture and cross-check the result against bias-function and partial-identification analyses of the same model.

title: Latent-U Bayesian QBA hides nonidentification behind a proper prior
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “A one-stage Bayesian ML-UMR model can introduce a latent omitted variable with priors for its prevalence, source association, outcome association and treatment interaction, and a fully joint Bayesian QBA can specify observed-data, validation, target-distribution and sensitivity models together. In both cases the likelihood contains little or no information about the sensitivity parameters, so the posterior for the causal contrast can be prior-driven while appearing fully probabilistic.”
What was wrong with it. The auditors disagreed with evidence on both sides. GPT-5.6 Sol read cpaic at commit 9d150e9 and found prior-to-posterior plotting and prior-sensitivity refitting already implemented, so the claim that no PAIC software displays prior movement is false there; it also rejected modular or cut feedback as a requirement, since full feedback is coherent when the joint likelihood is scientifically intended and cut feedback breaks ordinary Bayesian coherence, and noted that a proper prior guarantees a proper posterior only when the marginal likelihood is finite and positive. The literature auditor kept the entry open and confirmed the one-stage gap from the ML-UMR paper (arXiv:2606.20341), whose authors say QBA could be adapted for ML-UMR, meaning it has not been.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): The central warning is correct under the intended nonidentified latent-U model. If the likelihood is flat in a sensitivity parameter and the prior factorizes, that parameter’s posterior equals its prior, while a derived causal contrast can remain prior-driven. C1, C2, C7, and the transparency objectives in C3 and C8 are therefore sound with model-specific qualifications. A proper prior does not literally always guarantee a proper posterior without a finite, positive marginal likelihood, although it does in the usual bounded-likelihood setup. Convergence diagnostics assess computation, not identification. C4 and C9 are false as requirements: full feedback is coherent when the stated joint likelihood is scientifically intended. Cut feedback is useful when an external module is deliberately insulated or thought misspecified, but it breaks ordinary joint Bayesian coherence and is redundant when the likelihood truly contains no information. C5 describes plausible flexibility rather than a guarantee. C6 should supplement, not replace, a justified primary prior; power scaling also does not address every structural sensitivity. C10 is too broad. At the requested cpaic snapshot, plot_prior_posterior() displays prior-to-posterior movement and prior_sensitivity() refits tighter and looser priors. These are not latent-U QBA diagnostics and do not provide cut feedback or formal prior classes, so the core module remains open but part of the requested diagnostic infrastructure already exists.

open / supported. Retrieved Soutar et al. 2025 (PMC12066054). It is correctly described: Bayesian data augmentation treating the unmeasured confounder as missing data, imputed under user-specified exposure and outcome associations, with a dRMST estimand valid under proportional-hazards violation. title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text: QBA-17 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
Statement
When no single probability distribution over the bias parameters is defensible, reporting the set of effects compatible with a justified assumption set plus the decisions that survive across it is an honest option, though not the uniquely honest one, since arbitrarily narrow bounds mislead as readily as an arbitrary prior. The identified set must be distinguished from a sampling or posterior interval, while a confidence region for an identified set may legitimately carry nominal coverage, and a set alone is not a robust decision region, which additionally requires a threshold or loss function. Set-based decision rules (minimax, minimax regret, dominance, robust Bayes) are already well developed in the statistical decision-theory literature, so the gap is PAIC-specific: no PAIC package the auditors could inspect returns identified sets or robust decision regions, and HTA appraisal practice, built around a point estimate and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio, has no established procedure for acting on one. The gap is sharpened rather than removed by loss-based decision rules. Because a loss adjustment computed from the posterior scales with the uncertainty the model represents, applying it to an unanchored or bridged contrast, whose dominant uncertainty is nonidentified and absorbed by a proper prior, imposes the smallest penalty exactly where the evidence is weakest; a set-valued output is therefore not only an honesty device but what a risk-averse rule needs in order not to reward nonidentification.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
Why it is open
The honesty of the approach is purchased by shifting the burden from an untestable point assumption to an untestable range, and clinicians have little experience specifying the magnitude of a bias parameter, so the bounds require clinically defensible constraints that nobody has codified for PAIC estimands. There is no accepted criterion for how wide a stress-test range should be, so width becomes another analyst degree of freedom, and a set wide enough to be honest can be vacuous. Appraisal processes are built around a point estimate and an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio and provide no procedure for acting on an identified set, so honest wide ranges that span the decision threshold are experienced as uninformative and create direct pressure to narrow ranges without new evidence. Current PAIC software returns point estimates and intervals, so producing bounds requires bespoke code and the honest analysis is also the hardest one to produce.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ades et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Loss-adjusted expected value, a risk-averse decision rule that subtracts from each treatment’s expected value the Bayesian expected loss computed from the posterior of the contrast, recommending in two stages against the reference and against the best treatment. It satisfies a stated validity criterion that the alternatives fail, and across 10 NICE networks recommends a median of two fewer treatments than expected value. Its own scope statement is the limit that matters here: the penalty engages only uncertainty represented inside the decision model, with risk of bias, certainty ratings, model structure and data-source choice left outside it, and the rule is evaluated only on conventional randomized networks although its largest impact is predicted for non-randomized and unanchored evidence.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Instantiate the decision rules that already exist, minimax, minimax regret, dominance and robust Bayes, on PAIC estimands rather than developing decision theory from scratch; the missing pieces are clinically defensible restrictions for these estimands and a set-valued output object in reference PAIC software. Standardize how a stress-test range is constructed so its width is justified by an evidence hierarchy rather than chosen, and report the identified set separately from any confidence region for it. Translate bounds into decision tipping surfaces so they remain usable for reimbursement, and calibrate sensitivity parameters against measured covariates where that is possible.

title: Partial identification and robust decision regions for HTA
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “For high-stakes unanchored comparisons, disconnected bridges and settings where evidence about bias parameters is weak, the defensible output is the set of effects compatible with bounded assumptions or prior neighborhoods plus a robust decision region, not a single selected estimate. Partial identification is currently dismissed for not returning one number, and no PAIC software has any representation for a set.”
What was wrong with it. The literature auditor found the claim that HTA decision rules provide no procedure for acting on an identified set too strong as a statement about decision theory, since minimax-regret and related rules for treatment choice under partial identification are well developed in econometrics; it is defensible only about appraisal practice. GPT-5.6 Sol added that partial identification is an honest option rather than the uniquely honest one, that its practical difficulties go well beyond producing a range (choosing defensible restrictions, vacuous sets, sampling uncertainty, computation, mapping effects to losses), and that a set and a robust decision region are different outputs.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied full-text reading.

absorbed a proposal the reading raised separately: Risk-averse NMA decisions do not penalize nonidentified bias 1 citation(s) added

Verdict left unchanged

verdict left unchanged The only finding arguing for a change came from one paper and its reader marked it low confidence: Sensitivity of treatment recommendations to bias in network meta-analysis

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The entry cites nothing, and that is its weakness rather than its substance. Claims 1, 2, 4, 8, 11 are definitional statements about partial identification and are correct. Claims 13 and 14 (no PAIC software returns identified sets; HTA decision rules provide no procedure for acting on one) are no-method-exists assertions I could not falsify: I checked multinma, maicplus, drMAIC, outstandR and gemtc documentation surfaces and found only point estimates with intervals. However, a large and directly applicable statistical-decision-theory literature on acting under partial identification exists and is not acknowledged: minimax-regret and mean-square-regret optimal treatment choice under an identified set, and optimal decision rules under partial identification, are well developed in econometrics. Claim 14 as written (‘provide no procedure for acting on an uninformative identified set’) is therefore too strong as a statement about decision theory; it is defensible only as a statement about HTA appraisal practice. The genuinely open work is instantiating those decision rules on PAIC estimands with clinically defensible bounds and set-valued software output.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1, C2, C4, C8, and the narrow reading of C12 are correct. Partial identification returns values compatible with stated restrictions, and the identified set is not itself a probabilistic interval. C3 is generally true as a practical observation. C5 should call partial identification an honest option, not the uniquely honest option; arbitrary narrow bounds can be as misleading as an arbitrary prior. C6 understates the practical difficulties, which also include choosing defensible restrictions, vacuous sets, sampling uncertainty, computation, and mapping effects to losses. C7 and C9 are recommendations rather than technical necessities, and ranges should be justified rather than merely made deliberately wide. C10 should say can produce false precision: a diffuse or robust probabilistic model can instead be appropriately imprecise. C11 conflates outputs because partial identification yields a set, while a robust decision region additionally requires a decision threshold or loss function. C13 is a universal software claim not established here. C14 is false as a general technical claim: minimax, minimax-regret, dominance, and robust-Bayes rules can act on sets or prior classes. Whether particular HTA institutions operationalize those rules is a separate empirical question. The very-high severity applies when an unidentified point estimate is presented as identified, not simply because a method declines to return one number.

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text:
Statement
Multiple omitted variables need a joint sensitivity specification whenever their dependence can affect the bias, and each may require its source and target distribution, its outcome association under each treatment, and its dependence with measured covariates and with the other omitted variables; the entry’s five-quantity list double-counts, since source and target joint distributions determine the association with study membership and treatment-specific coefficients already encode effect modification. The two usual escapes are unvalidated here: independent variation can understate joint extremes when bias contributions are positively dependent and directionally aligned, though it can overstate them under negative dependence, and a scalar composite U is exact only when it is a sufficient index for selection and for every treatment-specific outcome regression, which nobody has characterized for unanchored PAIC. Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) handle several omitted covariates and flag the problem their own elicitation route creates, noting that eliciting a distribution for each separately would ignore the correlation structure between them.

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text:
Why it is open
None of the parameters is identified by the data, so the specification burden grows with the number of omitted variables while no compensating information arrives, and a tensor grid over p axes at k levels needs k to the power p evaluations, which makes joint deterministic exploration expensive. Independence is assumed because independent priors and independent grid axes are convenient to specify and sample, but the decision-relevant region is often the tail where several parameters are jointly extreme and aligned, which is exactly what independence suppresses. Whether a scalar composite is conservative depends on whether it is a sufficient index for the selection and treatment-specific outcome models, and no accepted parameterization for dependence among several omitted variables exists in a population-adjustment setting.

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Develop copula, latent-factor and robust moment-set specifications so dependence can be varied as part of the sensitivity region, and characterize the conditions under which a single composite index is sufficient rather than assuming the reduction is conservative. Require every QBA to state a non-redundant parameter set per omitted variable together with the assumed dependence, using treatment-specific outcome coefficients where interaction is in play and a common coefficient only under an explicit no-interaction assumption. Report how the tail of the joint distribution moves when independence is relaxed in both directions, since dependence can widen or narrow the decision-relevant region.

title: Multiple correlated omitted variables and their dependence structure
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 2 findings from 2 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “Each omitted variable requires at least five quantities (its source and target distribution, its association with study membership, its outcome association under each treatment, its treatment-effect modification, and its dependence with measured covariates and with other omitted variables), so a high-dimensional collection of omitted variables produces a sensitivity-parameter explosion. Varying each variable independently and collapsing everything into one composite U are the two usual escapes, and neither has been validated.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol found several claims too broad: the five quantities double-count, specifying a common outcome coefficient is sufficient under an explicit no-interaction assumption rather than being an error, independence understates tail scenarios only under positive and directionally aligned dependence, and the cost objection confuses parameter count, which grows roughly linearly (or quadratically for an unrestricted covariance), with grid size, which grows as k to the power p. The entry cited nothing; the literature auditor supplied Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13), which raises the same dependence problem in the PAIC setting.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 2 surviving findings from: Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data, S; Sensitivity analysis for an unobserved moderator in RCT-to-t. New citations: 10.1007/978-3-030-82673-4, 10.1214/16-AOAS1001

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. No prior_work and no citations, but the substantive claims survive scrutiny. Ren et al. 2025 explicitly handle multiple omitted covariates (their L can exceed 1) and explicitly flag the dependence problem their own elicitation route creates: ‘It may be easier to elicit a distribution for each U_i separately. However, this would ignore the correlation structure between the uncertain quantities U_i’, pointing readers to multivariate elicitation methods. That is direct support for claims 1 and 3 in the PAIC setting and should be cited. Claim 5 (treatment-specific outcome associations) is consistent with the unanchored identification problem. Claims 6 and 7 (the single-composite-U reduction has not been validated against copula or latent-factor alternatives for unanchored PAIC) are no-work-exists claims; I found no such validation and no PAIC copula or latent-factor sensitivity specification, but absence of a finding is not proof, so I do not treat them as verified. The general single-U-versus-multiple-confounder literature outside PAIC does exist and the entry would be stronger if it engaged with it.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The joint-dependence problem is technically real, but several claims are too broad. C1 is valid when independent variation substitutes for a joint analysis, although one-at-a-time variation remains useful diagnostically. C2 is correct for tensor grids, but the report confuses parameter count with grid size: p axes with k levels require k^p evaluations, while parameter count generally grows linearly, or quadratically for an unrestricted covariance. C3 is not universal. Independence understates joint extremes when bias contributions are positively dependent and directionally aligned, but may overstate them under negative dependence. Independence among sensitivity parameters is also distinct from independence among omitted variables. C4 double-counts quantities: source and target joint distributions can determine the study-membership association, while treatment-specific outcome coefficients already encode effect modification. C5 is false as a necessity because a common coefficient is sufficient under an explicit no-U-by-treatment-interaction assumption; a main effect plus interaction is equivalent to treatment-specific coefficients. C6-C7 are literature-validation claims that this technical audit cannot establish. A scalar composite can be exact when it is sufficient for both selection and every treatment-specific outcome regression. C8 identifies reasonable candidate approaches. The issue is decision-critical when several omitted variables plausibly contribute jointly, not automatically in every PAIC.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

text: QBA-13 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Statement
Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) extend the NORTA-based marginal unanchored STC of Ren et al. 2024 (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1718) by simulating an assumed synthetic joint distribution for covariates measured in the IPD but unreported in the comparator publication, averaging individual predictions on the natural outcome scale before transforming to the log odds scale, and presenting deterministic sensitivity curves with bootstrap confidence intervals; they do not present tipping-point plots, and the case study instead reads a significance-crossing value off the curve. This is the beginning of formal QBA for limited-aggregate-data PAIC rather than a completed solution: the workflow is implemented only for STC, and the authors restrict it there because a MAIC extension would suffer extreme effective-sample-size loss and might fail to produce feasible weights. Their statement that no additional assumptions are required cannot be read literally, since target marginals, dependence, source-to-target outcome associations, copula form and regression form are all assumed.

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Why it is open
The workflow is embedded in an STC and g-computation route, so it does not transfer to weighting, one-stage or network estimators, and the authors themselves rule out the direct MAIC extension on effective-sample-size and feasibility grounds. Its inputs, the outcome association of the omitted variable and its dependence with measured covariates, are estimated in the source study and assumed to hold in the target, which cannot be checked against the published comparator data. It also inherits the requirements of the underlying estimator, a sufficiently correct outcome model and adequate overlap, neither of which a covariate-omission sensitivity analysis can repair.

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Treat the simulated-covariate route as one family within a broader QBA framework, extend it to multiple correlated omitted variables and treatment-specific associations, and state its assumptions about target distributions, correlations, outcome associations, copula form and model form explicitly rather than describing it as assumption-free. Develop parallel routes for weighting and one-stage estimators so the same sensitivity question can be asked of any PAIC estimator, addressing the feasibility and effective-sample-size loss that led the authors to restrict the published version to STC. Report the sensitivity curve against a clinical or decision threshold rather than reading it off a significance boundary.

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Our study

A simulated-covariate bias analysis by STC and by MAIC
The question put to it. Is a MAIC version of the simulated-covariate bias analysis infeasible or too imprecise, as its authors assumed when restricting it to STC?
What it found. The MAIC extension of the simulated-covariate bias analysis was feasible in at least 99.8% of replicates across assumed target prevalences from 0.1 to 0.9, lost effective sample size to 85 to 109 of 300 only at the extreme, and had a reported SE 3% to 14% above STC’s. Both routes were unbiased. The restriction to STC was conservative rather than necessary. Both routes’ multiply imputed intervals widened along the sweep more than the estimate’s real spread (SE up to 0.28 against about 0.13), so coverage exceeded nominal.
Results.

Refuting sentence holds: feasibility 0.998 to 1.000; MAIC SE / STC SE 1.03 to 1.14.
Effective sample size 85 to 231 of 300 along the sweep.
Bias at most 0.009 for both routes; coverage 0.956 to 1.000 (conservative toward the extremes).

Design.

Estimand

A’s marginal log odds in a target with the assumed prevalence of the unmeasured covariate

Methods compared

simulated-covariate STC, simulated-covariate MAIC

Data-generating mechanism

Unanchored transport with an unmeasured binary covariate imputed from its assumed relations; STC and MAIC sensitivity curves over the assumed target prevalence, with feasibility and effective sample size. 2 cells, 500 replicates each.

Replicates

500 per scenario, 1,000 in total, each over a 5-point sweep with 10 imputations


What this does not answer. One binary unmeasured covariate, correct assumed relations, unanchored A side only, no decision reading. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Simulated-covariate QBA is an STC route, not a general solution
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Ren et al. (2025) extend a NORTA-based marginal unanchored STC by simulating covariates measured in the IPD but unreported in the comparator publication, then marginalizing predictions and presenting tipping plots. The report judges this the beginning of formal QBA for limited-AgD PAIC rather than a completed solution.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors found the entry’s description of tipping plots inaccurate: Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) present deterministic sensitivity curves with bootstrap confidence intervals and read a significance-crossing point off them, and the phrase tipping point appears only in background prose about QBA modes. GPT-5.6 Sol also corrected the claim that the method simulates the comparator population’s full covariate distribution; it simulates an assumed synthetic joint distribution.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Read the Ren et al. 2025 full text. Claims 1 to 6 and 8 verified verbatim. NORTA/Gaussian copula: ‘Ren et al. (2024) developed a novel way to implement unanchored STC by incorporating marginalisation and the NORmal To Anything (NORTA) algorithm (also is known as a Gaussian copula method)’. STC-only: ‘MAIC approach would suffer an extreme reduction of the effect sample size and may even fail to produce feasible weights. Hence, we will only present the QBA for the STC approach.’ Marginal estimand preserved: prediction is done ‘based on the natural scale … and then transformed to the log odds scale for the indirect comparison step’. Overlap and model requirements are stated verbatim in the discussion. Claim 7’s target text is real: ‘No additional assumptions are required for our approach.’ Caveat on the entry’s statement (not a numbered claim): the paper presents no tipping plots. ‘Tipping point’ appears once, in background prose describing QBA modes generally; the case study presents deterministic sensitivity curves with bootstrap CIs, from which the authors read off a significance-crossing point (‘If the proportion is greater than 28%, then the treatment effect becomes statistically significant’), which is the p=0.05-anchored reading QBA-25 criticises.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. The locally available full text supports C1-C8. Ren et al. follow the 2024 NORTA or Gaussian-copula STC, average individual predictions on the natural outcome scale before transforming, restrict the implemented QBA to STC, require correct outcome-model specification and overlap, rely on important omitted covariates being measured in the IPD source, and warn of severe MAIC effective-sample-size loss. The report is also correct that the paper’s statement that no additional assumptions are required cannot be literal: target marginals, dependence, source-to-target outcome associations, copula form, and regression form are assumed. Two caveats remain. C2 should say the method simulates an assumed synthetic joint distribution, not the comparator population’s known full distribution. The entry’s statement that the paper presents tipping plots is inaccurate; it presents deterministic sensitivity curves and significance-crossing interpretations rather than formal tipping plots. The broader estimator-general QBA problem remains open.

Decision path

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text: QBA-11 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising Tractability 2/5

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Statement
A linear STC applied where thresholds, splines or interactions operate produces outcome-model misspecification bias, and QBA for an omitted covariate holds the outcome model fixed, so it does not repair it. Double robustness is a property of the measured-data layer only: Campbell and Remiro-Azocar (doi:10.1017/rsm.2026.10106) place externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored ITCs in one causal framework and augment entropy-balancing MAIC with a conditional outcome model, giving robustness to misspecification of one of the two measured-data nuisance models, while identification still rests on conditional data-source ignorability and positivity with no bias-parameter indexing. No published unanchored-PAIC estimator is simultaneously doubly robust and indexed by explicit residual-bias parameters; drMAIC on CRAN offers doubly robust MAIC with E-values, weight trimming and variable-exclusion analyses, which is a generic screen rather than such an estimator.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Why it is open
Sensitivity analysis for an omitted variable holds the outcome model fixed, so misspecification of the retained model propagates untouched into every scenario on the grid, and model-form error is not a scalar that can be indexed by a prevalence or an association. Double robustness is silent about omitted variables, selection on unmeasured prognosis, outcome misclassification, target-distribution error and bridge drift, but the guarantee sounds strong enough to be read as protection against residual bias in general and to remove the perceived need for sensitivity analysis. Constructing an estimator that is doubly robust and indexed by explicit bias parameters requires the influence-function theory to be redone under a perturbed identification condition, which has not been done for population-adjusted transport, and flexible learners would need cross-fitting and extrapolation-aware prediction intervals that no current PAIC implementation supplies.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Campbell and Remiro-Azocar 2026, Doubly robust augmented weighting estimators for the analysis of externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect treatment comparisons, Research Synthesis Methods
Unifies externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored ITCs in one causal framework and augments entropy-balancing MAIC with a model for the conditional outcome expectation, giving double robustness against misspecification of the measured-data weighting or outcome model. Identification rests on conditional data-source ignorability and positivity; it contains no sensitivity analysis and no bias-parameter indexing.


Campbell and Remiro-Azocar, preprint of the same work (2025)
Preprint version of the doubly robust augmented weighting estimator for externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect treatment comparisons.


drMAIC 0.1.0 (CRAN)
Provides doubly robust MAIC with E-values, weight trimming and variable-exclusion analyses. A generic robustness screen rather than an estimator indexed by explicit residual-bias parameters, so it does not close the gap.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Take the doubly robust augmented MAIC that already exists and index it by bias parameters with cross-fitting, so the estimate is computed at every point of the sensitivity region and the measured-confounding layer and the residual-bias layer are reported separately, or apply bias functions and bounds to the existing doubly robust functional where that suffices. Publish an explicit demonstration of which failures double robustness does and does not cover. Treat unsupported target profiles as a positivity problem calling for support restrictions, bounds or stated extrapolation assumptions, and use flexible learner multiverses, residual-bias functions, model averaging across plausible forms and calibration against held-out trials as optional tools for functional-form error rather than as remedies for nonidentification.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Our study

Which failures double robustness covers
The question put to it. Does a doubly robust MAIC protect against an omitted confounder, and what happens to a sensitivity grid built on a misspecified outcome model?
What it found. Double robustness protects against one misspecified nuisance model and nothing else. With an omitted confounder the augmented estimator carried exactly the same bias as correctly specified weighting or outcome-regression estimators, and with both models wrong the misspecification and omitted-variable biases added. A sensitivity grid built on a misspecified analysis is therefore shifted by the misspecification bias. With exact-balance weights, augmentation by an outcome model built from the balanced terms reproduces MAIC.
Results.

Both models correct: augmented bias equal to the omitted-variable bias in all 16 scenarios; largest difference from correct outcome regression 0.0015.
Omitted variable absent, one model wrong: augmented estimator unbiased (second null control held); the wrong single-model estimator biased by up to 0.20.
Both models wrong: bias additive in misspecification and omitted-variable parts, largest interaction 0.008, within 3 MCSE in 16 of 16 scenarios.
Registered region-inclusion criterion not met as stated (0.888 against a 0.90 threshold) because the region omitted sampling error; the misspecified region was displaced by 0.195 to 0.201 at every omitted-variable strength.

Design.

Estimand

Target-population mean outcome under A (unanchored)

Methods compared

MAIC with correct or wrong weights, outcome regression with correct or wrong model, augmented (doubly robust) estimator under the four combinations

Data-generating mechanism

Unanchored transport with a nonlinear outcome, misspecifiable weighting and outcome models and an omitted binary confounder; MAIC, outcome regression and augmented estimators under every combination of model correctness; 16 cells crossing omitted-variable strength, imbalance and overlap. 2000 replicates per cell.

Replicates

2000 per scenario, 32,000 in total


What this does not answer. Continuous outcome only; no cross-fitting; drMAIC E-value screen and a formally bias-indexed doubly robust estimator not run. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Outcome-model misspecification and doubly robust QBA
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “A linear STC applied where thresholds, splines or interactions operate produces outcome-model misspecification bias with its own sensitivity parameters, and QBA for an omitted covariate does not repair it. Doubly robust estimators protect only against misspecification of one of two measured-data nuisance models under the identifying assumptions, so the correct research target is an AIPW or TMLE family indexed by bias parameters, not a claim that double robustness makes QBA unnecessary.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed what the entry demands: a functional-form class is a model set rather than a sensitivity parameter, unsupported target profiles are positivity and extrapolation failures that flexible learners and cross-fitting cannot repair, and a bias-indexed AIPW or TMLE is one coherent construction rather than the uniquely correct target, since bias functions or bounds can sometimes be applied to an existing doubly robust functional without redoing the influence-function theory.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Retrieved Campbell and Remiro-Azocar 2026 (Research Synthesis Methods, 10.1017/rsm.2026.10106; preprint arXiv 2505.00113), title ‘Doubly robust augmented weighting estimators for the analysis of externally controlled single-arm trials and unanchored indirect treatment comparisons’. Claims 8 and 9 verified: it presents a unified causal inference framework for both designs and ‘develop[s] an estimator that augments a popular weighting approach based on entropy balancing - matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) - by fitting a model for the conditional outcome expectation’, which is ‘doubly robust (DR), providing increased robustness against model misspecification’. Claim 10 is supported by the same retrieval: the paper’s identification rests on conditional data-source ignorability and positivity and contains no sensitivity analysis or bias-parameter indexing for unmeasured confounding. drMAIC 0.1.0 on CRAN provides doubly robust MAIC with ‘E-values, weight trimming, and variable exclusion analyses’, which is a generic screen rather than an estimator indexed by residual-bias parameters, so it does not falsify claim 10 either. Claims 5 to 7 are standard semiparametric facts and are correct.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 and C5-C9 are technically correct: double robustness concerns the measured-data outcome and selection or weighting models while identification, consistency, positivity, correct measurement, and the target law remain assumed. It does not protect against omitted confounding or the other listed violations. C2 nevertheless overstates what is required: a functional-form class is a model set, not a sensitivity parameter, and omitted interaction size covers only one misspecification. Unsupported target profiles are positivity or extrapolation failures, not merely outcome-model misspecification; flexible learners and cross-fitting cannot identify unsupported counterfactuals. C3-C4 list useful tools but not sufficient or mandatory remedies. Bias-indexed AIPW or TMLE is one coherent construction, not the uniquely correct one; bias functions or bounds can sometimes be applied to an existing doubly robust functional without rebuilding all influence-function theory. C10 and claims that research is still needed are literature-exhaustiveness claims outside this audit lens. At cpaic@9d150e9, no QBA, AIPW, TMLE, or cross-fitting API exists. The integrated residual-bias layer remains open, but its necessity and proposed implementation are inflated.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex
