title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text: QBA-09 Overstated High priority Emerging

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
Statement
Censoring-weighted estimation has already been combined with weighting to an aggregate-data target population: Yan et al.’s TADA (doi:10.1002/pst.70029) forms final weights as the product of time-varying inverse-probability-of-censoring weights and method-of-moments participation weights derived from target aggregate data, with a simulation study and an NSCLC case study. It adjusts under censoring at random given covariates, so what remains open is the sensitivity layer: no method indexes departures from that assumption inside a population-adjusted indirect comparison, by a selection, censoring-outcome association, pattern-mixture, copula or bounds formulation, and PAIC implementations propagate no uncertainty about the censoring assumption. Differential follow-up alone does not establish informative censoring, and the parameters the entry listed are alternative factorizations rather than a set that must all be specified.

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
Why it is open
The comparator’s censoring mechanism is unobservable from a published survival curve, so a departure from conditionally independent censoring is not identifiable from the observed follow-up and can only be indexed by assumption. Reweighting on baseline covariates addresses who enters the comparison, not the dependence between the censoring process and the unobserved event time, so the population-adjustment step leaves that dependence untouched even when a censoring model is fitted alongside it. Missingness also interacts with study selection and transport, so a censoring model fitted in the source carries its own transport assumption to the target. Ordinary inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting identifies the effect only under conditionally independent censoring unless it is augmented by an explicit departure parameter, and PAIC implementations typically assume administrative censoring and propagate no uncertainty about that assumption.

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Yan et al. 2025, Target Aggregate Data Adjustment Method for Transportability Analysis Utilizing Summary-Level Data From the Target Population, Pharmaceutical Statistics 24:e70029
Two-stage weighting whose final weights are the product of time-varying inverse probability of censoring weights and method-of-moments participation weights derived from target aggregate data, with simulations and an NSCLC case study. Adjusts under censoring at random given covariates; supplies no sensitivity-parameter layer, no bounds and no propagation of censoring-model uncertainty.

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend TADA-style joint censoring and transport adjustment with an explicit departure parameter rather than building a censoring-aware PAIC estimator from scratch: choose one justified formulation, whether a selection model, a pattern-mixture shift, a copula or bounds, and index departure from conditionally independent censoring by it. Combine it with the weighting or standardization step rather than applying it separately, and include censoring-model uncertainty among the propagated uncertainty layers. Trigger the analysis when censoring is plausibly outcome-dependent after conditioning on measured history, not merely because follow-up differs between the studies.

title: No sensitivity parameters index departures from censoring at random
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Censoring-weighted estimation has been combined with weighting to an aggregate-data target population, but no method indexes departures from non-informative censoring by explicit sensitivity parameters (selection odds, censoring-outcome association, pattern-mixture shift) inside a population-adjusted indirect comparison, and PAIC implementations propagate no uncertainty about the censoring assumption.
The source titled this. “Informative censoring and differential dropout as a bias model” The title presents censoring as an unbuilt bias model, but TADA already combines a censoring model with weighting to an aggregate-data target.
The source said. “Differential follow-up and treatment-related dropout between the IPD source and the external comparator require selection-odds, censoring-outcome association and pattern-mixture shift sensitivity parameters, addressed with IPCW sensitivity analyses, selection or pattern-mixture models and bounds. The report is explicit that these mechanisms are not forms of confounding and need their own bias models.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors judged the claim overstated on the same evidence: Yan et al. 2025 (doi:10.1002/pst.70029), which the entry did not cite, already combines a censoring model with weighting to an external aggregate-data target, contradicting the entry’s central claim that this has not been done. GPT-5.6 Sol added that differing censoring rates do not imply dependent censoring, and that selection odds, censoring-outcome association and pattern-mixture shift are alternative parameterizations rather than three jointly required parameters.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. Claim 5 (‘Sensitivity methods for dependent censoring have not been combined with weighting or standardization to an external target population’) is materially narrowed by Yan et al. 2025 (Pharm Stat 24:e70029, PMID 40765487), which the entry does not cite. TADA is a two-stage weighting framework whose final weights are the product of time-varying inverse probability of censoring weights and method-of-moments participation weights derived from target aggregate-level data. That is precisely the combination of a censoring model with weighting to an external aggregate-data target population that the entry says does not exist, with a simulation study and an NSCLC case study. The paper’s own framing also corroborates the entry’s premise: ‘AgD-based transportability methods in the presence of informative-censoring remain underexplored.’ What genuinely remains open is the sensitivity layer: TADA adjusts under a censoring-at-random-given-covariates assumption; it does not index departures from non-informative censoring by selection-odds or pattern-mixture shift parameters, does not return bounds, and does not propagate censoring-model uncertainty as a QBA layer. The entry also has zero prior_work, which understates a mature general literature on IPCW sensitivity analysis under non-ignorable dropout. Cites 10.1002/pst.70029: Combines time-varying inverse probability of censoring weights with method-of-moments participation weighting to an aggregate-data target population, directly contradicting the claim that censoring models have not been combined with weighting to an external target. Does not provide the sensitivity-parameter layer..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. Differential follow-up alone does not imply informative censoring: censoring rates may differ while remaining independent of event times conditional on measured history. C1 also incorrectly presents selection odds, censoring-outcome association, and pattern-mixture shifts as jointly required; these are alternative factorizations or sensitivity parameterizations. C2 names appropriate families, but ordinary IPCW identifies effects only under conditional independent censoring unless augmented by an explicit departure parameter. C3 and C4 correctly separate post-entry selection from baseline confounding. C5 is false under its broad reading because target participation weighting has been combined with time-varying censoring weights. That work does not, however, solve sensitivity to residual dependent censoring. At cpaic@9d150e9 there is no IPCW or censoring-sensitivity API, so that package does not close the residual layer. Cites 10.1002/pst.70029: Combines time-varying inverse-probability-of-censoring weights with method-of-moments target participation weights. It addresses joint censoring and transport adjustment under conditional censoring assumptions, but not residual MNAR sensitivity..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
Statement
Protocol-driven trial assessment and routine-care capture detect the same events at different times and with different completeness, so using detection time as event time can make progression curves depend on the assessment grid, and baseline covariate balancing generally cannot remove a residual study-specific observation process. Ackerman et al. 2024 (doi:10.3389/fdsfr.2024.1423493) quantify this for external control arms, simulating bias from misclassified progression events and irregular assessment timing and showing that together they may generate bias greater than the sum of their parts, but they measure the problem rather than correct it. The sub-mechanisms need different parameters and not all are always required: sensitivity and specificity address event classification, lag and interval endpoints address timing, linkage completeness addresses missing capture, and visit-process association parameters are needed only when observation is informative. Where visit times are noninformative given modeled covariates and the event is known to lie between visits, an interval-censored likelihood already accommodates different grids without an extra bias parameter, and cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) implements exactly that.

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
Why it is open
The event time recorded in an external data source is a function of the observation process as well as the underlying event, and that process differs systematically between a protocol-driven trial and routine care. Ascertainment parameters cannot be estimated from the comparison data because the true event process is never observed in either source, and assessment schedules and linkage completeness are rarely reported in enough detail in an aggregate publication to be bounded from protocol information. Missed events, informative visit intensity, death-recording lag and incomplete linkage each require their own sensitivity parameters or an explicit observation-process model, which sits outside the covariate-balancing toolkit and which no PAIC implementation attempts.

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Gray et al. 2024, Pharmacoepidemiology and Drug Safety
Illustrates QBA for external controls including an outcome-evaluation scenario, that is misclassification of survival, which matches the ascertainment element of this entry.


Ackerman et al. 2024, Measurement error and bias in real-world oncology endpoints when constructing external control arms, Frontiers in Drug Safety and Regulation
Simulates and quantifies bias from misclassified progression events and irregular assessment timing in external control arms, with disease-specific magnitudes, and shows the two mechanisms interact non-additively. A quantification and planning tool, not a correction framework, and not integrated with weighting or standardization.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
cmlnmr() implements exact likelihood contributions for observed events, right, left and interval censoring and delayed entry, which handles differing assessment grids when the observation process is conditionally noninformative. It does not model missed events, sensitivity, specificity, informative visit intensity, death-recording lag or incomplete linkage.

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build on the interval-censored likelihood that already exists for the noninformative case and add what it does not cover: event misclassification through sensitivity and specificity, informative visiting through a joint visit-outcome or inverse-intensity model, recording lag through a lag distribution, and incomplete linkage through a capture parameter, invoking the parameters the setting actually warrants rather than all of them by default. Integrate the correction with the weighting or standardization step rather than treating it as a separate appendix analysis, and report the sensitivity surface jointly with the confounding and censoring parameters. Require reporting of assessment schedules and linkage completeness in both studies so the parameters can be bounded.

title: Outcome ascertainment and the observation process in external data
text:
Our study

Outcome ascertainment in an external comparator
The question put to it. Does an interval-censored analysis cover the ascertainment differences between a trial and a routine-care comparator, or do missed detections and risk-dependent visiting still bias the RMST contrast?
What it found. Partly. With every progression detected, an interval-censored model removed the bias from the external arm’s sparser visits (within 0.05 months) and was not biased by visits that depended on patients’ risk at the strength simulated. When the external arm missed progression at some visits, every method was biased, by 0.25 to 0.38 months at a per-visit sensitivity of 0.85 and 0.67 to 0.94 at 0.7, against a true difference of 1.59 months. Missed detection needs its own bias parameter.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: interval-censored bias 0.25 to 0.94 months with missed detections.
Perfect detection: interval-censored bias -0.05 to 0.01 months; recorded times up to 0.42.
Risk-dependent visiting reduced the recorded-time bias and left the interval-censored model unbiased, contrary to DESIGN.md’s prediction.

Design.

Estimand

RMST at 24 months, external arm B minus trial arm A, from true event times

Methods compared

Kaplan-Meier on recorded times, interval midpoints, interval-censored Weibull

Data-generating mechanism

Trial arm with scheduled visits against an external arm with regular or risk-dependent visits and per-visit detection sensitivity of 1, 0.85 or 0.7; Kaplan-Meier, midpoint and interval-censored Weibull RMST. 12 cells, 1000 replicates each.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 12,000 in total


What this does not answer. No lag, linkage loss or false positives; one frailty and visiting strength; no sensitivity analysis over the detection parameter; no population adjustment. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
Statement
Trial eligibility, referral patterns, performance status, treatment candidacy and calendar time can leave source-to-target selection bias after conditioning on measured covariates, and a bias function that perturbs the assumed equality of source and target potential-outcome means expresses that departure directly. Dahabreh et al. (doi:10.1002/sim.9550, doi:10.1002/sim.70083) do this without positing a concrete latent variable, but Nguyen et al. 2017 (doi:10.1214/16-AOAS1001) is not a clean example of the contrast, because it represents unobserved moderation as a composite moderator U and only two of its five methods are bias-formula based. These templates were built for individual-level transportability and have not been adapted to the limited aggregate-data structure of PAIC, while a generic E-value, which inherits the population and estimand of the estimate it is applied to but carries no target, aggregate-data or bridge structure of its own, occupies the role by default.

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
Why it is open
Selection on unmeasured prognosis leaves no signature in the measured covariate distribution, so balance diagnostics are uninformative about it and only an explicit perturbation of exchangeability can express it. The bias-function parameterization avoids inventing a specific latent variable but is harder to elicit and defend unless it is indexed by treatment, covariates and target stratum, and no such indexing exists for the limited aggregate-data structure PAIC works with. An E-value is a scalar defined for one comparison on one association scale; it adds nothing about the target population, the marginal versus conditional choice, correlation with measured effect modifiers, non-collapsibility, outcome-definition differences or component-bridge assumptions, and it is cheap and familiar enough to displace analyses that would encode the operative mechanism.

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Nguyen et al. 2017, Annals of Applied Statistics
Sensitivity analysis for generalizing trial results, offered by the entry as a closer conceptual template than E-values. Two of its five methods are bias-formula based; its unobserved-moderator analysis explicitly introduces a composite moderator U, so it is not a latent-variable-free bias-function method.


Nguyen et al., preprint of the same work
Preprint carrying the counter-evidence quote both auditors cited: the concern that the treatment effect may be moderated by factors not observed even in the RCT, which we represent as a composite moderator U.


Dahabreh et al. 2023, Statistics in Medicine
Bias-function sensitivity analysis for extending trial inferences, parameterizing violations of source-target exchangeability directly.


Dahabreh et al. 2026, Global Sensitivity Analysis for Studies Extending Inferences From a Randomized Trial to a Target Population, Statistics in Medicine 45:13-14
Global sensitivity framework for transportability, modeling violations of conditional exchangeability through potential-outcome distributions. Built for individual-level data.


Leahy et al. 2023, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
HTA workshop recommendations whose first item restricts E-values to unknown-unknowns, corroborating the entry’s claim that an E-value is a screen rather than a primary sensitivity analysis.

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Adapt the direct potential-outcome bias functions to limited-aggregate-data PAIC by indexing the perturbation by treatment, covariates and target stratum, choosing one coherent parameterization rather than stacking a selection-odds parameter on top of a potential-outcome shift that already encodes the same departure. Calibrate them with negative controls and selection models rather than a generic latent confounder. Keep E-values as a rapid screen when only an effect estimate is available and treat them as supplementary rather than as the decision-grade sensitivity analysis for an unanchored comparison, which is the position the Leahy et al. 2023 workshop already takes.

title: Transport bias functions are not adapted to aggregate-data PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “Transport and selection bias functions rather than generic E-values” The title sets bias functions against generic E-values, a framing the audit softened, and the cited bias-function example itself posits a composite latent moderator.
The source said. “Trial eligibility, referral patterns, performance status, treatment candidacy and calendar time can leave source-to-target selection bias after conditioning on measured covariates, and the matching sensitivity object is a bias function that perturbs the assumed equality of source and target potential-outcome means directly. Existing bias-function templates were built for individual-level transportability and have not been adapted to limited aggregate data, while generic E-values, which encode none of the PAIC structure, occupy the role by default.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors found the entry’s use of Nguyen et al. 2017 (doi:10.1214/16-AOAS1001) cuts against its own claim that bias functions avoid positing a latent variable, since the paper represents the concern as a composite moderator U. GPT-5.6 Sol also rejected the requirement for both a selection-outcome association and a source-specific potential-outcome shift, which are alternative and often algebraically linked parameterizations that can double-count the same departure, and softened the blanket ban on E-values to insufficiency as the sole decision-grade analysis.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): Direct potential-outcome bias functions can parameterize departures from source-target exchangeability without specifying a concrete latent covariate, so C1-C4 are broadly sound for the Dahabreh approach. Nguyen et al. is not a clean example of that contrast, because its unobserved-moderator analysis explicitly introduces a composite U and only some proposed methods use bias formulas. C5 is mathematically wrong as a requirement: a potential-outcome-distribution shift and a selection-outcome association are alternative, often algebraically linked parameterizations. Requiring both can overparameterize or double-count the same departure. C7-C10 correctly note that a generic E-value does not itself carry PAIC target, estimand, target-summary, or bridge structure, although an E-value inherits the population and estimand of the effect estimate to which it is applied. C11 is too absolute. An E-value can be a legitimate sensitivity analysis when the scientific question and its confounding-association model match, but it is generally insufficient as the sole decision-grade analysis for an unanchored PAIC. Adaptation of direct bias functions to limited aggregate summaries remains a valid open task. Claims about default use and complete publication absence were not adjudicated under this lens.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Retrieved all three cited works. Dahabreh et al. 2026 verified as ‘Global Sensitivity Analysis for Studies Extending Inferences From a Randomized Trial to a Target Population’ (Stat Med 45:13-14), which models violations of conditional exchangeability through potential-outcome distributions, matching the entry’s description. Dahabreh et al. 2023 is verified by title as bias-function sensitivity analysis for extending trial inferences. The Nguyen et al. 2017 attribution is partly decorative and cuts against claim 1. Its own abstract frames situation (2) as concern ‘that the treatment effect may be moderated by factors not observed even in the RCT, which we represent as a composite moderator U’, and only two of its five methods ((iv) a bias formula and (v) partial weighting combined with a bias formula) are bias-function based. So the paper does posit a latent composite variable, which is exactly the parameterization claim 1 contrasts bias functions with. Claim 11 is independently corroborated by Leahy et al. 2023, whose first workshop recommendation restricts E-values to unknown-unknowns. Claim 6 (no adaptation to limited-AgD PAIC) I could not falsify; I found no PAIC-specific bias-function template.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
Statement
Bias correction, deterministic grid QBA, probabilistic QBA, partial identification and tipping-point analysis answer different questions and emit differently interpretable objects, yet applied analyses blur them and confidence, systematic-error, total-error and identified-set ranges are all published as 95% intervals. The distinctions are long established rather than new: they organize the Lash, Fox and Fink bias-analysis textbook (doi:10.1007/978-3-030-82673-4) and Greenland’s multiple-bias literature, and Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) make the PAIC-specific point that a deterministic grid treats every sensitivity-parameter value as equally likely. What remains open is narrower than the source said, because some labeling already exists: cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) tags contrasts by whether they are identified by IPD, by aggregate data or by neither, returns nonidentified effects as NA and diagnoses prior-driven movement, but no PAIC package carries the QBA mode or the interval type as metadata, and no ITC or PAIC reporting guideline enforces the taxonomy, including the 2025 PAIC framework of Ishak et al. (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1), which covers risk of bias and reporting but not interval semantics.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
Why it is open
All five modes emit an estimate and a range, and nothing in current PAIC software carries the mode or the interval type as metadata, so the distinction survives only in the analyst’s prose. Summarizing a grid as the fraction of scenarios favoring a decision imposes a uniform measure over an arbitrarily chosen and arbitrarily spaced set of points, producing a number that looks probabilistic with no elicited distribution behind it. Where bias parameters have no validation or auxiliary data behind them the observed-data likelihood does not update them, so a probabilistic output is the analyst’s input distribution passed through the estimator while presenting in the same visual form as a data-driven posterior. Because no ITC or PAIC reporting guideline enforces the taxonomy, economic models and appraisal committees downstream cannot tell a sensitivity envelope from a confidence interval.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Lash, Fox, Fink and colleagues, Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data (Springer)
Textbook whose organizing structure is the distinction between simple or deterministic, probabilistic and multiple-bias analysis, and between conventional confidence intervals, systematic-error intervals and total-error intervals. Supplied by the literature auditor as the source the entry presented uncited.


Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
States, in the exact PAIC setting, that a deterministic sensitivity analysis treats all possible sensitivity-parameter values as equally likely, which may not be realistic in practice.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Refutes the claim that no PAIC software labels identified versus analyst-specified quantities: estimable_effects_at() labels contrasts by identified_by (IPD, aggregate or none) and basis (exact, first-order screen or not identified), nonidentified effects are returned as NA, and prior_sensitivity() with plot_prior_posterior() diagnose prior-driven movement. It carries no QBA-mode or interval-type metadata.


Ishak, Chandler, Liu and Klijn 2025, A Framework for Reliable, Transparent, and Reproducible Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons, PharmacoEconomics 43:691-710
Published PAIC framework covering estimand definition, method and adjustment-variable selection, application, risk-of-bias assessment and comprehensive reporting. It occupies part of the reporting-guideline space but does not cover QBA mode or interval semantics.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the labeling that already exists rather than specify it from scratch: cpaic’s identification tags and prior-movement diagnostics show the pattern, and what is needed is QBA-mode and interval-type metadata on the result object so a systematic-error interval, a total-error interval and an identified set are never printed as one thing. Enforce a reporting vocabulary that names the mode and the interval type for every reported range and never labels a set with nominal coverage, while allowing a confidence region for an identified set to state its coverage explicitly. Attach a method-appropriate support or feasibility diagnostic to every grid point, using effective sample size where weights are involved and feasibility or overlap measures where they are not, so unsupported scenarios are not plotted with equal visual weight.

title: QBA modes and interval semantics are routinely conflated
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Bias correction, deterministic grid QBA, probabilistic QBA, partial identification and tipping-point analysis answer different questions and emit differently interpretable objects, yet applied analyses blur them: a deterministic envelope is read as a confidence interval, an MCMC-sampled bias posterior is read as data-identified, and a grid is summarized as if it were a probability distribution. The four interval types (confidence, systematic-error, total-error, identified set) are all published as 95% intervals.”
What was wrong with it. title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
Statement
Quantitative bias analysis for unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparison is fragmented rather than absent: the published methods are each tied to one estimator, one outcome type or one bias mechanism, and they share no common notation, no benchmark and no rule for choosing among them. Generic summary-level bias formulas can already be applied to a MAIC or STC estimate, as Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) state directly, so what is missing is a unified estimand-explicit parameterization and selection guidance, not a usable formula. The mathematics is narrower than the source claimed: under an additive identity-link conditional-mean model with a constant arm-specific coefficient for the omitted factor, arm-mean bias equals that coefficient times the difference in the omitted-factor prevalence the standardization actually uses, and on nonlinear or non-collapsible scales the correction requires integrating the conditional mean over the target covariate law, which finite summation, analytic formulas or quadrature can do exactly.

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
Why it is open
In an unanchored comparison treatment and study are the same unit, so any cross-study difference can contaminate the contrast, yet no shared parameterization links weighting, outcome-regression and one-stage estimators to a common bias object. A bias specified on a conditional linear predictor does not transfer mechanically to a marginal effect on a non-collapsible scale, so each estimand needs its own analytic summation, quadrature or simulation over the target covariate law, and corrections computed by different families are not comparable. Because the families return different kinds of object (a corrected point estimate, a distribution, or a set), an analyst can choose the one that yields the most convenient answer, and no published benchmark compares them on shared PAIC scenarios with known truth.

Work
What it contributes




Ren et al. 2025, Quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparisons, Research Synthesis Methods
Extends unanchored STC by simulating important covariates unreported in the comparator study; also states that the general class of bias formulas for mean difference, risk ratio and odds ratio can be applied directly to a MAIC or STC estimate as a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding.


Soutar et al. 2025, Flexible quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in subject-level indirect treatment comparisons with proportional hazards violation, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Bayesian data-augmentation QBA for subject-level indirect comparisons using the RMST difference under non-proportional hazards. Estimator-, outcome- and mechanism-specific.


Gray et al. 2024, Pharmacoepidemiology and Drug Safety
Illustrates QBA for external controls across three separately run scenarios: missing confounder, misclassification of exposure, and outcome evaluation. The literature auditor corrected the entry’s description of the second scenario as index-date error.


Nourredine et al. 2025, Statistics in Medicine
Likelihood correction and validation-informed likelihood for misclassified binary outcomes in unanchored external-control comparisons, in an unweighted design with no population adjustment.


Shi et al. 2024, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Systematic review counting 57 summary-level QBA methods, 53 designed for observational studies and 4 for meta-analyses. It never mentions indirect comparison, MAIC, STC, transportability or PAIC, so it cannot support a claim about PAIC frameworks specifically.


Leahy et al. 2023, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
HTA expert workshop recommending QBA to quantify magnitude, direction and uncertainty of residual bias, with ten recommendations on sourcing, transparency and use.


Chandler and Ishak 2026, Anchors Away: Navigating Unanchored Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR)
Supplies the ML-UMR estimator a general framework would have to cover, and asserts the gap: QBA could be adapted for ML-UMR by incorporating bias parameters or simulated unmeasured covariates into the outcome regression and standardization steps, meaning it has not been.

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build one estimand-explicit notation covering MAIC, STC and ML-UMR with marginal and conditional estimands and named target populations, and state for each estimand whether the correction is available in closed form, by finite summation or quadrature, or only by simulation, rather than letting collapsibility decide. Cover the ML-UMR estimator of Chandler and Ishak (arXiv:2606.20341), whose authors say QBA has yet to be adapted to it. Benchmark the families against one another on shared PAIC scenarios with known truth and publish selection guidance keyed to bias mechanism, available information, estimand and decision context, treating the QBA output as a decision object propagated into the economic model rather than an appendix table.

title: General estimand-specific QBA theory for unanchored PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 2 findings from 2 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “Quantitative bias analysis for unanchored population-adjusted indirect comparisons has no unified estimand-specific theory: the conventional primary analysis sets residual confounding, selection, measurement and design bias to exactly zero, and the few existing methods are each tied to one estimator, one outcome type or one bias mechanism. Six recognisable QBA families exist but share no notation, no common benchmark, and no rule for choosing among them.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol found the mathematical claims overstated against Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13): covariate dependence does not break the additive decomposition, arm-specific coefficients already accommodate treatment interaction, exact correction needs only the conditional mean integrated over the target covariate law rather than simulation of the full outcome distribution, and collapsibility is neither sufficient nor necessary for a closed form. The literature auditor verified the Shi et al. 2024 counts (57 summary-level QBA methods, 4 designed for meta-analysis, doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2024.111507) but found the review never mentions indirect comparison, MAIC, STC, transportability or PAIC, so it cannot testify that none of the 57 is a mature PAIC framework.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): The core need for estimand-specific sensitivity analysis remains real, but C15 and C17-C19 overstate the mathematics. The identity-link formula is exact only under an additive conditional-mean model with a constant arm-specific U coefficient and when p_S denotes the U prevalence actually induced by the standardization, not necessarily the raw source prevalence. Covariate dependence does not itself break that decomposition, and treatment interaction is already accommodated by using beta_U,a separately by arm, contrary to C18. For nonlinear or non-collapsible estimands, direct subtraction of a link-scale scalar is generally invalid, but one need only integrate the conditional mean over the target covariate law, not the full outcome distribution. Finite summation, analytic bias formulas, or quadrature may be exact; simulation is not required. Collapsibility is neither sufficient for a closed form nor necessary for exact calculation. C20 is a useful but overlapping, non-exhaustive taxonomy. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, NAMESPACE exposes bridge_fragility() for one bias mechanism but no general qba() interface, so the unification problem remains open. Publication-sparsity and no-framework claims were not used because literature coverage is outside this audit lens.

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text: OVL-05 Confirmed open High priority Promising

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text:
Statement
Matching a finite list of moments, the basis of MAIC and entropy balancing, leaves the rest of the distribution unconstrained, so source and target can agree on every balanced moment while differing in the tails and in the joint dependence structure. Optimal transport aligns fully specified empirical measures under an explicit cost function and makes the amount and location of transport visible, and it has already reached causal inference: Dunipace derives optimal-transport weights that minimize the transport distance between treatment and control (arxiv:2109.01991), and Gunsilius and Xu match for causal effects via multimarginal unbalanced optimal transport (arxiv:2112.04398). Neither addresses the PAIC data structure in which the target is known only through published marginal moments, which is where an adaptation would be new. Two auditors searched and found no such adaptation, so the absence is a negative search result rather than a verified fact, and the transport cost is a weaker diagnostic than the source claimed, since it measures separation under a chosen and scaled cost function rather than positivity failure as such.

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text:
Why it is open
Balancing a finite list of moments leaves tails and joint dependence unconstrained, exactly where nonlinear outcome models and survival estimands are most sensitive, so the failure mode the source identifies is real. Optimal transport addresses it in principle only when both measures are fully specified, and in PAIC the target usually is not: aligning entire distributions requires first imposing a synthetic joint distribution that published marginals do not identify, so the transport is computed against an assumption rather than against data. Robust optimal transport over a moment-constrained ambiguity set is a coherent response but naturally returns worst-case criteria or ranges rather than a unique target distribution or effect. Computation, per-covariate cost specification, and uncertainty quantification for transport-based weights in a network context are all unresolved, so there is no estimator to evaluate, and none of this would repair an identification failure in any case.

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Dunipace, Optimal transport weights for causal inference (2021)
derives weights by minimizing the optimal-transport distance between treatment and control groups, targeting distributional rather than moment balance; does not address the PAIC setting where the target is known only through published marginal moments


Gunsilius and Xu, Matching for causal effects via multimarginal unbalanced optimal transport

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build on the existing causal optimal-transport weighting and matching methods (arxiv:2109.01991, arxiv:2112.04398) rather than deriving PAIC transport from scratch, and treat the aggregate-data case as the genuinely new problem: transport to a target specified only by published marginals, using robust optimal transport over a moment-constrained uncertainty set and reporting the resulting range rather than a single aligned distribution. Add entropic regularization for computational stability, covariate-specific costs reflecting clinical plausibility, and partial transport that leaves unsupported target mass unmatched instead of forcing a match. Before transport cost can be reported as a diagnostic it needs clinical scaling, calibration against reference cases and decomposition by covariate direction, because an unscaled cost separates overlap from nonoverlap poorly in both directions. Frame the line of work as a research roadmap rather than as a prerequisite for decision-grade analysis, and never as evidence that positivity has been repaired.

title: Optimal transport for distributional balancing in PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Moment matching, the basis of MAIC and entropy balancing, can miss differences in the tails and in the dependence structure of the source and target covariate distributions. Optimal transport would align entire empirical distributions under an explicit cost function, with the amount and location of transport serving as a positivity diagnostic, but it has not been adapted to PAIC.”
What was wrong with it. The source read as if optimal-transport balancing for causal work were unbuilt; the literature auditor found two existing causal optimal-transport weighting and matching methods (arxiv:2109.01991, arxiv:2112.04398), neither covering the PAIC case where the target is only published moments, and recorded the absence claim itself as unverifiable rather than verified. GPT-5.6 Sol struck the claim that a large transport cost is a valid diagnostic of an unsupported target, since common support can coexist with a large Wasserstein distance, nonoverlap can produce a small cost, and a low cost can be falsely reassuring when effect-modifier directions are omitted, so cost needs clinical scaling, reference calibration and decomposition before it warns of anything.

Literature and prior-art check

open / unverifiable. Searched arXiv full text for ‘optimal transport’ AND ‘indirect comparison’ (zero results returned by the API), plus abstract queries pairing optimal transport with covariate balancing, transportability, external control and generalizability, plus PubMed. I found no adaptation of optimal transport to population-adjusted indirect comparison, and no source that asserts the absence. Per the standing rule, an absence cannot be verified by finding nothing, so the pivotal claim ‘Optimal-transport balancing has not yet been adapted to population-adjusted indirect comparison’ is unverifiable rather than verified. The generic OT facts asserted (distributional alignment under a cost function, entropic regularisation, partial transport, robust OT over uncertainty sets) are standard and correct. Two adjacent works exist and should be cited so the entry is not read as claiming OT-based causal weighting itself is novel: Dunipace, ‘Optimal transport weights for causal inference’ (arXiv:2109.01991), which minimises OT distance between treatment and control to target distributional balance, and Gunsilius and Xu, ‘Matching for causal effects via multimarginal unbalanced optimal transport’ (arXiv:2112.04398). Neither addresses the PAIC data structure in which the target is known only through published moments, which is the entry’s genuine novelty.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1-C6 and C8 are technically sound. A finite set of balanced moments need not determine tails or joint dependence; balanced OT constructs a minimum-cost coupling between fully specified empirical measures; entropic regularization smooths computation; and partial OT can leave mass unmatched. Important qualifications remain. In the usual PAIC setting, the target empirical distribution is unavailable, so an entire-distribution alignment is possible only after imposing a synthetic joint distribution that is not identified by marginal moments. Robust OT over a moment-constrained ambiguity set is a coherent research construction, but it naturally yields worst-case criteria or ranges rather than a uniquely identified target distribution or effect. C9 is too categorical: a large transport cost shows separation under the chosen, scaled cost function, not positivity failure as such. Common support can coexist with a large Wasserstein distance, nonoverlap can have a small cost, and omitted effect-modifier directions can make a low cost falsely reassuring. Cost requires clinical scaling, reference calibration, and decomposition before serving as a useful warning. C10 is a literature-absence claim and is not adjudicated here. The PAIC adaptation is therefore an open research direction, but it is a roadmap item rather than a prerequisite for decision-grade analysis, and it cannot repair identification failure.

title: No support diagnostic aggregates over a PAIC target distribution
text:
Statement
Outcome-regression PAIC such as STC, ML-NMR and parametric g-computation can rely on predictions at target covariate profiles that are sparsely represented or unsupported in the source data, and weight-concentration summaries such as ESS do not diagnose that reliance. General support diagnostics do exist and can be applied to a regression: covariate distance, convex-hull membership, density, prediction variance and classical leverage all flag risk, though none certifies that a transported causal effect is identified. What is missing is the PAIC-specific layer: aggregating those measures over a target distribution that is often known only as published moments, reporting them for a target-standardized marginal contrast rather than for a single prediction, and calibrating rules that map a flag to abstention, an explicit sensitivity model, or target redefinition. Two auditors searched and found no application of conformal prediction or representation-space out-of-distribution scoring to STC, ML-NMR or g-computation-based population adjustment; that is a negative search result rather than a verified absence.

title: No support diagnostic aggregates over a PAIC target distribution
text:
Why it is open
A regression has no weights to inspect, so a positivity violation shows up as a numerically well-behaved prediction rather than as an extreme weight, and while prediction variance does rise with leverage in linear and generalized linear models, no model-based interval represents misspecification or nonidentification. The general geometric and leverage diagnostics that could flag the risk do not aggregate cleanly to the quantity a PAIC reports, which is a target-standardized marginal contrast integrated over a target distribution known only through published marginals, in a hierarchical network where the relevant covariate joint distribution must be assumed rather than observed. Conformal and out-of-distribution scores inherit exchangeability-type assumptions that fail precisely under the unsupported covariate shift they are meant to detect, and in any case deliver predictive coverage or novelty rather than identification of a causal contrast. There is no established mapping from any of these scores to a decision, and interval widening is not one, because widening without an explicit sensitivity model, bound or prior does not repair nonidentification.

title: No support diagnostic aggregates over a PAIC target distribution
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Start from the support diagnostics that already exist for regression, namely covariate distance, convex-hull membership, density ratios, prediction variance and classical leverage, and solve the PAIC-specific problem, which is aggregating them over a target distribution reconstructed from published marginals and reporting them for a target-standardized marginal contrast rather than for a single prediction. Note that plot_leverage() in cpaic (https://github.com/choxos/cpaic, commit 9d150e9, an unreleased development package that cannot be installed from CRAN) is DIC point leverage computed from posterior deviance variance, so it is a model-fit diagnostic and not the covariate-support diagnostic proposed here; building the latter is genuinely new work. Treat conformal and out-of-distribution tools as candidates for the flagging step only in their weighted or anomaly-score forms, since ordinary conformal prediction carries no guarantee under the shift being diagnosed. Tie every flag to a stated response, whether abstention, target redefinition, or an explicit sensitivity model with declared bounds, rather than to ad hoc interval widening, and frame the whole battery as diagnostic so that a passing score is never read as certifying extrapolation.

title: No support diagnostic aggregates over a PAIC target distribution
text:
Our study

Unsupported target mass matters only where the effect is modified
This study was designed against OVL-01 and bears on this entry in part. What it does not answer is stated below.
The question put to it. When part of the target population lies outside the source trial’s support, do weight and covariate diagnostics identify the analyses that fail, or is the modification in the unsupported region, which they cannot see, what decides it?
What it found. Unsupported target mass caused bias only where the effect bent in the unsupported direction (up to 0.29 for G-computation and 0.30 for MAIC with 27% of the target unsupported), and none with linear modification or orthogonal alignment. title: No support diagnostic aggregates over a PAIC target distribution
text:
What this project measured
OVL-01 answers the refuting sentence of this entry. Its G-computation arm fitted natural-spline modification, whose prediction variance grows where the source has few patients, and integrated it over the target law including 27% of target mass outside the source’s support. When the modification bent in the unsupported region its interval covered 0.70 with a bias of -0.29 on a 0.04 truth, although it had widened there: prediction variance rises with leverage, but no model-based interval represents misspecification in a region the data do not reach. A diagnostic that multiplied unsupported distance by the estimated interaction discriminated failed analyses better than weight-based ones (AUROC 0.59 to 0.66 against 0.48 to 0.52) and was still not usable alone.
Not answered: how a support diagnostic should be aggregated over a target distribution that is itself reconstructed from published marginals (mean against tail functionals), and how the reconstruction error propagates into that diagnostic. OVL-01 used a known target law.

Verification

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I searched arXiv (full-text and abstract queries pairing conformal/out-of-distribution with transportability, generalizability and external validity) and PubMed, and found no application of conformal prediction or representation-space OOD scoring to STC, ML-NMR or g-computation-based population adjustment, and no extrapolation-leverage diagnostic for outcome-regression PAIC. So the entry’s own hedge that these tools are ‘speculative rather than established’ matches what I could retrieve, and the problem is open. Two caveats. First, the load-bearing negative claim (no support diagnostics exist for outcome-regression PAIC) is an absence claim and no source I retrieved asserts it, so it is unverifiable rather than verified. Second, the entry’s framing of extrapolation as pure hazard is one-sided: Remiro-Azocar et al. 2022 present extrapolation as the capability that lets regression-based adjustment beat MAIC exactly where overlap is worst, reporting that parametric G-computation is ‘more precise and more accurate than MAIC, particularly when covariate overlap is poor.’ The diagnostic gap is real; the implied verdict on outcome regression is not established.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1, the qualified form of C2, C6, and C8 are correct: weight-concentration diagnostics do not diagnose an outcome model, predictions can be computed outside empirical support, and neither conformal nor OOD scoring identifies a causal effect or validates extrapolation. The title and rationale nevertheless overstate the absence of diagnostics. Covariate-distance, convex-hull, density, prediction-variance, and classical leverage diagnostics can be applied to outcome regression, although none certifies causal transport. Model-based standard errors are not necessarily narrow outside support; linear and generalized regression prediction uncertainty can increase with leverage, while still failing to represent model misspecification or nonidentification. C4 is not true of ordinary conformal prediction: under unsupported covariate shift its exchangeability guarantee fails, and a conventional conformal interval need not flag the profile. Specialized conformal anomaly scores or weighted conformal procedures can be heuristic flags under additional assumptions. Representation-space OOD scores are likewise model-dependent heuristics. C7 is incomplete because ad hoc interval widening does not repair nonidentification; widening requires an explicit sensitivity model, bound, or prior. At cpaic@9d150e9, plot_leverage() is DIC point leverage based on posterior deviance variance, not the proposed covariate-support diagnostic. PAIC-specific aggregation of support diagnostics and calibrated abstention rules remains open, but general support diagnostics do exist.

title: Weak overlap leaves target regions the source data cannot support
text:
Statement
Weak overlap between the source individual patient data and the target population can produce highly variable MAIC weights, a low effective sample size and unstable inference, and can push outcome-regression predictions into regions where they rely heavily on extrapolation; applied work contains exactly this, with 93 pooled patients reduced to an effective sample size of 29 (doi:10.1016/j.clcc.2026.04.003). These are consequences that can occur, not necessities: finite-moment MAIC can retain a healthy effective sample size while still failing to cover unsupported regions or unbalanced features, so a comfortable ESS is not evidence of support. ESS is itself only a concentration functional of the weights, and Phillippo et al. 2018 record that the Kish approximation ‘is likely to be an underestimation of the true ESS’ because the weights are estimated and correlated with the outcome (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740); precision is additionally governed by estimator-specific influence, weighted outcome variance, treatment allocation, and for survival outcomes weighted risk-set and event information. What no estimator can fix is the nonparametric identification failure: where target covariate mass is absent from the source, reporting an effect requires stronger modeling assumptions, target redefinition, sensitivity analysis or abstention.

title: Weak overlap leaves target regions the source data cannot support
text:
Why it is open
Positivity is a property of the data rather than of the estimator, so weighting and outcome modeling both remain computable while their answers become determined by assumption rather than by observation, and no refinement of the weighting recovers support that the published aggregate data never described. The failure is not reliably visible in the diagnostics analysts report: weighting exposes it through concentrated weights only when the balancing constraints happen to load the unsupported directions, and regression returns smooth predictions whose model-based intervals reflect leverage but not misspecification or nonidentification. There is no accepted trimming rule or effective-sample-size threshold, so the same data can be made to look adequate or hollow depending on undocumented analyst choices. Outcome modeling can still recover efficiency or extrapolate under additional structural assumptions, so what cannot be restored is assumption-free identification, not information in general.

title: Weak overlap leaves target regions the source data cannot support
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Report precision in estimator-specific terms rather than through Kish ESS alone: weighted outcome and event information, influence-function variance, and local ESS or density-ratio maps that show where the weight mass sits, noting alongside that the robust sandwich variance estimator underestimates variability where effective sample sizes are small (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511). Couple trimming with explicit estimand redefinition rather than silent exclusion, add penalties for extrapolation, and adopt abstention rules that decline to report an effect where support is absent. Benchmarking should extend the existing simulation programme rather than start from scratch, since the 162-scenario anchored study (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511) and the parametric G-computation comparisons (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1565) already vary overlap; what would be new is entropy-balancing variants and overlap-aware shrinkage estimation, with ESS over n bands treated as stress-test strata rather than as validity thresholds.

text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed, on a single finding.
The source titled this. “Weak overlap collapses effective sample size and destabilizes weights” The title states effective sample size collapse and unstable weights as necessary consequences, which the audit found to be possible rather than automatic.
The source said. “When source and target covariate distributions overlap weakly, MAIC weights explode and the effective sample size collapses, regression-based methods extrapolate beyond the observed data, and the nominal target population becomes unsupported by the evidence. The report names weak overlap and unstable weighting as the first of the field’s most important open problems and as a principal unresolved weakness of anchored MAIC.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented ESS collapse and exploding weights as necessary consequences of weak overlap and treated ESS as the operative precision metric; GPT-5.6 Sol judged both too strong, since finite-moment MAIC can retain a healthy ESS while leaving unsupported regions uncovered, and the literature auditor added that Phillippo et al. 2018 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) call the reported Kish ESS a likely underestimate of the true ESS. The claim was unattributed in the source and is now sourced to that paper and to Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2022 (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1565), which treats regression extrapolation as a capability rather than as concealment and reports parametric G-computation as more precise and more accurate than MAIC particularly when covariate overlap is poor.

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 1 surviving finding from: Arbitrated Indirect Treatment Comparisons. New citations: 10.1007/s43441-026-00976-2

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Read the full text of Phillippo et al. 2018 (PMC5774635) and abstracts of Remiro-Azocar’s simulation programme. The core claims are all sourceable, and I supply the sources below since prior_work was empty. Two caveats. (1) The entry treats ESS as ‘the operative precision metric’; Phillippo et al. state the Kish ESS ‘is only accurate if the weights are fixed and known, or if they are uncorrelated with the outcome - neither of which is true here. As such, this approximation is likely to be an underestimation of the true ESS.’ The metric the entry leans on is a known-biased approximation, which the entry never says. (2) The entry frames regression extrapolation as concealment; Remiro-Azocar et al. 2022 frame it as a capability and find parametric G-computation ‘more precise and more accurate than MAIC, particularly when covariate overlap is poor,’ and the 162-scenario study concludes MAIC’s ‘bias reduction outweighs the loss in precision’ at low overlap. Positivity itself is a property of the data and remains open; the precision consequence is partly addressed. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740: Sources the unsourced claims that ESS is the reported diagnostic, that small ESS signals lack of overlap, and that anchored MAIC rests on conditional constancy of relative effects (all effect modifiers balanced) plus a valid common comparator.. Cites doi:10.1002/jrsm.1565: Sources both halves of the overlap claim: weighting cannot extrapolate and is overlap-sensitive, whereas outcome regression can extrapolate.. Cites arXiv:2112.08023: Sources the claim that anchored MAIC targets a marginal effect in the aggregate-data trial population.. Cites doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511: Sources ‘MAIC becomes brittle at small ESS’ but also narrows the entry’s severity framing.. Cites doi:10.1016/j.clcc.2026.04.003: A retrieved applied example of the ‘statistically hollow after balancing’ claim: 93 pooled patients reduced to ESS 29..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The nonparametric identification problem is real: an estimator cannot create support where the target population has covariate mass absent from the source. C3, C5, and C12-C15 are broadly correct. However, C2 and C10 incorrectly make ESS collapse and exploding weights necessary consequences of weak overlap. They occur when the fitted density-ratio or calibration problem exposes the unsupported directions, but finite-moment MAIC can retain a healthy ESS while missing unsupported regions or unbalanced features. C4 is too strong because Kish ESS is only a concentration functional of the weights. Actual precision also depends on arm-specific weighted outcome variance, estimated-weight uncertainty, treatment allocation, influence functions, and, for survival outcomes, weighted risk-set and event information. C11 applies when target mass lies outside or sparsely within source support, but regression standard errors can increase with leverage and regression can be more efficient under a correct extrapolation model. The statements that these are the principal or most important problems are priority judgments, not mathematical conclusions. Outcome modeling cannot restore assumption-free identification, but it can recover efficiency or extrapolate under additional structural assumptions, so the claim that discarded information cannot be recovered by any downstream modeling is also too broad. The proposed ESS bands are stress-test choices, not validity thresholds.

title: No treatment-invariance check for summed rating-scale outcomes
text:
Statement
Where the outcome entering an indirect comparison is a summed multi-item rating scale, the total score measures the intended construct equally across the treatments compared only if every item responds to each treatment through that construct. When a drug moves items through a side-effect channel such as sedation, appetite or weight, the sum records that movement as efficacy, and the resulting ranking is in part a ranking on side-effect profile rather than on the construct the network claims to compare. The magnitude is measured rather than hypothetical: in an item-based patient-level analysis of 5974 participants, the advantage of mirtazapine over selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors on the 17-item Hamilton sum disappeared once the three sleep items, the appetite item and the weight item were removed, with effect sizes between -0.02 and 0.07 across weeks 1 to 6 and no significant difference at any timepoint, while on the remaining core-symptom items the comparators were never inferior. That summed score is the outcome on which mirtazapine places among the most efficacious agents in the 21-drug antidepressant network meta-analysis. No indirect-comparison method, appraisal tool or reporting standard requires a composite outcome to be shown invariant across the treatments being compared, and no diagnostic with known operating characteristics exists for detecting differential item response by treatment.

title: No treatment-invariance check for summed rating-scale outcomes
text:
Why it is open
The failure is across treatment arms rather than across studies, so none of the cross-trial harmonization machinery applies: the instrument, endpoint definition, follow-up and analysis population can be identical in every trial and the contamination survives intact. Population adjustment cannot repair it either, because the problem sits in the outcome definition rather than in the covariate distribution, so balancing baseline characteristics leaves the contaminated contrast exactly where it was. Running the check requires item-level responses by arm, and publications report the total score, so the diagnostic cannot be computed from the aggregate data a network normally uses; the demonstration above needed sponsor individual patient data for 5974 participants, which is why the check is not made routinely. Measurement-invariance and differential-item-functioning theory is built for groups defined before treatment, and it does not transfer without modification to arms defined by a randomized intervention that is expected to change some items: an item moving under treatment is not by itself non-invariance, so the criterion has to separate a construct-mediated item response from a side-effect-mediated one, and that criterion has not been written for a treatment contrast. Core-symptom subscales exist for several instruments, but selecting one after seeing the result is a researcher degree of freedom, and no rule says when a network should be run on a subscale rather than on the full sum.

tests directly whether side-effect-driven item movement inflates measured antidepressant efficacy on the Hamilton scale using pooled patient-level data, establishing the mechanism as an empirical question rather than a theoretical worry

separates efficacy from side-effect experience within trials of two drugs, which is the within-arm analogue of the invariance question; it does not carry the separation into an indirect comparison or a network


Cipriani et al. 2018, Comparative efficacy and acceptability of 21 antidepressant drugs for the acute treatment of adults with major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis, The Lancet 391(10128):1357-1366
the reference network whose efficacy outcome is the change in a summed depression rating scale; it is the setting in which an item-composition artifact would propagate into published rankings, and it applies no invariance check to the composite


Fried and Nesse 2015, Depression sum-scores don’t add up: why analyzing specific depression symptoms is essential, BMC Medicine 13:72
shows that individual symptoms of a summed depression scale differ in their response and argues for symptom-level rather than sum-level analysis; it makes the case at the level of a single trial and does not state what a network or an indirect comparison should require


Meredith 1993, Measurement Invariance, Factor Analysis and Factorial Invariance, Psychometrika 58(4):525-543
the standard formalization of measurement invariance as equality of a measurement model’s parameters across groups; it is the machinery a treatment-invariance criterion would be built from, defined for groups fixed before measurement rather than for randomized arms whose treatment is expected to move some items

title: No treatment-invariance check for summed rating-scale outcomes
text:
Probable solution or research direction
State the criterion first: a composite is treatment-invariant for a contrast when the treatment’s effect on the total score is mediated entirely through the latent construct, which is a testable restriction in a measurement model that carries treatment as an exogenous variable, with a treatment-specific direct effect on an item as the parameter of interest. Specify the diagnostic and the data it needs, namely item-by-arm means and their covariance, and report the difference between the full-sum contrast and the construct-restricted contrast as an explicit item-contamination term alongside the estimate. Establish operating characteristics by simulation: how large a side-effect-mediated item shift must be to move a rank in a network of a given size and connectivity, and what power an item-level test has at the trial sizes typical of psychiatry and rheumatology. Fix the aggregate-data case separately, by requiring trials with composite primary outcomes to publish item-level or prespecified subscale results, and, until they do, by running the network on a prespecified core-symptom subscale alongside the full sum and reporting both. Where only summed scores exist, bound the contamination from external estimates of the side-effect-mediated item shift for the drug classes involved and report the bound as a quantitative bias analysis rather than as a limitation paragraph.

title: No treatment-invariance check for summed rating-scale outcomes
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the evidence is a single item-level patient-level analysis, which is a weaker basis than a multi-reader gap; the reviewer accepted it on the ground that an identical summed instrument can still reflect treatment-specific effects on components outside the intended construct. No criterion, diagnostic or reporting requirement for treatment invariance of a composite entering a network was found in the category or in the wider synthesis literature.

title: No estimand aligns outcomes reported on different assessment schedules
text: OUT-23 Partially addressed High priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: No estimand aligns outcomes reported on different assessment schedules
text:
Statement
Trials of the same condition report longitudinal outcomes on incompatible assessment grids; in one recent feasibility assessment the principal timepoints across a network ranged from 4 to 52 weeks, and where dosing is cyclical a nominated week may fall at a peak or at a trough of effect. Every population-adjustment method takes the outcome at a nominated timepoint as given, so the analyst must first choose or manufacture a common timepoint before any weighting or outcome model is fitted. The devices in use are picking each trial’s own principal timepoint, linear interpolation to an unreported timepoint, averaging over several timepoints, area under the curve, and carrying an earlier assessment forward to stand for a later one; published appraisals record a matching-adjusted comparison that carried 18-month motor-milestone results forward to represent 24 months, and another that compared 12-month results against a trial stopped at a mean of 9 months without using its extension data. None of these has a stated estimand, an identification argument from the summaries actually reported, or a variance that includes the alignment step. Time-course model-based network meta-analysis solves the aggregate-data version of the problem where trials report several timepoints each, and there is no population-adjusted counterpart and nothing at all for the common case in which each trial reports one timepoint, so the time-course shape is identified only by borrowing across trials. The choice is decision-relevant and signed, since reviewers report that the timepoint selected can favor one treatment over another.

title: No estimand aligns outcomes reported on different assessment schedules
text:
Why it is open
With one reported timepoint per trial the time course is not identified within a trial, so every alignment device is an extrapolation that borrows shape from other trials, and the borrowing assumption is least defensible in exactly the networks whose timepoints differ most. Carry-forward and interpolation change the estimand rather than estimate it: an 18-month result standing in for 24 months answers a different question, and this is not a missing-data problem with a principled correction because the later measurement was never taken. A time-averaged or area-under-the-curve contrast is a defensible estimand but is not what trials report, and reconstructing it from a few published means requires both a functional form for the trajectory and a within-patient correlation that aggregate publications do not supply. Population adjustment compounds all of this, because the covariates that modify the effect at one timepoint need not be those that modify it at another, so an alignment step performed before weighting can silently change the modifier set the weights were built to balance.

title: No estimand aligns outcomes reported on different assessment schedules
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Gilhus, Jacob, Hashim, Van Sanden et al. 2025, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research, e250009
Feasibility assessment of indirect treatment comparisons in generalized myasthenia gravis that documents the timepoint range across a real network and reviews the menu of responses in use, including a single reported timepoint, averaging across timepoints and area under the curve, and states that further investigation of the strengths and weaknesses of these approaches is needed and that multiple approaches should be explored to see how differences in timepoints affect results.


Pedder, Dias, Bennetts, Boucher & Welton 2019, Research Synthesis Methods 10(2):267-286
Time-course model-based network meta-analysis for continuous summary outcomes, which models the effect as a parametric function of time so that trials reporting at different times contribute to a common curve. Solves the aggregate-data version where repeated measurements are reported; supplies no population adjustment and needs more than one timepoint per study to identify the shape without borrowing.


MBNMAtime: Run Time-Course Model-Based Network Meta-Analysis Models (CRAN)
The maintained implementation of time-course model-based network meta-analysis, which shows the aggregate-data route is usable in practice and marks the absence of any equivalent for population-adjusted comparisons.


Dakin, Welton, Ades, Collins et al. 2011, Statistics in Medicine 30(20):2511-2535
Mixed treatment comparison of repeated measurements of a continuous endpoint, an early demonstration that repeated measurements across a network can be synthesized jointly rather than reduced to one timepoint per trial.


Trikalinos & Olkin 2012, Clinical Trials 9(5):610-620
Multivariate meta-analysis of effect sizes reported at multiple time points, which handles the within-study correlation between timepoints; requires that correlation to be known or assumed, which is the input aggregate publications withhold.


Musekiwa, Manda, Mwambi & Chen 2016, PLOS ONE 11(10):e0164898
General linear mixed model for meta-analysis of effect sizes reported at multiple time points, an alternative route to the same aggregate-data problem, again defined for studies that report a series rather than one value.

title: No estimand aligns outcomes reported on different assessment schedules
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Name the estimand before choosing a device: state whether the target is the contrast at a declared calendar time, the average contrast over a declared window, the area under the trajectory, or the contrast at a stated point in the dosing cycle, and note that these are different quantities that will not agree under a time-varying effect. For each device in use, derive the conditions under which the reported summaries identify that target, so that carry-forward and interpolation are either justified as estimating something or reclassified as estimand substitutions and reported as such. Build the population-adjusted counterpart of a time-course model, in which the trajectory parameters carry effect-modifier interactions and the target population is declared, so that alignment and weighting happen in one model rather than in sequence, and derive its variance including the alignment step. Then evaluate: simulate networks with a known trajectory and known modifiers, apply each device, and report bias and coverage for each named estimand, including the case that motivates this problem in which each trial reports a single timepoint.

title: No estimand aligns outcomes reported on different assessment schedules
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as well posed and specific to population-adjusted comparisons built from separately reported longitudinal outcomes, noting that existing longitudinal meta-analytic models do not supply the estimand, the identification conditions from the available summaries, or the uncertainty propagation. It is partially-addressed because time-course model-based network meta-analysis covers the aggregate-data case where trials report repeated measurements; only one of the two applied sources described in the proposal carries a verifiable identifier, so the direct evidence here is a single paper.
