title: Absolute effects across a network share no baseline risk or time horizon
text: OUT-21 Partially addressed Medium-high priority Established Tractability 5/5

title: Absolute effects across a network share no baseline risk or time horizon
text:
Statement
An absolute effect in a network meta-analysis, a number needed to treat, a risk difference or an absolute event rate, is manufactured by combining a relative effect with a baseline risk the analyst supplies. That baseline may be the mean control event rate across studies, a pooled estimate from a baseline model, or an elicited value, and it may be common to all comparisons or specific to each; the same network yields different absolute numbers under each choice. The trials informing different comparisons also have different follow-up durations, so two absolute effects in the same display can refer to different reference populations and to different time horizons at once. The displays in routine use place these numbers side by side as if they were commensurable: bar, Cates, forest, bubble, scatter and rank-heat formats, the last recommended precisely for showing many treatments across many outcomes in one figure. GRADE summary-of-findings guidance requires an assumed comparator risk and a time frame to be stated in the table, and the network adaptation of that table carries relative and absolute effects together, so part of the problem is addressed in tabular reporting. What no convention supplies is a requirement that every cell of a displayed set share one baseline and one horizon, or failing that be annotated with its own, and no checklist for network reports asks for either.

title: Absolute effects across a network share no baseline risk or time horizon
text:
Why it is open
Standardizing to one baseline risk reintroduces the question of whose baseline: different comparisons are informed by different trial sets, so a single control event rate is an extrapolation for every comparison whose trials were run in populations at different underlying risk, and choosing it is a judgment the display then hides. Standardizing to one horizon requires either that every comparison have evidence at that horizon, which is generally false, or an extrapolation model, which imports exactly the assumptions an absolute-effect display was meant to make transparent. Annotation is the cheaper fix and fails on the graphical formats, since a rank-heat cell or a bubble is a single mark with no room for a baseline and a follow-up, and moving them to a caption defeats the purpose of a display built for rapid comparison. The problem also has no owner: it falls between the synthesis methods literature, which treats absolute effects as a presentational step after estimation, and the reporting guidelines, which specify what a table must contain rather than what a set of numbers must have in common.

title: Absolute effects across a network share no baseline risk or time horizon
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Veroniki, Bender, Glasziou, Straus & Tricco 2019, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 111:11-22
Sets out six graphical methods for presenting the number needed to treat from a network meta-analysis and states the problem: the calculation requires a control event rate, different rates including the mean across studies, a pooled meta-analytic estimate and an expert-opinion value give different numbers, and because the number needed to treat depends on control event rate and study duration, comparing multiple treatments on that scale may be difficult. Advises caution rather than fixing a convention.


Veroniki, Straus, Fyraridis & Tricco 2016, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 76:193-199
Introduces the rank-heat plot for presenting many treatments across many outcomes in a single figure, the display format in which absolute effects computed from different baselines and horizons are most likely to be read as commensurable.


Yepes-Nunez, Li, Guyatt, Jack et al. 2019, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 115:1-13
Develops the GRADE summary-of-findings table for network meta-analysis through structured interviews with 32 stakeholders, with relative and absolute effect estimates, certainty and treatment ranking as required components. Establishes the tabular convention that partially covers this problem; it does not require that the absolute effects for different comparisons share a baseline risk and a follow-up.


Guyatt, Oxman, Santesso, Helfand et al. 2013, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 66(2):158-172
GRADE guidance on preparing summary-of-findings tables for binary outcomes, including how to choose and state assumed comparator risks and the follow-up to which they refer. This is the closest existing standard, written for pairwise comparisons rather than for a set of comparisons shown together.


Hutton, Salanti, Caldwell, Chaimani et al. 2015, Annals of Internal Medicine 162(11):777-784
The PRISMA extension for network meta-analysis, the reporting checklist that would be the natural home for a baseline-and-horizon requirement and does not contain one.


Dias, Sutton, Ades & Welton 2013, Medical Decision Making 33(5):607-617
The generalized linear modeling framework for evidence synthesis in which absolute effects are produced by combining a separately estimated baseline model with the pooled relative effects, which is where the baseline enters and where a common referent could be imposed.

title: Absolute effects across a network share no baseline risk or time horizon
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Adopt a default and make departures declare themselves: absolute effects displayed together should be computed from one named baseline risk and one named time horizon, with the source of that baseline stated as a pooled baseline model, an external registry estimate or an elicited value. Where a comparison has no evidence at the named horizon, mark the cell rather than filling it, and report the follow-up range of the contributing trials so a reader can see how far the number was carried. Extend network reporting checklists and the summary-of-findings format to require the baseline, its provenance and the horizon for every absolute quantity, including in figures, and specify a minimal annotation for dense displays such as a companion table keyed to the cells. Then test whether it matters: recompute published network absolute-effect displays under a common baseline and horizon and under the original comparison-specific choices, and report how often the implied treatment ordering on the absolute scale changes.

title: Absolute effects across a network share no baseline risk or time horizon
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as a specific commensurability problem rather than a restatement of the need to declare an estimand, since a declared absolute target outcome does not ensure that every displayed cell uses the same baseline-risk population and time horizon. It is partially-addressed because GRADE guidance and the network summary-of-findings format already require an assumed comparator risk and a time frame in tables; what nothing covers is commensurability across a displayed set or annotation in graphical formats.

title: No multivariate population-adjusted model for correlated outcomes
text: OUT-19 Overstated High priority Promising

title: No multivariate population-adjusted model for correlated outcomes
text:
Statement
Multivariate network meta-analysis of correlated efficacy and safety outcomes is established rather than promising methodology, covering borrowing of information across outcomes (PMC4142066), joint synthesis of multiple correlated outcomes in networks of interventions (PMC4481542), multivariate and network meta-analysis of multiple outcomes and treatments (PMC5596393) and applied Bayesian multivariate network meta-analysis (doi:10.1002/sim.8668). What has not been developed is the population-adjusted counterpart: no multivariate ML-NMR and no copula outcome model composed with transport. Running endpoints separately discards covariance only where the endpoint-specific fits are treated as independent, since a joint bootstrap, paired study-level estimates or shared posterior draws can retain it, and incoherence is not automatic either, because a decision based on expected net monetary benefit is coherent from marginal means while correlation affects its variance, the probability of cost-effectiveness, nonlinear utilities and patient-level joint quantities. The observation that different endpoints may have different effect modifiers, so separate population-adjusted analyses can standardize to subtly different populations, appears to be original to this entry.

title: No multivariate population-adjusted model for correlated outcomes
text:
Why it is open
The generic joint-synthesis problem is addressed while the population-adjusted version is not, so independent endpoint-specific PAICs can estimate target marginal means but do not identify within-patient outcome dependence and can misstate joint decision uncertainty wherever covariance is discarded. Within-patient correlation is not recoverable from separately reported marginal summaries, which is all aggregate publications provide, although between-study dependence may be estimable when the same studies report paired endpoints. Population adjustment compounds the problem because each outcome may have a different effect-modifier set, so separate analyses can be standardized to subtly different target populations without that being visible in the output. In cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, one outcome family is fitted per cmlnmr() call and its Gaussian copula models the target covariate distribution rather than cross-outcome dependence.

title: No multivariate population-adjusted model for correlated outcomes
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Achana et al., Network meta-analysis of multiple outcome measures accounting for borrowing of information across outcomes (PMC4142066)
network meta-analysis across multiple outcome measures that borrows information between outcomes, part of the established multivariate synthesis literature the entry treated as merely promising


Efthimiou et al. 2015, Joint synthesis of multiple correlated outcomes in networks of interventions, Biostatistics (PMC4481542)
establishes multivariate network meta-analysis for jointly synthesizing multiple correlated outcomes across networks of treatments, including estimation of between-outcome correlation


Riley et al., Multivariate and network meta-analysis of multiple outcomes and multiple treatments, BMJ (PMC5596393)
practical account of multivariate and network meta-analysis across multiple outcomes and treatments, showing the approach is standard rather than emerging

title: No multivariate population-adjusted model for correlated outcomes
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the population-adjusted counterpart of multivariate synthesis, namely target-standardized multivariate ML-NMR, rather than multivariate network meta-analysis itself, and state where the dependence inputs come from, since marginal aggregate data do not identify them. Where a full joint model is unavailable, preserve covariance by carrying joint posterior draws or a joint bootstrap through to the decision quantity instead of recombining independent marginal summaries. Make the effect-modifier set for each endpoint explicit so that separate analyses cannot silently standardize to different populations.

title: No multivariate population-adjusted model for correlated outcomes
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Multivariate network meta-analysis of correlated efficacy and safety outcomes is established methodology with a scoping review of its applied use; what has not been developed is its population-adjusted counterpart, so PAICs in practice are still run one endpoint at a time and can standardise different endpoints to subtly different populations when the effect-modifier sets differ.
The source titled this. “Efficacy and harms synthesized separately, ignoring correlation” The title says separate synthesis ignores correlation, but the audit found separate marginal models can retain covariance and that multivariate network meta-analysis is established.
The source said. “Reimbursement decisions depend on correlated efficacy, safety, quality of life, and cost outcomes, but population-adjusted comparisons are estimated one endpoint at a time in separate network meta-analyses, discarding the correlation structure and permitting internally incoherent decisions.”
What was wrong with it. The source rated multivariate network meta-analysis as promising and treated separate analyses as necessarily discarding correlation and producing incoherent decisions; the literature auditor documented a mature multivariate NMA literature (PMC4142066, PMC4481542, PMC5596393, doi:10.1002/sim.8668) plus a scoping review of its applied use, and the code auditor showed that separate marginal models can retain covariance and that expected net monetary benefit is linear in the marginal means. The same auditor narrowed the copula proposal, since copula association parameters are not identified from marginal aggregate data and require individual patient data, covariance summaries, assumptions or sensitivity analysis.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

closure-upheld

11 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors’ reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. None of the findings contradicts the mature multivariate-NMA literature on which closure relied. Several findings document non-adoption, unavailable within-study correlations, or practical limitations of aggregate-data multivariate models, all of which the closure already concedes. The new 2025 paper is aggregate-data multivariate synthesis without covariates or transport, so it reinforces rather than fills the multivariate population-adjustment gap. No finding supplies multivariate ML-NMR, a transport-composed outcome-dependence model, or evidence that the cited methods were mischaracterized. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening

12 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries overstated Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit’s closure needs the closure’s own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The claim that multivariate NMA is ‘promising’ for jointly modelling correlated decision outcomes understates a mature literature. I retrieved Achana et al., ‘Network meta-analysis of multiple outcome measures accounting for borrowing of information across outcomes’ (PMC4142066), Efthimiou et al., ‘Joint synthesis of multiple correlated outcomes in networks of interventions’ (Biostatistics, PMC4481542), Riley et al., ‘Multivariate and network meta-analysis of multiple outcomes and multiple treatments’ (BMJ, PMC5596393), Waddingham et al. (Stat Med 2020, doi 10.1002/sim.8668) applying Bayesian multivariate NMA to relapsing-remitting MS, and a 2023 J Clin Epidemiol scoping review of the conduct and reporting of multivariate NMAs, which by its existence establishes that these are routinely conducted. Multivariate NMA handling continuous, binary, time-to-event or mixed outcomes with or without within-study correlations is established methodology. What is genuinely open is the population-adjusted version: I found no multivariate ML-NMR and no copula outcome model composed with transport, and the point that different endpoints may have different effect modifiers so separate analyses standardise to subtly different populations appears to be original to this entry. Cites https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4481542/: Establishes multivariate NMA for jointly synthesising multiple correlated outcomes across networks of treatments, including estimation of between-outcome correlation.. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.8668: Applied Bayesian multivariate NMA exploiting cross-outcome relationships, showing the approach is in routine methodological use rather than merely promising..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. The generic joint-synthesis problem is partially solved by multivariate NMA; the population-adjusted multivariate extension remains open. C2 is true only when endpoint-specific fits are treated as independent. Separate marginal models can retain covariance through a joint bootstrap, paired study-level estimates, or shared posterior draws. C3 is therefore not automatic: a decision based on expected net monetary benefit can be coherent from marginal means because E(lambda Q minus C) equals lambda E(Q) minus E(C). Correlation affects its variance, probability of cost-effectiveness, nonlinear utilities, and patient-level joint quantities. C4 is correct for within-patient dependence from marginal summaries alone, but too broad for between-study dependence, which may be estimated when the same studies report paired endpoints. Copulas are a possible dependence model, but their association parameters are not identified from marginal AgD and require IPD, covariance summaries, assumptions, or sensitivity analysis. In cpaic@9d150e9, one outcome family is fitted per cmlnmr() call, and its Gaussian copula models the target covariate distribution, not cross-outcome dependence. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.8668: Demonstrates an implemented Bayesian multivariate NMA that jointly exploits relationships between outcomes, resolving the generic claim that efficacy and harms must be synthesized independently. It does not supply population adjustment or multivariate ML-NMR..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Transition-specific component effects in multistate PAIC
text: OUT-17 Confirmed open High priority Speculative Tractability 2/5

title: Transition-specific component effects in multistate PAIC
text:
Statement
A multistate component PAIC would treat ordinal categories as states and place additive component effects on the intensities of transitions between them, giving every transition its own component design and effect-modifier requirements. In sparse networks many transition-by-component-by-modifier coefficients will be weakly identified or nonidentified: a single occupancy vector at one time does not identify a transition generator, and different generators can produce the same vector. Hierarchical shrinkage cannot create likelihood identification; it regularizes by adding exchangeability assumptions, so it is useful rather than mathematically essential where the transition-specific designs already identify the parameters. No multistate extension of ML-NMR, transition-specific component model or bridge between ordinal synthesis and multistate models exists in the population-adjusted setting.

title: Transition-specific component effects in multistate PAIC
text:
Why it is open
Networks contain few studies and even fewer reporting transition-level data, so most transition-specific component and interaction parameters have no direct evidence and are determined by the prior. Trials report the ordinal distribution or state occupancy at fixed timepoints rather than transition counts, so transition intensities are not identified from published data. Component additivity would have to hold separately for each transition under the proposed parameterization, which is a stronger assumption than single-endpoint additivity. The nearest existing machinery stops short: multinma’s likelihood list has no multistate family and its class-effect machinery is single-endpoint, and netmeta’s component network meta-analysis is additive on a single contrast scale with no time dimension.

title: Transition-specific component effects in multistate PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




multinma (CRAN), class effects since 0.8.0
the literature auditor verified that its likelihood list contains no multistate family and that its component and class-effect machinery, including class effects added in 0.8.0, is single-endpoint, so it is the nearest existing machinery rather than a solution


netmeta (CRAN), component network meta-analysis
implements component network meta-analysis additive on a single contrast scale with no time dimension and no transition structure, confirming that the component half of the proposal also stops at a single endpoint

title: Transition-specific component effects in multistate PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Develop multistate extensions of population-adjusted synthesis in which ordinal categories are states and treatment effects are transition-specific, and be explicit that shrinkage and clinically structured constraints buy regularization under exchangeability rather than identification. Establish which transition-specific parameters the available transition-level evidence identifies before adding priors, and report the remainder as prior-determined. Treat this as a low-tractability research program rather than a requirement for every ordinal analysis.

title: Transition-specific component effects in multistate PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “A multistate component PAIC would let each treatment component act on each disease transition through a transition-specific main effect and a component-by-covariate interaction matrix, and would reinterpret ordinal categories as disease states; both create many parameters and severe identifiability challenges.”
What was wrong with it. The source said hierarchical shrinkage and clinically structured component effects will be essential; the code auditor corrected this to regularization under added exchangeability assumptions rather than a cure for non-identification, and noted that although the parameter count is proportional to transitions times components times one plus the number of modifiers, the evidence can still grow through observed transition events, so it is not literally fixed. The same auditor flagged that the source conflated categories with transitions, since ordinal categories are states while transitions are changes between states, and that transition-wise component additivity is a property of the proposed parameterization rather than of every multistate component model; the literature auditor separately noted that three of the entry’s eight claims are internal agenda bookkeeping rather than literature claims.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1, C7, and C8 are correct in the stated sparse-data setting. Each transition has its own component design and modifier-information requirements; a single occupancy vector at one time does not identify a transition generator, and different generators can yield the same vector. The parameter count is proportional to transitions times components times one plus the number of modifiers, but evidence can grow through observed transition events, so it is not literally fixed. Hierarchical shrinkage cannot create likelihood identification; it regularizes by adding exchangeability assumptions and is useful, not mathematically essential, when transition-specific designs already identify the parameters. C4 holds only for the proposed transition-wise additive parameterization, not for every multistate component model. The agenda scores in C3 are accurate, and it proposes multistate component PAIC, although the matrix does not explicitly say ML-NMR. C6 is mathematically wrong: ordinal categories are states, while transitions are changes between states. cpaic@9d150e9 has no multistate family. This remains an open, low-tractability program rather than an automatically critical requirement for every analysis.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I found no multistate extension of ML-NMR, no transition-specific component model, and no bridge between ordinal synthesis and multistate models in a population-adjusted setting; multinma’s likelihood list contains no multistate family and its component/class machinery (class effects added in 0.8.0) is single-endpoint. So the problem is unaddressed. Two caveats on the support axis. First, three of the eight claims are internal bookkeeping rather than literature claims: the impact/novelty/tractability ratings and ‘the report states these will be essential’ are self-referential to the agenda and cannot be audited against any source. Second, the identifiability claims are analytic rather than empirical (parameter count grows with transitions times components times covariates; a single-timepoint cross-sectional category distribution does not identify transition intensities), and these are correct as stated but are arguments, not findings. Per the audit calibration, a formalisation of severe identifiability problems strengthens rather than weakens the case that this is open, so the status vote is secure even though the sourcing is thin.

text: OUT-15 Confirmed open High priority Emerging

title: Treatment switching and subsequent therapies in survival PAIC
text:
Statement
Treatment switching and subsequent therapy are intercurrent events that change the estimand, and they differ across trials in a network, so an intention-to-treat survival comparison from a trial with high crossover answers a different question from one without. Switching adjustments such as RPSFTM, inverse probability of censoring weighting and two-stage estimation need switching times, treatment exposure histories and sometimes time-varying prognostic data, which in a population-adjusted comparison typically exist only on the individual-patient side; this follows from the usual design rather than being a theorem, since such histories or an already-adjusted published estimate may occasionally be available. Combining a switching-adjusted source estimate with an unadjusted comparator estimate creates an estimand mismatch where the two correspond to different intercurrent-event strategies, for example a hypothetical no-switch effect against a treatment-policy effect, and not merely because one is labeled adjusted and the other is not. Neither auditor found any switching-adjustment method embedded in an indirect comparison, MAIC, STC or network meta-analysis.

title: Treatment switching and subsequent therapies in survival PAIC
text:
Why it is open
Adjustment for switching is asymmetric by construction in the usual PAIC design, so the source side can be corrected while the comparator side cannot, and the resulting mismatch is invisible in the reported effect because both sides are presented as the same outcome. Subsequent therapy availability reflects the era and jurisdiction of the trial rather than patient characteristics, so covariate adjustment cannot balance it. At commit 9d150e9, cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, accepts event, censoring, interval and delayed-entry data but has no switching-history, subsequent-therapy or intercurrent-event strategy interface. How much this matters depends on whether switching patterns or strategies differ materially between the trials being combined.

title: Treatment switching and subsequent therapies in survival PAIC
text:
What has been tried
No prior work is identified for this problem in the reviewed sources.

title: Treatment switching and subsequent therapies in survival PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Make the intercurrent-event strategy an explicit part of the estimand and state which strategy each contributing trial’s reported effect corresponds to, so a strategy mismatch is visible instead of buried in a single reported hazard ratio. Develop transport methods that do not require symmetric individual-level switching data on both sides, and quantify the residual mismatch where only one side can be adjusted. Where the comparator publication reports an adjusted estimate or usable switching information, use it rather than assuming the asymmetry.

title: Treatment switching and subsequent therapies in survival PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Patients in survival trials switch treatments or receive different subsequent therapies, and these post-randomization events differ across trials in a network, contaminating the transported survival comparison.”
What was wrong with it. The source treated the estimand mismatch as automatic and the data asymmetry as definitional; the code auditor narrowed both, since the mismatch requires the two estimates to use different intercurrent-event strategies and comparator-side histories or an adjusted published estimate are sometimes available. The literature auditor noted that the claim that switching is an open problem for PAIC rests on a failed search rather than on any source asserting the absence, so it is recorded as unverified rather than established.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I searched for switching-adjustment methods embedded in indirect comparisons, MAIC, STC or network meta-analysis and retrieved nothing; the population-adjustment literature I did retrieve (NICE DSU TSD 18 material, ML-NMR, two-stage MAIC) does not address intercurrent events at all. The second claim is the strongest and is essentially definitional: RPSFTM, IPCW and two-stage estimation all require individual-level treatment histories and post-baseline covariates, which by construction exist only on the IPD side of a PAIC, so the asymmetry follows from the design rather than needing a citation. The third claim, that mixing a switching-adjusted source estimate with an unadjusted comparator creates an estimand mismatch, follows from the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework. The caveat is that I could not anchor claim one to any source that itself asserts the absence, so on the support axis ‘switching is an open problem for PAIC’ is unverifiable in the strict sense used elsewhere in this audit.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 is a genuine PAIC estimand-harmonization problem under asymmetric IPD and AgD. RPSFTM, IPCW, and two-stage switching adjustments generally need switching times, treatment exposure histories, and sometimes time-varying prognostic data, supporting C2. Unavailability on the comparator side is typical, however, not a theorem: histories or an appropriately adjusted published estimate may exist. C3 holds when the estimates use different intercurrent-event strategies, such as a hypothetical no-switch effect versus a treatment-policy effect. It does not follow merely from the labels adjusted and unadjusted if the comparator has no switching or both estimates target the same strategy. At cpaic@9d150e9, the survival path accepts event, censoring, interval, and delayed-entry data but has no switching-history, subsequent-therapy, or intercurrent-event strategy interface. This is decision-critical when switching patterns or strategies differ materially; otherwise it is a roadmap issue.

title: Reconstruction uncertainty from digitized Kaplan-Meier curves
text:
Statement
Survival indirect comparisons routinely digitize published Kaplan-Meier curves into pseudo individual patient data and carry the reconstruction downstream as if it were observed, and population-adjusted intervals do not propagate the reconstruction error. Part of the proposed remedy has been built: RESOLVE-IPD (arxiv:2511.01785) generates ensembles of mathematically valid labelings so that reconstruction uncertainty propagates into the downstream meta-analysis, and Rogula et al. (doi:10.1177/23814683221077643) reconstruct from marked censoring times and report curve-fit uncertainty the standard algorithm does not provide. Multiple reconstruction is therefore no longer merely promising, though it is a valid analogue of multiple imputation only where the repeated reconstructions are proper draws from a calibrated distribution conditional on the image, the risk table and the reported totals, rather than repeated runs of a deterministic algorithm or arbitrary tuning variants. Defining a Bayesian likelihood directly on the reported Kaplan-Meier ordinates and numbers-at-risk table remains unbuilt.

title: Reconstruction uncertainty from digitized Kaplan-Meier curves
text:
Why it is open
Reconstruction is deterministic given the image, so every standard method runs without complaint and repeating it reveals nothing; the error is silent while the reported interval ignores the extra variability. The published Kaplan-Meier ordinates are dependent derived statistics, so a likelihood defined on them needs an explicit digitization, rounding, censoring and risk-table observation model, which nobody has written. Population-adjusted implementations take reconstructed event and censoring rows straight into the likelihood as data: at commit 9d150e9, cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, has no observation model for digitization, risk-table interpolation, event allocation or alternative compatible reconstructions. How much this matters depends on image quality and on downstream sensitivity, so it is context-dependent rather than uniformly decisive.

title: Reconstruction uncertainty from digitized Kaplan-Meier curves
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Lang, Zhao, Gao and Xu 2025, RESOLVE-IPD: High-Fidelity Individual Patient Data Reconstruction and Uncertainty-Aware Subgroup Meta-Analysis (arxiv:2511.01785)
its MAPLE component generates ensembles of mathematically valid labelings, facilitating a propagating meta-analysis that quantifies and reflects uncertainty from subgroup reconstruction, with VEC-KM extracting coordinates and explicit censoring marks from vectorized figures; it is the multiple-imputation analogue the entry proposed


Rogula, Lozano-Ortega and Johnston 2022, A Method for Reconstructing Individual Patient Data From Kaplan-Meier Survival Curves That Incorporate Marked Censoring Times, MDM Policy and Practice
reconstruction method using marked censoring times that yields estimates of uncertainty in the curve fit, which the standard Guyot-style algorithm does not provide

title: Reconstruction uncertainty from digitized Kaplan-Meier curves
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Connect the existing ensemble reconstruction machinery to population-adjusted analysis rather than reinventing it, and state the calibration condition explicitly so the ensemble is a set of draws conditional on the image, risk table and reported totals rather than a set of arbitrary tuning variants. Build the Bayesian likelihood on the reported curve and numbers-at-risk table, which requires an explicit observation model for digitization, rounding, censoring and risk-table reporting. Report how far RMST and extrapolated survival move across reconstructions rather than assuming a uniform inflation, since curve error can partly cancel under integration and can be amplified or damped by the tail model.

title: Reconstruction uncertainty from digitized Kaplan-Meier curves
text:
Our study






NoteA study is running



Question. When individual data are reconstructed repeatedly from a published Kaplan-Meier curve, does the spread of the ensemble match the true reconstruction error, so that pooling it like multiple imputation is valid?
Design. Simulated trial data rendered as a pixel-rounded Kaplan-Meier figure with or without a risk table, reconstructed by Guyot’s algorithm; analyst-variant and observation-model ensembles scored by the ratio of their spread to the true reconstruction error for RMST, milestone and extrapolated survival. 13 cells, 300 replicates each.
The protocol is registered before any result is seen: read it.

title: Reconstruction uncertainty from digitized Kaplan-Meier curves
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Survival indirect comparisons routinely digitize published Kaplan-Meier curves to build pseudo individual patient data, then carry that reconstruction into every downstream analysis as if it were observed data, with no propagation of reconstruction uncertainty.”
What was wrong with it. The source listed multiple reconstruction as an unbuilt promising direction; the literature auditor found it implemented in RESOLVE-IPD (arxiv:2511.01785) and partially in Rogula et al. (doi:10.1177/23814683221077643). The code auditor added two qualifications: repeatedly applying a deterministic reconstruction or varying arbitrary tuning choices is not a valid multiple-imputation analogue, and reconstruction error does not monotonically compound, since RMST integrates curve error that can partly cancel while extrapolation can amplify or damp it depending on the tail model.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Routine practice does treat digitised pseudo-IPD as observed data, and I found no standard tool that propagates reconstruction error, so the description of practice holds. But the proposed direction has begun to be built. Rogula, Lozano-Ortega and Johnston (MDM Policy & Practice 2022, doi 10.1177/23814683221077643) reconstruct IPD using marked censoring times and report that the method yields estimates of the uncertainty in curve fits that traditional methods do not provide. More directly, RESOLVE-IPD (arXiv 2511.01785, Lang, Zhao, Gao and Xu) implements the multiple-reconstruction idea: its MAPLE component ‘generates ensembles of mathematically valid labelings, facilitating a propagating meta-analysis that quantifies and reflects uncertainty from subgroup reconstruction’, with VEC-KM extracting coordinates and explicit censoring marks from vectorised figures to minimise digitisation error. That is the multiple-imputation analogue named in the proposed direction, so it is no longer merely ‘promising’. The Bayesian-likelihood-on-reported-summaries route remains undeveloped; I found nothing implementing it. Cites arxiv:2511.01785: Implements ensemble (multiple-reconstruction) uncertainty propagation from KM digitisation into downstream meta-analysis, the analogue of multiple imputation the entry proposes.. Cites doi:10.1177/23814683221077643: Reconstruction method that yields estimates of uncertainty in the curve fit, unavailable from the standard Guyot-style algorithm..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. At the requested cpaic revision, aggregate survival input consists of reconstructed event and censoring rows that enter the likelihood as data. There is no observation model for digitization, risk-table interpolation, event allocation, or alternative compatible reconstructions, so ordinary cpaic posterior intervals do not propagate reconstruction uncertainty. C3 is directionally correct, although reconstruction errors need not monotonically compound: RMST integrates curve error, which can partly cancel, while extrapolation can amplify or damp it depending on the tail model. C4 is technically promising only if repeated reconstructions are proper draws from a calibrated distribution conditional on the image, risk table, and reported totals; repeatedly applying a deterministic reconstruction or varying arbitrary tuning choices is not analogous to valid multiple imputation. C5 is possible in principle, but the reported Kaplan-Meier ordinates are dependent derived statistics and require an explicit digitization, rounding, censoring, and risk-table observation model. The field-wide words ‘routinely’ and ‘standard’ are empirical claims outside this audit’s source-code scope. The priority is context-dependent because reconstruction uncertainty may be negligible or decision-changing depending on image quality and downstream sensitivity.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Non-proportional hazards and the transported hazard ratio
text: OUT-11 Overstated Very high priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: Non-proportional hazards and the transported hazard ratio
text:
Statement
The transported hazard ratio remains the default reported quantity in survival indirect comparisons, and on the marginal scale it can be population-dependent and time-varying through risk-set selection, while under non-proportional hazards a fitted Cox coefficient is a censoring- and event-weighted constant summary of a time-varying contrast. A conditional hazard ratio under a proportional-hazards model is constant by definition, so the instability belongs to the marginal scale or to non-proportionality rather than to the coefficient as such. The recommended alternatives are not missing from software: multinma has shipped survival models since 0.6.0 with predict() types including survival, hazard, cumulative hazard, mean, median, quantile and restricted mean survival time, marginal_effects() returns RMST and survival-probability differences standardized to a target population, and auxiliary parameters can be stratified by treatment to relax proportional hazards. The gap is between available methods and prevailing practice, and in the absence of any simulation benchmark comparing these estimators against proportional-hazards MAIC and STC under crossing hazards and differential censoring.

title: Non-proportional hazards and the transported hazard ratio
text:
Why it is open
Practice still reports a coefficient, so the mismatch between the estimand a reimbursement decision needs and the estimand produced persists even though the tooling exists in one package. Separating a baseline-hazard difference from an effect-modifier difference requires assumptions that published Kaplan-Meier curves cannot adjudicate, and the standard proportional-hazards test is often underpowered. No simulation study compares general-likelihood ML-NMR against proportional-hazards MAIC and STC on Weibull, Gompertz and multistate mechanisms with crossing hazards and differential censoring, so the relative operating characteristics of the recommended replacements are unknown. Component PAIC implementations such as cpaic still hold treatment effects proportional and lack target-marginal survival contrasts.

title: Non-proportional hazards and the transported hazard ratio
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo, Dias, Ades and Welton 2025, Multilevel network meta-regression for general likelihoods: synthesis of individual and aggregate data with applications to survival analysis, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
extends ML-NMR to individual-level likelihoods of any form, removing the closed-form aggregate-likelihood restriction that had prevented application to time-to-event outcomes, and delivers population-average marginal survival functions and restricted means in a target population by integrating the marginal survival function to a horizon


multinma (CRAN), survival models since 0.6.0 and marginal_effects() since 0.7.0
implements flexible survival likelihoods with auxiliary parameters that may be stratified by treatment to relax proportional hazards, predict() types covering survival probabilities, hazards, cumulative hazards, mean, median, quantile and restricted mean survival time, and marginal RMST and survival-probability differences standardized to a target population


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
provides survival likelihoods, flexible study baselines, delayed entry and interval censoring, but keeps treatment effects proportional, returns only a conditional hazard ratio at one covariate profile from relative_effects(), and averages survival over each observed arm rather than a common target distribution

title: Non-proportional hazards and the transported hazard ratio
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Run the benchmark rather than rebuild the estimators: compare general-likelihood ML-NMR and one-step exact-likelihood survival network meta-analysis against proportional-hazards MAIC and STC on Weibull, Gompertz and multistate data-generating mechanisms with crossing hazards and differential censoring, reporting RMST bias, hazard-ratio instability and calibration over time. Report target-standardized survival curves, milestone contrasts and RMST differences at prespecified horizons the data support, with the horizon declared as part of the estimand, without asserting that RMST is universally required. Add target-marginal survival contrasts and time-varying treatment effects to the component PAIC implementations that lack them.

title: Non-proportional hazards and the transported hazard ratio
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. The transported hazard ratio remains the default reported quantity in survival indirect comparisons even though it is non-collapsible, population-dependent and time-varying; RMST differences and target-standardised survival curves are already implemented in multinma and demonstrated in the general-likelihood ML-NMR paper, so the gap is between available methods and prevailing practice, and in the absence of any simulation benchmark comparing these estimators under crossing hazards and differential censoring.
The source said. “Proportional hazards frequently fails, especially in oncology and immunology, yet the hazard ratio remains the standard transported quantity in survival indirect comparison; it is simultaneously non-collapsible, population-dependent, and time-varying, and a single value can conceal crossing hazards entirely. The report states that the primary output should instead be the restricted mean survival time difference between target-standardized survival curves.”
What was wrong with it. The claim that target-standardized survival curves and milestone probabilities are outputs current PAIC software does not routinely produce is false; both auditors found them implemented in multinma, which is the software for the general-likelihood ML-NMR paper the entry already cited (doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169), and the File A material in this entry was unattributed in the source and is now anchored to that paper and to the multinma release notes. The code auditor also rejected the normative framing that RMST must be the primary estimand and that one-step exact-likelihood synthesis is automatically superior, and found that at commit 9d150e9 cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, still returns only a conditional hazard ratio at one covariate profile and averages survival over each observed arm rather than over a common target distribution.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

closure-upheld

10 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors’ reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. The new findings document widespread proportional-hazards failure, continued hazard-ratio reporting, and incomplete uptake of alternatives. Those are precisely the closure’s residual: available target-standardized survival and RMST methods have not displaced prevailing practice, and comparative benchmarking remains absent. The 2024 case study’s call for time-varying hazard ratios does not show that the cited ML-NMR methods cannot produce non-PH survival estimands; it shows that one applied implementation retained a PH model. None of the findings contradicts multinma’s documented prediction and marginalization capabilities or supplies the missing benchmark. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening

24 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries overstated Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit’s closure needs the closure’s own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The single prior_work citation is faithful: Phillippo, Dias, Ades and Welton, ‘Multilevel network meta-regression for general likelihoods’ (JRSSA, doi 10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169) does extend ML-NMR to survival, stating ‘implementation of this method so far has required the aggregate-level likelihood to have a known closed form, which has prevented application to time-to-event outcomes’ and ‘We extend ML-NMR to individual-level likelihoods of any form’. But the claim that target-standardised survival curves and milestone survival probabilities are ‘open outputs not routinely produced by current PAIC software’ is contradicted by the software that implements that very paper. multinma has shipped survival models since 0.6.0 (2024-01-24) with predict() types survival, hazard, cumhaz, mean, median, quantile and rmst, and marginal_effects() returns RMST differences and survival-probability differences standardised to a target population. Non-proportional hazards are also modellable: the NDMM vignette stratifies spline coefficients by treatment as well as study (aux_by = c(.study, .trt)). What is genuinely open is the benchmarking programme described in the proposed direction; I found no simulation study comparing general-likelihood ML-NMR against PH MAIC/STC on crossing-hazard mechanisms. Cites doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169: Delivers population-average marginal survival functions and restricted means in a target population from an ML-NMR fit.. Cites repo:dmphillippo/multinma NEWS 0.6.0 and 0.7.0: Ships RMST, survival-probability and quantile predictions plus marginal RMST/survival-probability differences standardised to a target population..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. The central warning is correct, but the scales must be named. A conditional hazard ratio under a proportional-hazards model is constant by definition. Under covariate heterogeneity, the corresponding marginal hazard ratio can be population-dependent and time-varying through risk-set selection; under non-proportional hazards, a fitted Cox coefficient is a censoring- and event-weighted constant summary of a time-varying contrast. C5-C6 and the RMST identity in C11 are sound. C10 and C13 are normative overstatements: RMST at a prespecified supported horizon is often preferable under non-proportionality, but it is not universally the required primary estimand, and exact-likelihood one-step synthesis is not automatically superior for every data configuration. C12 is false broadly because multinma produces survival, RMST, and marginal survival effects and can model treatment-specific auxiliary parameters. At the requested cpaic revision, survival likelihoods, flexible study baselines, delayed entry, and interval censoring exist, but treatment effects remain proportional; relative_effects() returns only a conditional hazard ratio at one covariate profile, and plot_survival() averages over each observed arm rather than a common target distribution. Cites doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169: Extends ML-NMR to general individual-level likelihoods, including survival.. Cites CRAN:multinma@0.6.0: Implements flexible survival likelihoods, treatment-stratified auxiliary parameters, survival predictions, and RMST predictions.. Cites CRAN:multinma@0.7.0: Implements marginal RMST differences and time-varying marginal hazard ratios..

title: Endogenous exposure time and target-standardized rate contrasts
text:
Statement
Rate outcomes divide counts by exposure time, and where exposure is affected by treatment, prognosis, death or discontinuation the resulting contrast needs an explicit causal estimand. The source’s framing that exposure cannot serve as an offset is not the issue: an offset is a modeling device that may contain a stochastic observed quantity, and the problem is the causal interpretation of the rate rather than the mechanics. Part of the reporting gap is already closed: cmaic() in cpaic reweights individual patient data to target covariate moments and fits a weighted Poisson model with a log-exposure offset, returning a marginal target-population rate ratio, and multinma fits Poisson models with a log time-at-risk offset. What remains open is joint exposure-count modeling, a common target exposure and follow-up strategy applied to both arms, marginal rate differences, and exposure-weighted aggregate covariate moments, since the aggregate Poisson path computes exposure times a covariate-averaged rate and explicitly assumes exposure is independent of covariates.

title: Endogenous exposure time and target-standardized rate contrasts
text:
Why it is open
If a treatment causes earlier discontinuation or death, patients on that arm accrue less exposure, so a rate computed from observed exposure can make a harmful treatment look favorable, and baseline covariate adjustment cannot repair a distortion that arises after randomization. Aggregate-data publications typically report total person-time without the joint distribution of exposure and events, so the dependence cannot be modeled from the reported summaries, although some publications do contain richer data. A rate difference is not directly available from a log-link coefficient and requires standardization over the target joint covariate distribution rather than the marginal moments aggregate data supply, and under overdispersed or zero-inflated likelihoods that marginalization is no longer analytic and carries its own integration uncertainty. The literature auditor found no literature at all on endogenous exposure time in indirect comparisons, so every claim here is a mechanism or an absence rather than a documented finding.

title: Endogenous exposure time and target-standardized rate contrasts
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Rate outcomes divide counts by exposure time, but exposure itself depends on prognosis and on treatment, so using it as a fixed offset conditions on a post-randomization variable. Rate results are then reported as conditional model coefficients rather than as marginal rate differences and rate ratios standardized to an explicit target population.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no standard implementation produces target-standardized marginal rate contrasts; the code auditor found that cmaic() already returns a marginal target-population rate ratio at commit 9d150e9 of cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, and the literature auditor independently asked for the claim to be softened to the packages actually checked. The same code auditor qualified the standardization claims: a full target distribution is needed for nonlinear or effect-modified marginal means, exposure can cancel from a constant multiplicative rate ratio under restrictive assumptions, and the target must specify a follow-up and intercurrent-event strategy rather than reproduce an empirical exposure distribution.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): The causal concern is real when observed exposure is affected by treatment, prognosis, death, or discontinuation. Nevertheless, an offset is a modeling device and may contain a stochastic observed quantity; the problem is its causal interpretation, not whether it can literally be an offset. C3 is too absolute because some publications contain richer data, while others report only totals. C5-C6 require qualification: a full target distribution is needed for nonlinear or effect-modified marginal means, but exposure can cancel from a constant multiplicative rate ratio under restrictive assumptions. The target must specify a follow-up and intercurrent-event strategy, not necessarily reproduce an empirical exposure distribution. At the requested cpaic revision, aggregate Poisson ML-NMR computes E times the covariate-averaged rate and explicitly assumes exposure is independent of covariates, so C7 identifies a genuine limitation. However, cmaic() already reweights IPD to target covariate moments and fits a weighted Poisson model with a log-exposure offset, returning a marginal target-population rate ratio. What remains open is joint exposure-count modeling, a common target exposure strategy, and marginal rate differences.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I found no literature at all on endogenous exposure time in indirect comparisons: no joint exposure-count model, no target-standardised marginal rate difference or rate ratio, and no treatment of exposure-weighted target moments. The mechanistic argument (offsetting by observed person-time conditions on a post-randomisation quantity) is sound and is a standard causal-inference point, and it is consistent with what implementations do: multinma’s poisson likelihood takes time at risk as an offset, which is exactly the fixed-offset practice described. The caveat is that every one of the seven claims is an absence claim or a mechanistic assertion, and none is anchored to a source that itself states the absence, so on the support axis this is closer to unverifiable than to verified. I would soften ‘no standard implementation produces such target-standardised marginal rate contrasts’ to a statement about the packages actually checked, since multinma’s marginal_effects() can in principle produce marginal contrasts for the Poisson likelihood and I did not test whether a rate difference is among them.

text: OUT-07 Partially addressed Very high priority Promising

title: Informative censoring and outcome-dependent missingness
text:
Statement
Continuous outcomes go missing and time-to-event outcomes are censored for reasons related to the outcome itself, and the source and comparator trials can have different mechanisms, so the biases do not cancel in an indirect comparison. Dependence between the dropout process and the outcome after dropout is not identified from observed event and censoring data alone without auxiliary information or restrictions, though observable censoring patterns and some model implications can still be examined, so the untestability is specific rather than total. Baseline covariate adjustment cannot correct selection driven by unobserved post-baseline outcomes, but correction is not ruled out in principle: baseline covariates may suffice under conditional independent censoring, and time-varying inverse probability of censoring weighting, congenial imputation or joint models can identify effects under further assumptions. Externally controlled comparisons are where the asymmetry bites hardest, and censoring there is documented to be often informative because it reflects discontinuation for toxicity, patient preference or early switch to alternative therapies.

title: Informative censoring and outcome-dependent missingness
text:
Why it is open
Ignorable missingness and non-informative censoring fail exactly where dropout is caused by toxicity or worsening disease, and the mechanisms can differ between the two trials, so the errors do not offset. Aggregate-data publications report at-risk tables rather than censoring reasons and give neither the missingness pattern nor the reasons in usable detail, so a missing-not-at-random sensitivity analysis has no anchor on the comparator side. Generic and calibrated inverse probability of censoring weighting adjust within a study rather than across the transport step, and the literature auditor found no method that makes such a sensitivity analysis compatible with a transport model. At commit 9d150e9, cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, handles right, left and interval censoring and delayed entry but models the outcome conditional on the supplied rows and has no censoring-process, dropout or informative-censoring sensitivity model.

title: Informative censoring and outcome-dependent missingness
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Informative censoring in externally controlled clinical trials: a potential source of bias, ESMO Open 2024
asserts in the externally controlled comparison setting that censoring is often informative because it reflects discontinuation due to toxicity, preference or early switch to alternative therapies, and that this can bias progression-free survival comparisons; it does not supply a transport-compatible correction

title: Informative censoring and outcome-dependent missingness
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build multiple imputation and inverse probability of censoring weighting that are congenial with the transport model rather than only with the within-study analysis, together with joint models of the outcome and the dropout or censoring process. Make missing-not-at-random and informative-censoring sensitivity analysis explicit, reporting how much outcome dependence would be needed to change the decision rather than assuming the mechanism away. State which features of the censoring process are being assumed and which are examinable, since observed censoring patterns can be inspected even though post-dropout dependence cannot.

title: Informative censoring and outcome-dependent missingness
text:
Our study

Informative censoring on the two sides of an indirect comparison
The question put to it. When censoring depends on latent risk in the source and comparator trials to different degrees, does the bias cancel in the indirect RMST contrast, what does source-side IPCW achieve, and does a one-sided comparator sensitivity analysis cover the truth?
What it found. Informative censoring cancels in an indirect RMST contrast only when the two mechanisms match. Unanchored, with differing mechanisms the bias was -2.3 to +1.4 months against a true difference of 0.62, reversing the comparison in up to 97% of analyses; equal mechanisms nearly cancelled. Anchored comparisons were protected (bias within 0.22) because both arms of each trial shared its mechanism. Adjusting only the source by inverse probability of censoring weighting helped partly where only the source was informative and broke the cancellation where both were.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: unanchored bias -2.326 to 1.416 months when mechanisms differed; -0.080 to 0.021 when equal.
Anchored: bias -0.202 to 0.219 months in all 12 scenarios.
Source-side IPCW with a proxy correlated 0.7 with latent risk: 1.42 to 0.99 months where only the source was informative; -0.08 to -0.52 where both were equally informative.
The comparator delta reproducing the truth lay outside 0.5 to 2 in up to 70% of analyses (median 2.4 with strong dependence at 50% censoring).

Design.

Estimand

RMST difference at 24 months, unanchored (A minus B) or anchored ((A minus C) minus (B minus C))

Methods compared

Kaplan-Meier RMST, source-side inverse probability of censoring weighting, one-sided comparator delta sensitivity analysis

Data-generating mechanism

Shared-frailty event and censoring processes with separate dependence in the source and comparator; 24 cells crossing the two dependences, censoring prevalence and anchored or unanchored design; naive Kaplan-Meier, source-side IPCW and a comparator delta-adjusted sensitivity analysis. 1000 replicates per cell.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 24,000 in total


What this does not answer. No covariate shift between trials; time-constant censoring hazards; one sensitivity parameterization; one baseline proxy. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 3 findings from 3 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “Continuous outcomes go missing and time-to-event outcomes get censored for reasons related to the outcome itself, such as lack of efficacy or toxicity, yet population-adjusted analyses assume ignorable missingness and non-informative censoring.”
What was wrong with it. The claim that non-informative censoring is simply untestable was narrowed by the code auditor to dependence between censoring and the unobserved post-dropout outcome, and the claim that population adjustment cannot correct such selection was narrowed to baseline weighting alone, since time-varying inverse probability of censoring weighting, congenial imputation and joint models can identify effects under further assumptions. The literature auditor supplied a real source for the asymmetry in the indirect-comparison setting, an ESMO Open 2024 article on informative censoring in externally controlled trials, and voted the entry supported rather than caveated; the weaker caveated reading is used here and the disagreement stays in the audit record.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): The core claim is structurally untestable and therefore cannot be closed by any paper: non-informative censoring and ignorable missingness are assumptions about the joint outcome-dropout distribution, so per the audit calibration this stays open regardless of how much sensitivity-analysis literature exists. I found no method that makes MNAR or informative-censoring sensitivity analysis compatible with a transport model, so the proposed direction is genuinely unbuilt. Generic IPCW and calibrated-IPCW sensitivity analyses exist but adjust within a study, not across the transport step.

title: Unequal variances, skew, and bounded scales in continuous outcomes
text: OUT-05 Confirmed open Medium-high priority Promising

title: Unequal variances, skew, and bounded scales in continuous outcomes
text:
Statement
Individual-level normal likelihoods in population-adjusted synthesis use one residual standard deviation for all individual patient data, which can mis-weight studies with genuinely different dispersion and misstate uncertainty. The stronger claim in the source does not hold: under an identity-link normal model the target-standardized mean is the target expectation of the fitted conditional mean and does not contain the residual variance, so heteroscedasticity affects likelihood weighting, uncertainty, shrinkage, predictive distributions and responder probabilities rather than that marginal mean. The restriction is also specific to the individual-level likelihood, since aggregate contrast synthesis ordinarily carries study-specific standard errors already. Bounded instruments, skew and floor or ceiling masses need endpoint-appropriate likelihoods, and reported means and standard deviations generally do not identify those features in a comparator trial.

title: Unequal variances, skew, and bounded scales in continuous outcomes
text:
Why it is open
Where the estimand is a responder probability, a predictive quantity or a tail summary rather than a mean, the residual distribution does enter, so a single pooled variance and an assumed normal shape propagate into the reported number and not only into its interval. Bounded instruments pile observations at the extremes, and population adjustment shifts the covariate distribution relative to the floor or ceiling, which makes the bias from ignoring truncation itself population-dependent. Aggregate-data publications report means and standard deviations only, so skewness and boundary piling in the comparator trial cannot be identified, although known scale bounds and extreme moments can flag a problem without identifying the distribution. cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, documents its common-sigma limitation but implements no heteroscedastic, skew or bounded alternative, and the continuous likelihood offered by multinma is normal only.

title: Unequal variances, skew, and bounded scales in continuous outcomes
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9, R/plot-mlnmr.R and inst/stan/cpaic_normal.stan
uses one residual standard deviation for all individual patient data and documents that limitation; the code auditor cites its note that a Gaussian model under the identity link is exact at the covariate means, which is the basis for rejecting the claim that residual variance enters the target-standardized mean

the literature auditor verified from the nma() documentation that the supported continuous likelihood is normal only, with no robust, skew or truncated alternative

title: Unequal variances, skew, and bounded scales in continuous outcomes
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Fit study-specific residual variances with hierarchical shrinkage where the number of studies is small, and report how far uncertainty, shrinkage and any responder or predictive summary move when the common-variance assumption is relaxed, rather than claiming movement in the standardized mean itself. For bounded or skewed endpoints use likelihoods that model the support and the point masses, not only heavier or asymmetric tails, since a robust or skew density on the real line does not represent a floor or a ceiling. Where aggregate reporting cannot identify the distributional shape, treat it as a declared assumption with sensitivity analysis rather than something the available data can settle.

title: Unequal variances, skew, and bounded scales in continuous outcomes
text:
Our study

The transported mean is safe and the responder probability is not
The question put to it. When a bounded continuous outcome is transported by G-computation with a pooled normal residual, is the mean contrast safe while the responder-probability contrast is biased, and does a floor make the bias depend on the target population?
What it found. Yes. With a pooled normal residual the transported mean contrast was unbiased while the responder-probability contrast was biased by up to 0.10 when the arms’ dispersions differed, with opposite signs at a threshold near the median and one in the tail. Arm-specific SDs fixed it only for normal errors without a floor; Tobit fixed the floor but not skew; logistic regression of the responder indicator was unbiased everywhere. A floor biased the mean contrast by under 2% of the effect, somewhat more at the larger target shift.
Results.

Dissociation confirmed: pooled-SD mean contrast within 3 MCSE without a floor; responder bias up to 0.102 at SD ratio 2.
Normal model with arm-specific SDs: responder bias up to 0.058 with a floor and 0.070 with skew.
Tobit: at most 0.003 with normal errors, 0.040 with skew; logistic responder model: at most 0.006 in every scenario.
Floor of 25%: linear mean-contrast bias -0.012 to 0.010 at shift 0.3 and -0.070 to 0.038 at shift 1.

Design.

Estimand

Target mean difference and target responder-probability differences at two thresholds

Methods compared

normal model, pooled SD, normal model, arm-specific SD, Tobit, arm-specific scales, logistic regression of the responder indicator

Data-generating mechanism

Source trial with arm-specific residual SDs, skewed or normal errors and a floor at 0, 10% or 25% mass, transported to targets at two shifts; normal pooled-SD, arm-specific SD, Tobit and direct logistic responder models; mean and responder contrasts at two thresholds. 24 cells, 1000 replicates each.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 24,000 in total


What this does not answer. One source trial, no ceiling, no intervals, no ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument · Code and data: studies/OUT-05-the-mean-is-safe-and-the-responder-probability-is-not · Protocol: registered before the run

title: Unequal variances, skew, and bounded scales in continuous outcomes
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Continuous-outcome models in indirect comparison and ML-NMR assume a shared residual variance and a normal-linear response, but residual variance genuinely differs across trials and clinical endpoints are frequently skewed, truncated, or subject to floor and ceiling effects.”
What was wrong with it. The source claimed residual variance affects target-standardized summaries and not only standard errors; the code auditor showed this is false for a target-standardized mean under a linear identity-link model, where the standardized mean is the target expectation of the conditional mean function. The same auditor narrowed the pooled-variance complaint to the individual-level Gaussian likelihood and noted that robust or skew distributions do not by themselves model bounded support, censoring or point masses at floor and ceiling values; the literature auditor could not confirm from documentation whether multinma stratifies its normal auxiliary parameter by study, so that specific point is left unasserted here.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C2 is a reasonable extension, and C4 identifies real risks. The statement overgeneralizes C1: aggregate contrast synthesis ordinarily uses study-specific standard errors, while cpaic’s single residual sigma applies to its IPD Gaussian likelihood. C3 is false for a target-standardized mean under a linear identity-link model. If E(Y|A,X)=m(A,X), the standardized mean is the target expectation of m(A,X) and does not contain the residual variance. Residual variance can alter likelihood weighting, uncertainty, posterior shrinkage, predictive distributions, and responder probabilities, but not that marginal mean. Individual-level skewness also does not automatically bias a correctly specified conditional-mean estimator, although it can invalidate likelihood-based uncertainty and tail summaries. C5 is incomplete: robust or skew distributions do not by themselves model bounded support, censoring, or point masses at floor and ceiling values. C6 is broadly right as a non-identification claim, although known scale bounds and extreme moments may flag a problem without identifying the distribution. cpaic documents its common-sigma limitation but implements no heteroscedastic, skew, or bounded alternative. The bundled priority is context-dependent: responder or boundary-sensitive decisions can be serious, whereas the common-sigma issue for a mean estimand may primarily concern efficiency and uncertainty.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I could not retrieve any PAIC-specific treatment of unequal residual variances, skewness or bounded scales, so the problem appears unaddressed in this setting. The caveat is scope: in standard aggregate-data NMA of continuous outcomes each study contributes its own standard error, so study-specific variance is already inherent there; the shared-residual-variance restriction the entry describes is specific to the individual-level normal likelihood in IPD meta-regression and ML-NMR. I confirmed from the multinma nma() documentation that the supported continuous likelihood is ‘normal’ only, with no robust, skew or truncated alternatives, which supports the software half of the claim. I could not confirm from the documentation whether multinma stratifies the normal auxiliary parameter (sigma) by study, so I do not assert that the pooled-variance restriction is actually imposed by the leading implementation; that is the one factual point a reader could challenge. The claim that residual variance propagates into target-standardised summaries is correct for any latent-normal responder derivation but I retrieved no paper quantifying it.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C2 is a reasonable extension, and C4 identifies real risks. The statement overgeneralizes C1: aggregate contrast synthesis ordinarily uses study-specific standard errors, while cpaic’s single residual sigma applies to its IPD Gaussian likelihood. C3 is false for a target-standardized mean under a linear identity-link model. If E(Y|A,X)=m(A,X), the standardized mean is the target expectation of m(A,X) and does not contain the residual variance. Residual variance can alter likelihood weighting, uncertainty, posterior shrinkage, predictive distributions, and responder probabilities, but not that marginal mean. Individual-level skewness also does not automatically bias a correctly specified conditional-mean estimator, although it can invalidate likelihood-based uncertainty and tail summaries. C5 is incomplete: robust or skew distributions do not by themselves model bounded support, censoring, or point masses at floor and ceiling values. C6 is broadly right as a non-identification claim, although known scale bounds and extreme moments may flag a problem without identifying the distribution. cpaic documents its common-sigma limitation but implements no heteroscedastic, skew, or bounded alternative. The bundled priority is context-dependent: responder or boundary-sensitive decisions can be serious, whereas the common-sigma issue for a mean estimand may primarily concern efficiency and uncertainty.
