title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text: OUT-03 Partially addressed High priority Promising

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
Statement
Binary outcomes can be misclassified differently in the source and comparator trials, and differential sensitivity and specificity can move an indirect contrast in either direction rather than only toward the null: if the true arm risk is p, the observed risk is Sep + (1-Sp)(1-p). The claim that population-adjusted analyses assume perfect and equal classification holds only where the intended estimand concerns a latent true outcome, since an ordinary model consistently estimates the effect on the recorded endpoint without that assumption. What requires measurement comparability or an explicit error model is the step of treating two trials as measuring the same true endpoint. Neither auditor found any quantitative bias analysis of outcome misclassification applied inside a population-adjusted synthesis.

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
Why it is open
Population adjustment balances baseline covariates and leaves the outcome measurement process untouched, so differential misclassification passes through weighting or outcome regression into the transported effect. Sensitivity and specificity of endpoint ascertainment are almost never reported in trial publications, so without validation data, a gold standard or replicate measurements the bias parameters are not identified from the data at hand and have to be supplied from outside. Because the parameters are not estimable from what publications report, this is structurally a sensitivity-analysis problem, which means no single paper can close it. cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, has no outcome-misclassification model at the audited commit.

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
What has been tried
No prior work is identified for this problem in the reviewed sources.

title: Outcome misclassification in binary indirect comparisons
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build sensitivity analyses for differential outcome misclassification into binary PAIC, parameterized by study- and arm-specific sensitivity and specificity, and report how much misclassification would be required to overturn the conclusion. State explicitly whether the estimand is the recorded endpoint or a latent true outcome, since the error model is needed only for the latter. Where validation data, a gold standard or replicate measurements exist for either trial, use them to anchor the bias parameters instead of eliciting them, and reserve the elicited version for endpoints where nothing better is available.

Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed, on a single finding.
The source said. “Binary outcomes in the source and comparator trials may be misclassified, and the misclassification may differ between studies, arms, or assessment schemes, yet population-adjusted analyses implicitly assume perfect and equal classification.”
What was wrong with it. The source said population-adjusted analyses implicitly assume perfect and equal classification; the code auditor narrowed this to analyses whose estimand is a latent true outcome, and added that true risk, sensitivity and specificity are not jointly identified from one fallible binary measurement but are not unestimable under every data design, since validation data, a gold standard, replicate measurements or identifying restrictions can identify them. The literature auditor noted that the absence of PAIC-specific work rests on a failed search rather than on any source asserting the absence, so the correct framing is unaddressed rather than unsolved.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 1 surviving finding from: Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data, S. New citations: 10.1007/978-3-030-82673-4

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I searched PubMed and the web for quantitative bias analysis of outcome misclassification applied to indirect comparisons, MAIC, STC or ML-NMR and retrieved nothing PAIC-specific; the general QBA apparatus for sensitivity/specificity bias parameters is long established in epidemiology but I found no application inside a population-adjusted synthesis. That supports the entry’s direction but means the three claims rest on my failure to find contrary work, which is weak evidence. The third claim, that differential misclassification can bias in either direction, is standard measurement-error epidemiology and is the strongest of the three; the first claim (that PAIC ‘implicitly assumes’ perfect equal classification) is really a statement that no PAIC paper models it, which I could not confirm from any source that asserts the absence. Because the bias parameters are not estimable from trial publications, this problem is structurally a sensitivity-analysis problem, and per the audit calibration no sensitivity-analysis paper could ever close it; the correct framing is ‘unaddressed’, not ‘unsolved’.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C3 is correct. If true arm risk is p, observed risk is Sep + (1-Sp)(1-p); study- or arm-specific sensitivity and specificity can therefore move an indirect contrast in either direction. C1 is accurate only when the intended estimand concerns a latent true outcome. An ordinary model can consistently estimate an effect on the recorded endpoint without assuming perfect classification, but interpreting trials as measuring the same true endpoint requires measurement comparability or an explicit error model. Without validation data, a gold standard, replicated measurements, external information, or identifying restrictions, true risk, sensitivity, and specificity are not jointly identified from one fallible binary measurement. They are not unestimable under every possible data design. C2’s claim that such analysis is non-standard is a practice or coverage claim outside this lens, although the proposed sensitivity analysis is technically appropriate. cpaic at the audited commit has no outcome-misclassification model. The issue can be decision-critical when ascertainment plausibly differs, but High priority is not automatic for well-defined, blinded, consistently assessed endpoints.

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
Statement
Outcome-regression population-adjusted comparisons that report covariate-conditional coefficients, namely plug-in-means STC and conditional ML-NMR effects, return odds ratios that are not the marginal contrast the aggregate-data trial published, because the odds ratio is non-collapsible. This is not a property of binary PAIC as a class: a MAIC that fits a weighted outcome model containing treatment only already returns a marginal effect in the target population. Estimators and software for target-standardized marginal risks, risk differences and risk ratios already exist, including parametric G-computation (pmid:35485582), multiple-imputation marginalization, outstandR, maicplus and multinma’s marginal_effects(). What remains is that these are not the reporting default in HTA submissions, and that marginal component effects are not generally additive, so the scale chosen for standardization has to be compatible with component synthesis.

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
Why it is open
The gap is between available methods and prevailing practice: conditional coefficients are still reported alongside marginal aggregate-data effects, and nothing in the output signals the mismatch because both are labeled odds ratios of plausible magnitude. Standardizing the conditional side requires both a fitted outcome model and an explicit target covariate distribution, which aggregate publications rarely supply, so the comparator side cannot be moved onto the conditional scale after the fact. Conditional and marginal odds ratios do coincide under the null, with no prognostic heterogeneity, or with a degenerate covariate distribution, so the mismatch is decision-critical when incompatible estimands are actually combined rather than automatically. Within cpaic, the unreleased development package, cML-NMR still has no marginal standardization path.

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The estimators exist, so the work is adoption and extension rather than construction. Make a named target-population estimand and marginal standardization the declared default in submissions, using the existing implementations, and add a marginal standardization path to cML-NMR where one is still missing. Check in each analysis that the effect scale chosen for standardization is compatible with component synthesis, since marginal component effects add exactly when the standardized treatment effects remain affine in the component design.

title: Target-standardized marginal risks are not the HTA reporting default
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Plug-in-means STC and conditional ML-NMR coefficients return covariate-conditional odds ratios that, because the odds ratio is non-collapsible, are not the marginal contrast published by the AgD trial; methods (parametric G-computation, multiple-imputation marginalisation, multinma marginal_effects) and software (outstandR, maicplus, multinma) that produce target-standardised marginal risks, risk differences and risk ratios already exist, but they are not yet the reporting default in HTA submissions.
The source titled this. “Odds-ratio default and conditional-marginal mismatch in binary PAIC” The title attributes the conditional-marginal mismatch to binary PAIC as a class, which both auditors rejected since weighted MAIC already returns a marginal target-population effect.
The source said. “Binary population-adjusted indirect comparisons report conditional odds ratios because logistic models are convenient, but the odds ratio is non-collapsible, so the covariate-adjusted coefficient estimated from individual patient data is neither the marginal contrast in any named population nor on the same scale as the marginal effect published by the aggregate-data trial it is combined with.”
What was wrong with it. The source attributed the conditional-marginal mismatch to binary PAIC as a class and to the convenience of logistic models, and both auditors rejected that scope. The literature auditor found the estimand problem already named in Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio (doi:10.1002/sim.9413), solved by parametric G-computation (pmid:35485582), and implemented in outstandR, maicplus and multinma; the code auditor confirmed at commit 9d150e9 of cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, that cmaic() returns a marginal weighted effect while cstc() and cmlnmr() return conditional ones.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict left unchanged

verdict left unchanged Later work reports progress, but on the chronology review the second reviewer judged it ‘no’ at high confidence: The later work demonstrates and recommends target standardization, but the earlier gap is specifically about routine reporting practice rather than methodological availability. Neither later claim shows that HTA submissions have adopted marginal risks, risk differences, or risk ratios as the default output.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. Retrieved Remiro-Azocar/Heath/Baio, ‘Target estimands for population-adjusted indirect comparisons’ (Stat Med 2022, doi 10.1002/sim.9413) and ‘Parametric G-computation for compatible ITCs with limited IPD’ (RSM 2022, PMID 35485582), plus the CRAN package outstandR, maicplus 0.1.2 NEWS (‘changed the link function to binomial for RD and RR in binary analysis’), and multinma NEWS 0.7.0 (‘The new marginal_effects() function produces marginal treatment effects’), whose docs describe mtype=‘difference’/‘ratio’/‘link’ standardised to a target population via newdata/baseline. The estimand-compatibility problem is named, formalised and implemented in three packages, so the methodological gap is largely closed; what remains is HTA default practice. The statement also over-generalises: MAIC fits a weighted outcome model containing treatment only, so its binary output is already a marginal effect in the AgD population. The conditional-marginal mismatch is specific to plug-in-means STC and to reporting ML-NMR conditional coefficients, not to ‘binary PAIC’ as a class. No source supports the motive claim about logistic convenience. Cites pmid:35485582: Provides an outcome-regression estimator that targets a marginal treatment effect compatible with the AgD trial’s published marginal effect, for binary outcomes.. Cites cran:outstandR: CRAN implementation of model-based standardisation for PAIC, producing marginal contrasts on user-chosen scales.. GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

Thus C2, C3, C5, and C6 are correct when read as general possibilities, not universal identities. Conditional and marginal odds ratios can coincide under the null, with no prognostic heterogeneity, or with a degenerate covariate distribution. C1’s motive claim and C7’s prevalence claim are not technically verifiable. C4 is too prescriptive: standardized risks, risk differences, and risk ratios are coherent named estimands, but require sufficient target-distribution and outcome information, and marginal component effects need not obey the component-additivity model. cpaic now documents the mismatch and already provides a marginal MAIC path, but cML-NMR still lacks marginal standardization. The issue is decision-critical when incompatible estimands are actually combined, not automatically for every binary PAIC. title: No valid selection criterion for cut points and powers in time-varying survival NMA
text: MOD-19 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: No valid selection criterion for cut points and powers in time-varying survival NMA
text:
Statement
Survival network meta-analyses that relax proportional hazards are chosen by a search whose outcome the usual criteria cannot defend. For piecewise or time-partitioned models the number and placement of cut points cannot be selected by DIC or AIC at all, because changing the intervals changes the data configuration the likelihood is evaluated on, so fit statistics for two candidates are not comparable quantities. For fractional polynomials the analyst fits up to 8 first-order and 36 second-order power combinations and reports the winner, so the number of models tried acts as unreported hidden parameters. The shortcut that makes the search affordable, selecting by frequentist AIC and then refitting the winner in Bayesian form, has never been checked for agreement with a Bayesian selection on the same data. In the absence of a statistical criterion, published practice falls back on prior knowledge, transparency, visual comparison against the observed curves and compatibility with the economic model, which is a statement that no criterion is available rather than a solution. Neither the interval on the reported time-varying contrast nor the extrapolated survival curve that carries the cost-effectiveness result reflects the search that produced the model.

title: No valid selection criterion for cut points and powers in time-varying survival NMA
text:
Why it is open
The cut-point obstacle is structural rather than computational: a likelihood built from interval-level event and exposure counts is a different likelihood for each partition, so information criteria that presuppose a fixed data configuration are not merely biased across candidates but undefined. A criterion that could compare them has to be defined on something invariant to the partition, such as the predictive density of the observed event times or a proper scoring rule on the survival function, and nothing in the applied literature has been written in those terms. Carrying the search into the reported uncertainty is harder here than in ordinary post-selection inference, because the target is not a coefficient but an extrapolated survival curve beyond the observed follow-up, where the candidates differ most and the data are silent, so a selection-adjusted interval would be widest exactly where it cannot be checked. Model averaging is the obvious alternative, but averaging over candidates that disagree about extrapolation produces a predictive band whose usefulness for a reimbursement decision has never been tested against current practice of choosing one model and defending it clinically.

title: No valid selection criterion for cut points and powers in time-varying survival NMA
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Freeman, Cooper, Sutton & Crowther 2022, Statistical Methods in Medical Research 31(5):839-861
Applies the competing non-proportional-hazards network models to a melanoma network and states the obstacle directly: comparing models with differing time intervals is not straightforward because the choice of intervals cannot be guided by model fit statistics, since the data to which the models are fitted change when the intervals change. Also records that agreement between frequentist AIC-based selection and Bayesian selection is unestablished, and falls back on non-statistical selection criteria.


Ouwens, Philips & Jansen 2010, Research Synthesis Methods 1(3-4):258-271
Network meta-analysis of parametric survival curves, which introduced the multi-parameter treatment effect whose functional form now has to be selected.


Jansen 2011, BMC Medical Research Methodology 11:61
Fractional polynomial network meta-analysis of survival data, the model class in which the analyst searches over first- and second-order power combinations and reports the best-fitting one.


Freeman & Carpenter 2017, Research Synthesis Methods 8(4):451-464
Bayesian one-step individual participant data network meta-analysis with Royston-Parmar models, a flexible spline alternative that accommodates time-dependent effects without cut points; it requires individual data, which is what the aggregate networks facing this problem lack, and it still requires choosing the number and position of knots.


Spiegelhalter, Best, Carlin & van der Linde 2002, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 64(4):583-639
Introduces DIC, the criterion applied networks use to choose among survival models; its comparability assumption is exactly what fails when the cut-point configuration changes the data the likelihood is evaluated on.


Berk, Brown, Buja, Zhang & Zhao 2013, Annals of Statistics 41(2)
Valid post-selection inference: intervals that remain valid over all models a search could have selected. The general machinery for pricing a model search, developed for linear models with a fixed design and not extended to survival syntheses whose candidates are fitted to differently constructed data.

text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define a selection criterion on a quantity that does not change with the partition: the leave-one-trial-out or leave-one-arm-out predictive density of the observed event times, or a proper scoring rule on the predicted survival function evaluated on a common time grid, so that piecewise models with different cut points and fractional polynomials of different orders can be scored against each other on the same footing. Check the frequentist-to-Bayesian shortcut empirically by running both selections on the same simulated and real networks and reporting how often they choose the same model and how much the extrapolations differ when they do not. Price the search by carrying it into the reported quantity, either by repeating the whole selection inside a bootstrap or by Bayesian model averaging over the candidate set with weights from the partition-invariant criterion, and report the resulting interval on the extrapolated survival difference and on the derived incremental cost-effectiveness ratio rather than on a coefficient. Publish the candidate set and the scores for every model tried, so the count of models fitted stops being an unreported parameter.

Verdict. Confirmed open. It rests on a single applied methods paper, which states both halves directly: fit statistics cannot guide the cut-point choice because the data change with the intervals, and the agreement of frequentist with Bayesian selection is unestablished.

title: No selection-adjusted interval for the treatment a network ranks best
text: MOD-17 Confirmed open High priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: No selection-adjusted interval for the treatment a network ranks best
text:
Statement
Applied network meta-analyses routinely report the effect of the treatment their own output identifies as best, using the ordinary interval for that contrast, computed as if the treatment had been named before the data were seen. Taking the maximum of a set of correlated estimates biases the selected estimate away from the null, and the exaggeration is a property of the selection rather than of the ranking metric, so it arises with SUCRA, P-scores, probability best or any other measure used to pick the winner. The size is not negligible: in a published multiplicity simulation the best-versus-reference effect was estimated at 2.37 when the true value was 1.00. The available mitigation is shrinkage through exchangeable priors on relative effects, which lowers mean absolute error and reduces average exaggeration but is not calibrated to the selection event, since the degree of shrinkage is governed by a between-treatment variance estimated from the same data and by an analyst-chosen exchangeability partition. No estimator supplies a conditional or selection-adjusted interval for the selected contrast with demonstrated coverage in a network, and no reporting convention requires the selection step to be declared, so a reader cannot tell whether the reported contrast was pre-specified or won a competition.

title: No selection-adjusted interval for the treatment a network ranks best
text:
Why it is open
Selection-adjusted and conditional inference exist in other fields, but the machinery is built for independent or simply structured estimates, whereas a network’s contrasts are correlated through shared arms, multi-arm trials and a common between-study variance, and that correlation is estimated rather than known. Conditioning on the event that a given contrast was the maximum has no closed form in that setting, and resampling schemes must repeat the entire fit, including variance estimation and the ranking step, inside every replicate. Shrinkage and selection adjustment answer different questions and are frequently conflated: shrinkage improves average error over all contrasts, while a selection-adjusted interval has to cover the particular contrast that won, which shrinkage does not guarantee. There is also no agreement on what the selection event is, since reporting the top-ranked treatment, reporting the top two, and reporting a pre-specified treatment that happened to rank first are three different selection rules requiring three different corrections, and nothing in current practice records which one occurred.

title: No selection-adjusted interval for the treatment a network ranks best
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Efthimiou & White 2020, Research Synthesis Methods 11(1):105-122
Documents multiplicity in network meta-analysis and shows that identifying the best or worst treatment risks overestimating the corresponding effect regardless of the measure used to identify it, with a simulation in which the selected best-versus-reference effect is 2.37 against a true 1.00. Proposes exchangeable priors as mitigation; reports no coverage or bias for the selected contrast conditional on selection.


Salanti, Ades & Ioannidis 2011, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 64(2):163-171
Defines the ranking summaries, including SUCRA, that turn a fitted network into the statement of which treatment is best; the selection whose consequences are unadjusted starts here.


Rucker & Schwarzer 2015, BMC Medical Research Methodology 15:58
Frequentist ranking by P-scores without resampling, showing the ranking step is cheap and therefore ubiquitous; the ranking is delivered without any adjustment to the interval of the contrast that is subsequently reported.


Trinquart, Attiche, Bafeta, Porcher et al. 2016, Annals of Internal Medicine 164(10):666-673
Reanalysis of published network meta-analyses showing that ranking uncertainty is large and that rankings are unstable, which is the empirical counterpart of the selection problem; it quantifies uncertainty in the rank rather than correcting the effect estimate for having been selected.


Andrews, Kitagawa & McCloskey 2024, Quarterly Journal of Economics 139(1):305-358
Inference on winners: conditional and hybrid confidence intervals with correct coverage for a parameter selected as the maximum of a set of correlated estimates. This is the machinery the network problem needs, developed for a known covariance and not adapted to a network with multi-arm trials and an estimated heterogeneity variance.


Benjamini & Yekutieli 2005, Journal of the American Statistical Association 100(469):71-81
False coverage-statement rate intervals for selected parameters, the alternative framework in which the guarantee is over the set of reported intervals rather than conditional on the selection event.


Efron 2011, Journal of the American Statistical Association 106(496):1602-1614
Tweedie’s formula and selection bias, the empirical Bayes correction that explains why shrinkage reduces average exaggeration and why the amount of correction depends on an estimated prior, which is the reason shrinkage does not by itself calibrate the selected interval.

title: No selection-adjusted interval for the treatment a network ranks best
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define the selection event that applied practice actually performs, namely reporting the contrast that maximizes a named ranking statistic in the fitted network, and derive the conditional distribution of that contrast given the event under the standard normal-likelihood network model, taking the contrast covariance from the fit. Build both a conditional interval and a hybrid interval that trades some conditioning for length, then evaluate them by simulation over network size, heterogeneity, number of treatments, multi-arm structure and the true gap between the best and second-best treatment, reporting coverage conditional on selection and expected length. Compare against the exchangeable-prior shrinkage already in use, so the choice between a Bayesian mitigation and a frequentist correction rests on measured conditional coverage. Alongside the estimator, add a reporting requirement that any network reporting a best treatment declare whether that treatment was pre-specified, since the correction depends on the selection rule and no correction is possible when the rule is not recorded.

title: No selection-adjusted interval for the treatment a network ranks best
text:

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as a genuine post-selection problem distinct from selecting a model or a bridge, because here the reported contrast itself is data-dependent while the estimand is unchanged. It rests on a single network meta-analysis methods paper for the magnitude, which establishes winner’s-curse exaggeration and offers a prior-based mitigation rather than conditional coverage.

title: No calibrated rule says when within- and across-trial interactions may be pooled
text: MOD-15 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: No calibrated rule says when within- and across-trial interactions may be pooled
text:
Statement
An individual participant data network meta-analysis carries two sources of information about a treatment-covariate interaction: the within-trial contrast between participants in the same trial, and the across-trial association between trial-level covariate means and trial-level effects. Standard practice separates them and rests modifier claims on the within-trial part, because the across-trial part is identified only under an untestable assumption of no unmeasured trial-level confounding. Pooling the two buys precision, and the only published criterion for deciding whether they agree closely enough to be pooled is a visual comparison plus a rule that the within-trial estimate should lie within half a standard error of the across-trial estimate, described in its source as relatively strict and justified by pointing at interactions later debunked rather than by any calibration. No study reports the operating characteristics of that rule or of any alternative: not its power to detect a real discrepancy, not its false-positive rate, and not the coverage of the combined estimate conditional on having passed. The decision changes conclusions rather than sharpening them; in the worked example that accompanies the rule, pooling would have moved a chemotherapy-plus-surgery interaction from +0.172 to -0.120, reversing its sign. The problem is not confined to full individual-data networks, since any mixed-granularity model that lets aggregate covariate variation inform an interaction makes the same pooling decision, usually without making it explicitly.

title: No calibrated rule says when within- and across-trial interactions may be pooled
text:
Why it is open
The identifying assumption behind the across-trial component is not testable from the data being pooled, so agreement between the two estimates is evidence about that assumption in one direction only: disagreement can come from ecological confounding or from sampling noise, and agreement can occur under confounding whenever the bias is small next to the standard errors. Any threshold rule therefore has operating characteristics that depend on the between-trial variance and the number of trials, and both are small in exactly the networks where the extra precision is wanted. Calibrating a rule requires simulating networks in which the ecological bias is set and varied, which requires a generative model for trial-level confounding that this literature has not standardized. There is also no agreement on what a pooling rule should protect: a test tuned to preserve coverage of the interaction coefficient is not the same as one tuned to protect the downstream decision that uses the modifier to select patients or to transport an effect.

title: No calibrated rule says when within- and across-trial interactions may be pooled
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Freeman, Fisher, Tierney & Carpenter 2018, Research Synthesis Methods 9(3):393-407
Framework for identifying treatment-covariate interactions in individual participant data network meta-analysis, separating within-trial from across-trial information and supplying the only published pooling criterion: agreement is taken to be shown if the within-trial interaction lies within half a standard error of the across-trial interaction.


Hua, Burke, Crowther, Ensor et al. 2017, Statistics in Medicine 36(5):772-789
Shows that one-stage individual participant data meta-analysis models must separate within-trial from across-trial information to avoid ecological bias in treatment-covariate interactions, which is the step that creates the pooling decision this problem is about.


Riley, Debray, Fisher, Hattle et al. 2020, Statistics in Medicine 39(15):2115-2137
Statistical recommendations for conduct and planning of individual participant data meta-analysis of treatment-covariate interactions, which set the default of relying on within-trial information; they do not supply a calibrated rule for when across-trial information may be added.


Berlin, Santanna, Schmid, Szczech et al. 2002, Statistics in Medicine 21(3):371-387
Demonstrates that group-level meta-regression can misattribute an ecological association to individual-level effect modification, which is the harm a pooling rule has to prevent.


Fisher, Copas, Tierney & Parmar 2011, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 64(9):949-967
Critical review of methods for assessing patient-level interactions in individual participant data meta-analysis with guidance for practitioners; catalogues the estimation options without proposing an agreement test with known operating characteristics.

title: No calibrated rule says when within- and across-trial interactions may be pooled
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Specify the decision as a test with a stated null and a stated alternative: the null that the within-trial and across-trial interaction estimate the same quantity, the alternative indexed by an ecological bias term. Simulate networks in which that bias term is set, crossing the number of trials, the between-trial variance of the covariate means, the covariate distribution overlap and the strength of the true within-trial interaction, and report for the half-standard-error rule and for candidate alternatives the rejection rate under the null, the power at each bias size, and the coverage and bias of the pooled interaction conditional on a pass. Compare threshold rules against continuous alternatives, such as a hierarchical model that shrinks the across-trial contribution toward the within-trial estimate with a data-driven weight, and against simply never pooling. Report the results in terms of the quantity the interaction is used for, namely the transported treatment effect in a target population, so that a rule can be chosen on decision cost rather than on interaction coverage alone.

title: No calibrated rule says when within- and across-trial interactions may be pooled
text:
Our study

The half-standard-error pooling rule for interactions is stated in the wrong standard error
The question put to it. The published rule pools within-trial and across-trial interaction estimates when they differ by less than half the across-trial standard error. What are its pass rate, the bias and coverage of what it reports, and how does it compare with a test stated in the difference’s own standard error?
What it found. The difference’s standard error is sqrt(sW^2 + sA^2), not sA, so under equality the rule pools with probability at most 0.383 (0.31 to 0.37 in the networks studied): it refuses valid pooling most of the time in every regime. When it pools under ecological bias, the pooled interval can cover as little as 22%. Its RMSE matches never pooling to within 0.3%, forgoing the 2% to 19% gain pooling offers when the estimates agree.
Results.

Pass probability under equality: 0.314 to 0.374, bounded above by P(|Z| < 0.5) = 0.383 in any network.
Coverage of the pooled interval given pooling falls with ecological bias: 0.72 at delta 0.1 and 0.22 at delta 0.2 with 20 trials and dispersed trial means, where the rule still pools in 6% and 0.04% of analyses.
Averaged over its decisions, the rule’s RMSE is within 0.3% of never pooling in every configuration.
Never pooling had the lowest worst-case RMSE over ecological bias 0 to 0.2 in five of six configurations; always pooling had it in one.
An individual-level check of 2000 networks per configuration reproduced the standard errors, the pass probability (0.366 against 0.374 exact) and the conditional coverage (0.951 against 0.950).

Design.

Estimand

The within-trial treatment-covariate interaction

Methods compared

never pool, always pool, half-SE rule, size-5% test on the difference, size-20% test

Data-generating mechanism

Exact bivariate-normal computation of pass probability, bias, RMSE and coverage for never pooling, always pooling, the half-SE rule and tests on the difference at 5% and 20%, over 24 configurations: 5, 10 or 20 trials of 200, trial covariate means spread with SD 0.25 or 0.75, ecological bias 0 to 0.4.

Replicates

Exact computation; individual-level check of 2000 networks in each of four configurations


What this does not answer. Independent normal estimates with known standard errors; no between-trial heterogeneity; all trials with individual data. The ML-NMR case, where aggregate trials inform only the across-trial component, is not computed. No agreement rule can detect trial-level confounding that is small relative to the across-trial standard error. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text: MOD-13 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging

title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text:
Statement
Posterior means, credible intervals, convergence diagnostics and ordinary fit diagnostics do not establish likelihood identification, and a proper prior yields a proper posterior for a contrast the likelihood does not touch. The tooling to expose this is not missing. Power-scaling sensitivity analysis (doi:10.1007/s11222-023-10366-5), shipped in the CRAN package priorsense and working with rstan, cmdstanr and brms, gives a diagnostic that indicates prior-data conflict or likelihood non-informativity and attaches to Stan-based models such as multinma with no new theory, and the development source cpaic already returns NA for contrasts its component design cannot uniquely identify, labels the information basis, refits under tighter and looser priors and plots prior against posterior (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9; an unreleased development package on GitHub that an auditor confirmed is not on CRAN). What is open is an ITC and PAIC reporting convention that makes this routine, plus exact identification diagnostics for nonlinear and aggregate-data likelihoods; GPT-5.6 Sol also notes the phenomenon is better named prior-dominated inference for a nonidentified contrast than prior-driven identification.

title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text:
Why it is open
A proper prior always produces a finite posterior for a nonidentified contrast, so a posterior mean plus credible interval cannot by itself separate an answer supplied by the data from one supplied by the prior, and routine convergence and fit diagnostics do not test whether the likelihood is flat in the specific contrast a decision depends on. The diagnostics that would catch the substitution exist but are requested by no reporting template, so nothing in the workflow forces their use. Every flexible direction proposed for this setting, including nonparametric mixtures, Gaussian processes, BART, commensurate and robust priors and generalized Bayes, adds prior structure, so the exposure problem grows as the models improve, and exact identification diagnostics for nonlinear or aggregate-data likelihoods are still missing.

title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Kallioinen, Paananen, Burkner & Vehtari 2024, Detecting and diagnosing prior and likelihood sensitivity with power-scaling, Statistics and Computing 34:57
Importance-sampling power-scaling of the prior and the likelihood, yielding a diagnostic that indicates prior-data conflict or likelihood non-informativity. This is the machinery the entry’s proposed direction asks for.


priorsense R package
Released implementation of power-scaling sensitivity analysis, working directly with rstan, cmdstanr and brms, so it attaches to Stan-based evidence-synthesis models such as multinma without new theory.


cpaic development source at commit 9d150e9 (choxos/cpaic)
Returns NA for relative effects the component design cannot uniquely identify rather than pseudoinverse or prior-driven artifacts, labels the information basis, refits under tighter and looser priors, and compares prior with posterior. cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub; an auditor confirmed it is not on CRAN.

title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Make the existing diagnostics routine rather than proposing new ones: require Bayesian ITC and PAIC analyses to run power-scaling or an equivalent prior and likelihood sensitivity check on each cross-gap or transported contrast, and to label parameters identified, partially identified or nonidentified. Use prior classes instead of one arbitrary prior, consider modular or cut-feedback models so outcome data do not spuriously update elicited sensitivity distributions, and report deterministic parameter grids alongside posterior mixtures. The research work left is exact identification diagnostics for nonlinear and aggregate-data likelihoods, plus bridge-deletion demonstrations.

title: No reporting convention exposes prior-dominated contrasts in PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Bayesian PAIC output does not expose prior-driven identification” The title says Bayesian output does not expose prior-driven identification, but power-scaling sensitivity ships on CRAN and prior-posterior comparison is already implemented.
The source said. “The report’s key requirement for Bayesian nonparametric and robust-Bayes methods in ITC and PAIC is that the model must expose prior-driven identification, because posterior precision is not data information when the likelihood is flat in the relevant contrast. Standard output does not distinguish the two.”
What was wrong with it. The source said standard output does not distinguish prior information from data information, with no prior work cited. The literature auditor supplied a packaged diagnostic that does exactly this (doi:10.1007/s11222-023-10366-5, CRAN package priorsense), and GPT-5.6 Sol found the universal output claim stale against choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, which already returns NA for non-identified contrasts and refits under alternative priors; cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub and is not installable from CRAN.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1, C3 and C4 are substantially correct for a well-defined posterior. If a likelihood is flat in a contrast and the prior factorizes, its posterior equals its prior; with prior dependence, data may move the contrast only through prior coupling to identified parameters, which is still not direct likelihood identification. A proper prior does not guarantee that a posterior mean exists or that the resulting interval is apparently precise, so ‘prior-driven identification’ is better called prior-dominated inference for a nonidentified contrast. The universal output claim is also stale at cpaic 9d150e9. relative_effects() returns NA for contrasts outside the relevant row space, estimable_effects_at() labels the information basis, prior_sensitivity() refits under tighter and looser priors, and plot_prior_posterior() compares prior and posterior distributions. These features partially expose the substitution already. Broader default reporting, exact nonlinear identification diagnostics and systematic prior-information decompositions remain open. The issue is decision-critical when a conclusion depends on a likelihood-null contrast, but not for every flexible Bayesian model.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The four claims are true: a proper prior yields a proper posterior for a nonidentified contrast, and standard convergence and fit diagnostics do not test likelihood flatness in a specific contrast. But the entry states this as if no tooling existed, and prior_work is empty. Kallioinen, Paananen, Burkner & Vehtari, ‘Detecting and diagnosing prior and likelihood sensitivity with power-scaling’, Statistics and Computing 2024;34:57 (doi 10.1007/s11222-023-10366-5) supplies exactly the diagnostic the proposed_direction asks for: importance-sampling-based power-scaling of the prior and the likelihood, yielding a diagnostic that indicates prior-data conflict OR likelihood non-informativity, implemented in the CRAN package priorsense and working directly with rstan, cmdstanr and brms, i.e. attachable to multinma-style Stan models with no new theory. The broader partial-identification framing (a proper prior concentrating inside an identification region purely by prior structure) is also long-established in the Bayesian partial-identification literature. What is genuinely open is the ITC/PAIC-specific reporting convention: labeling parameters identified, partially identified or nonidentified, and reporting prior-to-posterior movement per cross-gap contrast. That is a guidance gap, not a methods gap. Cites doi:10.1007/s11222-023-10366-5 (cran:priorsense): Provides a ready, packaged diagnostic that detects likelihood non-informativity and prior-driven posteriors via power-scaling, covering the power-scaling and prior-to-posterior movement elements of the entry’s proposed_direction..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

If a likelihood is flat in a contrast and the prior factorizes, its posterior equals its prior; with prior dependence, data may move the contrast only through prior coupling to identified parameters, which is still not direct likelihood identification. A proper prior does not guarantee that a posterior mean exists or that the resulting interval is apparently precise, so ‘prior-driven identification’ is better called prior-dominated inference for a nonidentified contrast. The universal output claim is also stale at cpaic 9d150e9. relative_effects() returns NA for contrasts outside the relevant row space, estimable_effects_at() labels the information basis, prior_sensitivity() refits under tighter and looser priors, and plot_prior_posterior() compares prior and posterior distributions. These features partially expose the substitution already. Broader default reporting, exact nonlinear identification diagnostics and systematic prior-information decompositions remain open. The issue is decision-critical when a conclusion depends on a likelihood-null contrast, but not for every flexible Bayesian model. title: No mixture-over-populations model transports to a declared target
text: MOD-11 Partially addressed Medium-high priority Emerging

title: No mixture-over-populations model transports to a declared target
text:
Statement
Dirichlet-process and finite-mixture representations are not undeveloped for this literature: Disher et al. (arXiv:2506.22154) put a Dirichlet-process prior with a regularized horseshoe base measure inside network meta-analysis, extend it to baseline-risk meta-regression so that clustering works under heterogeneity, and apply it to rheumatology and pain case studies. What has not been built is the narrower object this entry needs, a mixture over study populations combined with transport to a declared target population and aggregate-data integration. The generalized or safe Bayes half survives intact, since no calibrated learning-rate procedure exists for hierarchical evidence synthesis with transport. GPT-5.6 Sol also corrected two premises: with few studies these models can be strongly prior-sensitive but are not necessarily almost entirely prior-driven, and tempering does not widen intervals roughly uniformly, because it can change posterior location, shrinkage and the relative information of parts of a nonlinear hierarchical model.

title: No mixture-over-populations model transports to a declared target
text:
Why it is open
With the small number of studies typical of an ITC, a nonparametric mixture over study populations can be substantially prior-driven, so the apparent gain from non-normal heterogeneity or latent subpopulations is hard to separate from prior structure, although rich IPD or well-separated mixture components can supply real information. Tempering has the mirror problem: a learning rate must be chosen, no calibration procedure exists for a multi-study transport setting where the misspecification may sit in the outcome model, the study-effect structure or the integration over the target distribution, and a tempered posterior can look appropriately cautious while the structural error it was meant to guard against is untouched. Neither device identifies a cross-gap contrast that the likelihood does not touch. No worked implementation combines either with transport to a declared target and aggregate-data integration, so the trade-off between robustness and lost precision has never been quantified for ITC.

title: No mixture-over-populations model transports to a declared target
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Disher, Cameron & Hutton 2025, Bayesian non-parametric lumping and splitting of nodes in Network Meta-Analysis under heterogeneity
Implements a Dirichlet-process prior with a regularized horseshoe base measure inside network meta-analysis, extends it to baseline-risk meta-regression so clustering works under heterogeneity, and applies it to rheumatology and pain case studies. Does not address transport to a declared target population.

title: No mixture-over-populations model transports to a declared target
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Take the Dirichlet-process machinery that already works inside network meta-analysis and extend it to study-population heterogeneity with transport and aggregate-data integration, reporting prior sensitivity and prior-to-posterior movement for every contrast so the contribution of the nonparametric structure is visible, and use it for heterogeneity and non-normality rather than as a device to identify cross-gap contrasts. For generalized and safe Bayes, calibrate the learning rate against the specific estimator, data structure and misspecification being targeted, and test whether tempering reduces decision error compared with directly modeling the suspected structural failure. Report the tempering choice as a sensitivity dimension rather than a fixed analytic default.

title: No mixture-over-populations model transports to a declared target
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Robust heterogeneity and likelihood models undeveloped for ITC” The title says these models are undeveloped for ITC, but Dirichlet-process priors with meta-regression are already implemented and applied inside network meta-analysis.
The source said. “Dirichlet-process or finite mixture models for heterogeneous study populations, which would replace the usual normal random-effects assumption, and generalized or safe Bayes methods that temper or reweight the likelihood to reduce sensitivity to its misspecification, are both listed as potential methods for ITC and PAIC evidence synthesis. Neither has been developed, calibrated, or validated for this setting.”
What was wrong with it. The source said neither device has been developed, calibrated or validated for this setting; the literature auditor found Dirichlet-process priors already implemented and applied inside network meta-analysis with meta-regression (arXiv:2506.22154), which does not address transport to a declared target population. GPT-5.6 Sol rejected the claims that such models are almost entirely prior-driven and that tempering widens intervals roughly uniformly.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The claim that Dirichlet-process and mixture representations of heterogeneity have not been ‘developed, calibrated, or validated for this setting’ is too strong if ‘this setting’ includes network meta-analysis. Disher, Cameron & Hutton, ‘Bayesian non-parametric lumping and splitting of nodes in Network Meta-Analysis under heterogeneity’ (arXiv:2506.22154, 2025) introduces ‘a Bayesian non-parametric framework using a Dirichlet process prior with a regularized horseshoe base measure’, extends it to baseline-risk meta-regression so clustering works under heterogeneity, and applies it to rheumatology and pain case studies. That is a DP prior replacing a parametric random-effects structure inside an NMA with meta-regression, in an ITC method, with applied validation. It is not the same object as a mixture over study POPULATIONS transported to a declared target, so the entry’s narrower reading survives. The generalized/safe Bayes half I could not falsify: I found no calibrated learning-rate procedure for hierarchical evidence synthesis with transport, so that claim reads as open. I read abstracts, not full texts, hence the moderate confidence. Cites arXiv:2506.22154: Shows Dirichlet-process priors have already been implemented and applied inside network meta-analysis with meta-regression, narrowing the claim that DP/mixture models are undeveloped for ITC evidence synthesis; it does not address transport to a declared target population..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 and C4 describe legitimate candidate methods. C2 is correct only when the relevant cross-gap contrast is absent from, or invariant in, the observed-data likelihood; Bayesian nonparametrics cannot manufacture likelihood information in that case. C3 and C5 are maturity claims outside this audit’s lens. With few studies, mixture and Dirichlet-process models can be highly prior-sensitive, but the claim that they are almost entirely prior-driven is not universal, especially when rich IPD or well-separated mixture structure supplies information. Generalized-posterior tempering also does not merely widen intervals uniformly: it can change posterior location, shrinkage and relative information across a nonlinear hierarchical model. It offers no general guarantee against structural transport or bridge misspecification. Estimator-specific calibration and performance assessment remain open, but these methods are robustness and sensitivity devices, not solutions to disconnected identification.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

text: MOD-09 Partially addressed Very high priority Established

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
Statement
ML-NMR combines IPD and aggregate data in one model and avoids the aggregation bias of aggregate-data meta-regression (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579), now extends to general likelihoods including time-to-event outcomes (doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169), and allows key assumptions to be assessed but not eliminated, as the 2023 psoriasis application showed (PMID 35997006), while practice remains dominated by MAIC and STC (doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2023.09.004). The auditors split on the recommendation that follows. The literature auditor verified every checkable claim and read the adoption gap as open; GPT-5.6 Sol held that partial IPD plus suspected effect-modifier imbalance is not sufficient to declare ML-NMR the default, because method choice also depends on the estimand, network structure, target-distribution information, overlap and model credibility, and that the absence of a designated default is not itself an unresolved methodological problem. The premise that ML-NMR is harder to specify, fit, diagnose and explain is plausible and widely repeated but unmeasured; neither auditor found a study of it.

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
Why it is open
ML-NMR is harder to specify, fit, diagnose and explain than MAIC or STC, so the barrier to adoption is practical rather than theoretical and default behavior has not shifted. Conditional constancy, shared effect-modifier assumptions, overlap and target-population relevance remain only partially testable inside ML-NMR, so switching buys coherence rather than assumption relief and the case for the extra effort is not self-evident to analysts or reviewers. On the weaker reading the missing thing is not a default but the material that would let an analyst make the comparison at all: diagnostics, training and reporting templates that state what has and has not been relieved.

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




dmphillippo/multinma
R package implementing Bayesian NMA, NMR and ML-NMR with IPD plus aggregate data, time-to-event support, integration checks and target-population prediction.


Phillippo et al. 2020, Multilevel network meta-regression for population-adjusted treatment comparisons, JRSS-A (PMID 32684669)
Defines ML-NMR: an individual-level regression model whose aggregate data are fitted by integrating over the covariate distribution, avoiding the aggregation bias of standard meta-regression.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades & Welton 2025, JRSS-A (preprint arXiv:2401.12640)
Removes the requirement that the aggregate-level likelihood have a known closed form, which had prevented application to time-to-event outcomes. This is the general-likelihood and survival support the entry claims.


Phillippo et al. 2023, psoriasis application, Medical Decision Making 43(1):53-67 (PMID 35997006)
Demonstrates for the first time how ML-NMR allows key assumptions to be assessed, finding little evidence that conditional constancy or shared effect-modifier assumptions were invalid. Assumptions were assessed, not eliminated.


Serret-Larmande et al. 2023, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (PMID 37717707)
Methodological review of published PAIC analyses, overwhelmingly MAIC and STC, which is the evidence that practice has not moved to ML-NMR.


NICE quizartinib appraisal (PMID 39627603)
Cited by the literature auditor as one of the isolated applied appraisals using ML-NMR, consistent with adoption being sparse rather than absent.

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the operational layer rather than legislating a default: standardized integration and fit diagnostics, worked training material, and reporting templates that state which assumptions ML-NMR has and has not relieved. Set out explicit criteria for when ML-NMR is preferable and when it is infeasible, expressed in terms of estimand, network structure, available target-distribution information, overlap and model credibility, so the method choice is argued rather than asserted. Measuring the specification, fitting and communication burden against MAIC and STC would also convert the entry’s central unsourced premise into evidence.

title: No criterion says when ML-NMR should be preferred to MAIC or STC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 6 findings from 6 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source titled this. “ML-NMR is not the default despite being the most coherent framework” The title declares ML-NMR the most coherent framework and presumptive default, which the audit rejected since method choice also depends on estimand, network structure and overlap.
The source said. “The report recommends making ML-NMR the default upgrade path when IPD exist for a subset of trials in a connected network and clinically meaningful effect-modifier imbalance is suspected, because it is the most coherent framework currently available and now has survival and general-likelihood support. Practice has not moved, and the report is explicit that ML-NMR does not solve the underlying scientific problem.”
What was wrong with it. The source made a default-method recommendation with nothing cited. The literature auditor sourced each factual component (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579, doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169, PMID 35997006, doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2023.09.004), so the claim is now sourced, and voted the entry open; GPT-5.6 Sol voted it not a problem, because no universal default follows from partial IPD plus suspected imbalance. Both readings are kept above.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 6 surviving findings from: Anchors Away: Navigating Unanchored Indirect Comparisons wit; Assessing the performance of population adjustment methods f; Methods for Indirect Treatment Comparison: Results from a Sy; Network meta-interpolation: Effect modification adjustment i; Reframing Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons as a Tran; Response to discussant comments on “NMA, the first 20 years”. New citations: 10.1002/jrsm.1608, 10.1002/jrsm.1745, 10.1002/sim.8759, 10.3390/jmahp12020006

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Every checkable claim verified against retrieved sources. ‘Extends to general likelihoods including survival’: Phillippo, Dias, Ades & Welton, JRSS-A 2025 (doi 10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169, arXiv:2401.12640) states that ML-NMR ‘currently requires the aggregate-level likelihood to have a known closed form. Notably, this prevents application to time-to-event outcomes’ and then removes that restriction. ‘Integrates IPD and AgD and avoids aggregation bias’: Phillippo et al. 2020 JRSS-A and the 2023 Med Decis Making psoriasis paper, which says ML-NMR ‘coherently synthesizes evidence from IPD and AgD studies in networks of any size while avoiding aggregation bias and noncollapsibility bias’. The ‘2023 psoriasis application’ claim is exactly right: Phillippo et al., Med Decis Making 2023;43(1):53-67 (PMID 35997006) demonstrates ‘for the first time how ML-NMR allows key assumptions to be assessed’ and found ‘little evidence that the conditional constancy or shared effect modifier assumptions were invalid’ - assessed, not eliminated. ‘Practice has not moved’ is consistent with Serret-Larmande et al. 2023 (288 PAICs, overwhelmingly MAIC/STC) and with only isolated NICE applications such as the quizartinib appraisal (PMID 39627603). The one unsourced claim is that ML-NMR is harder to specify, fit, diagnose and explain; plausible and widely echoed, but I found no study measuring it.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

not-a-problem / overstated. C3 through C5 are broadly correct with important conditions. ML-NMR combines IPD and AgD coherently and can avoid conventional aggregation and non-collapsibility errors by integrating an individual-level model, but only when the outcome model, modifier structure, covariate distributions and numerical integration are adequate. It does not remove overlap, transportability or shared-modifier assumptions. C2 and C6 are comparative judgments rather than statistical results, and C1 is not a substantive claim. The presence of some IPD plus plausible modifier imbalance is insufficient to declare ML-NMR the default: method choice also depends on the estimand, network structure, target-distribution information, overlap and model credibility. C7 is a paper-specific claim outside this technical and cpaic-source audit. Training and implementation guidance may be useful, but failure to designate a universally preferred default is not an unresolved methodological problem, and the asserted very-high priority is inflated.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text: MOD-07 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising Tractability 2/5

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
Statement
No efficient influence function or TMLE is established for a mixed-IPD and aggregate-data, multi-arm network that transports arm-level potential outcomes to one declared population while retaining shared-arm covariance. The claim needs that narrowing, because adjacent problems are solved: Schnitzer et al. 2016 (doi:10.1515/jci-2016-0014) adapt doubly robust locally efficient TMLE to network meta-analysis with individual data, Dahabreh et al. (arXiv:1908.09230) build efficient robust transport estimators across multiple randomized trials, Su et al. (arXiv:2405.10769) derive the semiparametric efficiency bound of the transported average treatment effect from multi-source data, and Le et al. (arXiv:2408.04854) mix aggregate and individual data, though by M-estimation, without double robustness, and for two-arm binary treatment only. Two of the entry’s requirements also overreach: an aggregate study need not enter through a full aggregate likelihood, since summary-estimate covariance, calibration constraints or estimating equations can carry it, and small-study uncertainty is difficult rather than universally unsolved.

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
Why it is open
Standard semiparametric transport theory assumes one source sample and one target sample, whereas a network has many source studies with heterogeneous data granularity, multi-arm covariance and randomization inside each study that must survive estimation. Fluctuating or pooling an outcome model across studies can destroy the within-study randomization that supplies the network’s identification, and the usual workaround of replacing contrasts pairwise loses exactly the joint covariance the network needs. A network estimand is a vector of correlated contrasts rather than a scalar, so both a multivariate fluctuation and an influence function combining outcome models, study-participation models and aggregate contributions would have to be derived, and valid uncertainty would then have to come from a handful of studies where asymptotics in the number of studies are unavailable.

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Schnitzer, Steele, Bally & Shrier 2016, A Causal Inference Approach to Network Meta-Analysis, Journal of Causal Inference
Adapts single-study causal estimators, including doubly robust semiparametric locally efficient TMLE, to network meta-analysis. Requires individual data throughout.


Dahabreh, Robertson, Petito, Hernan & Steingrimsson, Efficient and robust transport estimators across multiple randomized trials
Builds efficient and robust estimators for transporting effects from multiple randomized trials to a target population. Requires IPD from every source.


Su, Rytgaard, Ravn & Eriksson, semiparametric efficiency for the transported average treatment effect from multi-source data
Derives the semiparametric efficiency bound of the transported average treatment effect and characterizes a class of doubly robust asymptotically linear estimators. Requires IPD from every source.


Le, Beclin, Afach & Vo, combining aggregate and individual data
Mixes aggregate and individual data, the granularity the entry cares about, but uses M-estimation, is not doubly robust, and covers binary treatment in two-arm trials only.

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Derive the efficient influence function for a connected network with IPD in a subset of studies and a declared target population, starting from the multi-trial transport and NMA-TMLE results that already exist rather than from first principles, with an estimator that respects within-study randomization, accounts for multi-arm covariance, targets arm-level potential outcomes in one population and permits cross-fitting by study. Let the aggregate studies enter through whichever coherent device fits the model, whether a likelihood contribution, a summary-estimate covariance or a calibration constraint, rather than assuming a full aggregate likelihood is required, and validate on multi-arm networks where the correct joint covariance is known by construction. A component extension replaces treatment indicators with component and interaction design vectors, which is valid only once component additivity and the interaction structure are assumed.

title: No influence-function theory for mixed-granularity multi-arm networks
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “No network efficient influence function or network TMLE exists” The title says no network efficient influence function or TMLE exists, but TMLE for network meta-analysis with individual data and multi-trial transport estimators are published.
The source said. “The report asks whether a network-level efficient influence function can be derived for evidence in which some studies contribute IPD and others contribute only aggregate data, and makes such an estimator the core of a proposed doubly robust network transport project. Its targeted counterpart, a network TMLE that preserves randomized within-study contrasts and multi-arm covariance while transporting to a declared population, is likewise stated not to exist.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no network-level efficient influence function has been derived, with an empty prior_work list; the literature auditor supplied four adjacent results (doi:10.1515/jci-2016-0014, arXiv:1908.09230, arXiv:2405.10769, arXiv:2408.04854) that narrow the novelty to the mixed-granularity multi-arm case. GPT-5.6 Sol rejected the requirement that aggregate studies must enter through a likelihood and the blanket claim that small-study uncertainty is unsolved.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Searched for a network-level efficient influence function and a network TMLE over mixed IPD and aggregate-data evidence and found nothing matching. The nearest prior art, all of which the entry omits (prior_work is empty), narrows the novelty claim considerably. Schnitzer, Steele, Bally & Shrier, ‘A Causal Inference Approach to Network Meta-Analysis’, J Causal Inference 2016 (doi 10.1515/jci-2016-0014) already adapts single-study causal estimators including a doubly robust semiparametric locally efficient TMLE to network meta-analysis, but with individual data. Dahabreh, Robertson, Petito, Hernan & Steingrimsson (arXiv:1908.09230) build efficient and robust transport estimators across MULTIPLE randomized trials to a target population, and Su, Rytgaard, Ravn & Eriksson (arXiv:2405.10769) ‘derive the semiparametric efficiency bound of the TATE’ from multi-source data; both need IPD from every source. Le, Beclin, Afach & Vo (arXiv:2408.04854) mix aggregate and individual data but use M-estimation, are not doubly robust, and cover binary treatment in two-arm trials only. So the genuinely open part is the mixed-granularity, multi-arm-covariance-preserving network version, which is a narrower and more defensible claim than ‘no network-level EIF has been derived’. The scoring claim (impact 5, novelty 5, tractability 2) is self-referential to the source report and unverifiable externally.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. At cpaic@9d150e9, cmlnmr() is a Bayesian mixed-IPD/aggregate network model, but NAMESPACE contains no EIF, AIPW, or TMLE estimator, so cpaic does not resolve C1-C2. Those absence claims are defensible only for the exact class specified: a target-transporting, mixed-granularity, multi-arm network estimator retaining shared-arm covariance. Absence is not a mathematical consequence and cannot be generalized to all network EIF or TMLE work. C3-C4 are valid design requirements in substance, although a valid joint arm-level model may respect randomization without literally preserving precomputed contrasts. C5 is false as a necessity: aggregate studies may enter through likelihoods, summary-estimate covariance, calibration constraints, or estimating equations. C6 is correct when pairwise replacement discards shared-arm covariance. C7 is too broad because small-study inference depends on the asymptotic regime and can use small-sample or Bayesian methods, although it remains difficult for the proposed semiparametric estimator. C8 works only after assuming component additivity and specified component interactions. C9 is a self-reported score, not technical evidence. The narrow mixed-granularity network target remains open, but the title and several ‘must’ or ‘unsolved’ formulations overreach.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex
