title: Synthetic-patient indirect comparisons lack a validation standard
text: EST-16 Confirmed open High priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Synthetic-patient indirect comparisons lack a validation standard
text:
Statement
Synthetic data generation trains a generative model on available individual patient data and emits artificial patient records that reproduce the source demographics, baseline characteristics and outcomes; it is now being proposed as an indirect-comparison route, carrying a claim of greater precision than MAIC where population overlap is poor. Nothing establishes what such a comparison identifies. Three questions have no answer: whether an apparent precision gain reflects information or the smoothing and extrapolation behavior of the generator, what the estimand is when synthetic records are compared against a real comparator arm, and how generator uncertainty propagates into the reported interval. The evidence base is thinner than the proposal: the precision claim is reported in a conference abstract, and the peer-reviewed review that repeats it states in print that validation evidence remains limited and that no comprehensive simulation studies have systematically assessed performance across a range of realistic rare-disease settings. No study scores the route across overlap, sample size and covariate-type regimes against MAIC, simulated treatment comparison and multilevel network meta-regression, and no reporting standard specifies which generator, which training data, and which fidelity and disclosure diagnostics must accompany a submission. The substantial adjacent literature on synthetic clinical trial data evaluates distributional fidelity, analytic utility and privacy risk; none of it addresses what a treatment contrast built on synthetic records means.

title: Synthetic-patient indirect comparisons lack a validation standard
text:
Why it is open
The claimed advantage lies exactly where the underlying data carry least information: poor overlap means few real patients resemble the target, so whatever the generator supplies in that region is model output rather than evidence, and separating the two requires a truth that the applied setting does not have. There is no estimand to check against either, because a generative model reproduces a joint distribution rather than a causal contrast, so the target quantity has to be imposed by whoever specifies the comparison and none of the current proposals does so. Uncertainty propagation is a further unresolved layer, since the generator is fitted, sampled from and then analyzed, and no published route carries fit uncertainty and synthetic sampling variability through to the interval. Evaluation also falls between two fields: the synthetic-data literature scores fidelity, utility and disclosure risk with no consensus metric and with most studies underestimating privacy risk, while the population-adjustment literature scores bias, coverage and mean squared error against a known truth, and the crossed evaluation this route needs has not been built. The work exists mainly as conference abstracts from a single group, so there is no full specification for anyone else to reproduce or refute.

title: Synthetic-patient indirect comparisons lack a validation standard
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Parkitny et al. 2026, Journal of Market Access and Health Policy
Reviews population-adjusted indirect comparison in rare disease; treats synthetic data generation as an experimental extension, repeats the precision claim from a conference abstract, and states that no comprehensive simulation studies have systematically assessed its performance across realistic rare-disease settings.


Aballea et al. 2024, Value in Health (ISPOR abstract MSR127)
Proposes synthetic data generation as a route to population-adjusted indirect comparison with an applied case in diabetic macular edema; the origin of the greater-precision-than-MAIC claim, published as a conference abstract.


Aballea et al. 2025, Value in Health (ISPOR abstract PT27)
Assesses the performance of the synthetic-data route against simulated treatment comparison for unanchored indirect comparison; the nearest thing to a benchmark, covering one comparator method and available only as an abstract.


Elvatun et al. 2025, PLOS Digital Health
Uses synthetic data as external control arms for scarce single-arm trials; the closest published relative, framed as external control rather than as indirect comparison, and inheriting the unanchored identification problem in full.


El Emam, Mosquera and Zheng 2021, JAMIA
Sequential-tree synthesis of clinical trial datasets with the variable order optimized against utility metrics; the generator technology being proposed, evaluated on distributional fidelity rather than against any causal target.


El Kababji et al. 2023, JCO Clinical Cancer Informatics
Compares sequential synthesis, conditional GAN and variational autoencoder on eight breast cancer trials, replicating published analyses and measuring attribution and membership disclosure risk; shows what a careful synthetic-data evaluation covers and what it leaves out.


Kaabachi et al. 2025, npj Digital Medicine
Scoping review of privacy and utility metrics for medical synthetic data; finds no consensus metric and that most studies underestimate privacy risk, so there is no ready-made scoring rule to borrow.


Yan et al. 2022, Nature Communications
Multifaceted benchmarking of synthetic health record generation models, establishing that no generator dominates across utility and privacy and that performance is task-dependent.


Pasculli et al. 2025, CPT: Pharmacometrics and Systems Pharmacology
Surveys definitions, regulatory frameworks and open issues for synthetic data in healthcare and drug development; the closest thing to a regulatory framing, since no agency has issued a position paper on synthetic evidence generation.


Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2022, Research Synthesis Methods
Parametric G-computation for indirect comparison, which also simulates pseudo-patients but from a specified covariate model inside a declared estimand; the disciplined comparator a generative route should be scored against.


Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2021, Research Synthesis Methods
Review and simulation study of population-adjustment methods whose factor grid over overlap, sample size and covariate structure is the standard against which any new route is evaluated.

title: Synthetic-patient indirect comparisons lack a validation standard
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define what a synthetic-data comparison identifies before scoring it: write the target as a marginal or conditional contrast in a declared population, then say which step of generate-then-analyze carries the identification, since a generator that reproduces a joint distribution supplies no causal content on its own. Score generator families against known truth on the standard population-adjustment factor grid, crossing overlap, sample size, covariate type and the strength of effect modification, with MAIC, simulated treatment comparison and multilevel network meta-regression as references and with mean squared error, coverage and interval width reported together, so that a precision gain accompanied by undercoverage is visible as such. Separate information from smoothing directly by holding the real data fixed and varying only the generator’s flexibility and its behavior outside the observed support. Build the uncertainty route, since an honest interval must carry generator fit uncertainty, synthetic sampling variability and outcome-model uncertainty; the natural candidates are a Bayesian generative model propagated through posterior predictive draws, or a bootstrap that refits the generator at every replicate. Write the reporting requirement in the same pass: generator family and hyperparameters, training data and provenance, number of synthetic records, fidelity and disclosure diagnostics, and a demonstration that the analysis reproduces the source-trial result when applied to synthetic records drawn from the source itself.

title: Synthetic-patient indirect comparisons lack a validation standard
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this from a single 2026 review, and the reviewer accepted it on the grounds that generating substitute patient records is not the same as using a flexible nuisance or outcome model inside a conventional population-adjusted comparison. An independent search of the literature confirms the thinness rather than merely the novelty: the route exists as conference abstracts from one group, the precision claim traces to a single abstract, and the peer-reviewed review states in print that no comprehensive simulation study of its performance exists.

title: Model-performance NMA lacks a target case-mix estimand

title: Model-performance NMA lacks a target case-mix estimand
text:
Statement
Network meta-analysis has been extended from treatment contrasts to contrasts in prognostic-model performance, so that scores validated in different cohorts can be ranked against each other through a shared cohort acting as a common comparator. Discrimination measures are functionals of the validation cohort’s case mix: the area under the ROC curve depends on the spread of predicted risk in the sample, so a difference in the area between two scores changes with the population even when both scores are applied without bias and both are correctly calibrated. The one published framework treats case-mix variation as a transitivity nuisance to be screened for balance across cohorts, naming characteristics such as the range of FEV1 percent predicted as variables that could affect discrimination in specific cohorts, and it reports a single pooled performance difference with no declared target population. Three objects do not exist: an estimand definition naming whose case mix a pooled performance contrast refers to, a standardization route that transports a performance difference to a declared target case mix, and a reporting rule showing how far the ranking of scores moves across the case mixes a decision might face. The single-cohort pieces have been built in the prediction-model literature, as benchmark values that separate a case-mix effect from incorrect coefficients and as a model-based concordance that predicts the c-statistic a model would attain under a different case mix. None of it has been carried into a network, where the contrast rather than the single score is the estimand and most nodes contribute only summaries.

title: Model-performance NMA lacks a target case-mix estimand
text:
Why it is open
Nothing forces the question, because a performance contrast looks like a treatment contrast: both are differences of study-level summaries, and network machinery accepts them without asking which population they refer to. Standardizing a discrimination measure to a target requires the joint distribution of predicted risk and outcome in that target, which external validation reports never publish; a single reported c-statistic does not determine what the same score would achieve elsewhere. The case-mix-corrected quantities that do exist were built for one model in one cohort and need individual data from that validation sample, so they do not compose across a network in which most cohorts supply only aggregate performance. And the decision the synthesis serves, which score to deploy in a named care setting, has no accepted target-performance estimand to be stated against, so nothing is violated when a pooled difference in discrimination is published with no population attached.

title: Model-performance NMA lacks a target case-mix estimand
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Haile et al. 2017, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Introduces Multiple Score Comparison, a network meta-analysis approach to comparing and externally validating prognostic scores across cohorts; handles case-mix variation by screening cohort characteristics for balance rather than by naming a target population for the pooled performance difference.


Vergouwe, Moons and Steyerberg 2010, American Journal of Epidemiology
Uses benchmark values computed under the validation cohort’s own case mix to separate a case-mix effect from incorrect model coefficients when a risk model performs differently on external validation; the single-study version of the standardization a network contrast would need.


van Klaveren et al. 2016, Statistics in Medicine
Defines a model-based concordance that gives the c-statistic a model would attain under a stated case mix, making discrimination comparable across validation settings; requires individual data from the validation sample.


Debray et al. 2015, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Framework for interpreting external validation studies that quantifies the relatedness of development and validation populations and separates case-mix differences from differences in predictor-outcome associations.


Debray et al. 2017, BMJ
Guide to systematic review and meta-analysis of prediction model performance; pools discrimination and calibration across validation studies and treats between-study variation in performance as heterogeneity to be summarized, not as a quantity to be transported to a target.


Debray et al. 2019, Statistical Methods in Medical Research
Meta-analysis framework for prediction model studies with binary and time-to-event outcomes, including random-effects pooling of the c-statistic with prediction intervals for performance in a new setting.


Pennells et al. 2014, American Journal of Epidemiology
Assesses risk prediction models using individual participant data from multiple studies and shows that measures of discrimination vary systematically with the case mix of the contributing cohort.


Snell et al. 2016, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Multivariate meta-analysis of individual participant data to validate a model’s discrimination and calibration jointly across studies, borrowing strength across performance measures.

title: Model-performance NMA lacks a target case-mix estimand
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define the estimand before the estimator: write a pooled performance contrast as a functional of a declared target joint distribution of predictors and outcome, so that a difference in the area under the ROC curve, in the Brier score or in net benefit at a stated threshold is indexed by the population it is claimed for. Then derive the standardization: with individual data in at least one validation cohort, a model-based concordance evaluated under the target predictor distribution gives a transportable discrimination estimate, and aggregate-only cohorts can enter through the same integration over a covariate distribution that multilevel network meta-regression already uses for treatment effects. Simulate a network of validation cohorts whose case mixes differ in predicted-risk spread while the score coefficients are held fixed, and report how often the ranking of scores reverses between cohort-specific and target-standardized contrasts. Standardize reporting to require the target case mix, the distribution of predicted risk in each contributing cohort, and a ranking-stability curve across the targets a decision might face. Characterize which performance measures transport most stably, since calibration slope and threshold-specific net benefit have different case-mix dependence from discrimination and may serve better as the primary decision output.

title: Model-performance NMA lacks a target case-mix estimand
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this from the single paper that introduced performance network meta-analysis, and the reviewer accepted it as a distinct estimand problem on the grounds that a performance contrast changes with the prediction cohort’s case-mix distribution rather than only with effect-modifier imbalance. The basis is one framework paper plus the adjacent prediction-model validation literature, so the absence of a target-standardized network performance contrast is an absence-of-evidence finding rather than a demonstrated impossibility.

title: Treatment hierarchies lack a declared target-population referent
text:
Statement
Ranking metrics in network meta-analysis, SUCRA, P-scores, probability of being best and rankograms, are functionals of the whole set of relative effects, so they inherit the population dependence of every contrast in the network at once. No ranking metric is defined with respect to a declared target covariate distribution, and no journal or health technology assessment template requires a published hierarchy to name the population it refers to. The dependence is demonstrated rather than theoretical: reweighting the trial samples in a four-medication cocaine dependence network to resemble successive target populations reordered the medications in both directions, with the medication ranked worst for abstinence becoming second best, while every pairwise interval still overlapped, so a reader of the unweighted hierarchy had no signal that the ordering was population-specific. Wigle and Moodie 2026 supply the conditional version, a hierarchy evaluated at one covariate profile from an individual participant data network meta-analysis with treatment-covariate interactions, and report a combination therapy ranked first for one hypothetical patient and fourth of six for another; they explicitly advise against the aggregate-data meta-regression route for this purpose because of ecological confounding, which closes it to the aggregate-only networks most submissions contain. What does not exist is the target-standardized version: a hierarchy computed from relative effects averaged over a named target population’s joint covariate distribution, a requirement that the population referent be stated, and a diagnostic that separates rank movement caused by sampling noise from rank movement caused by the choice of target.

title: Treatment hierarchies lack a declared target-population referent
text:
Why it is open
The ingredients sit on both sides of a join nobody has made. Population adjustment already returns population-average effects for a declared target from a mixed individual and aggregate network, and ranking metrics are computable from any posterior or covariance of relative effects, but the ranking machinery lives in packages that carry no target-population representation and the adjustment machinery ships no ranking output. The estimand is also awkward in a way a pairwise effect is not: a hierarchy is a discontinuous ordering, so uncertainty in the reported target moments propagates non-smoothly and a small change in the target distribution can flip ranks without moving any effect materially. There is no agreed answer to which population a hierarchy should refer to when one review serves several decision-makers, so the honest output is a family of hierarchies indexed by target rather than the single ordering that made rankings popular in the first place. Nothing forces the issue either: no reporting standard asks for the population referent, so an unlabeled hierarchy is never rejected.

title: Treatment hierarchies lack a declared target-population referent
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Wigle and Moodie 2026, Research Synthesis Methods
states that a standard hierarchy is not personalized to any patient and depends on the covariate distribution of the population, and adapts SUCRA to a single covariate profile from an individual participant data network meta-analysis with treatment-covariate interactions; conditional rather than target-standardized, and advised against for aggregate-data networks


Susukida et al. 2018, International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research
holds the evidence base fixed and reweights the trial samples to resemble target populations, showing that the ranking of four medications for cocaine dependence changes with the target alone


Salanti, Ades and Ioannidis 2011, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
defines SUCRA and rankograms as summaries of the posterior of relative effects, with no target covariate distribution anywhere in the definition


Rucker and Schwarzer 2015, BMC Medical Research Methodology
gives the frequentist P-score as a resampling-free analogue of SUCRA, computed from the point estimates and standard errors of relative effects and inheriting the same unstated population referent


Trinquart et al. 2016, Annals of Internal Medicine
reanalyzes published network meta-analyses to show how much sampling uncertainty rankings carry; quantifies the noise component of rank instability, which a target-sensitivity analysis would have to be separated from


Phillippo et al. 2020, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
multilevel network meta-regression produces population-average effects for an arbitrary declared target from a mixed individual and aggregate network, supplying the effect draws a target-standardized hierarchy would be computed from, but returns no ranking output


Wigle et al. 2026, arXiv:2605.15142
extends hierarchy construction to component network meta-analysis, including which hierarchy questions are estimable from a given design; extends the object without attaching a population referent to it


Phillippo et al. 2018, Medical Decision Making (NICE DSU TSD18)
requires the target population to be stated explicitly for population-adjusted indirect comparisons, the precedent this problem asks to be extended from effect estimates to hierarchies

title: Treatment hierarchies lack a declared target-population referent
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define SUCRA, P-score and probability of being best as functionals of target-standardized relative effects and compute them from a fit that already returns population-average effects for an arbitrary covariate distribution, so the hierarchy inherits a named target instead of an implicit one. Add a target-sensitivity display: recompute the hierarchy over a prespecified set of plausible targets, each contributing trial population, the pooled network population and the jurisdictional decision population, and report each treatment’s rank range across that set alongside its rank interval from sampling variability. Implement it where the target representation already exists, as a ranking method applied to the marginal effect draws produced by multilevel network meta-regression, so no new inferential machinery is needed. Require any reported hierarchy to state the population it refers to, in the way the target population is already required for population-adjusted effects in health technology appraisal.

title: Treatment hierarchies lack a declared target-population referent
text:
Our study

Treatment hierarchies across target populations
The question put to it. Does a treatment hierarchy move more across plausible target populations than across sampling variability, so that a hierarchy must name its population?
What it found. Yes: where effect modification changed the true ranking across plausible targets, the estimated hierarchy moved 1.6 to 2.4 places per treatment across targets against 0.1 to 1.4 places across sampling replicates, so a hierarchy must name its population. But estimated hierarchies also moved 0.2 to 2.1 places across targets where the true ranking did not change, through the uncertainty of meta-regression slopes away from the data’s center, so a changed hierarchy is not by itself evidence of population dependence.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: in all 10 scenarios with a true rank change, movement across targets exceeded movement across replicates beyond Monte Carlo error.
Spurious movement across targets with no true change: 0.23 to 2.07 places per treatment.
Best treatment misidentified at an outer target in up to 70% of analyses (two trials per comparison, closely spaced effects).

Design.

Estimand

Treatment ranks (P-scores) at declared target covariate means

Methods compared

fixed-effect meta-regression with P-scores at each target

Data-generating mechanism

Star networks of five treatments against a reference with treatment-specific linear modification; fixed-effect meta-regression and P-scores at three targets; rank movement across targets against movement across independent replicates. 24 cells, 1000 replicates each.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 24,000 in total


What this does not answer. Study-level meta-regression rather than ML-NMR; P-scores only; one covariate; fixed-effect. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Bucher ITC and aggregate-data NMA name no target population
text:
Statement
The Bucher adjusted indirect comparison and aggregate-data network meta-analysis produce relative effects whose formulas specify no target covariate distribution, and those effects are routinely read as common-population quantities. The assumption list is looser than the source states: what is required is transportability of same-scale direct effects to a common target, not literal balance of every effect modifier or identical trial designs, the direct evidence entering each contrast may itself synthesize several trials rather than one, and a random-effects network replaces homogeneity with an exchangeability model while also requiring connectedness. Neither method names the population its estimate refers to, and in wholly aggregate networks none can, since the population-adjusted successor that carries a network-wide target requires IPD from at least one study. The two auditors split on whether this leaves the problem open or partly solved.

title: Bucher ITC and aggregate-data NMA name no target population
text:
Why it is open
None of the identification conditions for Bucher or aggregate-data NMA pins down a covariate distribution, so there is no formal object against which population mismatch could be measured, and bias cannot even be defined until a target is chosen. Aggregate covariate summaries cannot separate individual-level effect modification from between-study gradients without strong assumptions, which is why assessment stays informal in practice. The successor that does carry a network-wide target needs IPD from at least one study, so it is unavailable exactly where the aggregate-only default is used. The maturity of the theory and software makes the common-population reading feel safe precisely where the underlying populations differ most.

title: Bucher ITC and aggregate-data NMA name no target population
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (NICE DSU TSD18)
States that a standard indirect comparison or fixed-effect network meta-analysis assumes constancy of relative effects on the linear predictor scale, requiring effect modifiers to be balanced between the trial populations, and tabulates those assumptions. It is the source for the descriptive claims about what Bucher and aggregate-data NMA assume; it does not supply a target covariate distribution for aggregate-only networks.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Its cML-NMR relative-effect path requires a named one-row effect-modifier profile, partially implementing explicit target labeling, and states that ML-NMR relative effects are population-specific whenever effect modifiers are present. It returns a conditional contrast at that profile rather than a marginal effect standardized over a population.

title: Bucher ITC and aggregate-data NMA name no target population
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Where IPD exist for at least one study, use ML-NMR as the successor that carries a network-wide target and label every network effect with the population it refers to. Where no IPD exist, the open work is different: state the population the network is being read as referring to and quantify how far the pooled parameter can sit from an effect in that population, since no aggregate-only estimator supplies one. Move effect-modification assessment from informal comparison of baseline tables to explicit modeling of within-study and between-study interaction components where the network supplies enough variation to identify them, and keep Bucher as a transparent estimator that remains decision-grade when its transport assumptions hold rather than demoting it by default.

title: Bucher ITC and aggregate-data NMA name no target population
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides. Reopened by the full-text reading: 2 findings from 2 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from unverifiable to partially-addressed.
The source said. “The Bucher adjusted indirect comparison identifies a relative effect in an implicitly common population defined only by the two connected trials sharing a comparator, and aggregate-data NMA produces network relative effects that are routinely read as common-population effects. Neither method names the population its estimate refers to, and population mismatch and effect modification across the network are only weakly assessed.”
What was wrong with it. The literature auditor confirmed every descriptive claim against NICE DSU TSD18 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) and voted the problem open for aggregate-only networks; GPT-5.6 Sol judged the same entry overstated, correcting that Bucher needs common-comparator direct evidence rather than exactly two RCTs, that the requirement is transportability rather than literal effect-modifier balance, that connectedness and exchangeability belong in the NMA assumption list, and that Bucher can still be decision-grade when its transport assumptions hold, so calling it a benchmark only inflates the severity. The disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 is accurate for the canonical Bucher calculation when relative effects are population-dependent: the formula itself does not specify a target covariate distribution. For C2 and C3, the actual requirement is transportability of the same-scale direct effects to a common target; literal balance of effect modifiers or identical designs is not necessary, and differences matter only when they modify effects or introduce bias. C4 is a reasonable practical judgment, not a mathematical result. C5 is false literally: Bucher needs direct evidence linked through a common comparator, but each direct estimate may synthesize multiple RCTs rather than exactly one trial. C6 describes sufficient fixed-effect NMA conditions incompletely: connectedness is also required, while random-effects NMA replaces homogeneity with an exchangeability/distributional model. C7 and the “usually” part of C8 are practice claims outside this audit; technically, aggregate summaries alone cannot separate within-study effect modification from between-study gradients without strong assumptions. C9 is broadly plausible but qualitative. The pooled NMA parameter is model- and weight-defined and need not equal an effect in any literal mixture population. cpaic partially addresses the target-labeling gap by requiring a named effect-modifier profile for cML-NMR output, but that output is conditional rather than marginally standardized. Bucher can still be decision-grade when its transport assumptions hold, so benchmark-only language inflates severity.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Every descriptive claim is confirmed by the full text of Phillippo et al. 2018 Med Decis Making: ‘A standard indirect comparison or (fixed effect) network meta-analysis assumes constancy of relative effects on the linear predictor scale … This requires that any and all effect modifiers are balanced between the 2 trial populations’, with Table 1 tabulating exactly those assumptions for the standard indirect comparison. Fragility to effect-modifier imbalance and design differences, the requirement of two connected RCTs sharing a comparator, and the maturity of aggregate-data NMA theory and software (netmeta, gemtc, multinma; the NICE DSU evidence-synthesis TSD series) are all uncontroversial. Weak assessment of population mismatch is corroborated by Phillippo et al. 2019 (NICE appraisal review) and Serret-Larmande et al. 2023 (3 of 133 PAIC articles reported all key methodological aspects adequately). I vote open rather than partially-solved because the entry’s scope is the aggregate-data-only setting: ML-NMR is the coherent successor that carries a network-wide target, but it requires IPD from at least one study, so for wholly aggregate networks no method names a target covariate distribution.

Bucher can still be decision-grade when its transport assumptions hold, so benchmark-only language inflates severity. title: Effect scales chosen by convention rather than transportability
text:
Statement
Odds ratios and hazard ratios are not automatically population-invariant, so they should not be treated as portable decision inputs without an explicit transport argument; that much holds. The source’s stronger claim, that risk differences, standardized risks, RMST differences and incremental net benefit are more portable across populations, does not: Dahabreh, Robertson and Steingrimsson (doi:10.1007/s10654-023-01067-4) show transportability for relative measures is largely incompatible with transportability for difference measures, and Xiao et al. (doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2021.08.002) conclude that neither the odds ratio nor the risk ratio is universally portable. The defensible core is narrower and already formalized: direct collapsibility makes marginal effects easier to standardize to a declared target (Remiro-Azocar, doi:10.1002/sim.10111), and Colnet et al. (arxiv:2303.16008) give formal criteria for which causal measure generalizes, so the selection theory the source calls missing partly exists. Incremental net benefit is the least portable quantity on the list, since it depends on local costs, utilities and willingness-to-pay thresholds.

title: Effect scales chosen by convention rather than transportability
text:
Why it is open
Choosing a scale trades off several things at once: how easily the estimand standardizes to a declared target, how stable it is across populations, how usable it is as a decision-model input, and how it behaves under random-effects synthesis, sparse events and censoring. Collapsibility settles only the first of these and no measure is stable everywhere, so an analyst who wants to switch still has no criterion that scores a measure jointly on transport and decision use for a given problem. The generalization theory that exists was developed for simple causal-inference settings rather than for indirect comparisons with aggregate targets, non-collapsible link functions and network structure. In component or additive-model settings the choice is further constrained, since marginal component effects are not generally additive, as documented at commit 9d150e9 of cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN.

title: Effect scales chosen by convention rather than transportability
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Dahabreh, Robertson and Steingrimsson 2024, European Journal of Epidemiology
Shows that transportability for relative effect measures is largely incompatible with transportability for difference effect measures unless the treatment has no effect on average, which contradicts a blanket ranking of absolute measures as more portable.


Xiao, Chu, Cole, Chen, MacLehose, Richardson and Greenland 2021, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Concludes that neither the odds ratio nor the risk ratio is universally portable, so no ratio measure can be assumed stable across populations by default.


Remiro-Azocar 2024, Transportability of model-based estimands in evidence synthesis, Statistics in Medicine 43(22):4217-4249
Gives the formal argument that directly collapsible measures facilitate the transportability of marginal effects between studies, which is the defensible core of the source’s Direction D and is about ease of standardization rather than empirical constancy.


Colnet, Josse, Varoquaux and Scornet, Risk ratio, odds ratio, risk difference… Which causal measure is easier to generalize?
Existing formal theory for selecting an effect measure for generalization, showing that only the risk difference has its conditional and average treatment effects disentangled from the baseline regardless of outcome type, and that the covariate set needed depends on the measure chosen. It is developed outside the indirect-comparison setting.


multinma: Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Individual and Aggregate Data (R package)
Its marginal_effects() defaults to a difference scale, contradicting the claim that software defaults push analysts toward odds ratios and hazard ratios.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Documents that marginal component effects are not generally additive and add exactly only when the standardized treatment effects remain affine in the component design, which constrains scale choice in component analyses.

title: Effect scales chosen by convention rather than transportability
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build on Colnet et al. rather than starting from nothing: extend measure-selection criteria to the indirect-comparison setting, where the target is described by aggregate summaries and the network imposes its own constraints, and score candidates on standardization cost and decision usability rather than on a presumed portability ranking. Establish how the candidate scales behave under random-effects synthesis, sparse events and censoring, so that a switch is statistically supported rather than advocated. Keep odds ratios and hazard ratios as modeling parameters where convenient, standardize to the declared target before any decision use, and check component additivity on whichever scale the analysis runs on.

title: Effect scales chosen by convention rather than transportability
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Directly collapsible measures make marginal effects easier to standardize to a declared target covariate distribution, because for non-collapsible measures even purely prognostic variables shift the marginal effect; this is a reason to standardize explicitly before decision use, not evidence that risk differences or RMST differences are empirically more constant across populations than odds or hazard ratios.
The source said. “Direction D proposes selecting the effect measure for transportability and decision usability, prioritizing risk differences and standardized risks, mean differences, survival-probability differences at clinically relevant times, RMST differences, cumulative incidence differences, and incremental net benefit. Odds ratios and hazard ratios may remain useful model parameters but should not automatically be treated as population-invariant decision inputs.”
What was wrong with it. The source ranked collapsible and absolute measures as more portable and said no theory exists for selecting a scale; the literature auditor found the ranking contradicted by Dahabreh et al. (doi:10.1007/s10654-023-01067-4) and Xiao et al. (doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2021.08.002), found existing selection theory in Colnet et al. (arxiv:2303.16008), and found the software-default claim false since multinma’s marginal_effects() defaults to a risk difference. GPT-5.6 Sol added that risk differences move with baseline risk under a constant conditional odds ratio, that standardized risks, survival differences, RMST and cumulative-incidence differences all depend on the target law, time horizon and competing events, and that incremental net benefit additionally depends on costs, utilities and thresholds.
Dissent. codex dissented (open): C2 and C3 are correct: marginal odds ratios are non-collapsible, and marginal hazard ratios depend on risk-set composition; neither is automatically population-invariant, although conditional log-odds and log-hazard parameters remain useful modeling devices. C1 and C4 conflate collapsibility, decision relevance, and transportability. Under a constant conditional odds ratio but differing baseline risks, risk differences vary across populations. Standardized risks, survival differences, RMST, and cumulative-incidence differences likewise depend on the target distribution, baseline hazards, competing events, and time horizon. Incremental net benefit additionally depends on costs, utilities, and willingness-to-pay. These quantities are often better decision outputs after target standardization, but they are not intrinsically more portable. Component PAIC also requires compatibility with the component model: cpaic at 9d150e9 documents that marginal component effects need not be additive. The context-specific scale-selection issue remains open, but the blanket prioritization and very-high severity are inflated.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

closure-upheld

9 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors’ reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. The findings support the residual already preserved by the closure: scale choice is consequential, data rarely identify the best modeling scale, and no universal portability ranking exists. The 2026 survival-PAIC finding directly reinforces the closure by showing that collapsible RMST is not automatically directly transportable when effect modification is modeled on the log-hazard scale. Earlier NMA papers establish that practical scale selection remains difficult, but do not contradict the cited formal generalization theory or establish that risk differences, standardized risks, RMST differences, or incremental net benefit are intrinsically more portable. The closure properly rejects the blanket ranking while leaving the context-specific network and decision-use selection problem open. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening

12 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries overstated Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit’s closure needs the closure’s own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The claim that collapsible and absolute measures are ‘more portable across populations’ than odds and hazard ratios conflates collapsibility with transportability, and the epidemiological literature actively contradicts it. Dahabreh, Robertson & Steingrimsson (Eur J Epidemiol 2024) note that ‘many epidemiologists and applied statisticians believe that relative effect measures … are transportable across populations or at least more likely to be transportable compared with difference (absolute) effect measures’, and prove that ‘transportability for relative effect measures is largely incompatible with transportability for difference effect measures’. Xiao, Chu, Cole, Chen, MacLehose, Richardson & Greenland (J Clin Epidemiol 2021) conclude ‘Neither the odds ratio nor the risk ratio is universally portable’. What is defensible is narrower and is already theorized: Remiro-Azocar (Stat Med 2024) shows directly collapsible measures ‘facilitate the transportability of marginal effects between studies’, and Colnet, Josse, Varoquaux & Scornet (arXiv:2303.16008) show only the risk difference disentangles CATE and ATE from baseline while stressing that the covariate set needed depends on the measure chosen. The claim about software defaults also fails: multinma’s marginal_effects() defaults to a risk difference. Incremental net benefit, being cost- and threshold-dependent, is the least jurisdiction-portable quantity on the list. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.10111: Provides the formal argument linking direct collapsibility to easier transport of marginal effects, i.e. the defensible core of Direction D.. Cites arxiv:2303.16008: Existing formal theory for selecting an effect measure for generalization, which the entry says does not exist..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C2 and C3 are correct: marginal odds ratios are non-collapsible, and marginal hazard ratios depend on risk-set composition; neither is automatically population-invariant, although conditional log-odds and log-hazard parameters remain useful modeling devices. C1 and C4 conflate collapsibility, decision relevance, and transportability. Under a constant conditional odds ratio but differing baseline risks, risk differences vary across populations. Standardized risks, survival differences, RMST, and cumulative-incidence differences likewise depend on the target distribution, baseline hazards, competing events, and time horizon. Incremental net benefit additionally depends on costs, utilities, and willingness-to-pay. These quantities are often better decision outputs after target standardization, but they are not intrinsically more portable. Component PAIC also requires compatibility with the component model: cpaic at 9d150e9 documents that marginal component effects need not be additive. The context-specific scale-selection issue remains open, but the blanket prioritization and very-high severity are inflated.

How the evidence falls in time

title: The MAIC paradox: swapping the IPD trial can reverse the comparison
text:
Statement
Reversing which trial supplies the IPD can reverse the direction of the apparent active-treatment comparison while each analysis remains internally coherent, because the two analyses estimate effects in different target populations. This is not new with Jiang et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10), who credit NICE DSU TSD18: Phillippo et al. 2018 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) documented the same reversal in a real appraisal, two competing manufacturers’ MAICs of secukinumab and adalimumab, and prescribed the remedy this entry proposes, namely deciding which population represents the decision target and transporting the comparison to it under the shared effect modifier assumption. Jiang et al.’s increment is that the paradox persists even when both analyses use the same covariate set. A target-population difference is also not the only way two MAICs can disagree; sampling error, different adjustment sets, model misspecification and measurement differences can each do it.

title: The MAIC paradox: swapping the IPD trial can reverse the comparison
text:
Why it is open
Pairwise MAIC contains no mechanism forcing both directions of an analysis to answer the same question, because the target is set by which trial supplies IPD rather than by the decision. The remedy has been on the books since 2018 and has not changed sponsor behavior, since each sponsor’s own trial is the natural source of its IPD and nothing obliges two competing submissions to share a target. Transporting both effects to one declared target also needs common support, compatible outcome definitions and enough information to carry both transports, which is often exactly what is missing when the two populations differ enough to produce the reversal. How often the reversal arises and under what covariate configurations is unmeasured, so it is still discovered after submission rather than anticipated.

title: The MAIC paradox: swapping the IPD trial can reverse the comparison
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Jiang et al. 2025, A critical assessment of matching-adjusted indirect comparisons in relation to target populations, Research Synthesis Methods
Describes the reversal, its internal coherence and its population explanation, stating that both conclusions are potentially valid within the context of the specific populations considered, and shows the paradox persists with a common covariate set. It credits TSD18 for the original example and recommends IPD sharing rather than ruling on averaging.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (NICE DSU TSD18)
Documents the two-way MAIC reversal in practice, with two MAIC analyses from competing manufacturers comparing treatments for ankylosing spondylitis, and prescribes the fix the entry proposes: decide which population represents the decision target and transport the comparison to it under the shared effect modifier assumption.


Fang and He 2026, Arbitrated Indirect Treatment Comparisons
A dedicated methodological response to the MAIC paradox that fixes a single common target, the overlap population, rather than a sponsor-specific one. It does not establish how often the reversal occurs or which target a committee should prefer.

title: The MAIC paradox: swapping the IPD trial can reverse the comparison
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Do not average conflicting MAICs unless the average is deliberately defined as an effect in a specified mixture population and the conditions for that definition hold. The remaining work is empirical and procedural rather than conceptual: characterize how often and under which covariate configurations the reversal arises, and give appraisal committees a rule for what to do when two sponsor submissions target different populations. Fang and He’s arbitrated indirect comparison (arxiv:2510.18071) is an existing methodological response that fixes a single common overlap target instead of a sponsor-specific one, so the task is to evaluate it against transporting both effects to an external decision target, not to reinvent it.

title: The MAIC paradox: swapping the IPD trial can reverse the comparison
text:
Our study

When two sponsors’ MAICs disagree: how often, why, and which common target resolves it
The question put to it. When two sponsors run MAIC on the same two trials, each weighting its own data to the other trial, how often do their conclusions reverse, how much of that is a real difference in target population rather than sampling error or differing adjustment sets, and which common-target remedy recovers the decision population’s effect?
What it found. Reversal is mostly a real target difference and it is common: with the modifier’s zero-effect point between the two populations, sponsors disagreed in sign in 23% to 56% of analyses at separations up to 1 SD and modification up to 0.4, and moving the point outside the populations cut that by a median 0.31. The two sponsors’ estimates are correlated, which a reversal calculation must use. Under linear modification the plain average of the two analyses is as accurate for the midpoint population as transporting both trials there.
Results.

Between-minus-outside reversal probability exceeded 0.20 in 11 of 18 common-set configurations (median 0.31); the refuting sentence, that reversals need extreme configurations, fails.
Correlation between the two sponsors’ estimates 0.14 to 0.99; a bivariate normal with that correlation predicted the reversal probability within 0.036, and ignoring it erred by up to 0.44.
A sponsor that left the modifier out of its weights was biased by 0.10 to 0.91 against its own target.
Transport of both trials to a declared population and the average of the two analyses: largest bias 0.024 and 0.027, median RMSE 0.231 and 0.239.

Design.

Estimand

B-versus-A mean difference in each sponsor’s target population and in a declared decision population

Methods compared

sponsor A MAIC, sponsor B MAIC, transport of both trials to a declared population, average of the two analyses

Data-generating mechanism

Two trials with linear modification of one treatment, analyzed by two sponsors each weighting its own trial to the other’s population; 108 scenarios crossing separation, modification strength, the position of the zero-effect point, trial sizes and adjustment sets, plus controls; transport of both trials to a declared population and the average of the two analyses as remedies.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 111,000 in total


What this does not answer. Linear modification and a continuous outcome; with nonlinear modification or a non-collapsible scale the average is not the midpoint effect. The arbitrated indirect comparison and measurement differences between trials were not run. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: The MAIC paradox: swapping the IPD trial can reverse the comparison
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Jiang et al. describe a target-population problem in which reversing which trial supplies the IPD can reverse the apparent active-treatment comparison, even when each analysis is internally coherent. The two analyses are not contradictory implementations; they estimate effects in different target populations.”
What was wrong with it. The source read as though Jiang et al. 2025 discovered the reversal and as though the ban on averaging came from them; the literature auditor found the reversal documented with an applied case in NICE DSU TSD18 nine years earlier (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740), along with the same prescribed fix, and found no recommendation against averaging in Jiang et al., who instead call for IPD sharing with HTA agencies. GPT-5.6 Sol added that a target-population difference is not the only cause of discordant MAICs and that a weighted average is not invalid in principle if it is deliberately defined as an effect in a specified mixture population.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. I read the full text of Jiang et al. 2025 (PMC12527493). The reversal, its internal coherence and its population explanation are all verbatim there (‘both conclusions … are potentially valid within the context of the specific populations considered’). But the entry reads as if Jiang et al. discovered the phenomenon. They did not, and they say so, crediting NICE DSU TSD18. Phillippo et al. 2018 Med Decis Making documented the same reversal with a real applied case nine years earlier and prescribed the entry’s own proposed direction: ‘the real conflict lies not in the different results produced by the 2 MAICs but in deciding which of the 2 study populations better represents the decision target population … the shared effect modifier assumption, if justified, may be used to transport indirect comparisons into the target population for the decision.’ Jiang et al.’s genuine increment is that the paradox persists with the same covariate set. Separately, the claim that averaging is invalid is not in Jiang et al.; they recommend IPD sharing to HTA agencies. Fang & He (arXiv:2510.18071, v2 May 2026) is an explicit methodological response targeting the overlap population. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740: Documents the two-way MAIC reversal in practice and prescribes the fix the entry proposes: declare the decision target and transport both effects to it under the shared effect modifier assumption.. Cites arxiv:2510.18071: A dedicated methodological response to the MAIC paradox that fixes a single common target (the overlap population) rather than a sponsor-specific one..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. C1 and C2 are technically possible: if swapping the IPD trial swaps the target population and the marginal treatment contrast varies across populations, the sign can reverse without a software error. C3 explains the constructed target-population paradox but is not the only possible cause of discordant MAICs; sampling error, different adjustment sets, model misspecification, and measurement differences can also reverse results. C4 is right for an unprincipled average of different estimands. A weighted average can be valid only if it is deliberately defined as an effect in a specified mixture population and the required linearity or standardization conditions hold. C5 states the correct design principle, subject to common support, compatible outcome definitions, and sufficient data or assumptions to transport both effects. C6 is acceptable as saying Jiang et al. describes the phenomenon, not that it uniquely discovered it. The conceptual cause and common-target remedy are already available; feasibility and empirical frequency remain open, so very-high severity is conditional rather than automatic. Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10: Demonstrates and explains the reversal as comparison of population-specific estimands rather than necessarily a software contradiction.. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740: Already prescribes choosing the decision target and transporting effects to it under stated assumptions.. Cites arxiv:2510.18071: Implements a common overlap-population target as one concrete response to sponsor-specific target reversal..

Decision path

section: How the evidence falls in time
text:
How the evidence falls in time
6 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2017 to 2026. The most recent paper to touch this reports progress on it, and every paper calling it open is older.
It is also being closed in pieces: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.
Does the later work answer the earlier work? Put to an independent reviewer with the older and newer claims side by side, it judged that the later work answers a component of it, leaving a named part (high confidence). Later work identifies the estimand mismatch mechanism, demonstrates that reversal can occur even with the same correct modifier set, and supplies an overlap-target estimator that removes the reciprocal discrepancy for that target. It does not establish that the overlap population is the appropriate decision target or solve the governance problem required to impose it. What remains: Selecting a decision-relevant common target population and establishing an institutional way to arbitrate it remain unresolved; disagreement can also arise from sampling, measurement, adjustment-set, and model failures.

title: Methods return incompatible marginal and conditional estimands
text:
Statement
MAIC targets a marginal effect while a regression-based analysis returns a conditional one, so results from different population-adjustment methods are not directly comparable, and effect modification together with non-collapsibility can drive conditional and marginal estimates to conflicting treatment rankings (Phillippo et al. 2025, doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2). The source’s description of standard STC as yielding a clean conditional effect is wrong: in typical use it subtracts a published marginal comparator contrast from a conditional coefficient, and is biased for either estimand (Phillippo et al. 2021, doi:10.1002/sim.8965). The reconciliation the source proposes already exists and has been evaluated: parametric G-computation (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1565) and multiple imputation marginalization (doi:10.1186/s12874-024-02157-x) marginalize an outcome regression over a target population, and outstandR ships both (arxiv:2601.07532). What is left is discipline in use rather than a missing method: comparative evaluations still have to hold the estimand fixed, and some implementations return only one of the two quantities.

title: Methods return incompatible marginal and conditional estimands
text:
Why it is open
The methods differ in where averaging over covariates happens, and on a non-collapsible scale averaging before and after the link function gives different numbers, so the discrepancy is not an artifact that better fitting removes. Applied comparisons of MAIC, STC and ML-NMR therefore often measure the estimand difference rather than estimator performance, and both quantities are printed on the same scale under the same name, so a reviewer cannot detect the switch from the output alone. Marginalization is available but is not the default everywhere: multinma returns conditional and marginal population-average effects as separately named outputs, while cpaic returns a conditional profile contrast from cML-NMR and documents that no population-standardized path exists yet. Marginalizing also requires a correctly specified outcome model, a defined target joint covariate law and adequate support, so it recovers a compatible marginal functional rather than making the conditional and marginal parameters identical.

title: Methods return incompatible marginal and conditional estimands
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo, Remiro-Azocar, Heath, Baio, Dias, Ades and Welton 2025, Effect modification and non-collapsibility together may lead to conflicting treatment decisions: A review of marginal and conditional estimands and recommendations for decision-making, Research Synthesis Methods 16(2):323-349
Supplies the missing citation for the conflicting-decisions claim and for reporting both estimands in the decision target population, and states that multilevel network meta-regression is currently the only population-adjustment method able to produce both conditional and marginal estimates in any decision target population.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades and Welton 2021, Target estimands for efficient decision making: Response to comments on Assessing the performance of population adjustment methods for anchored indirect comparisons: A simulation study, Statistics in Medicine
States that STC in typical usage estimates neither the marginal nor the conditional population-average treatment effect and is biased for either, because it combines conditional and marginal quantities. This contradicts the source’s description of standard STC as a conditional estimand.


Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2022, Parametric G-computation for compatible indirect treatment comparisons with limited individual patient data, Research Synthesis Methods
Provides and evaluates marginalization of an outcome regression over the relevant population so that regression-based PAIC returns an estimand compatible with MAIC’s marginal effect.


Model-based standardization using multiple imputation, BMC Medical Research Methodology 2024
Delivers the multiple imputation marginalization route the source proposed as future work, marginalizing over a target covariate distribution with simulation benchmarking under a correctly specified parametric outcome model.


Population-Adjusted Indirect Treatment Comparison with the outstandR Package in R, 2026
Unified software implementing maximum-likelihood and Bayesian G-computation plus multiple imputation marginalization explicitly to address non-collapsibility, so the compatible-estimand route is packaged rather than research-only.


multinma: Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Individual and Aggregate Data (R package)
Returns conditional and marginal population-average effects as separately named outputs from one fitted model, so the two estimands need not be conflated in a network analysis.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Labels cMAIC output as a marginal weighted effect and cSTC and cML-NMR output as conditional, and documents that there is no marginal population-standardized effect path yet, so only the conditional effect at a point is returned from cML-NMR.

title: Methods return incompatible marginal and conditional estimands
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Use the existing marginalization routes instead of proposing them as new work: parametric G-computation or multiple imputation marginalization, both implemented in outstandR, and multinma’s separately named conditional and marginal outputs. Report conditional and marginal quantities in the declared decision target population where each is policy relevant, following the recommendations in Phillippo et al. 2025. Hold the estimand fixed before comparing MAIC, STC and ML-NMR, so head-to-head evaluations measure estimator performance rather than an estimand difference. Where an implementation returns only one quantity, as cML-NMR does in cpaic, the concrete task is to add the standardization step rather than to relabel the output.

title: Methods return incompatible marginal and conditional estimands
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides. Reopened by the full-text reading: 4 findings from 4 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from unverifiable to partially-addressed.
The source said. “MAIC usually targets a marginal effect while standard STC often yields a conditional effect, and ML-NMR may return yet another quantity, so results from different population-adjustment methods are not directly comparable. The report states this mismatch can produce conflicting decisions if it is ignored.”
What was wrong with it. The claim was unattributed in the source and is now sourced: the literature auditor supplied Phillippo et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2) for the conflicting-decisions claim and for reporting both estimands, and Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021, Research Synthesis Methods 12(6):750-775, for the marginal versus conditional mismatch between MAIC and STC. The same auditor found the proposed reconciliation already built and benchmarked (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1565; doi:10.1186/s12874-024-02157-x), and both auditors rejected the description of typical STC as a clean conditional estimand. GPT-5.6 Sol added that in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, cML-NMR at commit 9d150e9 has no marginal standardization path at all, so the mismatch is live in that package even though the labeling is correct.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): This entry is flagged SOURCE-A-UNSOURCED; I can supply real sources for every claim. Phillippo, Remiro-Azocar, Heath, Baio, Dias, Ades & Welton, Research Synthesis Methods 16(2):323-349 (2025) is a direct source for the ‘conflicting decisions’ claim (‘effect modification can result in conflicting treatment rankings between conditional and marginal estimates’) and for reporting both (‘pragmatic comparisons of both conditional and marginal estimates in the decision target population’). Remiro-Azocar et al., Res Synth Methods 12(6):750-775 (2021) sources the MAIC-marginal / STC-conditional mismatch directly. But the methods half of the problem is largely solved, not open: parametric G-computation (Res Synth Methods 2022) and multiple imputation marginalization (BMC Med Res Methodol 2024) were built precisely to bring conditional regressions onto a compatible marginal scale, both with simulation evaluation, and outstandR (arXiv:2601.07532) ships both. multinma returns conditional and marginal population-average effects as separately named outputs. Caveat: Phillippo et al. contest the framing that typical STC yields a clean conditional effect - they say it mixes conditional and marginal quantities and is biased for either. codex dissented (supported-with-caveat): C1 is a placeholder, not a claim. C2 is correct for conventional anchored MAIC. C3 is correct only for the IPD regression contrast: a conventional anchored STC indirect comparison often subtracts a marginal published comparator contrast from that conditional coefficient and is therefore a hybrid, not a clean conditional A-versus-B estimand. C4, C5, and the possibility in C7 are sound. C6 is too vague to rank technically: ML-NMR can integrate nonlinear outcome models, but its reported estimand is implementation-specific. At cpaic@9d150e9, cmaic() returns a marginal weighted effect, cstc() a conditional effect at target means, and cmlnmr() only a conditional profile contrast; NAMESPACE has no marginal_effects export. C8 is valid under a correctly specified outcome model, a defined target joint law, and support; it estimates a compatible marginal functional rather than making conditional and marginal parameters identical. C9 is sensible. This mismatch can be decision-critical on non-collapsible scales, but established G-computation and multiple-imputation marginalization make it partly solved rather than a wholly open very-high-priority method gap.

title: Anchored PAIC needs a second transport to the decision population
text: EST-02 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging

title: Anchored PAIC needs a second transport to the decision population
text:
Statement
A conventional anchored PAIC with IPD for A versus C and aggregate data for B versus C identifies an A versus B effect defined in the comparator-trial population, and applying that effect to the index-trial baseline or to a jurisdictional decision population is a second, distinct transport step. Chandler and Ishak (arxiv:2602.17041) state both points explicitly, and Jiang et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10) independently confirm the comparator-population estimand. What is new is the explicit two-step framing rather than the identification condition: NICE DSU TSD18 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) already invoked the shared effect modifier assumption to transport an indirect comparison into the decision target population, and Phillippo et al. 2021 (doi:10.1002/sim.8965) warned that MAIC and STC estimates may not represent that population. How often the second step is left implicit in published analyses and submissions is an empirical claim this audit did not establish.

title: Anchored PAIC needs a second transport to the decision population
text:
Why it is open
The two transports are structurally different operations, but a standard PAIC workflow produces a single number that is then reused for whichever population the decision model needs. The first transport is performed by the estimator and the second by the economic modeler, so no one document states both sets of assumptions and the second is rarely assessed. On non-collapsible scales the second step changes the estimand rather than relabeling it, so the consequence is substantive rather than cosmetic. What is genuinely unsettled is not the identification theory, which is standard transport theory, but whether an analysis has the target covariate law, the covariate support, and an explicit second-stage model to carry the step out.

title: Anchored PAIC needs a second transport to the decision population
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Chandler and Ishak 2026, Reframing Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons as a Transportability Problem: An Estimand-Based Perspective and Implications for Health Technology Assessment
States that pairwise PAICs treat the index trial as source and the comparator trial as target, yielding effects defined in the comparator population, and that the Step 1 estimate is often applied to a different target without being formally identified as a second transport step. It makes the two-step structure explicit; it does not supply the reporting or software changes that would separate the steps in practice.


Jiang et al. 2025, A critical assessment of matching-adjusted indirect comparisons in relation to target populations, Research Synthesis Methods
Independently confirms that a pairwise MAIC estimand is defined in the comparator-trial population, and works through the consequences for target populations.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (NICE DSU TSD18)
Already states the need to define the decision target and to generate population-adjusted effects for it, and invokes the shared effect modifier assumption precisely to transport an indirect comparison into the decision target population, so the identification condition for the second step predates the two-step framing.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades and Welton 2021, Target estimands for efficient decision making: Response to comments on Assessing the performance of population adjustment methods for anchored indirect comparisons: A simulation study, Statistics in Medicine
Warns that MAIC and STC estimates may not be representative of the decision target population, and that marginal population-average effects depend more strongly on the population of interest than population-average conditional effects.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
For cML-NMR output it forces a target profile when effect modifiers are present and labels the returned estimand as conditional, stating that relative effects from a model with effect modifiers are population-specific so there is no population-free answer. This is estimand labeling in one unreleased package, not a general separation of first-stage and second-stage transport.

title: Anchored PAIC needs a second transport to the decision population
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The identification conditions for each step follow from existing transport theory, so the work is to separate the two estimands in reporting, software output and appraisal templates rather than to derive new conditions. Require every reported contrast to name its source and target population, and make the second-stage transport an explicit modeled step with stated inputs instead of an assumption absorbed into an economic model. Some software already labels the estimand this way: in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, the cML-NMR path at commit 9d150e9 forces a target profile when effect modifiers are present and prints the result as a conditional effect, which is the pattern to generalize. Where the target covariate law is unavailable, report the comparator-population effect as what it is and give sensitivity analysis over plausible decision targets.

title: Anchored PAIC needs a second transport to the decision population
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from unverifiable to partially-addressed, on a single finding.
The source titled this. “The hidden second transport step in anchored PAIC” The title calls the second transport step hidden, but the audit could not establish how often it is left implicit and found its identification condition already in NICE DSU TSD 18.
The source said. “A conventional anchored PAIC with IPD for A versus C and aggregate data for B versus C identifies an A versus B effect in the comparator-trial population, yet economic models routinely apply that effect to the index-trial baseline or to a jurisdictional decision population. That application is a second, distinct transport operation with its own identification requirements, and it is usually left implicit.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented the two-transport distinction as newly formalized and therefore unabsorbed by practice; the literature auditor confirmed the distinction verbatim in Chandler and Ishak (arxiv:2602.17041) but found the second step’s identification condition already in NICE DSU TSD18 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) and in Phillippo et al. 2021 (doi:10.1002/sim.8965), and the frequency claim about economic models unestablished. GPT-5.6 Sol judged the entry supported with caveats, holding that the identification conditions for a second transport are standard transport conditions and that moment balance alone does not identify the comparator population’s full covariate law; the two auditors disagreed over whether this leaves the problem open or partly solved, and the disagreement stands.
Dissent. codex dissented (supported-with-caveat): C1 is correct under anchoring, conditional-constancy or transportability, positivity, compatible effect-scale, and adequate balance assumptions. C2 is correct for a population-specific marginal effect: moving from the comparator-trial population to an index or jurisdictional population is a distinct transport. C3 and C4 are empirical frequency claims, not technical facts established here. C5 is faithful to the supplied source. C6-C8 overstate unresolvedness: identification conditions for a second transport are standard transport conditions, target choice is a design or policy decision, and non-collapsibility is a known property handled by target-specific standardization rather than a defect that can be eliminated. C9 is literally correct about balancing reported moments, but moment balance does not by itself identify the comparator population’s full covariate law. The conceptual separation and some software labeling already exist; the remaining open issue is whether analyses actually have the target data, support, and explicit second-stage model.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. I retrieved the abstract and HTML body of arXiv:2602.17041 (Chandler & Ishak, v3, revised 6 July 2026). Every attributed claim is present verbatim: ‘pairwise PAICs such as MAICs and STCs necessarily treat the index trial as the source population and the comparator trial as the target population, yielding relative treatment effect estimates defined in the comparator population’; and ‘the adjusted effect estimate from Step 1 is often applied directly to a different target population - typically, the index trial, implicitly assuming direct transportability … without being formally identified as a second transport step in practice.’ Jiang et al. 2025 (full text read) independently confirms the comparator-population estimand. The citation is load-bearing, not decorative. One calibration note for the why_open, not the claims: the second step’s identification condition is not new.
