title: Published PAIC analyses cannot be reconstructed from the record
section: How the evidence falls in time
text:
How the evidence falls in time
22 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2013 to 2026. The most recent paper to touch this reports progress on it, and every paper calling it open is older.
This problem is recurrent: three or more papers spanning at least eight years assert it independently. Sustained restatement by authors who mostly do not cite each other is the strongest evidence this reading can offer that a gap is real rather than one group’s framing.
It is also being closed in pieces: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.
Does the later work answer the earlier work? Put to an independent reviewer with the older and newer claims side by side, it judged that the later work answers a component of it, leaving a named part (high confidence). The later PA-NMA provides public code and identifies its software stack, so it addresses the code-availability component for that analysis. It withholds the confidential IPD and does not provide the broader reproducibility record required to independently rerun or audit published PAICs. What remains: Routine auditability of published PAICs, including access to usable inputs, executable environments, extraction provenance, and computational provenance, remains unresolved.

title: Intervals omit selection, reconstruction and target-summary error
text:
Statement
The estimated-weights component of this problem is solved and evaluated: Chandler and Proskorovsky 2024 (10.1002/jrsm.1759) compared four families of MAIC variance estimator across 108 scenarios and give guidance by overlap, effective sample size and outcome type, following Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021 (10.1002/jrsm.1511), which had shown the robust sandwich estimator understates variability at small ESS. What remains unpropagated is model-selection uncertainty where selection used the analyzed data, pseudo-IPD reconstruction uncertainty, target-summary uncertainty, and any decomposition separating sampling from prior and structural contributions. Bridge uncertainty belongs on that list only with a caveat: it is structural rather than sampling-based and should be reported through separate sensitivity or tipping analysis unless a defensible probability model supports joint propagation. The claim that standard software returns one interval with no components is also not true of cpaic, an unreleased GitHub development package not on CRAN, which re-estimates MAIC weights inside an arm-stratified bootstrap, preserves multi-arm covariance, and carries an integration-error diagnostic for component ML-NMR.

title: Intervals omit selection, reconstruction and target-summary error
text:
Why it is open
Interval estimates are conditional on the selected model, so a selection step carried out on the analyzed data leaves the reported interval too narrow, and no ITC reporting convention requires selection uncertainty to be accounted for. Each remaining component enters at a different stage of a multi-step pipeline, and the final stage that produces the interval has no access to what earlier stages introduced. Numerical integration error is a deterministic approximation error, so the fix is bounding and convergence assessment rather than treatment as another random variance component; the existing diagnostic traces nested approximations against the final grid rather than against the exact integral and is unavailable for survival models.

title: Intervals omit selection, reconstruction and target-summary error
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Chandler and Proskorovsky 2024
108-scenario simulation comparing four families of MAIC variance estimator; finds raw-weight conventional estimators understate variability under poor or moderate overlap, ESS-weighted conventional estimators accurate across most scenarios, and sandwich estimators downward-biased at small ESS without finite-sample adjustment.


Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2021
Earlier evidence that the robust sandwich variance estimator underestimates variability in MAIC where effective sample sizes are small.


cpaic (development package, audited at commit 9d150e9)
Unreleased development package on GitHub, confirmed by an auditor not to be on CRAN. Re-estimates MAIC weights and refits the outcome model inside an arm-stratified bootstrap, preserves multi-arm covariance through netmeta for the frequentist bridge and the standard 0.5 baseline-shift correlation for random effects, and provides a nested-Sobol integration-error diagnostic; selection, target-summary, pseudo-IPD and bridge-uncertainty decomposition remain unimplemented.

title: Intervals omit selection, reconstruction and target-summary error
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Adopt the published variance-estimation guidance for weights instead of treating it as open, and extend propagation to the stages still conditioned on: pseudo-IPD reconstruction, target summaries including their covariance, and model selection where the selection used the analyzed data. Require full model specification with priors and random-effects structure, explicit separation of within-study from between-study effect modification, justification of shared versus treatment- or component-specific interactions, and presentation of substantively plausible alternative models. Report structural bridge uncertainty and numerical error separately, as sensitivity regions and convergence bounds, rather than merging them into a single interval.

title: Intervals omit selection, reconstruction and target-summary error
text:
Our study

Coverage of an STC interval after selecting effect modifiers on the same data
The question put to it. When effect modifiers are selected on the analyzed data before an STC, does an interval that treats the selected model as fixed keep its coverage, and does resampling the whole procedure restore it?
What it found. Selecting effect modifiers on the analyzed data (interactions with p < 0.2) left the naive STC interval covering 0.887 to 0.927, because its SE ignored which model was selected; a bootstrap that repeats the selection restored 0.938 to 0.968. Lasso at the one-standard-error penalty dropped real modifiers and coverage fell to 0.33 with three modifiers at 1000 per arm. Fitting all candidate interactions kept coverage at 0.93 to 0.96.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: naive coverage after significance selection below 0.93 beyond Monte Carlo error in some scenarios (0.887 to 0.927); bias at most 0.046.
Whole-procedure bootstrap: 0.938 to 0.968.
Lasso (lambda 1se) kept on average 0.01 to 0.15 interactions; coverage as low as 0.333 and bias about -0.2 with three real modifiers.
The shortfall was not monotone in sample size with three modifiers (largest at 300 per arm), as registered.

Design.

Estimand

Target-population marginal log odds ratio, A versus C

Methods compared

all interactions, oracle interactions, no interactions, p < 0.2 selection with naive interval, p < 0.2 selection with whole-procedure bootstrap, lasso selection

Data-generating mechanism

G-computation STC with six candidate modifiers, five selection rules (all, oracle, none, p < 0.2, lasso), naive and whole-procedure bootstrap intervals, three sample sizes and one or three true modifiers. 400 replicates per cell.

Replicates

400 per scenario, 2,400 in total, each with a 60-resample bootstrap


What this does not answer. STC only; MAIC-based selection, overlap, larger candidate sets and target-summary uncertainty not run; 400 replicates. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Intervals omit selection, reconstruction and target-summary error
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Reported intervals omit selection, weighting and bridge uncertainty” The title lists weighting uncertainty as unpropagated, but the audit found the estimated-weights variance question settled across a 108-scenario evaluation with actionable guidance.
The source said. “Reported ITC and PAIC intervals are computed conditional on one selected model and on upstream inputs treated as fixed. Model specification and the selection process are not fully reported, and uncertainty from estimated weights, multi-arm covariance, pseudo-IPD reconstruction, target summaries, priors, numerical integration and the bridge itself is neither propagated nor decomposed.”
What was wrong with it. The source treated estimated-weight uncertainty in MAIC as unaddressed and said standard software offers no decomposition. The literature auditor found the variance-estimation question settled by a 108-scenario evaluation with actionable guidance (10.1002/jrsm.1759), and GPT-5.6 Sol found weight bootstrapping, multi-arm covariance and an integration-error diagnostic already implemented in cpaic and objected that structural bridge uncertainty should not be folded into a confidence interval.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 applies when model selection used the analyzed data, not to a genuinely prespecified model; its claimed frequency is not established here. C2-C3 are correct because between-study interaction gradients are ecologically confounded and shared interactions are structural assumptions. C4 is warranted for substantively plausible alternatives, not every imaginable model. C5 should say random-effects structures and priors can materially affect conclusions and must be reported. C6-C8 are sound when those stages are estimated, with target-summary covariance also needed where applicable. C7’s necessity is exact, but its frequency claim is unverified. C9 is important, but bridge uncertainty is structural and cannot be inserted into a confidence interval without a defensible probability model; sensitivity regions or tipping analyses should ordinarily remain separate. C10 should require convergence assessment and control of numerical error, not automatic treatment as a stochastic variance component. The blanket software claim is false for cpaic: cMAIC re-estimates weights inside an arm-stratified bootstrap, network engines preserve multi-arm dependence, and cML-NMR has an integration-error diagnostic. Selection, target-summary, pseudo-IPD, and full bridge-uncertainty decomposition remain unresolved.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. One component of this bundle has been formally settled. Chandler & Proskorovsky 2024 (Res Synth Methods, doi 10.1002/jrsm.1759, PMID 39323097) ran a 108-scenario Monte Carlo study comparing four families of variance estimator for MAIC (conventional with raw weights, conventional with ESS-rescaled weights, robust sandwich variants, bootstrap) across anchored and unanchored designs and binary and time-to-event outcomes, and gives concrete guidance: raw-weight conventional estimators understate variability under poor or moderate overlap, sandwich estimators are downward-biased at small ESS unless finite-sample-adjusted, bootstrapping is unstable at small ESS. Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021 (doi 10.1002/jrsm.1511) had already shown ‘the robust sandwich variance estimator underestimates variability where effective sample sizes are small’. So ‘uncertainty from estimated weights should be accounted for in MAIC standard errors’ is no longer an open problem; it is a solved-and-evaluated question with published recommendations. The remaining components, model-selection uncertainty, pseudo-IPD reconstruction uncertainty, target-summary uncertainty, multi-arm covariance preservation, numerical integration error, and a decomposition separating sampling from bridge and prior uncertainty, I found no work addressing, and they remain open. Cites 10.1002/jrsm.1759: Resolves the estimated-weights component: a 108-scenario evaluation of four variance-estimation approaches with actionable guidance by sample size, overlap and outcome type.. Cites 10.1002/jrsm.1511: Earlier evidence that the standard MAIC variance estimator misstates uncertainty at small effective sample size..

partially-solved / overstated. C1 applies when model selection used the analyzed data, not to a genuinely prespecified model; its claimed frequency is not established here. C2-C3 are correct because between-study interaction gradients are ecologically confounded and shared interactions are structural assumptions. C4 is warranted for substantively plausible alternatives, not every imaginable model. C5 should say random-effects structures and priors can materially affect conclusions and must be reported. C6-C8 are sound when those stages are estimated, with target-summary covariance also needed where applicable. C7’s necessity is exact, but its frequency claim is unverified. C9 is important, but bridge uncertainty is structural and cannot be inserted into a confidence interval without a defensible probability model; sensitivity regions or tipping analyses should ordinarily remain separate. C10 should require convergence assessment and control of numerical error, not automatic treatment as a stochastic variance component. The blanket software claim is false for cpaic: cMAIC re-estimates weights inside an arm-stratified bootstrap, network engines preserve multi-arm dependence, and cML-NMR has an integration-error diagnostic. Selection, target-summary, pseudo-IPD, and full bridge-uncertainty decomposition remain unresolved. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Resolves C6 for source-IPD sampling uncertainty by recalculating MAIC weights and refitting the outcome model in every bootstrap resample. Target moments remain fixed.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Addresses C7 through netmeta’s multi-arm covariance for the frequentist bridge and the standard 0.5 baseline-shift correlation for cML-NMR random effects.. It does not estimate error of the final grid against the exact integral and is unavailable for survival models..

title: Modifier selection and target moments reported without provenance
text:
Statement
Population-adjustment reports frequently omit the inputs that determine the adjustment: which variables were predefined as effect modifiers rather than prognostic-only, the clinical and empirical rationale, measurement definitions and harmonization, the provenance of each target moment, the assumptions used to reconstruct the target joint distribution, and any uncertainty in the target summaries. Farinasso et al. 2025 (10.1016/j.vhri.2025.101088) found evidence of effect-modifier status and adjustment for all effect modifiers among the least-reported items across 117 oncology MAICs. The joint-distribution assumption is an undisclosed requirement rather than an unrecognized one: multilevel network meta-regression (10.1111/rssa.12579) reconstructs the target joint distribution with a Gaussian copula whose correlations are borrowed from the IPD studies, and multinma implements it, so an analyst has a named convention to state. A correlation matrix alone does not identify a joint distribution, since marginal families and a dependence model are also needed, and moment-matching MAIC and identity-link models do not require a full joint distribution at all.

title: Modifier selection and target moments reported without provenance
text:
Why it is open
Modifier selection is usually made after seeing which variables the comparator publication happens to report, so predefinition would expose that availability rather than clinical reasoning drove the choice. Target summaries are published as point estimates, so treating them as fixed constants is the path of least resistance and no reporting rule forces the uncertainty to be propagated or its neglect justified; conditioning on them is defensible only for a fixed policy target or negligible sampling error. Software does not push back either: the component ML-NMR path in cpaic stores the copula, marginal families and correlation matrix in the fit, but no path records the source of each target moment, harmonization decisions or target-summary uncertainty, and its MAIC object retains target means without target standard deviations. cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub and is not on CRAN.

title: Modifier selection and target moments reported without provenance
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2020 (multilevel network meta-regression)
Reconstructs the target joint covariate distribution from published marginals using a Gaussian copula with correlations matched to the IPD studies, making explicit the assumption the entry says is undisclosed; implemented in multinma.


Farinasso et al. 2025
Finds evidence of effect-modifier status and adjustment for all effect modifiers and prognostic variables among the least-reported items across 117 oncology MAICs.


cpaic (development package, audited at commit 9d150e9)
Unreleased development package on GitHub, confirmed by an auditor not to be on CRAN. Its component ML-NMR path makes the Gaussian-copula dependence model, marginal families and correlation matrix explicit and retains them in the fit; it does not record moment sources, harmonization decisions or target-summary uncertainty, and its MAIC object stores target means but not target standard deviations.

title: Modifier selection and target moments reported without provenance
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Require the reporting elements the methods already imply: predefined effect modifiers with clinical and empirical rationale, harmonized measurement definitions, a complete listing of target moments with sources, an explicit statement of the marginal families and dependence model used to reconstruct the target joint distribution, and either propagation of target-summary uncertainty or a justification for treating it as negligible. Fix the estimand and effect scale first, because on a non-collapsible scale a variable that is only conditionally prognostic still moves the marginal effect, so prognostic-only cannot mean ignorable. Make the fit object carry the provenance so the disclosure is emitted by the software rather than asserted by the analyst.

title: Modifier selection and target moments reported without provenance
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Population-adjustment reporting omits the inputs that determine the adjustment: predefinition of effect modifiers as distinct from prognostic-only variables, clinical and empirical rationale for each variable, measurement definitions and harmonization, all target moments and their sources, the reconstruction of the target joint distribution with its correlation assumptions, and propagation of uncertainty in the target summaries.”
What was wrong with it. The source treated the correlation assumption behind a reconstructed target joint distribution as an unrecognized gap. The literature auditor found it is an explicit, documented component of multilevel network meta-regression (Phillippo et al. 2020, 10.1111/rssa.12579, implemented in multinma), so the claim narrows to non-disclosure; GPT-5.6 Sol added that correlations alone do not identify a joint distribution and that moment-matching MAIC does not need one.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): The reporting gap is documented. Farinasso et al. 2025 found that ‘evidence of effect modifier status’ and ‘adjustment for all effect modifiers and prognostic variables’ were among the least-reported items across 117 oncology MAICs, and Truong et al. 2023 found extensive heterogeneity assessment in only 37.0% of PAIC analyses. Caveat on the correlation sub-claim: the requirement is not an unrecognized gap but an explicit, documented component of an existing method. Multilevel network meta-regression (Phillippo et al. 2020, doi 10.1111/rssa.12579) reconstructs the target joint covariate distribution from published marginals using a Gaussian copula with a correlation matrix borrowed from the IPD studies, and this is implemented in multinma; Ren et al. 2025 similarly use the NORTA algorithm with an assumed correlation structure. So a willing analyst has a named convention to state, and the entry should say the assumption is rarely disclosed rather than that it is unrecognized. I could not verify with any measured figure how often correlation assumptions or target-moment provenance are actually reported, nor find a method paper propagating target-summary uncertainty; those sub-claims are plausible but unmeasured.

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. C1 and C5 are sound only after fixing the estimand and effect scale. On non-collapsible scales, a conditionally prognostic variable can alter a marginal treatment effect even without a conditional treatment interaction, so prognostic-only must not mean irrelevant. title: Estimand, effect scale and absolute target outcomes go undeclared
text: DEC-07 Partially addressed Very high priority Promising

title: Estimand, effect scale and absolute target outcomes go undeclared
text:
Statement
ITC and PAIC reports commonly do not declare the estimand: whether it is conditional, marginal, overlap-population or partially identified, which population it refers to, the intercurrent-event strategy and horizon, or the treatment versions compared; and they usually report relative effects without target-standardized absolute arm outcomes. The vocabulary and much of the requirement already exist: Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021 (10.1002/jrsm.1511) show that the typical usage of STC targets a conditional effect where the target is marginal and that the resulting incompatibility biases the indirect comparison on a non-collapsible scale, NICE DSU TSD 18 says population-adjusted absolute and relative effects should be constructed for the target decision population, and TSD 7 asks reviewers whether the absolute effects used in the economic model are reported. What is missing is a requirement that a submission declare these things, not the concepts to declare. Collapsibility should not be reported as the test of transportability: a collapsible effect can still vary through effect modification, and a conditional non-collapsible parameter can be transported under appropriate structural assumptions.

title: Estimand, effect scale and absolute target outcomes go undeclared
text:
Why it is open
The estimand framework entered practice through trial analysis, so ITC reporting templates predate it and have no field for intercurrent-event strategy or population labeling even where the underlying requirement exists in guidance. Because different methods inside one submission return conditional and marginal quantities on non-collapsible scales, omitting the declaration lets incompatible numbers be combined without anyone noticing. Synthesis models are parameterized in relative effects and most software returns those, so target-standardized absolute outcomes take an extra step; the economic modeler then supplies a baseline from a different source and the mismatch is never displayed. Stating the estimand precisely also makes visible that the analysis targets a comparator-trial population rather than the decision population.

title: Estimand, effect scale and absolute target outcomes go undeclared
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2021
Review and simulation study built on the marginal-versus-conditional distinction; shows that the typical usage of STC targets a conditional effect where a marginal one is required and that non-collapsibility makes the combined estimates incompatible.


Target estimands for population-adjusted indirect comparisons (arXiv preprint)
Develops the taxonomy of target estimands for population-adjusted indirect comparisons; named by the literature auditor as the same author’s follow-up to the 2021 review.


Jiang et al. 2025
Shows the indirect comparison result is valid only for the population represented by the aggregate-data trial, which may differ from the sponsor’s or the decision population, sourcing the requirement to name populations separately.


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 7 (2012)
Asks reviewers to assess target population, treatment definition, outcome and synthesis scale, and whether the absolute effects used in the cost-effectiveness analysis are reported. Read by the code auditor from a document corpus at the given commit.

title: Estimand, effect scale and absolute target outcomes go undeclared
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Turn the existing guidance into an explicit declaration: require every report to name the treatments with their versions, doses and schedules, the outcome, horizon, intercurrent-event strategy and effect measure, the source, comparator-trial and decision populations separately, and the estimand type. Require target-standardized absolute arm outcomes alongside relative effects wherever they are identifiable, which TSD 18 already recommends, so the baseline used by the economic model matches the population in which the effect was estimated. Justify the effect scale on clinical and modeling grounds and state the standardization performed, rather than treating collapsibility as a license to transport.

title: Estimand, effect scale and absolute target outcomes go undeclared
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “ITC and PAIC reports do not state what is being estimated: intervention versions, doses, schedules and strategies; outcome, time horizon, intercurrent-event strategy and effect measure; the source, comparator-trial and final decision populations named separately; whether the estimand is conditional, marginal, overlap-population or partially identified; and whether the chosen effect scale is collapsible. They also report relative effects alone, without the target-standardized absolute arm outcomes that the decision and the economic model require.”
What was wrong with it. The source said ITC reporting conventions have no slot for these declarations and that collapsibility determines whether an effect is transportable. GPT-5.6 Sol found TSD 18 and TSD 7 already ask for target-population absolute and relative effects, and that collapsibility is neither necessary nor sufficient for transportability; the literature auditor added that the marginal-versus-conditional taxonomy has been developed since 2021 (10.1002/jrsm.1511, arXiv:2112.08023).

I could not verify the sub-claim about absolute target-standardized arm outcomes being outside every default workflow, since I did not check what current software returns. codex dissented (overstated): The reporting proposal has a strong technical core, but its absolute claims and collapsibility argument are incorrect. Existing ITC and PAIC guidance already asks for treatment definition, target population, effect scale, and absolute treatment effects, so the claim that reporting conventions have no such slots is false. C2, C5, C6, and C7 are technically sound. For C3, time horizon and an applicable intercurrent-event strategy belong in the estimand, but frequent nonreporting is an empirical claim. C4 is false: collapsibility is neither necessary nor sufficient for transportability. A collapsible effect can vary through effect modification, while a conditional non-collapsible parameter can be transported under appropriate structural assumptions. C8 is correct for a marginal effect naively combined with an aggregate baseline from another population, but too broad for conditional models. Non-collapsibility means that marginal effects depend on the covariate distribution even without conditional effect modification; valid target standardization, rather than a blanket prohibition, is the remedy.

title: Committees get no one-page statement of what an estimate rests on
text:
Statement
No agency template requires a single committee-facing page that states, together, what is being estimated, for which population, what connects disconnected evidence, where overlap is weak, which results are prior- or bridge-driven, and how much assumption violation would change the decision. Parts of this already exist: NICE DSU TSD 7 provides a pro forma reviewer checklist covering the decision problem, evidence structure, assumptions, sensitivity and absolute outcomes, TSD 18 requires the target population for the decision problem to be stated explicitly, and threshold analysis (10.7326/M18-3542) already reports how much the evidence could change before the recommendation changes. What is missing is that none of it is consolidated into one required artifact, and that no method supplies the data-driven versus prior-driven versus bridge-driven decomposition the source asks for.

title: Committees get no one-page statement of what an estimate rests on
text:
Why it is open
The answers are spread across a long technical appendix and several separate checklists, and no template forces them into one place where inconsistencies would become visible; because the artifact is never required, its absence is never penalized. Committees include clinicians and lay members who cannot extract these answers from a statistical appendix, so translation falls on whoever is least equipped to do it. The decomposition into data-driven, prior-driven and bridge-driven contributions has no unique additive definition, so it must be operationally defined before it can be required.

title: Committees get no one-page statement of what an estimate rests on
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “No appraisal process requires a committee-facing one-page assumptions map, diagnostics summary and sensitivity hierarchy, so the nine questions that decide whether an ITC can support a decision are never answered in one place: what is being estimated, for which population, which comparisons are randomized, what connects disconnected evidence, which variables are assumed to remove population differences, where overlap is weak, what is data-driven rather than prior- or bridge-driven, which residual biases were quantified and from what parameter sources, and how much assumption violation changes the decision. Interpretability therefore rests on the individual reviewer, and methods that are easy to narrate are favored over methods whose assumptions are weaker but whose explanation is harder.”
What was wrong with it. The source asserted, without attribution, that HTA committees remain skeptical of weakly justified unanchored analyses; the literature auditor sourced it to Phillippo et al. 2019 (10.1017/S0266462319000333), which found that committees received population-adjusted results with caution and looked for greater cost effectiveness to minimize decision risk. GPT-5.6 Sol found the questions already partly consolidated by the TSD 7 checklist and TSD 18, and rejected as unsupported the claims that one page is inherently more informative than an appendix, that MAIC is popular because it is easy to narrate, and that narrative simplicity implies stronger assumptions.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): I found no reporting instrument, agency template or published proposal for a one-page committee-facing assumptions map answering these nine questions, and Farinasso et al. 2025 and Truong et al. 2023 both document that the underlying information is not reported consistently anywhere, let alone in one place. Two of the entry’s sub-claims are now sourceable rather than unsourced. Phillippo et al. 2019 (IJTAHC, doi 10.1017/S0266462319000333) reviewed NICE TAs and found ‘Appraisal committees received results of population-adjusted analyses with caution and typically looked for greater cost effectiveness to minimise decision risk’, supporting HTA skepticism toward weakly justified unanchored analyses; 89% (16/18) of those applications were unanchored. Jiang et al. 2025 supports the specific need to state the target population plainly, since failing to do so permits opposing conclusions from the same data. Caveat: the ‘sensitivity hierarchy’ element is partly pre-existing, since Phillippo et al. 2019 (Ann Intern Med, doi 10.7326/M18-3542) proposed threshold analysis precisely to tell committees how robust a recommendation is. The claims that MAIC is popular because it is easier to narrate, and that narrative simplicity hides stronger assumptions, are plausible but I found no source measuring either. codex dissented (overstated): A one-page committee artifact of the exact proposed form may be absent, but it is incorrect that the relevant questions are never consolidated or that no template exists. TSD 7 already provides a pro forma decision-facing checklist, and TSD 18 adds PAIC-specific reporting for target population, overlap, weights, uncertainty, and systematic error. Neither source makes such a page mandatory or supplies a complete data-versus-prior-versus-bridge decomposition, so a communication gap remains. C3 and C5 are unsupported comparative claims: one page is not inherently more informative, and fastest route is not a statistical conclusion. C7-C9 are reasonable reporting requirements, although the amount that is data-, prior-, or bridge-driven may lack a unique additive decomposition and must be operationally defined. C10 is an unsupported causal claim. C11 is false generally because assumption strength depends mainly on anchored status, identification, overlap, and model restrictions, not narrative simplicity or computational complexity. C12 is an institutional-prevalence claim outside this audit.

title: Value of information is not extended to IPD or bridge acquisition

title: Value of information is not extended to IPD or bridge acquisition
text:
Statement
Value-of-information machinery for evidence-synthesis networks already exists: Jackson et al. 2019 (10.1080/01621459.2018.1562932) give EVPPI and EVSI for Bayesian evidence-synthesis models fitted by MCMC, compare the expected value of additional data from two candidate sources, and trade expected benefit against cost to choose a sample size. What it does not cover is what is specific to indirect comparison: the IPD-versus-aggregate distinction, propagation of structural bridge, transport and drift uncertainty, and the combinatorial question of which decision contrasts a new study would render estimable. EVSI is also a research-design and acquisition criterion, not a performance measure for ranking ITC estimators in a simulation study.

title: Value of information is not extended to IPD or bridge acquisition
text:
Why it is open
Generic EVSI is well defined for a candidate design once the joint network, transport, decision and sampling model is fully specified, with network placement entering through the design-specific likelihood and structural uncertainty through a model indicator. The difficulty in indirect comparison is that bridge and transport uncertainty is often only partially identified, with no probability model, prior or bound, in which case EVSI is not unique; that is an incomplete specification rather than proof that no method exists. Which contrasts a new study renders estimable is a combinatorial design question on top of the variance calculation, and computation for realistic networks remains heavy.

title: Value of information is not extended to IPD or bridge acquisition
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Jackson, Presanis, Conti and De Angelis 2019
EVPPI and EVSI for multi-parameter Bayesian evidence-synthesis models fitted by MCMC; compares candidate new data sources and trades expected benefit against sampling cost to pick a design.


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 6 (2011)
Establishes the general route for propagating evidence-synthesis uncertainty through a probabilistic decision model and performing value-of-information analysis. Read by the code auditor from a document corpus at the given commit.

title: Value of information is not extended to IPD or bridge acquisition
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the existing evidence-synthesis EVSI machinery rather than build a parallel one: add a design-specific likelihood that distinguishes IPD from aggregate data, represent structural bridge and transport uncertainty through a model indicator or an explicit partial-identification bound, and score candidate designs by which decision contrasts they render estimable. Address the computational cost of network-specific EVSI directly, since that is the practical obstacle. Report the result as a research-prioritization criterion for IPD acquisition and bridge-trial design, not as a simulation performance measure.

title: Value of information is not extended to IPD or bridge acquisition
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Value-of-information machinery for evidence-synthesis networks exists and can already rank candidate data collections by expected value, but it has not been extended to the features specific to indirect treatment comparison: the IPD-versus-aggregate distinction, structural bridge and transport uncertainty, and which decision contrasts a new study would render estimable. EVSI is also not reported as a performance measure in ITC simulation studies.
The source titled this. “No value-of-information basis for acquiring IPD or bridge trials” The title says no value-of-information basis exists, but EVPPI and EVSI for Bayesian evidence-synthesis networks were published in 2019 and can already rank candidate data collections.
The source said. “There is no method or evidence to answer which new IPD study or which new comparison would have the greatest expected value for a given decision problem. Evidence acquisition and bridge-trial design therefore proceed on availability rather than on a value-of-information calculation.”
What was wrong with it. The source said there is no method for deciding which new IPD study or comparison has the greatest expected value. Such a method has existed since Jackson et al. 2019 (10.1080/01621459.2018.1562932), which does exactly that for evidence-synthesis networks, and the general route through probabilistic decision models was already in NICE DSU TSD 6; the residual gap is the ITC-specific features, and the proposal to report EVSI as a simulation performance measure was a misclassification.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. I read the full text of Jackson, Presanis, Conti & De Angelis 2019 (JASA, doi 10.1080/01621459.2018.1562932). It builds an EVPPI/EVSI framework specifically for Bayesian evidence-synthesis models represented as DAGs and fitted by MCMC, generalizing Strong et al.’s regression method from finite-action decisions to point estimation and vector outputs. In their application they directly compare the expected value of additional data from two different sources (GUM Anon vs GMSHS) at a range of sample sizes, and compute the expected net benefit of sampling to pick an optimal sample size (166 participants). That is precisely ‘which new study has greatest expected value in a network of evidence’. Welton et al.’s EVPPI research-prioritization work and Mohiuddin et al.’s review of VoI in 25 NIHR HTA reports predate it. What Jackson et al. do not cover, and what remains open, is the IPD-versus-aggregate distinction, propagation of structural bridge/transport/drift uncertainty, and the combinatorial question of which contrasts a new study renders estimable. ‘There is no method’ is therefore wrong as stated; ‘no method for the PAIC-specific features’ is defensible. Cites 10.1080/01621459.2018.1562932: Provides EVPPI and EVSI methods for multi-parameter evidence-synthesis networks fitted by MCMC, compares candidate new data sources, and trades expected benefit against sampling cost to choose an optimal design..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 and the assertion that standard EVSI requires a single well-identified model are too strong. For candidate design s, EVSI can be defined as E_Z[max_d E{NB(d,theta)|Y,Z,s}] minus max_d E{NB(d,theta)|Y}. Network placement enters through the design-specific likelihood for Z; structural uncertainty can enter through a model indicator and its joint posterior. If bridge or transport uncertainty has no probability model, prior, or identified bound, EVSI is not unique, but that is an incomplete specification rather than proof that no method exists. C3 is correct because placement determines which parameters and contrasts receive information. C2 misclassifies EVSI: it is principally a research-design or acquisition criterion, not a generic performance measure for comparing ITC estimators. Network-specific computation and robust treatment of poorly identified structural uncertainty may remain open. Cites choxos/NICE-DSU-TSD-RAG@75abcb9c226a9f8fa7a0a4ffeba42874f1712ecb: Establishes the general technical route for propagating evidence-synthesis uncertainty through a probabilistic decision model and performing value-of-information analysis..

Decision path

title: Method evaluations score estimator error, not decision error
text:
Statement
ADEMP does not require, and its performance-measure inventory does not contain, any decision or net-benefit measure: Table 6 of Morris et al. 2019 lists bias, EmpSE, relative precision, MSE, model standard error, coverage and rejection percentage only. Whether ITC and PAIC method comparisons routinely omit decision metrics such as wrong-decision probability, net-benefit error or rank reversal is contested: the literature auditor searched and found no such evaluation, while GPT-5.6 Sol holds that this prevalence claim is not established by the cited paper. Decision-level assessment already exists outside method-comparison simulation, in threshold analysis for applied network meta-analysis (Phillippo et al. 2018) and in NICE DSU TSD 7’s probability that a strategy is optimal at a threshold willingness to pay. Expected value of perfect or sample information does not belong on the list of estimator-quality metrics: it measures the value of collecting information and can rise as uncertainty rises.

title: Method evaluations score estimator error, not decision error
text:
Why it is open
The link from estimator error to decision error runs through a decision threshold and a loss function, neither of which ADEMP requires, so a method that wins on RMSE can lose on the recommendation; Figure 1 of Morris et al. already shows RMSE and coverage ranking methods differently. Computing a decision metric means simulating a decision rule and usually an economic model, machinery that method authors treat as outside statistical scope and that no ITC benchmark provides. The blocker is therefore adoption inside method-comparison simulation rather than missing technical machinery, since threshold-based decision assessment already exists for applied syntheses.

title: Method evaluations score estimator error, not decision error
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Morris, White and Crowther 2019
Defines ADEMP; Table 6 enumerates the performance measures, none of which is a decision or net-benefit measure, and its methods element explicitly allows a decision rule.


Phillippo et al. 2018
Derives bias-adjustment thresholds, the smallest changes to the data that change the treatment decision, giving decision-level assessment for applied network meta-analysis.


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 7 (2012)
Reviewer’s checklist for evidence synthesis in decision making; uses an explicit decision model, willingness-to-pay threshold and probability that a strategy is optimal. Read by the code auditor from a document corpus at the given commit.

title: Method evaluations score estimator error, not decision error
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Carry the existing threshold-and-loss machinery into method-comparison simulation instead of inventing decision metrics: report wrong-decision probability, net-benefit error and rank reversal alongside bias, RMSE and coverage under a prespecified decision model, threshold and loss, which the ADEMP performance-measure element is broad enough to hold. Re-score published benchmark scenarios on both axes so the estimation ranking and the decision ranking can be compared. Keep expected value of information out of that set and use it where it belongs, as a research-design criterion.

title: Method evaluations score estimator error, not decision error
text:
Our study

Do estimation and decision rankings of population-adjustment methods agree?
The question put to it. When population-adjustment methods are ranked by the decisions their estimates lead to rather than by RMSE, does the ranking change, and how does it depend on where the truth sits relative to the decision threshold?
What it found. For a threshold on a known side of the truth, yes: near the threshold in poor-overlap scenarios the RMSE and expected-loss rankings correlated at only 0.45, and the disagreement was reproducible, not noise. It came from the direction of bias: a biased method decided wrongly far less often when its bias pointed away from the threshold (0.11 against 0.64). Averaged over the two sides of the threshold, as an analyst who does not know the truth must, the rankings agreed (0.93, the same best method in every poor-overlap scenario). RMSE is therefore an adequate proxy for decision error unless the side of the threshold is known.
Results.

Registered primary (near threshold, poor overlap, symmetric loss): mean Spearman correlation 0.45 (95% bootstrap interval 0.29 to 0.60); RMSE-best also loss-best in 38% of strata; verdict CONFIRMED.
Exploratory: split-half reliability of the rankings 1.00 (RMSE) and 0.96 (expected loss) in poor-overlap scenarios, against a cross-measure correlation of 0.44.
Biased methods (|bias| > 0.05), threshold 0.1 from the truth: wrong-decision probability 0.114 with bias pointing away from the threshold and 0.635 toward it.
Exploratory: loss averaged over both sides of the threshold correlated with RMSE at 0.93 (distance 0.1) and 0.96 (0.3) in poor-overlap scenarios.

Design.

Estimand

Wrong-decision probability and expected loss of adopting B over A, against the true recommendation

Methods compared

unadjusted, MAIC on means, MAIC on means and variances, MAIC on the prognostic index variance, G-computation

Data-generating mechanism

Re-scoring of COV-03’s 108,000 stored replicates (five methods) against thresholds 0.1 or 0.3 above or below the truth, with loss ratios 1, 2 and 5; rank correlation between RMSE and expected-loss rankings by stratum, plus exploratory split-half reliability and two-sided averaging.

Replicates

108,000 replicates re-scored (108 scenarios x 1000), 5 methods, 12 threshold-loss settings


What this does not answer. Decision on the relative effect only, without a net-benefit model; one source of replicates (COV-03) and five methods; no ML-NMR; priors on the side of the threshold not modeled. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument · Code and data: studies/DEC-01-when-the-two-rankings-disagree · Protocol: registered before the run

title: Method evaluations score estimator error, not decision error
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides. Reopened by the full-text reading: 5 findings from 5 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from unverifiable to partially-addressed.
The source said. “ITC and PAIC method comparisons are scored on bias, RMSE and coverage, and ADEMP contains no decision element, so no evaluation reports how often a method produces the wrong reimbursement decision. Decision measures such as wrong-decision probability, incremental net-benefit error, expected regret, rank-reversal frequency, probability of selecting a dominated treatment and expected value of sample information are absent from the standard reporting set.”
What was wrong with it. The source listed EVPI and EVSI among decision-quality metrics for scoring estimators; GPT-5.6 Sol found this a category error, since value-of-information measures the value of collecting data rather than estimator quality. The premise that decision-level assessment is possible was unattributed in the source and is now sourced to Phillippo et al. 2018 (10.1111/rssa.12341) and NICE DSU TSD 7, and the ADEMP claim was checked line by line against Table 6 of Morris et al. 2019.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): I read the full text of Morris, White & Crowther 2019 (PMC6492164). ADEMP is Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods, Performance measures; Table 6 enumerates exactly bias, EmpSE, relative % increase in precision, MSE, average ModSE, relative % error in ModSE, coverage, bias-eliminated coverage, and rejection % (power/type I error). No loss function, net benefit, regret or decision metric appears anywhere. The citation is used accurately. Two narrowings worth noting: the paper’s Estimands element says ‘Define estimands and/or other targets’, and it states a method ‘might refer to a design or some procedure (such as a decision rule)’, so ADEMP accommodates decision rules without requiring a decision-consequence element. Figure 1 also demonstrates that RMSE and coverage can rank methods differently, which is the mechanism behind the entry’s ‘lower RMSE, more wrong decisions’ claim. Prior art exists for decision-based assessment of applied NMAs (Phillippo threshold analysis, nmathresh), but I found no ITC/PAIC method-comparison simulation scoring wrong-decision probability, net-benefit error or rank reversal. The problem is open. ‘Most important metric addition’ is opinion, not verifiable. codex dissented (overstated): C5-C7 are mathematically correct. For example, with true incremental net benefit 1 and threshold 0, an estimator fixed at -0.1 has RMSE 1.1 and always gives the wrong decision, while one fixed at 3 has RMSE 2 and never does. C2 is also correct: ADEMP does not require a decision element. However, the report conflates estimator losses with value-of-information measures. Wrong-decision probability and regret are valid only after specifying actions, a threshold, and a loss or net-benefit model. EVPI and EVSI measure the value of resolving or collecting information, not estimator quality, and can increase when uncertainty increases. C3, C4, and C11 are literature-prevalence claims not established by the cited ADEMP paper; C10 is an unsupported priority judgment. Existing decision-analysis guidance already connects evidence synthesis to threshold-based decisions, so the remaining gap is routine PAIC application, not missing technical machinery.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. I read the full text of Morris, White & Crowther 2019 (PMC6492164). ADEMP is Aims, Data-generating mechanisms, Estimands, Methods, Performance measures; Table 6 enumerates exactly bias, EmpSE, relative % increase in precision, MSE, average ModSE, relative % error in ModSE, coverage, bias-eliminated coverage, and rejection % (power/type I error). No loss function, net benefit, regret or decision metric appears anywhere. The citation is used accurately. Two narrowings worth noting: the paper’s Estimands element says ‘Define estimands and/or other targets’, and it states a method ‘might refer to a design or some procedure (such as a decision rule)’, so ADEMP accommodates decision rules without requiring a decision-consequence element. Figure 1 also demonstrates that RMSE and coverage can rank methods differently, which is the mechanism behind the entry’s ‘lower RMSE, more wrong decisions’ claim. Prior art exists for decision-based assessment of applied NMAs (Phillippo threshold analysis, nmathresh), but I found no ITC/PAIC method-comparison simulation scoring wrong-decision probability, net-benefit error or rank reversal. The problem is open. ‘Most important metric addition’ is opinion, not verifiable. Cites 10.1002/sim.8086: Confirms the cited claim: ADEMP has five elements and its performance-measure inventory contains no decision or net-benefit measure.. Cites 10.1111/rssa.12341: Real reference for the entry’s unsourced premise that decision-level assessment is possible and already formalized for applied NMA (not for method-comparison simulations), so the proposed direction is building on existing machinery rather than starting fresh..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C5-C7 are mathematically correct. For example, with true incremental net benefit 1 and threshold 0, an estimator fixed at -0.1 has RMSE 1.1 and always gives the wrong decision, while one fixed at 3 has RMSE 2 and never does. C2 is also correct: ADEMP does not require a decision element. However, the report conflates estimator losses with value-of-information measures. Wrong-decision probability and regret are valid only after specifying actions, a threshold, and a loss or net-benefit model. EVPI and EVSI measure the value of resolving or collecting information, not estimator quality, and can increase when uncertainty increases. C3, C4, and C11 are literature-prevalence claims not established by the cited ADEMP paper; C10 is an unsupported priority judgment. Existing decision-analysis guidance already connects evidence synthesis to threshold-based decisions, so the remaining gap is routine PAIC application, not missing technical machinery. Cites 10.1002/sim.8086: Provides the general ADEMP framework, including a performance-measures element broad enough to contain a prespecified decision loss, although it does not require one.. Cites choxos/NICE-DSU-TSD-RAG@75abcb9c226a9f8fa7a0a4ffeba42874f1712ecb: Shows that evidence-synthesis appraisal can already use an explicit decision model, willingness-to-pay threshold, and probability that a strategy is optimal..

Decision path

title: No review method for assembling transferable effect-modifier sets
text: COV-13 Confirmed open High priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: No review method for assembling transferable effect-modifier sets
text:
Statement
Every population-adjusted analysis begins by assembling a candidate list of effect modifiers and prognostic variables from external evidence, and no method governs that step. Freitag, Gurskyte and Sarri 2023 reviewed guidance from payer and non-payer organizations, published indirect comparisons and prior submissions in two indications, and found the most explicit guidance, from NICE, recommends a literature review or structured discussion with clinical experts without saying how the review should be designed, which evidence types are admissible, what criteria establish that a modification finding transfers from another population to the trials being compared, or whether a hierarchy should govern the final selection. Practice matches the guidance: of 511 unique records screened, 17 described any selection process, and those rested on prior literature, trial subgroup analyses or clinical input, with no reference to systematic identification. The demand has since outrun the method: EU joint clinical assessment guidance now requires a second comprehensive review to identify potential effect modifiers, in addition to the review of clinical evidence, and consultation with clinicians experienced in the disease area. What does not exist is a review methodology scoped to identify modifiers rather than to estimate an effect: an admissibility rule covering randomized subgroup analyses, individual participant data meta-analyses of interactions, observational heterogeneity studies and mechanistic argument; a ranking or filtering rule over the resulting candidates; and above all a transferability criterion. Appraisers therefore have no basis on which to judge whether a submitted candidate list was assembled adequately, only whether the statistics applied to it were correct.

title: No review method for assembling transferable effect-modifier sets
text:
Why it is open
The candidate list bounds everything downstream: a variable absent from it can never be balanced, tested or entered into a sensitivity analysis, so an omission at this step is invisible to every later diagnostic, yet the step sits in evidence retrieval rather than in statistics and neither field has claimed it. The indirect comparison methods literature takes the list as given and studies what to do with it; systematic review methodology is built around estimating an effect, not around identifying which covariates modify one, and has no design for a review whose output is a variable list rather than a pooled estimate. Transferability is the hard part and is genuinely unsolved rather than merely unwritten, because a modification finding is itself specific to a population, an effect scale, a treatment version and a follow-up horizon, so importing it into a new comparison requires an argument of exactly the type the indirect comparison is trying to make; the criterion is circular unless something external, such as a mechanistic argument or invariance across several source populations, breaks the loop. Because no standard exists, the list is assembled in practice from prior submissions in the same indication and from whichever subgroup analyses the available trials happened to run, which selects on reporting rather than on relevance and systematically favors indications with a long appraisal history.

title: No review method for assembling transferable effect-modifier sets
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Freitag, Gurskyte and Sarri 2023, Increasing transparency in indirect treatment comparisons: is selecting effect modifiers the missing part of the puzzle?, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research 12
Reviews guidance documents, published indirect comparisons and prior submissions in non-small cell lung cancer and psoriasis. Finds that guidance names literature review and expert opinion without specifying review design, admissible evidence, transferability criteria or a selection hierarchy, and that of 511 records screened only 17 reported any selection process, none of it systematic.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making 38:200-211 (the peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18)
The guidance that names literature review and clinical expert discussion as the routes to identifying effect modifiers, and that is the target of the review’s finding that the route is named but not specified.


Phillippo et al. 2019, Population Adjustment Methods for Indirect Comparisons: A Review of NICE Technology Appraisals, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care 35:221-228
Documents what submissions actually do with population adjustment across NICE appraisals, including the reporting of covariate handling, which is the record against which a designed review protocol would be judged.


Aballea et al. 2026, Between Rigor and Relevance: Why the EU HTA Guidelines on Indirect Comparisons Miss the Mark, Journal of Market Access and Health Policy 14:30
Records that EU joint clinical assessment guidance now requires a second comprehensive review to identify potential effect modifiers plus documented consultation with disease-area clinicians, and argues that these operational requirements are imposed without methodological evidence behind them. The obligation now exists in regulation while the method does not.

title: No review method for assembling transferable effect-modifier sets
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Specify the review as a protocol-driven step with its own reporting standard: a question of the form which covariates modify the effect of treatment class X on outcome Y on scale Z, a search that covers randomized subgroup analyses, individual participant data meta-analyses of interactions and observational heterogeneity studies, and prespecified inclusion criteria stating what counts as evidence of modification rather than of prognosis. Add an explicit transferability appraisal for each imported finding, scoring the source’s population, treatment version, follow-up, outcome definition and effect scale against the trials being compared, and record the appraisal in the submission so it can be contested item by item. Pair the review with formal expert elicitation for candidates the literature cannot supply, and require the final adjustment set to be traceable to specific rows of the review with a stated reason for every inclusion and every exclusion. Pilot the protocol in an indication with a long appraisal history, where the list assembled from prior submissions can be compared directly against the list a designed review produces, and report how much they differ; that comparison is the evidence the new EU requirement currently lacks.

title: No review method for assembling transferable effect-modifier sets
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as well posed and upstream of statistical adjustment-set selection, noting that the cited review explicitly identifies missing methods for review design, evidence admissibility, transferability and hierarchical selection. The evidence is a single paper, but that paper is itself a systematic survey of guidance, published analyses and submissions across two indications, so the absence it reports is documented rather than asserted.

title: Landmark external controls lack covariate inputs for population adjustment
text: COV-11 Confirmed open High priority Emerging Tractability 2/5

title: Landmark external controls lack covariate inputs for population adjustment
text:
Statement
A growing family of external controls is defined at a post-baseline landmark rather than at randomization: post-progression survival from a prior-line trial, time to progression on a patient’s own previous line of therapy, or any cohort whose time zero is a disease event. Population adjustment of such a control requires the distribution of effect modifiers and prognostic factors as they stood at that landmark, but trials publish, and frequently only collect, baseline characteristics measured at their own randomization; Hatswell and Sullivan 2020, proposing two such constructions, state that adjustment here is more complicated than in a standard cross-trial comparison because data on patient characteristics are not routinely collected or reported at disease progression. Two distinct problems follow. There is no target moment vector at the landmark, so matching-adjusted indirect comparison has nothing to weight toward, simulated treatment comparison has nothing to plug in, and standardization has no distribution to integrate over. And the index trial applies its eligibility criteria at its own baseline, so patients who deteriorated between the prior-line landmark and that baseline are present in the external cohort but would have been screened out of the index trial; the worked instance is a trial of ofatumumab requiring ECOG performance status 0 or 1 at entry while the alemtuzumab cohort supplying the historical control is observed at progression, when some of those patients had deteriorated. That selection is a function of post-landmark evolution, so no baseline covariate set can capture it. No method and no reporting convention addresses either half.

title: Landmark external controls lack covariate inputs for population adjustment
text:
Why it is open
The information is destroyed by the design rather than merely unreported: a trial whose covariate collection ends at randomization never measures performance status, laboratory values or disease burden at the landmark, so no reanalysis of the published record can recover the target moments and the fix has to be prospective. Existing work on time-zero problems in external controls treats index-date misalignment, immortal time and delayed entry as biases in the survival contrast and assumes the adjustment inputs exist; here the contrast may be aligned correctly and still be unadjustable. The eligibility-timing half is worse than an ordinary covariate imbalance, because the selection operates on the trajectory between the landmark and the index trial’s baseline, a quantity unobserved in both data sources, so it cannot be balanced, weighted or standardized even in principle without a model for how patients evolve after the landmark event. Landmark analysis as a statistical device is well established, but it was built to remove immortal time within one cohort, not to make two cohorts with different time origins comparable on covariates, so there is nothing to borrow.

title: Landmark external controls lack covariate inputs for population adjustment
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Hatswell and Sullivan 2020, Creating historical controls using data from a previous line of treatment: two non-standard approaches, Statistical Methods in Medical Research 29:1563-1572
Proposes two historical-control constructions from a previous line of treatment, using either a patient’s own time to progression on the prior line or published outcomes for that line extrapolated forward, and states the obstruction as an unresolved limitation of its own proposal: characteristics are not routinely collected or reported at progression, and eligibility applied at the index trial’s baseline can exclude patients who had deteriorated by the landmark.


Dafni 2011, Landmark Analysis at the 25-Year Landmark Point, Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes 4:363-371
Gives the standard treatment of landmark analysis, conditioning on survival to a fixed time point within one cohort to remove guarantee-time bias. It says nothing about transporting covariate distributions between cohorts whose time origins differ.


Suissa 2008, Immortal Time Bias in Pharmacoepidemiology, American Journal of Epidemiology 167:492-499
Characterizes the outcome-side consequence of misaligned time zero, the problem that landmark and delayed-entry methods address. It is a bias in the effect estimate, not an absence of the covariate summaries needed to adjust for population differences.


Hernan and Robins 2016, Using Big Data to Emulate a Target Trial When a Randomized Trial Is Not Available, American Journal of Epidemiology 183:758-764
Requires eligibility assessment, treatment assignment and start of follow-up to be aligned at a single time zero, which names the defect precisely. It offers no repair for the case where covariates at that time zero were never measured in one of the two data sources.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making 38:200-211 (the peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18)
Specifies matching-adjusted indirect comparison and simulated treatment comparison as requiring published summaries of effect modifiers and prognostic variables in the comparator population. There is no variant for a comparator population defined at a post-baseline landmark, and no statement of what should be done when the summaries refer to a different time point than the cohort does.

title: Landmark external controls lack covariate inputs for population adjustment
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Act in two directions, because neither alone is sufficient. Prospectively, specify a short list of characteristics to be re-recorded at progression or at any other landmark likely to define a future external control, covering performance status, key laboratory values, disease burden and time since randomization, and add it to trial data standards and to what comparator publications are asked to report, so a prior-line cohort can serve as an adjustable control at all. Analytically, derive a transport estimator for a landmark-defined cohort that uses baseline summaries plus an explicit model for covariate evolution between baseline and the landmark, fitted wherever individual participant data from a comparable cohort exist, and state what it identifies under what assumptions about that evolution. Treat the eligibility-timing selection as a separate, explicit selection model: express the index trial’s entry criteria as a function of landmark covariates and report bounds, or a single interpretable sensitivity parameter, for the fraction of the external cohort that would have failed screening. Until either exists, require any report using a landmark-defined comparator to state that the target moments are unavailable at the landmark rather than silently substituting the comparator trial’s randomization-time summaries.

title: Landmark external controls lack covariate inputs for population adjustment
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it, judging that QBA-08 covers time-zero bias in the survival contrast but not the absence of landmark covariate distributions or the eligibility selection driven by post-baseline evolution. The evidence is a single methods paper, which states the obstruction as an unresolved complication of its own proposal rather than solving it; no counter-evidence of a method for this case surfaced.
