title: References
text: Every reference below resolved correctly against CrossRef, arXiv, or PubMed during verification. Entries are cited from the individual problem pages.

title: The method landscape
text: The catalog is organized by problem. This page is organized by method: which approach answers which question, what each one assumes, and where each one fails. It exists so an entry in the catalog can be read against the method it constrains.

title: The method landscape
text:
Choosing a method





flowchart LR
    A[Decision problem] --> B{Connected randomised network?}
    B -- Yes --> C{Effect modifiers plausibly balanced?}
    C -- Largely yes --> D[Standard ITC / NMA]
    C -- No, IPD available in subset --> E[Anchored PAIC]
    E --> F[ML-NMR preferred when feasible]
    E --> G[MAIC or STC only with explicit diagnostics]
    B -- No --> H{Single-arm or disconnected evidence?}
    H -- Yes --> I[Unanchored comparison]
    I --> J{Conditional constancy plausible?}
    J -- Weak --> K[Do not make strong causal claims]
    J -- Strong but uncertain --> L[Unanchored MAIC / STC / ML-UMR plus aggressive sensitivity analysis]
    H --> M[Alternative linking: ALM, baseline RE, dose-response MBNMA, class effects]






The branch that matters most is the one ending in “do not make strong causal claims.” That is a legitimate destination, not a failure of the analysis.

title: The method landscape
text:
Where the bias enters





flowchart TB
    X[Measured baseline covariates] --> S[Study membership]
    X --> Y[Outcome]
    Z[Effect modifiers] --> T[Treatment effect]
    Z --> S
    T --> Y
    U[Unmeasured design / care differences] --> S
    U --> Y
    O[Overlap quality] --> W[Weight stability / extrapolation]
    W --> Y






Read this for what it says about \(U\). Weighting and outcome regression both act on \(X\) and \(Z\). If the determinants of the cross-study outcome difference sit in \(U\) instead, no amount of balancing on \(X\) repairs the comparison; at best it disguises the bias more elegantly. That observation is why quantitative bias analysis is the largest category in this catalog.

title: The method landscape
text:
What each method identifies











Method
Evidence structure
Nominal estimand
Main identifying assumptions
Principal unresolved weakness




Bucher adjusted ITC
Two connected RCTs, common comparator
Relative effect in an implicitly common population
Transitivity; compatible effect scale; no material modifier imbalance
No explicit target population; fragile to modifier imbalance and design differences


Aggregate-data NMA
Connected RCT network
Network relative effects
Homogeneity, transitivity, consistency
Population mismatch and effect modification often only weakly assessed


IPD-NMA
IPD from all or many trials
Conditional or standardized effects
Correct individual-level model; exchangeability; IPD availability mechanism
IPD availability is selective; high-dimensional interactions remain difficult


Anchored MAIC
IPD index trial, AgD comparator, common comparator
Usually a marginal effect in the AgD trial population
All relevant modifiers balanced; overlap; correct weighting moments
ESS collapse, incomplete moments, target ambiguity, non-collapsibility, second-stage transport


Anchored STC
IPD index trial, AgD comparator, common comparator
Often a conditional effect at target means unless standardized
Correct outcome model; all relevant modifiers included; valid extrapolation
Model misspecification; conditional and marginal incompatibility; target joint distribution unavailable


Parametric g-computation
IPD source plus target summaries
Compatible marginal effect in a specified target
Correct outcome model and target-distribution model
Sensitive to misspecification; target-summary uncertainty usually ignored


ML-NMR
Mixed IPD and AgD in a connected network
Population-specific effects from one hierarchical model
Conditional constancy; individual-level model; integration distribution
Computational burden; partial identifiability; within and between interaction conflation


Unanchored MAIC or STC
Disconnected trials or single-arm studies
Cross-study contrast in a chosen target
All prognostic factors and modifiers that differ across studies measured and correctly adjusted
No randomization anchor; extreme vulnerability to omitted variables and design heterogeneity


Baseline synthesis, reference prediction
Disconnected AgD, possibly single-arm
Relative effects linked through baseline-outcome structure
Exchangeable or modelled baseline effects; correct arm-level model
Baseline risk is not a universal bridge; ecological and design confounding remain


Dose-response MBNMA
Treatments linked through dose or exposure
Effects along a shared dose-response function
Common pharmacologic curve form and modifiers
A wrong curve or class assumption produces precise but artificial links


Class-effect NMA
Treatments grouped into classes
Shrunk treatment effects and class contrasts
Within-class exchangeability; correct class variance
Class definitions are contestable and may hide genuine heterogeneity


Additive CNMA
Multicomponent treatments sharing components
Component and reconstructed treatment effects
Additivity; stable component effects across subnetworks
Cross-gap component constancy; synergy and treatment-version differences may invalidate the bridge


Component ML-NMR
Component network with mixed IPD and AgD
Component-adjusted contrasts at target covariate values
CNMA assumptions plus transportability and stable component-by-modifier interactions
Strong, partly untestable structural assumptions; marginal standardization incomplete


Doubly robust transport
Source IPD plus target IPD or adequate summaries
Target-population marginal effect
Conditional exchangeability plus either a correct weight model or a correct outcome model
No protection against unmeasured modifiers, positivity failure, or both models being wrong


Partial identification
Any structure with uncertain assumptions
Bounds or a bias-adjusted set
Explicit bounds rather than point identification
Requires defensible sensitivity parameters; less convenient for decision models




This table is not a ladder. A richer model helps only when its added structure is scientifically defensible and adequately informed by data. A faster sampler does not cure non-identification, a doubly robust estimator does not cure positivity failure, perfect covariate balance does not cure unmeasured effect modification, and a narrow interval does not establish that the target population was the right one.

title: The method landscape
text:
How to evaluate a method
Simulation studies in this field routinely report bias without naming the population-specific estimand the bias is relative to, which makes the number uninterpretable. A usable evaluation covers six families at minimum.








Metric family
Minimum metrics




Estimand recovery
Bias, relative bias, RMSE, mean absolute error, sign error, target-standardized bias


Uncertainty calibration
95% coverage, empirical to nominal standard-error ratio, posterior calibration, type I error, power


Decision quality
Incremental net-benefit decision error, wrong-treatment probability, rank-reversal frequency


Overlap and weighting
ESS, ESS over nominal \(n\), coefficient of variation of weights, maximum weight, entropy, proportion trimmed


Model adequacy
Calibration slope, posterior predictive checks, leave-one-study-out predictive error, divergence counts, \(\hat{R}\), effective posterior draws


Computation and reproducibility
Runtime, failure rate, seed sensitivity, sensitivity to starting values, container reproducibility




The decision-quality row is the one most often omitted. A method that is slightly more biased but better calibrated for a reimbursement decision may be preferable to one that looks efficient but is anti-conservative when overlap is weak.





flowchart LR
    A[Define estimand] --> B[Data-generating mechanism]
    B --> C[Connected / disconnected evidence]
    C --> D[Manipulate: overlap, modifiers, misspecification]
    D --> E[Fit competing methods]
    E --> F[Evaluate against the declared estimand]
    F --> G[Publish code, seeds, manifests]

Two packages that appear in older workflows are no longer maintained. maic was archived from CRAN on 22 July 2025 because the maintainer’s email had become undeliverable, and Roche/MAIC states in its own README that it “is no longer developed”, recommending maicplus instead. Legacy installs belong in reproducibility archaeology, not in a new workflow.
No package unifies target-population definition, connected and disconnected evidence, marginal and conditional estimands, doubly robust transport, component structure, complex outcomes, missing data, sensitivity analysis, and regulatory reporting. That gap is itself catalogued, under software and benchmarks.

title: The chronology of the evidence
text:
Every finding in this catalog carries the publication year of the paper that made it, so a problem’s evidence can be read as a sequence rather than a pile. That answers three questions a pooled count cannot: has later work answered what an earlier paper left open, is a problem being closed in pieces by different groups, and is a problem simply being restated across the years with nothing happening in between.
195 problems carry at least one dated finding, drawn from a full-text reading of 687 papers published between 2010 and 2026.

title: The chronology of the evidence
section: Did the later work answer the earlier work?
text:
Did the later work answer the earlier work?
27 problems had progress as their newest evidence and every assertion of openness older. Publication order alone proves nothing there: two papers can straddle a date and be about different questions, and a later paper can close a corner of a problem whose earlier statement was about something else. Each was put to an independent reviewer with the older and newer claims side by side, and without the classification, so it could not agree with the mechanism by reading its label.

title: The chronology of the evidence
section: The same gap, named again and again
text:
The same gap, named again and again
Papers name the gaps they leave behind, in their own words. Across the corpus the same gap gets named repeatedly by authors who never cite each other, and that repetition is invisible while the gaps sit as free text under the paper that wrote them. Clustering the text does not find it, because a recurrence is a paraphrase rather than a near duplicate. So all 3619 future-research gaps were read and attached to a theme instead, and the chronology falls out.
139 themes were named by three or more papers across eight or more years; 78 of those have no paper in the corpus reporting any progress at all.
The most-restated of them are not registered problems yet. They are candidates from this reading, and they need the same scrutiny as any other entry before they become one.

title: A prioritized agenda
text:
The catalog lists problems. This page ranks them, in three tiers plus a list of work the field does not need. Tier 1 requires no new methodology: every item is something an analyst could do differently in the next analysis. Tiers 2 and 3 are research programs.
Priorities carried in the source material are weak evidence and are treated as such. Of the 46 rows in the source’s own master matrix, 30 are graded “Very high” and 15 “High”, which is under half a bit of information. Where a priority appears in this catalog it reflects three observable things instead: whether the problem blocks a decision-grade estimand, whether any method addresses it at all, and whether any software implements it.

title: A prioritized agenda
text:
Tier 1: change current practice now
These need no new theory. They are conventions the field could adopt in its next submission.

Declare one decision target population. Do not let data availability choose it implicitly. See estimands and target populations.
Separate conditional and marginal estimands. Do not combine a conditional regression coefficient with a published marginal effect without justifying the combination.
Prefer anchored analyses whenever a credible randomized path exists. Label unanchored methods as cross-study causal reconstructions, not routine adjustments. See the method landscape.
Require formal quantitative bias analysis for any decision-grade unanchored comparison. At minimum quantify omitted prognostic and modifier bias plus the most credible selection, measurement, or design threat. Otherwise label the result exploratory. See quantitative bias analysis.
Report support and influence, not effective sample size alone. An adjusted study that does not influence the decision contrast is not evidence for that contrast. See positivity, overlap and extrapolation.
Expose the bridge in a disconnected network. State exactly which parameter carries information across the gap. See disconnected networks.
Use target-standardized outcomes for non-collapsible and survival measures. Do not treat odds ratios and hazard ratios as population-invariant decision inputs.
Distinguish sampling, target-distribution, sensitivity, prior, and bridge uncertainty. An ordinary confidence or credible interval usually conditions on every major structural assumption being true.
Make sensitivity analysis decision-based, and joint where biases could interact. Report how much plausible bias changes the recommendation, and whether biases cancel or reinforce. One-at-a-time analyses can make a cancellation accident look like robustness.







NoteThe one-page test



A committee-facing summary should answer nine questions. If an analysis cannot, the problem is not the statistics.
What is being estimated? For which population? Which comparisons are supported by randomization? What connects any disconnected evidence? Which variables are assumed to remove population differences? Where is overlap weak? What is data-driven versus prior-driven or bridge-driven? Which residual biases were quantified, from what parameter sources? How much assumption violation changes the decision?

title: A prioritized agenda
text:
Tier 2: develop and validate next
Tractable programs where a first publishable contribution is within reach.

Estimand-specific deterministic and probabilistic bias analysis for matching, outcome regression, and unanchored meta-regression
Multiple-bias analysis combining confounding, selection, measurement, censoring, and design drift, with dependence preserved between bias parameters
Target-standardized multilevel network meta-regression, including the component case
Doubly robust network transport with study-level cross-fitting, nested inside explicit residual-bias analysis rather than presented as a substitute for it
Partial-identification and bias-function modules in mainstream software
Separation of within-study from between-study effect modification
Subnetwork-specific component drift with robust borrowing
Non-proportional-hazards, restricted-mean-survival, and multistate population adjustment, plus survival-specific bias analysis
Target-distribution uncertainty and distributionally robust standardization
Optimal individual-patient-data acquisition and bridging-trial design
Public validation datasets and cross-package benchmarks

title: A prioritized agenda
text:
Tier 3: high risk, high reward
Where the payoff is large and the probability of a clean result is not.

Federated cross-sponsor evidence synthesis
Mechanistic and statistical hybrid bridges
Invariant component effects across environments
Probabilistic component ontologies and treatment embeddings
Proximal methods using validated proxies for unmeasured modifiers
Graph-learning tools for design and diagnostics
Sequential and dynamic-regime indirect comparisons
Privacy-preserving release of target joint-distribution summaries

title: A prioritized agenda
section: What the field does not need
text:
What the field does not need
Stated plainly, because an agenda that only adds is not an agenda.

Another weight optimizer with no estimand contribution
Another package reproducing conventional matching under different function names
Simulation studies restricted to linear models, good overlap, measured modifiers, and correctly specified outcomes, which is to say studies run where every method works
Disconnected-network analyses reporting one narrow interval and no bridge sensitivity
Black-box machine-learning outcome regression evaluated only by predictive accuracy
Component models that add every pairwise interaction without identification or hierarchy
Ranking metrics presented without uncertainty or decision relevance

title: A prioritized agenda
text:
The organizing discipline

No effect estimate without an estimand, no disconnected estimate without a stated bridge, no population-adjusted estimate without a named target, and no structural bridge without fragility or partial-identification analysis.

Each row links to the full entry: what the problem is, why it is open, what has already been tried, and the probable solution or research direction.
Read the verdict column first. It records what happened when the claim was checked against the literature and against two independent external auditors, not what the source document asserted. A verdict is a judgment about the claim, not about the problem’s importance.






NoteWhat the verdicts mean












Verdict
Meaning




Confirmed open
Genuinely open. Auditors agreed and no counterevidence was found.


Partially addressed
Real, but existing work covers part of it. The entry names which part.


Overstated
The underlying difficulty is real, but a claim about its severity, or about no method existing, is stronger than the evidence supports.


Resolved since report
Closed in the literature or in code, either already or since the source was written. Kept because knowing something was recently closed is as useful as knowing it is open.


Not supported
No accessible source substantiates the claim as stated. Retained, with the reasons shown.


Unverifiable
Auditors disagreed with evidence on both sides, or the evidence was insufficient to decide. The disagreement is shown on the entry.

title: Open Problems in Indirect Treatment Comparisons
text:
The field is not short of estimators. It is short of identification discipline, estimand discipline, target-population discipline, and diagnostics that expose how much of an answer is supplied by data rather than by assumption.
This site catalogs the open problems, one entry at a time. Each says what the problem is, why it stays open, what has already been tried, and the most probable route to a solution.

title: Open Problems in Indirect Treatment Comparisons
text:
Start here


Browse the catalog
Every problem in one filterable table. Sort by priority, filter by category or verdict, or search across all fields.


The prioritized agenda
What should change in practice now, what should be built next, and what is high-risk and high-reward.


The method landscape
What each approach identifies, where it breaks, and a decision path from a comparison problem to a defensible method.


How this was verified
The provenance of this material, the audit protocol, and an honest account of what the verdicts do and do not establish.

title: Open Problems in Indirect Treatment Comparisons
text:
The organizing distinction
The decisive division in this field is anchored versus unanchored evidence, not matching versus regression versus multilevel modeling.
In an anchored comparison, randomization still identifies the within-trial relative effect, and population adjustment is mainly about transporting effect modification. In an unanchored or disconnected comparison, the analyst has to reconstruct a causal contrast across studies: every prognostic factor and effect modifier that creates cross-study outcome differences becomes relevant, and residual confounding is generally not testable. Most of the hardest entries in this catalog live on the unanchored side of that line.
Three consequences run through the whole collection:
Adjustment to one trial population is not transport to the decision population. Pairwise matching and regression approaches usually target the population of the trial that supplied aggregate data. Applying that effect to a reimbursement population is a second transport step, and it is commonly hidden.
Weak overlap is not a nuisance diagnostic; it changes the scientific question. When weights are extreme or a model extrapolates beyond its support, the nominal target estimand may cease to be credibly identified. Reporting an effective sample size does not repair that.
In a disconnected network, some assumption carries the information across the gap. Baseline risk, a dose-response curve, a treatment class, a shared component — each answers a different question and imports different bias. That software produced a connected posterior is not evidence that the effect is identified.

title: Open Problems in Indirect Treatment Comparisons
text:
Reading a verdict
Every entry carries a verdict recording what happened when its claims were checked against the literature and against two independent external auditors. A verdict of Overstated does not mean the problem is not real; it usually means the underlying issue is real and a claim about its severity was pitched too strongly. Entries marked Resolved since report are kept rather than deleted, because knowing that something was recently closed is as useful as knowing it is open.
The source material for this catalog was produced by a large language model and then audited. How this was verified explains what that means in practice, including where the audit’s own limits are.

title: How this was verified
text:
This catalog is derived from a set of deep-research documents produced by a large language model (ChatGPT deep research) in July 2026, covering open methodological problems in indirect treatment comparisons, population-adjusted indirect comparisons, component methods, and quantitative bias analysis.
That origin is the reason this page exists. A machine-generated research agenda is a plausible-sounding artifact whether or not it is correct, and publishing one as settled fact would be a disservice. Nothing from the source documents appears on this site without a verification verdict attached, and the evidence behind each verdict is shown on the entry itself.
The source documents are kept as working material and are not published here.

title: How this was verified
text:
The audit
Every problem carries a set of atomic, falsifiable claims extracted from the source. Those claims, not the prose around them, are what was tested.

Literature verification
For each problem, an agent with web and PubMed access checked that each cited work actually supports the claim attributed to it, and searched for later work that would resolve or narrow the problem.


Adversarial refutation
A second agent was instructed to refute the proposition that the problem is open, and to default to “not open” when uncertain. Asking an agent to confirm a claim and asking it to break the claim produce different results; only the second is informative.


Independent external auditors
Two frontier models outside this system were given the same claims, blind to each other and to the verdicts above:

GPT-5.6 Sol at maximum reasoning effort, via the codex CLI
Grok 4.5 at high reasoning effort, via the grok CLI

Both were constrained to answer from their own knowledge of the evidence-synthesis and causal inference literature, and asked to return a graded verdict, a reason, and any counterevidence.
Coverage was not equal, and that matters. Grok’s usage balance was exhausted partway through the run, so it reached only a fraction of the catalog. Entries it never saw carry two independent opinions rather than three. This is recorded rather than smoothed over, because an entry judged by two auditors is weaker evidence than one judged by three.



Auditor
Entries covered




Literature and prior-art check (Claude)
232 of 232


GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
232 of 232


Grok 4.5, recency lens
47 of 232





Checking the auditors
An audit is only worth what its auditors are worth, so their own load-bearing claims were spot-checked by hand against primary sources. Every checked claim held: marginal_effects() does exist in multinma 0.7.0, nmathresh is on CRAN, the Behaviour Change Intervention Ontology papers resolve, and Ishak et al. 2025 in PharmacoEconomics is real. No invented locator, version number, or function name was found.
One auditor finding is worth stating on its own, because it changed several entries: the source report proposes a reporting and credibility standard for population-adjusted indirect comparisons without citing Ishak et al. 2025, which published one.
Using two auditors rather than one is the point. On a pilot run they agreed that a claim about the emptiness of the quantitative bias analysis literature was overstated, both citing the mature epidemiological bias-analysis toolkit. On a different claim, about whether cross-subnetwork component constancy is testable at all, they disagreed — and the disagreement was substantive rather than noise. Where auditors disagree, this site shows the disagreement rather than resolving it silently.


Code verification
Problems that describe limitations of a specific software implementation were re-checked against that package’s current source, not against the report’s description of it. Some had already been fixed; those are marked as resolved rather than deleted, because the underlying methodological problem is still worth recording.


Adjudication
Verdicts follow a fixed rule, applied to the evidence gathered above:







Condition
Verdict




Later work resolves it, in the literature or in code
Resolved since report


At least two of the three independent checks call it overstated
Overstated


All checks agree it is open and no counterevidence surfaced
Confirmed open


Existing work covers part of it
Partially addressed


Checks disagree, or evidence is insufficient
Unverifiable, with the dissent shown


No support could be found
Not supported





What a verdict is about, and what a simulation study is about
These are different questions, and six entries now carry both. The verdict grades whether the entry’s characterization of the literature is accurate: whether the problem is as unaddressed as the entry claims, given what has already been published and shipped. A verdict of Overstated means the entry overstated the gap, not that the underlying methodological concern is unfounded.
A simulation study answers the methodological question directly, by measuring what the methods do. Those two can point in opposite directions without either being wrong, and on this site they sometimes do.
DIA-03 is the clearest case. The entry says PAIC diagnostics have not been evaluated as classifiers of realized error. That was graded Overstated, because two partial evaluations exist. The study then performed the full evaluation and found the panel does not classify realized error at the thresholds in use. Both hold: the entry overstated how unexamined the question was, and the answer to the question is that the diagnostics fail.
So a reader should not take a verdict as a judgment on the method, or a study result as a correction to the verdict. Where an entry has a study, the section headed What this project measured carries the measurement, and it is the part that speaks to what a method actually does.

title: How this was verified
section: Which fields are audited, and which are editorial
text:
Which fields are audited, and which are editorial
Not everything on an entry page is a verified claim, and the difference matters.
Audited. The statement, the reasons the problem is open, the cited prior work, and every claim extracted from them. These went through the process above and carry the verdict.
Editorial. Maturity and tractability are not stated anywhere in the source material. The source has no such fields; these values are a classification applied during extraction to make the catalog browsable. They are one reader’s judgment, they were not audited, and they should not be cited as findings.
Deliberately rebuilt. Priority is not carried over from the source either. The source’s own master matrix grades 30 of its 46 rows “Very high” and 15 “High”, which is under half a bit of information and not usable as a ranking. Priority here reflects three observable things instead: whether the problem blocks a decision-grade estimand, whether any method addresses it at all, and whether any software implements it.

title: How this was verified
section: What the verdicts do not mean
text:
What the verdicts do not mean
A verdict of Confirmed open means the claim survived the checks described above. It does not mean the problem is provably unsolved. Absence of counterevidence in a targeted search is weaker evidence than a systematic review, and this was not a systematic review: there was no protocol registration, no duplicate screening, and no formal risk-of-bias assessment.
A verdict of Overstated is a refinement, not a dismissal. In almost every case the underlying problem is real and the correction concerns how strongly it was stated.
Model-based auditors have their own failure modes. They can be confidently wrong, they share training data with the system that produced the source documents, and their knowledge has a cutoff. They were used because two independent expert opinions are better than none, not because they are authoritative.
Where an entry matters to a decision, read the cited primary sources. This catalog is a map of where the problems are, and a record of how hard each claim was pushed on. It is not a substitute for the literature it points to.

title: How this was verified
text:
Reproducing this
The site source, the build script, and the workflow definitions are in the repository. Entry pages are generated from a structured registry rather than hand-written, so the audit metadata on each page is the same data the adjudication used.

title: Studies
text:
The catalog records what is open. This is the attempt to close some of it: one study a week, each aimed at a single entry, taken in priority order.
Scope is population-adjusted indirect comparison only, meaning MAIC, STC, ML-NMR, ML-UMR and NMI. Standard network meta-analysis is out of scope because it does not adjust for population differences, which is where these problems live.

title: Studies
text:
Completed

ADJ-04 — Weighted conformal prediction keeps its marginal guarantee under shift by returning infinite intervals where the source has no data
Question. Does weighted conformal prediction give valid intervals for target patients under covariate shift, including where the source has no data?
Answer. No. Weighted conformal intervals kept marginal coverage over the target (0.904 to 0.919 at nominal 0.9), but beyond the source’s largest covariate value they covered 0.70 at a small shift and 0.83 at a moderate one, and at the largest shift they covered 0.99 only because 83% of those intervals were infinite. The method makes the support problem visible; it does not solve it. Estimating the density ratio changed nothing.
What it does not answer. Prediction intervals for individual outcomes rather than a marginal treatment effect; one covariate and one outcome model; no BART or Gaussian process arm; no support diagnostic scored as a classifier. Peer review has not been done.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument


ADJ-09 — An invariance screen for a bridging assumption, scored as a classifier
Question. Does instability across observed trials predict failure of a bridge used in a gap with no data, and does a screen on marginal effects fire under a valid bridge through non-collapsibility?
Answer. A stability screen across observed trials cannot confirm a bridge and refutes it rarely. With 4 or 10 trials, drift visible across them that biased the gap estimate by 0.28 was flagged in only 20% to 24% of analyses, and drift confined to the gap never above the null rate; passing the screen did not improve coverage of the reported analyses. Screening marginal log odds ratios raised false abstention under a valid bridge from 0.11 to 0.19 to 0.24 through non-collapsibility; screening conditional or standardized effects removed that.
What it does not answer. One event-rate level, no measurement shift, Cochran’s Q only; environments valid by construction. Peer review has not been done.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument


ADJ-10 — Modifier discovery across trials: no penalty is both stable and powerful, and study-level heterogeneity creates a false modifier that more trials entrench
Question. Are effect modifiers discovered from pooled trial data stable and correct enough to use, and do study-level confounders create false modifiers that more data do not remove?
Answer. No. Lasso discovery at the minimum-error penalty found the true modifiers but added 1.7 to 2.8 false ones among seven null covariates, and sets from independent datasets agreed with Jaccard similarity 0.37 to 0.57; the one-standard-error rule was stable only by selecting nothing (a single modifier found in 3% to 5% of analyses). With an unmeasured study-level cause of effect heterogeneity, pooled discovery selected the covariate whose trial means tracked it in 69% of analyses with 3 trials and 93% with 12 at the same total size, and raised false discoveries among the other covariates from 1.7 to 2.8 per analysis to 3.6 to 3.9; trial-specific treatment effects removed both.
What it does not answer. Lasso only (no multi-study causal forests); continuous outcome; linear modification; one overlap level; post-selection inference for the target not studied here. Peer review has not been done.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument


ADJ-15 — Target moments released under differential privacy
Question. When a target trial releases covariate moments under differential privacy, how much does ignoring the added noise cost MAIC coverage at realistic arm sizes and budgets, does propagating its known variance repair it, and when do extra released moments stop paying for their share of the budget?
Answer. Privacy noise is not negligible at usable budgets for trial-sized targets: at epsilon 1 and 150 patients it was 8% to 60% of the estimate’s variance and ignoring it cut coverage to 0.88 to 0.94; at 40 patients to 0.73. Its variance is known exactly, and adding it restored coverage in every scenario, conservatively where noise dominated. Releasing second moments pays only at larger budgets; at small ones it made MAIC infeasible in up to 87% of replicates.
What it does not answer. Laplace mechanism only; Gaussian mechanism, released correlations and overlap not varied. Results are conditional on feasible weights. Budget choice and governance are outside the study. Peer review has not been done.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument


CMP-12 — Splitting a multi-arm trial’s adjusted contrasts is conservative for one contrast and anticonservative for another
Question. When a three-arm trial’s population-adjusted contrasts share an arm and a weight vector, what is lost by treating them as independent, is the error ever anticonservative, and is dropping the trial cheaper?
Answer. Ignoring the within-trial covariance errs in a direction set by the contrast, not by how the arms’ effect modification aligns. The trial’s own B-versus-C interval became conservative in every scenario, while the network A-versus-B interval, which borrows through the trial, fell below nominal in 15 of 30 scenarios. The shared-weighting part of the covariance took both signs but never reversed a contrast’s error. Dropping the trial widened the network interval by 29% to 91%.
What it does not answer. Continuous outcome, linear modification, one three-arm trial in a fixed two-trial aggregate network; four-arm trials, the one-stage ML-NMR comparator and a bootstrap are not run, and target moments are fixed. Peer review has not been done.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument


CMP-13 — Separating within-trial from across-trial component effect modification
Also bears on IDN-06.
Question. Component ML-NMR fits one shared interaction on a globally centered covariate, which algebraically forces the causal within-trial interaction to equal the confounded across-trial association. How much does that cost, when, and is the damage really caused by aggregate data as the catalog claims?
Answer. Fitting one shared interaction matrix on a globally centered covariate is not pooling: for a binary modifier with study prevalence p_s it is algebraically identical to imposing that the causal within-trial coefficient equals the confounded across-trial one. In the model simulated, coverage of a nominal 95% interval for the causal interaction falls from 93.8% when that happens to be true to 17.2% when the two are equal and opposite, and further in networks whose contrasts move two components at once. Separating them costs about 5% in interval width and removes an order of magnitude of bias. The catalog’s stated cause is incomplete: the loss is present with all twelve trials supplying individual data, so aggregate data are not necessary for it, but removing individual data roughly doubles the bias, so they amplify it.
What it does not answer. The registered global analysis is uninformative and the regime split that produced a usable answer was prompted by observing that failure, so it is not prespecified. The general headline about component ML-NMR is not established: the likelihood and nuisance structures are not mapped onto the fixed- and random-effect specifications the implemented method offers, and free study-by-treatment effects or priors can absorb or alter the term the identity isolates. A maximum-likelihood analogue of component ML-NMR. Implemented ML-NMR is Bayesian and priors matter most where interactions are weakly identified, so the coverage numbers do not transfer to multinma; the algebra does, and therefore so does the direction. One binary modifier, a log link, a Poisson outcome, additive components with no synergy, no random treatment-effect heterogeneity, no inconsistency, and exactly reported study prevalences. Under the discordance patterns the split model is correctly specified, so the study measures the cost of an algebraically known restriction rather than establishing that real networks contain within/across disagreement or how large it typically is. Continuous or multiple correlated modifiers, misspecified aggregate covariate distributions, and time-to-event outcomes are untested. It does not touch IDN-05.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument


CMP-14 — Prior-to-posterior contraction and effective likelihood rank measure information, not bias
Question. CMP-14 asks for two default summaries, prior-to-posterior contraction per interaction and an effective likelihood rank, so an analyst sees when an aggregate-only interaction is held up by its prior. Would those summaries tell the analyst whether the reported interval covers?
Answer. Not reliably, and the reason is structural. On an exact identity-link arm of 504 scenarios and a logit arm of 72, no threshold on contraction, on either effective-rank reading, or on the estimability screen separates scenarios whose 95% interval covers nominally from those that fail. The summaries are functions of Fisher information and the prior, so within one design they are exactly constant while coverage ranges from 0 to 0.96. They partly catch the failure they were designed for: contraction flags 59% of failures caused by a tight prior. They catch none of the 142 failures caused by a biased route, where the ecological route carries between-study confounding or the additivity route a synergy, because confounding moves the posterior mean and not its information. A clean contraction says the likelihood spoke, not that it was right. Every result is exploratory.
What it does not answer. Nothing here is confirmatory: E1 was computed before its protocol existed, E2’s separation rules were rebuilt after its output was read, and the cause decomposition was added for the manuscript. E1 is exact for a design realized at its quadrature nodes and E2 is asymptotic, so no posterior was sampled and neither is an average over realized designs. The exact invariance of the summaries holds for known-variance Gaussian models; with estimated variances or random effects they would move with a departure and whether that movement could ever warn is untested. One target component, one covariate, one network geometry, a normal within-study covariate law on the logit arm, and departures acting on the mean only. The protocol went through thirteen rounds of critique; the manuscript has not been peer reviewed.

CMP-22 — Which trials supply individual data, and what selection on it does
Question. When the trials that supply individual data are selected on observed trial variables or on their own effect modification, how biased is the interaction evidence, does combining with aggregate trials help, and can a leave-IPD-out diagnostic reveal it?
Answer. Selection of which trials supply individual data on an observed trial variable caused no bias, but selection on the trials’ own effect modification biased the within-trial interaction evidence by up to 0.14 (true 0.3), with coverage down to 0.59. Combining with the across-trial association in all trials halved the bias. A leave-IPD-out influence diagnostic did not respond to the selection, so the problem is invisible without a stated selection model.
What it does not answer. Pairwise continuous-outcome meta-analysis rather than component ML-NMR; no selection-model sensitivity analysis; one network size. Peer review has not been done.

CMU-02 — Do prior-sensitivity diagnostics catch the analyses that are actually wrong?
Question. In a population-adjusted network a proper prior yields a proper posterior even where the likelihood identifies nothing, so a narrow interval can reflect the prior rather than the evidence. The diagnostics that would expose this exist. What are their operating characteristics: do they flag the analyses whose intervals actually miss the truth, and how often do they cry wolf?
Answer. At the thresholds the literature suggests, they miss most of it. Pairing each warning with whether that replicate’s own interval missed, a composite of four diagnostics has sensitivity 0.37 at a false-alarm rate of 0.16, falling to 0.13 outside two engineered geometries; the one sensitive rule fires on half the sound analyses too. Used as continuous scores the same statistics reach AUC 0.51 to 0.78, so this is a failure of thresholds rather than of the statistics. What no threshold repairs is that these diagnostics measure the prior’s influence while the harm comes from the prior’s location: with disconnected evidence and a tight prior four standard deviations from the truth, going from 100 to 400 per arm drops the warning rate from 0.98 to 0.01 while coverage stays near zero.
What it does not answer. The other half of CMU-02, wiring these diagnostics into released software, is untouched; neither multinma nor cpaic is run. The model is conjugate Gaussian with an identity link, a correctly specified linear mean and known variances, so nothing transfers directly to a non-conjugate posterior where MCMC error enters and the diagnostics behave differently. Only automated thresholds are evaluated; a plot read by an experienced analyst is a different instrument. Thresholds were taken from the source literature and not tuned. CMP-14 is touched only for the generic aggregate-only interaction, not for component models, and IDN-06 is not addressed at all because this design contains no within-versus-between discrepancy.

COV-02 — The adjustment set is a property of the scale
Question. Does the set of covariates whose imbalance changes a transported contrast differ between the risk difference, risk ratio, marginal odds ratio and conditional odds ratio scales?
Answer. The covariates a transported contrast depends on change with the scale, but not in the nested way DESIGN.md predicted. Prognostic non-modifiers never affected the conditional log odds ratio and affected some marginal scale by more than 5% in 13 of 24 scenarios, the risk difference included, because with a logistic model every prognostic variable modifies the risk difference; the risk difference was in fact the most sensitive scale (median 4.5% change per unbalanced prognostic variable, against 1.6% for the marginal odds ratio). Sets differed between the risk difference, marginal and conditional odds ratio in 10 of 24 scenarios, below the registered threshold of half, so the refuting sentence holds as registered.
What it does not answer. No time-to-event scale; no sampling or estimation of the sets; independent normal covariates. Peer review has not been done.

COV-03 — What an anchored comparison must balance on a non-collapsible scale
Question. On the log odds ratio scale a purely prognostic covariate changes the marginal effect. Does an anchored MAIC that balances only covariate means, as practice does, leave material bias, and does balancing the variance of the prognostic index remove it at acceptable cost in effective sample size?
Answer. Yes. On the log odds ratio scale a difference in the spread of prognosis between trials biases an anchored MAIC that balances only means by up to 0.11, even with no effect modification. Balancing variances or the variance of the prognostic index removes the bias, but when the source is less dispersed than the target the loss of effective sample size makes RMSE worse than not balancing. G-computation was unbiased with the lowest RMSE throughout.
What it does not answer. Independent normal covariates and a correctly specified outcome model favor G-computation. Hazard ratios, skewed covariates and augmented estimators not run; MAIC intervals treat weights as fixed. Peer review has not been done.

COV-04 — Shrinkage priors on interactions do not give honest intervals for a transported effect
Question. Do posterior intervals from shrinkage or selection priors on treatment-by-covariate interactions keep frequentist coverage for the transported effect when the whole procedure is repeated?
Answer. No. Continuous shrinkage does not select, but its intervals still undercovered: 95% posterior intervals for the transported effect covered 0.794 to 0.948 with an empirical-Bayes ridge prior and 0.868 to 0.959 with a hierarchical normal prior, against 0.939 to 0.955 for a flat prior. When the interactions the target weights push the effect the same way, their joint shrinkage biases the transported effect (up to 0.19) and the narrower interval does not carry the bias. Integrating the prior scale recovers only part of the loss.
What it does not answer. Continuous outcome with conjugate priors; no horseshoe, heredity constraints or projection-predictive selection; aligned modifiers only, no null scenario. Peer review has not been done.

COV-09 — The same covariate name, two instruments
Question. When the source and target measure a matched effect modifier with different instruments, how is the MAIC estimate biased, does a reliability correction recover it, and can a bounded analysis over declared instrument differences contain the truth?
Answer. MAIC’s bias from a modifier measured by different instruments follows a closed form in the instruments’ offsets, slopes and the source reliability. A reliability correction removes it only when both trials use the same instrument; with differing instruments it left bias up to 0.18 and could undo a chance cancellation. An envelope of corrected intervals over declared instrument differences covered the truth at 1.4 to 2.9 times the naive width.
What it does not answer. Linear instruments and identity link only; misclassification of binary covariates and bridging-sample correction not run; target sampling error absent. Peer review has not been done.

COV-10 — Interaction coefficients have their own consistency equation
Question. When direct and indirect paths carry opposing treatment-by-covariate interactions, does the pooled network meta-regression mask the modifier while the effect-consistency check passes, and can an interaction-consistency check detect it?

Opposing interactions on direct and indirect paths attenuate the pooled network meta-regression interaction toward zero, fully at the balance point and partly across a continuum, while the effect-consistency check stays at its null rate. The target effect was biased by 0.13 to 0.30 whether or not the covariate was selected. A direct interaction-consistency check detects it when studies per path and covariate spread are adequate (up to 1.00) and has little power otherwise (0.16 with two studies and narrow spread).

COV-12 — Reconstructing a target covariate from a median: when the mean is enough and when it is not
Question. When a target publication reports a skewed covariate as a median with IQR or range, how much error does reconstructing its marginal put into a target-standardized contrast, and is that error a function of the reconstructed mean alone?
Answer. Under an identity link with linear effect modification, yes: the contrast error is exactly the modification coefficient times the mean error. Under a logit link, no: the mean explains only 60% of the error’s variance, because the reconstruction’s spread and shape also enter. With strong skew and a reported range, a normal reconstruction biased the contrast by more than 1 on the identity scale and 0.4 on the log odds ratio scale, growing with sample size; a lognormal matched to the reported quantiles kept bias below 0.1.

COV-14 — Covariate sets that differ across comparators, and the ranking read from them
Question. When one individual-data trial is compared with several aggregate comparators that report different covariates, does adjusting each contrast for everything it reports give a worse ranking than adjusting all contrasts for the common set, even though each contrast is less biased?

The registered inversion was not confirmed in the primary scenarios, whose pattern turned out to widen the top comparator’s lead, but held in all six Fawsitt-like scenarios with similar populations. The intersection’s per-contrast bias was a median 2.4 times the maximal. A bounded analysis over the other comparators’ reported means covered at least 0.93 with similar comparator populations at little extra width.

DEC-01 — Do estimation and decision rankings of population-adjustment methods agree?
Question. When population-adjustment methods are ranked by the decisions their estimates lead to rather than by RMSE, does the ranking change, and how does it depend on where the truth sits relative to the decision threshold?
Answer. For a threshold on a known side of the truth, yes: near the threshold in poor-overlap scenarios the RMSE and expected-loss rankings correlated at only 0.45, and the disagreement was reproducible, not noise. It came from the direction of bias: a biased method decided wrongly far less often when its bias pointed away from the threshold (0.11 against 0.64). Averaged over the two sides of the threshold, as an analyst who does not know the truth must, the rankings agreed (0.93, the same best method in every poor-overlap scenario). RMSE is therefore an adequate proxy for decision error unless the side of the threshold is known.
What it does not answer. Decision on the relative effect only, without a net-benefit model; one source of replicates (COV-03) and five methods; no ML-NMR; priors on the side of the threshold not modeled. Peer review has not been done.

DEC-02 — Which analysis choice flips a decision
Question. Within one decision question, which analysis choices most often flip a population-adjusted recommendation, and how does that compare with the change in the question when the target population changes?
Answer. The choices are ordered rather than dominated by one. Near a decision threshold, adjusting or not flipped a population-adjusted decision in 36% of analyses, weighting against an outcome model in 20%, linear against quadratic STC in 13% and MAIC on means against means and SDs in 7%. Changing the target population moved the true log odds ratio by 0.39 to 0.59, more than any estimator choice moved the estimate, so the target belongs to the question, not the sensitivity analysis.

DEC-11 — Coverage of an STC interval after selecting effect modifiers on the same data
Also bears on COV-01.

Lasso at the one-standard-error penalty dropped real modifiers and coverage fell to 0.33 with three modifiers at 1000 per arm. Fitting all candidate interactions kept coverage at 0.93 to 0.96.

DEC-28 — The covariate value at which the better treatment changes is often not estimable as a point, and borrowed precision can make its interval wrong
Question. Is the covariate boundary between two treatments’ optimality well enough determined at achievable interaction precision to report as a point, and do standard intervals for it hold when interaction information comes partly from between-trial variation?
Answer. No. From one trial of 400 patients at a moderate interaction the exact (Fieller) 95% confidence set for the boundary was unbounded in 66% to 69% of replicates, while the delta-method interval was always finite and covered as little as 0.86 at the weakest interaction. Borrowing interaction precision from aggregate trials at different covariate means (81% of the precision) made the sets bounded, but a between-trial ecological term of 0.1 cut their coverage to 0.68 to 0.70 for a boundary away from the trials’ mean covariate value. Treating by the point estimate at the moderate interaction lost 31% to 95% of the value of individualized treatment with one trial.

DIA-02 — The reported weight panel cannot see where support is missing
Question. Every member of the overlap panel MAIC reports (Kish ESS, ESS percentage, entropy efficiency, maximum weight, top-share) is a symmetric function of the weights, so none can depend on where in covariate space the source fails to cover the target. Does that blindness matter in an ordinary covariate law, or do weight concentration and support geometry move together tightly enough that the panel is an adequate proxy?
Answer. It matters. Two source populations that remove the same mass at the same threshold, one in the effect-modifying coordinate and one in a prognostic coordinate, give panels that agree to within 1.6% while one estimate is biased by 0.016 on the marginal risk difference and the other by less than 0.0001, and material error is 24 times as frequent in the first. Across the two placements every panel member sits within 0.005 of chance; region-specific ESS separates them almost perfectly and sliced optimal transport cost at 0.73, but a convex hull distance maximized over coordinates is as blind as the panel. The registered within-arm primary outcome reads the other way (panel 0.574, best geometric 0.592, rule returns refuted) because within one arm the hole placement is fixed and the outcome measures sampling noise, not geometry. Both readings are reported. Balance on the omitted moment, the comparator most likely to overturn the headline, was never fairly tested.
What it does not answer. Balance on the omitted moment, the free check registered as most likely to overturn the headline, was not tested: every cell where it had anything to see was removed by the matched-multiset control. Region-specific ESS was handed the easiest instance, since the region it examines is the region the hole empties, so its near-perfect separation is an upper bound; a hole in a high-modification region the analyst did not think to examine is untested and there it would fail like the panel. No diagnostic is calibrated to a threshold. The analysis subgrid was chosen by a mechanical rule written after the run was read. The realized high-modification hole holds 22% of the modification mass against a registered 25%. MAIC weights only, a binary outcome, normal covariates, one rectangular hole, good overlap only after the null control, and two of the three published ESS definitions. Peer review has not been done.

DIA-03 — Effective sample size tracks the error an analysis got by chance better than the error it got from adjusting on the wrong covariates
Also bears on DIA-06.
Question. Every population adjustment arrives with a panel of numbers beside it: effective sample size, the same figure as a percentage, the largest weight, standardized differences before and after adjustment, a distance between populations. A committee reads them as evidence about whether to believe the estimate, and a widely quoted rule says to worry below an effective sample size of about 30 to 35. Scored as classifiers of realized error, with discrimination and calibration, against known truth and under a declared distribution of analyses, what are they worth?
Answer. At the level at which a diagnostic is actually read, one analysis at a time, effective sample size tracks the error a study got by chance far better than the error it got from adjusting on the wrong covariates: AUROC 0.847 against the outcome-noise component and 0.813 against chance covariate imbalance between the source arms, both of which are functions of the covariates, the assignment and the weights, against 0.653 for the transport component that adjustment exists to remove. At the quoted cutoff of 35 it catches between a quarter and a third of material errors in every misspecification stratum, 0.309 where an effect modifier is omitted and the omission is diagnosable in principle, at specificity 0.926. No evaluated fixed cutoff met the registered requirement of sensitivity 0.80 at specificity 0.50 in every stratum. Three of the panel’s members are provably one statistic, since ESS/n = 1/(1+CV^2(w)) exactly and area under the ROC curve is invariant to monotone transformation; a fourth, the post-weighting balance on matched moments, is zero at the solution of the calibration equations and among converged analyses cannot discriminate anything. On a decision-curve basis every rule in the panel is beaten by scrutinizing every analysis, up to an action threshold of 0.3.
What it does not answer. The second half of DIA-03 is untouched: no PSIS-LOO is computed at any hierarchical level and grouped study-level leave-one-out is no more implemented here than in the packages, so the mismatch between the level at which cross-validation is reported and the level at which the prediction is made remains open. DIA-06 is answered only in part; two estimator families and no adjustment are compared on identical replicates, but ML-NMR, NMI, doubly robust estimators and flexible learners are absent. The outcome is continuous with an identity link, which is what buys the exact error decomposition and is also the largest restriction: nothing here transfers to non-collapsible effect measures or time-to-event outcomes, where part of the error is a collapsibility artifact rather than an adjustment failure. Covariates are normal, comparisons are anchored, conditional constancy holds, and target moments are exact. The deployment weights are a declared judgment and nothing in this program measured them, which is why the primary results are within strata.

DIA-08 — Does the generator’s effect-modification structure decide the method ranking?
Question. When effect modification departs from the shared linear form most simulations use, does the ranking of population-adjustment methods change?

STC with linear interactions ranked first everywhere even though the departures biased it by up to 0.12, because weighting methods lost more to variance at poor overlap. Question. When population adjustment transports a time-to-event outcome with a competing cause, does a correctly transported cause-specific hazard ratio give the right cumulative incidence in the target, and what repairs it?

DIA-13 — Do bias mechanisms in an unanchored MAIC combine additively?
Also bears on QBA-22.
Question. When an omitted confounder, comparator outcome misclassification and covariate measurement error act together on an unanchored MAIC, is their joint bias the sum of their separate biases, and does a one-at-a-time analysis bound it?
Answer. No. An omitted confounder and misclassification of the comparator’s outcome interacted by up to 0.16 on the log odds ratio scale: with both at their largest the joint bias was about half the sum of the separate biases, and with the confounder reversed the joint bias had the opposite sign to that sum. Measurement error in a matched covariate combined nearly additively with either. The joint bias exceeded the largest single-mechanism bias in 22 of 36 combinations, so one-at-a-time analyses neither add up to nor bound it.

DIA-14 — A quantitative bias analysis verdict scored as a classifier
Question. How often does a QBA declare a MAIC decision robust when the true bias would reverse it, how does that depend on the elicited region rather than the method, and does oracle recovery reveal it?

When the region contains the true bias the grid never reassures falsely (an exact property); with elicitation errors scaled to the region it reassured falsely at most 17% of the time the true bias reversed the decision, but with the common region centered at zero bias it did so 78%, 37% and 9% of the time at half-widths 0.05, 0.15 and 0.3.
