title: Cross-environment invariance as a screen for bridges and modifiers
text: ADJ-09 Confirmed open High priority Promising

title: Cross-environment invariance as a screen for bridges and modifiers
text:
Statement
No invariant-causal-prediction screen for bridge or component assumptions exists in evidence synthesis, so the proposal stands. The nearest published precedent is Tanboga (arXiv:2604.18646), a transport meta-analysis with a precision-weighted sign-stability diagnostic and a two-condition abstention rule that declines to report a pooled estimate when stability is not supported; it operates within a connected evidence base and is a single-author preprint, so it does not certify a bridge across a disconnected gap. Two qualifications belong in the claim: a trial, era, country or subnetwork is not automatically a valid environment, since that requires harmonized variables, suitable exogenous shifts and adequate within-environment treatment support, and strong instability should flag a bridge for sensitivity analysis rather than trigger automatic rejection, because sampling error, measurement change, case mix and effect-scale non-collapsibility produce instability too.

title: Cross-environment invariance as a screen for bridges and modifiers
text:
Why it is open
The bridging assumption that matters concerns the gap where no data exist, so every stability check is necessarily performed somewhere else; passing the check is consistent with the bridge failing exactly where it is used, which makes the procedure able to refute but never to confirm. Invariance methods also need enough distinct environments to separate stable structure from noise, and evidence networks supply very few trials. The environment assumptions themselves, that studies differ in the right way and that an invariant set exists, cannot be verified from the network alone.

title: Cross-environment invariance as a screen for bridges and modifiers
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Tanboga, Stable Transport Meta-Analysis for Heterogeneous Cardiovascular Trials: A Nuisance-Anchor Framework with a Sign-Stability Diagnostic (2026)
Nearest published precedent for invariance-style screening with abstention in evidence synthesis: a precision-weighted sign-stability diagnostic with a two-condition abstention rule. Operates within a connected evidence base and says nothing about disconnected-gap bridges.

title: Cross-environment invariance as a screen for bridges and modifiers
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build invariance-based screening that estimates treatment or component effects separately by environment while letting baselines vary, and that flags bridges whose effects are unstable where they can be checked. Establish what counts as a valid environment in a trial network, given harmonization, exogenous shift and treatment support, and characterize how many environments are needed before the signal is usable. Present the output as screening and calibration rather than validation, routing failures into sensitivity analysis rather than into a pass/fail gate.

title: Cross-environment invariance as a screen for bridges and modifiers
text:
Our study

An invariance screen for a bridging assumption, scored as a classifier
The question put to it. Does instability across observed trials predict failure of a bridge used in a gap with no data, and does a screen on marginal effects fire under a valid bridge through non-collapsibility?
What it found. A stability screen across observed trials cannot confirm a bridge and refutes it rarely. With 4 or 10 trials, drift visible across them that biased the gap estimate by 0.28 was flagged in only 20% to 24% of analyses, and drift confined to the gap never above the null rate; passing the screen did not improve coverage of the reported analyses. Screening marginal log odds ratios raised false abstention under a valid bridge from 0.11 to 0.19 to 0.24 through non-collapsibility; screening conditional or standardized effects removed that.
Results.

Primary confirmed: under a valid bridge with strong prognosis, marginal minus conditional abstention 0.077 (SE 0.016) with 4 trials and 0.113 (SE 0.017) with 10; standardized within 0.03 of conditional.
Visible drift of 0.15 per unit (gap bias about 0.28): abstention 0.20 to 0.24; of 0.3 per unit (gap bias about 0.56): 0.50 to 0.67.
Gap-only drift: abstention within Monte Carlo error of the valid-bridge rate while the gap estimate was biased by up to 0.60.
Coverage among analyses that passed the screen differed from coverage among all analyses by at most 0.011.
Controls: identical trials 0.099 to 0.104; collapsible risk-difference model, marginal screen 0.117; large drift 0.990 or more.

Design.

Estimand

Conditional log odds ratio in the gap environment

Methods compared

Cochran’s Q screen on marginal log odds ratios, on conditional log odds ratios, on standardized marginal log odds ratios

Data-generating mechanism

K trials with differing covariate laws and a gap environment; Cochran’s Q screen with abstention on marginal, conditional and standardized log odds ratios; valid bridge, drift visible in the trials, and drift confined to the gap; 20 cells and 3 controls, 1000 replicates each.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 23,000 in total


What this does not answer. One event-rate level, no measurement shift, Cochran’s Q only; environments valid by construction. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument · Code and data: studies/ADJ-09-a-screen-that-can-refute-and-never-confirm · Protocol: registered before the run

title: Cross-environment invariance as a screen for bridges and modifiers
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Treating each trial, era, country or subnetwork as an environment, one can search for treatment-by-covariate or component-effect structures that remain stable while nuisance baselines vary, and reject or down-weight a candidate bridge whose effect varies strongly where it can be checked. The report labels invariant causal prediction speculative and calls the limitation of invariance-based bridge screening serious.”
What was wrong with it. The source said a candidate bridge should be rejected or down-weighted when its effect varies across environments; GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed that to flagging and sensitivity analysis, because instability has several innocent sources. The literature auditor also named the nearest precedent, arXiv:2604.18646, which the source did not cite.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. I found no invariant-causal-prediction screen for bridge or component assumptions in evidence synthesis, so the entry stands. The generic machinery exists (Peters, Buhlmann & Meinshausen’s invariant causal prediction; ‘Active Invariant Causal Prediction: Experiment Selection through Stability’, NeurIPS 2020), and one 2026 preprint does implement a stability screen inside transport meta-analysis: Tanboga, ‘Stable Transport Meta-Analysis for Heterogeneous Cardiovascular Trials: A Nuisance-Anchor Framework with a Sign-Stability Diagnostic’ (arXiv:2604.18646), which ‘incorporates a precision-weighted sign-stability diagnostic with a two-condition abstention rule to avoid reporting a single pooled estimate when stability is not supported’, evaluated in a pre-specified ADEMP simulation. That is the entry’s screen-and-abstain idea, but applied to pooling across connected trials, not to certifying a bridge across a disconnected gap; it is a single-author unrefereed preprint. The entry’s central logical point, that a stability check performed where data exist cannot license the gap where they do not, is correct and is not contradicted by anything I retrieved. Cites arxiv:2604.18646: Does NOT resolve this entry. It is the nearest published precedent for invariance-style screening with abstention in evidence synthesis, and the entry should cite it as such; it operates within a connected evidence base and says nothing about disconnected-gap bridges..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 and C2 are plausible for an adaptation of invariance methods, but ordinary invariant causal prediction targets invariant conditional laws or parent sets, not treatment-by-covariate interactions automatically. C3, C4, C7, and C8 capture the main limitations: observed invariance can be tested, while the causal environment assumptions and extrapolation across an unobserved gap cannot be established from those tests. C5 requires harmonized variables, suitable exogenous shifts, and enough within-environment treatment support; a trial, era, country, or subnetwork is not automatically a valid environment. Under C6, strong instability should flag the bridge and enter sensitivity analysis, not trigger automatic rejection or down-weighting without accounting for sampling error, measurement changes, case mix, and effect-scale non-collapsibility. C9 accurately reports the label. The adaptation and calibration problem remains open; its seriousness is conditional on using such a screen to support a decision-grade bridge.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Invariant causal prediction is a real multi-environment method for stable predictors/interactions, but aggressive search did not surface a peer-reviewed ITC/NMA/PAIC implementation that screens component or treatment bridges and is evaluated as operational practice. The report’s core epistemic claims match the method’s known limits: stability can be checked only where environments exist, so a pass never confirms the gap where the bridge is used; few trials supply few environments; environment assumptions are untestable from the network alone. That package of limitations means the problem is still open as stated (speculative screening tool, not validation). No RSM/SIM/MDM/JCE online-first 2024–2026 paper, arXiv stat.ME hit, or package PR closed invariance-based bridge screening for evidence networks. Queries: invariant causal prediction network meta-analysis; invariant prediction multi-trial effect modification; ICP transportability trials.

title: No proximal ITC method works with an aggregate-only comparator
text: ADJ-11 Partially addressed Medium priority Speculative

title: No proximal ITC method works with an aggregate-only comparator
text:
Statement
Proximal causal inference for indirect comparison is no longer speculative. Su, Rytgaard, Ravn and Eriksson, ‘Proximal indirect comparison’ (doi:10.1093/biomet/asaf044; arXiv:2405.10773), give identification and a doubly robust estimator for anchored ITC under unmeasured shifted effect modifiers, using an adjustment proxy in both trials and a reweighting proxy in the source, and Song et al. (arXiv:2603.04544) carry out a full proximal analysis of an external-control comparison in HIV prevention using baseline sexually transmitted infection status as a negative control outcome and geographic region as a negative control exposure. Both require individual data on each side, so the routine PAIC setting, where the comparator is a published baseline table, is untouched: no proxy’s negative-control role can be established from a summary table, and completeness and bridge-function conditions remain untestable.

title: No proximal ITC method works with an aggregate-only comparator
text:
Why it is open
Proximal identification requires proxies occupying specific structural roles plus bridge-function existence, completeness and positivity, and those conditions are not nonparametrically testable. The published methods assume individual patient data in both trials; in the usual PAIC setting the comparator is a published baseline table, from which no candidate proxy’s role can be checked. Unanchored comparisons and multi-arm networks also lie outside the two-trial construction that has been solved.

title: No proximal ITC method works with an aggregate-only comparator
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Proximal causal inference with proxies for unmeasured modifiers” The title presents proximal causal inference for unmeasured modifiers as the open problem, but the audit found a published method paper and an applied analysis for exactly this setting.
The source said. “Proximal causal inference is proposed as a route to identification in ITC settings with unmeasured effect modifiers or confounders, using proxy variables in place of the unmeasured quantity. The report labels it speculative for this field.”
What was wrong with it. The source called proximal causal inference speculative for this field, said suitable proxies are rarely available and cited nothing. Grok 4.5 found a method paper for exactly this setting (doi:10.1093/biomet/asaf044) and the literature auditor found an applied external-control analysis (arXiv:2603.04544); both weaken the rarity claim, though both need individual data on each side.
Dissent. literature dissented (overstated): A full applied proximal analysis of an unanchored indirect comparison now exists and the entry cites nothing. Song, Wu, Landovitz, … Shi, Gao, Donnell, Janes & Ye, ‘Proximal Learning for Trials With External Controls: A Case Study in HIV Prevention’ (arXiv:2603.04544, Mar 2026) applies proximal causal inference to estimate counterfactual placebo outcomes in an active-controlled trial using an external placebo-controlled trial, with baseline sexually transmitted infection status as negative control outcome and geographic region as negative control exposure. That is an external-control/unanchored ITC, and the proxies are ordinary trial baseline variables, not exotic instruments. This materially weakens ‘Suitable proximal proxy variables are rarely available in trial publications’ and ‘That makes the method inapplicable in most real ITCs.’ The narrow version survives: proxies were available because the authors had IPD from both trials; from a published baseline table you cannot verify a negative-control role. The completeness-condition claim is correct and untestable, as the entry says.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. A full applied proximal analysis of an unanchored indirect comparison now exists and the entry cites nothing. Song, Wu, Landovitz, … Shi, Gao, Donnell, Janes & Ye, ‘Proximal Learning for Trials With External Controls: A Case Study in HIV Prevention’ (arXiv:2603.04544, Mar 2026) applies proximal causal inference to estimate counterfactual placebo outcomes in an active-controlled trial using an external placebo-controlled trial, with baseline sexually transmitted infection status as negative control outcome and geographic region as negative control exposure. That is an external-control/unanchored ITC, and the proxies are ordinary trial baseline variables, not exotic instruments. This materially weakens ‘Suitable proximal proxy variables are rarely available in trial publications’ and ‘That makes the method inapplicable in most real ITCs.’ The narrow version survives: proxies were available because the authors had IPD from both trials; from a published baseline table you cannot verify a negative-control role. The completeness-condition claim is correct and untestable, as the entry says. Cites arxiv:2603.04544: Covers the external-control (unanchored ITC) case with IPD on both sides: proximal identification using baseline STI status as negative control outcome and geographic region as negative control exposure. Does not cover the aggregate-comparator PAIC case..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 is correct only under an explicit proximal ITC or transport causal structure with treatment-inducing and outcome-inducing proxies or their transport analogues, bridge-function existence, completeness, positivity, and compatible source and target data. Arbitrary correlates of an unmeasured modifier are not enough. C2 is essentially correct, although completeness is a property of conditional expectation operators and distributions, not of a proxy variable in isolation, and is generally not nonparametrically testable. C3 is plausible for aggregate trial publications but is an uncited empirical prevalence claim that this technical and source-code audit cannot verify. C4 accurately reports the label. The narrow adaptation and data-requirement problem remains open; Medium is proportionate because the method is inapplicable when the required proxy structure is absent.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. A direct method paper now exists for this exact setting: Su, Rytgaard, Ravn, Eriksson, Proximal indirect comparison (Biometrika, published 2025 / volume dating into 2026; arXiv:2405.10773), extending proximal causal inference to anchored ITC with unmeasured shifted effect modifiers via adjustment and reweighting proxies, with identification results and a doubly robust estimator under IPD in both trials. That means C1 is no longer purely speculative: proximal ITC is a formalized option in some IPD-rich anchored cases. The problem remains only partially closed because (i) completeness / bridge-function existence and structural proxy roles remain unverifiable assumptions, (ii) the paper itself requires suitable proxies (reweighting proxy in the source, adjustment proxy in both) and IPD, which most AgD-only trial publications do not supply, and (iii) unanchored and multi-arm network settings are not solved by this two-trial construction. C2–C3 and the practical inapplicability claim therefore still hold for routine HTA ITCs. Cites 10.1093/biomet/asaf044: Provides proximal identification and a doubly robust estimator for anchored indirect comparison under unmeasured shifted effect modifiers using reweighting and adjustment proxies (IPD setting).. Cites arXiv:2405.10773: Preprint of the Biometrika paper; same ITC-specific proximal method..

title: Topology-only graph neural network output cannot identify effects
text: ADJ-13 Confirmed open Medium priority Speculative

title: Topology-only graph neural network output cannot identify effects
text:
Statement
No graph neural network has been applied to a treatment or component evidence network, so the proposal is untested; the closest retrieved work is graph-theoretic rather than neural, including a preprint on the bipartite treatment-trial structure (arXiv:2505.18036). The claim that survives is narrow: a model reading topology alone can rank candidates or emulate simulations but cannot certify that any bridge is valid, because identification is a property of the assumptions attached to edges rather than of the shape of the graph. The stronger version, that a graph neural network’s output must never be an effect estimate, is too broad; such a model may legitimately serve as a nuisance or outcome model inside an otherwise identified estimator, and what is invalid is treating a topology-only prediction as an identified causal effect.

title: Topology-only graph neural network output cannot identify effects
text:
Why it is open
Identification in an evidence network is carried by the assumptions attached to edges, so a topology-reading model can rank candidates but cannot establish that any of them holds. A trained model nevertheless emits a number, and no current tooling or reporting convention types that number differently from an estimated treatment effect, so nothing structural prevents a topology-only prediction from being consumed as one. Because no such model has been applied in this field yet, this is a design principle for a technology that has not arrived rather than a documented failure.

title: Topology-only graph neural network output cannot identify effects
text:

Work
What it contributes

title: Topology-only graph neural network output cannot identify effects
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Restrict graph neural network tooling to simulation emulation, bridge-candidate ranking, prior construction and design prioritization, and validate the emulator against the simulations it replaces. Establish reporting conventions that type emulator output differently from estimated treatment effects so the distinction survives into submissions. Where such a model is used as a nuisance or outcome model inside an identified estimator, say so explicitly and carry valid inference for the learned component.

title: Topology-only graph neural network output cannot identify effects
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “Graph neural networks must output hypotheses, not effect estimates” The title asserts a graph neural network must never output an effect estimate, which the audit rejected as too broad since such a model may serve as a nuisance model inside an identified estimator.
The source said. “Graph neural networks are proposed to encode treatment-network and component-network topology so as to inform priors, rank bridge candidates and emulate expensive simulation studies. The report is explicit that they must not decide causal validity: the appropriate output is a hypothesis or design recommendation, not an effect estimate.”
What was wrong with it. The source said the appropriate output of a graph neural network here is a hypothesis or design recommendation and never an effect estimate; GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed that, since such a model can be a nuisance or outcome model inside an identified estimator, so the prohibition attaches to topology-only predictions rather than to the architecture. The literature auditor added that the governance risk is a prediction about a practice that does not yet exist rather than an observed failure mode.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I found no graph neural network applied to a treatment or component evidence network; searches returned graph-theoretic but not neural work (random walks on NMA networks, Rucker/Davies; the bipartite treatment-trial structure preprint arXiv:2505.18036). So the technical proposal is open. The caveat is about what kind of claim this entry is making. ‘Network topology alone cannot establish causal identification’, ‘a GNN should not decide causal validity’ and ‘the appropriate output is a hypothesis or design recommendation’ are normative positions, not findings; no source asserts them, and no source contradicts them. Likewise the governance claim, that nothing prevents a GNN number being consumed as an effect estimate, is a prediction about practice with no evidence base because the practice does not yet exist. The entry is defensible but should be worded as a design principle for a technology not yet in the field rather than as an observed failure mode.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

not-a-problem / overstated. C1 through C3 are feasible only as learned surrogates trained on relevant simulations or data and validated within their training domain. C4 and C5 are correct when restricted to topology alone: graph shape contributes to structural estimability, but it cannot establish the causal assumptions attached to a bridge. C6 is too broad and architecture-specific. A GNN may legitimately be a nuisance or outcome model inside an otherwise identified causal estimator, and could contribute to an effect estimate with valid design and inference. What is invalid is treating a topology-only prediction or simulation surrogate as an identified causal effect. C7 accurately reports the label. The stated governance risk is generic model misuse, not a distinct unresolved statistical problem; the technically correct restriction can be imposed by defining the estimand, role, and output type. This is a speculative roadmap item rather than a decision-grade gap.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Search for GNN applications to evidence-network topology, NMA bridge ranking, simulation emulation, or prior construction for ITC found no field-closing work. Broader GNN ranking papers exist for general pairwise comparison graphs, and GNN causal-learning surveys exist, but none establish permissible, evaluated tooling that ranks ITC bridges or emulates NMA simulations under governance that prevents topology-trained numbers from being read as causal effect estimates. The identification claim that topology alone cannot certify causal validity is standard and unrefuted; the open part is tooling-plus-convention so that GNN output is typed as hypothesis/design recommendation rather than estimate. Queries: graph neural network network meta-analysis; GNN treatment ranking evidence synthesis; GNN bridge candidates NMA.

title: Privacy guarantees and governance for shared trial-level data
text: ADJ-15 Partially addressed High priority Emerging

title: Privacy guarantees and governance for shared trial-level data
text:
Statement
Differential privacy would let data holders publish richer target-population summaries under a formal guarantee, and adjacent work exists: differentially private covariate balancing propagates privacy noise into weighted treatment-effect estimators (arXiv:2410.14789), FedECA delivers federated inverse-probability-weighted external-control analysis without pooling individual data (arXiv:2311.16984), and methods exist for choosing the privacy parameter for trial data release (PMC11031247). None calibrates a budget for the target moments PAIC needs, and no PAIC estimator treats released summaries as noisy inputs and propagates that noise into the transported effect. Two claims need narrowing: a correctly calibrated guarantee does not cease to hold because an arm is small, with utility rather than validity the casualty, and the assertion that no governance framework exists in evidence synthesis was not verifiable by any auditor.

title: Privacy guarantees and governance for shared trial-level data
text:
Why it is open
Trial arms are small, so aggregate quantities computed on them have high sensitivity: gradients, sufficient statistics or likelihood contributions from a few dozen patients need large noise to be protected, and standard federated privacy analyses assume per-site samples far larger than a 40-patient arm. The guarantee is bought with injected noise, so extra moments arrive already degraded, and PAIC estimators must propagate that noise into the effect rather than treating the summaries as fixed; nobody has established what privacy budget yields target moments precise enough to change a PAIC conclusion. Governance is the second constraint, since cross-sponsor analysis requires legal agreement about who runs the code, who sees intermediate quantities and who is accountable.

title: Privacy guarantees and governance for shared trial-level data
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ohnishi & Awan (arXiv:2410.14789), differentially private covariate balancing
Privatizes propensity-score and balancing steps and propagates privacy noise into weighted treatment-effect estimators with privacy-utility rates. Does not calibrate a budget for the target moments PAIC needs.


FedECA (Nature Communications 2025; arXiv:2311.16984)
Federated inverse-probability-weighted external-control analysis for time-to-event outcomes without pooling individual data, with discussion of differentially private variants.


PMC11031247 (data-driven choice of the privacy parameter for clinical trial data release)
Addresses privacy-parameter selection for trial data release, the nearest existing answer to the budget-calibration question, but not for PAIC target moments.


PMC8449619 (scoping review of differential privacy in health research)
Surveys differential privacy applications in health research, establishing the privacy-utility trade-off and the state of adoption.

title: Privacy guarantees and governance for shared trial-level data
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Characterize the privacy attack surface of evidence synthesis when trial arms are small, and design release mechanisms and noise calibration for exactly the target moments PAIC needs in that regime, extending the differentially private balancing work that already propagates privacy noise into weighted estimators. Build PAIC estimators that treat released summaries as noisy inputs and carry the uncertainty into the transported effect. Develop governance conventions for cross-sponsor analyses covering code custody, intermediate quantities and accountability, and document what already exists before claiming a vacuum.

title: Privacy guarantees and governance for shared trial-level data
text:
Our study

Target moments released under differential privacy
The question put to it. When a target trial releases covariate moments under differential privacy, how much does ignoring the added noise cost MAIC coverage at realistic arm sizes and budgets, does propagating its known variance repair it, and when do extra released moments stop paying for their share of the budget?
What it found. Privacy noise is not negligible at usable budgets for trial-sized targets: at epsilon 1 and 150 patients it was 8% to 60% of the estimate’s variance and ignoring it cut coverage to 0.88 to 0.94; at 40 patients to 0.73. Its variance is known exactly, and adding it restored coverage in every scenario, conservatively where noise dominated. Releasing second moments pays only at larger budgets; at small ones it made MAIC infeasible in up to 87% of replicates.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: coverage ignoring the noise was as low as 0.883 at epsilon of at least 1 and targets of at least 150.
Propagating the known noise variance gave coverage of at least 0.926 in every private scenario, the minimum matching the non-private analysis’s own misspecification; it reached 1.000 where noise dominated.
Releasing means and second moments with a split budget left no feasible weights in 45% to 87% of replicates at 40 to 150 patients and epsilon 0.5 to 1.
Under quadratic modification at epsilon 4 and 150 patients second moments cut RMSE from 0.229 to 0.171.

Design.

Estimand

Target-population mean difference, A versus C, at the target trial’s own covariate moments

Methods compared

MAIC to non-private moments, MAIC to private moments, noise ignored, MAIC to private moments, noise variance propagated

Data-generating mechanism

MAIC to Laplace-privatized target means or means and second moments, 48 cells crossing target size (40 to 500), privacy budget, released statistics and linear or quadratic effect modification; non-private, noise-ignored and noise-propagated analyses. 1000 replicates per cell.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 48,000 in total


What this does not answer. Laplace mechanism only; Gaussian mechanism, released correlations and overlap not varied. Results are conditional on feasible weights. Budget choice and governance are outside the study. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument · Code and data: studies/ADJ-15-noise-whose-variance-is-known-exactly · Protocol: registered before the run

title: Privacy guarantees and governance for shared trial-level data
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 2 findings from 2 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “Differential privacy is proposed so data holders can publish richer target-population summaries, including more moments, correlations and joint structure, under a formal guarantee, while the report separately names privacy attacks arising from small trial arms and the governance of cross-sponsor analyses as key open questions. Together these determine what can safely be released and who is accountable for the result.”
What was wrong with it. The source implied that small trial arms defeat formal privacy guarantees and that no cross-sponsor governance framework exists. GPT-5.6 Sol pointed out that a correctly calibrated guarantee still applies at small n and that the universal governance claim is not established, and the literature auditor could not verify it either; Grok 4.5 supplied the adjacent differentially private causal work the source did not cite.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 2 surviving findings from: Arbitrated Indirect Treatment Comparisons; Identifying back pain subgroups: developing and applying app. New citations: 10.1007/s43441-026-00976-2, 10.3310/pgfar04100

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. I found differential privacy applied to clinical trial data sharing, including a data-driven method for choosing the privacy parameter for trial data release (PMC11031247) and a scoping review of DP in health research (PMC8449619), plus the standard precedent that published aggregate summaries alone permitted large-scale reconstruction of the 2010 US Census. Nothing I retrieved releases DP-protected target-population moments and propagates the injected noise through a PAIC estimator, which is the entry’s specific gap, and nothing establishes what privacy budget still yields target moments precise enough to change a PAIC conclusion. The privacy-utility trade-off, the requirement to account for injected noise, and the elevated re-identification risk of statistics computed on small arms are all standard and documented. The governance claim (‘no such framework exists in evidence synthesis’) is a no-method-exists assertion; I found no source stating the absence, so treat that specific sentence as unverified rather than verified.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1, C2, C4, C6, and C8 are technically sound with conditions. A differential-privacy guarantee requires a defined neighboring unit, bounded contributions, a specified mechanism, and privacy accounting; releasing more or higher-dimensional moments generally consumes privacy budget or increases error. Small arms worsen sensitivity and utility, but a correctly calibrated formal guarantee does not cease to apply merely because n is small. Attack feasibility also does not follow from sample size alone. Privacy-induced randomness should normally be propagated for unconditional inference, although an explicitly conditional analysis can condition on the released value. Cross-sponsor governance is a legitimate implementation question, but the universal claim that no framework exists is not established technically. This remains open PAIC-specific work, but it is a decision-grade blocker only when privacy-constrained sharing is required.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported-with-caveat. Inverted-prior search found adjacent DP-plus-causal and federated ECA work, but not a solution to the PAIC-specific package as stated. Differentially private covariate balancing (Ohnishi and Awan, arXiv:2410.14789) shows how to privatize propensity-score / balancing steps and propagate privacy noise into weighted ATE/WATE estimators with privacy-utility rates; FedECA (Nature Communications 2025; arXiv:2311.16984) delivers federated IPTW for time-to-event external control arms without pooling IPD and discusses DP variants. Neither calibrates a privacy budget for richer target-population moments (means, correlations, joints) that classic AgD PAIC needs, nor builds PAIC estimators that treat those released moments as noisy inputs, nor characterises the small-arm (tens of patients) attack surface specific to evidence-synthesis statistics, nor supplies a cross-sponsor governance framework for code custody and intermediate quantities. Gradient-leakage and federated DP literature confirm C5–C6 as general facts, not as ITC closures. C1–C4 are standard DP properties (supported as framing), not evidence that the PAIC adaptation is done. C7 remains open. C8 is a report-internal maturity label and was not independently auditable beyond consistency with the sparse PAIC-DP literature. Queries run: differential privacy + (MAIC|PAIC|NMA|indirect comparison|target moments); FedECA DP; DP covariate balancing causal inference; small-sample federated gradient leakage; ISPOR/EUnetHTA/NICE federated HTA governance 2024–2026.

title: Representation learning for low-dimensional population encodings
text: ADJ-17 Confirmed open Medium priority Speculative

title: Representation learning for low-dimensional population encodings
text:
Statement
No learned population representation has been used inside an indirect comparison or population adjustment, so the ITC-specific problem is open, though the underlying machinery is well developed elsewhere in balanced representation learning for causal effect estimation and in cross-institution record harmonization. For an encoding to support valid transport, the relevant conditional treatment effect must be representable from the encoding, with exchangeability, positivity and measurement comparability still holding, and no data-only objective can guarantee that unknown effect modifiers survive compression. The auditability objection needs softening: a learned encoding is harder to audit than a declared mapping, but transparent encoders, reconstruction checks, interaction-preservation checks and external validation can reveal some losses.

title: Representation learning for low-dimensional population encodings
text:
Why it is open
A representation is optimized for some objective, and unless that objective explicitly preserves treatment-effect-relevant variation, compression can discard exactly the modifier information the transport depends on; no objective can guarantee retention of modifiers that are unknown. Because the encoding is learned rather than declared, a reviewer cannot readily see which covariate contrasts were preserved and which were collapsed, which conflicts with the reporting expectations placed on population adjustment. Nothing in current practice reports what a representation dropped, so a loss that does occur goes unnoticed.

title: Representation learning for low-dimensional population encodings
text:
What has been tried
No prior work is identified for this problem in the reviewed sources.

title: Representation learning for low-dimensional population encodings
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Investigate representation learning for high-dimensional biomarker harmonization under a stated sufficiency condition that says which heterogeneity the encoding must retain, and require diagnostics that report what the representation dropped, using reconstruction and interaction-preservation checks rather than asserting opacity. Compare against declared, human-readable harmonization mappings before accepting an opaque encoding in a submission.

title: Representation learning for low-dimensional population encodings
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Learned low-dimensional representations of populations are proposed to handle high-dimensional biomarkers and to harmonize covariates measured differently across trials. The report labels the idea speculative.”
What was wrong with it. The source said a learned encoding makes population transport opaque and that nothing in current practice would reveal a dropped modifier. GPT-5.6 Sol called that categorical, since reconstruction, interaction-preservation and external-validation checks can expose some losses, even though they cannot rule out loss of an unmeasured modifier.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I found no learned population representation used inside an indirect comparison or population adjustment, so the ITC-specific problem is open. The caveat is that ‘Speculative’ understates the maturity of the underlying machinery, which is well developed elsewhere: balanced representation learning for causal effect estimation maps covariates into a latent space where treatment groups are distributionally similar while retaining prognostic information, and cross-institution EHR harmonization by representation learning is now published at scale (Nature Communications 2026, harmonized embeddings across US and French health systems enabling federated joint clustering). The entry’s two risk claims are the right ones and are not contradicted by anything I retrieved: an objective that does not explicitly preserve treatment-effect-relevant variation can discard modifier information, and a learned encoding is not auditable in the way NICE-style population adjustment reporting expects. I did not find a source that states the auditability objection, so that part rests on reasoning rather than citation.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1-C3 and C5 are defensible. For an encoding Z=phi(X) to support valid transport, the relevant conditional treatment effect must be representable using Z, with the required exchangeability and positivity conditions still holding; harmonization also requires measurement comparability across trials. No learning objective can guarantee preservation of unknown effect modifiers without assumptions about the modifier class or outcome structure. C4 is directionally correct, but saying learned adjustment becomes unauditable and that nothing can reveal lost information is categorical overstatement. Transparent encoders, reconstruction checks, interaction-preservation checks, and external validation can reveal some losses, although they cannot rule out loss of unmeasured modifiers. This is a speculative roadmap item, not a current requirement for decision-grade PAIC.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. No cited prior_work. Search for representation learning / embeddings applied to ITC, PAIC, transportability, or multi-trial population encoding found no evaluated method that (i) compresses high-dimensional biomarkers into low-dimensional population encodings for PAIC, (ii) provably retains effect-modifying variation, and (iii) exposes audit diagnostics of what was collapsed. Adjacent work is batch harmonization for imaging biomarkers (ComBat, DeepResBat and variants), which is declared or residual-batch correction rather than learned population encodings for transported treatment effects, and does not meet the auditability bar the problem raises. C1–C2 remain speculative proposals; C3–C4 correctly flag silent loss of modifiers and regulatory opacity. C5 is a report maturity label consistent with absence of PAIC-specific methods. Queries: representation learning + (transportability|MAIC|indirect comparison|population adjustment); embedding harmonization biomarkers meta-analysis; deep residual batch harmonization 2024–2026.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Shapley attribution of regimen effects to treatment components
text: ADJ-19 Confirmed open Medium priority Emerging

title: Shapley attribution of regimen effects to treatment components
text:
Statement
Attributing a combination regimen’s effect to its components in component network meta-analysis by Shapley value remains untested. Model-based attribution of effect to drug versus context has been done in psoriasis (doi:10.1016/j.jaad.2026.07.030), but not as a Shapley decomposition over a component design matrix. A Shapley value is defined relative to a fitted model, so any such attribution inherits that model’s additivity assumption rather than testing it.

title: Shapley attribution of regimen effects to treatment components
text:
Why it is open
A Shapley allocation exists for any fitted value function, so nothing in the numbers distinguishes an attribution supported by contrast information from one manufactured by the model’s structure, while the output looks like evidence that a component works. Unsupported coalitions require the model to extrapolate to component combinations no trial studied, and the allocation of interaction terms is a convention rather than a fact. Component estimability is not visible in a network diagram, so a reader has no way to tell which attributions rest on evidence.

title: Shapley attribution of regimen effects to treatment components
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Li, Shih & Tu, Graphical evaluation of evidence structure within a component network meta-analysis, Res Synth Methods 2023;14:596-607
Shows that component identifiability cannot be deduced from the network plot and requires a dedicated signal-flow analysis; the estimability report that must accompany any Shapley attribution.


netmeta (R package, netcomb for component network meta-analysis)
Existing component network meta-analysis estimation, which estimates component effects where the design identifies them; a different estimand path from post-hoc Shapley allocation.


Ellenberg et al. 2026

title: Shapley attribution of regimen effects to treatment components
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Use Shapley-style attribution to communicate interaction structure within component models, and report component estimability alongside it so an attribution can never be mistaken for an identified causal component effect. State the estimability condition correctly: in a linear component model a linear attribution is identified exactly when its coefficient vector lies in the row space of the design, and a nonlinear attribution must be invariant over the observational equivalence class. Label attributions that fail that test as unidentified rather than reporting them as component effects.

title: Shapley attribution of regimen effects to treatment components
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Cooperative game theory and Shapley values are proposed to attribute a combination regimen’s effect to its individual components under a fitted model, improving interpretability of component interactions. The report calls this an emerging interpretive tool.”
What was wrong with it. An earlier pass of this audit dropped a real reference here. Grok supplied a correct PubMed identifier next to a placeholder DOI ending in ‘xxx’; the synthesis agent rejected both as fabricated. The PMID resolves to Ellenberg et al., Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology, whose real DOI is 10.1016/j.jaad.2026.07.030. A placeholder beside an identifier does not make the identifier fake.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. I found no application of Shapley values or cooperative game theory to attributing a combination regimen’s effect to its components in component network meta-analysis. Shapley attribution is well established in machine-learning feature attribution and has been applied to biological networks, and component NMA has its own additive and interaction models, but the two have not been joined in the literature I retrieved. The entry’s key warning is correct and is independently corroborated by the CNMA identifiability literature: Li, Shih & Tu (Res Synth Methods 2023;14:596-607, doi:10.1002/jrsm.1623) show that whether all component effects are identifiable is not readable off the network and requires a dedicated signal-flow analysis, which is precisely the condition under which a Shapley decomposition would still return a full, confident-looking allocation. Confidence is moderate: absence of a Shapley-CNMA paper is a negative search result rather than a positive finding.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 is correct only after defining a player set, a coalition value for every required component subset, a reference population, and an interaction-allocation convention. Shapley values then allocate a model-implied contrast. C2 is possible but not automatic, especially when unsupported coalitions require extrapolation. C3 is the essential limitation, and C4 matches the report. The claim that Shapley attribution always supplies a meaningful decomposition is too broad. The proposed null-space diagnostic is also imprecise: components do not generally lie in a design matrix’s null space. In a linear component model X beta, a linear attribution l-transpose beta is identified exactly when l lies in the row space of X, equivalently when l-transpose n equals zero for every n in null(X). A nonlinear attribution must likewise be invariant over the observational equivalence class. Safe PAIC reporting remains open, but this is an interpretive roadmap item rather than evidence that component effects are identified.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. No cited prior_work. Component NMA (additive/interaction CNMA; netmeta::netcomb and related methods) already estimates component effects when design information identifies them; that is a different estimand path from post-hoc Shapley allocation of a regimen effect under an arbitrary fitted value function. Search found clinical model-based Shapley/SHAP attributions (including Ellenberg et al. 2026 JAAD online-first on model-based attribution of biologic effectiveness in psoriasis: drug vs context, doi:10.1016/j.jaad.2026.07.xxx as indexed under S0190-9622(26)03104-X / PubMed 42456775) and many SHAP applications for feature importance, none of which solve the identification-versus-attribution gap for multi-component regimens in ITC: a Shapley decomposition always exists relative to the model even when component effects are not identified by the network design. C1 is true as a computational fact under a fitted model. C2 is a soft interpretability claim, not a solved methodological standard. C3 is the correct caution and is strengthened, not resolved, by applications that emit attributions without reporting design null-space / estimability. C4 is a report label consistent with the literature. Queries: Shapley + (component network meta-analysis|CNMA|combination regimen|multi-component intervention); cooperative game theory treatment components meta-analysis 2023–2026.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Cross-subnetwork component constancy is the untestable bridge
text: CMP-01 Confirmed open Very high priority Emerging

title: Cross-subnetwork component constancy is the untestable bridge
text:
Statement
In a disconnected network the additive component bridge identifies a cross-gap contrast only when the requested component contrast lies in the row space of the pooled design, and the subnetwork-specific drift that would invalidate it has no data behind it. Petropoulou et al. 2023 state the point directly: for disconnected networks the additivity assumption cannot be tested, and the nested Q statistic comparing CNMA with NMA is unavailable because standard NMA cannot be fitted across the gap. The untestability is narrower than a blanket claim, because a common component parameter does impose observable compatibility restrictions, and any component functional lying in the intersection of two subnetworks’ row spaces can be estimated in each and compared. What cannot be tested is a bridge-relevant drift functional that is not separately estimable in at least two subnetworks, and that is exactly the functional carrying the cross-gap comparison.

title: Cross-subnetwork component constancy is the untestable bridge
text:
Why it is open
Writing subnetwork component effects as beta^(s) = beta + Delta^(s), the bridge requires the particular contrast of drifts loading the target comparison to be zero, and no randomized evidence inside either subnetwork bears on it. The pooled additive lack-of-fit statistic can detect some cross-subnetwork incompatibility, but it conflates that with other misfit, and the nested additivity test is unavailable precisely when the network is disconnected. The drift is also mis-parameterized in the only sensitivity tool that exists for it: the cross-gap bias is C_t’ Delta_s minus C_u’ Delta_r across two different subnetworks, not (C_t - C_u)’ Delta, so a shared-drift formula can cancel a component exactly when differential subnetwork drift is what matters. Component labels additionally conceal dose, schedule, and delivery differences that can make the same nominal component a different intervention on each side of the gap.

title: Cross-subnetwork component constancy is the untestable bridge

Work
What it contributes




Rucker et al. 2020
gives the foundational frequentist formulation of component network meta-analysis and shows the models can be applied to disconnected networks when subnetworks share components


Wigle and Beliveau 2022

title: Cross-subnetwork component constancy is the untestable bridge
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Reparameterize the fragility calculation so the perturbed quantity is the subnetwork-indexed drift contrast that actually loads the cross-gap comparison, and report partial-identification bounds over plausible drift sets together with commensurate priors that shrink toward but do not impose equality. Report which component functionals are estimable in more than one subnetwork, since those can be compared directly and are the only empirical purchase on constancy that a disconnected network provides. Where the decision matters enough, seek external bridge evidence or a trial spanning the gap, and otherwise follow the published recommendation to analyze subnetworks separately unless strong external clinical evidence supports additivity.

title: Cross-subnetwork component constancy is the untestable bridge
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “The additive component bridge that reconnects a disconnected treatment graph requires component effects to be constant across subnetworks, and that constancy cannot be tested against the observed evidence. It is the assumption that actually identifies the cross-gap comparison, so the same shared parameter that reconnects the network is also what makes the reconnection fragile.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no data could bear on cross-subnetwork constancy and that every computable goodness-of-fit statistic is structurally insensitive to it. GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed both from the design algebra: a shared component parameter imposes observable compatibility restrictions, the pooled additive Q can detect some cross-subnetwork incompatibility, and functionals estimable in two subnetworks can be compared directly, so only a drift functional not separately estimable in two subnetworks is untestable; the literature auditor supplied the missing source for what survives, doi:10.1186/s12874-023-01959-9.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Retrieved both cited works. Rucker/Petropoulou/Schwarzer 2020 (Biom J 62:808-821) is indeed the foundational frequentist CNMA formulation (weighted least squares, netmeta) and its abstract ends: ‘we show that these models can even be applied to disconnected networks, if the composite treatments in the subnetworks contain common components’ - supporting the reconnection claim. Wigle and Beliveau 2022 is titled ‘Bayesian unanchored additive models for component network meta-analysis’, so the attribution is literally accurate; caveat for the site editor: ‘unanchored’ there means ‘no anchor intervention in the additivity parameterisation’, NOT the anchored/unanchored ITC distinction used elsewhere in this catalog. The untestability claim is independently asserted by a source the entry does not cite: Petropoulou et al. 2023 states plainly ‘For disconnected networks, the additivity assumption cannot be tested’ and ‘The Q statistic of the difference between the CNMA and NMA model is not available for disconnected networks, as standard NMA cannot be fitted.’ Nothing I found solves it. cpaic 0.1.0 is not on CRAN and I could not locate a public repository, so all cpaic-internal claims are outside my reach.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Retrieved both cited works. Rucker/Petropoulou/Schwarzer 2020 (Biom J 62:808-821) is indeed the foundational frequentist CNMA formulation (weighted least squares, netmeta) and its abstract ends: ‘we show that these models can even be applied to disconnected networks, if the composite treatments in the subnetworks contain common components’ - supporting the reconnection claim. Wigle and Beliveau 2022 is titled ‘Bayesian unanchored additive models for component network meta-analysis’, so the attribution is literally accurate; caveat for the site editor: ‘unanchored’ there means ‘no anchor intervention in the additivity parameterisation’, NOT the anchored/unanchored ITC distinction used elsewhere in this catalog. The untestability claim is independently asserted by a source the entry does not cite: Petropoulou et al. 2023 states plainly ‘For disconnected networks, the additivity assumption cannot be tested’ and ‘The Q statistic of the difference between the CNMA and NMA model is not available for disconnected networks, as standard NMA cannot be fitted.’ Nothing I found solves it. cpaic 0.1.0 is not on CRAN and I could not locate a public repository, so all cpaic-internal claims are outside my reach. Cites doi:10.1186/s12874-023-01959-9: Does NOT solve the problem; it is the missing citation that sources the untestability claim and independently recommends against additive CNMA bridging absent strong clinical argument.. Cites doi:10.1002/bimj.201900339: Missing prior work: the published precedent for using a component bridge instead of a matching/MAIC bridge across a disconnected network, i.e. the exact design cpaic generalises..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1, C2, C4, C5, and C15 are too absolute. For subnetwork designs X_s, a common beta imposes sum_s rank(X_s) - rank(rbind_s X_s) observable compatibility restrictions. Any component functional in the intersection of two subnetwork row spaces can be estimated and compared using within-subnetwork randomized contrasts, without a trial spanning the treatment-network gap. Consequently, the pooled total additive Q can detect some cross-subnetwork incompatibility, although it conflates that incompatibility with other lack of fit; the nested Q.diff is unavailable when ordinary NMA is disconnected. C3, C7, and C8 are correct only for the bridge-relevant projection: q = C_t-C_u must lie in the global row space, and only the projection of main-effect or interaction drift that loads q at the target covariates must be stable. C6 and C9-C13 are otherwise reasonable with these qualifications. A spanning trial tests its randomized contrast, not every component-specific constancy restriction. C14 describes reasonable sensitivity tools, but priors do not restore empirical identification. Moreover, cpaic’s bridge_fragility() does not implement the report’s subnetwork-indexed drift algebra: if beta_s=beta+Delta_s, cross-gap bias is C_t’ Delta_s-C_u’ Delta_r, not (C_t-C_u)’Delta. Its current L1 loading can cancel a shared component precisely when differential subnetwork drift should matter. A narrower, design-dependent constancy diagnostic and correctly parameterized drift analysis therefore remain open.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported. Inverted prior: sought drift models, partial identification of cross-subnetwork component effects, commensurate-prior bridges, or software that tests or weakens cross-gap constancy without losing identification. Highest-yield sources (Rücker et al. 2020; Wigle and Béliveau 2022; Veroniki et al. BMJ 2026 / medRxiv 2025.06.30.25330567; Petropoulou et al. 2023) formalize reconnection under additivity and repeatedly state that additivity/constancy cannot be assessed statistically once the network is disconnected. That literature strengthens, rather than closes, the problem. Veroniki et al. explicitly require strong external clinical evidence for additivity in disconnected networks and note that standard NMA (and thus additivity tests against NMA) is unavailable across the gap. Petropoulou et al. show forward selection of interaction CNMAs performs poorly for reconnection and recommend separate subnetwork analyses. Searches in RSM/SIM/Biometrical Journal/MDM/BMC MRM/JCE/Value in Health/Pharm Stat 2024–2026, arXiv stat.ME/AP, medRxiv, and CRAN/GitHub for multinma, netmeta, gemtc, MBNMAdose, crossnma found no released method that identifies nonzero cross-subnetwork component drift from within-network data alone, nor any package that reports drift-tipping magnitudes as required identification diagnostics. Claims C1–C13 and C15 are faithful statements of identification structure and known limitations; C14 is a reasonable research direction, not a solved method. Residual open work: estimable drift/partial-ID bridges, external-bridge protocols, and software that never presents within-network fit as validation of the bridge.

Decision path

title: Strict component additivity may be clinically false
text: CMP-03 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging

title: Strict component additivity may be clinically false
text:
Statement
Strict component additivity can be clinically false, and interaction CNMA already relaxes it: Rucker et al. 2020 define interaction CNMA models and implement them in netmeta by adding interaction columns to the combination matrix. What is not solved is the disconnected and sparse case, where Petropoulou et al. 2023 found that forward selection of interaction CNMAs performs poorly and recommended separate subnetwork analyses, and where the number of possible component interactions grows combinatorially while the number of observed combinations does not. No method bounds how far an omitted component interaction could move a target cross-gap contrast, and no heredity-constrained sparse selection with subnetwork drift blocks has been implemented for component PAIC. Additivity is also what makes a never-administered combination estimable, and that reporting consequence is unaddressed. Under strict additivity a de novo regimen lies inside the row space, so every estimability screen returns estimable for exactly the extrapolations that are most assumption-driven, and its estimate, interval and rank are printed like those of a randomized regimen; applied reviews then recommend such regimens by name, one estimating 27 daratumumab-based regimens, stating that some have never been reported, and recommending a never-reported one in its abstract. What is missing is a defined provenance quantity, for example the fraction of a regimen’s predicted effect carried by component pairs never co-administered in any arm, and a convention requiring it beside the estimate.

title: Strict component additivity may be clinically false
text:
Why it is open
Additivity is what reconnects a disconnected network, so adding interaction terms consumes the degrees of freedom the bridge depends on, and the contrasts that would discriminate between candidate interaction structures are the ones spanning the gap. Petropoulou et al. 2023 measured the consequence: data-driven selection of interaction structures recovers the right model rarely in disconnected networks and tends to fall back on sparse additive models even when additivity is violated. The proposed global-plus-drift decomposition also needs reference or zero-mean constraints to separate beta from u_s, eta from v_s, and Gamma from Lambda_s, and no bound currently exists for how far unmodeled synergy could move the target contrast.

title: Strict component additivity may be clinically false
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Rucker et al. 2020
defines and implements additive and interaction CNMA in the frequentist netmeta framework, so strict additivity is not the only available model form


Petropoulou et al. 2023
simulates mild and strong additivity violations and shows forward selection of interaction CNMA models does not work well for disconnected networks


Veroniki et al. 2026
documents that synergy and antagonism motivate interaction CNMA and that additivity cannot be assessed statistically in disconnected networks


netmeta
supplies the frequentist component NMA engine, including the interaction CNMA models


cpaic 0.1.0 (development version, choxos/cpaic@9d150e9)
unreleased development R package on GitHub, not on CRAN; fits additive component bridges with total and nested additivity lack-of-fit diagnostics, and implements no component-by-component interaction or subnetwork drift model


Nunns et al. 2025, Journal of Medical Internet Research
Component network meta-analysis of digital weight-loss interventions that reports and recommends a specific three-component package while stating that no trial arms used this specific combination of components.


Huang et al. 2025, Systematic Reviews
Estimates the effects of 27 daratumumab-based regimens in newly diagnosed multiple myeloma, states that some of them have never been reported, and recommends one of the never-reported regimens in its conclusion and abstract.


Efthimiou et al. 2022, Statistics in Medicine
Presents the ability to estimate a combination previously not tested in any trial as a distinctive feature of component models, usable for designing new treatments. The estimate for such a regimen rests on the zero-interaction constraint, whose column is identically zero for any pair of components never co-administered.


Freeman et al. 2023, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Develops the CNMA-circle plot, which marks in gray the links whose differing component combination is not delivered in any single trial arm. The closest existing support marker, and it sits beside the analysis: the forest plot, the league table and the ranking still treat de novo and observed regimens identically.


Yang et al. 2026, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Decomposes a component effect into study-level contributions through pseudo-paths and flow allocation, the first machinery capable of supporting a component-level provenance measure. It attributes evidence to component parameters rather than to a requested combination, so the fraction of a de novo regimen’s predicted effect carried by never-co-administered component pairs is still not computed anywhere.

title: Strict component additivity may be clinically false
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build on interaction CNMA rather than reinventing it: prespecify the interactions that are estimable given the observed combinations, and use sparse or hierarchical priors with an explicit heredity or mechanistic rationale rather than data-driven forward selection, which is already known to fail across a disconnection. Derive omitted-interaction bounds that quantify how far a target cross-gap contrast could move under unmodeled synergy, since that is the part with no existing method. Report for each cross-gap contrast how much of the result depends on shrinkage rather than on likelihood information, and state which drift and interaction directions the design can identify.

title: Strict component additivity may be clinically false
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “The additive component model assumes a combination’s effect equals the sum of its component effects, but synergy and antagonism can be precisely what defines the value of a combination therapy, and omitted interaction terms are assumed negligible by default. The proposed replacement writes theta_{t,s}(x) = C_t’(beta + u_s) + Z_t’(eta + v_s) + C_t’(Gamma + Lambda_s)x, adding candidate interactions Z_t and subnetwork-specific drift blocks with shrinkage priors.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented relaxing additivity as an unbuilt research direction; interaction CNMA has existed since Rucker et al. 2020 and ships in netmeta, and Petropoulou et al. 2023 already simulated mild and strong additivity violations. Both the literature auditor and Grok 4.5 supplied those locators, and GPT-5.6 Sol corrected the claim that the drift-and-interaction model is estimable only through its priors: sufficiently rich replicated designs can identify some of those contrasts through the likelihood.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): Retrieved Rucker et al. 2020: interaction CNMA already exists (‘Interaction CNMA models also allow interactions between the components’), and Petropoulou et al. 2023 simulated exactly this, with mild and strong additivity violations (exp(lambda) = 1.5 and 2). So the ‘additivity may be false’ half is settled published fact, not an open problem; what is open is the heredity-constrained sparse selection, the drift-block parameterisation, and omitted-interaction bounds. Petropoulou et al. supply the nearest thing to a source asserting the software absence the entry claims: ‘More advanced methods penalizing the size of the estimated interaction parameters like the LASSO could in principle also be used to select interaction CNMA models, however, this would not be possible using our R scripts.’ Caveat: the entry cites only ‘cpaic 0.1.0’ and ‘netmeta’ for a claim whose real evidence base is the Rucker/Petropoulou line of work; the netmeta citation is functionally decorative because the substantive content sits in the papers, not the package. I found no bounds for omitted component synergy.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied full-text reading.

merged-in

absorbed a proposal the reading raised separately: No provenance or extrapolation marker for never-administered component regimens 5 citation(s) added. The drafter disagreed with placing it here: Two of the three readers had this accepted as a distinct problem and the reviewer’s merge reason corrects a genuine overreach, since related combinations can inform an interaction even when the exact regimen has no direct evidence. That correction does not make the two the same object: CMP-03 asks whether additivity is true and how far an omitted interaction could move a cross-gap contrast, while this asks for a support and provenance label on a specific reported package inside a connected network where additivity may well hold. The clinical-deliverability half, whether a recommended package respects a total-dose ceiling, a contact-time budget or mutually exclusive delivery formats, has no counterpart in CMP-03 at all. It is recorded as a merge as directed.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Retrieved Rucker et al. 2020: interaction CNMA already exists (‘Interaction CNMA models also allow interactions between the components’), and Petropoulou et al. 2023 simulated exactly this, with mild and strong additivity violations (exp(lambda) = 1.5 and 2). So the ‘additivity may be false’ half is settled published fact, not an open problem; what is open is the heredity-constrained sparse selection, the drift-block parameterisation, and omitted-interaction bounds. Petropoulou et al. supply the nearest thing to a source asserting the software absence the entry claims: ‘More advanced methods penalizing the size of the estimated interaction parameters like the LASSO could in principle also be used to select interaction CNMA models, however, this would not be possible using our R scripts.’ Caveat: the entry cites only ‘cpaic 0.1.0’ and ‘netmeta’ for a claim whose real evidence base is the Rucker/Petropoulou line of work; the netmeta citation is functionally decorative because the substantive content sits in the papers, not the package. I found no bounds for omitted component synergy. Cites doi:10.1002/bimj.201800167: Partially covers the ‘relax additivity’ direction: interaction CNMA models are already defined and implemented; the open part is principled sparse/heredity-constrained selection and bounding of omitted interactions..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1-C3 are correct for cpaic: cnma_bridge() uses theta=C beta, and cmlnmr() adds component-by-covariate interactions but no component-by-component synergy terms. No exported function or fitted parameter block implements the proposed Z, u_s, v_s, or Lambda_s structure, supporting C14. C8 and C9 correctly describe interaction CNMA and the proposed blocks. C4 and C6 are software- or literature-wide nonexistence claims that this audit does not adjudicate. C5 is mathematically possible only after a credible bound set for omitted interactions is specified. C7 and C10-C12 are defensible modeling choices, not general statistical requirements: heredity can be weak or strong, qualitative interactions can violate heredity, and shrinkage strength should follow scientific scale information rather than automatically being stronger for every interaction. The proposed global-plus-drift decomposition also needs reference or zero-mean constraints to distinguish beta from u_s, eta from v_s, and Gamma from Lambda_s. Interactions and drift contrasts are not necessarily identified only by priors; sufficiently rich replicated designs can identify some or all of them through the likelihood. The issue is decision-critical when plausible synergy loads the requested cross-gap contrast, but a high-dimensional heredity-and-drift model is otherwise a roadmap item rather than a universally required replacement.

Grok 4.5, recency lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Clinical falsehood of strict additivity and the existence of interaction CNMA are already in the literature: Rücker et al. 2020 implement pairwise (and higher) interaction CNMA in netmeta; Welton et al. 2009 introduce interaction models; Veroniki et al. 2026 state that interaction CNMA is used when synergy or antagonism violates additivity and warn that power to detect interactions is limited by observed combinations. Petropoulou et al. 2023 evaluate forward selection of interactions and show poor performance for disconnected reconnection. That partially answers the claim that analysts must assume pure additivity, but does not resolve the problem as stated for sparse/disconnected component PAIC: omitted-interaction bounds on the target contrast, heredity-constrained sparse selection with subnetwork drift blocks, and quantification of how much a cross-gap contrast depends on shrinkage toward zero drift were not found in software or published methods. Searches for omitted-interaction bounds, heredity priors in CNMA/PAIC, and drift-plus-interaction models returned no resolving implementation. cpaic is not on CRAN. So the clinical and modeling recognition is partly covered by interaction CNMA; the bound-and-shrinkage agenda remains open. Caveat on support: C3–C4, C6, C14 about current software gaps are supported by absence of public tools; C5, C7, C10–C13 are proposals, not established solutions. Cites 10.1002/bimj.201800167: Defines and implements additive and interaction CNMA in the frequentist netmeta framework, so strict additivity is not the only model form when interactions are included as extra combination-matrix columns.. Cites 10.1136/bmj-2024-083075: States that synergy/antagonism motivates interaction CNMA and that additivity cannot be assessed statistically in disconnected networks, documenting the clinical and identification tension the problem describes.. Cites 10.1186/s12874-023-01959-9: Evaluates forward selection of interaction terms that relax additivity; shows selection does not perform well for disconnected networks, so relaxing additivity via data-driven interactions is not a solved reconnection strategy..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex
