A review of what ITC and PAIC simulation studies actually report would put a number on the field-specific gap that is currently assumed.

title: Computational diagnostics and Monte Carlo error go unreported
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Simulation studies in this field publish performance summaries without the computational context that produced them or the precision of the summaries themselves: runtime and memory, optimizer and sampler failure rates, divergent transitions and maximum tree depth, R-hat and bulk/tail effective sample size, numerical integration error, sensitivity to initialization and seed, replicate-level outputs, and the Monte Carlo standard error of each reported performance measure are all routinely absent.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented this as an unmet methodological need. The literature auditor found the reporting standard and the tooling already exist (Siepe et al. 2024, doi:10.1037/met0000695; SimDesign on CRAN), so the gap is adoption rather than invention, and noted that the prevalence figures are from psychology because no ITC or PAIC specific review has been done. The source-code auditor narrowed the ranking claim: separating two methods needs the MCSE of their paired difference, and a close ranking is not automatically indeterminate.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 and C6 are empirical prevalence claims not established by the supplied evidence. C2 is correct whenever numerical integration is approximate. C3 is correct: diagnostic failure rates should be stratified by scenario rather than hidden in an average. C4 is useful when optimization or sampling is initialization-sensitive, but seed sensitivity is not automatically a separate method-performance estimand; ordinary simulation variation should instead be quantified by MCSE. C5 is plausible under informative failure but is not a theorem. C7 is too absolute: if replicate counts or raw outputs are available, uncertainty can sometimes be derived or bounded, and method rankings require the MCSE of paired differences rather than merely separate MCSEs. C8 is correct when raw outputs include truths, estimates, and failure indicators. cpaic now records fit-level divergences, tree-depth saturation, E-BFMI, R-hat, and ESS, but supplies no simulation-level runtime, memory, failure aggregation, performance-measure MCSE, or replicate archive.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. I retrieved Siepe, Bartos, Morris, Boulesteix, Heck & Pawel (2024, Psychological Methods, doi 10.1037/met0000695, PMID 39541533; full text PMC7616844). It reviewed 321 articles, 100 of which report a simulation study, and reports: 77% did not report uncertainty of performance measures; convergence reported in 19%; full computational-environment information in 2%; code unavailable for 64%. That is direct empirical support for the general claims, and the same paper supplies MCSE formulae and a repetition-count calculation, so the methodological prescription is solved and packaged (ADEMP-PreReg, building on Morris/White/Crowther’s ADEMP). SimDesign (CRAN 2.25.5) already catches errors and warnings, re-simulates non-convergent results, and records sessioninfo. Caveat, and it is the material one: none of this evidence is field-specific. I found no review of ITC, PAIC or ML-NMR simulation studies quantifying failure-rate, divergence, R-hat or MCSE reporting, so every claim qualified ‘in PAIC and ML-NMR simulation studies’ is an extrapolation from psychology and general biostatistics. Separately, the integration-error sub-claim is now automated by multinma int_check (default TRUE since 0.6.0). Cites doi:10.1037/met0000695: Supplies the empirical rates of non-reporting and a complete reporting/preregistration template with MCSE formulae and repetition-count calculation; solves the prescription, not the field’s adoption.. Cites cran:SimDesign 2.25.5: Provides the infrastructure for automatic re-simulation of non-convergent results, error/warning capture, and high-quality parallel RNG..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 and C6 are empirical prevalence claims not established by the supplied evidence. C2 is correct whenever numerical integration is approximate. C3 is correct: diagnostic failure rates should be stratified by scenario rather than hidden in an average. C4 is useful when optimization or sampling is initialization-sensitive, but seed sensitivity is not automatically a separate method-performance estimand; ordinary simulation variation should instead be quantified by MCSE. C5 is plausible under informative failure but is not a theorem. C7 is too absolute: if replicate counts or raw outputs are available, uncertainty can sometimes be derived or bounded, and method rankings require the MCSE of paired differences rather than merely separate MCSEs. C8 is correct when raw outputs include truths, estimates, and failure indicators. cpaic now records fit-level divergences, tree-depth saturation, E-BFMI, R-hat, and ESS, but supplies no simulation-level runtime, memory, failure aggregation, performance-measure MCSE, or replicate archive. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Automates collection and warning for the main HMC convergence and geometry diagnostics at the fitted-model level..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported-with-caveat. General simulation-study methodology has long required Monte Carlo standard errors and computational transparency (White 2010; Morris, White & Crowther 2019 ADEMP tutorial; Williams et al. 2024 TRISS checklist for reporting MCSE). Those works propose standards; they do not show that PAIC/ML-NMR simulation papers now report optimizer/sampler failure rates, divergences, tree-depth, R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, integration error, seed/init sensitivity, or MCSE of performance measures per scenario severity. Field-focused searches (RSM, SiM, Pharm Stats, Value in Health, 2024–2026; multinma/maicplus simulation vignettes) did not surface a convention shift that would close C1, C3, C5–C7 as practice claims. C2 remains tied to ML-NMR (integration vs MC error), where multinma diagnostics help applied fits more than published simulation tables. C8 (share replicate-level outputs) is technically trivial and still uncommon. Problem remains open as an ITC/PAIC reporting practice gap, not as absence of general methodology.

title: Simulation studies publish no registry, seeds, or environment locks
text:
Statement
Large simulation programs in this field publish neither a navigable scenario registry (stable scenario identifiers, exact per-scenario estimands, data-generating code) nor the provenance needed to re-run a specific cell (a reproducible RNG stream assignment, an immutable implementation identifier, environment information, and tests against analytic special cases). The prescriptions and the tooling exist outside the field: Siepe et al. (doi:10.1037/met0000695) recommend RNG streams rather than a single seed under parallelism together with environment capture, and report that full computational-environment information appeared in 2% of studies; the RepliSims project (doi:10.1098/rsos.231003) shows that missing information, not cost, is what blocks replication; and SimDesign supplies parallel substreams and session capture. Two of the source’s requirements do not survive as requirements: a dashboard is one way of serving a machine-readable registry and not the only one, and a container or lock file supports reproducible results without guaranteeing bitwise identity across hardware and numerical libraries. No review of ITC or PAIC simulation studies was found, so the field-specific absence claims are unrefuted rather than verified.

title: Simulation studies publish no registry, seeds, or environment locks
text:
Why it is open
A factorial program over topology, covariates, modification structure, outcomes, missingness, information and bias mechanisms produces thousands of cells that cannot be communicated in a journal table, so results are compressed into averages that hide the method-by-scenario interaction a reader needs, and without stable scenario identifiers a later paper cannot re-run or extend a specific cell, so evidence does not accumulate. Reproduction fails for a separate reason: a single reported seed suffices only when the code deterministically derives per-worker streams, which is rarely documented, and the realized numbers also depend on the whole toolchain. Journals reward the narrative rather than the registry and no venue requires either set of artifacts, so producing them is unpaid work.

title: Simulation studies publish no registry, seeds, or environment locks
text:
What has been tried

title: Simulation studies publish no registry, seeds, or environment locks
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Adopt the existing prescriptions rather than restate them: publish the scenario registry as a machine-readable table with stable identifiers, exact per-scenario estimands and generator code, an immutable implementation identifier (a release tag, source archive or content digest, of which a commit hash is one form), the RNG algorithm and the task-to-stream mapping, environment information, and tests against analytic special cases with closed-form answers. A queryable result table is the deliverable and a dashboard over it is optional. Frameworks such as SimDesign already provide the parallel substreams and environment capture, so the work is to run an ITC simulation program through them and to publish the registry as the primary output with the paper as a summary of it.

title: Simulation studies publish no registry, seeds, or environment locks
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Simulation programs in this field publish neither the artifacts that make a large factorial study navigable (a scenario registry with human-readable IDs, exact per-scenario estimand definitions, data-generating code, and a dashboard filterable by assumption violation) nor the artifacts required to reproduce one bitwise (seeds together with the parallel RNG substream strategy, a container image or environment lock file, package versions and commit hashes, and automated tests against analytic special cases).”
What was wrong with it. The source asked for artifacts that already have published prescriptions and working tooling. The literature auditor named Siepe et al. 2024 (doi:10.1037/met0000695) for the seed, substream and environment-capture recommendations and RepliSims (doi:10.1098/rsos.231003) for the evidence that missing information blocks replication, so the gap is adoption in this field rather than invention. The source-code auditor knocked down two framings: a dashboard is not required because a machine-readable registry with a queryable result table does the same job, and containers or lock files do not deliver bitwise reproduction across toolchains.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1-C3 are field-practice claims that cannot be established under the assigned lens. C4 overstates what is required: an immutable release, source archive, or content digest can identify an implementation without a Git commit, although stronger provenance is preferable. C5 is false as a requirement; a documented machine-readable registry and queryable result table can replace a dashboard. C6 is correct when averaging masks method-by-scenario interactions. C7 should require a reproducible RNG algorithm and task-to-stream mapping, but a single master seed can be sufficient when the code deterministically derives task streams. C8 conflates bitwise identity with reproducible scientific results; containers and lock files are useful but neither necessary nor sufficient across hardware and numerical libraries. C9 is sound. At 9d150e9, cpaic records package and backend versions, the Stan-source hash, seed, integration count, and assumptions, and has analytic special-case tests. It still has no tracked scenario registry, lock file, container, or public simulation pipeline; the local validation tree is ignored and therefore is not resolving public work.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Retrieved three sources. Siepe et al. 2024 (doi 10.1037/met0000695, PMC7616844) gives the empirical rates (‘Of the 36% of studies in which code was provided, 21% also provided a seed’; ‘Full information on the computational environment was only reported in 2% of the studies’) and makes exactly the recommendations the entry proposes, including using RNG streams rather than seeds when parallelizing and using Docker plus sessionInfo(). The RepliSims project (doi 10.1098/rsos.231003, PMID 38234442) attempted to replicate eight highly cited simulation studies and found replicability ‘mainly impeded by lack of information and sustainability of information sources’, with some studies providing too little to implement any reported simulation. SimDesign (CRAN 2.25.5) already delivers parallel RNG substreams, error capture and environment capture. So the seeds/substreams/lock-file half of this entry is solved as prescription and tooling; adoption in ITC/PAIC is the residual gap. Caveats: the scenario-registry-with-human-readable-IDs and the ‘dashboard filterable by assumption violation’ are normative assertions for which I found no supporting source, and no ITC-specific review exists, so the field-specific absence claims are unverifiable. Cites doi:10.1098/rsos.231003: Empirically establishes that missing implementation detail, not cost, blocks reproduction of simulation studies, and identifies which artifacts matter.. Cites doi:10.1037/met0000695: Supplies the seed/stream, environment-lock and preregistration prescriptions this entry asks for, plus the non-reporting base rates..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1-C3 are field-practice claims that cannot be established under the assigned lens. C4 overstates what is required: an immutable release, source archive, or content digest can identify an implementation without a Git commit, although stronger provenance is preferable. C5 is false as a requirement; a documented machine-readable registry and queryable result table can replace a dashboard. C6 is correct when averaging masks method-by-scenario interactions. C7 should require a reproducible RNG algorithm and task-to-stream mapping, but a single master seed can be sufficient when the code deterministically derives task streams. C8 conflates bitwise identity with reproducible scientific results; containers and lock files are useful but neither necessary nor sufficient across hardware and numerical libraries. C9 is sound. At 9d150e9, cpaic records package and backend versions, the Stan-source hash, seed, integration count, and assumptions, and has analytic special-case tests. It still has no tracked scenario registry, lock file, container, or public simulation pipeline; the local validation tree is ignored and therefore is not resolving public work. Cites choxos/cpaic@ae63da32171aa12fbfb0311ede1066213342b483: Adds automatic fit provenance covering the package, sampler engine, Stan source, seed, integration count, and core assumptions.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Provides tracked tests comparing survival integration calculations with analytically known values..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported-with-caveat. Queries for ITC/PAIC simulation programs publishing human-readable scenario registries, assumption-filter dashboards, parallel RNG substream strategies, container/lockfiles with commit hashes, and analytic special-case tests (arXiv, RSM/SiM, CRAN/GitHub for multinma/maicplus/netmeta/gemtc/MBNMAdose, 2024–2026) found no field standard that would falsify C1–C3 or C6–C9 as practice claims. General reproducibility tools (renv/packrat, Docker, rngtools/L’Ecuyer streams, ADEMP structure from Morris et al. 2019) exist outside the field, so C4, C7, and C8 are technically correct requirements but not invented by this agenda. C5 (‘required’ dashboard) is a design preference for very large factorials rather than a solved or refuted scientific claim. Evidence accumulation across studies via stable scenario IDs remains largely absent in PAIC simulation literature. Confidence capped because some individual open-code studies may partially meet subsets of artifacts without a public registry narrative.

title: No cross-package benchmark or reference pipeline for ITC software
text:
Statement
No cross-package agreement harness, containerized reference pipeline, or published benchmark output with expected values exists for ITC and PAIC methods, so a third party cannot re-run a submitted analysis and compare it against a reference result. Individual packages are further along than ‘method demonstration’ implies: multinma ships more than thirty testthat files including snapshot tests plus vignettes that reproduce the published NICE TSD analyses, and maicplus is maintained by the hta-pharma consortium with continuous integration and was presented as a package to support analysis and reporting of MAIC for HTA dossiers (doi:10.1016/j.jval.2023.09.2992). cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, has seeded analyses, expected-value regression tests, rendered end-to-end vignettes, multi-platform R CMD check, a smoke test comparing its rstan and cmdstanr backends, and one narrow numerical agreement test against multinma, while lacking a dependency lock file, a container specification, and a publicly tracked simulation-validation pipeline.

title: No cross-package benchmark or reference pipeline for ITC software
text:
Why it is open
Packages are funded and published on the criterion that the method runs on a worked example, so nothing in the incentive structure asks whether an outside analyst can regenerate a submission, and no single maintainer is rewarded for manifests, expected outputs, container images or cross-package agreement tests that only pay off across the ecosystem. Cross-package agreement is also a weaker check than it sounds: one comparison of four MAIC packages on a shared unanchored simulation, cited by the recency auditor without a locator (Taylor and Hatswell, Value in Health 2025), found identical weights, effective sample sizes and outcomes because the packages reuse the same NICE DSU TSD 18 code, so agreement can reflect shared lineage rather than independent verification. And reproducibility infrastructure buys computational auditability only: it can expose an implementation error but it does not repair non-identification, estimand mismatch, non-collapsibility or an untestable bridging assumption, so the claim that it would materially improve decisions holds only conditionally.

title: No cross-package benchmark or reference pipeline for ITC software
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the ecosystem-level artifacts that no single package has an incentive to build: published benchmark datasets with expected outputs, a containerized reference pipeline, and an agreement harness across implementations. Design the agreement tests to compare implementations with independent lineage, since packages descended from the same TSD 18 code will agree without verifying anything. Add the cheap per-package pieces where they are missing, namely dependency lock files, container specifications, and publicly tracked simulation-validation pipelines. Claim the benefit as computational auditability rather than as better decisions, because the assumptions that drive a population-adjusted estimate are untouched by reproducibility.

title: No cross-package benchmark or reference pipeline for ITC software
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. No cross-package agreement tests, containerized reference pipelines, or published benchmark outputs with expected values exist for ITC and PAIC methods, so a submitted analysis cannot be independently re-run and compared against a reference result; individual packages such as multinma and maicplus do already ship test suites, reproducible vignettes and HTA-reporting-oriented documentation.
The source titled this. “ITC and PAIC software are method demos, not reference workflows” The title calls the whole software ecosystem method demonstrations, which the audit contradicted with multinma’s snapshot tests and TSD-reproducing vignettes and maicplus’s HTA reporting remit.
The source said. “ITC and PAIC packages are built and published as demonstrations that a method runs on an example, not as reference implementations with which a third party can reproduce a submitted analysis end to end. The report ranks moving the ecosystem from method demonstrations to reference-grade reproducible workflows as its fourth most consequential open question.”
What was wrong with it. The source called the whole ecosystem method demonstrations and cited nothing for it; the entry was flagged source_unsourced. Auditors found multinma’s snapshot tests and NICE TSD-reproducing vignettes and maicplus’s HTA-reporting remit (doi:10.1016/j.jval.2023.09.2992) contradict the categorical framing, and the original second sentence, which ranked the problem fourth most consequential in the source report, was cut as an unverifiable self-reference. What survives is the ecosystem-level absence.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): This entry is source_unsourced and its second sentence (‘the report ranks … as its fourth most consequential open question’) is a self-reference to a document with no retrievable citation, so it is unverifiable and should be cut or reworded. On the substance I inspected the artifacts rather than searching for opinions. multinma’s repository contains 30+ testthat files including snapshot tests and vignettes that reproduce the published NICE TSD analyses, i.e. reference examples with expected outputs already exist for at least one package. maicplus is maintained by the hta-pharma consortium with CI, coverage reporting and a package website, and was presented as a package ‘to Support Analysis and Reporting of Matching Adjusted Indirect Treatment Comparisons (MAIC) for HTA Dossiers’ (Chen et al., Value in Health 2023, doi 10.1016/j.jval.2023.09.2992), which is a reporting-workflow aim, not a method demo. What I could not find any instance of is the ecosystem-level element: cross-package agreement tests, containerized reference pipelines, or published benchmark outputs against which a submitted analysis could be re-run. That narrower claim is defensible and still open.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

closure-upheld

6 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors’ reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. None of the new findings contradicts the closure’s counterevidence that individual packages already provide tests, reproducible examples, and limited agreement checks. crossnma’s call for large-scale comparison, the clinical Python implementation, and the historical package discrepancies all illustrate the ecosystem-level gap the closure explicitly retained. The optimizer paper establishes an important implementation-risk case, but the closure already says reference workflows can expose implementation errors without establishing statistical validity. Taylor and Hatswell’s shared-code agreement point was already considered by the closure and reinforces, rather than refutes, its residual. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening

7 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries overstated Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit’s closure needs the closure’s own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

open / overstated. This entry is source_unsourced and its second sentence (‘the report ranks … as its fourth most consequential open question’) is a self-reference to a document with no retrievable citation, so it is unverifiable and should be cut or reworded. On the substance I inspected the artifacts rather than searching for opinions. multinma’s repository contains 30+ testthat files including snapshot tests and vignettes that reproduce the published NICE TSD analyses, i.e. reference examples with expected outputs already exist for at least one package. maicplus is maintained by the hta-pharma consortium with CI, coverage reporting and a package website, and was presented as a package ‘to Support Analysis and Reporting of Matching Adjusted Indirect Treatment Comparisons (MAIC) for HTA Dossiers’ (Chen et al., Value in Health 2023, doi 10.1016/j.jval.2023.09.2992), which is a reporting-workflow aim, not a method demo. What I could not find any instance of is the ecosystem-level element: cross-package agreement tests, containerized reference pipelines, or published benchmark outputs against which a submitted analysis could be re-run. That narrower claim is defensible and still open.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 is confirmed: the report supplies no source for its ecosystem-wide and incentive-structure assertions. C2 is not established for ITC/PAIC software generally, and cpaic@9d150e9 is material counter-evidence to the categorical method-demo framing: it has seeded analyses, expected-value regression tests, rendered end-to-end vignettes, multi-platform R CMD check, an installed-package smoke fit comparing rstan with cmdstanr, and a narrow agreement test against multinma. The remaining gap is real but narrower: cpaic calls itself research software, has no dependency lockfile or container specification, and explicitly says its simulation-validation code is not in the public repository. C3 holds only conditionally. Reproducible workflows improve computational auditability and can expose implementation errors, but they do not repair non-identification, estimand mismatch, non-collapsibility, extrapolation, or an untestable bridging assumption; cross-implementation agreement also does not establish statistical validity when implementations share assumptions or defects. C4 is a comparative literature-coverage claim, outside the specified technical/source-code lens, and cannot be inferred from one repository or from the absence of cited evidence. Accordingly, the workflow work is valuable quality infrastructure, but the asserted ecosystem prevalence, guaranteed material effect on decision quality, estimator-versus-implementation shortage, and very-high ranking are inflated. The checkout itself was at aaa76c9, two commits beyond the supplied revision; all quoted evidence was read from the exact 9d150e9 Git object. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Partially implements an automated, installed-package, end-to-end reference check and compares the two supported Stan backends.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Provides executable vignette sources, self-contained rendered outputs, installed-source freshness checks, and cache keys tied to the analysis and package inputs.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Implements one narrow cross-package numerical agreement test, though not full independent-method validation.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Records random seeds as fit provenance, covering one reproducibility requirement identified by the report..

Grok 4.5, recency lens

open / supported-with-caveat. Inverted prior: treated the gap as closed if any released package ecosystem or guidance had delivered reference-grade, third-party-rerunnable ITC/PAIC workflows (manifests, fixed seeds, expected benchmark outputs, containers, and sustained cross-package agreement tests for submitted analyses). Nothing retrieved does that. (1) No prior_work was listed on the problem, so search went straight to packages and 2024–2026 literature. (2) Taylor & Hatswell (Value in Health 2025; ISPOR Europe 2024 SA88) is the highest-yield hit: they compared maic, MAIC, maicplus, and maicChecks on a shared unanchored simulation and found identical weights/ESS/outcomes because all reuse NICE DSU TSD 18 code; maicChecks is the only partial alternative. That is diagnostic work exposing shared demo lineage and optimizer sensitivity, not an installed reference pipeline. Their conclusion still calls for comparative studies of weight methods. (3) New or maturing packages (outstandR, arXiv:2601.07532 / CRAN 2026; drMAIC CRAN 2026 with “submission-ready” reporting language; ongoing maicplus / multinma / netmeta / gemtc vignette+testthat culture) remain method-and-dossier tools with synthetic or example vignettes. outstandR’s own paper frames use as “illustrative examples using synthetic datasets,” which is the method-demo pattern the claim describes. (4) No CRAN NEWS or GitHub signal was found for dockerized reference pipelines, published expected-output gold files for third-party re-run of HTA submissions, or continuous cross-package agreement harnesses across MAIC/NMA stacks. (5) NHS Open Analytics RAP material (2026) and ISPOR HARPER/ICH M14 reproducibility templates target general analytics or RWE protocols, not ITC/PAIC estimator agreement or re-execution of PAIC submissions. NICE DSU TSD 18 remains the 2016 methods/code anchor; no 2025–2026 DSU/EUnetHTA revision establishing reference software workflows was found. Caveats on support: C2 and C4 are faithful as of mid-2026 (estimators and packages proliferate; reference-grade end-to-end auditability does not). C3 (material decision-quality gain from reference workflows) is a priority/impact judgment, not something the literature has established as an empirical result; treat that sub-claim as aspirational. C1 correctly flags the problem statement as unsourced. Status remains open: partial packaging and one-off package-comparison studies do not solve incentive-structure or reference-workflow gaps.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: No evidence on how the modifier set changes across effect scales
text:
Statement
Effect-modifier status is defined relative to a treatment contrast and an effect scale, so candidate adjustment sets can differ by estimand; that is an established definition rather than an unsettled question. The estimand-first rule the source says is missing has been stated: effect modification is defined on a conditional measure while population-level decisions need marginal effects, and under non-collapsibility purely prognostic variables can modify marginal effects (Remiro-Azocar 2024, doi:10.1002/sim.10111); a transportability framing ties modifier identification explicitly to the chosen measure (Chandler and Ishak 2026, arxiv:2602.17041). What is undone is uptake and evidence: neither paper reports how the modifier set changes across the candidate scales a decision might use, and learning which heterogeneity matters from sparse PAIC data remains uncertain.

title: No evidence on how the modifier set changes across effect scales
text:
Why it is open
Under non-collapsible measures a variable can be purely prognostic on the conditional scale and still shift the marginal contrast, so the modifier set is a property of the estimand rather than of the variable, and a set that is right for the fitted model can be wrong for the decision. The scale-first principle is available but not routine, and no published analysis shows how the modifier set moves when the same data are read on the risk difference, odds ratio and hazard ratio scales, so scale sensitivity stays absorbed in the adjustment step. Population adjustment is also not only about transporting conditional effect modification: unanchored comparisons need prognostic adjustment, and marginal non-collapsible estimands vary with the prognostic distribution even without a conditional interaction.

title: No evidence on how the modifier set changes across effect scales
text:

What it contributes




Remiro-Azocar, 2024
Transportability of model-based estimands in evidence synthesis: effect modification is defined with respect to a conditional measure while marginal effects are required for population-level decisions, and for non-collapsible measures purely prognostic variables can modify marginal effects.


Chandler and Ishak, 2026

cpaic, commit 9d150e9
Unreleased development R package on GitHub, not on CRAN and not installable by a reader; its estimand documentation distinguishes the conditional contrast at a covariate profile from the marginal effect standardized over a population, which is the distinction the source said is never surfaced.

title: No evidence on how the modifier set changes across effect scales
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Apply the estimand-first rule rather than rediscover it: declare the contrast and the scale, derive the modifier set from them, and require the reported estimand, adjustment set and contrast to sit on the same scale. The research contribution left is the diagnostic, which is to report how the modifier set and the resulting estimate move across the candidate scales a decision might use, plus evidence on how often that changes an appraisal. Implementations can help by labeling outputs as conditional profile contrasts or marginal standardized effects, as the development package cpaic does; cpaic is an unreleased GitHub development version, commit 9d150e9, and is not installable from CRAN.

title: No evidence on how the modifier set changes across effect scales
text:
Our study

The adjustment set is a property of the scale
The question put to it. Does the set of covariates whose imbalance changes a transported contrast differ between the risk difference, risk ratio, marginal odds ratio and conditional odds ratio scales?
What it found. The covariates a transported contrast depends on change with the scale, but not in the nested way DESIGN.md predicted. Prognostic non-modifiers never affected the conditional log odds ratio and affected some marginal scale by more than 5% in 13 of 24 scenarios, the risk difference included, because with a logistic model every prognostic variable modifies the risk difference; the risk difference was in fact the most sensitive scale (median 4.5% change per unbalanced prognostic variable, against 1.6% for the marginal odds ratio). Sets differed between the risk difference, marginal and conditional odds ratio in 10 of 24 scenarios, below the registered threshold of half, so the refuting sentence holds as registered.
Results.

Registered verdict: refuting sentence HOLDS (sets differ in 42% of scenarios against a 50% threshold).
Marginal odds ratio set containing the risk-difference set (DESIGN.md’s prediction): 19 of 24 scenarios.
Median relative change from one unbalanced prognostic variable: 0.045 (risk difference), 0.035 (log risk ratio), 0.016 (marginal log odds ratio), 0 (conditional log odds ratio). Near-null contrasts inflate relative changes.

Design.

Estimand

Target A-versus-C contrast on the risk difference, log risk ratio, marginal and conditional log odds ratio scales

Methods compared

mean balancing with each covariate in turn left unbalanced

Data-generating mechanism

Population-level numerical study: logistic outcome with 0 to 3 conditional modifiers and 2 or 6 prognostic non-modifiers, two prognostic strengths and two imbalances; each covariate’s omission scored by its relative change in the target contrast on four scales.

Replicates

Population-level calculation, 24 scenarios, 10^6 common random draws each


What this does not answer. No time-to-event scale; no sampling or estimation of the sets; independent normal covariates. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Effect-modifier status is uncertain and scale-dependent” The title calls effect-modifier status uncertain, but the audit found scale-dependence to be an established definition and the estimand-first rule already stated in the literature.
The source said. “Whether a covariate modifies the treatment effect depends on the effect scale, so the correct adjustment set is not a property of the variable alone. The report states that identification of which covariates are effect modifiers remains uncertain and scale-dependent.”
What was wrong with it. The entry was unattributed in the source and said the literature offers no rule for declaring the scale first and deriving the modifier set from it; it is now sourced, and that rule turns out to be stated in doi:10.1002/sim.10111 and arxiv:2602.17041, so the gap is uptake and benchmarking rather than the principle. The code auditor added that scale-conditional modifier status is a definition rather than an open problem, that effect-modifier transport is not the only reason population adjustment exists, and that software does surface the distinction between conditional and marginal effects; the two auditors split on whether the entry is open or partly solved, and it is published at the weaker claim.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): All three claims are supportable from retrieved text. Remiro-Azocar 2024 (Stat Med) states verbatim that ‘effect modification is defined with respect to a conditional measure, but marginal effect estimates are required for population-level decisions in health technology assessment’, and that ‘For non-collapsible measures, purely prognostic variables that are not determinants of treatment response at the individual level may modify marginal effects’ — the precise mechanism the entry describes. Chandler & Ishak 2026 (arXiv 2602.17041) reframes PAIC as transportability and ties modifier identification to the chosen effect measure. The caveat is on the why_open text, not the claims: the entry asserts ‘the literature offers no rule for declaring the scale first and deriving the modifier set from it’. Both retrieved papers articulate exactly such a rule (define the marginal estimand and its scale first; prefer directly collapsible measures partly because they facilitate covariate selection). What is missing is uptake and benchmarking, not the principle. Neither paper reports how modifier sets change across candidate scales, so the diagnostic proposed here is genuinely undone. codex dissented (overstated): C2 is mathematically correct: with a constant conditional odds ratio of 2, control risks 0.10 and 0.40 imply treated risks 0.1818 and 0.5714, hence risk differences 0.0818 and 0.1714. The assertion that the mismatch is never surfaced is also contradicted by cpaic@9d150e9, which explicitly distinguishes conditional profile contrasts from marginal standardized effects.

Does the later work answer the earlier work? title: Selection uncertainty in PAIC interaction shrinkage is uncalibrated
text: COV-04 Partially addressed High priority Promising

title: Selection uncertainty in PAIC interaction shrinkage is uncalibrated
text:
Statement
Shrinkage on treatment-by-covariate interactions in place of stepwise selection is already a benchmarked recommendation in evidence synthesis: LASSO, ridge, adaptive LASSO, Bayesian LASSO and stochastic search variable selection were compared against stepwise regression and the all-interactions model for IPD meta-analysis, with shrinkage recommended and stepwise regression advised against (Seo et al. 2021, doi:10.1002/sim.8859), and Bayesian variable selection has been carried into component network meta-analysis combining aggregate data and IPD (Efthimiou et al. 2022, doi:10.1002/sim.9372). What survives as open is the honest-uncertainty half: neither evaluation covers the regularized horseshoe, heredity constraints or projection-predictive selection, and both report mean squared error rather than interval coverage with the selection step included. A posterior interval reported conditional on a data-selected model, with the selection event ignored, is not automatically honest, and that calibration has not been checked for decision-grade PAIC use.

title: Selection uncertainty in PAIC interaction shrinkage is uncalibrated
text:
Why it is open
The number of candidate treatment-by-covariate interactions grows with covariates times treatments or components while a sparse network holds little information to estimate them, so some restriction is unavoidable, although prespecification or dimension reduction can substitute for shrinkage. The priors and selection rules on offer differ in how hard they shrink and how wide the resulting intervals are, and those properties have not been characterized for PAIC. Reporting an interval from a model chosen on the same data leaves nominal coverage unguaranteed unless the inference accounts for the procedure as a whole, and multi-task shrinkage across treatment classes and components adds a layer whose calibration in decision-grade use is untested.

title: Selection uncertainty in PAIC interaction shrinkage is uncalibrated
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Seo et al., 2021
Compares LASSO, ridge, adaptive LASSO, Bayesian LASSO and stochastic search variable selection against stepwise regression and the all-interactions model for treatment-covariate interactions in IPD meta-analysis, and recommends shrinkage over stepwise regression.


Efthimiou et al., 2022
Bayesian models for aggregate and individual patient data component network meta-analysis using stochastic search variable selection and the Bayesian LASSO, with prior information about important interactions; the component-level shrinkage the source proposes.

title: Selection uncertainty in PAIC interaction shrinkage is uncalibrated
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the existing benchmarks rather than repeat them: add the regularized horseshoe, hierarchy-respecting group lasso and spike-and-slab priors, heredity constraints that require inclusion of the main-effect term, projection-predictive selection from a rich reference model, and treatment-class or component-level multi-task shrinkage to the comparisons already run in doi:10.1002/sim.8859 and doi:10.1002/sim.9372. Report interval coverage for the whole procedure with the selection step included, not mean squared error conditional on the selected model. Coherent Bayesian model averaging over scientifically plausible modifier sets is one way to make the interval account for selection; sample splitting and resampling the entire procedure are others.

title: Selection uncertainty in PAIC interaction shrinkage is uncalibrated
text:
Our study

Shrinkage priors on interactions do not give honest intervals for a transported effect
The question put to it. Do posterior intervals from shrinkage or selection priors on treatment-by-covariate interactions keep frequentist coverage for the transported effect when the whole procedure is repeated?
What it found. No. Continuous shrinkage does not select, but its intervals still undercovered: 95% posterior intervals for the transported effect covered 0.794 to 0.948 with an empirical-Bayes ridge prior and 0.868 to 0.959 with a hierarchical normal prior, against 0.939 to 0.955 for a flat prior. When the interactions the target weights push the effect the same way, their joint shrinkage biases the transported effect (up to 0.19) and the narrower interval does not carry the bias. Integrating the prior scale recovers only part of the loss.
Results.

Worst cell, three moderate modifiers at 100 per arm: empirical-Bayes ridge 0.794, hierarchical normal 0.868, spike-and-slab averaging 0.908, median-probability model 0.785, flat 0.954.
Plugging in the fitted prior scale costs up to 0.074 coverage relative to integrating it; the remainder is prior-truth conflict at a fixed nonzero truth.
The median-probability model’s conditional interval, the Bayesian form of DEC-11’s selection, was the worst prior at 300 per arm (0.840 with three moderate modifiers).
With one strong modifier at 300 per arm every prior except the median-probability model covered at least 0.948.

Design.

Estimand

Target-population mean difference, A versus C, -0.5 + 0.5 times the sum of the interactions

Methods compared

flat prior, empirical-Bayes ridge, hierarchical normal (half-Cauchy scale), spike-and-slab model averaging, median-probability model

Data-generating mechanism

Continuous-outcome STC with eight candidate interactions, one strong or three moderate modifiers, two sample sizes; flat, empirical-Bayes ridge, hierarchical normal, spike-and-slab averaging and median-probability-model priors. 4 cells, 1000 replicates each.

Replicates

1000 per cell, 4 cells


What this does not answer. Continuous outcome with conjugate priors; no horseshoe, heredity constraints or projection-predictive selection; aligned modifiers only, no null scenario. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Selection uncertainty in PAIC interaction shrinkage is uncalibrated
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Hierarchical sparse interaction models with honest uncertainty” The title presents hierarchical sparse interaction models as the open object, but the audit found shrinkage already benchmarked and recommended for IPD meta-analysis and built into component NMA.
The source said. “High-dimensional effect modification should be handled by structured regularization rather than stepwise selection, using shrinkage priors and hierarchy constraints on treatment-by-covariate interactions. The resulting coverage must incorporate selection uncertainty, because a posterior interval from a model selected on the same data is not automatically honest.”
What was wrong with it. The source framed ‘structured regularization rather than stepwise selection’ as open; the literature auditor found it benchmarked and recommended (doi:10.1002/sim.8859) and component-level Bayesian variable selection already built (doi:10.1002/sim.9372), so only the coverage claim survives. The code auditor corrected two side claims: shrinkage changes the estimator and its prior sensitivity rather than the causal estimand, and heredity should require that the main-effect term be included, not that its coefficient be nonzero, because an interaction can exist with a zero main effect.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The headline claim, ‘structured regularization rather than stepwise selection’, is not an open question in evidence synthesis; it is a benchmarked recommendation. Seo et al. 2021 (Stat Med) simulated LASSO, ridge, adaptive LASSO, Bayesian LASSO and stochastic search variable selection against the all-interactions model and stepwise regression for treatment-covariate interactions in IPD meta-analysis and concluded: ‘We recommend that future IPD meta-analysis that aim to estimate patient-specific treatment effects using multiple effect modifiers should use shrinkage methods, whereas stepwise regression should be avoided.’ Efthimiou et al. 2022 carries Bayesian variable selection (SSVS, Bayesian LASSO) into component network meta-analysis combining aggregate data and IPD, with priors on which interactions matter. What is genuinely undone in these papers: the regularized horseshoe specifically was not among the evaluated priors, heredity constraints and projection-predictive selection were not assessed, and both papers report MSE rather than interval coverage with the selection step included. The honest-coverage element of the entry survives; claim 1 does not. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.8859: Benchmarks shrinkage on treatment-covariate interactions against stepwise selection in evidence synthesis, settling the entry’s first claim. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.9372: Component-level Bayesian variable selection for interactions in a network combining aggregate data and IPD, the multi-task/component shrinkage the entry proposes.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 is a reasonable high-dimensional default, not a theorem: some restriction is needed when interactions exceed information, but prespecification or dimension reduction can also be defensible. C2 is suitable only when approximate sparsity and prior scaling are credible. C3, C5, and C6 are legitimate constructions, but none automatically supplies PAIC identification or calibrated intervals. C4 is a useful hierarchy convention, not a causal law; an interaction can exist with a zero prognostic main effect, and hierarchy should usually require inclusion of the main-effect term rather than force a nonzero coefficient. C7-C8 are correct when an interval is reported conditional on a data-selected model while the selection event is ignored; coherent model averaging or inference for the entire procedure can account for it. Shrinkage generally changes the estimator and prior sensitivity, not the causal estimand itself. cpaic@9d150e9 offers only global normal or Student-t priors for interaction coefficients and a cSTC inclusion hierarchy, not horseshoe, group-lasso, spike-and-slab, projection-predictive, or model-averaged PAIC. The decision-grade calibration problem remains open, but it is high priority only when the analysis is genuinely high-dimensional.

text:
Statement
Causal forests give a principled framework for heterogeneous treatment effects (Wager and Athey 2018), and the study-aware half of the PAIC adaptation is largely off the shelf: grf performs subsampling and honest splitting on whole clusters when clusters are declared (github.com/grf-labs/grf), and study-aware multi-trial CATE estimation has been developed and simulated (Brantner et al. 2024, doi:10.1002/sim.9955; Venkatasubramaniam and Wolfson 2025, arxiv:2502.02110). What none of that covers is the case that defines PAIC: a target population known only through published marginal summaries, and the variance of averaging individual-level effects over it. The requirements are also narrower than the source states, since whole-trial splitting matters when the trial is the sampling unit or when trial-level generalization is the goal rather than always, and target-aware aggregation is needed for a marginal target-population effect but not for a conditional effect at a fixed covariate profile.

title: No causal forest aggregates to a target known only by marginals
text:
Why it is open
The remaining gap is the aggregate-data target: individual-level effects have to be averaged over a distribution known only through published summaries, so the aggregation can be unidentified before it is estimated, and the variance of the two-stage procedure has not been worked out. Trial clustering and non-random IPD availability still matter when the trial is the sampling unit or when the estimand is trial-level generalization, and the existing cluster machinery handles the splitting but not the transport. Validation against held-out trials tests across-study generalization but does not establish identification, and it is unstable when the number of trials is small.

title: No causal forest aggregates to a target known only by marginals
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Wager & Athey, 2018
provides a principled framework and asymptotic theory for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects with causal forests


Brantner et al., 2024
Compares S-learner, X-learner and causal forest for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects across multiple randomized trials by simulation; covers the multi-IPD-trial case but not an aggregate-data target.


Venkatasubramaniam and Wolfson, 2025

title: No causal forest aggregates to a target known only by marginals
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Use the cluster-level honest splitting grf already provides and the multi-study forest work that exists, and put the research effort into target-aware aggregation: state when averaging conditional effects over a target known only through published marginal summaries is identified, and derive uncertainty that propagates through both the forest and the aggregation. Where identification fails, report bounds or sensitivity over the target distribution rather than a point estimate. Held-out-trial validation is worth running but should be read as a generalization check rather than as evidence of identification, with its instability under few trials reported.

title: No causal forest aggregates to a target known only by marginals
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Study-aware and target-aware causal forests for PAIC” The title names study-aware causal forests as undeveloped, but cluster-level honest splitting ships in grf and study-aware multi-trial causal forests are already published.
The source said. “Causal forests give a principled framework for heterogeneous treatment effects, but their adaptation to PAIC is unsolved because it requires study-aware sample splitting and target-aware aggregation rather than the standard single-sample procedures.”
What was wrong with it. The source said both study-aware sample splitting and target-aware aggregation still have to be developed. Cluster-level honest splitting already ships in grf and study-aware multi-trial causal forests already exist (doi:10.1002/sim.9955, arxiv:2502.02110), per the literature auditor; the code auditor added that forest honesty does not by itself require leaving whole trials out, that study is not a confounder of randomized treatment within a trial, and that with a target known only through marginal summaries the aggregation step may not be identified at all.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The prior_work citation is accurate: Wager & Athey 2018 is exactly the principled framework with asymptotic theory the entry attributes to it. But the study-aware half of the stated gap is available off the shelf. grf’s documentation states that with clusters specified, ‘all subsampling procedures operate on entire clusters as opposed to individual examples’, and honest splitting ‘split[s] these cluster IDs in half’ — cluster-level honest splitting, which is what trial clustering requires. Multi-trial CATE estimation with study structure has also been developed and simulated: Brantner et al. 2024 compares S-learner, X-learner and causal forest across trials and finds that methods allowing cross-trial heterogeneity perform better; Venkatasubramaniam & Wolfson 2025 give a Multi-Study Causal Forest for between-study heterogeneity. What none of these cover is the PAIC-defining case: a target population known only through published marginal summaries, and the variance of aggregating individual effects over it. Claim 4 as written is an unverifiable absence claim; narrowed to the aggregate-data target it is defensible. Cites doi:10.1002/sim.9955: Study-aware multi-trial CATE estimation including causal forests, evaluated by simulation; covers the multi-IPD-trial case, not the aggregate-data-target case. Cites arxiv:2502.02110: Causal forest adapted to between-study heterogeneity and varying treatment allocation across studies. Cites repo:github.com/grf-labs/grf: Cluster-level honest sample splitting already implemented, which is the study-aware splitting the entry says must be developed.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 is supported by the cited Wager-Athey work. C2 is required only when within-study dependence, clustered sampling, or trial-level generalization makes the trial the sampling unit; forest honesty means separating split selection from estimation and does not by itself require leaving whole trials out. Study is not a confounder of randomized treatment within a trial, although study selection and treatment-effect heterogeneity matter for transport. C3 is required for a marginal target-population effect, but not for a conditional effect at a fixed covariate profile. If the target is available only through marginal summaries, target averaging may itself be unidentified. C4 is a literature-existence claim and cannot be verified under this audit lens. Consequently an off-the-shelf forest does not automatically violate two universal requirements; the needed splitting and aggregation depend on the data structure and estimand. Held-out-trial validation tests across-study generalization but does not establish identification and can be unstable with few trials.

Decision path

title: Entropy balancing has no network extension or variance theory
text: COV-08 Overstated High priority Promising

title: Entropy balancing has no network extension or variance theory
text:
Statement
Entropy balancing with target summary information supplies a causal-generalization framework when consistency, exchangeability, positivity and sufficient calibration hold, and in indirect comparisons the machinery is not new: standard MAIC weights already are entropy-balancing weights, on any suitable scale such as log odds ratios, log hazard ratios or mean differences (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1416). The nonlinear-outcome extension exists for the single-source pairwise case: an augmented, doubly robust entropy-balancing estimator with a conditional outcome model has been developed and simulated with binary outcomes and a logistic outcome model (Campbell and Remiro-Azocar 2025, arxiv:2505.00113) and ships as drMAIC for binary and time-to-event outcomes (cran:drMAIC), while MAIC read as calibration estimation supplies a model-independent standard error (Wang 2021, arxiv:2107.11687). What remains undeveloped is the network case: multiple sources, multiple adjusted edges, consistency constraints across contrasts, and a variance theory that jointly accounts for estimated weights, shared estimated target summaries and network structure.

title: Entropy balancing has no network extension or variance theory
text:
Why it is open
A network involves several sources calibrated to one target, several adjusted edges and consistency constraints across contrasts, and the covariance induced by sharing the same estimated target summaries across edges is not handled by single-source estimating equations. The identification limit is separate from the software limit: balancing a finite set of target moments does not identify a nonlinear marginal estimand unless the relevant conditional response lies in the span of the balanced functions, which bites hardest for non-collapsible estimands where arm-specific outcomes must be marginalized before being contrasted. The network gap is an implementation and packaging gap rather than an impossibility, since trial-specific calibrations to a common target can be stacked and sandwich or bootstrap methods can propagate weight and shared-target uncertainty; until that is assembled, network applications lean on justification derived for the single-source case.

title: Entropy balancing has no network extension or variance theory
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Chen et al., 2023
establishes entropy balancing with target summary information as a causal-generalization method, for a single source sample generalized to one target described by moments, subject to its identification and calibration conditions


Campbell and Remiro-Azocar, 2025
Augments entropy-balancing MAIC with a conditional outcome model to give a doubly robust estimator, simulated with binary outcomes and a logistic outcome model; the nonlinear-outcome extension for the single-source unanchored case.


drMAIC (R package, version 0.1.0)
Shipped implementation of standard MAIC by entropy balancing plus augmented weighting with outcome regression, for binary and time-to-event outcomes.


Wang, 2021
Places MAIC inside calibration estimation and proposes a model-independent standard error estimator, a partial answer to the variance-theory gap.


Equivalence of entropy balancing and the method of moments for MAIC, 2020
Shows that the field’s standard MAIC weights already are entropy-balancing weights and that weighted outcomes are contrasted on a suitable scale such as log odds ratios, log hazard ratios or mean differences, so the foundation is neither new to indirect comparisons nor restricted to linear outcomes.

title: Entropy balancing has no network extension or variance theory
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Assemble the network estimator from parts that exist: stack trial-specific calibrations to a common target, impose the consistency constraints, and propagate weight and shared-target uncertainty with a joint sandwich or bootstrap, rather than developing nonlinear-outcome entropy balancing that is already available in the pairwise case. State the conditions under which the balanced moment set identifies the nonlinear marginal estimand, and report sensitivity or bounds when it does not. Benchmark the result against MAIC and ML-NMR on the same networks so the gain from distributional balancing over moment matching is measured rather than asserted.

title: Entropy balancing has no network extension or variance theory
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Entropy balancing with target summary information has been extended to non-linear outcome models only in the single-source, pairwise (externally-controlled or unanchored) case, where doubly robust augmented estimators with logistic outcome models exist and are implemented. Extension to evidence networks with multiple sources, multiple adjusted edges and consistency constraints, together with a variance theory that jointly accounts for estimated weights, estimated target moments and network structure, remains undeveloped.
The source titled this. “Entropy balancing extensions to networks and nonlinear outcomes” The title names the nonlinear-outcome extension as open, but the audit found a doubly robust augmented estimator with a logistic outcome model already published and shipping as drMAIC.
The source said. “Entropy balancing with target summary information already supplies a causal-generalization foundation for adjusting an IPD sample to published target moments, but its extensions to evidence networks and to nonlinear outcome models remain underdeveloped.”
What was wrong with it. The source said extensions of entropy balancing to nonlinear outcome models remain underdeveloped; both auditors disagreed for the single-source case, where a doubly robust augmented estimator with a logistic outcome model exists and ships as drMAIC (arxiv:2505.00113, cran:drMAIC) and a model-independent standard error is available (arxiv:2107.11687). The code auditor added that entropy balancing is outcome-agnostic calibration weighting rather than a linear-outcome method (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1416), and that with finitely many target moments a nonlinear marginal estimand is identified only if the relevant conditional response lies in the span of the balanced functions or the target law is identified some other way.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The prior_work citation is accurate: Chen, Chen & Yu 2023 is ‘Entropy Balancing for Causal Generalization with Target Sample Summary Information’, and it is indeed a single-source-to-one-target method. The network half of the claim holds. The nonlinear-outcome half does not. Campbell & Remiro-Azocar 2025 (Research Synthesis Methods) augments entropy-balancing MAIC with a conditional outcome model and demonstrates it ‘in a simulation study with binary outcomes and a logistic outcome model’, reporting the doubly robust property; the method ships as drMAIC 0.1.0, whose description states it provides ‘standard MAIC via entropy balancing / exponential tilting’ alongside augmented IPW-plus-outcome-regression, for binary and time-to-event outcomes. Partial variance theory also exists: Wang 2021 treats MAIC as calibration estimation and proposes ‘a model-independent SE estimator’. What remains genuinely undeveloped is the network case with multiple sources, multiple adjusted edges and consistency constraints, plus a variance theory covering estimated weights, estimated target moments and network structure jointly. Cites arxiv:2505.00113: The nonlinear-outcome extension of entropy-balancing weighting with target summary information, for the single-source unanchored case. Cites cran:drMAIC: Shipped software implementing entropy-balancing MAIC augmented with outcome regression for binary and time-to-event outcomes. Cites arxiv:2107.11687: Places MAIC inside calibration estimation and supplies a model-independent standard error estimator, a partial answer to the variance-theory gap. Cites doi:10.1002/jrsm.1416: Establishes that the field’s standard MAIC weights already are entropy balancing weights, so the ‘foundation’ is not new to ITC.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 is correct only under consistency, source treatment exchangeability, sampling exchangeability, positivity, and sufficient calibration or a correctly specified target-to-source density ratio. C3 is misframed: entropy balancing is an outcome-agnostic calibration-weighting method, not inherently a linear-outcome estimator. If its weights recover the density ratio, weighted standardization can transport arbitrary integrable potential-outcome means. With only finitely many target moments, however, a nonlinear marginal quantity is not generally identified unless the relevant conditional response lies in the span of the balanced functions or the target joint distribution is otherwise identified. This is especially important for non-collapsible estimands, which require marginalizing arm-specific outcomes before contrasting them. C2 describes a plausible implementation gap, but not a mathematical impossibility: separate trials can be calibrated to one common target and their estimating equations stacked. Generic joint sandwich or bootstrap methods can propagate weight and shared-target uncertainty when the required influence information or target microdata exist. Intervals that explicitly condition on published target summaries are not automatically unjustified. The genuinely incomplete part is a coherent, readily usable network implementation under limited aggregate target information. Its severity is high only for analyses that actually depend on such network-wide calibration or nonlinear marginal estimands. Cites 10.1111/biom.13825: Establishes the single-source causal-generalization foundation using target summary moments, resolving C1 subject to its identification and model conditions.. Cites 10.1002/jrsm.1416: Establishes entropy balancing as the standard MAIC moment-weighting solution and places weighted treatment outcomes on general link scales, contradicting an inherent restriction to identity-scale linear outcomes. It does not resolve joint network calibration or finite-moment identification..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Entropy balancing has no network extension or variance theory
section: How the evidence falls in time
text:
How the evidence falls in time
4 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2012 to 2024. The most recent paper to touch this reports progress on it, and every paper calling it open is older.
It is also being closed in pieces: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.
Does the later work answer the earlier work? Put to an independent reviewer with the older and newer claims side by side, it judged that the later work answers a component of it, leaving a named part (high confidence). Later work supplies pairwise indirect-comparison implementations and inference procedures that do not simply treat entropy-balancing weights as fixed, and clarifies its equivalence to MAIC calibration weighting. Those advances answer the single-source pairwise variance component, but not the network component of the earlier gap. What remains: A network-level extension with multiple IPD and aggregate sources, coherent constraints across adjusted contrasts, and joint variance theory for estimated weights, shared target summaries, and network dependence.

title: Effect-modifier selection does not check interaction consistency
text: COV-10 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: Effect-modifier selection does not check interaction consistency
text:
Statement
Treatment-by-covariate interaction coefficients satisfy a consistency equation of their own, and when it fails, direct and indirect evidence can carry interactions of opposite sign that cancel in a pooled network meta-regression, so the fit reports no effect modification for a covariate that strongly modifies the effect within each evidence path. Donegan, Dias and Welton 2019 construct the case explicitly: in a fabricated antimalarial network the interaction coefficients from direct evidence were 0.0000 (95 percent credible interval -0.0115 to 0.0116) while the corresponding indirect coefficients were 0.0399, -0.0400 and 0.0800, and the network meta-regression concluded that no interaction exists. The ordinary consistency check passes at the same time: the posterior probability that direct and indirect evidence agree was 0.9976 to 1.000 for the log odds ratios and 0 for the interaction coefficients, so an analyst who checks treatment effects for inconsistency sees nothing wrong. Effect-modifier sets for population adjustment are routinely assembled from meta-regression, network meta-regression and published interaction estimates, and no selection procedure, guidance document or software checks the consistency of the interaction coefficients before a covariate is accepted or rejected. The result is a matching-adjusted indirect comparison, simulated treatment comparison or multilevel network meta-regression balanced on a modifier set that omits a real modifier because it was cancelled rather than absent, and the omission is invisible to every downstream balance, overlap and effective sample size diagnostic, all of which are computed after the set is fixed.

title: Effect-modifier selection does not check interaction consistency
text:
Why it is open
The methods that would detect this exist only as bespoke Bayesian models. Donegan, Dias and Welton extend node splitting, the design-by-treatment interaction model and the unrelated mean effects model to carry treatment-by-covariate interactions, and state that before their paper no method had been introduced for assessing the consistency assumptions underlying network meta-regression; those models are not implemented in netmeta, gemtc, multinma or any population-adjustment package, so running the check means writing the code by hand. The check also needs a covariate that varies across trials and enough studies on each of the direct and indirect paths to estimate two interaction coefficients, which is rarely available in the small sparse networks where population adjustment is used, and it inherits the low power that afflicts every inconsistency test, so a null result is weak evidence either way. Above all, modifier selection is treated as an input to the analysis rather than as an inference: the candidate set is fixed before any network model is fitted, so the workflow never creates an occasion at which a network-level diagnostic on the set could be run. Population adjustment then compounds the problem, because the shared effect modifier assumption it usually relies on presumes the interaction structure is coherent across the network, which is exactly what goes untested.

title: Effect-modifier selection does not check interaction consistency
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Donegan, Dias and Welton 2019, Assessing the consistency assumptions underlying network meta-regression using aggregate data, Research Synthesis Methods 10:207-224
Extends node splitting, the design-by-treatment interaction model and the unrelated mean effects model to include treatment-by-covariate interactions for aggregate data, demonstrates that an interaction present in both direct and indirect evidence can be masked by inconsistency in the pooled fit, and states that no method for assessing the consistency assumptions underlying network meta-regression existed before it. The models are not implemented in standard software.


Dias, Welton, Caldwell and Ades 2010, Checking consistency in mixed treatment comparison meta-analysis, Statistics in Medicine 29:932-944
Establishes node splitting for treatment effects, the machinery the interaction check extends. It tests agreement of effects across direct and indirect paths, which is precisely the check that passes while the interaction structure is inconsistent.


Donegan, Williamson, D’Alessandro and Tudur Smith 2013, Assessing key assumptions of network meta-analysis: a review of methods, Research Synthesis Methods 4:291-323
Surveys the methods available for assessing similarity, homogeneity and consistency, showing that the assessment literature is aimed at treatment effects rather than at the interaction coefficients that determine which covariates are modifiers.


Saramago, Sutton, Cooper and Manca 2012, Mixed treatment comparisons using aggregate and individual participant level data, Statistics in Medicine 31:3516-3536
Shows how individual participant data recover within-trial interactions that aggregate-level covariate summaries confound with across-trial associations, which is the other way an interaction estimate can be wrong and is separately catalogued; it does not address cancellation across evidence paths.


Phillippo et al. 2020, Multilevel Network Meta-Regression for Population-Adjusted Treatment Comparisons, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 183:1189-1210
Fits one network-level interaction model that removes aggregation bias and, in small networks, assumes effect modifier interactions are shared across treatments. That assumption presumes the interaction structure is consistent across the network rather than providing a way to test it.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making 38:200-211 (the peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18)
Specifies how effect modifiers should be handled once selected and points to literature review and clinical expert discussion as the routes to selecting them. No network-level coherence check on the candidate set appears anywhere in the workflow.

title: Effect-modifier selection does not check interaction consistency
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Make the interaction consistency check part of modifier selection rather than a separate methodological exercise: implement interaction node splitting and the interaction design-by-treatment model in a maintained package so a candidate covariate can be screened against the network before it is accepted or discarded, and report the direct and indirect interaction coefficients side by side with the posterior probability that they agree. Establish operating characteristics before recommending it, since the diagnostic will be used to keep covariates as well as to drop them: simulate networks with opposing path-specific interactions of known size and report the probability of recovering the masked modifier as a function of the number of trials per path, the between-trial variation in the covariate and the size of the cancellation. Where the network is too sparse to split, require the report to state that the check could not be run instead of citing the pooled coefficient as evidence of no modification. Define the action when the check fires: a covariate whose interaction differs across paths is a modifier on at least one of them, so balancing on it is defensible even though the pooled coefficient says otherwise, and the analysis should say which path drove the decision.

title: Effect-modifier selection does not check interaction consistency
text:
Our study

Interaction coefficients have their own consistency equation
The question put to it. When direct and indirect paths carry opposing treatment-by-covariate interactions, does the pooled network meta-regression mask the modifier while the effect-consistency check passes, and can an interaction-consistency check detect it?
What it found. Opposing interactions on direct and indirect paths attenuate the pooled network meta-regression interaction toward zero, fully at the balance point and partly across a continuum, while the effect-consistency check stays at its null rate. The target effect was biased by 0.13 to 0.30 whether or not the covariate was selected. A direct interaction-consistency check detects it when studies per path and covariate spread are adequate (up to 1.00) and has little power otherwise (0.16 with two studies and narrow spread).
Results.

Effect-consistency check flag rate 0.094 to 0.107 in every interaction-inconsistent scenario without effect inconsistency (blindness confirmed).
Refuting sentence fails: partly opposing interactions biased the target by -0.13 to -0.26.
Cancelling configuration: pooled interaction mean near 0 but replicate SD 0.13 to 0.67 against model SE 0.03 to 0.38 (1.5 to 4.2 times), so the Wald test selected the covariate in 31% to 88% of analyses.
Interaction-consistency check power 0.16 to 1.00, rising with studies per comparison and covariate spread.

Design.

Estimand

C versus A effect at a covariate value of 1.5, with the AC path’s modification as truth

Methods compared

consistency network meta-regression with covariate selection, interaction-consistency test, effect-consistency (Bucher) test

Data-generating mechanism

Triangle networks with path-specific interaction slopes (consistent, partly opposing, cancelling), two to eight studies per comparison, two covariate spreads and effect inconsistency absent or present; consistency meta-regression, modifier selection, interaction and effect consistency checks. 36 cells, 2000 replicates each.

Replicates

2000 per scenario, 72,000 in total


What this does not answer. Stylized triangles with continuous estimates; design-by-treatment interaction model and larger networks not run. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.
