title: No error control for repeated looks at a living network
text: DEC-14 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: No error control for repeated looks at a living network
text:
Statement
A living or cumulative network meta-analysis re-fits an accumulating network on a fixed cadence, and every release is read as the current answer, yet no convention states what error rate is being controlled across the series of looks. Sequential monitoring machinery exists for the single-contrast case: Nikolakopoulou et al. 2018 (doi:10.1177/0962280216659896) build efficacy and futility boundaries from each network estimate’s z-score and its accrued information fraction, and applied sequential network meta-analyses use them. Four things that machinery does not supply are missing at once: a required information size for a contrast when treatments and loops keep entering, an error-rate target for the K(K-1)/2 comparisons that are re-tested at every update and are correlated through the shared basic parameters and the consistency equations, a rule stating which assumptions must be re-checked at each update and which may be inherited, and a rule for retiring a settled comparison from the update cycle. The network case is not the pairwise case with more contrasts, because a comparison can cross its boundary purely on indirect evidence contributed by trials of other comparisons; the same methods paper shows a stent-versus-surgery contrast becoming significant when only stent-versus-stent studies are published. Living protocols decline adjustment explicitly and record it as a design choice: one cumulative antidepressant program states it will not adjust for multiple comparisons in successive network meta-analyses, and a live cumulative lung-cancer network planning updates every four months with about two new treatments per cycle declines adjustment on the stated grounds that Bayesian inference is not affected by repeated updates. Guideline panels consume these releases between updates, so a reader of update k has no stated basis for interpreting the reported interval, and no report says how many looks a conclusion has survived.

title: No error control for repeated looks at a living network
text:
Why it is open
Alpha spending requires a fixed information target and a fixed hypothesis set, and a living network supplies neither: adding a treatment changes the required information size for contrasts nobody looked at, and adding an indirect path changes an estimate with no new direct trial, so the information fraction is not well defined per contrast. The monitored quantity also moves, because the best of k treatments and any rank summary are defined relative to the treatment set, so a node added, merged or split between looks redefines the estimand rather than adding information about it. The Bayesian defense is correct as far as it goes and does not reach the problem: a posterior for a fixed parameter is unaffected by optional stopping, but selecting a maximum over a growing set, and the decision rules a guideline consumer applies at each release, are not fixed-parameter inference. The dependence among comparisons is analytically available from the network covariance matrix, so an efficient simultaneous procedure is derivable in principle; what is absent is a decision about which family is being controlled, and that choice sits outside any model. Living-review methodology has developed the production side in detail while the statistical updating series stops at pairwise synthesis, so the network case has no owner.

title: No error control for repeated looks at a living network
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Nikolakopoulou et al. 2018, Statistical Methods in Medical Research
Extends sequential monitoring to network meta-analysis: efficacy and futility boundaries per network estimate from the z-score and the information accrued after each study enters, with the demonstration that a contrast can become conclusive through indirect evidence alone. Adjusts for repeated looks at one comparison, defines no family-level error target, and declines multiplicity adjustment for the accompanying inconsistency tests.


Wetterslev et al. 2008, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Trial sequential analysis for cumulative pairwise meta-analysis: heterogeneity-adjusted required information size plus monitoring boundaries, finding early potentially spurious P below 0.05 in five of six neonatal meta-analyses. Assumes one fixed comparison and a monotone information target, which is what a living network breaks.


Simmonds et al. 2017, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Living systematic reviews part 3: compares the law of the iterated logarithm, the Shuster method, trial sequential analysis and sequential meta-analysis as ways of controlling type I and type II error under repeated updating, and states that the type I error rate rises rapidly as more updates are performed. Pairwise only, with a fixed comparison set.


Elliott et al. 2017, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Defines the living systematic review, its update cadence and the conditions under which continuous updating is worth doing, setting the production framework within which the inferential question arises.


Tsai et al. 2020, Journal of Clinical Periodontology
Applies sequential network meta-analysis to an updated 60-trial periodontal network specifically to control the type I error rate from multiple testing, and reports that the stricter sequential criteria give different conclusions from the ordinary analysis. A single application rather than a framework, with a fixed treatment set.


Vandvik, Brignardello-Petersen and Guyatt 2016, BMC Medicine
Sets out living cumulative network meta-analysis as a program and enumerates the challenges that must be solved before it can become routine. Error control across repeated releases is not among them, which is itself evidence that the question is unformulated.


Xin et al. 2022, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Interactive re-analysis and sensitivity analysis of a living COVID-19 network through the MetaInsight app, and surveys what exists for the repeated-looks problem: trial sequential analysis has been proposed, its network extension and R packages have started to be developed, and issues such as futility boundaries still need further work.


Crequit, Trinquart and Ravaud 2016, BMJ Open
Protocol for a live cumulative network meta-analysis in second-line non-small-cell lung cancer with updates every four months, which declines any adjustment for multiple testing on the stated grounds that Bayesian inference is not affected by repeated updates.


Luo et al. 2018, BMJ Open
Protocol for cumulative network meta-analyses of new-generation antidepressants feeding practice guidelines, which states that no adjustment for multiple comparisons will be made across successive network meta-analyses because particular hypotheses for specific comparisons are not being tested.

title: No error control for repeated looks at a living network
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Fix the monitored family before deriving anything: state whether the target is a per-contrast rate, a family-wise rate over the decision-relevant contrasts at one release, or a false-discovery rate across the whole update series, and take the correlation among contrasts from the network covariance matrix, which already supplies it analytically. Redefine the information fraction so it survives node entry and exit, for example by anchoring it to a declared decision contrast and treating a newly opened indirect path as information accrual rather than as a change of target. Write an assumption-inheritance rule saying which transitivity, heterogeneity and node-partition checks must be re-run when new studies or new nodes arrive and which results may carry over. Add a retirement rule that drops a settled comparison from further monitoring, plus a reporting convention stating how many looks a conclusion has survived and what fraction of the required information has accrued. Evaluate the result by simulating an accruing network and reporting the realized probability that at least one comparison crosses an efficacy boundary spuriously, as a function of the number of treatments, the update cadence and the rate at which new nodes enter.

title: No error control for repeated looks at a living network
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Four independent readers proposed this from four different papers and the reviewer accepted each, holding that repeated publication and decision use of an evolving network raise questions that neither pairwise trial sequential analysis nor the fixed-parameter Bayesian argument answers. The basis is not only applied protocols: the methods paper that defines sequential boundaries for networks adjusts solely for repeated looks at one contrast, and a living-review feasibility study records that the network extensions of trial sequential analysis still leave issues such as futility boundaries unresolved.

title: No joint error rate for the many claims a network asserts
text: DEC-16 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: No joint error rate for the many claims a network asserts
text:
Statement
Network meta-analysis reports per-treatment marginal summaries such as SUCRA, P-scores and rankograms, plus a league table of pairwise intervals each at nominal 95 percent, while a recommendation uses several of those statements together. Nothing reports the joint posterior or family-wise confidence of the conjunction that is acted on, and nothing defines a tie by reference to a minimal clinically important difference rather than to exact equality of parameters. Both halves are computable and the omission is material: in the 12-drug antidepressants network the full set of 66 pairwise ordering statements holds jointly with posterior probability below 0.01, and only a heavily trimmed set survives at 0.97 (doi:10.1093/jrsssc/qlae038). The GRADE minimally contextualised framework interrogates each contrast against a decision threshold at nominal 95 percent and then builds effectiveness categories by iterative promotion; its worked 27-treatment example produces 351 comparisons, and the guidance states that how seriously multiplicity might compromise inferences remains uncertain and that no satisfactory or widely accepted strategy exists for dealing with it. Part of the clinical half is built: Mavridis et al. 2020 (doi:10.1002/bimj.201900026) extend the P-score to measure the mean certainty that a treatment beats its competitors by at least a stated minimum important difference, across several outcomes at once. What remains absent is an error-rate target for the family of claims a network report makes, a procedure that exploits the correlation among contrasts that the network covariance matrix already supplies, and any convention fixing the joint-probability target or choosing among the several distinct trimmed sets that reach it. This concerns the many claims made from one network at one time; error control across the repeated looks of a living network is a separate gap.

title: No joint error rate for the many claims a network asserts
text:
Why it is open
The family is not defined, and until it is no procedure can be evaluated: a network report asserts pairwise superiorities, category memberships and an ordering at the same time, and which of these a committee acts on jointly varies by decision, so the correction depends on a choice that sits outside the model. Standard corrections are also a poor fit, because the contrasts are strongly dependent through the shared basic parameters and the consistency equations, so a Bonferroni-style adjustment over T(T-1)/2 comparisons is badly conservative while the efficient alternative requires carrying the network covariance into a simultaneous procedure nobody has written. Making equality expressible at all requires a prior with an atom at zero, so a joint-probability report is a change of model rather than post-processing of an existing analysis. Even once computed the report is not unique, since several distinct trimmed sets of ordering statements can reach the same joint probability with no rule for choosing among them and no default for the target. The clinically meaningful half is blocked upstream by elicitation: an equivalence region needs a minimum important difference per outcome, network meta-analyses rarely declare one, and without it a statistically detected difference far below any plausible margin still produces an arrow in a ranking.

title: No joint error rate for the many claims a network asserts
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Barrientos, Page and Lin 2024, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C
Nonparametric Bayesian model whose prior has an atom, so exact equality of treatment effects is expressible, and which reports the joint posterior probability of a whole set of ordering statements. On the 12-drug antidepressants network the untrimmed set of relationships holds jointly with probability below 0.01. Leaves the trimming threshold undefined and concedes that several distinct trimmed graphs can reach the same joint probability.


Brignardello-Petersen et al. 2020, BMJ (minimally contextualised framework)
Official GRADE guidance for drawing conclusions from a network: each contrast is interrogated against a decision threshold and treatments are sorted into effectiveness categories by iterative promotion. Names multiplicity as unresolved, states that no satisfactory or widely accepted strategy exists, and declines to address it.


Brignardello-Petersen et al. 2020, BMJ (partially contextualised framework)
The companion framework that additionally assigns magnitude labels from the same nominal intervals, so the unaddressed multiplicity carries through into the wording of the published conclusion.


Mavridis et al. 2020, Biometrical Journal
Extends the P-score so that it measures the mean certainty that a treatment is better than the competing treatments by at least a minimum clinically important difference, and so that several outcomes can be combined with an explicit benefit-harm tradeoff. Addresses the clinical-margin half for a per-treatment metric, not the joint credibility of a set of ordering statements.


Trinquart et al. 2016, Annals of Internal Medicine
Reanalyzes 58 networks and reports that the median width of the 95 percent credible interval for SUCRA is 65 percentage points and that in 28 percent of networks there is a 50 percent or greater probability that the best-ranked treatment is not the best. Quantifies the imprecision of one rank; says nothing about the credibility of a conjunction of claims.


Salanti, Ades and Ioannidis 2011, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Introduces SUCRA and the rank-based presentation that decisions are read off, including probabilities of lying within an acceptable range from a reference treatment. Each summary is marginal in the treatment, which is the form the joint statement is missing from.


Rucker and Schwarzer 2015, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Defines the frequentist P-score as the mean of one-sided p-values, the metric that Mavridis et al. later extended to a clinically important margin. Also marginal per treatment, and the paper itself notes it offers no major advantage over inspecting intervals.

title: No joint error rate for the many claims a network asserts
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Fix the family before the procedure: write down the exact set of claims a network report asserts, separating pairwise superiorities, category memberships and the full ordering, and state which of them a committee acts on jointly. For that family, derive a simultaneous procedure that uses the network covariance matrix rather than treating contrasts as independent, and report both the joint credibility of the asserted set and the largest subset reaching a stated target. Standardize the equivalence side by requiring an outcome-specific minimum important difference in the protocol, then define a tie as a contrast whose interval lies inside that region, which puts ranking metrics on the same scale as the decision and makes the Mavridis-style P-score extension usable by default. Settle the reporting conventions that the joint-probability approach leaves open: a default target probability and a deterministic rule for choosing among trimmed sets that reach it. Score every candidate on realized decision error by simulating networks with known orderings and reporting how often a category separation or a superiority claim is spurious as a function of the number of treatments.

title: No joint error rate for the many claims a network asserts
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Two independent readers proposed this and the reviewer accepted both, but real work covers parts of it: Barrientos et al. 2024 compute the joint posterior of a set of ordering statements and Mavridis et al. 2020 build a minimum important difference into a ranking metric. What no work supplies is an error-rate target for the family of claims a network report makes, a procedure that uses the known correlation among contrasts, or a convention for the joint-probability threshold, and the GRADE working group’s own guidance states that no satisfactory or widely accepted strategy exists.

title: NMA rank output lacks a decision-theoretic reconciliation with net benefit
text: DEC-18 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: NMA rank output lacks a decision-theoretic reconciliation with net benefit
text:
Statement
Evidence synthesis reports treatment orderings as probability-best, rankograms, SUCRA or P-scores computed on a clinical outcome, while the economic model reports a separate ordering on net benefit, and no convention reconciles the two. SUCRA is an unweighted average of the cumulative rank probabilities, and Epstein 2019 states that this leaves it without empirical or theoretical grounding, such as utility theory, for preference-based choice. The two orderings can conflict inside a single model: in a seven-option varicose-vein appraisal a dominated option had a 33 percent probability of greatest net benefit at a threshold of 20,000 pounds per quality-adjusted life year while ranking fifth or worse in 27 percent of simulations, and SUCRA placed it above an option that was more likely to be in the top four, 86 percent against 72 percent on cumulative rank probability. Rank probabilities had not previously been used for economic evaluation at all, so nothing links the synthesis-stage ordering that submissions publish to the decision-stage ordering that determines reimbursement. The synthesis side has moved: the treatment hierarchy question has been formalized as something the analyst must state before selecting a ranking metric, and complex hierarchy statements can now be evaluated as posterior probabilities in released software. What is still missing is the mapping from a rank functional to a loss function, a rule for what to do when the clinical-outcome ordering and the net-benefit ordering diverge, and an agreed partial order that is reportable without assuming a risk attitude.

title: NMA rank output lacks a decision-theoretic reconciliation with net benefit
text:
Why it is open
Rank statistics discard exactly what a reimbursement decision needs. A rank is invariant to the magnitude of the differences between options, so two networks with the same ordering and wildly different effect sizes yield identical SUCRA values, while net benefit is a function of magnitudes, costs and utilities; no transformation of the rank distribution can recover information the ranking threw away. Rank metrics are also defined relative to the set of options in the network, so adding or removing a comparator changes every treatment’s rank without any new evidence about it, whereas net benefit at a given threshold is a per-option quantity that does not move. The work that has been done sits on one side of a boundary: hierarchy questions have been formalized inside the synthesis and against clinical outcomes, and it stops at the economic model, so nobody owns the join, because the synthesis team does not hold the cost and utility inputs and the economic team does not publish a rank distribution. And the divergence has never been measured, so there is no evidence base saying how often a SUCRA ordering and a net-benefit ordering actually disagree in appraisals that contain both.

title: NMA rank output lacks a decision-theoretic reconciliation with net benefit
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Epstein 2019, Beyond the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve: the appropriateness of rank probabilities for presenting the results of economic evaluation in multiple technology appraisal, Health Economics 28:801-807
Argues SUCRA is inappropriate for economic evaluation because it is an unweighted average of cumulative rank probabilities with no utility-theoretic basis, computes rank probabilities of net benefit in a seven-option case study, and shows a dominated option with a 33 percent probability of greatest net benefit that nonetheless ranks fifth or worse in 27 percent of simulations. States that rank probabilities had not previously been used in economic evaluation.


Salanti, Ades and Ioannidis 2011, Graphical methods and numerical summaries for presenting results from multiple-treatment meta-analysis, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 64:163-171
Introduces the rankogram, the cumulative ranking curve and SUCRA as presentational summaries of a network’s posterior ordering. They are defined as descriptive quantities, not as solutions to a decision problem.


Rucker and Schwarzer 2015, Ranking treatments in frequentist network meta-analysis works without resampling methods, BMC Medical Research Methodology 15
Defines the P-score, the frequentist analogue of SUCRA computed from point estimates and standard errors. It inherits the same absence of a loss function.


Salanti et al. 2022, Introducing the Treatment Hierarchy Question in Network Meta-Analysis, American Journal of Epidemiology 191:930-938
The closest existing thing to the mapping this entry asks for: it requires the analyst to state the clinical question a hierarchy is meant to answer before choosing a metric, and matches metrics to questions. It works with clinical outcomes and stops short of a loss function or of the economic model’s net benefit.


Papakonstantinou et al. 2022, Answering complex hierarchy questions in network meta-analysis, BMC Medical Research Methodology 22, with the nmarank package on CRAN
Evaluates the posterior probability of arbitrary specified hierarchy statements, which supplies the machinery for reporting a decision-relevant ordering once someone specifies which statement the decision needs.


Rucker and Schwarzer 2017, Resolve conflicting rankings of outcomes in network meta-analysis: partial ordering of treatments, Research Synthesis Methods 8:526-536
Reports a partial order rather than forcing a total ranking when outcomes conflict, which is the form of preference-free output this entry asks for on the multi-outcome side. It does not extend to conflict between a clinical ordering and a net-benefit ordering.


Trinquart, Attiche, Bafeta, Porcher and Ravaud 2016, Uncertainty in treatment rankings: reanalysis of network meta-analyses of randomized trials, Annals of Internal Medicine 164:666-673
Reanalyzes published network meta-analyses and shows how wide the uncertainty around a reported ranking is, which is the reason a point ordering cannot substitute for a decision rule.


Chiocchia et al. 2020, Agreement between ranking metrics in network meta-analysis: an empirical study, BMJ Open 10:e037744
Measures agreement among ranking metrics computed on the same clinical outcome. It establishes the template for the divergence study this entry asks for while stopping inside the synthesis.


Claxton 1999, The irrelevance of inference: a decision-making approach to the stochastic evaluation of health care technologies, Journal of Health Economics 18:341-364
The decision-theoretic argument that adoption should follow expected net benefit rather than inferential statements about which option is superior. It is the standard against which a rank statistic used as a decision quantity has to be justified.


Hopkin et al. 2019, Combining Multiple Treatment Comparisons with Personalized Patient Preferences, Medical Decision Making 39:264-277
Builds a patient-facing statin selection platform whose treatment ordering is a preference-weighted average of SUCRA values drawn from two separate network meta-analyses, which is the practice this entry says has no decision-theoretic justification.


Ades, Welton, Dias, Phillippo and Caldwell 2024, Twenty years of network meta-analysis: continuing controversies and recent developments, Research Synthesis Methods 15:702-727
Surveys the state of the field including the continuing dispute over ranking metrics, confirming that the interpretation of ranks remains contested within evidence synthesis independently of the economic question.

title: NMA rank output lacks a decision-theoretic reconciliation with net benefit
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Write down the loss functions and match each reported rank statistic to the one that makes it optimal, so a reader can tell which decision a SUCRA or a probability-best is the answer to: probability-best is the Bayes rule under a zero-one loss on the identity of the top option, which is defensible only when exactly one option will be recommended and all errors are equally costly, and it is not the rule for a reimbursement decision on net benefit. Require the rank distribution of net benefit at the relevant threshold to be reported alongside the clinical-outcome ranking, since the probabilistic economic model already generates the simulations that produce it, and require both orderings to be shown together with an explicit note when they diverge. Measure how often they diverge by re-running a set of completed appraisals that contain both a network meta-analysis and a probabilistic economic model, reporting the proportion in which the SUCRA ordering and the net-benefit ordering disagree in the top three. Where no threshold or utility set can be agreed, report a partial order instead of a ranking: the set of options not dominated by first-order stochastic dominance of net benefit is preference-free within the class of increasing utility functions and is computable from the same simulations.

title: NMA rank output lacks a decision-theoretic reconciliation with net benefit
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as a distinct decision-theoretic reporting and interpretation gap rather than the simulation-performance issue in DEC-01, on the ground that rank probabilities and SUCRA encode no effect magnitudes, costs, utilities or loss function. It is recorded as partially addressed rather than confirmed open because the synthesis half has moved: the treatment hierarchy question has been formalized and arbitrary hierarchy statements can be evaluated as posterior probabilities in released software, so what remains absent is the loss function and the reconciliation with the economic model’s net-benefit ordering.

title: No rule says what proves similarity from an indirect comparison
text: DEC-20 Confirmed open Very high priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: No rule says what proves similarity from an indirect comparison
text:
Statement
Reimbursement pathways that turn on whether a new treatment is clinically similar to an existing one, such as the NICE cost-comparison route, are routinely decided from indirect comparisons, and no guidance states what the estimate must show before similarity may be concluded. A systematic review of all 41 NICE cost-comparison evaluations from the pathway’s introduction in 2017 to April 2025 found companies relying heavily on statistically non-significant indirect comparison results, external assessment groups objecting, and only about 32% of appraisals applying any formal method to explore the uncertainty in those results. Absence of a detected difference and demonstrated similarity are different claims, and nothing requires a non-inferiority margin to be prespecified, fixes the posterior probability or interval position that suffices, or says what to do when no clinically validated margin exists. The disagreement is public: one external assessment group has concluded that non-significant differences or overlapping 95% intervals may be sufficient to demonstrate clinical similarity, and another has published the opposite position, with a comment and reply exchange in the record. The estimate carrying the claim is an indirect one, so it already rests on transitivity and, in population-adjusted analyses, on transportability, and none of that enters the threshold. The single published framework reports the posterior probability that a contrast lies within a margin and derives a hypothetical threshold by empirical distribution function where no validated margin exists, but concedes its own 95% probability cutoff is arbitrary and does not extend to population-adjusted comparisons.

title: No rule says what proves similarity from an indirect comparison
text:
Why it is open
The rule has to be set by the agency that uses it, and the NICE methods manual is silent, so no submission is ever rejected for lacking one and no submitter has an incentive to propose a stricter bar than the one accepted last time. Where a clinically validated margin does not exist, any rule needs a convention for manufacturing one, and manufacturing a margin from the evidence being tested is circular unless the convention is fixed in advance. A defensible threshold would also have to price the extra assumptions of the indirect route, a quantity nobody has calibrated and which cannot be estimated from the data that produced the comparison. The pathway’s attraction to all parties is speed, so requirements that add analysis are resisted from both sides. Because the two assessment groups disagree in print and neither position has been evaluated against realized decision error, there is no empirical basis on which the agency could choose between them.

title: No rule says what proves similarity from an indirect comparison
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Edwards et al. 2026, Clinical similarity in cost-comparison evaluations: a systematic review of current methods in NICE appraisals and the development of a framework for the formal assessment of clinical similarity, BMJ Open
Reviews all 41 NICE cost-comparison evaluations from 2017 to April 2025, states that NICE gives no guidance on interpreting non-significant indirect comparison results to prove clinical similarity, finds only about 32% applied any formal method, and proposes point-and-density plots reporting the probability of non-inferiority against a margin; applied to appraisal TA1019 it returns 95.9% and 86.3% probabilities of non-inferiority where the frequentist comparison was non-significant.


Lee et al. 2025, How Similar Is Similar Enough? Assessment of Indirect Treatment Comparisons to Support Similarity for National Institute for Health and Care Excellence’s Cost Comparison Route, Value in Health
An assessment group’s review of indirect comparisons used to support similarity in the cost-comparison route, raising concerns about reliance on non-significant results and recommending methods that would improve transparency.


Poley et al. 2025, Cost Comparisons in NICE Technology Appraisals: An External Assessment Group Perspective, PharmacoEconomics
States the opposing assessment-group position that a lack of statistically significant differences or overlapping 95% intervals may suffice to demonstrate clinical similarity; the disagreement is recorded in a published comment (doi 10.1007/s40273-025-01551-7) and reply (doi 10.1007/s40273-025-01553-5).


Hashim et al. 2021, A systematic review of noninferiority margins in oncology clinical trials, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research
Documents how non-inferiority margins are chosen when direct evidence exists, which is the comparison case against which an indirect-comparison rule would have to be set.


Bucher et al. 1997, The results of direct and indirect treatment comparisons in meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Gives the anchored indirect estimator whose interval position is what similarity claims are read off in practice.


NICE health technology evaluations: the manual (2023)
The process document governing the cost-comparison route; it contains no rule for interpreting a statistically non-significant indirect comparison as evidence of similarity.

title: No rule says what proves similarity from an indirect comparison
text:
Probable solution or research direction
State the rule as a decision problem rather than a significance test: fix a margin on the scale the committee acts on, require the posterior probability that the contrast lies within it, and set the threshold from the error rate the pathway is willing to accept rather than from convention. Require the margin to be prespecified in the final scope, so that it cannot be chosen after the estimate is seen, which is the one procedural change the review recommends and no guidance imposes. Establish operating characteristics by simulation: for realistic cost-comparison evidence structures, compute how often a stated probability threshold declares similarity when a clinically meaningful difference exists, as a function of network sparsity, heterogeneity and the size of a transitivity violation. Extend the rule to population-adjusted comparisons, where the effective sample size after weighting rather than the nominal sample size determines what probability is attainable, so that a threshold set for an unadjusted comparison is not silently reused.

title: No rule says what proves similarity from an indirect comparison
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as a decision-methods gap distinct from reporting requirements, noting that a single proposed Bayesian framework does not establish an agreed or validated rule. The evidence is a single systematic review, but it covers the complete population of 41 relevant appraisals and records a published disagreement between two assessment groups.

title: No confidence rating covers a network that mixes designs
text: DEC-22 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: No confidence rating covers a network that mixes designs
text:
Statement
Joint synthesis of randomized trials and real-world data in one network is now done at scale, and the instrument the field uses to rate confidence in network estimates does not accept it. A network combining individual participant data from the Finnish and Swedish national registries with aggregate randomized evidence on antipsychotic relapse prevention published its joint estimates with no formal appraisal at all, stating that CINeMA does not currently accommodate observational studies. CINeMA rates six domains per network estimate (within-study bias, reporting bias, indirectness, imprecision, heterogeneity, incoherence) and computes them from the contribution matrix over a randomized design, so there is no way to report, per contrast, how much of the confidence rests on randomized and how much on non-randomized contributions, and no way to downgrade a contrast carried entirely by registry edges. The synthesis side is not the gap: design-adjusted, bias-adjusted and hierarchical models for combining randomized and non-randomized evidence in a network have been published since 2013 and are now used in applied reviews. What is missing is the appraisal side, namely a within-study bias domain appropriate to non-randomized comparisons, a per-contrast contribution split by design, and a rule for combining the two into one confidence rating. In the absence of that instrument, ratings are either omitted, as here, or produced by applying a randomized-evidence instrument outside its stated scope.

title: No confidence rating covers a network that mixes designs
text:
Why it is open
A rating for a mixed network needs a contribution split by design before it can weight the domains, and the contribution matrix is defined over a randomized design, so the appraisal instrument is blocked on the same provenance quantity that has not been generalized. The two designs also fail differently: within-study bias in a trial concerns randomization integrity, allocation concealment and blinding, while in a registry it concerns confounding, time-varying treatment assignment and outcome ascertainment, so the domains have no common scale that could be averaged into one judgment. Bias-adjustment models already absorb design differences into the estimate, which makes double counting a live risk, because downgrading for non-randomized contribution after the model has adjusted for it penalizes the same problem twice, and no rule states whether the rating applies to the naively pooled or the adjusted estimate. GRADE’s architecture assumes one body of evidence per comparison, so a per-contrast mixture of designs has no place in it. Meanwhile the analyses are being published regardless, so the omission carries no cost to anyone who publishes one.

title: No confidence rating covers a network that mixes designs
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Efthimiou et al. 2024, Efficacy and effectiveness of antipsychotics in schizophrenia: network meta-analyses combining evidence from randomised controlled trials and real-world data, The Lancet Psychiatry
Combines Finnish and Swedish registry individual participant data with aggregate randomized evidence in one network and states that no formal appraisal of the joint network was performed because CINeMA does not currently accommodate observational studies; the joint estimates are published without a rating.


Nikolakopoulou et al. 2020, CINeMA: An approach for assessing confidence in the results of a network meta-analysis, PLOS Medicine
Defines the six-domain per-estimate confidence framework and its scope, which is randomized evidence; it is the instrument the joint analysis could not use.


Papakonstantinou et al. 2020, CINeMA: Software for semiautomated assessment of the confidence in the results of network meta-analysis, Campbell Systematic Reviews
Ships the framework as software and fixes its input format, so admitting non-randomized studies is a specification change and not only a conceptual one.


Efthimiou et al. 2017, Combining randomized and non-randomized evidence in network meta-analysis, Statistics in Medicine
Sets out the design-adjustment, bias-adjustment and hierarchical options for synthesizing the two designs in one network, establishing that the estimation problem is solved while the appraisal problem is not.


Schmitz et al. 2013, Incorporating data from various trial designs into a mixed treatment comparison model, Statistics in Medicine
Earlier model for admitting several trial designs into one mixed treatment comparison, showing how long the estimation side has been available.


Jenkins et al. 2021, Methods for the inclusion of real-world evidence in network meta-analysis, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Reviews the available routes for adding real-world evidence to a network, none of which is paired with a confidence-rating instrument.


Hussein et al. 2023, Hierarchical network meta-analysis models for synthesis of evidence from randomised and non-randomised studies, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Develops hierarchical models that treat design as a level, giving the structure from which a design-split contribution could in principle be read.


Sterne et al. 2016, ROBINS-I: a tool for assessing risk of bias in non-randomised studies of interventions, BMJ
Supplies the study-level bias instrument for non-randomized studies that a mixed-design network framework would have to fold into a per-contrast rating.


Izcovich et al. 2023, A guide and pragmatic considerations for applying GRADE to network meta-analysis, BMJ
Current practical guidance for rating certainty in network meta-analysis; its architecture assumes randomized evidence per comparison and offers no route for a per-contrast mixture of designs.

title: No confidence rating covers a network that mixes designs
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the split before the instrument: extend contribution accounting so that each network estimate reports the share of information arriving from randomized and from non-randomized edges, which is a design-matrix computation once non-randomized studies are admitted as rows. Define the within-study bias domain by design, applying a randomized-trial tool to randomized contributions and ROBINS-I to non-randomized ones, then combine them by contribution weight, which is exactly what CINeMA already does within the randomized case. State the double-counting rule explicitly, so that a rating declares whether it applies to a naively pooled estimate or to a bias-adjusted one and, in the latter case, downgrades for residual rather than total design bias. Validate against networks where a randomized-only answer is also available, checking whether the rating separates contrasts on which joint and randomized-only estimates agree from those on which they diverge; that is the operating characteristic a confidence rating for mixed evidence would have to demonstrate.

title: No confidence rating covers a network that mixes designs
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it, noting that the application supplies direct evidence that CINeMA could not be used for a mixed randomized and observational network and that the joint estimates were published anyway. The evidence is a single application rather than a survey, but the statement it makes about the instrument’s scope is a property of the instrument, not of that analysis.

title: Borrowing intensity has no scale that spans sharing mechanisms
text: DEC-24 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: Borrowing intensity has no scale that spans sharing mechanisms
text:
Statement
Synthesis models that borrow strength across populations, treatments, outcomes or study designs each impose some degree of sharing between direct and indirect evidence, and the parameters that nominally control it (the power-prior exponent, a mixture weight, a commensurability parameter, a between-class standard deviation) sit on incommensurable scales. A classification of the field sorted the available devices into four core relationships (functional, exchangeability-based, prior-based and multivariate) and recorded that the few studies assessing the degree of sharing consider precision gains only, not the movement of the point estimate, which is what changes a recommendation. Part of this is now solved: three metrics (point-estimate divergence, precision increase and Kullback-Leibler divergence) have been standardized to run from zero at splitting to one at lumping and used to place power priors, commensurate priors and exchangeability models on a common axis in one case study, where odds ratios ranged from 0.55 to 0.90 and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios from about 16,000 to 52,000 pounds per quality-adjusted life year across sharing models. That same work shows why the problem is not closed: the strength of sharing imposed by a given model varies across the three metrics, so there is no single invariant number, and Kullback-Leibler divergence is asymmetric and interpretable only comparatively. The metrics are demonstrated on one adult-to-children borrowing problem, are not defined per contrast within a network, have no published operating characteristics, and nothing requires them to be reported. The direction of borrowing is not guaranteed either: multivariate synthesis can borrow weakness, and across 40 published networks the network estimate was less precise than the direct estimate for 104 of 181 comparisons (57.5%) informed by a single head-to-head study.

title: Borrowing intensity has no scale that spans sharing mechanisms
text:
Why it is open
Sharing intensity is a property of the model and the data together rather than of a parameter, so any scalar must be computed after fitting and depends on which functional of the posterior is being compared; point-estimate movement and precision gain can point in opposite directions and no argument privileges one of them. Anchoring at splitting and lumping fixes the endpoints but not the path between them, so two metrics can agree at zero and one and disagree everywhere in between, which is what is observed. Reparameterization invariance conflicts with interpretability: a divergence between posteriors is invariant but has no natural units, while a metric on an estimate has units but is scale-dependent. Sharing intensity also varies contrast by contrast with how much direct evidence each contrast carries, so a single model-level number is the wrong resolution for a decision that concerns one comparison. Finally, reporting the quantity can only make a modeling choice look more consequential than it did, so nothing pushes it into submissions.

title: Borrowing intensity has no scale that spans sharing mechanisms
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Nikolaidis et al. 2021, Classifying information-sharing methods, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Classifies information-sharing methods into four core relationships, states that the few studies assessing the degree of sharing typically consider only precision gains rather than movement of the point estimate, and records that multivariate methods sometimes borrow weakness rather than strength.


Nikolaidis et al. 2025, Methods for information-sharing in network meta-analysis: Implications for inference and policy, Research Synthesis Methods
Implements the range of sharing methods on an intravenous immunoglobulin sepsis case study and supplies three metrics standardized between splitting and lumping; shows odds ratios from 0.55 to 0.90 and cost-effectiveness ratios from about 16,000 to 52,000 pounds per quality-adjusted life year across models, and that a given model’s sharing strength changes with the metric used to read it.


Jackson et al. 2017, Borrowing of strength and study weights in multivariate and network meta-analysis, Statistical Methods in Medical Research
Defines the borrowing of strength statistic as the percentage reduction in uncertainty attributable to indirect evidence, the one borrowing measure that is already defined per contrast in a network.


Lin et al. 2019, Borrowing of strength from indirect evidence in 40 network meta-analyses, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Applies the borrowing of strength statistic to 40 networks and 915 comparisons: 484 (53%) had no direct evidence, and among 181 comparisons with one direct study, 104 (57.5%) had reduced rather than increased precision under the network model.


Chen and Ibrahim 2000, Power prior distributions for regression models, Statistical Science
Defines the power prior, whose exponent is the archetype of a control parameter that quantifies sharing only within its own family.


Hobbs et al. 2011, Hierarchical Commensurate and Power Prior Models for Adaptive Incorporation of Historical Information in Clinical Trials, Biometrics
Introduces the commensurability parameter, a second and incompatible control scale for the same underlying quantity.


Morita, Thall and Muller 2008, Determining the Effective Sample Size of a Parametric Prior, Biometrics
Gives prior effective sample size, the closest thing the field has to a common unit for borrowing; it is defined for a prior rather than for a synthesis model and is extended to conditionally independent hierarchical models in the companion paper (doi 10.1214/12-BA720).


Zhang et al. 2025, Prior Effective Sample Size When Borrowing on the Treatment Effect Scale, Statistics in Medicine
Extends prior effective sample size to borrowing on the treatment-effect scale, showing the unit is being generalized but remains tied to prior-based devices rather than covering exchangeability or multivariate sharing.


Achana et al. 2014, Network meta-analysis of multiple outcome measures accounting for borrowing of information across outcomes, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Borrows across outcomes through a multivariate structure, one of the mechanisms whose sharing intensity is not comparable with a prior-based device.


Ye et al. 2023, When we shouldn’t borrow information from an existing network of trials for planning a new trial, Frontiers in Pharmacology
Identifies conditions under which borrowing degrades rather than improves an answer, which is what a reported sharing intensity would let a reader check.

title: Borrowing intensity has no scale that spans sharing mechanisms
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Treat the splitting-to-lumping anchoring as settled and attack the disagreement between metrics directly: characterize analytically when point-estimate divergence and precision increase order two models differently, and report both rather than continuing to search for one scalar. Define the metrics per contrast rather than per model, since sharing intensity varies with how much direct evidence each contrast carries; the borrowing of strength statistic already does this for network borrowing and supplies the template. Give the metrics operating characteristics: simulate a known discrepancy between the direct and the borrowed source and report how each metric behaves as the discrepancy grows, so that a reported value tells a reader something about the risk being taken rather than only about the model that was fitted. Require the sharing metric alongside the estimate in any submission that uses a prior-based or exchangeability-based device, which is the reporting step that turns a diagnostic into a check.

title: Borrowing intensity has no scale that spans sharing mechanisms
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it on the condition that it be framed as the absence of a model-agnostic, contrast-level scale rather than the absence of any borrowing quantity. It is partially addressed because a 2025 case study supplies three standardized sharing metrics anchored at splitting and lumping, including one based on point-estimate movement; what remains is that the metrics disagree, are demonstrated once, are not defined per contrast, and are required by nobody.

title: Nothing predicts whether a network will beat separate comparisons
text: DEC-26 Confirmed open Medium-high priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Nothing predicts whether a network will beat separate comparisons
text:
Statement
The choice between a network meta-analysis and a set of separate comparisons against a common comparator is made on the theoretical ground that the network uses more data, not on any criterion evaluated before the models are fitted. The network can add nothing: in a 261-trial, 39,753-patient acute postoperative pain review covering 52 drug and dose combinations, the network and the placebo-anchored Cochrane estimates differed by an average of 0.04 number-needed-to-treat units, with no significant difference for almost all comparisons apart from those with small patient numbers or small effects. It can also make matters worse: across 40 published networks and 915 possible comparisons, 484 (53%) had no direct evidence at all, and among the 181 comparisons informed by a single head-to-head study the network estimate was less precise than the direct estimate for 104 (57.5%), with reliable gains appearing only where at least two head-to-head studies existed. What does not exist is a rule that takes observable features of the assembled evidence, such as the number of head-to-head studies per contrast, loop structure, homogeneity of outcome definition and trial quality, and predicts before fitting whether the network will change a decision. Nor is there a reporting convention requiring both estimates where it will not, although both empirical studies recommend one. The choice is consequential because the network carries transitivity and consistency assumptions across the whole graph that the separate anchored comparisons only partly incur.

title: Nothing predicts whether a network will beat separate comparisons
text:
Why it is open
The comparison has been answered retrospectively and neither answer transfers: the pain review attributes the agreement after the fact to stringent trial quality criteria and consistent outcome definitions, which are properties visible only once the review is complete. Borrowing of strength is computed from the fitted network, so the quantity that would drive a rule is available after the analysis rather than before it, and turning it into a prediction requires modeling what the network would produce from study counts and graph structure alone. The assumption side cannot be predicted at all, since transitivity and consistency are not testable in sample, so a criterion could at best price the precision half of the trade. Nothing penalizes running the more complex analysis, and only the network yields a ranking, so the incentive runs one way regardless of what the precision comparison would have shown.

title: Nothing predicts whether a network will beat separate comparisons
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Moore et al. 2018, Estimating relative efficacy in acute postoperative pain: network meta-analysis is consistent with indirect comparison to placebo alone, Pain
Compares a 261-trial, 39,753-patient network across 52 drug and dose combinations with the corresponding placebo-anchored analyses, finds an average difference of 0.04 number-needed-to-treat units, and concludes that neither this network nor other pain networks produced insights beyond what was already known.


Lin et al. 2019, Borrowing of strength from indirect evidence in 40 network meta-analyses, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Quantifies the incremental precision of network over pairwise analysis in 40 networks and 915 comparisons, finds reduced precision for 104 of 181 comparisons with a single direct study, and recommends that both analyses be reported routinely.


Jackson et al. 2017, Borrowing of strength and study weights in multivariate and network meta-analysis, Statistical Methods in Medical Research
Defines the borrowing of strength statistic that quantifies the gain a network delivers over direct evidence, the quantity a prospective criterion would have to predict.


Caldwell, Ades and Higgins 2005, Simultaneous comparison of multiple treatments: combining direct and indirect evidence, BMJ
Makes the standing theoretical case for the network over separate comparisons, which is the argument currently used in place of a criterion.


Song et al. 2009, Methodological problems in the use of indirect comparisons for evaluating healthcare interventions: survey of published systematic reviews, BMJ
Surveys how indirect comparisons are used and misused, establishing that the choice between synthesis strategies is made without a stated rule.


Thom et al. 2019, Automated methods to test connectedness and quantify indirectness of evidence in network meta-analysis, Research Synthesis Methods
Supplies connectedness tests and indirectness measures computable from the graph before any effect model is fitted, which are the natural inputs to a prospective criterion.


Ye et al. 2023, When we shouldn’t borrow information from an existing network of trials for planning a new trial, Frontiers in Pharmacology
Identifies conditions under which borrowing from a network is inappropriate, the closest existing attempt at a prospective rule, posed for trial planning rather than for choosing the analysis.


Shourick and Garbayo-Salmons 2026, A tale of two meta-analyses: Similarity, consistency and avoiding overinterpretation in network meta-analysis, Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology
Shows two syntheses of the same evidence reaching different presentations, illustrating that the analysis choice is consequential even where the underlying trials are fixed.

title: Nothing predicts whether a network will beat separate comparisons
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the predictor from quantities available before fitting: direct-study counts per contrast, path lengths, the indirectness measures already computable from the graph, and a prior on heterogeneity, then calibrate it against realized borrowing of strength in a database of published networks such as nmadb. Score the criterion on decision change rather than on precision: for each network in the calibration set, record whether the network and the anchored analysis would have produced the same recommendation, and ask whether the pre-fit features predict that. Make the fallback explicit, so that where the predicted gain is small a report must show both estimates, which is what both empirical studies recommend and no guidance requires. Keep the assumption side separate, since a criterion that predicts a precision gain says nothing about whether transitivity holds; preferring the network should require both a predicted gain and an argument for the assumption, reported as two conditions rather than one.

title: Nothing predicts whether a network will beat separate comparisons
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it, noting that the cited review is a strong counterexample to the assumption that a full network necessarily adds decision-relevant information over a common-comparator analysis. The evidence is two empirical studies, both retrospective; neither attempts a prospective criterion and both recommend only that the two analyses be reported side by side.

title: No inference is reported for an estimated optimal-treatment boundary
text: DEC-28 Confirmed open High priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: No inference is reported for an estimated optimal-treatment boundary
text:
Statement
When an effect measure is non-collapsible and effect modification is present, the population-average conditional and population-average marginal estimands can rank treatments oppositely; a worked logistic example gives conditional log odds ratios of -4 and -3 favoring one treatment while the marginal effects of -2.36 and -2.49 favor another, so deciding on the marginal effect assigns the inferior treatment to 75% of the population. The published resolution is to stratify the decision: boundaries between optimal treatment choices can be determined mathematically in the L-dimensional effect-modifier space, and cut-points are read off plots of fitted individual-level effects. Both the covariate that defines the partition and the location of the cut-point are therefore functions of estimated interaction coefficients, yet the resulting subgroup recommendation is issued as a point statement. No population-adjustment implementation reports a posterior or bootstrap distribution over the boundary, a probability that a given covariate profile lies on the recommended side of it, or subgroup-specific contrast intervals that account for the partition having been estimated from the same data. Applied work inherits the omission: a two-stage network meta-regression prediction model reports which treatment is preferable for high-risk and for low-risk patients, and a cost-effectiveness model built on risk-specific network estimates reports that one drug carries the higher net monetary benefit up to a baseline risk of 55% after which another takes over, neither with an interval on where the switch occurs. The missing object is inference on a partition rather than on a contrast, and the two are not interchangeable: a narrow interval on every contrast is compatible with a boundary that could sit almost anywhere.

title: No inference is reported for an estimated optimal-treatment boundary
text:
Why it is open
The optimal-treatment partition is defined by an argmax over treatments, so the parameters indexing it are nonregular wherever two treatments are close, and standard bootstrap and Taylor-series arguments break down exactly at the boundary, which is the region the decision turns on. The remedies developed for that nonregularity live in the single-dataset dynamic-regime literature and have never been carried into evidence synthesis, where the interaction coefficients come from a network rather than from one trial. Selection compounds it: which covariate defines the partition is chosen by comparing induced variation in individual effects, subgroup-detection analyses have low power and invite spurious findings when many candidate factors are screened, and reporting the cut-point the same data produced leaves any subgroup interval too narrow. In a network the interaction is estimated partly from across-study variation, which is ecologically confounded, so part of the boundary’s error is not sampling error at all and will not show up in a posterior width. Only multilevel network meta-regression produces the individual-level event probabilities the boundary needs; matching-adjusted indirect comparison and simulated treatment comparison return population averages, so for most submitted analyses the object cannot be computed at all.

title: No inference is reported for an estimated optimal-treatment boundary
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Proves that population-average conditional and marginal estimands can rank treatments oppositely, and only when individual treatment effects cross within the population; recommends treating rank conflict as a signal to stratify the decision and states that boundaries between optimal choices can be determined mathematically in the effect-modifier space, with no uncertainty statement attached to them.


Phillippo et al. 2020, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
Multilevel network meta-regression, the only population-adjustment method producing individual-level predicted probabilities for an arbitrary target population and therefore the only one whose posterior could be turned into a distribution over the boundary; its reported output object is a treatment effect, not a partition.


Chalkou et al. 2021, Statistics in Medicine
Two-stage model combining a prognostic baseline risk score with network meta-regression to give risk-specific treatment effects; concludes that the relapse-minimizing treatment differs between high-risk and low-risk patients without an interval on where the preference changes.


Hamza et al. 2026, Value in Health
Carries risk-specific network meta-regression effects into a cost-effectiveness model, reporting incremental cost-effectiveness ratios across baseline risk quintiles and a net monetary benefit crossing point at a baseline risk of 55%; the crossing point is reported as a point estimate.


Chakraborty, Laber and Zhao 2013, Biometrics
Adaptive m-out-of-n bootstrap giving asymptotically correct confidence sets for the parameters indexing an optimal treatment regime under the nonsmoothness that argmax operations create; the closest available inference technology, built for single-study data.


Luedtke and van der Laan 2016, Annals of Statistics
Inference for the mean outcome under a possibly non-unique optimal treatment strategy, addressing the nonregularity that arises when treatments are effectively tied over a region of covariate space.


Foster, Taylor and Ruberg 2011, Statistics in Medicine
Virtual Twins subgroup identification with cross-validated and bootstrap bias-corrected estimates of the enhanced-effect subgroup; the single-trial analogue of correcting a subgroup effect for the search that found it.

title: No inference is reported for an estimated optimal-treatment boundary
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define the estimand before the estimator: the optimal-treatment partition as a functional of the fitted interaction vector, and for each covariate profile the posterior probability that a named treatment is optimal, which is smooth even where the argmax is not and can be mapped over a declared target population directly from existing multilevel network meta-regression draws. Report that probability map alongside any cut-point, with a pointwise credible band obtained by recomputing the boundary in every posterior draw, and state which part of its variability comes from within-study and which from across-study interaction estimation. Score the procedure in a simulation crossing modifier strength, overlap and network topology, using the probability of assigning the wrong treatment at profiles near the boundary and the coverage of subgroup contrast intervals when the same data chose the partition. For frequentist population adjustment, port the m-out-of-n bootstrap to the boundary parameters and check whether its coverage survives the extra layer of target-population standardization. Then make it a reporting requirement, so that a stratified recommendation cannot be published as a bare cut-point.

title: No inference is reported for an estimated optimal-treatment boundary
text:
Our study

The covariate value at which the better treatment changes is often not estimable as a point, and borrowed precision can make its interval wrong
The question put to it. Is the covariate boundary between two treatments’ optimality well enough determined at achievable interaction precision to report as a point, and do standard intervals for it hold when interaction information comes partly from between-trial variation?
What it found. No. From one trial of 400 patients at a moderate interaction the exact (Fieller) 95% confidence set for the boundary was unbounded in 66% to 69% of replicates, while the delta-method interval was always finite and covered as little as 0.86 at the weakest interaction. Borrowing interaction precision from aggregate trials at different covariate means (81% of the precision) made the sets bounded, but a between-trial ecological term of 0.1 cut their coverage to 0.68 to 0.70 for a boundary away from the trials’ mean covariate value. Treating by the point estimate at the moderate interaction lost 31% to 95% of the value of individualized treatment with one trial.
Results.

Fieller sets bounded from one trial: 84% to 85% at interaction 0.3, 31% to 34% at 0.15, 7% to 9% at 0.05.
The pointwise probability that A is better, thresholded at 0.5, is the plug-in rule; its (0.025, 0.975) region is the Fieller set, so it changes the report, not the decision.
With the ecological term, combined-estimator coverage 0.68 to 0.70 at boundary 1.5 and 0.92 to 0.93 at 0.5; individual-trial coverage 0.95.
At interaction 0.05, treating by the estimated boundary did worse than treating everyone with the better treatment on average (regret share up to 3.6).

Design.

Estimand

The boundary x* = -delta/beta between two treatments’ optimality, and regret of treating by its estimate

Methods compared

plug-in cut-point, delta-method interval, Fieller confidence set, pointwise optimality probability

Data-generating mechanism

One individual-data trial plus five aggregate trials; interaction 0.3, 0.15 or 0.05, two boundary positions, an ecological term absent or present; within-trial and combined estimators; delta-method and Fieller intervals, regret and the pointwise optimality map. 12 cells, 2000 replicates each.

Replicates

2000 per cell, 12 cells, two estimators each


What this does not answer. Two treatments and one modifier; no modifier selection; closed-form frequentist estimators rather than ML-NMR; declared linear ecological term. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: ROB-MEN reliability is unmeasured and CINeMA agreement collapses on large networks
text: DEC-30 Partially addressed Medium-high priority Established Tractability 4/5

title: ROB-MEN reliability is unmeasured and CINeMA agreement collapses on large networks
text:
Statement
CINeMA and ROB-MEN attach graded labels to individual network estimates, confidence in the result and risk of bias due to missing evidence respectively, and those labels are carried into guidelines and appraisals as if they were properties of the evidence. The ROB-MEN guidance states that the reproducibility of CINeMA and ROB-MEN assessments has not been studied and that interrater agreement work would be informative. For CINeMA that has since been partly answered: 13 assessors applying both CINeMA and GRADE to four networks of differing size and complexity produced interrater agreement, measured by Gwet’s AC, between 0.02 and 0.73 for CINeMA against 0.49 to 0.70 for GRADE, with the 0.02 falling on the largest and most complex network, while concordance between the two approaches fell from 1 to 0.42 as the number of comparisons and the share of indirect evidence rose. Nothing comparable exists for ROB-MEN, whose judgment-based inputs are not incidental: the assessor sets the suspected direction of bias for each comparison, decides what percentage contribution from suspect evidence counts as substantial (set at 15% by user choice in the guidance paper’s own case study), and reads a difference between network meta-analysis and network meta-regression estimates as evidence of small-study effects, while the quantitative across-study assessment needs 10 studies per comparison and was therefore unavailable for all 15 comparisons of that example. Because both instruments compute the final label algorithmically from those inputs, the output looks objective while inheriting whatever variability sits upstream, and neither reports how far its label would move if an input were set differently. What is missing is a reliability estimate for ROB-MEN, a replication of the CINeMA result over more networks and assessors, and any evidence that either label is stable enough to be treated as a property of the evidence rather than of the assessor. The instrument landscape has since widened without closing the question: a 2026 map counts 22 appraisal instruments for network meta-analysis, 11 of them NMA-specific, and finds measurement-property data reported for only 9, while the RoB NMA tool published in 2025 reports no reliability estimate at all beyond a pilot completion time.

title: ROB-MEN reliability is unmeasured and CINeMA agreement collapses on large networks
text:
Why it is open
Measuring reliability requires a designed duplicate-assessment study across multiple assessors and multiple networks, it produces no new method, and the one study that exists needed 16 authors and 150 to 481 minutes of assessor time per network per tool. That study also shows a single summary agreement coefficient will not settle the question, since agreement was acceptable on small networks and collapsed on the largest, so any replacement design has to vary network size, connectivity and share of indirect evidence deliberately. ROB-MEN is harder to study than CINeMA because its most consequential input is unavailable in most real networks: funnel plots and small-study-effect tests need 10 studies per comparison, so in typical networks the across-study assessment reduces to unanchored qualitative judgment. ROB-MEN also consumes a percentage contribution matrix whose construction is itself contested, so its reliability cannot be separated from a definitional choice the field has not settled. Tool developers have little incentive to run a study that can only reduce confidence in their own instrument, and reliability measurement of an appraisal tool is not treated as a fundable research output.

title: ROB-MEN reliability is unmeasured and CINeMA agreement collapses on large networks
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Chiocchia, Holloway and Salanti 2023, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Guidance paper for the ROB-MEN web application; documents the judgment-based inputs, sets the substantial-contribution threshold at 15% by user choice in its worked example, reports no funnel plot or small-study-effect test was applicable to any comparison there, and states that reproducibility of CINeMA and ROB-MEN has not been studied.


Chiocchia et al. 2021, BMC Medicine
The ROB-MEN framework itself: per-comparison within-study and across-study judgments combined with the contribution matrix into a risk-of-bias label for every network estimate.


Nikolakopoulou et al. 2020, PLoS Medicine
CINeMA: the domain framework producing per-comparison confidence ratings, weighting study-level judgments by contribution.


Minozzi et al. 2025, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Thirteen assessors applied GRADE and CINeMA to four networks chosen for differing size and complexity; reports interrater agreement of 0.02 to 0.73 for CINeMA and 0.49 to 0.70 for GRADE by Gwet’s AC, overall concordance between approaches from 1 to 0.42, and median assessment times of 150 to 330 minutes for CINeMA and 160 to 481 for GRADE. Covers CINeMA, not ROB-MEN.


Battain et al. 2026, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Companion qualitative survey of the same assessors: CINeMA’s automation made application fast but reduced understanding of how the conclusion was reached, GRADE was judged transparent but slow and subjective, and both were said to need further training before correct use.


Noori et al. 2024, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Applies GRADE and CINeMA to the same opioid network: ratings differed for 36 of 105 pain-relief comparisons and 11 of 66 function comparisons, all by one level, with CINeMA typically lower because of transitivity and heterogeneity assessment. Measures agreement between approaches, not between assessors.


Minozzi et al. 2020, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Interrater reliability study of RoB 2, reporting low agreement and application difficulties; the design template that a ROB-MEN reliability study would follow.


Minozzi et al. 2019, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Interrater reliability of ROBINS-I across five raters and 31 studies, with only slight agreement on the overall judgment and a recommendation for calibration exercises and intensive training; shows how far an instrument’s labels can depend on who applies them.


Lunny et al. 2025, BMJ
publishes the RoB NMA tool, a 17-item instrument covering network geometry and node definition, effect modifiers and transitivity, and statistical synthesis including multi-arm handling, heterogeneity assumptions, direct-versus-indirect conflict and selective reporting; its only reported operating characteristic is a pilot completion time of 79 minutes (range 30 to 150), so it inherits the reliability question this entry describes rather than answering it


Mondragon et al. 2026, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
maps 22 appraisal instruments applicable to network meta-analysis, 11 of them NMA-specific, and finds that only 9 of the 22 report any measurement-property data

title: ROB-MEN reliability is unmeasured and CINeMA agreement collapses on large networks
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Run for ROB-MEN what has been run for CINeMA: a duplicate-assessment study in which independent assessors label the same networks, powered to estimate agreement separately for the within-study component, the across-study component and the overall label, and deliberately sampling networks that do and do not reach 10 studies per comparison. Report agreement as a function of network size, connectivity and share of indirect evidence rather than as a single coefficient, since the CINeMA result shows the answer is not constant across networks. Instrument both applications to emit their own sensitivity: given an assessor’s inputs, each can recompute the label over a grid of substantial-contribution thresholds and suspected bias directions and report which labels are stable, at essentially no extra computational cost. Where agreement is poor because assessors differ, the response is calibration exercises and worked training examples before application, as recommended after the ROBINS-I study; where it is poor because the input is unavailable, the honest output is an explicit no-information label rather than a judgment.

title: ROB-MEN reliability is unmeasured and CINeMA agreement collapses on large networks
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this from the ROB-MEN guidance paper’s own statement that reproducibility is unstudied, and the reviewer accepted it as distinct from developing a population-adjustment credibility instrument or validating numeric diagnostics. It is not confirmed-open because a 13-assessor study has since measured CINeMA’s interrater reliability; the unmeasured half is ROB-MEN, and the CINeMA result itself rests on four networks.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied full-text reading.

prior-work-added

added 2 citations and widened the statement to the current instrument landscape Surfaced while assessing a labeller-reported absence, ‘no validated instrument appraises NMA conduct’, which was rejected as resolved by the RoB NMA tool. The residue of that candidate, that reliability is reported for a minority of instruments, is this entry’s problem, so the tool and the instrument map belong here as prior work. Previously: “CINeMA and ROB-MEN attach graded labels to individual network estimates, confidence in the result and risk of bias due to missing evidence respectively, and those labels are carried into guidelines and appraisals as if they were properties of the evidence. The ROB-MEN guidance states that the reproducibility of CINeMA and ROB-MEN assessments has not been studied and that interrater agreement work would be informative. For CINeMA that has since been partly answered: 13 assessors applying both CINeMA and GRADE to four networks of differing size and complexity produced interrater agreement, measu”
