title: Non-collapsible marginal effects are not portable across populations
text:
Statement
Odds ratios and hazard ratios can vary across populations even without confounding, so the shared effect modifier assumption alone does not make a marginal effect portable to an arbitrary population. The result is not new and does not belong to the citation the source gave it: Remiro-Azocar (doi:10.1002/sim.10111) established the stronger result that under non-collapsibility even purely prognostic variables shift the marginal effect, Phillippo et al. 2021 (doi:10.1002/sim.8965) had already noted that marginal effects are less transportable than population-average conditional ones, and Chandler and Ishak (arxiv:2602.17041) restate it inside an explicit two-step transportability framing for PAIC. Collapsibility is also not the same as transportability: a risk difference or an RMST difference marginalizes cleanly but still varies across populations when effects are heterogeneous, and a standardized risk is a target-specific absolute quantity rather than a treatment-effect scale.

title: Non-collapsible marginal effects are not portable across populations
text:
Why it is open
Non-collapsibility is a property of the effect measure rather than a bias, so it cannot be removed by better adjustment, better models or larger samples. An assumption about effect modification of the conditional contrast does not license moving the marginal contrast, because the marginal effect depends on the covariate distribution it is averaged over, and under non-collapsibility even purely prognostic variables move it. What remains open is propagation rather than theory: the formal results are published and target-specific standardization is implemented, but reporting conventions and HTA submission scales still carry marginal odds ratios and hazard ratios without a population index. Because the same number is valid in its own population and invalid in the target, no diagnostic run on the source analysis reveals the error.

title: Non-collapsible marginal effects are not portable across populations
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Remiro-Azocar 2024, Transportability of model-based estimands in evidence synthesis, Statistics in Medicine 43(22):4217-4249
Establishes that for non-collapsible measures purely prognostic variables that are not determinants of treatment response can modify marginal effects even under individual-level treatment effect homogeneity, which is why an assumption about effect modifiers cannot suffice for portability. This is the work that establishes the entry’s central result.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades and Welton 2021, Target estimands for efficient decision making: Response to comments on Assessing the performance of population adjustment methods for anchored indirect comparisons: A simulation study, Statistics in Medicine
States that marginal population-average treatment effects depend more strongly on the population of interest than population-average conditional effects and are less generalizable as a result, foreshadowing the formal result by three years.


Chandler and Ishak 2026, Reframing Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons as a Transportability Problem
Restates that the shared effect modifier assumption alone does not guarantee direct transportability of marginal effects, inside an explicit two-step transportability framing for PAIC. It restates rather than establishes the result.


Jiang et al. 2025, A critical assessment of matching-adjusted indirect comparisons in relation to target populations, Research Synthesis Methods
Documents the population dependence of MAIC results in relation to target populations.


multinma: Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Individual and Aggregate Data (R package)
Implements target-population marginal-effect calculation, with marginal_effects() defaulting to a risk difference, so the standardization step is available and the collapsible default is already in software.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Distinguishes a conditional profile contrast from a marginal population-standardized effect in its documentation, stating that the returned value is the conditional contrast at the covariate profile rather than the marginal effect standardized over a population. The labeling is correct; the marginal path is absent.

title: Non-collapsible marginal effects are not portable across populations
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Index every marginal estimand by the population it is defined in and standardize explicitly to a named target covariate law before any decision use, rather than assuming scale invariance. Directly collapsible contrasts make that standardization easier, so prefer them where the decision permits, but do not present them as empirically constant across populations, since the target still has to be declared. The concrete work is in outputs rather than derivations: get the population index into reporting templates and into packages that do not yet separate a conditional profile contrast from a population-standardized marginal effect, as in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, where at commit 9d150e9 the cML-NMR path returns only the conditional contrast at a covariate profile.

title: Non-collapsible marginal effects are not portable across populations
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work and the entry names which part. The source additionally attributed the claim to the wrong work, which is corrected in the entry.
The source said. “Odds ratios and hazard ratios can vary across populations even in the absence of confounding, so a marginal effect estimated in one population is not automatically transportable to another. The shared-effect-modifier assumption, routinely invoked to justify population adjustment, does not by itself make non-collapsible marginal effects portable to an arbitrary population.”
What was wrong with it. The source credited Chandler and Ishak (arxiv:2602.17041) with establishing that shared effect modification does not make non-collapsible marginal effects portable; the literature auditor found the result established two years earlier by Remiro-Azocar (doi:10.1002/sim.10111) and foreshadowed by Phillippo et al. 2021 (doi:10.1002/sim.8965), and found the claim that it has not reached software defaults false, since multinma’s marginal_effects() defaults to a risk difference. GPT-5.6 Sol separately struck the equation of collapsibility with portability and the treatment of a standardized risk as an effect scale.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): Chandler & Ishak 2026 does say what is attributed (‘SEMA alone does not guarantee direct transportability of marginal treatment effects’; non-collapsible marginal effects ‘are not directly transportable, even when SEMA holds’), so claims 1-3, 5 and 6 hold. Claim 4 does not: Chandler & Ishak are not the work that establishes this. Remiro-Azocar, Statistics in Medicine 43(22):4217-4249 (2024) establishes a strictly stronger result two years earlier - for non-collapsible measures even purely prognostic variables that are not determinants of treatment response modify marginal effects - which is exactly why an assumption about effect modifiers cannot suffice. Earlier still, Phillippo, Dias, Ades & Welton (Stat Med 2021) wrote that marginal effects ‘depend more strongly on the population of interest than the population-average conditional treatment effects, and are less generalizable/transportable as a result’. The why_open assertion that the result ‘has not propagated into guidance, software defaults’ is also wrong at the software level: multinma’s marginal_effects() defaults to mtype = ‘difference’, a collapsible absolute scale. Status stays open because these are formalizations of an unfixable property. codex dissented (overstated): C1-C3 are mathematically correct: a marginal odds ratio or hazard-ratio projection can change with baseline risk, prognostic covariate distribution, or follow-up composition despite no confounding and a stable conditional treatment parameter. C4 is a priority-attribution claim outside this assigned technical lens; the result is an established consequence of non-collapsibility, not something that can be credited from technical truth alone. C5 is sloppy: risk differences and RMST differences are collapsible linear contrasts, but collapsibility neither guarantees transportability under effect modification nor makes them universally preferable; a standardized risk is target-specific and is not itself a treatment-effect scale. C6 should require a named target population, and numerical standardization needs a target covariate or outcome law, but the abstract marginal estimand need not encode one particular covariate representation. Target-specific standardization is established and implemented, so the management problem is partly solved; no population-free marginal OR or HR exists.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

It does not show that target-specific standardization is unavailable or that a population-free marginal odds ratio or hazard ratio can be recovered. title: Non-collapsible marginal effects are not portable across populations
section: How the evidence falls in time
text:
How the evidence falls in time
3 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2025 to 2026. The most recent paper to touch this reports progress on it, and every paper calling it open is older.
Does the later work answer the earlier work? Put to an independent reviewer with the older and newer claims side by side, it judged that the later work answers a component of it, leaving a named part (medium confidence). Chandler and Ishak give the requested general transportability classification for the principal non-collapsible PAIC measures, and ML-UMR quantifies the consequence even without effect modification. Neither makes marginal odds ratios or hazard ratios portable across populations, so the practical problem survives despite the theoretical question being substantially clarified. What remains: A method for producing decision-relevant portable effects, or for handling the population dependence in practice, remains; the later work mainly characterizes and quantifies the limitation.

title: Nothing requires declaring whether a result is marginal or conditional
text: EST-05 Overstated Very high priority Promising

title: Nothing requires declaring whether a result is marginal or conditional
text:
Statement
No journal or HTA template requires an analysis to declare all four of target population, target estimand, effect scale, and whether the result is marginal or conditional; the marginal versus conditional element in particular is nowhere mandated. Two of the four are already required for NICE submissions: NICE DSU TSD18 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) requires the target population to be stated explicitly and requires indirect comparisons to be carried out on the linear predictor scale. A published PAIC framework also codifies definition of the comparison as an estimand as its first element (Ishak et al. 2025, doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1), and Phillippo et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2) give recommendations for reporting marginal and conditional estimands in the decision target population, so what is missing is a single enforcement point rather than a standard to enforce. Population-superscripted notation likewise already appears in the methods literature, including TSD18; what has not happened is its adoption in applied reports.

title: Nothing requires declaring whether a result is marginal or conditional
text:
Why it is open
The requirements that exist are scattered across a technical support document, a framework paper and a recommendations paper, so there is no one field where a reviewer checks all four and no error signal when one is missing; the marginal versus conditional element has recommendations behind it but no template that demands it. Writing the declaration forces the analyst to fix the target population before seeing the data, which conflicts with the current practice of choosing the adjustment set from whatever the comparator publication reported. Because nothing pushes the population into the name of the estimand in applied reports, two numerically different quantities are published under one label and inherited unlabeled by appraisal templates and economic models. The mismatch changes the number rather than breaking the analysis, so nothing forces the field to correct itself.

title: Nothing requires declaring whether a result is marginal or conditional
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (NICE DSU TSD18)
Requires the target population to be stated explicitly and requires indirect comparisons to be carried out on the linear predictor scale with the usual link functions, covering two of the four declaration elements for NICE submissions, and uses population-indexed estimand notation. It does not require a marginal versus conditional declaration.


Ishak et al. 2025, A Framework for Reliable, Transparent, and Reproducible Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons, PharmacoEconomics
Six-element PAIC reporting and risk-of-bias framework whose first element is definition of the comparison of interest in terms of an estimand. It is a published framework rather than a mandated field in journal or submission templates, and it does not impose population-indexed notation.


Phillippo, Remiro-Azocar, Heath, Baio, Dias, Ades and Welton 2025, Effect modification and non-collapsibility together may lead to conflicting treatment decisions, Research Synthesis Methods
Provides published recommendations for declaring and jointly reporting marginal and conditional estimands in the decision target population, the element TSD18 does not cover.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Requires a target profile for effect-modified cML-NMR output and prints the result as a conditional effect at that profile, stating that relative effects from a model with effect modifiers are population-specific. Partial enforcement of the declaration inside one unreleased package.

title: Nothing requires declaring whether a result is marginal or conditional
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Assemble the declaration from the pieces that exist rather than writing a new standard: TSD18 fixes target population and scale, Ishak et al. 2025 supply a PAIC framework whose first element is estimand definition, and Phillippo et al. 2025 supply the marginal versus conditional recommendation, so the work is binding them into one mandatory field in analysis plans, journal templates and submission templates. Require every reported contrast to identify its population, by superscript or by an equally explicit structured field, since the point is unambiguous identification rather than one notation. Forbid silent reinterpretation of a conditional effect as a marginal one, or of a comparator-trial effect as a decision-target effect, and treat software that already enforces part of this, such as cpaic requiring a target profile for effect-modified cML-NMR output, as a pattern to generalize rather than as a finished solution; cpaic is an unreleased development package on GitHub and is not installable from CRAN.

title: Nothing requires declaring whether a result is marginal or conditional
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. No journal or HTA template requires a four-part declaration; in particular nothing requires an analysis to state whether its result is marginal or conditional, even though NICE DSU TSD18 has required an explicit target population and a pre-specified linear-predictor scale since 2016, and population-superscripted notation already exists in the methods literature without being adopted in applied reports.
The source titled this. “No required estimand declaration or population-indexed notation” The title says population-indexed notation is missing, but the audit found it already used in TSD 18 and the methods literature; only applied adoption is absent.
The source said. “Nothing in the publication or submission pipeline requires an analysis to declare its target population, target estimand, effect scale, and whether the result is marginal or conditional, so the literature continues to tolerate analyses that switch interpretations without admitting it. The report also requires population-indexed notation of the form Delta_AB^{P2} versus Delta_AB^{P*}, and asserts that a report should never call both quantities simply the treatment effect.”
What was wrong with it. The claim was unattributed in the source and is now sourced, and both auditors judged it overstated: the literature auditor found that NICE DSU TSD18 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) already requires an explicit target population and a pre-specified linear-predictor scale and already uses population-indexed notation, and that Phillippo et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2) supplies the marginal versus conditional recommendations TSD18 does not cover. A PAIC reporting and risk-of-bias framework established elsewhere in this audit, Ishak et al. 2025 (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1), makes definition of the comparison as an estimand its first element. GPT-5.6 Sol added that population-superscripted notation is a useful convention rather than a mathematical necessity, since explicit prose or structured fields identify the population equally well.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

closure-upheld

5 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors’ reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. The new findings reinforce the closure’s residual: no cited checklist or decision-facing framework requires declaration of marginal versus conditional status, and estimand uptake in evidence synthesis remains limited. They also independently confirm the closure’s qualification that target population and effect scale have existing reporting requirements or checklist items. The 2026 JCA framework is later than some closure evidence, but it does not supersede or contradict TSD18’s requirements and merely lacks the missing enforcement element already identified. Thus the current statement correctly distinguishes scattered partial standards from the absent single four-part mandate. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening

6 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries overstated Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit’s closure needs the closure’s own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. Also SOURCE-A-UNSOURCED. Reading the full text of Phillippo et al. 2018 Med Decis Making (the published NICE DSU TSD18) contradicts the framing that ‘nothing in the publication or submission pipeline requires an analysis to declare its target population … [and] effect scale’. Recommendation 6 requires the target population to be explicitly stated; Recommendation 5 requires the scale: ‘Indirect comparisons should be carried out on the linear predictor scale, with the same link functions that are usually employed for those outcomes.’ TSD18 is the reference document for NICE submissions, so an enforcement point exists for two of the four declaration elements. That same paper already uses population-indexed notation of exactly the requested form, writing estimands with a population superscript and stating the transport relation between two populations P and Q, so ‘no established standard uses source-target notation’ is too strong for the methodological literature even if true of applied reports. What genuinely remains undeclared and unenforced is the marginal-versus-conditional element; Phillippo et al. 2025 RSM is the closest thing to a normative recommendation there. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740: Supplies an existing enforcement point for two of the four declaration elements (target population, effect scale) and already uses population-indexed estimand notation.. Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2: Provides published recommendations for declaring and jointly reporting marginal and conditional estimands in the decision target population, the element TSD18 does not cover..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 is a placeholder. C2, C3, C5, C6, C9, and C10 are claims about current practice, prevalence, or standards that cannot be established from technical correctness alone. C4 is a sound minimum declaration, although a full estimand also needs outcome, treatment conditions, time horizon, and handling of intercurrent events where relevant. C7 is useful notation, not a mathematical necessity; equally explicit prose or structured fields can identify the population. C8 is a sound communication rule unless the quantities have been shown to coincide and that fact is stated. The absolute statement that nothing in the pipeline requires target or scale declaration is false, and cpaic itself requires a target for effect-modified cML-NMR output and labels it as conditional. Existing guidance and package behavior partly solve declaration; universal four-part enforcement and routine source-target notation remain operational issues. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740: Requires explicit target-population declaration and specifies the synthesis scale, covering two of the proposed four fields.. Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2: Supplies an explicit framework for distinguishing and reporting marginal and conditional estimands.. title: Reported target moments are treated as known constants
text:
Statement
Reported target-population means and standard deviations are estimates, and standard PAIC estimators condition on them as fixed inputs, so the reported interval omits that variability whenever the inference is to a superpopulation rather than to the realized finite target sample. The first of the four uncertainty sources the source bundles together has been solved, though outside the ITC literature: Sheng, Sun and Huang (arxiv:2603.02474) give asymptotic normality and a variance estimator for an entropy-balancing transport estimator, which is MAIC-equivalent, that accounts for uncertainty in covariate summaries, and Chen, Chen and Yu (doi:10.1002/sim.70358) construct resampling-based perturbation intervals for a target effect estimated from summary-level target information. The other three sources are not sampling error and do not belong in the same interval: uncertainty in reconstructed correlations is model uncertainty, inclusion-criteria ambiguity is estimand ambiguity, and secular change is a transport bias over time. The claim that no software propagates target-moment uncertainty was verified only for cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, where at commit 9d150e9 cmaic() bootstraps IPD patients while holding target means and standard deviations fixed.

title: Reported target moments are treated as known constants
text:
Why it is open
Conditioning on published summaries as if exact omits variability from the reported interval in a way no convergence diagnostic reveals, and the fix is not a bootstrap of the source IPD, which carries no information about how the target summaries were estimated. Propagating that uncertainty needs target microdata, a sampling design, or at least the covariance or influence information behind the published summaries, which aggregate publications rarely provide. Two of the four listed sources have no conventional variance representation at all, so they need declared alternative estimands or explicit bias models rather than a wider interval. The solutions that do exist sit in the transportability literature and have not been carried into PAIC estimators or packages, which still take reported moments as given.

title: Reported target moments are treated as known constants
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Sheng, Sun and Huang 2026, Transportable inference using target population summary statistics under covariate shift
Establishes asymptotic normality for the entropy balancing estimator, which is MAIC-equivalent, and proposes a variance estimator that accounts for uncertainty in covariate summaries, plus a second method handling covariate shift and summary uncertainty together. It is framed as transportability rather than PAIC and has not been carried into ITC software.


Chen, Chen and Yu 2026, Confidence Interval Construction for Causally Generalized Estimates With Target Sample Summary Information, Statistics in Medicine 45(1-2):e70358
Proposes a resampling-based perturbation method for constructing confidence intervals for an estimated target average treatment effect using summary-level target information with entropy balancing weights.


Gao, Heath and Baio 2025, Regression augmented weighting adjustment for indirect comparisons in health decision modelling (G-MAIC), Research Synthesis Methods
Uses Bayesian bootstrap to propagate the uncertainty of population-adjusted estimates, but treats the reported comparator summaries as fixed balancing targets, so it addresses uncertainty from the matching process rather than sampling error in the target moments.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
At commit 9d150e9, cmaic() holds target means and standard deviations fixed while bootstrapping only IPD patients, cstc() centers on fixed target means, and cmlnmr() builds fixed integration points from aggregate means, standard deviations and a supplied or borrowed correlation. This confirms the conditioning behavior in one unreleased package rather than across all PAIC software.

title: Reported target moments are treated as known constants
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Port the existing target-summary variance results into PAIC rather than deriving them again: the entropy-balancing variance estimator and the perturbation interval both apply to MAIC-equivalent weighting, so the work is validation under PAIC conditions and implementation in packages that currently hold target moments fixed. A Bayesian formulation placing a distribution over the target covariate law is a reasonable complement, but its posterior is identified only through the target data and the chosen law or prior, so that prior has to be stated rather than absorbed. Handle inclusion-criteria ambiguity and secular drift as declared alternative estimands or explicit bias models with sensitivity ranges, not as extra variance in one interval. Uncertainty in reconstructed correlations remains the genuinely unaddressed component and is the natural next target.

title: Reported target moments are treated as known constants
text:
Our study

What conditioning on sampled target moments costs
This study was designed against MIS-03 and bears on this entry in part. What it does not answer is stated below.
The question put to it. Population adjustment treats a target trial’s published covariate means and standard deviations as exact, though they are sample estimates. By how much does that cost interval coverage at realistic sample sizes, and what would a publication have to report for a correction to work?
What it found. Two things, established by different means. Analytically: the variance a standard interval omits is (1-2k)Var_T(tau)/n_T to first order, where k is how far the target trial’s own treatment effect is modified by the same covariates as the source trial’s, so the sign is set by a quantity the usual inputs do not identify; and a correction adding only the positive term is closer to the right variance than doing nothing only when k < 1/4. Empirically, and only in an exploratory subset: the omission runs from 9.5% too much variance to 14.9% too little and moves coverage between 92.1% and 96.2%. The registered analysis is uninformative and the confirmatory coverage question remains open.
Results.

The prespecified analysis returned uninformative. Its gates require the reference interval and the negative controls to be nominal, and at poor overlap the Wald sandwich undercovers by up to 7 points for every method including scenarios with no effect modification at all, where the population omission is exactly zero. That is a source-variance failure, not a target-moment one.
The sign of the omission is an analytic identity, not a simulation finding: (1-2k)Var_T(tau)/n_T. Regressing the measured omission on it across all 216 scenarios with effect modification gives a slope of 1.003 (SE 0.042). An earlier draft claimed the simulation located the cancellation point; peer review corrected that and the claim was retracted.
The two corrections an analyst can deploy add only the positive term and omit the cross-covariance. They beat doing nothing only when k < 1/4, and are worse than doing nothing between 1/4 and 1/2. The design has no interior k with which to test this, so no recommendation is made for intermediate alignment. A draft claim that they help whenever k < 1/2 was wrong and was corrected in review.
In the exploratory subset the status quo was the only method to leave 93% to 97% coverage, and it left in both directions. Magnitude tracks the ratio of source to target information, so a large source trial matched to a small target publication is the worst case, not a small target trial.
Peer review left a standing recommendation of major revision. The confirmatory question needs a fresh registered run with an ex ante overlap restriction or a validated source variance estimator.

Design.

Estimand

Target-superpopulation marginal A versus B mean difference, exact in closed form

Methods compared

status quo (target moments held fixed), normal reconstruction (deployable today), reported moment covariance (enhanced reporting), full joint score (all target information)

Data-generating mechanism

Anchored MAIC on a continuous outcome, with the target trial’s participants generated and then discarded so the estimator sees only a published baseline table. 252 scenarios crossing source size, target size, overlap, effect-modification strength calibrated to a fixed target-population standard deviation, the alignment between the two trials’ effect modification, and whether the analyst’s borrowed correlation is correct.

Replicates

5000 per scenario, 1,260,000 in total


What this does not answer. The registered coverage question is not confirmatorily answered: every usable coverage result comes from a post-run restriction conditioning on an observed outcome. One estimator, one outcome type, one information structure. Covariates are multivariate normal, which is also the assumption the deployable correction is derived under, so it is measured under conditions favorable to it; skewed, bounded and categorical covariates are untested. The outcome is continuous and the effect additive, so marginal and conditional effects coincide, and nothing transfers directly to binary or time-to-event outcomes, where MAIC is most used. Effect modification lies exactly in the span of the matched moments, so this is a variance result under correct identification and says nothing about bias. The target moments and the target treatment effect come from the same trial, which is the common case but not the only one. STC, ML-NMR, ML-UMR and NMI have different sensitivities and are not covered. EST-07’s other components, model uncertainty in reconstructed correlations, inclusion-criteria ambiguity and secular drift, are not sampling error and are untouched. The alignment parameter imposes exact non-negative proportionality between source and target modifier coefficients, so modifier sets differing in direction or overlapping only partially are untested.
Peer review. 2 rounds, two independent reviewers. The reports, the point-by-point responses and the editorial decision are published in full: read the review.

text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Reported target-population means and standard deviations are estimates, not known constants, yet standard PAIC estimators condition on them as fixed inputs. Direction B holds that a joint model should propagate sampling uncertainty in target moments, uncertainty in reconstructed correlations, ambiguity in target inclusion criteria, and secular change between the trial and current practice.”
What was wrong with it. The source treated all four uncertainty sources as unaddressed; the literature auditor found the first already solved for MAIC-equivalent estimators (arxiv:2603.02474; doi:10.1002/sim.70358) and noted that G-MAIC (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10021) propagates uncertainty by Bayesian bootstrap of the IPD only, leaving the target summaries fixed. GPT-5.6 Sol judged the entry overstated for treating the moments as necessarily random when the estimand may condition on the realized finite target, for bundling estimand ambiguity and secular drift with sampling variance, and for a universal software negative that source code confirms only for cpaic.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 is correct for superpopulation inference from a finite target sample, but not when the estimand deliberately conditions on the realized finite target population and its exact summaries. C2 is an empirical ecosystem claim; source code confirms it for cpaic. At 9d150e9, cmaic() holds target means and SDs fixed while bootstrapping only IPD patients, cstc() centers on fixed target means, and cmlnmr() constructs fixed integration points from aggregate means, SDs, and a supplied or borrowed correlation. C3 improperly bundles sampling uncertainty, reconstructed-law model uncertainty, estimand ambiguity, and temporal transport bias. Inclusion criteria and secular change need explicit alternative estimands, scenarios, or bias models, not automatic addition to one interval. C4 is possible but posterior uncertainty is identified only through the target data and chosen law or prior. C5 requires target microdata, a sampling design, or at least the covariance or influence information for the reported summaries; bootstrapping source IPD alone cannot do it. C6 is an unsupported universal software negative, although it is true of cpaic. Frequentist methods already address target-summary sampling uncertainty, so only the broader structural components remain open. The priority is very high only when the target sample is small, the effect is sensitive to its law, or the decision changes.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The descriptive half checks out. G-MAIC (Gao, Heath & Baio, Res Synth Methods 2025) uses the reported comparator summaries as fixed balancing targets and propagates uncertainty only by Bayesian bootstrap of the IPD; Chandler & Proskorovsky’s 108-scenario MAIC variance study (Res Synth Methods 2024) compares conventional, ESS-rescaled, sandwich and bootstrap estimators, all of which address uncertainty from the matching process, none the sampling error in the target moments; maicplus matches weighted moments to reported moments taken as given. But the first of the four listed uncertainty sources has been solved outside the ITC literature, using estimators that are equivalent to MAIC. Sheng, Sun & Huang (arXiv:2603.02474, March 2026) apply entropy balancing to transportability and ‘propose a variance estimator to account for uncertainty in covariate summaries’, then give a second method handling covariate shift and summary uncertainty simultaneously; Chen, Chen & Yu (Stat Med 45(1-2):e70358, 2026) give a resampling-perturbation confidence interval for a target ATE estimated from target summary-level information. The other three sources (reconstructed correlations, inclusion-criteria ambiguity, secular drift) remain genuinely unaddressed. C2 is an empirical ecosystem claim; source code confirms it for cpaic. Frequentist methods already address target-summary sampling uncertainty, so only the broader structural components remain open. The priority is very high only when the target sample is small, the effect is sensitive to its law, or the decision changes. title: No convention for reading divergence between estimand rungs
text: EST-09 Partially addressed High priority Emerging

title: No convention for reading divergence between estimand rungs
text:
Statement
Reporting a single pooled effect hides population dependence, scale dependence and identification fragility, and the source’s response is a ladder of estimands whose divergence is read as informative. The lower rungs are already obtainable from one fitted model: multinma returns study-specific conditional effects, population-average marginal effects and predictions in an arbitrary target through newdata, and Phillippo et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2) recommend comparing conditional and marginal estimates in the decision target population, calling multilevel network meta-regression the only population-adjustment method able to produce both in any target. An overlap-population rung has a dedicated method in arbitrated indirect comparisons (arxiv:2510.18071). What does not exist is the top rung and the packaging: no software produces partially identified bounds under unmeasured effect modification as routine PAIC output, and there is no accepted convention for reading divergence between rungs.

title: No convention for reading divergence between estimand rungs
text:
Why it is open
A single number conflates population dependence, scale dependence and identification fragility, and none of the three can be recovered from it afterwards. The rungs that exist are not assembled: they come from different functions, papers and packages, and no output presents them together with each one labeled by its population, so the comparison Phillippo et al. recommend is not what the reader of a submission actually sees. The partially identified rung needs bias-function machinery that is not integrated with PAIC estimators, and bounds are informative only when a defensible sensitivity model and range are specified, otherwise they are vacuous. There is also no convention for how a committee should read divergence between rungs, so an analyst who reports one invites the charge of indecisiveness, which removes the incentive to produce it.

title: No convention for reading divergence between estimand rungs
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo, Remiro-Azocar, Heath, Baio, Dias, Ades and Welton 2025, Effect modification and non-collapsibility together may lead to conflicting treatment decisions, Research Synthesis Methods
Establishes that multilevel network meta-regression can deliver conditional and marginal estimands in any decision target population from one model, which covers the lower rungs jointly, and supplies the published justification for reading their divergence rather than treating it as failure.


multinma: Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Individual and Aggregate Data (R package)
Implements relative_effects(), predict() and marginal_effects() from a single fitted model, each targetable at an arbitrary population through newdata, so the conditional, trial-population marginal and target-population marginal rungs are already computable together.


Fang and He 2026, Arbitrated Indirect Treatment Comparisons
Supplies the overlap-population rung as a dedicated method that fixes a single common overlap target.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
At commit 9d150e9 its namespace exposes no ladder, overlap-target or partial-identification bound interface, and cML-NMR lacks marginal standardization, so cSTC and cMAIC supply separate conditional and marginal analyses rather than an integrated ladder.

title: No convention for reading divergence between estimand rungs
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Assemble rather than invent: wire the conditional, trial-population marginal, target-population marginal and overlap rungs into one labeled output built on the estimators that already produce them. Fix the number and content of rungs to the decision at hand rather than to a list of five, since marginal effects in each trial population multiply with the network and the rungs are different kinds of object. Develop the partial-identification rung as declared sensitivity models with defensible ranges, and report model and overlap diagnostics alongside each rung so divergence can be attributed to population dependence rather than to misspecification or positivity failure. In cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, none of this is exposed at commit 9d150e9, so the ladder is a concrete build there rather than a research question.

title: No convention for reading divergence between estimand rungs
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “No estimand ladder: analyses report a single pooled effect” The title says there is no estimand ladder, but the lower rungs are already obtainable from a single multinma fit and an overlap-population method exists.
The source said. “Direction C proposes that each analysis estimate a ladder of estimands rather than one effect: a conditional effect at a clinically interpretable profile, marginal effects in each trial population, the marginal effect in the policy target, an overlap-population effect, and partially identified bounds under plausible unmeasured effect modification. Divergence between rungs is treated as scientifically informative rather than as analytic failure.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no standard workflow or software computes the rungs jointly; the literature auditor found the first three obtainable from a single multinma fit and the fourth addressed by arbitrated indirect comparisons (arxiv:2510.18071), and found the justification for treating divergence as informative already published in Phillippo et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2). GPT-5.6 Sol rejected the count of exactly five rungs, noted that divergence can also come from misspecification, positivity failure or numerical error, and held that partial-identification bounds are informative only under a specified sensitivity model rather than as routine output.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. I found no published or implemented five-rung estimand ladder, so the packaged proposal is genuinely new. But the why_open claim that ‘no standard workflow or software computes the rungs jointly’ is too strong for the first three rungs. From one fitted multinma model, relative_effects() returns study-population-specific (conditional) effects, marginal_effects() returns population-average marginal effects on difference, ratio or link scales, and both accept newdata for an arbitrary policy target - and Phillippo et al. (Res Synth Methods 2025) both recommend comparing conditional and marginal estimates in the decision target population and state that ‘multilevel network meta-regression is the only population-adjustment method capable of producing both conditional and marginal estimates, in any decision target population’. That same paper also supplies the missing justification for the entry’s claim that divergence between rungs is informative rather than a defect. Rung 4 has a dedicated method (overlap-population targeting, arXiv:2510.18071). Rung 5 is closest to open: Ren et al. (Res Synth Methods 2025) give quantitative bias analysis with code for unmeasured confounding in unanchored PAIC, but that is sensitivity analysis, not partial identification, and does not restore identification. Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.2: Establishes ML-NMR as able to deliver conditional and marginal estimands in any decision target population from one model, i.e. rungs 1-3 jointly, and recommends reading their divergence.. Cites cran:multinma: Implements relative_effects(), predict() and marginal_effects() from a single fitted model, each targetable at an arbitrary population via newdata..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 has no basis for exactly five rungs: “marginal effect in each trial population” generates as many estimands as there are trial populations, and a conditional profile effect, population-marginal effects, an overlap effect, and a partial-identification set are different kinds of objects. C2 is conditional: divergence can reveal population dependence or non-collapsibility when every rung is correctly defined and estimated, but it can also reflect model misspecification, positivity failure, or numerical error. C3 is generally right under effect heterogeneity or non-collapsibility, although a single effect explicitly labeled for the decision target is not intrinsically defective. C4 is false as a routine claim: informative bounds require a specified sensitivity model, defensible ranges for unmeasured modification, adequate target information, and support; otherwise bounds may be vacuous. At cpaic 9d150e9, NAMESPACE exposes no ladder, overlap-target, or partial-identification-bound API, and cML-NMR explicitly lacks marginal standardization; cSTC and cMAIC instead provide separate conditional and marginal analyses. Thus the integrated ladder remains open in cpaic. C5 is supported for cpaic but unverifiable as a universal statement about all ITC/PAIC software under this audit’s no-literature constraint.

It is also being closed in pieces: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.
Does the later work answer the earlier work? Put to an independent reviewer with the older and newer claims side by side, it judged that the later work answers a component of it, leaving a named part (high confidence). The 2025 paper provides a concrete decision rule for divergence between conditional and marginal effects in the decision population, including a subgroup-decision response when rankings conflict. That is only one pair of rungs, whereas the earlier gap concerns a broader ladder and its unmeasured-effect-modification bounds. What remains: There is no accepted interpretation framework spanning study-specific, target-standardized, overlap, and partially identified estimands, and routine PAIC software still lacks the partially identified bounds rung.

title: No simulation crosses target choice with second-stage transport error
text:
Statement
No published PAIC simulation crosses a full menu of target-population choices with correct versus incorrect second-stage transport and with uncertainty in the reported target moments, and a simulation that defines truth by the estimator’s own implicit target makes target-mismatch error invisible. The blanket version of the claim is false: Chandler and Ishak’s ML-UMR simulation (arxiv:2606.20341) treats the target population as a design factor over index and comparator populations, crosses it with effect-modification strength, overlap and covariate dependence including a misspecified between-population correlation, uses two effect measures, and scores bias and coverage against true marginal effects computed externally from simulated populations of ten million. The count of eight factors is also not defensible as exact or orthogonal, since target choice, overlap and distributional difference cannot always be varied independently, and dimensions such as network geometry, baseline risk and censoring are equally material.

title: No simulation crosses target choice with second-stage transport error
text:
Why it is open
What has not been mapped is the interaction between a full menu of target choices, including pooled, registry and overlap populations, and the correctness of the second-stage transport; no study varies uncertainty in the reported target moments at all. Judging bias against an externally declared decision estimand presupposes the target-declaration discipline the field does not enforce, so simulations keep inheriting the estimator’s implicit target as truth, and an estimator that answers the wrong question scores as unbiased. The full crossed design is large and expensive to summarize, and because comparative simulations are the main evidence used to recommend methods, the metric propagates directly into method-selection guidance.

title: No simulation crosses target choice with second-stage transport error
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Chandler and Ishak 2026, Anchors Away: Navigating Unanchored Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR)
Runs a 24-scenario factorial simulation at 500 replications that treats the target population as a design factor over index and comparator populations, crosses effect modification, population imbalance and covariate dependence including a misspecified between-population correlation, uses two effect scales, and computes true marginal effects externally from populations of ten million rather than from any estimator’s implicit target. It does not vary a five-level target menu, second-stage transport correctness, or target-moment uncertainty.

title: No simulation crosses target choice with second-stage transport error
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend the existing design rather than start one: Chandler and Ishak’s simulation already varies the target population and defines truth externally, so the increment is a wider target menu including pooled, registry and overlap populations, a correct versus incorrect second-stage transport factor, and target-moment uncertainty, run as a coherent fractional-factorial design rather than a full crossing of eight nominally independent factors. Separate the effect-modification factor into functional form and whether modification is shared or treatment-specific, instead of treating four levels as mutually exclusive. Report bias, RMSE and coverage against the declared decision estimand for every method, and report each estimator’s error for its own native estimand separately, so target-mismatch error and estimation error can be read apart.

title: No simulation crosses target choice with second-stage transport error
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. No published PAIC simulation crosses a full menu of target-population choices with second-stage transport correctness and target-moment uncertainty, although at least one 2026 study (Chandler & Ishak’s ML-UMR simulation) does treat target population as a design factor, uses two effect measures, and scores bias and coverage against an externally defined target estimand rather than the estimator’s implicit target.
The source titled this. “No factorial simulation of target choice, judged against the target” The title says no factorial simulation of target choice exists, but a 2026 ML-UMR simulation treats target population as a design factor and scores against externally computed truth.
The source said. “Section 5.4 specifies a target-population simulation program crossing eight factors (target choice; effect measure; effect-modification structure; prognostic effect strength; overlap; covariate-distribution difference; target-moment uncertainty; and correct versus incorrect second-stage transport), and no such crossed study is reported as existing. Its principal outcome should be bias relative to the declared target estimand, not bias relative to whichever population the estimator implicitly targets.”
What was wrong with it. The source stated that no crossed study exists and that existing PAIC simulations judge bias against the estimator’s implicit target; the literature auditor falsified the blanket version with Chandler and Ishak’s ML-UMR simulation (arxiv:2606.20341), which varies the target population as a design factor and evaluates against externally computed true marginal effects. GPT-5.6 Sol rejected the fixed count of eight factors as neither exhaustive nor orthogonal and abstained on how much published simulation coverage exists, holding that question outside a technical audit’s reach.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The two blanket negative claims are falsified by a 2026 preprint from the same authors the neighbouring EST entries already cite. Chandler & Ishak’s ML-UMR paper (arXiv:2606.20341, 18 June 2026) runs a factorial simulation that treats the target population as a design factor - the methods section states ‘For a target population P in {index, comparator}’ and reports bias and coverage in both - and defines truth externally rather than by any estimator’s implicit target: ‘True marginal treatment effects were computed for each scenario using large simulated populations (N = 10,000,000) to approximate the data-generating distributions’, on two effect scales (log odds ratio and log risk ratio). Its Table C.1 crosses effect modification (none / weak / strong), population imbalance (moderate / high overlap), covariate dependence including a misspecified between-population correlation, and sample size, for 24 scenarios at 500 replications. So target choice has been crossed with effect measure, effect-modification structure and overlap. What survives is narrower: no study crosses a five-level target choice (IPD trial, AgD trial, pooled, registry, overlap) with correct-versus-incorrect second-stage transport, and no study varies target-moment uncertainty. Cites arxiv:2606.20341: Demonstrates a PAIC simulation that varies the target population as a design factor, crosses it with effect-modification strength, overlap and covariate dependence, uses two effect measures, and evaluates bias against externally computed true marginal effects..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

abstain / overstated. C1 is not defensible as “exactly eight.” The dimensions are sensible but neither exhaustive nor orthogonal: nonlinear effect modification can also be shared or treatment-specific, and target choice, overlap, and distributional difference cannot always be varied independently. Other potentially material dimensions include network geometry, sample size, baseline risk, censoring, measurement error, and outcome-model misspecification. C4 and C5 are useful simulation dimensions when defined coherently. C6 should separate functional form from whether modification is shared or treatment-specific rather than treating them as four mutually exclusive levels. C7 is correct for decision-focused method comparison, although native-estimand estimation error should be reported separately from target-mismatch error. C9 follows directly: an estimator unbiased for θ(P) has bias θ(P)-θ(Q) for decision target Q. C10 is correct because precision conditional on an estimand cannot validate that estimand’s policy relevance. C2, C3, and C8 are claims about published simulation coverage, explicitly outside this audit’s lens and unsupported by cited works here; therefore the open-status vote is an abstention rather than an inference from absence.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Network intervals condition on plugged-in variance components
text: EST-13 Partially addressed Medium-high priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: Network intervals condition on plugged-in variance components
text:
Statement
Standard frequentist network meta-analysis estimates the between-study heterogeneity variance, and where fitted the inconsistency variance, then treats both as known when computing treatment-effect standard errors and confidence intervals, so the reported interval answers a question conditional on quantities that were themselves estimated from few designs. In sparse networks the omission is large rather than technical: in a Cochrane topical antibiotics network of 13 studies and four treatments the plug-in estimate of one contrast is -1.92 with standard error 0.64, where the Bayesian posterior for the same contrast under the same normal approximations has mean -2.07 and standard deviation 1.09 (Jackson et al. 2016, doi:10.1002/sim.6752). The univariate corrections do not transfer mechanically, because multi-arm trials make contrast-level estimates dependent and because a model carrying both a heterogeneity and an inconsistency variance requires the two to be handled jointly. What information there is about those variances comes from the number of distinct designs rather than the number of studies: coverage falls below nominal whenever inconsistency is present, 50 studies spread over 5 designs performed no better than 10 studies over the same 5 designs, and only a network with 10 designs approached nominal coverage. Part of the problem has since been solved for likelihood-based fits, where Kenward-Roger-type corrections and Bartlett-type or bootstrap adjustments restore coverage for restricted-maximum-likelihood network meta-analysis and meta-regression and are the defaults of one CRAN package. The moments-based case with two variance components, which is where the question was raised, remains unaddressed, and the most widely used frequentist implementation still reports random-effects intervals conditional on a plugged-in heterogeneity variance.

title: Network intervals condition on plugged-in variance components
text:
Why it is open
Variance-component uncertainty enters the treatment-effect interval through a nonlinear function of quantities that are poorly estimated exactly when the network is sparse, and it is the design count rather than the study count that governs how much information there is about them, so asymptotics in the number of studies do not describe the situation the correction is needed for. The moments-based estimator has no likelihood, so the Kenward-Roger and Bartlett machinery that repaired the restricted-maximum-likelihood case does not apply to it, and truncating negative variance estimates at zero introduces a positive bias that any interval method has to accommodate. Which resampling scheme is appropriate is itself unstudied for networks, since resampling studies changes the design structure and can drop a design or disconnect the network entirely. And because the plug-in interval is narrow rather than visibly wrong, nothing in the output signals the problem, and a wider Bayesian interval on the same data is usually attributed to the prior instead.

title: Network intervals condition on plugged-in variance components
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Jackson et al. 2016, Statistics in Medicine
gives the moments-based estimator for a network model with separate heterogeneity and inconsistency variances, states that interval estimation for those components does not extend immediately to networks because multi-arm trials make estimates dependent and two variances are involved, offers bootstrapping as an unvalidated stopgap, and reports the coverage and design-count results


Hartung and Knapp 2001, Statistics in Medicine
gives the refined variance estimator and t reference distribution for pairwise meta-analysis that accounts for estimation of the heterogeneity variance, the univariate fix whose network extension is the open question


Veroniki et al. 2019, Research Synthesis Methods
inventories and compares methods for calculating uncertainty in the summary effect of a random-effects meta-analysis, the pairwise reference set for which no network counterpart exists


Jackson and Riley 2014, Statistics in Medicine
supplies a refined multivariate meta-analysis and meta-regression method that allows for estimation of the between-study covariance matrix, the closest multivariate precedent for what a network version would need


Noma et al. 2018, Statistics in Medicine
develops likelihood-ratio and score-based inference for network meta-analysis with Bartlett-type corrections and parametric bootstrap adjustments, showing that small-sample invalidity of the standard intervals can be corrected within the likelihood framework


Noma et al. 2023, Research Synthesis Methods
gives Kenward-Roger-type corrected covariance estimators and t approximations for restricted-maximum-likelihood network meta-analysis and meta-regression, reporting that standard Wald intervals seriously underestimate error with few trials while the corrected intervals hold their nominal coverage


Noma et al. 2023, Research Synthesis Methods
extends the same correction to prediction intervals for network meta-analysis through bootstrap and Kenward-Roger adjustments, with an implementation in the PINMA package


NMA (CRAN 3.1-1)
implements contrast-based network meta-analysis with the improved restricted-maximum-likelihood methods as defaults and also fits Jackson’s random inconsistency model, so the corrected inference and the two-variance-component model are available in one package but have not been shown to work together


netmeta (CRAN 3.6-1)
the most widely used frequentist implementation, whose random-effects estimates use the estimated heterogeneity variance as if known; neither its reference paper nor its package description lists a variance-component uncertainty correction

title: Network intervals condition on plugged-in variance components
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Take the two extensions in order. Derive an interval for the moments-based estimator that accounts for both variance components under dependent multi-arm contrasts, for example by constructing a Q-based confidence region for the pair of variances and taking the union of treatment-effect intervals over that region, and test it in the design-count regime where coverage is known to fail. Settle the resampling question by comparing study-level, design-level and parametric bootstraps on networks that lose designs when resampled, reporting coverage and interval width against the number of designs rather than the number of studies. Separately, check whether the Kenward-Roger and Bartlett corrections built for consistency models keep their coverage once a random inconsistency variance is added, since that is the model behind the applied question. Whatever survives belongs in the general-purpose frequentist packages as a default rather than in a specialist one as an option, and every reported interval should state which variance components were treated as known.

title: Network intervals condition on plugged-in variance components
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed it from a single methods paper whose discussion states the problem is open, and the reviewer accepted that the multi-arm and joint heterogeneity-inconsistency setting makes this more than a routine univariate correction. It is partially-addressed because Kenward-Roger-type and Bartlett-type corrections now restore coverage for likelihood-based network meta-analysis and ship as defaults in one CRAN package; the moments-based two-variance-component case and the mainstream implementations are untouched.

title: No bound for effect-measure non-transitivity in anchored survival comparisons
text: EST-15 Confirmed open Very high priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: No bound for effect-measure non-transitivity in anchored survival comparisons
text:
Statement
An anchored indirect comparison presumes that the chosen effect measure is statistically transitive, so that the common comparator cancels and the A versus B effect equals the A versus C effect minus the B versus C effect on that scale. The Cox hazard ratio does not have this property in general: it holds in expectation if and only if hazards are proportional across all three arms, because each pairwise Cox fit conditions on its own nuisance baseline hazard, so the anchor does not cancel. This is a third identification requirement alongside comparator comparability and effect-modifier balance, and it bites when the two trial populations are identical and the comparator drug is the same, which places it outside every population-adjustment remedy. A simulated three-arm case with 2000 patients per arm produces a direct hazard ratio of 0.896 (95% CI 0.840 to 0.956) favoring one drug and an indirect hazard ratio of 1.296 (95% CI 1.117 to 1.440) favoring the other, so the sign of the comparison reverses and the answer depends on which treatment serves as the anchor. What does not exist is a bound or sensitivity parameter for the magnitude of the non-transitivity bias in a given analysis, a procedure that estimates it from the digitized comparator survival curve and reported follow-up, or any account of how it interacts with reweighting in a population-adjusted comparison.

title: No bound for effect-measure non-transitivity in anchored survival comparisons
text:
Why it is open
The condition that would license the anchored subtraction is proportionality across all three arms jointly, and in the usual data configuration the third arm is never observed alongside the other two: the comparator trial publishes a hazard ratio and at best a Kaplan-Meier curve, so the cross-trial proportionality that matters cannot be tested. Where a proportional-hazards test can be run at all it is underpowered, so failing to reject is not evidence of transitivity. The remedy the literature offers is to change measure, to a difference in restricted mean survival time or in absolute survival probability, which does not help when the decision requires a hazard ratio as an input to an extrapolation or when the comparator publishes nothing else. Bounding the bias needs a class of departures from proportionality that is both parameterized and pinned down by what gets published, and the natural candidates such as an arbitrary time-varying log hazard ratio are not identified from a single reported summary. The failure is also invisible in standard output: each pairwise Cox fit is internally well behaved, and no diagnostic in the anchored workflow inspects whether the anchor cancels.

title: No bound for effect-measure non-transitivity in anchored survival comparisons
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Jiang et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Proves that statistical transitivity of the Cox hazard ratio holds if and only if hazards are proportional across all arms, exhibits a simulated three-arm case in which the direct and indirect comparisons have opposite signs, and recommends switching to a transitive measure; concedes the enabling condition is untestable in the usual configuration.


Bucher et al. 1997, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
The adjusted indirect comparison whose validity rests on the assumed algebraic cancellation of the common comparator; the estimator whose scale requirement this problem names.


Hernan 2010, Epidemiology
Shows that a hazard ratio at any time conditions on survivors, so it carries a built-in selection component and varies over time even under randomization; the mechanism that makes the Cox coefficient a fit-specific summary.


Aalen, Cook and Roysland 2015, Lifetime Data Analysis
Demonstrates that Cox analysis of a randomized survival study does not in general return a causal treatment effect, because frailty selection in the risk set makes the hazard contrast depend on the accumulated history.


Martinussen, Vansteelandt and Andersen 2020, Lifetime Data Analysis
Formal account of what hazard contrasts identify and why they are not causal contrasts in a fixed population; the theory a bias functional for non-transitivity would build on.


Daniel, Zhang and Farewell 2021, Biometrical Journal
Sets out the consequences of comparing non-collapsible effect estimators fitted with different covariate sets, the closest existing treatment of why two hazard-ratio estimates need not be on a common footing.


Uno et al. 2014, Journal of Clinical Oncology
Argues for restricted mean survival time as a between-group summary that does not require proportional hazards; the class of measures the switch-the-measure remedy points to.


Wiksten et al. 2020, Value in Health
Model-building and analysis strategies for non-proportional hazards in network meta-analysis, showing how far the synthesis literature has gone in relaxing proportionality without addressing anchor cancellation.


Ouwens, Philips and Jansen 2010, Research Synthesis Methods
Network meta-analysis of parametric survival curves, synthesizing whole hazard functions rather than one hazard ratio, so no cancellation of a scalar anchor is required.


Jansen 2011, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Fractional polynomial network meta-analysis of survival data, giving time-varying contrasts from published Kaplan-Meier information; the whole-curve alternative to a transported hazard ratio.

title: No bound for effect-measure non-transitivity in anchored survival comparisons
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Write the non-transitivity bias down as a functional: with arm-specific hazard functions, express the difference between the population Cox coefficient for A versus B and the difference of the two pairwise Cox coefficients, then parameterize departures from proportionality, for instance a piecewise-constant or log-linear time-varying log hazard ratio, and derive the induced bias as a function of those parameters, the follow-up and the censoring distribution. Bound that functional over the set of hazard shapes compatible with the published comparator Kaplan-Meier curve, its reconstructed pseudo-individual data and the reported censoring pattern, so that the reported output is an interval rather than a point. Establish how the bias behaves under population adjustment, since reweighting changes the composition of the risk set and therefore the weights the Cox coefficient places on the time-varying contrast. Add an anchor-invariance check to the anchored workflow: refit the comparison with each available common comparator in turn and report the spread, which is a computable lower bound on the problem wherever more than one anchor exists. Where the decision needs a survival curve, synthesize whole curves and report a hazard ratio only as a derived summary with the time window it applies to stated explicitly.

title: No bound for effect-measure non-transitivity in anchored survival comparisons
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this from a single 2025 methods paper that proves the if-and-only-if condition and demonstrates a sign reversal, and the reviewer accepted it as distinct from OUT-11 because comparator-dependent failure of the anchor to cancel arises with zero population difference. The identification result itself is not in dispute; resting on one paper, what is undocumented is how large the bias is in real appraisals and whether it can be bounded from published summaries.
