title: Multi-arm covariance is lost when contrasts are adjusted pairwise
text:
Statement
MAIC-style weighting is defined for one pairwise comparison against one aggregate study, so a two-stage weighting workflow that outputs separately adjusted contrasts with only marginal standard errors loses the covariance induced by a shared common arm and the covariance induced by shared weight estimation. Regression-based population adjustment already solves this at the network level: multilevel network meta-regression is a one-stage arm-level likelihood valid for networks of any size (Phillippo et al. 2020, doi:10.1111/rssa.12579), implemented in multinma since 2020, where multi-arm studies carry correlated multivariate-normal random effects (Perren et al. 2025, doi:10.1177/0272989X251389887). What is open is the weighting branch: there is no arm-level MAIC-style estimator, and no sandwich or multivariate bootstrap variance estimator for weighted multi-arm contrasts that also carries weight-estimation uncertainty has been derived or benchmarked. The same split holds in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN: at commit 9d150e9 cmlnmr() gives within-study deviations from a study baseline the standard 0.5 NMA correlation, while cmaic() and cstc() refuse IPD studies with more than two arms rather than processing them pairwise. The same covariance is lost without any multi-arm trial present. Where a sparse network admits single-arm studies by matching each to a comparator arm of an existing randomized trial, several pseudo-contrasts can be built from the same comparator arm, so their errors are correlated through shared control observations exactly as contrasts are correlated within a multi-arm trial; published implementations nonetheless enter them into the network likelihood as independent evidence, and in a late-onset Pompe disease network admitting the matched single-arm studies reversed the direction of the headline comparison.

title: Multi-arm covariance is lost when contrasts are adjusted pairwise
text:
Why it is open
Multi-arm trials produce correlated contrasts because they share a common arm, and a network likelihood needs that correlation; a two-stage pipeline that adjusts one contrast at a time and passes on only marginal standard errors has nowhere to store it. Weight estimation adds a second source of correlation between contrasts that naive variance formulas ignore. Neither is a theoretical obstacle, because one weight set can feed a joint arm-level outcome model and a multivariate bootstrap that re-estimates the weights recovers the full contrast covariance; the obstacle is that nobody has derived, implemented or benchmarked this for the weighting branch. The consequence surfaces as distorted precision and as spurious or masked inconsistency rather than as an obvious failure, which is why nobody is forced to confront it.

title: Multi-arm covariance is lost when contrasts are adjusted pairwise
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al., 2020, Multilevel network meta-regression for population-adjusted treatment comparisons, JRSS-A
Defines an individual-level regression model and fits aggregate data by integrating over the covariate distribution to form the likelihood; this is the arm-based one-stage population-adjusted estimator the source says does not exist, and it is valid for networks of any size including multi-arm trials.


multinma: Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Individual and Aggregate Data (version 0.9.1)
Working implementation: nma() fits ML-NMR with arm-based likelihoods, and multi-arm studies receive correlated multivariate-normal random effects.


Perren, Pedder, Welton and Phillippo, 2026, Network Meta-Analysis with Class Effects: A Practical Guide and Model Selection Algorithm
States the multi-arm covariance parameterization used in multinma, confirming that studies with more than one non-baseline arm have multiple correlated random effects modeled as multivariate normal.


Phillippo et al., 2019, Population adjustment methods for indirect comparisons: a review of NICE technology appraisals
Cited by the audit as counter-evidence that the problem is real in practice: larger treatment networks were commonplace in NICE appraisals (10 of 18) while the population adjustment methods in use could not account for them.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
cmlnmr() jointly fits IPD and aggregate arms by integrating the individual-level model over each aggregate study’s covariate distribution, and cmlnmr_random.R gives multi-arm deviations from a study baseline the standard 0.5 NMA correlation; cmaic() and cstc() support two-arm IPD studies only.


Shohet et al. 2024, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research
Builds a rare-disease network by pairing each single-arm study with the comparator arm of an existing randomized trial chosen to minimize a distance over aggregate baseline characteristics, then enters the resulting pseudo-contrasts as independent evidence in the network likelihood while recording the reuse of comparator-arm evidence as a limitation; admitting the matched single-arm studies reverses the direction of the headline comparison.


Goring et al. 2016, Research Synthesis Methods
Sets out the analytic options for treatment networks having no common comparator, the sparse-network setting in which single-arm studies are matched to existing comparator arms rather than left out.

title: Multi-arm covariance is lost when contrasts are adjusted pairwise
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Do not rebuild the one-stage arm-level likelihood, which ML-NMR in multinma already provides; extend the weighting branch to match it. Derive a MAIC-style estimator that applies one weight set to a joint arm-level model, with a sandwich or multivariate bootstrap variance that accounts for weight estimation as well as the outcome model, and give two-stage implementations a joint covariance matrix to export instead of marginal standard errors. Benchmark it in simulations that inject three-arm and four-arm studies with correlated contrasts and unequal variances, reporting variance recovery, inconsistency inflation and undercoverage, with ML-NMR as the reference rather than as the thing being replaced. In cpaic the concrete step is multi-arm support for cmaic() and cstc(), which currently reject such studies outright.

title: Multi-arm covariance is lost when contrasts are adjusted pairwise
text:
Our study

Matched single-arm studies built against one comparator arm
The question put to it. When several single-arm studies are each matched to the same comparator arm and their pseudo-contrasts enter a network as independent, how much does that overstate precision, and does it change the conclusion?
What it found. Entering pseudo-contrasts built against one comparator arm as independent counts that arm once per study. Its reported SE shrank as studies were added while the estimate’s spread did not, so coverage fell from 0.88 with one study to 0.57 with eight (comparator arm of 50). Modeling the shared covariance kept coverage at 0.95. In this fixed-effect network the point estimate barely changed; the error is in the stated precision.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: naive coverage 0.567 to 0.884 with two or more pseudo-contrasts; correct 0.945 to 0.955.
Naive SE with a comparator arm of 50: 0.137 (one study) to 0.059 (eight), against a true spread of 0.167 to 0.147.
Mean absolute difference between naive and correct point estimates small; sign disagreement rare.

Design.

Estimand

A versus C mean difference in the network

Methods compared

generalized least squares with the shared-arm covariance, pseudo-contrasts entered as independent

Data-generating mechanism

Network with two randomized trials and one to eight single-arm studies sharing one comparator arm; fixed-effect generalized least squares with the correct block covariance or with independence. 8 cells, 4000 replicates each.

Replicates

4000 per scenario, 32,000 in total


What this does not answer. Fixed-effect continuous network without a weighting step; heterogeneity and conflicting evidence, where the point estimate can also move, not run. Peer review has not been done.

title: Multi-arm covariance is lost when contrasts are adjusted pairwise
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. MAIC-style weighting is defined for a single pairwise comparison against one aggregate study, so weighting-based PAIC applied contrast by contrast loses the covariance induced by a shared common arm. Regression-based population adjustment already solves this: multilevel network meta-regression (Phillippo et al. 2020, implemented in multinma) is a one-stage arm-level likelihood that keeps multi-arm structure intact. The open part is a weighting-based arm-level estimator and a variance estimator for it that accounts for weight estimation.
The source said. “MAIC-style weighting is defined for one pairwise comparison against one aggregate study, so a multi-arm trial is processed contrast by contrast and the covariance induced by the shared common arm is never carried into the network likelihood. Standard NMA software handles that structure correctly, but it sits downstream of the weighting step and is not wired into it.”
What was wrong with it. The source claimed no arm-based or multivariate PAIC estimator preserving multi-arm covariance is available, and cited nothing; the literature auditor found that multilevel network meta-regression is exactly that estimator and has been on CRAN in multinma since 2020 (doi:10.1111/rssa.12579), and the code auditor found cpaic’s cmlnmr() already implements the shared-baseline multi-arm correlation. The code auditor also rejected the framing that it is not established whether weighting before contrast formation preserves the correct covariance: weighting is not inherently pairwise, and the weighted covariance is estimable by joint estimating equations or a bootstrap that re-estimates the weights, so this is undone work rather than an unverifiable assumption.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied full-text reading.

merged-in

absorbed a proposal the reading raised separately: Single-arm matching into networks leaves induced dependence unmodelled 2 citation(s) added. The drafter disagreed with placing it here: The covariance half of this proposal merges cleanly: reusing one comparator arm across several matched pseudo-contrasts induces the same shared-data correlation that a two-stage pipeline exporting only marginal standard errors cannot carry, and the fix is the same joint covariance HET-02 already asks for. The second half does not merge as neatly. Residual bias from imperfect matching between a single arm and its chosen comparator is an unanchored-comparison problem with no randomized anchor, closer to the external-control and overlap entries than to multi-arm covariance, and HET-02 as written proposes no diagnostic for matching adequacy. If HET-02 takes on matched single-arm pseudo-contrasts, its research direction should either name a matching-adequacy diagnostic or hand that half to an unanchored-comparison entry rather than let it fall between the two.

Citation corrected

normalized a citation year: ‘Perren, Pedder, Welton and Phillippo, 2025, Network Meta-Analysis with Class Effects: A Practical Guide and Model Selection Algorithm’ -> ‘Perren, Pedder, Welton and Phillippo, 2026, Network Meta-Analysis with Class Effects: A Practical Guide and Model Selection Algorithm’ 10.1177/0272989X251389887 is cited with two different years across the registry. CrossRef gives 2025 online and 2026 in print; the issue year is used throughout.

closure-upheld

6 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors’ reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. None of the findings contradicts the closure’s cited one-stage ML-NMR result or show that its multi-arm likelihood fails to retain shared-arm covariance. The 2019 review and the gastric-cancer example document exactly the residual already conceded: applied pairwise workflows can treat dependent adjusted inputs as independent. The other findings concern standard NMA implementation, contribution matrices, or analogous non-PAIC settings, not an arm-level MAIC estimator or a joint weighted variance procedure. They therefore support the retained narrow problem in the weighting branch rather than reopen the stronger claim. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening

10 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries overstated Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit’s closure needs the closure’s own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The claim ‘No arm-based or multivariate PAIC estimator that preserves multi-arm covariance is currently available’ is contradicted by work the entry does not cite. Phillippo et al. (2020) multilevel network meta-regression is exactly a one-stage individual-level (arm-based) likelihood for population adjustment: ‘An individual level regression model is defined, and aggregate data are fitted by integrating over the covariate distribution to form the likelihood’, and it applies to ‘networks of any size’. It is implemented in multinma 0.9.1. Perren, Pedder, Welton & Phillippo (2025) describe the same package’s multi-arm handling verbatim: ‘Studies with more than 1 nontreatment arm therefore have multiple RE, which are correlated and modeled using a multivariate normal distribution.’ So the arm-based, multi-arm-preserving population-adjusted estimator exists and has been in CRAN software since 2020. What remains open is narrower and real: MAIC-style weighting itself has no arm-based extension, and no sandwich or multivariate bootstrap variance estimator for weighted multi-arm contrasts that also carries weight-estimation uncertainty has been derived or benchmarked. The ‘Standard NMA software handles multi-arm correlated contrasts maturely’ claim is correct. Cites doi:10.1111/rssa.12579: Provides the arm-based one-stage likelihood for population adjustment that the entry says does not exist, valid for networks of any size including multi-arm trials.. Cites cran:multinma 0.9.1: Working implementation: nma() fits ML-NMR with arm-based likelihoods; multi-arm studies get correlated multivariate-normal random effects.. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X251389887: States the multi-arm covariance parameterization used in multinma, confirming multi-arm correlation is carried in the likelihood..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C2, C5, C7, and C8 are technically sound with appropriate implementation. Weighting is not inherently pairwise: one set of patient weights can feed a joint arm-level outcome model, and joint estimating equations or a multivariate bootstrap that re-estimates the weights can recover the full contrast covariance. Thus C4 is framed incorrectly; the weighted covariance need not equal the unweighted covariance, but it is estimable rather than an intrinsically unverified assumption. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, cmaic() and cstc() reject IPD studies with more than two arms rather than processing them pairwise. More importantly, cmlnmr() is already a population-adjusted, joint arm-level estimator and implements the standard shared-baseline multi-arm random-effects correlation. This directly refutes C6 and the statement that covariance is never carried. The remaining open part is multi-arm support for the two-stage cMAIC and cSTC paths, including export of their joint covariance. C3’s claim about what workflows often do is unsourced. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Implements a one-stage model that jointly fits IPD and aggregate arms while integrating over aggregate-study covariate distributions.. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Preserves the standard covariance among random-effects contrasts sharing a baseline arm in cMLNMR..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text: HET-04 Partially addressed High priority Emerging

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Statement
Standard aggregate-data node splitting, as implemented in netmeta and gemtc, compares direct and indirect evidence without standardizing either path to a common target population, so a population difference between the paths and a genuine loop conflict arrive as a single number. Node splitting is local to a comparison rather than a global test of the network, and it can already be fitted inside a population-adjusted regression: multinma has supported consistency = ‘nodesplit’ since 0.4.0 and the same call accepts a regression formula and integration points, so both paths can be compared after adjustment (Phillippo et al. 2022, doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162 assess inconsistency inside a population-adjusted psoriasis model with estimates produced for three external target populations). Two things remain undone: that adjusted split reports a conditional inconsistency factor rather than one standardized to a named target population on the marginal scale, and no study has quantified how often the unadjusted diagnostic flags population mismatch as inconsistency or misses true inconsistency that a compensating mismatch has masked. Whether consistency is population-indexed at all needs care, because marginal effects on non-collapsible measures are population-dependent (Chandler and Ishak, arxiv:2602.17041) but a loop whose every effect is defined in the same population telescopes algebraically, so population-varying inconsistency requires different populations along the evidence paths, design-specific effect surfaces, or an inconsistency-by-covariate interaction.

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Why it is open
Unadjusted node splitting takes the direct estimate from the studies that made that comparison and the indirect estimate from a different set of studies, so the two paths carry different covariate distributions; a population difference registers as inconsistency, a real conflict can be cancelled by a compensating population difference, and one number is returned for both explanations. Fitting the split inside a population-adjusted regression removes that confounding at the conditional level, but only under the usual transport conditions: consistent estimands, positivity, measured effect modifiers, and correctly specified outcome and transport models. Even then the output is a conditional inconsistency factor, so no diagnostic is reported at a named target population on the marginal scale a decision uses. And the false-positive and masking rates of the unadjusted test, which is the one applied work actually runs, have not been measured for the population-indexed comparison this entry describes, though Song et al. 2012 measured them for the ordinary unadjusted test by simulation, so nobody knows how much reported inconsistency in the literature is population mismatch.

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




multinma: Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Individual and Aggregate Data (version 0.9.1), nma(consistency = “nodesplit”)
Node splitting, added in 0.4.0 (2022-01-18), can be fitted within a covariate-adjusted ML-NMR with a regression formula and numerical integration, so the two evidence paths are compared after population adjustment rather than on raw aggregate contrasts.


Phillippo et al., 2023, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis
Examines residual heterogeneity and inconsistency inside a population-adjusted model and relaxes the shared effect modifier assumption for each covariate in turn, with estimates produced for three external target populations.


Chandler and Ishak, 2026
Shows that even when effect modifiers are shared across treatments, marginal effects are generally population-dependent for commonly used non-collapsible measures including hazard ratios and odds ratios; the audit used it as the support for consistency being population-indexed.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
relative_effects() evaluates a conditional contrast at one covariate profile and explicitly does not marginally standardize over a target distribution, and the NAMESPACE exposes no node-splitting or design-by-treatment diagnostic.

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The immediate work is measurement rather than method: run the simulation that quantifies how often unadjusted node splitting flags population mismatch as inconsistency and how often a compensating mismatch masks a real conflict, since that number decides whether the adjusted version is worth its cost. Beyond that, marginalize the ML-NMR node split so the inconsistency factor is reported at a named target population on the decision scale rather than at a covariate profile, and treat population-indexed inconsistency parameters as the harder remaining case. Any such diagnostic inherits the transport assumptions and cannot separate genuine inconsistency from unmeasured population or design differences, so it should be reported with that limit stated. In cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, neither piece exists at commit 9d150e9: relative_effects() evaluates a conditional contrast at a single covariate profile without marginal standardization, and no node-splitting or design-by-treatment diagnostic is exported.

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Our study

A population difference arriving as inconsistency
The question put to it. When the studies supplying the direct and indirect paths of a loop differ in an effect modifier, how often does unadjusted node splitting flag the population difference as inconsistency or miss a real conflict that the difference cancels, and what does an adjusted split achieve?
What it found. Unadjusted node splitting tests inconsistency plus population mismatch. With no true inconsistency it flagged 14% to 98% of analyses when the direct and indirect study sets differed in an effect modifier, and it fell to its null rate when the mismatch cancelled a real conflict. A split adjusted for the modifier held size (4% to 6%) and recovered some masked conflicts, but its precision fell as the gap between the study sets grew.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: unadjusted flag rate 0.141 to 0.982 with no inconsistency and differing populations; adjusted 0.041 to 0.058.
Exact masking: unadjusted 0.058 to 0.105; adjusted 0.074 to 0.254.
Adjusted inconsistency SE rose from 0.10 to 0.30 as the covariate gap went from 0 to 1 (four studies per comparison, modification 0.4); power against 0.2 fell from 0.54 to 0.12.
Unadjusted split at 0.10 even with no gap under modification 0.4, from covariate-driven heterogeneity.

Design.

Estimand

Loop inconsistency factor for the B versus C contrast

Methods compared

unadjusted node split, meta-regression-adjusted node split

Data-generating mechanism

Triangle networks with a covariate gap between the direct and indirect study sets, modification strength, true loop inconsistency and two or four studies per comparison; unadjusted and meta-regression-adjusted node splits. 54 cells, 2000 replicates each.

Replicates

2000 per scenario, 108,000 in total


What this does not answer. Continuous study estimates, one loop, no Bayesian node split or marginalization to a named target. Peer review has not been done.

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Consistency is population-indexed but tested as a global property” The title calls consistency tested as a global property, but node splitting is local to a comparison and can already be fitted inside a population-adjusted regression.
The source said. “A network loop can be consistent in one population and inconsistent in another, so consistency is a population-indexed property; standard node splitting and design-by-treatment interaction models nonetheless test it as a global property of the network.”
What was wrong with it. The source said node splitting and design-by-treatment models test consistency as a global property with no population standardization; the literature auditor found node splitting can already be fitted inside a covariate-adjusted ML-NMR (multinma since 0.4.0; Phillippo et al. 2022, doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162), and the code auditor noted that node splitting is local to a comparison rather than global, and that non-collapsibility on its own does not make consistency population-dependent because a loop defined in one population telescopes algebraically. The auditors split on whether the entry is open or partly solved, and it is published at the weaker claim.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Corrected

why_open: corrected a factual claim Song et al. 2012 (BMC Med Res Methodol 12:138) ran 5000 replicates per scenario across four heterogeneity levels and six network sizes, reporting type I error and power for the unadjusted test. The flat claim that these were never measured is false; the narrower population-indexed claim in the statement stands. Previously: “Unadjusted node splitting takes the direct estimate from the studies that made that comparison and the indirect estimate from a different set of studies, so the two paths carry different covariate distributions; a population difference registers as inconsistency, a real conflict can be cancelled by a compensating population difference, and one number is returned for both explanations. Fitting the split inside a population-adjusted regression removes that confounding at the conditional level, but only under the usual transport conditions: consistent estimands, positivity, measured effect modifi”

Citation corrected

normalized a citation year: ‘Phillippo et al., 2022, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis’ -> ‘Phillippo et al., 2023, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis’ 10.1177/0272989X221117162 is cited with two different years across the registry. CrossRef gives 2022 online and 2023 in print; the issue year is used throughout.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Claim 1 is supported. Chandler & Ishak (arXiv 2602.17041, in this corpus) state: ‘even when effect modifiers are shared across treatments, marginal effects are generally population-dependent for commonly used non-collapsible measures, including hazard ratios and odds ratios.’ If the effects being compared are population-dependent, then so is any consistency relation among them. Claim 2 needs a qualifier. It is true of aggregate-data node splitting in netmeta and gemtc, but false as stated for multinma: node-splitting was added in multinma 0.4.0 (consistency=‘nodesplit’) and the same nma() call accepts a regression formula and integration points, so a node-split can be fitted inside a covariate-adjusted ML-NMR where direct and indirect paths are compared at a common covariate profile and estimates can be produced in any target population. Phillippo et al. (2022) do exactly this: ‘We examine residual heterogeneity and inconsistency and relax the shared effect modifier assumption for each covariate in turn.’ What is genuinely open is the evaluation the entry asks for. I found no study quantifying how often standard node splitting flags population mismatch as inconsistency, or how often a compensating mismatch masks true inconsistency, and ML-NMR node splitting reports a conditional inconsistency factor, not a target-population-standardized marginal one. Cites cran:multinma 0.9.1: Node splitting can already be fitted within a covariate-adjusted, population-adjusted ML-NMR, so the two evidence paths are compared after adjustment rather than on raw aggregate contrasts. Feature added in multinma 0.4.0 (2022-01-18).. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162: Demonstrates assessment of inconsistency inside a population-adjusted model with estimates produced for three external target populations..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 is possible, but non-collapsibility alone does not make consistency switch across populations. If each effect is coherently defined as delta_jk(P) = g(mu_k(P)) - g(mu_j(P)) in the same population P, loop consistency telescopes algebraically for every P. Population-varying inconsistency requires different populations along the evidence paths, design-specific effect surfaces, or an inconsistency-by-covariate interaction. C2 is correct for ordinary node splitting, which generally compares estimates from their contributing study populations rather than transporting both paths to an explicit common target. Node splitting is local to a comparison, however, so describing it as a global test is inaccurate. C3 is promising only under consistent estimands, positivity, measured effect modifiers, and correctly specified outcome and transport models; it cannot separate genuine inconsistency from unmeasured population or design differences. At cpaic 9d150e9, relative_effects() evaluates a conditional contrast at one covariate profile and explicitly does not marginally standardize over a target distribution, while NAMESPACE exposes no node-splitting or design-by-treatment diagnostic. The proposed diagnostic therefore remains open in the package.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Node splitting compares paths without standardizing to a target
section: How the evidence falls in time
text:
How the evidence falls in time
17 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2013 to 2023. The most recent paper to touch this reports progress on it, and every paper calling it open is older.
This problem is recurrent: three or more papers spanning at least eight years assert it independently. Sustained restatement by authors who mostly do not cite each other is the strongest evidence this reading can offer that a gap is real rather than one group’s framing.
It is also being closed in pieces: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.
Does the later work answer the earlier work? Put to an independent reviewer with the older and newer claims side by side, it judged that the later work answers a component of it, leaving a named part (high confidence). The 2017 and 2018 regression-based node-splitting work separates discrepancies in treatment effects from discrepancies in treatment-by-covariate coefficients, which meaningfully addresses the original conflation. But these are conditional covariate-value analyses, not standardization of both paths to a target covariate distribution, and they do not quantify the practical frequency or consequences of misclassification. What remains: A direct-versus-indirect diagnostic standardized marginally to a named target population, and empirical evidence on how often conventional node splitting mistakes population mismatch for inconsistency or masks real inconsistency.

title: Diagnostic-driven study deletion in NMA lacks a calibrated rule
text: HET-06 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: Diagnostic-driven study deletion in NMA lacks a calibrated rule
text:
Statement
When a network shows substantial heterogeneity in a contrast or poor fit under the consistency model, one response used in health technology assessment is to delete the offending studies or arms, refit, and repeat until the diagnostics pass, then report the surviving network as the primary result. Detection tooling for this is mature: influence and outlier diagnostics, forward-search monitoring and mixture models all identify which studies drive heterogeneity and inconsistency. What is missing is everything after detection: no stopping criterion for the iteration, no principled ceiling on how much evidence may be removed, no requirement to report which contrasts became data-poor as a result, and no simulation quantifying the bias, interval coverage or ranking distortion that fit-driven deletion introduces. A worked instance in an antidepressant network, deleting until residual deviance plus leverage fell to 3 or less for every study arm, reports 7 changes in direction of effect and 7 changes in statistical significance across the 78 possible contrasts, and in every one of those 7 significance changes the effect became significant only after deletion; the 20 percent exclusion ceiling used to bound the damage is itself acknowledged to be open to the criticism that it is arbitrary. The alternatives to deletion, namely bias-adjusted synthesis, meta-regression on the offending study feature, down-weighting rather than removal, and excluding a whole node, have not been compared against deletion on coverage, bias or agreement with the correct decision. Nothing in a reported credible interval records that the network was selected to be consistent.

title: Diagnostic-driven study deletion in NMA lacks a calibrated rule
text:
Why it is open
Deletion selected by a fit statistic removes exactly the studies that disagree with the rest of the network, so the network is consistent by construction afterward and the estimate is pulled toward the majority of the evidence whether or not the majority is right; the diagnostic that licensed the deletion cannot then be used to check it. Pricing the deletion in the interval is a post-selection inference problem in which the selection event is a sequence of data-dependent refits rather than a single variable-selection step, and the valid post-selection machinery developed for regression has no network analogue. A defensible ceiling would have to be a function of network topology and information contribution rather than a single percentage, because removing a tenth of the studies from a densely connected network and a tenth from a star-shaped one do different amounts of damage, and no work characterizes that dependence. There is also a genuine conflict of requirements: pooling across grossly heterogeneous studies is itself indefensible, so a rule forbidding all deletion is not the answer, and no criterion distinguishes removal that is repair from removal that is selection. The practice leaves no trace in the reported output, so nobody is forced to defend it.

title: Diagnostic-driven study deletion in NMA lacks a calibrated rule
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Reken, Sturtz, Kiefer, Bohler and Wieseler 2016, PLOS ONE
The worked instance and the numbers: stepwise exclusion of studies and arms until residual deviance plus leverage is at most 3 for every study arm, a 20 percent exclusion ceiling conceded to be open to the criticism that it is arbitrary, and 7 changes in direction of effect plus 7 changes in statistical significance across 78 contrasts when the consistent network is compared with the pre-deletion one, all 7 significance changes running toward significance after deletion.


Noma, Gosho, Ishii, Oba and Furukawa 2020, Research Synthesis Methods
Outlier and influence diagnostics for network meta-analysis; supplies the detection half of the problem with no accompanying deletion policy or post-deletion inference.


Petropoulou, Salanti, Rucker, Schwarzer, Moustaki and Mavridis 2021, Statistics in Medicine
Forward search algorithm for detecting extreme study effects in network meta-analysis, with monitoring plots and the NMAoutlier package; explicitly a visual diagnostic that identifies candidate sources of heterogeneity and inconsistency rather than a rule for removing them.


Viechtbauer and Cheung 2010, Research Synthesis Methods
Outlier and influence diagnostics for pairwise meta-analysis; the origin of the tooling, and the source of the standing advice that flagged studies prompt investigation rather than automatic exclusion.


Beath 2014, Research Synthesis Methods
Finite mixture model that accommodates outlying studies by assigning them to a separate component instead of deleting them; a concrete alternative to removal that has never been benchmarked against removal in a network.


Turner, Spiegelhalter, Smith and Thompson 2009, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
Bias-adjusted synthesis with elicited, design-stratified priors for internal and external bias; the down-weighting-by-belief alternative to deletion, defined for meta-analysis and never compared with deletion on decision agreement.


Berk, Brown, Buja, Zhang and Zhao 2013, The Annals of Statistics
Valid post-selection inference for linear models; the framework whose network analogue would price an iterative deletion sequence in the reported interval, and which does not currently extend to selection over which studies to retain.


Salanti, Del Giovane, Chaimani, Caldwell and Higgins 2014, PLOS ONE
Framework for rating the quality of evidence from a network, downgrading for heterogeneity and incoherence; the alternative response in which disagreement lowers confidence in the estimate rather than removing the evidence that produced it.


Nikolakopoulou et al. 2020, PLOS Medicine (CINeMA)
Operationalizes confidence in network estimates with heterogeneity and incoherence as scored domains; a deletion sequence that clears both domains improves the rating without the rating recording that it was cleared by removing evidence.

title: Diagnostic-driven study deletion in NMA lacks a calibrated rule
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Simulate the policies rather than argue about them: generate networks with known heterogeneity and known inconsistency, apply each candidate policy (no deletion, delete until a fit threshold passes, delete at most a fixed fraction, down-weight by influence, model the offending feature as a covariate, bias-adjust with an elicited prior) and report bias, interval coverage, rank stability and agreement with the true decision, broken out by network topology and by whether the flagged studies were genuinely aberrant or merely the minority. That produces the missing object, a stopping criterion with known operating characteristics and a ceiling defined by topology and information contribution rather than by a round percentage. Pending it, make the practice visible: require the full deletion sequence with diagnostics before and after each step, report the pre-deletion estimate alongside the post-deletion one, and label contrasts whose direct evidence was removed. Bootstrapping the entire deletion algorithm, selection included, is the crude but immediate way to obtain an interval that prices the search, and it can be assembled today from existing packages.

title: Diagnostic-driven study deletion in NMA lacks a calibrated rule
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted post-fit deletion as a selection mechanism distinct from evidence-set eligibility and from model-selection uncertainty, while noting that the claim it is standard practice is broader than the single worked example supports. It is partially addressed because detection of influential and outlying studies in networks is published, evaluated and implemented; what has no published rule, stopping criterion or performance evaluation is the deletion policy itself and its cost in coverage.

title: Inconsistency conclusions depend on an uncalibrated heterogeneity error specification

title: Inconsistency conclusions depend on an uncalibrated heterogeneity error specification
text:
Statement
The standard checks for network inconsistency, the design-by-treatment interaction test, generalized Cochran’s Q and node splitting, are conditional on how heterogeneity is specified, because the trial-by-treatment interaction is nested within the design-by-treatment interaction and therefore supplies the error term against which inconsistency is judged. On a single ten-treatment diabetes network of fifteen designs the two defensible specifications give opposite answers: with the trial-by-treatment interaction taken as fixed the inconsistency statistic is chi-squared 22.53 on 7 degrees of freedom, p = 0.0021, and with the same interaction taken as random and Kenward-Roger denominator degrees of freedom the test is F = 0.32 on 7 and 11 degrees of freedom, p = 0.9268. The residual diagnostics reverse with the test: two designs carry conspicuous studentized and PRESS residuals under the fixed specification and unremarkable ones under the random specification. A third specification in common use, dropping the heterogeneity term altogether, changes the effective weighting again, since the fixed specification weights all trials equally while dropping the term weights each trial by the variances of its means. No published criterion, calibration study or simulation says which specification a decision-grade analysis should use. Because consistency status decides whether a pooled network estimate is reported at all, and feeds credibility instruments in which incoherence is a scored domain, the specification is an analyst degree of freedom sitting at the gate and it is not reported as a choice.

title: Inconsistency conclusions depend on an uncalibrated heterogeneity error specification
text:
Why it is open
The specifications encode genuinely different positions about what heterogeneity is, a nuisance to be conditioned on or a random error term against which design differences should be judged, and both are defensible in the abstract, so the question cannot be settled by argument and has to be settled by operating characteristics that nobody has computed. Calibrating them means simulating networks with known inconsistency and known heterogeneity and reporting type I error and power for each specification, which is straightforward and unglamorous; it also requires deciding what error rate is acceptable for a test whose consequence is refusing to pool, and the field has never stated one. The random specification carries an estimated variance component into the reference distribution, so its small-sample behavior depends on the denominator degrees-of-freedom approximation as well as on the specification, and those two sources have not been separated. Heterogeneity and inconsistency are also not cleanly separable in a sparse network, so at realistic sizes the specifications compete for the same variation and any calibration will be topology-dependent rather than universal.

title: Inconsistency conclusions depend on an uncalibrated heterogeneity error specification
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Piepho 2014, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Formulates network meta-analysis as a factorial analysis of variance and demonstrates the reversal on the Senn diabetes network: inconsistency chi-squared 22.53 on 7 degrees of freedom with heterogeneity fixed against F = 0.32 on 7 and 11 degrees of freedom with the same effects random, with the studentized and PRESS residuals for two designs conspicuous under the first and unremarkable under the second, and states a preference rather than a calibration.


Piepho, Williams and Madden 2012, Biometrics
The two-way linear mixed model formulation of multitreatment meta-analysis in which the nesting of the heterogeneity interaction inside the inconsistency interaction is explicit, and in which fixed or random is an ordinary model option.


Higgins, Jackson, Barrett, Lu, Ades and White 2012, Research Synthesis Methods
Defines the design-by-treatment interaction model, the global inconsistency framework whose test statistic the heterogeneity specification determines.


White, Barrett, Jackson and Higgins 2012, Research Synthesis Methods
Estimates the design-by-treatment model by multivariate meta-regression, where the same fixed-versus-random heterogeneity choice appears as a fitting option with no guidance on which to select.


Jackson, Barrett, Rice, White and Higgins 2014, Statistics in Medicine
Design-by-treatment interaction model with random inconsistency effects, adding a second variance component and therefore a second specification choice on top of the one this entry concerns.


Dias, Welton, Caldwell and Ades 2010, Statistics in Medicine
Node splitting, the local consistency check that inherits the same dependence, since the direct and indirect estimates it compares are both conditioned on the assumed heterogeneity structure.


Krahn, Binder and Konig 2013, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Net-heat plot for locating inconsistency in a network under a baseline-contrast parameterization; the analysis of the same diabetes network whose fixed-specification statistic the reversal reproduces, which is what establishes that the disagreement is about specification rather than about parameterization.


Veroniki, Vasiliadis, Higgins and Salanti 2013, International Journal of Epidemiology
Applies competing inconsistency evaluation methods across many published networks and reports how often each flags inconsistency; the closest thing to an empirical calibration, and it varies the method rather than the heterogeneity specification.


Kenward and Roger 1997, Biometrics
Small-sample approximation to the denominator degrees of freedom for Wald-type F statistics from restricted maximum likelihood fits; the correction the random specification depends on, whose contribution to the reversal has not been separated from the specification’s own.


Nikolakopoulou et al. 2020, PLOS Medicine (CINeMA)
Confidence framework in which incoherence is a scored domain taking the inconsistency assessment as an input; establishes that the undisclosed specification choice propagates into a published confidence rating.


Dias, Welton, Sutton, Caldwell, Lu and Ades 2013, Medical Decision Making
Decision-making guidance on inconsistency in networks of randomized trials; sets out the checks a submission is expected to run without specifying the heterogeneity structure under which they are to be run.

title: Inconsistency conclusions depend on an uncalibrated heterogeneity error specification
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Run the calibration: simulate networks over a grid of topology, studies per design, true heterogeneity and true inconsistency, and report type I error and power for the design-by-treatment test with the heterogeneity term taken as fixed, as random, and omitted, with and without the Kenward-Roger correction, so the choice can rest on measured error rates. Report the same curves for node splitting, which inherits the specification through the same error term. Convert the result into a default with a stated condition, for instance the random specification whenever the heterogeneity variance is estimable and the fixed specification only below a stated number of studies per design, and require the analysis plan to name the specification before the data are seen. Where specifications disagree on real data the honest output is both results together with the statement that consistency status is not determined by the evidence, rather than the one the analyst prefers; a sensitivity display of the inconsistency p-value across specifications is a small addition to existing software and would make the degree of freedom visible immediately.

title: Inconsistency conclusions depend on an uncalibrated heterogeneity error specification
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as a well-posed operating-characteristics problem, since the heterogeneity specification changes the reference distribution and the practical conclusion of a global inconsistency assessment, which is distinct from the untestability of consistency itself. The reversal is demonstrated on one network in one paper, a narrow empirical base for how often the specifications disagree, though sufficient for the claim that no calibration of their error rates exists.

title: No calibrated small-study interval method for population-adjusted NMA
text:
Statement
Random-effects inference in multivariate and contrast-based network meta-analysis rests on a large-sample approximation in the number of studies, and it fails when that number is small: across 24 scenarios with 8, 12 and 16 studies, coverage of extended DerSimonian-Laird, maximum likelihood and restricted maximum likelihood confidence regions fell materially below the nominal 95 percent, worst for joint inference and, among marginal inferences, at small study counts with large heterogeneity. Exact permutation regions repair this for aggregate-data multivariate and contrast-based models. The repair does not carry to population-adjusted synthesis: a network fed by matching-adjusted or simulated treatment comparison estimates, or fitted as multilevel network meta-regression, combines estimated weights or a fitted outcome surface with a handful of studies, so the exchangeability under permutation of study labels that the exact method needs does not hold, and weights estimated from one individual-patient dataset supply several contrasts at once. Variance estimation for a single matching-adjusted comparison has been benchmarked across 108 scenarios, with sample size, population overlap and outcome type identified as what decides whether a given estimator is adequate, but that is a within-comparison question and says nothing about the interval for a network estimate assembled from few such comparisons under heterogeneity. No published work reports the realized coverage of population-adjusted network intervals as a function of the number of studies, and no exact, permutation-based or small-sample-calibrated alternative has been derived for that setting. Population-adjusted networks are where study counts are smallest, commonly two to a dozen trials, so this is the regime the methods are used in rather than an edge case.

title: No calibrated small-study interval method for population-adjusted NMA
text:
Why it is open
The permutation argument needs a null under which study-level contributions are exchangeable, and a two-stage weighting workflow breaks it structurally, because the weights are estimated from one individual-patient dataset that supplies several contrasts, so the studies are not independent units and permuting their labels does not leave the null distribution unchanged. A one-stage mixed-granularity likelihood does not obviously possess the symmetry either, since individual-level and aggregate-level studies enter through different terms and are not interchangeable. Bayesian population-adjusted intervals do not escape by construction, because with a handful of studies the heterogeneity variance is determined by its prior, so the interval inherits a choice rather than the data. The natural fallbacks from pairwise meta-analysis, the Hartung-Knapp adjustment and its relatives, have no derivation for a network whose inputs carry estimated weights, and importing them would produce an interval of unknown coverage in exactly the situation where coverage is the question. Measuring the problem is cheap and nobody has done it, which is the more awkward half: the realized coverage of population-adjusted network intervals as a function of the number of studies is a simulation, not a theorem.

title: No calibrated small-study interval method for population-adjusted NMA
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Noma, Nagashima and Furukawa 2020, Biometrics
Demonstrates serious undercoverage of extended DerSimonian-Laird, maximum likelihood and restricted maximum likelihood confidence regions across 24 scenarios at 8, 12 and 16 studies, and supplies exact permutation-based joint and marginal inference for multivariate meta-analysis and contrast-based network meta-analysis; the remedy that does not transfer to estimated-weight settings.


Chandler and Proskorovsky 2024, Research Synthesis Methods
Monte Carlo comparison of variance estimators across 108 anchored and unanchored matching-adjusted indirect comparison scenarios, covering conventional estimators with raw and with effective-sample-size weights, sandwich estimators with and without finite-sample adjustment, and bootstrap variants, and finding that raw-weight conventional estimators understate variability under poor overlap while bootstrapping is unstable at small sample sizes; settles the single-comparison part of the problem and leaves the few-studies network part untouched.


IntHout, Ioannidis and Borm 2014, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Shows the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method substantially outperforms DerSimonian-Laird for random-effects meta-analysis with few studies; the small-study interval fix that has no population-adjusted network analogue.


Noma, Nagashima, Maruo, Gosho and Furukawa 2018, Statistics in Medicine
Bartlett-type corrections and bootstrap adjustments to likelihood-based inference for network meta-analysis; the other small-sample route for aggregate-data networks, likewise derived without estimated weights or a mixed-granularity likelihood.


Higgins and Thompson 2004, Statistics in Medicine
Permutation approach to meta-regression to control spurious findings from few studies; the origin of the exchangeability argument that population adjustment breaks.


Phillippo et al. 2020, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
Multilevel network meta-regression, the one-stage mixed-granularity likelihood in which individual and aggregate studies enter through different terms; its small-sample interval behavior as a function of the number of studies has not been studied.


Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2021, Research Synthesis Methods
Review and simulation study of population adjustment with limited individual patient data, reporting bias and precision for the competing estimators; does not report coverage as a function of the number of studies in a network, which is the quantity at issue.


Remiro-Azocar 2022, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Two-stage matching-adjusted indirect comparison, which separates weight estimation from outcome modeling; the workflow whose estimated weights and reused individual-patient data destroy the permutation symmetry the exact method needs.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Medical Decision Making
Methods guidance for population-adjusted indirect comparisons in health technology appraisal; establishes that these comparisons are routinely built from very few studies, which is the regime in which the asymptotic interval is never justified.

title: No calibrated small-study interval method for population-adjusted NMA
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Measure first: simulate population-adjusted networks over the number of studies from two upward, the number of individual-patient studies, population overlap and heterogeneity, and report realized coverage and interval width for the intervals actually used, namely sandwich and bootstrap matching-adjusted contrasts combined in a network and credible intervals from multilevel network meta-regression under standard heterogeneity priors. Then derive the calibration: the promising route is a bootstrap that resamples at the level of the study and re-estimates the weights inside each replicate, giving a null that respects the dependence a naive permutation destroys, together with a Hartung-Knapp-style variance inflation whose degrees of freedom account for the estimated weights. Establish whether any permutation scheme is exact for the one-stage mixed-granularity likelihood, because if none is, the field should stop waiting for one and calibrate approximations instead. Report everything by number of studies rather than averaged over it, since the small-count regime is the point of the exercise, and state a minimum study count below which no population-adjusted network interval should be presented as calibrated.

title: No calibrated small-study interval method for population-adjusted NMA
text:
Our study

Interval coverage for population-adjusted synthesis with few studies
The question put to it. How does interval coverage of population-adjusted random-effects synthesis depend on the number of studies, when one individual-data trial supplies the adjusted contrast for several aggregate trials?
What it found. Coverage fails in two ways. Meta-analyzing per-trial adjusted contrasts that reuse one individual-data trial as if independent lost coverage as trials were added (down to 0.55 at twelve trials with DerSimonian-Laird), because the shared error does not average out. Pooling the aggregate trials first and subtracting the transported contrast once fixed that; with DerSimonian-Laird it stayed within 0.93 to 0.97 from four trials, and Hartung-Knapp was conservative (up to 1.00) at two or three.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: coverage at two to four trials was 0.774 to 0.888 for the per-trial analysis and 0.909 to 0.962 for the two-step DerSimonian-Laird analysis.
Minimum trial count with coverage 0.93 to 0.97 at every heterogeneity level: 4 for two-step DerSimonian-Laird; none for the per-trial analyses or two-step Hartung-Knapp.
Per-trial analysis coverage fell with the number of trials even without heterogeneity.

Design.

Estimand

B versus A mean difference in the target population

Methods compared

per-trial adjusted contrasts, DerSimonian-Laird, per-trial adjusted contrasts, Hartung-Knapp, two-step, DerSimonian-Laird, two-step, Hartung-Knapp

Data-generating mechanism

One individual-data trial transported by MAIC and 2 to 12 aggregate trials with heterogeneity; naive and two-step random-effects analyses with DerSimonian-Laird or Hartung-Knapp intervals. 18 cells, 2000 replicates each.

Replicates

2000 per scenario, 36,000 in total


What this does not answer. Pairwise synthesis with one individual-data trial; continuous outcome; no one-stage or Bayesian analysis; one overlap level. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: No empirical prior exists for residual heterogeneity after covariate adjustment
text:
Statement
The empirically derived predictive distributions that supply informative heterogeneity priors describe unadjusted random-effects heterogeneity: Turner et al. 2012 built them from 14,886 Cochrane meta-analyses, Turner et al. 2015 published 80 log-normal distributions for binary outcomes indexed by outcome type and comparison type, and Rhodes et al. 2015 did the same on the standardized mean difference scale. Network meta-regression and multilevel network meta-regression estimate a residual heterogeneity after conditioning on a specific covariate set, which is a different quantity whose plausible magnitude depends on which covariates were adjusted for. No empirical distribution exists for that residual, and no principle deflates an unadjusted distribution by the adjustment made. Turner et al. 2018 state that the same prior machinery carries to network meta-regression but that prior evidence for the residual is unlikely to be available, and note that reusing an unadjusted empirical distribution is conservative in only one direction, supporting larger heterogeneity than necessary. Population-adjusted network methods inherit the problem in full, since ML-NMR fits a single network-wide residual tau alongside the interaction model. The analyst is therefore left choosing between a prior known to be too diffuse and a vague prior that leaves the residual variance close to unidentified in exactly the sparse networks where adjustment is used.

title: No empirical prior exists for residual heterogeneity after covariate adjustment
text:
Why it is open
The residual is defined relative to a covariate set chosen anew in every analysis, so there is no single target quantity around which a corpus can be indexed; a database organized by outcome type and comparison type would additionally have to be organized by adjustment set, and adjustment sets are not comparable across reviews. The empirical ratio of adjusted to unadjusted heterogeneity cannot be recovered from the published literature at scale, because meta-regressions rarely report both variances side by side, so the corpus would have to be built by refitting rather than by extraction. Study-level meta-regressions are fitted with few studies, so each adjusted tau estimate is itself imprecise, and a predictive distribution assembled from such estimates is a distribution of noise unless the extraction model is hierarchical. The conservative fallback is not neutral either: an over-diffuse heterogeneity prior widens intervals and weakens shrinkage, which is not uniformly the safe direction once the output feeds a decision rule.

title: No empirical prior exists for residual heterogeneity after covariate adjustment
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Turner, Dominguez-Islas, Jackson, Rhodes and White 2019, Statistics in Medicine
Builds four ways of attaching externally derived informative priors to heterogeneity variances in a network, and states in its discussion that the same approaches apply to network meta-regression but that prior evidence for the residual heterogeneity after adjustment for a specific covariate combination is unlikely to be available, with the unadjusted distributions serving only as a conservative substitute.


Turner, Davey, Clarke, Thompson and Higgins 2012, International Journal of Epidemiology
Derives predictive distributions for between-study heterogeneity from 14,886 meta-analyses in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, indexed by outcome type and intervention comparison type; this is the corpus method that would have to be repeated for an adjusted parameter.


Turner, Jackson, Wei, Thompson and Higgins 2015, Statistics in Medicine
Publishes log-normal predictive distributions for heterogeneity in 80 settings defined by outcome and comparison type, usable directly as priors; these are the unadjusted distributions currently reused in adjusted models.


Rhodes, Turner and Higgins 2015, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
Supplies the corresponding predictive distributions for continuous outcomes on the standardized mean difference scale, extending the coverage of the unadjusted corpus without addressing adjustment.


Rhodes, Turner, White, Jackson, Spiegelhalter and Higgins 2016, Statistics in Medicine
Gives a pseudo-data device for implementing informative log-normal heterogeneity priors inside standard meta-analysis and meta-regression software; it transfers the priors into a regression setting but does not recalibrate them for the adjustment.


Dias, Sutton, Welton and Ades 2013, Medical Decision Making (NICE DSU TSD 3)
The standard applied account of network meta-regression and of residual heterogeneity after covariate adjustment; it defines the parameter whose prior is missing without supplying evidence about its magnitude.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades, Belger, Brnabic, Schacht, Saure, Kadziola and Welton 2020, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
Defines multilevel network meta-regression, which fits an individual-level regression with treatment-covariate interactions and a single network-wide residual heterogeneity term; the parameter that needs the missing prior in the population-adjusted setting.


Rover, Bender, Dias, Schmid, Schmidli, Sturtz, Weber and Friede 2021, Research Synthesis Methods
Guidance on weakly informative heterogeneity priors when very few studies contribute, the current fallback when an empirical prior is judged inapplicable; it is calibrated for unadjusted heterogeneity as well.

title: No empirical prior exists for residual heterogeneity after covariate adjustment
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the missing evidence by refitting rather than by extraction: take a sample of published networks and pairwise meta-analyses that carry the covariates needed for meta-regression, fit each with and without adjustment under matched weakly informative priors, and report the distribution of the ratio of residual to unadjusted heterogeneity, stratified by the kind of adjustment (a single study-level covariate, baseline risk, a patient-level effect modifier in ML-NMR). Fit that extraction hierarchically so each network’s imprecision is carried into the predictive distribution rather than averaged away, and validate the resulting deflation factor by leave-one-network-out prediction against both the unadjusted prior and a vague prior. Until that exists, make prior sensitivity a reporting requirement for adjusted networks: fit with the unadjusted empirical prior, a deflated version of it, and a weakly informative prior, and report how far the treatment contrasts and the interval widths move. Because the residual variance also absorbs unmodeled inconsistency, estimate the deflation inside models that keep heterogeneity and inconsistency separate, otherwise the deflation factor will be contaminated by whatever inconsistency the adjustment failed to explain.

title: No empirical prior exists for residual heterogeneity after covariate adjustment
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it on the ground that the quoted passage distinguishes residual heterogeneity after a specified covariate adjustment from the unadjusted empirical distributions used for existing priors. The evidence is a single paper, which is a weaker basis, but that paper is the state of the art for external heterogeneity priors in networks and names the absence itself.

title: No evidence base or reporting rule governs the heterogeneity versus inconsistency split
text: HET-14 Partially addressed Medium-high priority Established Tractability 4/5

title: No evidence base or reporting rule governs the heterogeneity versus inconsistency split
text:
Statement
In a network meta-analysis with random inconsistency effects the excess variation must be apportioned between a between-study heterogeneity variance and an inconsistency variance, and three classical estimators are available to do it: a generalization of DerSimonian and Laird, a generalization of Paule and Mandel, and REML. Which one is used can change the apportionment qualitatively. On a network of nine cognitive enhancers for Alzheimer’s dementia with 41 studies, Paule-Mandel returns 0.51 for heterogeneity and 0.91 for inconsistency, REML returns 0.68 and 0.54 with profile-likelihood intervals of (0.31, 1.55) and (0, 2.94), and DerSimonian-Laird returns 1.20 and zero, so the fitted model collapses to the consistency model and produces markedly smaller standard errors for the treatment effects. On an osteoarthritis-of-the-knee network Paule-Mandel returns a heterogeneity variance of 0.35 while DerSimonian-Laird and REML both return 0.18, and the Paule-Mandel value lies above the REML profile-likelihood interval of (0.09, 0.31). REML is nominated as the gold standard and Paule-Mandel as a semiparametric sensitivity analysis, but no simulation or empirical study establishes in which networks the decomposition is estimator-sensitive, and no reporting convention requires the alternatives to be shown. Since an estimated zero inconsistency variance is read in practice as a license to pool, an estimator-dependent zero is a decision-relevant artifact rather than a nuance.

title: No evidence base or reporting rule governs the heterogeneity versus inconsistency split
text:
Why it is open
The two components are weakly separated by construction: the inconsistency variance is informed only by the loops, of which a typical network has few, so the likelihood surface has a near-flat ridge along which heterogeneity and inconsistency trade off, and different estimating equations settle at different points on it. The mature evidence on variance estimators, including the comprehensive review of between-study variance methods and the large simulation comparing them, concerns a single variance in pairwise meta-analysis, and the ordering it produces does not transfer to a two-component decomposition where the second component is boundary-prone. The people who generalized the estimators state that the large-scale simulation and empirical investigation needed to turn the observation into guidance is beyond the scope of a methods paper and encourage others to do it, and no one has; the models involved are still uncommon in applied practice, so there is no user base demanding the answer. Guidance would also have to settle what an analyst does when the estimators disagree, which is a reporting question with no natural home in an estimation paper.

title: No evidence base or reporting rule governs the heterogeneity versus inconsistency split
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Jackson, Veroniki, Law, Tricco and Baker 2017, Research Synthesis Methods
Extends the Paule-Mandel estimator to network meta-analysis with random inconsistency effects, applies all three classical estimators to four networks, documents the qualitative disagreements including a collapse to the consistency model under DerSimonian-Laird, recommends REML as the gold standard with Paule-Mandel as a sensitivity analysis, and states that the simulation and large-scale empirical work needed is beyond its scope.


Law, Jackson, Turner, Rhodes and Viechtbauer 2016, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Provides the Bayesian importance-sampling route and the REML plus profile-likelihood route for the same two-variance model, including the code used to compute the intervals against which the semiparametric estimates are judged.


Jackson, Barrett, Rice, White and Higgins 2014, Statistics in Medicine
Defines the model and the original method-of-moments estimator that the DerSimonian-Laird generalization implements, so it fixes what is being estimated in each component.


Higgins, Jackson, Barrett, Lu, Ades and White 2012, Research Synthesis Methods
The design-by-treatment interaction model that gives inconsistency its own variance component, and the framework within which the split is defined for multi-arm studies.


White, Barrett, Jackson and Higgins 2012, Research Synthesis Methods
Estimates the same consistency and inconsistency structure by multivariate meta-regression, giving a fourth estimation route whose behavior in the decomposition has likewise not been compared with the others.


Veroniki, Jackson, Viechtbauer, Bender, Bowden, Knapp, Kuss, Higgins, Langan and Salanti 2016, Research Synthesis Methods
Reviews the available estimators of the between-study variance and its uncertainty in pairwise meta-analysis and issues recommendations; the univariate template whose conclusions do not settle the two-component case.


Langan, Higgins, Jackson, Bowden, Veroniki, Kontopantelis, Viechtbauer and Simmonds 2019, Research Synthesis Methods
The large simulation comparing heterogeneity variance estimators in pairwise meta-analysis; the design that the missing network study would extend to a two-variance decomposition.


Jackson, White and Riley 2013, Biometrical Journal
The matrix-based method of moments for multivariate random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression that the network DerSimonian-Laird estimator generalizes, which is where its boundary behavior originates.

title: No evidence base or reporting rule governs the heterogeneity versus inconsistency split
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Run the simulation that was deferred: vary the number of designs, the number of independent loops, the replication within designs, and the true pair of variances including boundary cases where one is zero, and report for each estimator the bias in each component, the frequency of a spurious zero inconsistency variance, the coverage of the treatment-effect intervals that follow, and how often the three estimators disagree about whether inconsistency is present. Pair it with an empirical pass over a database of published networks reporting how often the three disagree about a zero and how far the treatment-effect standard errors move when they do. Turn the result into a reporting rule rather than a single recommendation, since the informative output is whether the pooling decision is invariant to the estimator: report all three decompositions, or report REML with a profile-likelihood interval for the inconsistency variance so that a zero is presented with its uncertainty instead of as a point. Extending profile-likelihood or bootstrap intervals to the semiparametric estimators is the enabling step, since at present only the likelihood route can attach an interval to either component.

title: No evidence base or reporting rule governs the heterogeneity versus inconsistency split
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it because alternative standard estimators demonstrably change the decomposition and the resulting uncertainty. It is scored partially-addressed rather than confirmed-open because a weak ordering does exist, REML as gold standard with Paule-Mandel as a semiparametric sensitivity analysis, and the estimator-comparison literature for a single variance is mature; what is absent is any evidence on the two-variance decomposition and any convention for reporting sensitivity to the choice.
