title: Exchangeable and comparison-specific heterogeneity priors are blocked by the covariance constraint
text: HET-16 Confirmed open Medium-high priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: Exchangeable and comparison-specific heterogeneity priors are blocked by the covariance constraint
text:
Statement
Letting between-study heterogeneity variances differ across comparisons in a network requires the induced random-effects covariance matrix to remain positive semidefinite, the condition Lu and Ades call second-order consistency, because the variance of a contrast not involving the reference treatment is a function of two diagonal entries and their covariance. Four structures have been built under that constraint: one common variance; proportional variances whose prior means differ by comparison type; separate priors on the variances together with a prior on the correlations, whose hyperparameters are found by numerically solving a nonlinear moment-matching system; and an informative Wishart prior on the precision matrix. Two structures that a sparse network most needs are still unavailable. An exchangeable model that borrows heterogeneity information across comparisons has no known specification that also meets second-order consistency, and a model in which each comparison receives its own externally derived informative prior cannot be delivered by the Wishart route, whose moments cannot be matched comparison by comparison, and can be delivered by the separate-prior route only by solving a fresh moment-matching system for every new network. The setting where this matters is the ordinary one: in the reference review of network characteristics the median network holds 21 studies with a median of 2 studies per comparison, so per-comparison heterogeneity is essentially uninformed by the data and has to come from outside.

title: Exchangeable and comparison-specific heterogeneity priors are blocked by the covariance constraint
text:
Why it is open
The constraint is a joint condition on the whole covariance matrix while both missing structures are specified marginally. An exchangeable hierarchical prior on the comparison-specific variances, and a set of separate external priors on them, both place distributions on quantities that are constrained functions of the underlying matrix, and no construction is known that induces prescribed marginals for those quantities while guaranteeing the matrix stays positive semidefinite. The routes that do guarantee validity either fix the borrowing strength through a single degrees-of-freedom parameter, as the Wishart family does, or make the induced marginals an awkward function of the parameterization, so matching them to published targets requires numerical solution network by network, which is the impracticality that keeps the approach out of applied use. Because the parameter is close to unidentified in the networks concerned, a wrong variance structure does not show up in the fit, which removes the empirical pressure that would otherwise force the construction to be found. Any solution also has to be implementable by applied analysts in general-purpose samplers rather than merely derivable, which is a stiffer requirement than the derivation itself.

title: Exchangeable and comparison-specific heterogeneity priors are blocked by the covariance constraint
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Turner, Dominguez-Islas, Jackson, Rhodes and White 2019, Statistics in Medicine
Builds and compares the four approaches to informative priors for multiple heterogeneity variances under second-order consistency, and states in its discussion both that it is not clear how to assume exchangeability while meeting the requirement and that an approach allowing unequal variances with different informative priors would be desirable but is not available.


Lu and Ades 2009, Biostatistics
Models between-trial variance structure in mixed treatment comparisons and establishes the second-order consistency condition that any unequal-variance structure must satisfy; the constraint that blocks both missing structures.


Lu and Ades 2004, Statistics in Medicine
Defines the contrast-based mixed treatment comparison model in which heterogeneity variances attach to comparisons rather than arms, fixing the parameters whose priors are at issue.


Thorlund, Thabane and Mills 2013, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Builds and compares four replacements for the homogeneous variance assumption, including exchangeable and consistency-constrained variance structures and two informative variance-prior schemes, evaluated on two illustrative datasets; the earlier attempt at the same problem, without external predictive distributions attached comparison by comparison.


Turner, Jackson, Wei, Thompson and Higgins 2015, Statistics in Medicine
Supplies the 80 predictive distributions by outcome and comparison type that a comparison-specific prior structure would attach edge by edge; the external evidence that currently cannot be used at that granularity.


Rhodes, Turner and Higgins 2015, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
The corresponding predictive distributions for continuous outcomes, extending the set of external priors that the missing structure would need to accommodate.


Rhodes, Turner, White, Jackson, Spiegelhalter and Higgins 2016, Statistics in Medicine
A pseudo-data device for implementing informative lognormal heterogeneity priors in standard software, which addresses the implementation half of the problem for a single variance but not the joint validity constraint for many.


Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe 2009, Journal of Multivariate Analysis
Vine and onion constructions for random correlation matrices, the separation-strategy machinery that would let a valid covariance be built from standard deviations and a correlation matrix with a tunable borrowing structure.


Nikolakopoulou, Chaimani, Veroniki, Vasiliadis, Schmid and Salanti 2014, PLoS ONE
The description of 186 published networks that supplies the median of 21 studies per network and 2 studies per comparison, which is why per-comparison heterogeneity cannot be estimated from within the network.

title: Exchangeable and comparison-specific heterogeneity priors are blocked by the covariance constraint
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Attack the construction rather than the constraint: parameterize the covariance by the separation strategy, a vector of standard deviations for the reference contrasts and a correlation matrix under a vine or onion prior, then derive by simulation-based calibration the map from that parameterization to the marginals of the comparison-specific variances, and choose hyperparameters so those marginals match the published predictive distributions. Tabulate the solution once per network size and comparison-type pattern so an analyst does not solve a nonlinear system for every new network, which is the step that currently makes the approach impractical. For exchangeability, place the hierarchy on the parameters of the valid construction rather than on the constrained variances themselves, and measure by simulation how much borrowing that actually achieves relative to a common variance. Evaluate all of it on the criteria a decision cares about, interval coverage for treatment contrasts and how often the ranking changes, at network sizes drawn from the empirical distribution, and ship the survivor in multinma or netmeta, since a structure that has to be hand-coded will not be used.

One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it because the cited source expressly identifies both exchangeability under second-order consistency and comparison-specific informative priors as unresolved. The evidence is a single paper, but it is the state of the art for the problem and the two gaps are named in its own discussion rather than inferred.

title: Arm-based between-treatment correlations are imposed as exchangeable with no way to test or vary the structure
text: HET-18 Confirmed open Medium-high priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: Arm-based between-treatment correlations are imposed as exchangeable with no way to test or vary the structure
text:
Statement
Arm-based network meta-analysis models the study-specific treatment effects as a multivariate normal vector whose covariance carries a correlation matrix among treatments. In practice that matrix is forced to be exchangeable, a single scalar shared by every treatment pair, because typical networks are too sparse to identify unequal correlations, and the prior on the scalar is bounded below at minus one over the number of treatments minus one so the matrix stays positive definite. The restriction is consequential rather than technical, because the correlation governs how much absolute-effect information is borrowed across arms and therefore how much relative effects are shrunk: moving it within its own posterior range flips the interval conclusion for 13 of 112 treatment pairs, 11.6%, across 14 real networks, and moves the point estimate by more than 15% for 29 pairs, 25.9%. The posterior median correlation across those 14 networks runs from 0.266 to 0.996, so the shared scalar is neither near-constant across settings nor pinned at a boundary, and the default cannot be defended as harmless. No method estimates, screens or performs sensitivity analysis over a heterogeneous correlation structure in a sparse network, and no evidence establishes how large or how well connected a network must be before competing correlation structures can be distinguished at all.

title: Arm-based between-treatment correlations are imposed as exchangeable with no way to test or vary the structure
text:
Why it is open
The correlation is only weakly informed by the data in exactly the networks where arm-based models are most attractive, star-shaped or thinly connected ones, so a richer structure is at best nominally identified and its posterior is driven by the prior rather than by the evidence. Any structured alternative must keep the covariance positive definite, which restricts what can even be posed: block correlations by class, or correlations decaying with some notion of treatment distance, are not automatically valid matrices and need constructions rather than declarations. Screening for a heterogeneous structure requires a model comparison whose power at realistic network sizes has never been established, so a null result from such a screen currently cannot be interpreted as evidence that exchangeability holds. The restriction is understood rather than overlooked: it is named as the first limitation of the tipping-point method and attributed explicitly to sparse data, which means the obstacle is identification and not oversight.

title: Arm-based between-treatment correlations are imposed as exchangeable with no way to test or vary the structure
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Wang, Murray, Han, Lin, Siegel and Chu 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Develops a Bayesian tipping-point analysis for the shared correlation parameter in arm-based network meta-analysis, reports tipping points in 13 of 112 treatment pairs for interval conclusions and 29 for magnitude change across 14 networks with posterior median correlations from 0.266 to 0.996, and names the exchangeable structure as its first limitation, attributed to sparse data.


Han, Wang, Xiao, He, Chu and Lin 2024, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Tipping-point analysis for the between-arm correlation in a two-arm arm-based evidence synthesis, the precursor that fixed the sensitivity-analysis format later carried to networks.


Zhang, Carlin, Neaton, Soon, Nie, Kane, Virnig and Chu 2014, Clinical Trials
Sets out the arm-based network meta-analysis formulation with a correlated multivariate random-effects vector across treatments, which is where the correlation matrix at issue is introduced.


Hong, Chu, Zhang and Carlin 2016, Research Synthesis Methods
A Bayesian missing-data framework for generalized arm-based mixed treatment comparisons, extending the same covariance structure to multiple outcomes and making the correlation assumption load-bearing for more parameters.


Wang, Lin, Hodges and Chu 2020, Statistics in Medicine
Examines how the choice of covariance prior affects arm-based Bayesian network meta-analysis with binary outcomes, which establishes that the covariance specification is influential but keeps the exchangeable structure fixed.


Wang, Lin, Hodges, MacLehose and Chu 2021, Statistical Methods in Medical Research
A variance shrinkage method for arm-based Bayesian network meta-analysis, the current answer to sparse estimation of the standard deviations, with the correlation still handled by a single shared parameter.


Lin, Zhang, Hodges and Chu 2017, Journal of Statistical Software
The pcnetmeta implementation of arm-based network meta-analysis, which fixes the exchangeable correlation as what an applied analyst can actually fit.


White, Turner, Karahalios and Salanti 2019, Statistics in Medicine
Compares arm-based and contrast-based network models and shows where their assumptions diverge, which locates the correlation parameter as a structure with no contrast-based analogue and therefore no borrowed evidence base.


Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe 2009, Journal of Multivariate Analysis
Vine and onion constructions for random correlation matrices, the machinery available for posing a structured alternative that is positive definite by construction rather than by constraint checking.


Lu and Ades 2009, Biostatistics
The contrast-based analogue of structuring the between-trial covariance under a validity constraint, which shows both the form the arm-based work would take and how long the corresponding contrast-side question has been open.

title: Arm-based between-treatment correlations are imposed as exchangeable with no way to test or vary the structure
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Establish distinguishability first, because without it neither a screen nor a structured fit can be interpreted: simulate arm-based networks under known heterogeneous structures, block correlations by treatment class, a single outlying treatment, and decay with treatment distance, and report the number of studies, treatments and loops at which a model comparison separates them from exchangeable at useful power. Pose the alternatives through the separation strategy, putting a vine or onion prior on the correlation matrix with a hierarchical or class-blocked mean, so positive definiteness holds by construction and the borrowing strength is not controlled by a single degrees-of-freedom parameter. Extend the tipping-point analysis from a scalar to a structure, reporting which treatment pairs’ conclusions are sensitive to relaxing exchangeability rather than only to moving a common correlation. Make the sensitivity output a default of the arm-based packages, since an analysis that reports only the exchangeable fit gives its reader no way to see that one interval conclusion in nine is at stake.

One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it because the between-study correlation structure in arm-based models is distinct from within-study multi-arm covariance and from a common heterogeneity variance. The evidence is a single paper, which is a weaker basis, but it quantifies the decision impact across 14 networks and names the restriction as its own first limitation.

title: The design-by-treatment inconsistency test has no small-sample null
text: HET-20 Confirmed open High priority Established Tractability 4/5

title: The design-by-treatment inconsistency test has no small-sample null
text:
Statement
The design-by-treatment interaction model is the standard global consistency check in network meta-analysis, and it is applied by referring a Wald statistic for all inconsistency parameters to a chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to their number. That reference distribution is derived treating the within-design heterogeneity variance as known, so its accuracy improves as the degrees of freedom rise and as within-design heterogeneity falls; the failure is therefore directional, since with few degrees of freedom and appreciable within-design heterogeneity a small p-value read as evidence of inconsistency can be an artifact of the approximation rather than a direct-indirect conflict. The configuration that would make the approximation safe is not the one real networks have: across 201 published networks the median number of loops was three and the median number of inconsistency parameters four, 186 of 201 networks (92.5 percent) contained at least one comparison informed by a single study, and the test returned p below 0.05 in 14 percent of networks and below 0.10 in 20 percent (Veroniki et al. 2021, doi:10.1186/s12874-021-01401-y). No corrected null, small-sample or resampling calibration, or reported type I error rate exists for the test as it is run in netmeta and in the Stata network suite. The nearest measurement covers a different regime: false-positive rates of 15.2 to 22.8 percent were reported for the graph-theoretical between-designs Q statistic at a nominal 0.20 level, but only for networks of at most five treatments with five two-arm studies per direct comparison and tau-squared fixed at 0.01 or 0.1 (Kiefer et al. 2020, doi:10.1186/s12874-020-0917-3), which is the well-determined end of the range rather than the sparse, heterogeneous end where the approximation is suspect. This is a different problem from the documented low power of global inconsistency tests, which concerns false negatives under a correct null; what is unknown here is whether the null holds at all.

title: The design-by-treatment inconsistency test has no small-sample null
text:
Why it is open
The statistic’s distribution depends on a nuisance parameter, the within-design heterogeneity variance, that is estimated and then conditioned on as though known, and it is least well determined precisely when designs contribute one or two studies each, so the approximation error is largest where the test is most used. Refinements for exactly this difficulty exist one level up, in multivariate meta-analysis and meta-regression with an estimated between-study covariance matrix (Jackson and Riley 2013, doi:10.1002/sim.5957), but nobody has carried them into the design-by-treatment decomposition or shown what they cost in effective degrees of freedom when the number of designs is small. Simulation work on network consistency screening has scored decision rates for a menu of statistics rather than the null calibration of any one of them, so the type I error rate of the design-by-treatment test at realistic network topologies is not among the quantities anyone has measured. Nothing in practice forces the issue, because a global test that returns a small p-value is read as a finding rather than as a diagnostic of its own approximation, and the two candidate explanations produce identical output. The test meanwhile feeds prevalence estimates, CINeMA and GRADE inconsistency ratings and the decision whether a network may be pooled at all, so a miscalibrated null propagates into appraisal without ever surfacing as a statistical failure.

title: The design-by-treatment inconsistency test has no small-sample null
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Higgins, Jackson, Barrett, Lu, Ades and White 2012, Consistency and inconsistency in network meta-analysis: concepts and models for multi-arm studies, Research Synthesis Methods 3:98-110
Defines the design-by-treatment interaction model, the framework in which all inconsistency parameters are tested jointly; the model is stated without a small-sample distributional theory for the resulting test.


White, Barrett, Jackson and Higgins 2012, Consistency and inconsistency in network meta-analysis: model estimation using multivariate meta-regression, Research Synthesis Methods 3:111-125
Gives the multivariate meta-regression estimation route and the Wald test of all inconsistency parameters that constitutes the global check in practice, with the heterogeneity variance plugged in.


Jackson, Barrett, Rice, White and Higgins 2014, A design-by-treatment interaction model for network meta-analysis with random inconsistency effects, Statistics in Medicine 33:3639-3654
Extends the model to random inconsistency effects, adding a second variance component that is also estimated and then conditioned on when the global test is formed.


Veroniki, Tsokani, White, Schwarzer et al. 2021, Prevalence of evidence of inconsistency and its association with network structural characteristics in 201 published networks of interventions, BMC Medical Research Methodology 21
Applies the test to 201 published networks, reports the structural characteristics that make the chi-squared reference doubtful (median three loops, median four inconsistency parameters, 92.5 percent of networks with at least one single-study comparison), and states in its limitations that validity improves with more degrees of freedom and smaller within-design heterogeneity, without proposing a remedy.


Kiefer, Sturtz and Bender 2020, A simulation study to compare different estimation approaches for network meta-analysis and corresponding methods to evaluate the consistency assumption, BMC Medical Research Methodology 20
The only simulation reporting false-positive rates for global consistency screens; the between-designs Q statistic gave 15.2 to 22.8 percent at a nominal 0.20 level, but only for networks of at most five treatments, two-arm studies, five studies per direct comparison and tau-squared of 0.01 or 0.1, which does not cover the sparse, heterogeneous regime at issue.


Jackson and Riley 2014, A refined method for multivariate meta-analysis and meta-regression, Statistics in Medicine 33:541-554
Improves inference in multivariate meta-analysis and meta-regression when the between-study covariance matrix is estimated rather than known; this is the closest available template for a corrected null and it has not been carried into the design-by-treatment decomposition.


Krahn, Binder and Konig 2013, A graphical tool for locating inconsistency in network meta-analyses, BMC Medical Research Methodology 13:35; implemented as decomp.design() in netmeta 3.6-1
The decomposition of the network Q statistic into within-design heterogeneity and between-design inconsistency that netmeta reports, with chi-squared p-values and no small-sample correction.


Zarin, Veroniki, Nincic, Vafaei et al. 2017, Characteristics and knowledge synthesis approach for 456 network meta-analyses: a scoping review, BMC Medicine 15
The assembled collection of published networks from which the 201-network sample was drawn, so real topologies and design sparsity are available as a simulation grid rather than having to be invented; it was served programmatically by the nmadb package, which was archived from CRAN on 2025-01-23 and is now available only from the archive.

title: The design-by-treatment inconsistency test has no small-sample null
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Derive or approximate the null distribution of the design-by-treatment Wald statistic with the within-design heterogeneity variance estimated rather than known, taking the refined multivariate meta-analysis and meta-regression inference of Jackson and Riley as the starting template and reporting the effective degrees of freedom it implies. Where an analytic correction is unattractive, calibrate by parametric bootstrap or by permutation across designs, and ship the corrected p-value alongside decomp.design so that the corrected version is what practice actually uses. Then measure what is missing: simulate at the topologies that occur, drawing network structures from the published collections that already exist rather than constructing five-treatment examples, and report type I error as a function of inconsistency degrees of freedom, within-design heterogeneity and the presence of multi-arm trials, so the region in which the chi-squared reference is safe can be stated rather than assumed. Until that exists, report the inconsistency degrees of freedom and the estimated within-design heterogeneity next to every design-by-treatment p-value, since those are the two quantities that decide whether the p-value can be believed.

title: The design-by-treatment inconsistency test has no small-sample null
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as a well-posed calibration problem specific to the design-by-treatment test, distinct from low power and from the general non-testability of transitivity. The evidence is a single empirical study whose authors record the concern in a limitations paragraph and propose no remedy, which is a thin basis; the accompanying network characteristics and the absence of any published calibration make the gap credible rather than proven.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

title: Transitivity and conditional constancy cannot be tested in-sample
text:
Statement
Transitivity, consistency and conditional constancy restrict counterfactual quantities that are never jointly observed, so they cannot be verified nonparametrically from the data and passing any check does not establish transportability. Prespecifiable screens nevertheless exist: Spineli et al. (doi:10.1002/sim.70068) compute dissimilarities between treatment comparisons from study-level characteristics and cluster them to locate hot spots of potential intransitivity, backed by the tracenma database of 217 network datasets assembled to develop exactly this methodology, and Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162) assess conditional constancy through residual heterogeneity and inconsistency, though only in sufficiently large networks. What survives is narrower than the source claimed: each screen tests one observable implication, a calibrated failure is evidence against at least one assumption without saying which, and no catalogue states which implications a population-adjusted comparison should prespecify or what action a failure triggers. The judgment also governs whether the analysis happens at all, and nothing governs the judgment: reviews that prespecify a network meta-analysis and then cannot assess whether potential effect modifiers are similar across comparisons abandon it on an unquantified reading, with no threshold, no requirement to report network estimates that were fitted and then withheld, and no convention for signaling the abandonment where readers will see it. Three 2017 Cochrane reviews from one group abandoned an identical prespecified Bayesian protocol this way, one of them after fitting the models and detecting inconsistency, and the Cochrane Central Editorial Unit required the phrase ‘attempted network meta-analysis’ to be removed from one title on the grounds that it might confuse readers. The screens are also not always executable, and nothing says when that matters: no rule states which covariates must be reported, by what fraction of the trials contributing to each comparison and at what level of detail, before a transitivity screen counts as runnable, nor what an analyst owes when it cannot be run, whether to proceed and label the network as assumption-laden, restrict to a subnetwork with adequate reporting, or decline. The consequence is visible divergence rather than acknowledged uncertainty: two Cochrane reviews abandoned planned network meta-analyses of hepatocellular carcinoma treatments because effect-modifier similarity could not be assessed, one of them across a connected 18-trial evidence base (doi:10.1002/14651858.CD011650.pub2, doi:10.1002/14651858.CD011649.pub2), while other teams synthesize and rank the same interventions, and neither the go nor the no-go decision can be checked against any stated criterion.

title: Transitivity and conditional constancy cannot be tested in-sample
text:
Why it is open
The restriction is on treatment contrasts in study and population cells that are never jointly observed, so no function of the observed data has power against every violation, and covariate balance or model fit can look excellent under severe residual confounding. The screens that exist do not close this. The dissimilarity and clustering approach works on reported study-level characteristics and returns a semi-objective judgment rather than a verdict, and in 209 real networks a likely intransitivity prevailed in all of them while statistical tests were feasible in only 61 percent and often disagreed with the dissimilarity reading. For population-adjusted comparisons the residual-heterogeneity route needs a network large enough to support it, which is not the setting where conditional constancy does the most identifying work.

title: Transitivity and conditional constancy cannot be tested in-sample
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Spineli et al. 2024, Low awareness of the transitivity assumption in complex networks of interventions: a systematic survey from 721 network meta-analyses, BMC Medicine
sources the previously unattributed claim that transitivity is examined poorly in practice: most reviews evaluated it statistically rather than conceptually (40 percent versus 12 percent before PRISMA-NMA, 54 percent versus 11 percent after), with consistency evaluation the most preferred device (34 percent to 47 percent)


Spineli 2024, An empirical study on 209 networks of treatments revealed intransitivity to be common and multiple statistical tests suboptimal to assess transitivity, BMC Medical Research Methodology
empirical evidence that a likely intransitivity prevailed in all datasets examined and that statistical tests were feasible in only 61 percent of them and often conflicted with a study-dissimilarity reading


Spineli et al. 2025, Exploring the Transitivity Assumption in Network Meta-Analysis: A Novel Approach and Its Implications, Statistics in Medicine
gives a prespecifiable quantitative transitivity screen from dissimilarity matrices and hierarchical clustering that detects hot spots of potential intransitivity and supports semi-objective judgments; it does not verify the assumption


tracenma R package v0.1.1 (2025), database for developing transitivity methodology in network meta-analysis; companion paper doi:10.1186/s12874-025-02634-x
public benchmark database of 217 network meta-analysis datasets with extracted study-level candidate effect modifiers, built expressly to develop transitivity methodology


Phillippo et al. 2023, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis, Medical Decision Making
assesses population-adjustment assumptions inside a nine-study network: splits the common class interaction into treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time, checks conditional constancy through residual heterogeneity and inconsistency in sufficiently large networks, and reports that the shared-interaction restriction was required to identify the model where a treatment was informed only by aggregate data


Mantzoukis et al. 2017, Pharmacological interventions for acute hepatitis B infection: an attempted network meta-analysis, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
Shows what happens when the transitivity screen cannot be run: the planned network meta-analysis was abandoned because it was not possible to assess whether potential effect modifiers were similar across comparisons, and the Cochrane Central Editorial Unit then required the phrase ‘attempted network meta-analysis’ to be removed from the review title on the grounds that it might confuse readers, so the abandonment is invisible in the Cochrane Library record while PubMed retains it.


Lombardi et al. 2017, Pharmacological interventions for non-alcohol related fatty liver disease (NAFLD): an attempted network meta-analysis, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
A second review from the same group with the same prespecified Bayesian protocol, abandoned on the identical unquantified judgment that it was not possible to assess whether potential effect modifiers were similar across comparisons; 77 trials and 6287 participants were then synthesized pairwise instead.


Buzzetti et al. 2017, Pharmacological interventions for alcoholic liver disease (alcohol-related liver disease): an attempted network meta-analysis, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
The case where the models were fitted and the results withheld: in the subgroup where effect modifiers appeared reasonably similar across comparisons there was evidence of inconsistency, so the network results were not reported and 81 trials were synthesized pairwise. It shows the abandonment decision arising after fitting as well as before it.


van der Mark et al. 2012, A systematic review with attempted network meta-analysis of asthma therapy recommended for five to eighteen year olds in GINA guidelines, BMC Pulmonary Medicine
An earlier attempted network meta-analysis, establishing that abandonment after prespecification predates the 2017 group of reviews and is not confined to one editorial group.


Boonpattharatthiti et al. 2025, Reporting and evaluation of assumptions and certainty of evidence in network meta-analyses, Research Synthesis Methods
Surveys how assumptions and certainty of evidence are reported and evaluated across published network meta-analyses, which is the reporting-practice side of the same transitivity judgment.


Majumdar, Roccarina, Thorburn, Davidson, Tsochatzis and Gurusamy 2017, Management of people with early- or very early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma: an attempted network meta-analysis, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews CD011650
A planned network meta-analysis of 18 eligible randomized trials abandoned on the stated ground that it was not possible to assess whether the potential effect modifiers were similar across different comparisons, so performing a network meta-analysis in this scenario can be misleading; the review reverts to pairwise comparisons and issues no ranking.


Roccarina, Majumdar, Thorburn, Davidson, Tsochatzis and Gurusamy 2017, Management of people with intermediate-stage hepatocellular carcinoma: an attempted network meta-analysis, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews CD011649
The companion review reaching the same abstention on the same grounds in an adjacent evidence base, showing that the no-go decision is a repeated practice of one group rather than a single reviewer’s judgment, and still resting on no stated criterion.

title: Transitivity and conditional constancy cannot be tested in-sample
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The screening step no longer needs inventing, so the work is calibration and prespecification: characterize the operating characteristics of the dissimilarity and clustering screen against the tracenma datasets, and fix in advance which implications are checked, on what scale, and what a failure obliges the analyst to do. Around it, assemble the falsification devices that population adjustment still lacks, including held-out-trial contrast prediction, bridge deletion, negative controls, transported versus observed control-arm comparison, cross-trial interaction replication, and transport checks separated by calendar time, geography and setting. Report all of them with an explicit statement that passing does not establish transportability, and where falsification is impossible attach an explicit bias function to the restriction instead of asserting it.

title: Transitivity and conditional constancy cannot be tested in-sample
text:
Our study

What each transitivity screen can see
The question put to it. Do the available transitivity screens (covariate dissimilarity, loop inconsistency, heterogeneity), run together, detect the violations that bias a network estimate, and can their pattern of flags identify the mechanism?
What it found. No. Each screen sees one direction of violation, and an unmeasured modifier that makes one treatment look better in every comparison that includes it is invisible to all three: at size 0.4 it biased the network estimate by 0.40 with coverage near zero while the screens together fired at their null rate (0.28). Loop breaks and drift were detected with power rising in the number of studies, but the pattern of flags identified the mechanism poorly, and a measured modifier was always flagged although adjustment removed its bias.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: loop-consistent unmeasured modification of 0.4, any-screen detection 0.281 and 0.279 against 0.274 and 0.283 with no violation; bias -0.40.
Loop break of 0.4: detected in 0.77 (2 studies per comparison) and 0.98 (5); drift of 0.4: 0.95 and 1.00.
Measured modifier: dissimilarity flagged 100% of analyses; meta-regression bias at most 0.003.
Mechanism read from the flag pattern: loop breaks 43% correct, drift 34%; drift often triggered the loop test.

Design.

Estimand

B versus C effect in a declared target population

Methods compared

covariate dissimilarity screen, Bucher loop inconsistency test, Cochran’s Q heterogeneity screen, their union

Data-generating mechanism

Triangle networks with two or five studies per comparison and five violation mechanisms, including a loop-consistent unmeasured modifier constructed to be invisible to every screen; 26 cells, 2000 replicates each; detection, bias, coverage and mechanism identification.

Replicates

2000 per scenario, 52,000 in total


What this does not answer. Stylized triangle networks with continuous estimates; calendar drift as random shifts; abandonment records not scored. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Transitivity and conditional constancy cannot be tested in-sample
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 4 findings from 4 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “Standard ITC requires transitivity, consistency and a sensible effect scale, and PAIC adds conditional constancy of relative effects, yet these assumptions cannot be fully tested from the observed data. Research should therefore be redirected from impossible assumption tests towards prespecified falsification opportunities, accepting that success does not prove transportability while failure is highly informative.”
What was wrong with it. The source carried no citations and asserted both that there is no agreed catalogue of which implications to check or how to prespecify them and that a failed check is highly informative. The literature auditor sourced the practice claims (doi:10.1186/s12916-024-03322-1, doi:10.1186/s12874-024-02436-7) and found a prespecifiable transitivity screen already published (doi:10.1002/sim.70068, with cran:tracenma), so the entry is now sourced; the source-code auditor cut ‘highly informative’ back to evidence against at least one unidentified assumption, since a failure can equally reflect sampling variation, support failure, outcome-version differences or an invalid control.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied full-text reading.

merged-in

absorbed a proposal the reading raised separately: No standard governs abandoning a prespecified NMA 5 citation(s) added. The drafter disagreed with placing it here: The merge is right about the trigger and incomplete about the consequence. The reason for abandonment is exactly the in-sample untestability IDN-01 describes, so it belongs here. What does not fit IDN-01’s scope is the reporting half: no requirement to disclose fitted-but-withheld network estimates, no convention for signaling abandonment in the title or abstract, and no accounting of what the fallback to pairwise synthesis discards. That is a transparency requirement of the kind DEC-13 covers for population-adjusted analyses, and it will not be visible to a reader who arrives at IDN-01 looking for an identification problem.

merged-in

absorbed a proposal the reading raised separately: No criterion decides whether covariate reporting licenses NMA 2 citation(s) added

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 4 surviving findings from: A process for assessing the feasibility of a network meta-an; Comparative effectiveness of biological medicines in rheumat; Exploring the Transitivity Assumption in Network Meta-Analys; Network meta-analysis including treatment by covariate inter. New citations: 10.1002/jrsm.1257, 10.1002/sim.70068, 10.1136/bmj.m2288, 10.1186/1741-7015-12-93

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Retrieved Spineli et al. 2024 (BMC Med, 721 NMAs) and Spineli 2024 (BMC Med Res Methodol, 209 networks), which supply exactly the empirical backing this unsourced entry lacks: transitivity is mostly evaluated statistically rather than conceptually (40% vs 12% pre-PRISMA-NMA; 54% vs 11% post), consistency evaluation is the single most-used device (34% -> 47%), and likely intransitivity ‘prevailed in all datasets’. Phillippo et al. 2023 independently states that conditional constancy ‘may be assessed by checking for residual heterogeneity and inconsistency’ only ‘in sufficiently large networks’. The core claim (the restriction is on counterfactuals never jointly observed, so no in-sample test has power against every violation) is unsolvable by construction and stays open. Caveat: why_open asserts ‘no agreed catalogue of which implications are worth checking, how to prespecify them’. That is now materially narrowed. Spineli et al. 2025 (Stat Med) give a prespecifiable dissimilarity-plus-clustering transitivity screen with empirically derived thresholds, backed by the public tracenma CRAN database (217 NMA datasets) built expressly to develop such methodology. The entry cites none of this and should. Cites 10.1186/s12916-024-03322-1: Sources the unsourced claims that transitivity is poorly examined in practice and that NMA diagnostics lean on after-the-fact inconsistency. Cites 10.1186/s12874-024-02436-7: Empirical evidence that intransitivity is common and that statistical tests are a poor device for assessing it. Cites 10.1002/sim.70068: Provides a prespecifiable, quantitative transitivity screen (dissimilarity matrices plus hierarchical clustering) that narrows the entry’s claim that no catalogue or prespecification procedure exists. Cites cran:tracenma: A public benchmark database of 217 NMA datasets with extracted study-level candidate effect modifiers, built specifically to develop transitivity methodology.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The central nonidentification point is correct: observed data cannot verify equality of counterfactual treatment contrasts across unobserved study-treatment cells, and balance or model fit cannot rule out residual bias. However, C6 is a false scientific-versus-statistical dichotomy because these are formal statistical restrictions informed by science, sometimes with testable implications. C13 is materially too strong: a failed held-out prediction or negative control may reflect sampling variation, heterogeneity, support failure, outcome-version differences, model misspecification, or an invalid negative control. It is not automatically highly informative about transitivity. C14 additionally requires that withholding the trial preserve identification and that prediction and observation target the same population-specific estimand. C15 requires a valid negative control sharing the relevant bias pathway. C8-C10 are empirical literature claims outside this audit lens.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: No procedure shows an unanchored adjustment set is complete
text: IDN-03 Partially addressed Very high priority Established

title: No procedure shows an unanchored adjustment set is complete
text:
Statement
Anchored versus unanchored is a primary identification distinction: Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) state that unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions that are widely regarded as infeasible, and NICE DSU TSD 18 calls the requirement that all effect modifiers and prognostic factors be accounted for largely impossible to meet. It is not the only axis that matters, because MAIC, STC and ML-NMR still differ in estimand, model dependence, extrapolation and uncertainty, and anchored adjustment is not modifier-only on a non-collapsible scale, where shifting the distribution of a purely prognostic covariate moves the marginal odds ratio even with a constant conditional odds ratio and no interaction. What is unresolved is completeness: unanchored identification needs a measured set sufficient to block the study-selection paths for absolute potential outcomes, that set is fixed by a scientific claim rather than by the data, and no accepted procedure demonstrates that a proposed set is complete. ML-UMR (arXiv:2606.20341) extends unanchored comparison beyond the pairwise case and makes its assumptions explicit for sensitivity testing, which is an estimation and reporting advance rather than a completeness result.

title: No procedure shows an unanchored adjustment set is complete
text:
Why it is open
With a common comparator, randomization still identifies the within-trial contrast and the analyst is fixing an imbalance in modifiers of that contrast; once the anchor is gone, study membership and treatment are inseparable and every cross-study difference in absolute outcomes loads onto the treatment effect. That is a change in what must be known rather than in how well it is estimated, so no choice of estimator recovers it and larger samples do not help. Because the required set is a claim about what drives cross-study outcome differences, any proposed list is an argument rather than a result, and method debates conducted at the estimator level let an analysis lose the anchor with no corresponding change in what is reported or how the result is labeled.

title: No procedure shows an unanchored adjustment set is complete
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2018, Medical Decision Making
sets out population-adjustment methods for HTA and distinguishes anchored from unanchored comparisons according to whether a common comparator arm is used, stating that unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions that are widely regarded as infeasible


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 18: Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Submissions to NICE
official guidance stating that unanchored MAIC and STC assume all effect modifiers and prognostic factors are accounted for, an assumption it calls very strong and largely considered impossible to meet, and that anchored approaches are preferred whenever a connected network exists


Chandler and Ishak 2026, Anchors Away: Navigating Unanchored Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR), arXiv:2606.20341
extends unanchored comparison beyond the pairwise case and makes its assumptions explicit so they can be varied in sensitivity analysis; it does not supply a procedure for demonstrating that an unanchored adjustment set is complete

title: No procedure shows an unanchored adjustment set is complete
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Make anchored versus unanchored the primary axis for guidance, reporting and appraisal, and route unanchored analyses into a transportability frame with explicit residual-confounding analysis instead of treating them as a variant of the same estimator family. State the required adjustment set as a causal restriction attached to the declared estimand and effect scale, separating modifiers of the randomized contrast from the prognostic drivers of cross-study outcome differences, and say where non-collapsibility makes prognostic standardization necessary even in the anchored case. Treat completeness as a target for quantitative bias analysis, partial identification, negative controls, proximal methods and hidden-truth calibration, and allow no strong causal reading of an unanchored comparison without one of these or an explicit statement that the result is exploratory.

title: No procedure shows an unanchored adjustment set is complete
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed, on a single finding.
The source titled this. “Anchored versus unanchored is the decisive identification split” The title calls the anchored versus unanchored split decisive, but the audit found it is not the only axis that matters and that anchored adjustment is not modifier-only on a non-collapsible scale.
The source said. “The decisive methodological fault line is anchored versus unanchored, not MAIC versus STC versus ML-NMR: an anchored PAIC needs only effect modifiers of the within-study randomized contrast, whereas an unanchored PAIC needs every prognostic factor and every effect modifier that explains cross-study outcome differences. The asymmetry is widely stated but not operationalized, because no procedure exists for enumerating or defending the completeness of the unanchored adjustment set.”
What was wrong with it. The source framed the split as decisive against the choice among MAIC, STC and ML-NMR and said anchored comparisons need only effect modifiers; the source-code auditor rejected both, since the estimators differ in estimand and extrapolation and non-collapsible marginal estimands can require prognostic standardization. The completeness claim held up, and this previously unattributed entry is now sourced to Phillippo et al. 2018 and NICE DSU TSD 18, whose own text asserts the gap, with ML-UMR (arXiv:2606.20341) named as the nearest recent work.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 1 surviving finding from: A process to validate prognostic factors for unanchored matc. New citations: 10.57264/cer-2024-0235

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Retrieved the Phillippo et al. 2018 abstract verbatim; it carries the entry’s central asymmetry claim word for word: ‘We distinguish between anchored and unanchored comparisons according to whether a common comparator arm is used or not. Unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions, which are widely regarded as infeasible.’ NICE DSU TSD 18 states that an unanchored MAIC or STC ‘effectively assumes that absolute outcomes can be predicted from the covariates; that is, it assumes that all effect modifiers and prognostic factors are accounted for. This assumption is very strong, and largely considered impossible to meet’ (retrieved via search of the TSD text, not the PDF directly, hence confidence 0.8 not higher). That guidance sentence is itself the source assertion that licenses the entry’s ‘no accepted procedure for demonstrating completeness’ claim, so it is not an unverifiable absence claim. Nothing I found resolves the identification problem. The most recent relevant method, ML-UMR (arXiv 2606.20341, Chandler and Ishak, June 2026), extends unanchored comparison beyond the pairwise case and makes assumptions explicit for sensitivity testing; that is an estimation and reporting advance, not a completeness result, and the entry does not cite it.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. Anchoring is a major identification distinction, but C2 creates a false choice: MAIC, STC, and ML-NMR still differ in estimand, model dependence, extrapolation, and uncertainty. C3 is valid only for suitable conditional or collapsible relative-effect estimands under conditional constancy and support. On non-collapsible marginal scales, a purely prognostic covariate can matter without a conditional interaction. For example, a logistic model with constant conditional OR 3 and no treatment-covariate interaction gives marginal ORs 1.958 and 2.581 when Pr(X=1) changes from 0.1 to 0.9. C4 is therefore too reassuring: randomization identifies within-trial effects, not their transport, and network connectivity alone supplies neither overlap nor transitivity. Unanchored identification requires a sufficient set blocking study-selection paths for the relevant potential outcomes, not literally every prognostic variable. QBA characterizes sensitivity but does not itself license a causal interpretation. Claims about what NICE documents say are outside this technical audit.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: The shared effect modifier check has low and uncalibrated power
text: IDN-05 Overstated Very high priority Promising

title: The shared effect modifier check has low and uncalibrated power
text:
Statement
A published, software-implemented check on the shared effect modifier assumption already exists: Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162) split the common class interaction into treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time and compare posteriors and model fit, inside a single nine-study network and with no second IPD trial, and multinma implements the hierarchical relaxation this entry proposed through nma(class_interactions = c(‘common’, ‘exchangeable’, ‘independent’)). The check has low and uncharacterized power, which its authors concede, no calibration threshold and no agreed stability metric, and it is least feasible in the small, IPD-poor networks where the assumption does the most identifying work. The restriction is also not the universal mechanism that makes anchored adjustment work; it becomes an identifying restriction in particular class, component and sparse ML-NMR parameterizations, and hierarchical pooling regularizes weak information rather than creating identification.

title: The shared effect modifier check has low and uncalibrated power
text:
Why it is open
Interaction terms are estimated far less precisely than main effects, so the existing check can pass on intervals wide enough to accommodate almost any drift, while apparent discrepancies can come from non-collapsibility, differing covariate ranges or different outcome definitions instead of genuine modifier drift. Nothing states how much interaction stability is enough, so comparing posteriors and model fit returns a judgment rather than a calibrated verdict. The networks where the restriction carries the most identifying weight are the ones with the least data to relax it, and treatment-specific interactions are rarely estimable where one arm contributes only aggregate summaries.

title: The shared effect modifier check has low and uncalibrated power
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo et al. 2023, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis, Medical Decision Making
assesses population-adjustment assumptions inside a nine-study network: splits the common class interaction into treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time, checks conditional constancy through residual heterogeneity and inconsistency in sufficiently large networks, and reports that the shared-interaction restriction was required to identify the model where a treatment was informed only by aggregate data


multinma R package, nma() argument class_interactions
documents common, exchangeable (hierarchically shrunk) and independent treatment-class effect-modifier interactions. Correction, from study IDN-05: "exchangeable" is accepted by the argument but not implemented. In version 0.9.1.9002 (commit 8489bd83) make_nma_formula() aborts with “Exchangeable treatment class interactions (class_interactions = "exchangeable") not yet supported.” Only "common" and "independent" can be fitted, so the relaxation the source proposed as future work remains future work. The separate class_effects argument does support "exchangeable", but that shrinks treatment class effects, not effect-modifier interactions

title: The shared effect modifier check has low and uncalibrated power
text:
Probable solution or research direction
The estimator and the diagnostic exist, so the work is characterization: establish the power of the split-interaction check across network sizes and IPD availability, define a stability metric reporting how far interactions can drift before conclusions move rather than a binary verdict, and set a calibration threshold. Use estimated between-trial interaction drift to set priors or sensitivity envelopes on modifier drift, and report how conclusions move as the restriction is relaxed from common to exchangeable to independent, which multinma already supports. Where mechanistic pharmacology or biomarker evidence exists, use it to inform the shrinkage prior instead of defaulting to a common interaction.

title: The shared effect modifier check has low and uncalibrated power
text:
Our study

A violation twice the size that would change a decision raises the shared effect modifier check’s alarm rate from 1.3% to 4.5%
The question put to it. Population adjustment across a network assumes that a covariate modifies the effect of every active treatment in a class in the same way. There is one published within-network check on that assumption: fit the model with a single interaction shared across the class, refit with treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time, and compare the posteriors and the model fit. Its authors say it likely has low power. Nobody has measured it, there is no threshold that separates a pass from a failure, and there is no statement of what a pass licenses. Scored against a known truth under a declared distribution of networks, what is it worth?
What it found. The check does not have the resolution to test the assumption it is read as testing. Against a violation already twice the size that would change a decision, the DIC rule fires in 0.045 [0.029, 0.070] of analyses, against 0.013 [0.005, 0.029] when the assumption holds exactly: a violation that doubles the error that matters moves the alarm rate by about three percentage points. The result does not depend on where the cut is put. Scored threshold-free, the DIC difference ranks a violated network above an intact one with an AUROC of 0.557 [0.517, 0.596] at that violation, so no threshold recovers a ranking the statistic does not contain. The posterior standard deviation of the interaction contrast runs 0.30 to 1.64 against the 0.153 that would make a transported estimate materially wrong, which is why. The equivalence reading, the only one that could confirm rather than merely fail to contradict, fired zero times in 3,200 opportunities, including every replicate where the assumption held exactly; that is a statement about precision, and partly about the prior, since independent normal(0, 2.5) priors already place 0.965 of the contrast beyond the margin. Following the check is still better than not: relaxing exactly what it fires on beats relaxing everything at every target displacement and beats imposing the restriction at every displacement except zero, where the two are indistinguishable.
Results.

Detection barely moves with the violation. Pooled over all eight design strata, 400 replicates each, the DIC cut at 5 fires in 0.013 [0.005, 0.029] under the global null, 0.045 [0.029, 0.070] at a contrast of 0.30 that leaves the transported estimate wrong by twice the material threshold, 0.147 at 0.60 and 0.453 at 1.20, which is eight times the decision boundary and a stress test rather than a plausible violation.
The finding survives without any threshold. Scored as a classifier, the DIC difference separates a violated network from an intact one with an AUROC of 0.557 [0.517, 0.596] at a contrast of 0.30, 0.681 [0.644, 0.718] at 0.60 and 0.843 [0.815, 0.870] at 1.20; against material error itself it reaches 0.666 at a target one standard deviation away. This analysis was prespecified, computed from the first run onward, and omitted from the first two drafts until three reviewers asked for it.
The reason is resolution. The posterior standard deviation of the difference between the two treatments’ effect modifiers runs 0.30 to 1.64 on the log-odds scale across strata, against 0.153 for the difference that makes the transported estimate materially wrong. An earlier draft led with a prior-removed version of this quantity; its own sensitivity arm showed the quantity is unstable, so the measured posterior standard deviation is what is reported.
The procedure cannot give an all-clear. The equivalence reading, P(|difference| <= 0.153) > 0.95, fired in 0 of 3,200 covariate-checks, including every replicate where the two modifiers were identical by construction. This is a precision result: firing needs a posterior standard deviation below about 0.078 and the tightest stratum reaches 0.30. It is also prior-dependent in the other direction, since independent normal(0, 2.5) priors on the two coefficients put 0.965 of their contrast beyond the margin before any data are seen, above the 0.95 threshold at which the complementary margin rule fires.
The registered verdict fails, and a perfect check would have failed it too. The upper 95% bound on the probability that a passed analysis is materially wrong is 0.697, deployment- weighted, against a registered 0.10. But an oracle that knows the true interaction specification is materially wrong 0.639 of the time on the same replicates, so the check’s excess over that oracle is 0.036 and is negative at small target displacements. With a threshold of 0.03 absolute risk, the estimation error of a six-study network alone exceeds it in about half of analyses when the assumption holds exactly. A threshold on total error charges a diagnostic for noise it was never built to detect.
The check is blind to what determines the harm. Its output reads only the fitted network, so its pass rate is identical at every target displacement to the last digit. Over the same fits the probability that a passed analysis is materially wrong rises from 0.427 to 0.723, an excess over the noise floor of 0.296 against a registered 0.20. The first half of that is an algebraic identity that verifies the bookkeeping; the second is empirical.
The three readings are not three procedures. The DIC rule fires without the interval rule in 0.0006 of covariate-checks and the interval rule fires without DIC in 0.106, so the DIC cut is very nearly a strict subset of the interval rule rather than a second opinion. Under the global null they differ in type I error by 0.080 on the drifting covariate and 0.087 pooling both. The 95% interval rule runs at about twice its nominal rate, 0.075 [0.046, 0.120] with no treatment-effect heterogeneity and 0.110 [0.074, 0.161] with it, so avoiding covariate selection does not deliver nominal coverage.
A fire is not a diagnosis. When a violation is present the interval rule fires on the covariate that is shared exactly in up to 0.388 of replicates.
Following the check beats the alternatives, but not uniformly, and the ranking of the alternatives is the surprise. Deployment-weighted and paired on the same replicates, relaxing exactly what fired beats relaxing everything at every displacement on both absolute and squared error, and beats imposing the restriction at displacements 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 but is indistinguishable from it at 0 (-0.00005, 95% CI [-0.00069, 0.00059]), where there is nothing to transport. Relaxing everything is worse than imposing the restriction, because the relaxed model spends precision the network does not have; it also fails its sampler diagnostics in 0.068 of replicates and 0.24 in the worst cell. The worst diagnostic reached by any model is R-hat 5.13 with effective sample size 1.03, in a singly-relaxed fit.
Knowing the target is worth more than knowing the check statistic. Held out across design factors, the check statistic alone discriminates material error at an AUROC of 0.48 to 0.63, close to chance; adding the target displacement raises it to 0.69 to 0.83. A one-term mapping from the statistic to the probability of material error transports across network size, covariate spread and heterogeneity with absolute errors of 0.013 to 0.058, and fails across drift with an error of 0.469.
On a decision-curve basis, distrusting every adjusted analysis has higher net benefit than every rule in the panel at every action threshold from 0.05 to 0.60. This restates the noise floor rather than measuring the check: with material error present in 0.675 of passing analyses, most of it sampling noise no covariate check can predict, treat-all dominates almost regardless of what the check does.
Two software findings, against multinma 0.9.1.9002 (commit 8489bd83). The package documents class_interactions = ‘exchangeable’ and raises ‘not yet supported’, so the hierarchical relaxation this catalog entry proposed as the way forward cannot be fitted; the entry’s claim that it ships in the package is wrong for this version. And under the default class_interactions = ‘common’, an x:.trt term in a regression formula is silently demoted to the class level, so an analyst who follows the published recipe by editing the formula alone fits the shared model twice and can never find evidence against sharing.
Two adversarial critiques before the run found nine issues between them that changed the design, and each found something the other missed. Peer review then found more, including two errors in this study’s own code: contraction was divided by the standard deviation of a prior the prior-sensitivity arm was not fitted under, which inverted the reported direction of that arm’s result, and the primary bound was a Wilson interval on the unweighted risk printed beside a deployment-weighted point estimate. Both were derived by reviewers from the published numbers alone, without access to the code.

Design.

Estimand

Marginal risk difference for the aggregate-only treatment versus the individual-data treatment in a target population, with the population-average conditional log-odds effect as the mechanism scale

Methods compared

shared class interaction, treatment-specific interaction for one covariate, treatment-specific interactions for all covariates, check first, then relax exactly what fired

Data-generating mechanism

A multilevel network meta-regression with a binomial outcome and a logit link, one individual-level study and the rest aggregate, two active treatments in one class of which only one has individual data. Drift is carried by one covariate and parameterized as the contrast between the two treatments’ interactions; a second covariate is shared exactly and supplies a type I error observation from the same fits. 32 cells crossing drift, network size, between-study covariate spread and treatment-effect heterogeneity, 50 replicates each, four fits per replicate forming the complete model lattice, plus eight amendment cells at the decision boundary, a prior-sensitivity arm and an integration-sensitivity check. The target population is not a design factor because the check reads only the fitted network and cannot depend on it; one set of fits is scored at four target displacements, and the reference intercept is solved separately for each so displacement moves the treatment contrast and not the baseline risk.

Replicates

50 per cell, 2,000 networks and 8,960 ML-NMR fits: 6,400 over the 32 registered cells, 1,600 in the amendment arm, 960 in the prior-sensitivity arm. That last arm ran at 30 replicates per cell against the 100 registered, a departure found in round-two review and disclosed in the protocol.


What this does not answer. The design is a best case in several specific ways that favour the check, and failures attributable to those idealizations are conservative; no general lower-bound claim is made, because three features cut the other way. The true marginal reference risk in the target is supplied to the estimator. Covariates are normal with known target moments and study covariate means are drawn independently of study baselines and of the random treatment effects, so the ecological route identifying the aggregate-only treatment’s interaction is unbiased by construction. Conditional constancy holds and only one covariate drifts, linearly. Against that: the fits are fixed-effect while half the cells generate random treatment effects, which is a second specification error that inflates firing; the likelihood is integrated over 64 quadrature points and refitting at 256 changes the DIC verdict in 8.3% of a 24-network subset, which is noise belonging to the implementation and not to the evidence, and 256 points is not demonstrated to be converged; and a single individual-level study is an assumption about the network rather than necessarily a pessimistic one. Beyond that: what a second individual-level study would buy is not measured, that factor having been dropped to pay for treatment-effect heterogeneity. With two active treatments and two covariates, multiplicity across covariates and the selection involved in reading the widest of several pairwise differences are not measured. Where treatment-effect heterogeneity is present the estimand is not cleanly defined, since truth is set at a random effect of zero while a fixed-effect model targets a function of the realized studies; primary results are repeated on the sixteen homogeneous cells and do not change. The hierarchical middle ground between shared and independent interactions could not be fitted because the package does not implement it, and we did not implement it ourselves: that is a reason for its absence, not a justification. The five decision rules scored here are our formalizations of an exploratory published practice, not published rules, and their operating characteristics are ours. Fifty replicates per cell gives a per-cell standard error of 0.065, so nothing is read off a single cell.
Peer review. 2 rounds, two independent reviewers. The reports, the point-by-point responses and the editorial decision are published in full: read the review.

title: The shared effect modifier check has low and uncalibrated power
text:
What this project measured
Study studies/IDN-05-shared-modifier-check-power, run and decided against a rule registered before the run. Six-study networks, deployment-weighted over a displacement grid.
Registered rule. The check earns the reassurance it is read as giving if the upper 95% confidence bound on P(material error | the check did not fire) is below 0.10, where material error is a C-versus-A marginal risk difference wrong by more than 0.03 absolute risk.
Result: the rule fails. Upper bound 0.697 on realized error and 0.563 on systematic error, against a 0.10 threshold.
The qualification matters more than the verdict. An oracle that knows which specification is true, fitted to the same replicates, is materially wrong 0.639 of the time at the same displacement. The check’s excess over that oracle is 0.036, and at displacements 0 and 0.5 the excess is negative. A perfect check would have failed this gate too: with a 0.03 absolute-risk threshold, the estimation error of a six-study network alone exceeds it in 0.46 to 0.58 of replicates when the assumption holds exactly. The registered threshold was unreachable by any procedure, so this is evidence about what a six-study network can support, not only about the check.
Mechanism claims: decoupling confirmed (conditional risk rises 0.296 while the pass rate is flat in displacement); identification asymmetry partly confirmed (contraction gap widens monotonically, clearing 0.20 in 5 of 8 strata); the two rules differ on the null confirmed (type I gap 0.087); the two rules disagree not clearly met (0.107, 95% CI [0.096, 0.118], against a 0.10 threshold).

title: The shared effect modifier check has low and uncalibrated power
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. A published, software-implemented check on the shared effect modifier assumption exists (split the common class interaction into treatment-specific interactions and compare posteriors and model fit, as in Phillippo et al. 2023 with multinma’s class_interactions argument), but it has low and uncharacterized power, no calibration threshold, and no agreed stability metric, and it is infeasible in the small, IPD-poor networks where the assumption does the most identifying work.
The source titled this. “Shared effect modification is assumed rather than estimated or tested” The title says shared effect modification is never estimated or tested, but a published within-network check exists. (Its hierarchical relaxation does not ship in multinma: see the correction in the sources table.)
The source said. “Population adjustment commonly assumes that a covariate modifies the effects of different treatments in the same way, although the same modifier may act differently on different treatments. The only empirical check on offer, testing whether modifier interactions estimated in one IPD trial predict the treatment-effect heterogeneity observed in another, is not standardized and is rarely feasible.”
What was wrong with it. The source called cross-trial replication with two IPD trials the only empirical check on offer and proposed hierarchical shrinkage of treatment-specific interactions as future work. Both auditors found the check published in 2023 as a within-network procedure needing no second IPD trial (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162) and the shrinkage already shipped in multinma’s class_interactions argument, so what remains open is power, calibration and a stability metric rather than the method itself.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

closure-upheld

15 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors’ reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. The new findings restate the closure’s residual: the Phillippo check exists but has low, uncalibrated power and is often infeasible when only one IPD study or sparse aggregate evidence is available. The 2022 Phillippo paper expressly concedes low power and multiplicity, which was already central to the closure rationale. Applied examples imposing a common interaction because flexible interactions are not estimable show non-adoption or non-feasibility in particular data structures, not that the cited within-network method fails to exist or falls outside its claimed scope. The 2026 transportability finding also supports the closure’s qualification that shared effect modification is not universally required for anchored pairwise adjustment. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening

16 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries overstated Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit’s closure needs the closure’s own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. I read the full text of Phillippo et al. 2023 (Med Decis Making), which the entry does not cite, and it directly contradicts the statement’s ‘only empirical check on offer’. They assess the shared effect modifier assumption inside a single 9-study network with no second IPD trial, by splitting the common class interaction into treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time and comparing posteriors and DIC, and they report a result (weak evidence against sharing for weight). The entry’s own proposed direction, hierarchical shrinkage of treatment-specific interactions, is already released software: multinma’s nma() takes class_interactions = c(“common”, “exchangeable”, “independent”) (verified in man/nma.Rd), so exchangeable within-class interactions are fittable today. What remains genuinely open is exactly what Phillippo et al. concede: ‘It is likely that this approach to assessing the shared effect modifier assumption has low power, particularly when data are lacking.’ Power, calibration, a stability metric rather than a binary verdict, and the data conditions under which the check is informative are unresolved. So the problem is real but the framing overstates the void by roughly one decade and one R package. Cites 10.1177/0272989X221117162: Provides and applies a standardized within-network empirical check on the shared effect modifier assumption, not requiring two IPD trials. Cites cran:multinma: Implements common, exchangeable (hierarchically shrunk) and independent treatment-class effect-modifier interactions, i.e. the entry’s proposed direction.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 and C2 are correct: treatment-specific modification can differ, and shared conditional interactions do not make marginal odds or hazard ratios population-invariant. Hierarchical pooling is a coherent relaxation but regularizes weak information rather than creating identification. The shared-interaction restriction is not the universal mechanism that makes anchored PAIC work; an anchored analysis targeting the comparator-trial population can transport the IPD trial contrast and subtract the contrast observed in the target trial without assuming identical interactions for every treatment. Shared interactions become identifying restrictions in particular class, component, or sparse ML-NMR parameterizations. The proposed two-trial replication is also not the only empirical check and does not invariably require two complete IPD datasets: treatment-specific interactions can be compared within a mixed network, and sufficiently detailed subgroup aggregate data may support a limited check. Existing within-network relaxation and model comparison partially address the problem; power, calibration, and prior sensitivity remain open. Cites 10.1177/0272989X221117162: Demonstrates a within-network empirical assessment of shared effect modification by relaxing common interactions to treatment-specific interactions and comparing the resulting models, so cross-trial replication using two IPD trials is not the only available check..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)
