title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text: IDN-07 Unverifiable Very high priority Promising

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Statement
Refitting an ITC or PAIC model with one connected trial withheld and comparing the predicted contrast with the observed one is a coherent falsification design, but only if removing the trial leaves the required contrast identifiable and the withheld population’s target covariate distribution can be specified without using its outcome contrast. We are not aware of a standardized protocol saying how to run it or when a discrepancy counts as falsifying, and neither auditor could certify that absence: the literature auditor found no source asserting it, and the source-code auditor treated a literature-wide absence claim as outside the technical lens. The nearest work found is adjacent rather than on point, namely leave-one-trial-out influence and outlier diagnostics for network meta-analysis (arXiv:1910.13080) and formal falsification tests for external validity with defined test statistics and error control from outside the ITC literature (Hussain et al., AISTATS 2023). The two secondary claims survive: study-level held-out prediction and patient-level cross-validation answer different questions, and withholding a trial changes the evidence base and can change the implied target population, though not when the target is externally prespecified.

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Why it is open
There is no agreed pass or fail rule: the predictive interval has to absorb weight estimation, target-moment uncertainty and between-study heterogeneity, and neither the discrepancy metric nor a calibration threshold is defined. Networks contain few trials, so the check has low power and its verdict depends heavily on which trial is withheld. Because predicted and observed contrasts can refer to different populations once the evidence base changes, a discrepancy is ambiguous between an estimand mismatch and a genuine transport failure, and current practice further conflates study-level held-out prediction with patient-level cross-validation, which answers a different question.

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Write the protocol rather than the method: specify the identifiability precondition for removal, a target-standardized comparison of predicted and observed contrasts, a discrepancy metric, prespecified failure thresholds, and full propagation of weight and target-moment uncertainty. Calibrate it where held-out truth is available so the threshold has known operating characteristics instead of being asserted, and keep it explicitly distinct from patient-level cross-validation in reporting. The conditional-moment falsification machinery developed for external validity is the closest formal template and is worth adapting rather than reinventing.

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Our study

Calibrating a held-out-trial falsification rule
The question put to it. When one trial is withheld and its contrast predicted from the rest, which pass or fail rule holds its type I error, how much power does it have, and what does omitting a variance component or mis-targeting the prediction do?
What it found. A held-out-trial check has a controllable size if the prediction targets the withheld trial’s own population and its variance includes between-trial heterogeneity: the full rule’s size was 0.035 to 0.073 (registered limit 0.07, exceeded by 0.003 in one scenario). Omitting heterogeneity raised size to 0.104, and aiming the prediction at the remaining trials’ population raised it to 0.96. Power against a violation as large as the effect was only 0.21 to 0.47, so a pass licenses very little.
Results.

Registered verdict: FULL RULE SIZE NOT HELD, by 0.003 in one of 8 null scenarios (MCSE 0.006); every other null scenario 0.035 to 0.064.
Power of the full rule: 0.07 to 0.17 at violation 0.15 and 0.21 to 0.47 at violation 0.3.
Null mean of the discrepancy: at most 0.009 with the external target, down to -0.60 with the reduced-network target.
Sign-disagreement rule: flagged 0.02 to 0.44 of valid analyses depending on the effect’s distance from zero.

Design.

Estimand

The withheld trial’s contrast in its own population, and the discrepancy between prediction and observation

Methods compared

full-variance standardized discrepancy, naive-variance discrepancy, prediction at the reduced-network target, sign-disagreement rule

Data-generating mechanism

One individual-data trial and five aggregate trials with a continuous outcome and linear effect modification; 24 cells crossing violation size, heterogeneity, covariate spread and withheld-trial position; full, naive, mis-targeted and decision-flip rules. 2000 replicates per cell.

Replicates

2000 per scenario, 48,000 in total


What this does not answer. Continuous outcome and G-computation only; no MAIC weight variance, no Bayesian predictive or conditional-moment rule; five aggregate trials. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: No agreed criterion for when a held-out-trial discrepancy falsifies
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source titled this. “No protocol for held-out-trial falsification of predicted contrasts” The title asserts flatly that no protocol exists, an absence neither auditor could certify, so the entry now says only that it is not aware of one.
The source said. “An ITC/PAIC method can be refit with one connected trial withheld and used to predict that trial’s treatment contrast, which is then compared with the observed contrast. No standardized protocol defines how such a leave-one-trial-out emulation should be conducted or when a discrepancy should count as falsifying the analysis.”
What was wrong with it. The source asserted flatly that no standardized protocol exists. Neither auditor could verify a literature-wide absence, so the claim is now stated as one we are not aware of, and the nearest work is named: arXiv:1910.13080, an ISPOR 2024 abstract on predictive cross-validation for network meta-analysis that the literature auditor could not retrieve in full (Value in Health, PII S1098-3015(24)05231-8), and Hussain et al. 2023 on falsification of external validity via conditional moment restrictions.

Literature and prior-art check

open / unverifiable. The headline claim is an absence claim (‘no standardized protocol defines how leave-one-trial-out emulation should be conducted or when a discrepancy counts as falsifying’), and I found no source that asserts that absence, so by the audit’s own rule this is unverifiable rather than supported. I searched PubMed and the web and found only adjacent work, none of which is an ITC/PAIC held-out-trial falsification protocol with prespecified thresholds: leave-one-trial-out influence and outlier diagnostics for NMA (arXiv 1910.13080); an ISPOR 2024 conference abstract on predictive cross-validation for NMA that I could not retrieve in full (Value in Health S1098-3015(24)05231-8); and, outside the ITC literature, formal falsification tests for external validity with defined test statistics and error control (Hussain et al., ‘Falsification of Internal and External Validity in Observational Studies via Conditional Moment Restrictions’, PMLR v206, AISTATS 2023). The two secondary claims are sound: study-level held-out prediction and patient-level LOO-CV do answer different questions, and in ML-NMR the target population is study-indexed, so withholding a trial does change the implied estimand. Publish the sub-claims; soften the absence claim to ‘we are not aware of’.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

abstain / unverifiable. The technically assessable subclaims need conditions. A held-out-trial prediction is feasible only if removal leaves the required contrasts identifiable and the withheld population’s target distribution is specified without using its outcome contrast. Study-level prediction and patient-level cross-validation do answer different questions. Withholding changes the evidence base, but it need not change the target population when that target is externally prespecified; C4 correctly says only that it can. The headline assertion that no standardized protocol currently exists is a literature-wide absence claim. Verifying it would require the novelty and literature review that this audit was expressly instructed not to perform, so neither openness nor support for that central claim can be established under the assigned lens.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R10:no-accessible-source

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Statement
Prespecified negative-control outcomes and negative-control covariates can provide qualitative falsification for indirect comparisons under explicit null-effect, shared-bias and estimand-scale conditions, and a calibrated signal is evidence against a joint set of assumptions rather than a measurement of bias in the primary contrast. The calibration machinery the source treats as nonexistent does exist outside this setting: control outcome calibration corrects estimates for unobserved confounding using control outcomes and comes with a sensitivity analysis for its own identifying assumption (doi:10.1093/aje/kwt303), and empirical calibration of confidence intervals from banks of negative and synthesized positive controls is routine in OHDSI network studies (doi:10.1073/pnas.1708282114, cran:EmpiricalCalibration). Both were built for unmeasured confounding within observational data and have not been adapted to cross-study transport, and for indirect comparisons specifically there are no disease-area catalogues of design-sensitive control outcomes, no power or specificity characterization under correlated baseline covariates and non-collapsible scales, and no validated mapping from a control signal to a bias parameter for the primary contrast.

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Why it is open
A valid negative-control outcome must have no causal treatment effect on the specified scale while sharing the confounding, selection, measurement and follow-up pathways of the primary outcome, and a valid negative-control covariate must be known not to modify the effect, which is exactly the knowledge that is incomplete and that data-driven modifier selection cannot supply. The data are usually absent as well, since control outcomes are rarely reported in the aggregate publications indirect comparisons rely on, which is where the check is most needed. With few trials and correlated baseline covariates an apparent placebo interaction can reflect collinearity with a true modifier, a scale artifact or multiplicity, so specificity is unknown. The existing calibration methods assume a confounding structure within one data source rather than a transport gap between two, so importing them is real work rather than a citation.

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Tchetgen Tchetgen, the control outcome calibration approach, American Journal of Epidemiology
goes beyond using control outcomes for detection and corrects causal effect estimates for bias due to unobserved confounding, with a sensitivity analysis for its identifying assumption; developed for observational confounding, not cross-study transport


Schuemie et al. 2018, empirical calibration of confidence intervals from negative and synthesized positive controls, PNAS
calibrates confidence intervals using banks of negative and synthesized positive controls, the calibration step the source says does not exist, again for observational confounding rather than for transport across studies


EmpiricalCalibration R package
ships the empirical calibration procedure used routinely in OHDSI network studies, along with the negative-control concept sets that are the kind of catalogue the source says is absent, in a neighboring field

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Adapt rather than invent: take control outcome calibration and empirical calibration from the observational-confounding setting and re-derive what they require when the bias is cross-study transport instead of within-source confounding. Build disease-area catalogues of candidate control outcomes and prespecified control-covariate lists elicited from clinicians, and require their reporting in trial publications and submissions so comparator studies can be checked at all. Characterize the power and specificity of placebo-covariate tests under realistic covariate correlation and non-collapsible scales, and wire a positive test into modifier selection so it forces respecification rather than being reported as an incidental finding.

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Our study

A negative-control outcome for transport bias
The question put to it. Can a negative-control outcome detect and calibrate transport bias in an unanchored MAIC, and when does the calibration fail?
What it found. Only in a knife-edge case. A negative-control outcome with no treatment effect detects a population difference (flag rate up to 0.83) but calibrates the primary contrast correctly only when its dependence on the unmeasured covariate equals the primary outcome’s and that covariate does not modify the treatment effect (bias 0.001). Otherwise the calibrated contrast was biased by -0.18 to 0.40: it missed the modification part, overcorrected with a more strongly dependent control, and cancelled by coincidence in one scenario.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: calibrated bias -0.183 to 0.399 wherever the control’s bias differed from the primary’s.
Control test size 0.039 to 0.056 without a shift; power 0.04 to 0.83 with a 0.5 SD shift, rising with the control’s dependence on the unmeasured covariate.
With modification by the unmeasured covariate and a matched control, calibration left 0.19 of 0.41 naive bias.

Design.

Estimand

Marginal log odds ratio of the primary outcome, B versus A, in the target

Methods compared

naive unanchored MAIC, negative-control test, negative-control calibrated contrast

Data-generating mechanism

Unanchored MAIC with an unmeasured covariate shifted between populations, a negative-control outcome sharing some, all or more of its prognostic dependence, and effect modification absent or present; naive, control-test and calibrated contrasts. 16 cells, 2000 replicates each.

Replicates

2000 per scenario, 32,000 in total


What this does not answer. One control outcome rather than a bank with empirical calibration; unanchored only; availability of control outcomes not surveyed. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Negative controls for ITC lack catalogues, power and calibration
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Negative-control outcomes and negative-control covariates have no disease-area catalogues, no power or specificity characterization, and no calibration mapping validated for the cross-study transport bias that indirect comparisons face; calibration machinery that converts negative-control signals into bias corrections does exist (control outcome calibration, empirical calibration of confidence intervals) but has been developed for unmeasured confounding in observational data and not adapted to ITC/PAIC.
The source said. “Two negative-control devices are proposed for indirect comparisons: outcomes unlikely to be modified by treatment but sensitive to design differences, whose nonzero apparent contrast signals residual cross-study bias, and covariates that should not modify the treatment effect, whose apparent interaction falsifies the effect-modification model. Neither has the catalogues, operating characteristics or calibration needed to be used as evidence.”
What was wrong with it. The source said no accepted transfer function converts a negative-control discrepancy into a bias magnitude and that neither device can be used as evidence at all. The literature auditor found that machinery in use since 2013 and 2018 for unmeasured confounding in observational data (doi:10.1093/aje/kwt303, doi:10.1073/pnas.1708282114 with cran:EmpiricalCalibration), so the correct claim is that it has not been adapted to indirect comparison, and the source-code auditor added that negative controls already carry qualitative evidence.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. The ITC-specific problem is real and I found nothing that solves it: no disease-area catalogue of design-sensitive negative-control outcomes for indirect comparisons, and no power or specificity study under correlated baseline covariates and non-collapsible scales. But why_open’s assertion that ‘no accepted transfer function converts an observed negative-control discrepancy into a bias magnitude’ is wrong as stated. Tchetgen Tchetgen’s control outcome calibration approach does exactly that and has done since 2013, with an accompanying sensitivity analysis for its identifying assumption; and Schuemie et al. (PNAS 2018, 10.1073/pnas.1708282114) calibrate confidence intervals from banks of negative and synthesized positive controls, shipped as the CRAN package EmpiricalCalibration and used routinely in OHDSI network studies. Both live in the confounding-in-observational-data setting, not the cross-study transport setting, so importing them is a genuine open task; but the entry should say ‘not yet adapted to ITC’ rather than ‘does not exist’. Note also that OHDSI-style negative-control concept sets are precisely the kind of catalogue the entry says is absent, in a neighbouring field.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1-C2 require a sharper negative-control null: no causal treatment effect on the control outcome on the specified estimand scale, plus sufficiently shared bias pathways. An outcome that is merely unlikely to be affected and sensitive to design is not enough, and a discrepancy rejects a joint set of assumptions rather than transportability alone. C4 is correct. For C5-C6, a prespecified covariate null can be a placebo check, but a nonzero point estimate is expected under sampling and can arise from proxy correlation with a true modifier, scale or non-collapsibility, omitted modifiers, or multiplicity; only calibrated incompatibility with the null falsifies the joint model. C7 is substantially correct because the structural null needs external or design knowledge, whereas C8’s instability claim is not universal. C3 is an empirical prevalence claim outside this audit. Negative controls can already contribute qualitative evidence, so saying that calibration is required before they can be used as evidence inflates the gap; quantitative mapping to primary-outcome bias remains open.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text: IDN-11 Partially addressed High priority Emerging

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
Statement
Trial participation can itself affect outcomes through monitoring, adherence support, visit frequency, diagnostic intensity and access to rescue care, and because engagement is a property of the protocol rather than of the patient, reweighting or regressing on baseline covariates cannot remove it. The source’s dichotomy, that transport assumes either no engagement effect or an explicitly incorporated one, misses a third case established in the paper it cites: Ung, VanderWeele and Dahabreh (doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001863, erratum doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001891) define engagement-aware estimands and show that under a no participation-by-treatment-assignment interaction condition the identifying functionals are the same as those obtained under the stronger conditions invoked previously. What stays open is the ITC and PAIC specific part: where engagement is study-constant it is absorbed into the study intercept and is observationally identical to prognostic imbalance, and in a single-arm versus randomized comparison engagement is confounded with treatment, which is exactly where the no-interaction condition fails.

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
Why it is open
An anchored randomized contrast can cancel an engagement main effect, so the problem is not universal; it bites when engagement interacts with treatment and in unanchored comparisons. Where engagement is constant within a study it is collinear with study membership, so covariate-balance diagnostics say nothing about it and it cannot be told apart from baseline-risk differences. The protocol features that would let it be modeled, visit schedules, imaging frequency, adherence-support programs and rescue-therapy rules, are recorded as narrative design descriptions rather than analyzable variables and are rarely reported in aggregate publications. Study-design bias parameters can represent the remainder but they are sensitivity parameters, not identified corrections.

title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Carry the engagement-aware estimands and identification results into the ITC and PAIC setting instead of restating the problem: say whether the no participation-by-treatment interaction condition is being assumed, and say what breaks in the single-arm versus randomized case where it cannot hold. title: Trial-engagement effects are mistaken for prognostic imbalance
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Trial participation itself can affect outcomes through monitoring, adherence support, visit frequency, diagnostic intensity and access to rescue care, so cross-study outcome differences are not fully explained by patient characteristics. Standard transportability assumes either that no relevant engagement effect exists or that it has been explicitly incorporated, and in PAIC engagement differences masquerade as prognostic imbalance or baseline-risk heterogeneity.”
What was wrong with it. The source cited Ung et al. as background while stating the assumption as a two-way choice. Both auditors found that the cited paper supplies the missing third case, identification under no participation-by-treatment interaction, so the usual functionals still apply with engagement effects present; the literature auditor also flagged the paper’s erratum, doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001891.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. The citation is accurate and the abstract supports it verbatim: ‘Most work on extending (generalizing or transporting) causal inferences from a randomized trial to a target population has, explicitly or implicitly, assumed that trial engagement effects are absent.’ But the paper the entry cites as background is also the paper that partly resolves the problem, and the entry does not register this. Ung et al. define estimands and give identification results for transport in the presence of engagement effects under no interaction between trial participation and treatment assignment, and show ‘The identifying observed data functionals under these no-interaction assumptions are the same as those obtained under the stronger identifiability conditions that have been invoked in prior work.’ That is a third option the why_open dichotomy excludes: engagement effects present, standard estimators reinterpreted rather than assumed away or explicitly modelled. Genuinely open: the ITC/PAIC-specific case where engagement is absorbed into a study intercept and is observationally identical to prognostic imbalance, and the single-arm-versus-randomized case where engagement is confounded with treatment (which violates Ung et al.’s no-interaction condition). Housekeeping: an erratum exists (Epidemiology 2025;36(5):e25, 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001891) and should be cited alongside. Cites 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001863: Supplies estimands and identification results for transport when trial-engagement effects are present, under no participation-by-treatment interaction; partially answers the entry’s call for explicit engagement causal models.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. C1 and C4 are correct: a study-level engagement exposure is not changed by reweighting baseline patient covariates. C2 needs an estimand- and scale-specific third case: engagement may affect outcomes yet cancel from the randomized treatment contrast under a suitable no trial-participation-by-treatment interaction condition, without estimating an engagement coefficient. C3 holds when engagement or protocol intensity is study-constant and collinear with source, especially in a single-arm-versus-randomized comparison; it is not universal when crossed protocol variation, measured engagement, or multiple studies exist, and engagement-by-treatment heterogeneity is not merely baseline-risk heterogeneity. C5 describes sensitivity parameters, not identified corrections. C6 is accurate. Ung et al. partly resolves the causal estimand and identification problem, while the PAIC-specific confounded single-arm setting remains open. This is high priority for unanchored comparisons but less universal for anchored randomized contrasts whose engagement main effect cancels. Cites 10.1097/EDE.0000000000001863: Defines engagement-aware transport estimands and identification under a no trial-participation-by-treatment-assignment interaction condition; it does not resolve the ITC or PAIC setting where engagement is confounded with treatment or study..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text: IDN-13 Confirmed open High priority Emerging

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
Statement
When calendar period, geography and care setting are each constant within each of two non-crossed studies, all three are affine functions of the binary study indicator, so only one composite between-study difference is identified and a failed transport check cannot be attributed to a dimension. This is a property of non-crossed evidence rather than of indirect comparison as a whole: once a network carries crossed structure, network meta-regression and multilevel network meta-regression can carry region, period or setting as study-level covariates, which multinma supports. Separating the dimensions therefore requires crossed variation, external information or explicit identifying restrictions, and no estimator can do it by computation alone.

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
Why it is open
Assembling evidence with crossed structure, such as multi-regional or multi-period trials and registries spanning more than one care setting, is rarely done for an indirect comparison, so the standard two-study case carries the collinearity by construction. Without separation a failed transport check yields no targeted remedy, and a bias parameter elicited for undifferentiated study differences mixes mechanisms whose plausible magnitudes and directions differ, which degrades both elicitation and sensitivity analysis. The remedy is evidence design, measurement and explicit restriction rather than a better estimator, and tooling reflects that: in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, study intercepts and generic covariates are available but no calendar-time, geography or setting specific transport diagnostics are exported.

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Design evidence sets with separately indexed transport dimensions, using multi-regional and multi-period trials plus real-world data to estimate dimension-specific drift, and report dimension-specific transport diagnostics so that failures are attributable. Where crossed structure is unavailable, state the identifying restriction that assigns the composite difference to a dimension instead of leaving it implicit, and elicit separate bias parameters for period, region and setting rather than one undifferentiated study effect. Since study-level regression already exists in released software, the work is assembling the crossed evidence and the diagnostics on top of it, not building a new estimator.

title: Time, geography and setting are confounded in non-crossed evidence
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “Calendar time, geography and setting are not separately identified” The title states the non-identification as a general fact, but both auditors narrowed it to non-crossed evidence, since crossed networks can carry these as study-level covariates.
The source said. “Transportability should be tested separately across calendar time, geography and care setting rather than conflated into a single study or source indicator, but standard practice indexes everything by a study identifier so these dimensions cannot be separated.”
What was wrong with it. The source stated the non-identification as a fact about ITC and PAIC practice in general. Both auditors narrowed it to non-crossed evidence in which each dimension is constant within a study, and the literature auditor noted that regression on study-level terms such as region or period is already available in multinma, so the missing qualifier belongs in the statement.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I found no work resolving this and no work asserting the absence, so I am judging the claims on their merits. The load-bearing claim, that in a two-study indirect comparison calendar time, geography and care setting are not separately identified, is a straightforward collinearity fact: with two studies the study indicator is binary and every study-level covariate is a deterministic function of it, so no contrast can attribute a discrepancy to a dimension. That is defensible without citation. The caveat is scope. The title generalizes to ITC/PAIC as a whole, but the identification failure is specific to two-study (and more generally to non-crossed) evidence structures; network meta-regression and ML-NMR can and do carry study-level covariates such as region or period once the network has enough crossed structure, and multinma supports regression on study-level terms including baseline risk. The entry’s own why_open concedes this (‘separating them requires evidence with crossed structure’), so the fix is to move that qualifier into the title and statement rather than to change the vote. The remaining claims are descriptive of practice and I found nothing contradicting them.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 and C4 are sound when all three dimensions are relevant to the target decision. C3 is a rank statement only under the missing qualifier that each dimension is constant within each of two studies: then every dimension is an affine function of the binary study indicator, so the design identifies at most one composite between-study contrast, not three dimension-specific effects. A two-study label alone does not imply failure if multiregional, multiperiod, site-level, or registry data provide crossed variation. C2 is a broad practice claim, not a mathematical necessity. At cpaic@9d150e9, study intercepts and generic covariates are available but no separate calendar-time, geography, or setting transport diagnostics are exported. No estimator can solve perfect collinearity without external restrictions; the open task is evidence design, measurement, and sensitivity analysis rather than computation. The asserted high severity is context-dependent.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Global inconsistency diagnostics lack calibrated operating characteristics
text: IDN-15 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: Global inconsistency diagnostics lack calibrated operating characteristics
text:
Statement
The global statistics used to interrogate the consistency assumption in network meta-analysis, namely the graph-theoretical Q statistics with their I-squared analogues, residual-deviance and DIC comparison of a consistency model against an inconsistency model, and stepwise removal of studies flagged in a leverage plot, are deployed as screens without a decision rule of known error rates. The one study that measured them found none acceptable: across networks of three to five treatments, residual deviance and stepwise leverage removal declared inconsistency in 37.8 to 66.1 percent and 32.2 to 87.8 percent of replications when none was present, DIC almost never gave a false positive (0.7 to 2.5 percent) but detected true inconsistency in at most 28.3 percent of replications, and detection by the total Q statistic of a fixed injected inconsistency rose from 6.9 to 63.1 percent purely by raising tau-squared from 0.01 to 0.1 (Kiefer et al. 2020, doi:10.1186/s12874-020-0917-3). That last result is the structural one: these statistics respond to heterogeneity and to inconsistency together, so a screen cannot report which of the two it has found. What is missing is not another statistic but a decision rule with stated false-positive and detection rates over the range of network sizes, sparsity and heterogeneity that published networks occupy, and practice acts on these screens regardless, since prevalence estimates, CINeMA and GRADE inconsistency ratings and the decision whether to pool at all rest on them. The evidence for the calibration itself is also thin: a single simulation with at most five treatments, two-arm studies only, five studies per direct comparison and tau-squared of 0.01 or 0.1, so the operating characteristics of these screens outside that grid are unmeasured rather than known to be bad.

title: Global inconsistency diagnostics lack calibrated operating characteristics
text:
Why it is open
Heterogeneity and inconsistency both inflate the same residual variation, and separating them requires either replication within designs or an assumption about how the two variance components relate, so a global statistic built on total discrepancy is confounded by construction rather than by carelessness. Calibrating a screen requires a known truth, so the work has to be done in simulation, and the scenario grid needed is large: topology, number of studies per design, multi-arm structure, heterogeneity, and the size and placement of the injected inconsistency all move the answer, and the one published grid varied only a few of them. Multi-arm trials, present in 142 of 201 surveyed networks, were excluded from that simulation for ease of implementation, so the structure most common in practice is the least examined. There is also no agreed operating point to calibrate to: global consistency tests are known to have low power, so a threshold that controls false positives leaves the screen nearly useless while one that detects inconsistency flags networks that are merely heterogeneous, and nobody has stated which error the field prefers to make. The absence goes unfelt in applied work because a screen returns a p-value or a fit comparison that reads as a result, and no reference standard exists in a real network against which the verdict could be checked.

title: Global inconsistency diagnostics lack calibrated operating characteristics
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Kiefer, Sturtz and Bender 2020, A simulation study to compare different estimation approaches for network meta-analysis and corresponding methods to evaluate the consistency assumption, BMC Medical Research Methodology 20
Measures false-positive and detection rates for the standard global consistency screens for the first time, concludes that none is suitable, and states that reliable methods for evaluating the consistency assumption in complex networks are missing; the grid covers at most five treatments, two-arm studies and tau-squared of 0.01 or 0.1.


Veroniki, Tsokani, White, Schwarzer et al. 2021, Prevalence of evidence of inconsistency and its association with network structural characteristics in 201 published networks of interventions, BMC Medical Research Methodology 21
Gives the empirical landscape a calibration study would have to reproduce: median 20 studies and seven interventions per network, median three loops, multi-arm trials in 142 of 201 networks, and 92.5 percent of networks containing at least one comparison informed by a single study.


Krahn, Binder and Konig 2013, A graphical tool for locating inconsistency in network meta-analyses, BMC Medical Research Methodology 13:35
Derives the decomposition of the network Q statistic into within-design and between-design parts and the net heat plot built on it, the screen whose false-positive behavior is at issue.


Balduzzi, Rucker, Nikolakopoulou, Papakonstantinou et al. 2023, netmeta: An R Package for Network Meta-Analysis Using Frequentist Methods, Journal of Statistical Software 106(2)
Documents the implementations that make these screens the default in applied work, including the design decomposition and node splitting, with conventional significance thresholds and no calibration guidance.


Spineli 2021, A Revised Framework to Evaluate the Consistency Assumption Globally in a Network of Interventions, Medical Decision Making 42:637-648
Repairs the unrelated mean effects model so multi-arm trials are accommodated and all observed comparisons are estimated, and adds deviance-contribution plots; it improves the diagnostic without attaching error rates to any decision rule based on it.


Spineli 2024, Local inconsistency detection using the Kullback-Leibler divergence measure, Systematic Reviews 13
Replaces the significance test for local inconsistency with an average Kullback-Leibler divergence between direct and indirect estimates compared against what the work itself calls a semi-objective threshold; it shows how far test-based verdicts and divergence-based verdicts diverge, and inherits the absence of calibrated error rates.


Nikolakopoulou, Higgins, Papakonstantinou, Chaimani et al. 2020, CINeMA: An approach for assessing confidence in the results of a network meta-analysis, PLOS Medicine 17:e1003082
The downstream consumer that converts an inconsistency screen result into a confidence rating for a network estimate, so the screen’s unmeasured error rates propagate into a graded conclusion.


Zarin, Veroniki, Nincic, Vafaei et al. 2017, Characteristics and knowledge synthesis approach for 456 network meta-analyses: a scoping review, BMC Medicine 15
Supplies the published network structures needed to build a calibration grid from real topologies instead of constructed examples; the nmadb package that served them programmatically was archived from CRAN on 2025-01-23, and the 217 datasets in tracenma are a maintained alternative.

title: Global inconsistency diagnostics lack calibrated operating characteristics
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Run the calibration study the field has never run: fix the decision rules currently in use, then measure false-positive and detection rates over a scenario grid built from real topologies, using the published network collections rather than constructed examples, crossed with heterogeneity and with the size and placement of an injected inconsistency, and including multi-arm trials rather than excluding them. Report the two error rates as functions of the design characteristics an analyst can see before testing, so the output is a statement of when a screen can be believed rather than a global verdict on the screen. Separate the two signals rather than only measuring their confusion: statistics computed from within-design replication alone, or from the difference between consistency and inconsistency fits at a fixed heterogeneity, are candidates that are not confounded by construction and have never been compared on this criterion. Choose the operating point explicitly, since a screen used to license pooling and a screen used to trigger investigation need different thresholds, and both should be prespecified with measured error rates attached rather than inherited from a 0.05 or 0.10 convention. Where a screen cannot be calibrated, say so in the guidance that consumes it, because CINeMA and GRADE currently turn an uncalibrated test result into a confidence rating.

Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this from a single simulation study, and the reviewer accepted the gap while noting that the absolute claim that these operating characteristics are unreported is overstated, since the cited simulation reports them. Partially addressed is the accurate reading: false-positive and detection rates have been measured once and found unacceptable, but only for networks of at most five treatments with two-arm studies, so no calibrated decision rule exists for the networks these screens are actually applied to.

title: No criterion for discarding a present but non-exchangeable anchor
text: IDN-17 Confirmed open Very high priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: No criterion for discarding a present but non-exchangeable anchor
text:
Statement
Guidance makes the connectedness of the randomized evidence decide whether an unanchored comparison is admissible, but an analyst can declare a connected network effectively disconnected by judging that the nominally common comparator is not the same condition across trials, for example because the placebo response depends on the mode of administration or because rescue and subsequent therapies differ. Nothing governs that declaration. There is no test or threshold for how much comparator drift is enough, no requirement to report the anchored analysis beside the unanchored one, no sensitivity analysis over the disconnection decision itself, and no way to price the exchange being made: a partially checkable constancy assumption on relative effects is traded for an untestable constancy assumption on absolute outcomes. The two assumptions are not on a common scale, so the trade has no natural currency, and the resulting bias is unsigned in both directions, since comparator drift biases the anchored estimate by an amount nobody computes and disconnection introduces residual confounding by an amount nobody computes either. The election is consequential: in a migraine example a fixed-effects network meta-analysis and a network meta-regression found few differences between anti-CGRP antibodies, while an unanchored simulated treatment comparison run on the premise that mode of administration creates a distinct contextual effect came out strongly in favor of one product, and the same analysis found no evidence of a non-zero placebo-response coefficient because too few studies contributed to each comparison (Fawsitt et al. 2023, doi:10.57264/cer-2023-0021). The discretion has been named without being closed: population adjustment methods were criticized for giving very considerable leeway to investigators to choose anchored or unanchored approaches (Phillippo et al. 2018, doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740), and no criterion has followed.

title: No criterion for discarding a present but non-exchangeable anchor
text:
Why it is open
Comparator drift is real and sometimes large, so a blanket rule that a connected network must always be analyzed anchored would be wrong; the remedy therefore has to be a criterion, and criteria are harder to write than prohibitions. The evidence needed to check the premise is largely the evidence the disconnection discards, because whether the comparator arms differ beyond chance is a question the anchored model would answer, and it is underpowered in exactly the small networks where the question arises. There is no scale on which to express the exchange, since the anchored bias is a function of unobserved comparator drift and the unanchored bias is a function of unobserved prognostic imbalance, and neither quantity is identified from the data at hand. The declaration is also made by the party that assembles the evidence and that benefits from the outcome, and because the anchored analysis is often not reported at all a reviewer cannot see what the decision cost. Reporting conventions have not caught up: nothing obliges a submission to present both analyses, so the discretion leaves no audit trail.

title: No criterion for discarding a present but non-exchangeable anchor
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Fawsitt, Thom, Regnier, Lee, Kymes and Vase 2023, Comparison of indirect treatment methods in migraine prevention to address differences in mode of administration, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research 12
Runs network meta-analysis, network meta-regression and unanchored simulated treatment comparison on the same connected evidence base, reaches materially different conclusions, and justifies treating the network as disconnected by a contextual effect of administration route that its own regression could not support because too few studies informed each comparison.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making 38:200-211
States that unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions widely regarded as infeasible, and identifies the specific discretion at issue here, that MAIC and STC give very considerable leeway to investigators to choose anchored or unanchored approaches, without proposing a criterion for the choice.


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 18: Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Submissions to NICE
Makes connectedness of the randomized evidence the admissibility rule for unanchored analysis; it does not say what qualifies a nominally shared comparator as non-exchangeable, which is where the rule is circumvented.


Bucher, Guyatt, Griffith and Walter 1997, The results of direct and indirect treatment comparisons in meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 50:683-691
The anchored indirect comparison whose validity rests on the common comparator being the same condition in both trials; the requirement is stated qualitatively and has never been operationalized as a checkable threshold.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades and Didelez 2018, Sensitivity of Treatment Recommendations to Bias in Network Meta-Analysis, JRSS-A 181:843-867
Threshold analysis: computes how much bias in a piece of evidence would have to be present before the recommendation changes; this is the existing machinery for pricing the anchored-versus-unanchored election and has not been applied to it.


Chandler and Ishak 2026, Anchors Away: Navigating Unanchored Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR), arXiv:2606.20341
Extends unanchored comparison beyond the pairwise case and makes its assumptions explicit so they can be tested in sensitivity analysis; it improves what happens after the election is made rather than constraining the election.

title: No criterion for discarding a present but non-exchangeable anchor
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Write the decision as a comparison of two bias budgets rather than as a judgment: express the anchored estimator’s bias as a function of comparator drift, express the unanchored estimator’s bias as a function of residual prognostic imbalance, and require the analysis to report the drift magnitude at which the two are equal, which is a threshold analysis of a kind already built for network meta-analysis. Require both analyses to be presented, so an unanchored analysis of a connected network appears alongside the anchored one it replaced with the difference attributed, and a reviewer sees the cost of the election rather than only its result. Test the premise wherever the data allow: a comparator-arm contrast, a network meta-regression on the proposed contextual variable, or a design decomposition restricted to the comparator arms each give an observable implication of the claim that the anchor is not shared, and reporting the result of that check should be a precondition rather than an optional extra. Prespecify the criterion, since the choice is currently made after both answers are visible. Where the premise cannot be checked at all, the disconnection should be presented as a sensitivity analysis rather than as the base case.

title: No criterion for discarding a present but non-exchangeable anchor
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this from a single applied comparison, and the reviewer accepted it as a real design-election problem not settled by the ordinary rule that randomized connectedness permits an anchored analysis, while declining the broader empirical claim that unanchored analyses generally give larger and more precise effects. The evidence for the gap is one worked case plus the long-standing observation that the choice is left to investigator discretion; no survey has measured how often connected networks are analyzed unanchored or what it changes.

title: No principled basis for shared effect-modifier treatment classes

title: No principled basis for shared effect-modifier treatment classes
text:
Statement
The shared effect modifier assumption is defined relative to a set of treatments assumed to carry identical interaction vectors, and it is the restriction that makes most small-network multilevel network meta-regression and most target-transportable MAIC or STC identifiable at all. Nothing governs how that set is chosen. In practice it is enlarged until the model is estimable: one metastatic prostate cancer analysis grouped every treatment except the reference into a single class spanning docetaxel chemotherapy, androgen deprivation, a non-steroidal antiandrogen and three androgen-receptor pathway inhibitors, across twelve studies with individual patient data from one of them (Shore et al. 2026, doi:10.57264/cer-2025-0100); a relapsed refractory myeloma application shares interactions across a CAR-T product, a nuclear export inhibitor and an antibody-drug conjugate (Maciel et al. 2024, doi:10.1016/j.jval.2024.04.017); and the psoriasis application that validated the method used mechanism-defined classes (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162). Widening the class strictly weakens the identifying assumption while strictly improving estimability, so the incentive runs toward the widest partition a reviewer will accept, and the partition is typically settled after the analyst has seen which version converges. What does not exist is a criterion linking class membership to an observable implication, a measure of how much a target contrast moves across admissible partitions, or a requirement to report the partition and its justification as an identifying assumption rather than as a modeling detail. The relaxations software provides operate within a fixed partition rather than over it: multinma’s class_interactions argument moves between common, exchangeable and independent interactions for a given class structure, and the class-effect model selection algorithm of Perren et al. (doi:10.1177/0272989X251389887) selects among class-effect structures on the treatment effects, not among partitions of the interaction assumption.

title: No principled basis for shared effect-modifier treatment classes
text:
Why it is open
The assumption restricts interaction vectors for treatments whose interactions are, by hypothesis, not separately estimable, so it is only testable in networks that do not need it, and any diagnostic is weakest exactly where the partition carries the most identifying weight. Class membership is a scientific claim about shared mechanism of effect modification, which is not the same as shared mechanism of action and is rarely the subject of any direct evidence, so there is often nothing external to appeal to. Widening the class is not visibly wrong: a wider class fits, converges and returns narrower intervals, so the diagnostic signature of an indefensible partition looks like success. A partition-sensitivity analysis is easy to describe and nobody has built it, partly because the number of possible partitions grows quickly and there is no agreed way to restrict the candidate set to clinically defensible ones. Reporting practice hides the choice, since the partition is usually stated in a single clause of a methods section, if at all, and does not appear among the items that appraisal checklists ask for.

title: No principled basis for shared effect-modifier treatment classes
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo, Dias, Ades, Belger et al. 2020, Multilevel Network Meta-Regression for Population-Adjusted Treatment Comparisons, JRSS-A 183:1189-1210
Defines the model in which the shared effect modifier assumption becomes the identifying restriction when aggregate-data arms cannot support treatment-specific interactions; the assumption is stated relative to a treatment set whose construction is left to the analyst.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades, Welton et al. 2023, Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis, Medical Decision Making
Uses mechanism-defined classes and relaxes the shared interaction one covariate at a time, comparing posteriors and model fit; the relaxation is over covariates within a fixed partition rather than over the partition itself, and its power is conceded to be low.


multinma R package, nma() argument class_interactions
Implements common, exchangeable and independent interaction structures for a class of treatments, so the strength of the sharing can be varied; the classes themselves are supplied by the user and no diagnostic reports sensitivity to that input.


Perren, Pedder, Welton and Phillippo 2026, Network Meta-Analysis with Class Effects: A Practical Guide and Model Selection Algorithm, Medical Decision Making 46:275-295
Gives a model selection algorithm for class-effect structures and sharing of within-class variability across sparse classes; it applies to class effects on the treatment effects, and its adaptation to partitions of the interaction assumption has not been made.


Shore, Morgans, Paracha, Thom et al. 2026, Population-adjusted network meta-analyses provide new insights into the efficacy of treatment alternatives for metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research 15
Groups all treatments except the reference into one class with identical effect-modifier impact, over twelve studies with individual patient data from one trial; the partition is stated in a sentence and is not accompanied by a justification or a sensitivity analysis.


Maciel, Jansen, Klijn and Towle 2024, Implementing Multilevel Network Meta-Regression for Time-To-Event Outcomes: A Case Study in Relapsed Refractory Multiple Myeloma, Value in Health 27:1012-1020
A second application that shares effect-modifier interactions across mechanistically dissimilar agents in order to estimate the model, showing that the widest-class strategy is not confined to one therapeutic area.


NICE DSU Technical Support Document 18: Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Submissions to NICE
Sets out what a population-adjusted submission must justify; the treatment set over which effect modification is assumed shared is not among the items it requires to be reported or defended.

title: No principled basis for shared effect-modifier treatment classes
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the partition-sensitivity diagnostic first, since it is the cheapest change that would alter practice: refit under every clinically defensible partition and report the induced range of the target contrast next to the point estimate, so a contrast whose sign depends on the class structure becomes visible. Define the admissible candidate set with clinicians before fitting and record it in the protocol, so the partition is a prespecified identifying assumption rather than a consequence of which model converged. Adapt the existing class-effect model selection algorithm from treatment effects to interaction vectors so partitions can be compared on fit where the network supports it, and state the network size at which that comparison has power rather than assuming it does. Where the partition cannot be checked, replace the equality constraint with a hierarchical prior over interaction vectors around a class-level mean and report how the contrast moves as the shrinkage is loosened, which multinma supports within a partition and would need extending across partitions. Finally, require the partition and its justification in reporting, on the same footing as the covariate list.

title: No principled basis for shared effect-modifier treatment classes
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this from a single applied analysis, with two further published applications cited as corroboration, and the reviewer accepted the treatment partition as an identifying modeling choice distinct from covariate selection and from the power to test a fixed shared-interaction restriction. No methodological work addresses partition choice; the evidence that it is unconstrained is that published applications range from one class containing everything to mechanism-defined classes with no stated criterion in any of them.

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Statement
PAIC missingness spans three layers that rest on different assumptions and admit different remedies: participant-level missing covariates or outcomes inside the IPD, trial-level non-reporting in the aggregate publication, and structurally unavailable IPD for whole studies. Fang et al. (2026, doi:10.1007/s43441-026-00914-2) closes the first layer for MAIC by multiplying an inverse-probability-of-being-observed weight into the matching weights, with simulation evidence; the other two layers are untouched, and multiple imputation congenial with the transport model, missing-not-at-random sensitivity analysis, and imputation of missing target summaries remain unbuilt. Complete-case handling is not a single default that collapses all three, because it acts on individual records while an absent aggregate summary and an unavailable IPD study are identification and data-access problems it cannot reach. What survives is narrower: complete-case deletion changes the identifying sample, and any imputation, weighting, or standardization has to preserve the target estimand and the conditional distributions the transport step relies on.

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Why it is open
Deleting a record for a missing covariate does not only lose a variable; it removes a patient from the balancing constraint set, so the population actually being matched shifts with nothing in the output to signal it. The other two layers resist the same treatment: an unreported aggregate moment cannot be imputed from nothing without auxiliary information or an identified model, and a study with no IPD is an access problem rather than a missing-data problem. The one solution that exists is specific to MAIC and to missingness inside the IPD, so nothing yet propagates uncertainty jointly across imputation, weighting, and target-summary estimation, and packages still do not record which strategy was used; the literature auditor found that maicplus 0.1.2 and outstandR 2.0.0 declare no missing-data dependency at all. Missing-not-at-random departures stay unidentifiable from the data, so sensitivity analysis is needed wherever a missing-at-random assumption is not defensible rather than as a blanket requirement.

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Fang, Li, Lai and He 2026, Missing Data Handling in the Application of Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison, Ther Innov Regul Sci 60(4):1103-1111
states that the literature lacks guidance on how to handle missing data in the application of MAIC, then proposes weighting-based methods for missing outcomes and covariates inside the IPD, formed as the product of an inverse probability of not missing the outcome and the usual MAIC balancing weights, with extensive simulation studies; it does not address unreported aggregate summaries or structurally unavailable IPD


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
handles the three layers differently rather than collapsing them: cstc() delegates NA handling to glm() and coxph(), cmaic() rejects nonfinite weights caused by missing matching covariates, cmlnmr() rejects missing covariates and outcomes outright, missing aggregate moments raise an error, and aggregate-only edges keep their published study-population contrast; it has no coherent missing-data framework

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Layer one now has a weighting solution for MAIC, so the work there is validation and extension: test it outside MAIC, against multiple imputation, and under conditions the original simulations did not cover. Multiple imputation congenial with a transport model still has to be built, with imputation variables chosen by their causal role rather than from a fixed checklist, since a selection indicator is usually unavailable when target microdata do not exist. Missing target summaries need auxiliary information or an explicit identified model rather than imputation from nothing, and missing-not-at-random departures need declared sensitivity analysis. At minimum, software should record which missing-data strategy was applied, because the choice is currently invisible in the output; a negligible-missingness threshold is the wrong test, since it is neither necessary nor sufficient for complete-case validity.

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Our study

Missing covariate values in the individual-data trial of a MAIC
The question put to it. When a matched covariate is missing for some patients in the individual-data trial, when is complete-case MAIC biased, and do inverse-probability-of-observation weighting and multiple imputation repair it?
What it found. Complete-case MAIC bias is set by the missingness mechanism, not the rate. It is unbiased when missingness depends only on matched covariates, including the missing covariate itself, and biased already at 15% missingness when it depends on an unmatched effect modifier, the outcome with modification, or an unmatched covariate in one arm only. Weighting and imputation repair the missing-at-random cases (imputation with arm interactions most reliably) but are biased by up to 0.22 when missingness depends on the missing covariate itself, where complete case is not.
Results.

Complete case within 3 MCSE of zero in all 24 scenarios predicted unbiased and beyond 3 MCSE in all 4 predicted-biased scenarios at 15% missingness.
Missingness in one arm driven by an unmatched prognostic covariate: complete-case bias -0.34 at 15% and -0.65 at 30%, with no effect modification.
Missingness driven by the missing covariate: complete case within 0.035; observation weighting and imputation biased by up to 0.22.
Imputation without arm interactions carried small systematic bias (up to 0.05); observation weighting failed with extreme weights when 60% to 95% of one arm was missing.

Design.

Estimand

Target-population mean difference, A versus C, in the anchored MAIC

Methods compared

complete-case MAIC, observation weighting, multiple imputation with arm interactions, multiple imputation without arm terms

Data-generating mechanism

Continuous-outcome MAIC with one partly missing matched covariate, one observed matched covariate and one unmatched covariate; 36 cells crossing missingness rate, six mechanisms and whether the unmatched covariate modifies the effect; complete case, observation weighting and congenial or generic imputation. 1000 replicates per cell.

Replicates

1000 per scenario (997 in 4), 36,000 in total


What this does not answer. Missing outcomes, binary outcomes, STC, overlap levels and pattern-mixture sensitivity analysis not run; single-driver mechanisms only. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Missing aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD have no remedy
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides. Reopened by the full-text reading: 4 findings from 4 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from unverifiable to partially-addressed.
The source titled this. “Three missingness layers in PAIC collapse to a complete-case default” The title says all three missingness layers collapse to a complete-case default, which the audit found too strong since the layers are handled differently and layer one has been closed by weighting.
The source said. “PAIC missingness has three distinct layers with different mechanisms: participant-level missing covariates or outcomes inside the IPD, trial-level non-reporting in the aggregate publication, and structurally unavailable IPD for whole studies. Packages default to complete-case handling that collapses all three, and standard imputation is not automatically compatible with the transport model, so imputations valid in the source need not be valid in the target.”
What was wrong with it. The three-layer taxonomy was unattributed in the source, and its central claim, that packages default to a complete-case handling that collapses all three layers, was too strong. The literature auditor supplied the missing source, Fang et al. 2026 (doi:10.1007/s43441-026-00914-2), which states that the literature lacks guidance on handling missing data in MAIC and then closes layer one by weighting; the code auditor found that at commit 9d150e9 of the unreleased cpaic development package the layers are handled differently rather than collapsed, since cmlnmr() rejects missing covariates and outcomes outright, missing aggregate moments raise an error, and aggregate-only edges keep their published contrast.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Retrieved Fang, Li, Lai & He (2026), Ther Innov Regul Sci 60(4):1103-1111, which both confirms the absence claim and partly closes it. The paper states outright: ‘However, the literature lacks guidance on how to handle missing data in the application of MAIC.’ That is a source asserting the absence, which is what the entry’s unsourced claims need. It then proposes a solution for layer one only: ‘we propose some weighting-based methods to handle missing data in the outcome variable and/or covariates when applying MAIC. These weights can be expressed as products of the inverse probability of not missing the outcomes and weights that account for the difference in baseline characteristics… Extensive simulation studies are conducted.’ So participant-level missing covariates and outcomes inside the IPD are now handled, by inverse-probability weighting nested inside the MAIC weights, with simulation evidence. The other two layers are untouched: trial-level non-reporting in the aggregate publication, and structurally unavailable IPD. Multiple imputation congenial with the transport model remains unbuilt (Fang et al. use weighting, not MI), as does MNAR sensitivity analysis and imputation of missing target summaries. maicplus 0.1.2 and outstandR 2.0.0 declare no missing-data dependency, consistent with the complete-case-default claim. codex dissented (open): C2 is a useful taxonomy, but complete-case analysis cannot collapse all three layers: it acts on individual records, while absent aggregate summaries and unavailable IPD create different identification or data-access problems. C3, C4, and C6 are unsourced prevalence or maturity claims. C5 is correct when the missing variables are required for identification. C7 is possible, not inevitable; dependence between missingness, study selection, and transport must be represented by an explicit causal or selection model. C8 and C9 are broadly sound as conditional recommendations. C10 is too prescriptive: treatment, outcome, study, and selection indicators belong in an imputation model only when their variation and causal roles require them, and a selection indicator cannot ordinarily be used in standard MI when target microdata do not exist. C11 is not universally required, although MNAR sensitivity analysis is warranted when MAR is not defensible. C12 requires auxiliary information or an identified model; missing target summaries cannot simply be imputed from nothing. C13 uses the wrong criterion: negligible missingness is neither necessary nor sufficient for complete-case validity. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, cstc() delegates NA handling to glm()/coxph(), cmaic() rejects nonfinite weights caused by missing matching covariates, cmlnmr() explicitly rejects missing covariates and outcomes, missing AgD moments cause errors, and aggregate-only edges are retained rather than complete-cased. Thus cpaic does not collapse the three layers, although it lacks a coherent missing-data framework. The issue is decision-critical only when missingness or data availability threatens identification or materially changes precision.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

C3, C4, and C6 are unsourced prevalence or maturity claims. C5 is correct when the missing variables are required for identification. C8 and C9 are broadly sound as conditional recommendations. C10 is too prescriptive: treatment, outcome, study, and selection indicators belong in an imputation model only when their variation and causal roles require them, and a selection indicator cannot ordinarily be used in standard MI when target microdata do not exist. C11 is not universally required, although MNAR sensitivity analysis is warranted when MAR is not defensible. C12 requires auxiliary information or an identified model; missing target summaries cannot simply be imputed from nothing. C13 uses the wrong criterion: negligible missingness is neither necessary nor sufficient for complete-case validity. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, cstc() delegates NA handling to glm()/coxph(), cmaic() rejects nonfinite weights caused by missing matching covariates, cmlnmr() explicitly rejects missing covariates and outcomes, missing AgD moments cause errors, and aggregate-only edges are retained rather than complete-cased. Thus cpaic does not collapse the three layers, although it lacks a coherent missing-data framework. The issue is decision-critical only when missingness or data availability threatens identification or materially changes precision.

How the evidence falls in time
