title: Network meta-interpolation has no stated estimand and no implementation
text: MOD-14 Partially addressed High priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Network meta-interpolation has no stated estimand and no implementation
text:
Statement
Network meta-interpolation adjusts for effect modification by using published subgroup results to impute treatment effects at a covariate profile common to every trial, through a best linear unbiased predictor, and then running a standard network meta-analysis on the interpolated contrasts. Its inputs are the marginal contrasts trials publish, while the interpolation equations treat those contrasts as conditional at a covariate value, so the quantity the fitted network returns is neither a population-average marginal effect nor a conditional effect at a declared profile, and it yields no absolute predictions. The only simulation evidence is the development study itself: across two four-treatment networks it reported root mean squared error of 0.228 for interpolation against 0.241 for standard network meta-analysis, 0.447 for multilevel network meta-regression and 0.541 for aggregate network meta-regression in the base-case non-shared-modifier scenario, with credible interval coverage following a similar pattern. No evaluation separates bias from variance or asks whether the variance propagated through the interpolation step is adequate, and no independent group has replicated the comparison. There is no package: every application adapts bespoke code, which a 2026 oncology application states explicitly while noting that its comparator method ships in multinma. Missing are a statement of what interpolation identifies, an independent evaluation reporting bias and variance separately across overlap, subgroup completeness and covariate type, and a maintained implementation.

title: Network meta-interpolation has no stated estimand and no implementation
text:
Why it is open
The estimand question cannot be settled by simulation, because a simulation scores an estimator against a target that has already been named, and this target has not been. The freedom that makes the method attractive is the same freedom that makes its target hard to write down: it deliberately avoids the shared effect modifier assumption, and the covariate profile it interpolates to is fixed by whichever subgroup breakdowns the trials happened to publish, so the estimand is set by reporting practice rather than by the decision. An independent evaluation needs a data-generating mechanism that produces realistic subgroup summaries, including partially reported and mutually incompatible breakdowns, and no published simulation framework in this literature supplies one. Packaging is unattractive work: a usable implementation must own the subgroup data model, the imputation and its variance, and the handover to a network fit, which is three components for a method with a small user base and a published correction rather than a maintained code base.

title: Network meta-interpolation has no stated estimand and no implementation
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Harari, Soltanifar, Cappelleri, Verhoek, Ouwens, Daly & Heeg 2023, Research Synthesis Methods 14(2):211-233
Introduces network meta-interpolation: subgroup and study-level treatment effects are converted by best linear unbiased prediction into effects and standard errors at effect-modifier values common to all studies, without assuming shared effect modification, then synthesized by standard network meta-analysis. Reports the simulation study that is still the only evaluation, scoring root mean squared error and credible interval coverage against standard NMA, network meta-regression and ML-NMR.


Correction to Network Meta-Interpolation, Research Synthesis Methods 2024;15(2):369
Published correction to the method article, which is the closest thing the method has to maintenance.


Phillippo, Remiro-Azocar, Heath & Baio 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Review of marginal and conditional estimands for decision making that assesses network meta-interpolation directly: it mixes incompatible estimates within the model, cannot produce marginal effects or absolute predictions, and its properties are not yet fully understood because simulation studies have not directly investigated bias or the adequacy of variance estimation.


Shore, Morgans, Paracha & Thom 2026, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research
Applies interpolation alongside ML-NMR to a decision-relevant metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer network and records that no package currently exists to implement it, while ML-NMR is available in multinma and saves the user from developing custom code.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams & Welton 2018, Medical Decision Making 38(2):200-211
Sets out the population-adjustment framework for health technology appraisal and the shared effect modifier assumption that interpolation is designed to avoid, which is the benchmark against which its estimand claim has to be judged.

title: Network meta-interpolation has no stated estimand and no implementation
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Write the estimand down first: state, for a given collection of published subgroup summaries, what function of the trial populations the interpolated contrast at a common covariate profile equals, and the conditions under which the interpolation is unbiased for it. Then run an evaluation that is not by the developers, reporting bias, empirical standard error, model-based standard error and coverage separately, crossing departure from shared effect modification with subgroup completeness, number of reported modifiers, continuous versus categorical modifiers, and the correlation of modifiers across trials, with ML-NMR fitted on matched information as the comparator. Score it on the marginal target-standardized quantity a decision needs as well as on the interpolated contrast, so an estimand mismatch shows up in the performance table instead of being absorbed into root mean squared error. Package the imputation and the network fit together, exposing the subgroup data model, the imputation variance and the propagated standard errors, so that an analysis using it can be reproduced and audited.

title: Network meta-interpolation has no stated estimand and no implementation
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as an estimator-level gap distinct from the general marginal-versus-conditional estimand problem, because it concerns this method’s particular interpolation construction and variance calculation. The verdict is partially-addressed rather than confirmed-open because the development study does contain an extensive simulation reporting root mean squared error and coverage; what is absent is any independent evaluation, any separation of bias from variance, a statement of the estimand, and an implementation.

title: No criterion chooses pooled or arm-separate matching in anchored MAIC
text: MOD-16 Confirmed open High priority Established Tractability 5/5

title: No criterion chooses pooled or arm-separate matching in anchored MAIC
text:
Statement
In an anchored matching-adjusted indirect comparison the analyst may estimate one weight vector matching the pooled individual patient data trial to the pooled aggregate trial, or two weight vectors matching the active arm to the aggregate active arm and the control arm to the aggregate control arm separately. The two choices identify different quantities and fail in opposite directions. Arm-separate matching reproduces whatever arm imbalance the aggregate trial had and was more precise and less biased in the simulation that introduced it; it also reweights the two arms of a randomized trial by different functions, so the within-trial balance that randomization supplied on covariates outside the matching set is no longer guaranteed. The evaluation that introduced it recommends it while stating that the approach might break the randomization, that covariates might be imbalanced after weighting, and that further investigation under a more diverse array of situations is needed. No diagnostic reports whether randomization-induced balance on unmatched covariates survived a particular arm-separate weighting, and no rule maps the observed arm imbalance in the aggregate trial and the prognostic strength of unmatched covariates onto a choice. Because arm-level aggregate summaries are routinely published the choice arises in most anchored analyses, it is exposed as an ungoverned user option in the tooling built around the method, and no reporting requirement asks which was used.

title: No criterion chooses pooled or arm-separate matching in anchored MAIC
text:
Why it is open
The two options trade one bias against another and neither bias is estimable from the data at hand: matching each arm separately protects the comparison against arm-level covariate differences that a pooled match would average away, while differential reweighting of randomized arms can introduce confounding through covariates that were never in the matching set. A diagnostic for the second failure would have to demonstrate balance on covariates that are by construction not reported for the comparator trial, so the check needs precisely the information the design lacks. The two published simulation-based positions were generated under different data-generating mechanisms, so reading them against each other cannot settle which is right; a resolution requires a study whose factors include the size of the aggregate trial’s arm imbalance and the prognostic strength of unmatched covariates, which is the combination nobody has crossed. Practice leaves no trail either, since submissions need not state which weighting was used, so the field cannot learn retrospectively which choice moved which result.

title: No criterion chooses pooled or arm-separate matching in anchored MAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Petto, Kadziola, Brnabic, Saure et al. 2019, Value in Health 22(1):85-91
Introduces and evaluates weighting each arm of the individual-data trial to the corresponding arm of the aggregate trial via the common comparator, reports better precision and lower bias than pooled matching in simulation, and states that the approach might break the randomization, that covariates might be imbalanced after weighting, and that further investigation across a more diverse array of situations is needed.


Jiang, Cappelleri, Gamalo, Chen, Thomas & Chu 2024, Research Synthesis Methods 15(4):671-686
Comprehensive review of matching-adjusted indirect comparison, its derivation, assumptions and connection to calibration estimation in survey sampling, accompanied by the Shiny-MAIC application that offers anchored and unanchored analyses and alternative variance estimators as user settings. Reproduces the weighting options without adjudicating between them.


Remiro-Azocar 2022, BMC Medical Research Methodology 22:217
Two-stage matching-adjusted indirect comparison, the closest formal treatment of arm-differential weighting: a treatment-assignment model inside the individual-data trial produces inverse probability weights that are combined with trial-assignment odds weights, so arms are weighted differently in order to correct chance imbalance in the randomized trial rather than to reproduce the aggregate trial’s imbalance.


Signorovitch, Wu, Yu, Gerrits et al. 2010, PharmacoEconomics 28(10):935-945
The original matching-adjusted indirect comparison, which matches on pooled trial-level summaries and so sets the pooled option as the default from which the arm-separate variant departs.


Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams & Welton 2018, Medical Decision Making 38(2):200-211
The appraisal-facing framework for population-adjusted indirect comparison, which sets out what an anchored analysis is assumed to preserve; it does not address how the weighting problem should be partitioned across randomized arms.

title: No criterion chooses pooled or arm-separate matching in anchored MAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Run one simulation study whose factors are the ones that separate the two options: the size and direction of arm imbalance in the aggregate trial, the prognostic strength and the number of covariates outside the matching set, the effective sample size after weighting, and the true effect modification. Score bias, coverage and precision for pooled and arm-separate weighting together with balance on the unmatched covariates, so the randomization-breaking failure appears as a measured quantity rather than a warning. Derive and report the estimand each option targets, since a comparison that reproduces the aggregate trial’s arm imbalance and one that removes it are answers to different questions, and state which corresponds to the decision population. Where the choice cannot be made on evidence, make it disclosable: require that the weighting partition, the resulting per-arm effective sample sizes and the balance achieved on all covariates be reported, and offer both fits as a standard sensitivity pair.

title: No criterion chooses pooled or arm-separate matching in anchored MAIC
text:
Our study

Arm-separate matching cancels the aggregate trial’s chance imbalance; pooled matching carries it
The question put to it. Arm-separate matching weights each individual-data arm to the corresponding aggregate arm; pooled matching uses one weight function. When does each give a biased anchored comparison, and is the bias of arm-separate matching the product of unmatched prognostic strength and aggregate arm imbalance, as the design claims?
What it found. The product claim is wrong. Given an aggregate-trial imbalance kappa, pooled matching is biased by kappa (beta/2 + gamma_X + gamma_U rho_T) and arm-separate matching by kappa gamma_U (rho_T - rho_S); simulation matched both (slopes 1.00 and 0.96). Arm-separate matching reproduces the aggregate imbalance in the individual-data contrast so it cancels, and is biased only when an unmatched prognostic covariate relates to the matched one differently in the two trials. It had smaller bias than pooled matching in every scenario with an imposed imbalance and 10% to 27% lower RMSE under chance imbalance.
Results.

With the matched-unmatched correlation shared between trials, arm-separate bias was within Monte Carlo error of zero in all 16 scenarios with an unmatched prognostic covariate and an imposed imbalance (largest 0.011).
Slope of simulated on predicted bias: pooled 1.004 (SE 0.011); arm-separate 0.958 (SE 0.035).
Under chance imbalance, arm-separate RMSE over pooled 0.73 to 0.90; its sandwich interval overcovered (0.965 to 0.991) because the two trials’ imbalances are positively correlated.
Two-stage MAIC behaved like pooled matching, correcting the individual trial’s imbalance but not the aggregate trial’s.
The design’s candidate diagnostic, the weighted difference in the unmatched covariate between arms, estimates rho_S kappa and cannot see rho_T; its correlation with arm-separate bias was -0.41.

Design.

Estimand

Anchored B-versus-A mean difference in the target

Methods compared

unadjusted Bucher, pooled MAIC, arm-separate MAIC, two-stage MAIC

Data-generating mechanism

Anchored MAIC with a continuous outcome, 300 per arm; 96 scenarios crossing an imposed aggregate-arm imbalance in the matched covariate (0, 0.1, 0.2 SD or chance), the unmatched covariate’s prognostic strength, the matched-unmatched correlation in each trial and shared effect modification; unadjusted, pooled, arm-separate and two-stage MAIC.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 96,000 in total


What this does not answer. Continuous outcome, linear model, one matched and one unmatched covariate, shared effect modification; the non-collapsible case, where arm-separate matching compares arms in different populations, is not studied, and the arm-separate interval’s conservatism is not repaired. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Risk-modeling network meta-regression treats a fitted risk score as observed
text: MOD-18 Confirmed open Medium-high priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: Risk-modeling network meta-regression treats a fitted risk score as observed
text:
Statement
Risk-modeling approaches to treatment effect heterogeneity fit a prognostic model for baseline risk in one dataset, optionally recalibrate it in the trial data, then enter the fitted risk score into a network meta-regression as a prognostic covariate and as an effect modifier. Where the stages are fitted separately the synthesis conditions on that score as though it were observed, so the sampling and shrinkage uncertainty of the prognostic model and of the recalibration never reaches the treatment-effect posterior. This is the generated-regressor problem arriving in evidence synthesis: standard errors computed as if an estimated regressor were data are too small, and the understatement grows where the regressor is least well estimated, which in risk modeling is the tails of the risk distribution and therefore exactly where risk-stratified treatment recommendations are made. The three-stage version that combines a cohort-based prognostic model, recalibration in the trials, and a network meta-regression on the resulting score names a single Bayesian model implementing all three stages as the way to incorporate uncertainty from all stages and avoid spuriously overprecise conclusions, and does not build it; no published risk-modeling meta-analysis or network meta-analysis does. The magnitude of the interval understatement has not been quantified for any published network, so the reported credible intervals on risk-stratified benefit are too narrow by an unknown amount.

title: Risk-modeling network meta-regression treats a fitted risk score as observed
text:
Why it is open
Fitting the stages jointly requires a likelihood linking the prognostic cohort to the trials, and whether that joint model is identified depends on whether the same score means the same thing in both, which is a transportability assumption rather than a modeling detail; where it fails, the recalibration parameters carry the difference and there is no settled answer on whether they should be shared, stratified or partially pooled across trials. Two requirements then conflict. The prognostic cohort is usually far larger than the trials, so a fully joint fit lets a handful of trials influence the prognostic model in ways the analysis did not intend, which is the standard motivation for cutting feedback; cutting feedback is precisely what discards the uncertainty at issue. A bootstrap over the prognostic model is available in principle but has to be propagated through recalibration and a Bayesian network fit for every replicate, which is expensive enough that nobody has reported it. Because nobody has measured the understatement, there is also no demonstrated harm to motivate paying that cost.

title: Risk-modeling network meta-regression treats a fitted risk score as observed
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Chalkou, Hamza, Benkert, Kuhle et al. 2024, Research Synthesis Methods 15(4):641-656
The three-stage model: a prognostic model for baseline risk fitted in a large cohort, recalibrated for trial participants, then used as an effect modifier in a network meta-regression combining aggregate and individual randomized data. States that implementing the three stages in a single Bayesian model would naturally incorporate uncertainty from all stages and avoid spuriously overprecise conclusions, and stops short of doing so.


Chalkou, Steyerberg, Egger, Manca et al. 2021, Statistics in Medicine 40(20):4362-4375
The two-stage predecessor, in which a baseline risk score from a prognostic model enters a network meta-regression as a single prognostic factor and effect modifier; establishes the design in which a fitted score is treated as a covariate.


Kent, Paulus, van Klaveren, D’Agostino et al. 2020, Annals of Internal Medicine 172(1):35-45
The PATH statement, which establishes risk modeling as the recommended route to treatment effect heterogeneity and therefore drives the use of fitted risk scores as covariates in synthesis; it does not address how the uncertainty of the fitted score should propagate.


Pagan 1984, International Economic Review 25(1):221-247
The generated-regressor result: when a regressor is an estimate from a first-stage model, conventional second-stage standard errors are wrong, and the correction depends on the first-stage covariance. This is the general statement of the failure and the reason it is not a small-sample artifact.


Plummer 2015, Statistics and Computing 25(1):37-43
Cuts in Bayesian graphical models: a formal account of what happens when feedback from one module to another is cut, showing the cut distribution is not a posterior and has no general convergence guarantee. This is the trade-off any staged risk-modeling synthesis is implicitly making.

title: Risk-modeling network meta-regression treats a fitted risk score as observed
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Quantify the understatement first, because it is cheap and decides whether the rest is worth doing: refit a published risk-modeling network meta-regression with the prognostic model and recalibration bootstrapped, and report how much the credible intervals on risk-stratified treatment effects widen, separately at the median and at the tails of the risk distribution. Then write the joint model: one Bayesian specification in which the cohort likelihood, the recalibration and the network meta-regression share parameters, and state the conditions under which the treatment-by-risk interaction is identified when the cohort and the trials differ in population. Compare the joint fit against a cut-feedback fit and against the staged fit on interval width, calibration of the predicted benefit and stability of the recalibration parameters, so the cost of protecting the prognostic model from trial feedback is measured rather than assumed. Report the risk score with its own uncertainty in the output, so that a stratified recommendation at the tail can be seen to rest on a weakly estimated score.

title: Risk-modeling network meta-regression treats a fitted risk score as observed
text:
Our study

An estimated risk score used as a regressor
The question put to it. When a risk score estimated in a prognostic cohort is used as a regressor for treatment-effect heterogeneity, does treating it as data understate the interval, and is the understatement worst at the tails of risk?
What it found. Little, given a prognostic cohort of about a thousand patients or more: propagating the score’s estimation uncertainty widened intervals by at most 2.4%, and plug-in coverage stayed near nominal. With 300 cohort patients the widening reached 7% at the risk tails against about 1% at the median, confirming that the understatement is worst where recommendations are made, and plug-in coverage fell to 0.924. The registered rule (plug-in coverage at least 0.93 everywhere) was missed in that one scenario, so the refuting sentence fails as registered.
Results.

Widening ratio 1.001 to 1.024 with cohorts of 1000 or 5000; 1.011 to 1.073 with 300.
Tails against median with 300: widening 1.065 to 1.073 against 1.011 to 1.012.
Plug-in coverage 0.924 to 0.970; propagated 0.932 to 0.974.

Design.

Estimand

Treatment log odds ratio at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of true risk

Methods compared

plug-in interval treating the score as data, interval adding bootstrap variance of the score

Data-generating mechanism

Logistic prognostic score from cohorts of 300 to 5000, used in a six-trial individual-data meta-regression with calibration drift; plug-in and bootstrap-propagated intervals for the treatment effect at the 10th, 50th and 90th risk percentiles. 6 cells, 500 replicates each.

Replicates

500 per scenario, 3,000 in total, each with 20 bootstrap refits


What this does not answer. Pairwise six-trial analysis; frequentist bootstrap rather than a joint or cut Bayesian model; well-specified score. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: No criterion or error-based evidence selects arm-synthesis over contrast-synthesis
text: MOD-20 Confirmed open High priority Established Tractability 4/5

title: No criterion or error-based evidence selects arm-synthesis over contrast-synthesis
text:
Statement
Two model families synthesize a network of trials. Contrast-synthesis holds the study intercepts fixed, so relative effects are estimated from within-study differences alone; arm-synthesis makes them random, which recovers between-study information and lets the model return absolute as well as relative effects. The conditions under which the extra between-study information biases a treatment effect are established theoretically, including a constructed dataset in which a true odds ratio of 1 is estimated as 1.35, but nothing establishes whether those conditions arise in real networks or how large the error is when they do. The one large empirical comparison re-analyzed 118 published networks with binary outcomes under three contrast-synthesis and two arm-synthesis models: against the Bayesian contrast-synthesis reference, arm-synthesis with a common variance returned odds ratios a factor 0.69 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.95) apart and standard errors a factor 0.69 (0.68 to 0.71) apart, while arm-synthesis with treatment-specific variances returned 0.47 (0.37 to 0.61) and standard errors 1.64 times those of the common-variance arm model, with regression-based limits of agreement at the midpoint of the log odds ratios running from minus 0.7 to 0.4 and from minus 1.3 to 0.8; treatment ranks moved with them, and 28 of the 118 arm-synthesis fits either produced no estimate or failed convergence diagnostics. An agreement study of real networks can measure disagreement but never error, and no simulation has scored bias, coverage, interval width and rank recovery for the two families under realistic network conditions, so nothing ranks them by accuracy. There is consequently no rule an analyst can apply before fitting: the standing advice is to prespecify a model and justify it, or to run both as complementary sensitivity analyses. Two subsidiary questions are equally unsettled: whether adding a fixed study main effect makes arm-synthesis equivalent to contrast-synthesis by removing the recovery of between-study information, which has been proposed but never compared; and whether the random-effect variance should differ by treatment or by contrast, which was introduced as a stated belief and left undecided by a deviance information criterion of 298.4 against 298.6 in the worked example that proposed it.

title: No criterion or error-based evidence selects arm-synthesis over contrast-synthesis
text:
Why it is open
An empirical comparison of published networks is the only design that keeps realism, and it can never say which model was right, because the truth is unobserved; only simulation can rank the families by error, and a simulation has to fix the exact quantity in dispute, namely whether study intercepts are associated with treatment effects, so its verdict is written into its data-generating mechanism before a single replicate runs. The comparison is also not purely about bias, because the two families target different estimands: contrast-synthesis returns a study-specific conditional effect while arm-synthesis returns a population-averaged marginal one, so a scoring exercise must first choose which target it is scoring against, and choosing determines much of the answer. Within arm-synthesis the data cannot separate the competing variance structures either, which is why the choice is defended by argument rather than by fit. Worse, the regimes where the choice matters most are the regimes the evidence excludes: empirical comparisons screen out networks failing an inconsistency test because the models being fitted do not represent inconsistency, and sparse networks drop out through convergence failure of the arm-synthesis fits, so the available agreement statistics are computed on the subset where the two families were always going to agree.

title: No criterion or error-based evidence selects arm-synthesis over contrast-synthesis
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Karahalios, White, Turner, Salanti, Herbison, Veroniki, Nikolakopoulou and McKenzie 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
The largest empirical comparison: 118 published binary-outcome networks re-analyzed under three contrast-synthesis and two arm-synthesis models, reporting ratios of odds ratios and of standard errors, Bland-Altman limits of agreement, rank and SUCRA differences, and 28 arm-synthesis fits that failed to estimate or converge; states in its own future-research section that simulation evidence, a test of the fixed-study-effect equivalence and an assessment of the effect of model choice on inconsistency are all still needed.


White, Turner, Karahalios and Salanti 2019, Statistics in Medicine
Derives the four differences between the families, shows that random study intercepts admit between-study information that can cause important bias, gives the constructed example in which a true odds ratio of 1 is estimated as 1.35, and concludes that both families are suitable but that random study intercepts require a strong rationale; supplies the theory a criterion would have to operationalize.


Karahalios, McKenzie and White 2022, Methods in Molecular Biology volume 2345
Sets out both models, their estimands, symmetry and use of between-study information, reviews the simulation and empirical evidence available, and records that this evidence is limited, that it is unknown whether the extra between-study information is a problem in practice, and that simulation studies under realistic scenarios crossing network geometry, sparsity and outcome type are needed.


Dias and Ades 2016, Research Synthesis Methods
The case against arm-synthesis: pooling arm-level summaries breaks the within-trial randomized comparison, and an underlying risk needed for absolute effects is better taken from an external source than from the network; one of the two positions the field has polarized into.


Hong, Chu, Zhang and Carlin 2016, Research Synthesis Methods
Casts arm-synthesis as a Bayesian missing-data problem in which absent arms are imputed under exchangeability of absolute effects; the formulation whose weaker missingness assumption is the main argument in its favor.


Zhang, Carlin, Neaton, Soon, Nie, Kane, Virnig and Chu 2014, Clinical Trials
The arm-synthesis formulation with a correlated multivariate random-effects vector across treatments, from which absolute risks and marginal contrasts are reported; the model implemented in the software applied studies use.


Piepho, Madden and Williams 2024, Research Synthesis Methods
Argues that recovery of between-study information in arm-synthesis is prevented by fitting a fixed study main effect, so the principle of concurrent control can be honored inside an arm-based analysis; the proposed reconciliation that no study has yet compared against either family.


Piepho and Madden 2022, Research Synthesis Methods
Implements the fixed-study-main-effect device in standard generalized linear mixed model procedures, establishing that the reconciliation is routinely fittable and therefore that the missing item is evidence rather than software.


Chu, Lin, Wang, Wang, Chen and Cappelleri 2024, WIREs Computational Statistics
Review of the assumptions, advantages and limitations of the two families for binary outcomes; declines to supply a selection rule and instead recommends fitting both as complementary sensitivity analyses, which is the current state of guidance.


Hawkins, Scott and Woods 2016, Research Synthesis Methods
Introduces the arm-based parameterization with treatment-specific rather than contrast-specific random-effect variances, states as a belief that variation by treatment is the more realistic assumption for many applied studies, and reports deviance information criteria of 298.4 and 298.6 for the two structures, which cannot separate them.


Lin, Zhang, Hodges and Chu 2017, Journal of Statistical Software
The pcnetmeta implementation, the only R package used to fit arm-synthesis in the empirical comparison; settles the dispute over exchangeability of absolute rather than relative effects by citing that both assumptions are accepted in the literature, which is the position a criterion would have to replace.


Lin, Chu and Hodges 2016, Epidemiology
Earlier empirical comparison on 14 networks using treatment exclusion as the perturbation, finding arm-synthesis estimates more stable on average but with large changes in some networks, and recommending that analysts consider both models; the precedent for measuring disagreement rather than error.


Li, Shih, Song and Tu 2023, Research Synthesis Methods
Simulates how bias in one direct comparison propagates through the network under contrast-based, baseline and arm-based models, showing the propagation depends on geometry; the closest existing error-based comparison, scored on how an injected bias spreads rather than on which family recovers the truth.


Luney et al. 2026, BMJ
A 158-trial, 52-intervention network meta-analysis of drugs to prevent postoperative delirium fitted with a Bayesian arm-based model; establishes that the family whose operating characteristics are unmeasured is carrying headline results in general medical journals rather than sitting in the methods literature.

title: No criterion or error-based evidence selects arm-synthesis over contrast-synthesis
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Settle the analytic question first, because it is cheap and it partitions the rest: if fitting a fixed study main effect does remove the recovery of between-study information, then the disagreement measured across the 118 networks is attributable to the random intercepts alone, and what remains is an estimand choice rather than a bias problem. Then run the simulation the field has been asking for since 2022, crossing the presence and strength of association between study intercepts and treatment effects, the degree of inconsistency, the number of studies per treatment, event rarity and network geometry, and scoring bias, coverage, interval width and rank recovery separately against a conditional and a marginal target so that the two families are each judged on the estimand they claim. Report non-convergence as a performance measure rather than an exclusion, since a family that fails on roughly one network in four is telling an analyst something the surviving fits cannot. Convert the output into a rule that can be applied before fitting, stated over network features an analyst can read off the data, and ship it as a default check in the packages that fit these models, because a criterion published as a table will not be consulted.

title: No criterion or error-based evidence selects arm-synthesis over contrast-synthesis
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. This came from an absence reported by 2 of 12 gap labelers at the end of their labeling rather than from a paper arguing for it, so it rests on weaker provenance than its neighbors. The evidence spans five papers, of which two carry it, the 2025 empirical comparison and the 2022 chapter, both of which state the missing item in their own words; the other three are secondary, being a software paper that resolves the exchangeability dispute by citation, an applied study whose complaint is about inconsistency detection under both frameworks and belongs to the inconsistency entries rather than here, and a parameterization paper that states a belief about the variance structure. The registry was searched for arm-based and contrast-based content and the near neighbors were read in full: HET-18 covers the between-treatment correlation matrix inside arm-based models, HET-16 the comparison-specific heterogeneity variances under the second-order consistency constraint, EVB-07 the missing-data assumption on trial design that separates the two likelihoods, and DIA-22 the exclusion of inconsistent networks from the empirical comparison; none of them states that no criterion and no error-based evidence selects between the families. PubMed was searched to July 2026 for a simulation comparison of arm-synthesis and contrast-synthesis and none has appeared, and the most recent review declines to give a rule and recommends fitting both.

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
Statement
Rare events and concentrated weights leave the binary likelihood weakly informative, so estimates can separate and become strongly sensitive to the prior or penalty that is then doing the identification work. The failure is narrower than the source said: a contrast-level log-odds estimate is infinite or undefined with a zero cell, but zero counts can enter an arm-based binomial, Bayesian or penalized likelihood without a continuity correction, and a double-zero study carries no conditional odds-ratio information that any likelihood choice can recover. Rare-event machinery does exist in the unweighted network meta-analysis literature, specifically penalized likelihood regression (Evrenoglou et al., arxiv:2109.10221, PMC9805041), which the source asserted without citing. Weight diagnostics still report a patient effective sample size that says nothing about how many events support the contrast, and no effective event sample size convention has been implemented.

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
Why it is open
Reweighting concentrates the effective sample on few individuals without reducing the number of covariates, so the weighted binary likelihood can flatten exactly where population adjustment is most needed. Where the prior or penalty supplies the identification, the resulting interval is still finite and reads as evidence, and there is no accepted way to report how much of the answer came from the data rather than the penalty. Effective sample size is computed from the weights alone and ignores the outcome, so it cannot detect that the weights landed on patients who contribute no events, and neither an effective event sample size nor a rare-event-plus-overlap workflow has been implemented anywhere the auditors looked. The literature auditor searched for any composition of rare-event likelihoods with MAIC weighting, STC or ML-NMR integration and found none, an absence they could not confirm from a source, so that part is recorded as unverified rather than established.

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Evrenoglou, White, Afach, Mavridis and Chaimani, Network meta-analysis of rare events using penalized likelihood regression, Statistics in Medicine (PMC9805041)
penalized-likelihood machinery for rare-event network meta-analysis that avoids continuity corrections and handles zero-event arms; it does not touch population adjustment, so it is the unweighted half the entry said already exists


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9, inst/stan/cpaic_binomial.stan, R/fit_checks.R, R/bayesian_diagnostics.R
accepts zero-count aggregate arms in the Bayesian population-adjusted binomial likelihood, rejects two-stage cSTC and cMAIC fits showing separation or non-identification rather than returning a misleading finite contrast, reports entropy, weight concentration and residual balance alongside ESS, and refits under tighter and looser priors as an identification diagnostic; it has no effective event sample size

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Compose the existing penalized and Bayesian rare-event likelihoods with the weighting and integration steps that population adjustment adds, and report the prior or penalty contribution explicitly instead of only a finite interval. Define and report an effective event sample size alongside the weighted patient effective sample size, paired with local ESS, leverage, influence and density-ratio diagnostics, since the diagnostics that already exist stop at the weights and do not reach the outcome. Drop the expectation that a beta-binomial or noncentral hypergeometric likelihood rescues individual-level separation or double-zero studies, and benchmark the remaining candidates in a simulation that varies event risk independently of nominal sample size, includes single-zero and double-zero studies, and reports type I error, coverage and prior dominance.

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
Our study

Effective sample size counted in events: right direction, no gain over ESS times the event rate
The question put to it. With rare binary outcomes, does an effective sample size counted in events (EESS) predict when a MAIC interval fails better than the reported ESS multiplied by the event rate, and in which direction do the two diverge?
What it found. EESS is the reciprocal of the sandwich variance of a weighted log odds, and it differs from ESS times the event rate by E_w[w]E_w[p]/E_w[wp]: below 1 when weights concentrate on high-risk patients, above 1 on low-risk ones (the design had the direction reversed). As a predictor of failure the two were equivalent (AUROC 0.839 and 0.858) and ESS alone was poor (0.662). Their predictive value comes from zero-event analyses; once an estimate exists, non-coverage is near nominal and neither predicts it.
Results.

Median EESS / (ESS p): 0.47 to 0.79 when weights concentrate on high-risk patients, 1.28 to 2.40 on low-risk patients, 1.00 to 1.03 when the shift is in a non-prognostic covariate.
AUROC for failure (no estimate or non-coverage) over 108,000 analyses: EESS 0.839, ESS x event rate 0.858, ESS 0.662; the registered rule, requiring EESS to be better by 0.05, is refuted.
No estimate (an arm with no events) in up to 86% of analyses at risk 0.005 and 300 per arm.
Among analyses with an estimate, non-coverage was 5.7% and the diagnostics’ AUROC 0.54 to 0.59 (exploratory).

Design.

Estimand

Target-population marginal log odds ratio, A versus C; failure of its interval

Methods compared

event-based ESS (EESS), ESS times the event rate, Kish ESS

Data-generating mechanism

Binary-outcome MAIC with one prognostic covariate among three, 108 scenarios crossing event risk (0.005 to 0.1), size and direction of the target shift relative to risk, sample size and effect; EESS, ESS times the event rate and ESS as per-analysis predictors of failure.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 108,000 in total


What this does not answer. One prognostic covariate, MAIC on means; the penalized, Firth, Bayesian and fail-closed estimators were not run, and unanchored comparisons and multivariable separation are outside the design. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Rare events, separation, and zero-event studies in weighted synthesis
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “With rare events, weighting estimators and generalized linear models become unstable and can separate, zero-event and double-zero studies cannot enter a standard log-odds likelihood, and priors or penalties rather than data determine the answer. Diagnostics report a weighted patient effective sample size that can look adequate while the effective number of events is negligible, and no simulation program benchmarks the competing rare-event remedies in this regime.”
What was wrong with it. The claim that rare-event NMA methods already exist was unattributed in the source and is now sourced to Evrenoglou, White, Afach, Mavridis and Chaimani, penalized likelihood regression for rare-event NMA (arxiv:2109.10221, PMC9805041), supplied by the literature auditor. The code auditor found several mechanisms overstated at commit 9d150e9 of cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN: zero-event aggregate arms already enter its Bayesian binomial likelihood, two-stage fits fail closed on separation, weight diagnostics already report entropy, concentration and residual balance beyond ESS, and prior-sensitivity refits already expose weak identification; the same auditor rejected the beta-binomial remedy for individual-level separation and the noncentral hypergeometric remedy for double-zero studies.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): This is a source_unsourced entry. I can source the claim ‘rare-event NMA methods already exist’: Evrenoglou, White, Afach, Mavridis and Chaimani, ‘Network meta-analysis of rare events using penalized likelihood regression’ (Stat Med; PMC9805041, arXiv 2109.10221), which is exactly the penalised-likelihood machinery the entry says exists in the unweighted NMA literature. I searched for any composition of rare-event likelihoods with MAIC weighting, STC or ML-NMR integration and found none; per the audit rules an absence claim cannot be confirmed by not finding anything, so ‘no settled rare-event likelihood has been integrated with population-adjustment machinery’, ‘no PAIC method combines rare-event likelihoods with overlap-aware diagnostics’, ‘no standard effective-event-sample-size convention’, and ‘no existing simulation study varies event risk independently of nominal sample size’ are all unverifiable rather than verified. The mechanistic claims (weighting concentrates mass, ESS ignores the outcome) are sound but I retrieved no paper demonstrating MAIC-induced separation empirically. The internal priority claim is not a literature claim. codex dissented (overstated): C2, C4, C5, C11 through C13, and the broad simulation recommendation in C16 are technically sound. C3 overstates prior or penalty influence as exclusive determination by the prior rather than joint influence from a weak or monotone likelihood. A zero cell makes a standalone saturated contrast-level log-odds estimate infinite or undefined, but zero counts can enter an arm-based binomial likelihood, and one zero cell need not make a shared multi-study effect’s MLE infinite. A double-zero study has no conditional odds-ratio information, so a noncentral hypergeometric likelihood cannot make it informative merely by avoiding a continuity correction. C9 conflates remedies for separation with models for overdispersion or sparse counts; a beta-binomial model does not itself cure individual-level separation. C6 through C8, C14, C15, and C18 are literature-absence or practice claims outside this audit lens. C17 is not an exhaustive operating-characteristic set, and C19 merely reproduces the agenda’s priority label. At the audited cpaic commit, Bayesian cML-NMR accepts zero-event aggregate arms, two-stage methods fail closed on separation, weight diagnostics go beyond ESS, and prior-sensitivity refits expose weak identification. No effective-event ESS or specialized rare-event-plus-overlap workflow is implemented, so the problem is only partially addressed.

Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text: OUT-04 Partially addressed High priority Promising

title: Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text:
Statement
Trials in a network may measure the same construct with different instruments, and a linear rescaling makes them equivalent only where the instruments are defensibly affine-equivalent and measurement-invariant. Latent-variable linking is not a new proposal: common-metric and item-response linking of different patient-reported instruments is deployed methodology (PMC5069858) and has been built for individual participant data across studies (PMC6582193), so what is missing is its integration into network or population-adjusted synthesis together with the anchor items, co-administration or calibration data it requires. On the standardized mean difference side, the standardizer is a property of the population in which it was measured, which is documented (PMC12358740; doi:10.1002/sim.10114), so the same mean difference yields different SMDs in populations with different outcome variability. The transport behavior of an SMD is not mathematically undefined; it is a mean difference divided by a specified reference standard deviation, so the real problem is choosing and identifying a scientifically meaningful common scale, and no transport theory for the standardized scale is established.

title: Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text:
Why it is open
Instruments differ in item content, scoring range and precision, and publications rarely include the co-administration, anchor items or calibration data a linking model needs, so the mapping is unidentified from what is published. Because the standardizer is a population property, transporting an SMD mixes a change in the effect with a change in the standardizing variance, and the target-population standard deviation is one of several defensible denominators rather than the compelled one. The native-scale fallback does not rescue this, since it cannot create a common metric across different instruments without a mapping. In cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, Gaussian individual-patient analyses accept mean differences only and explicitly reject SMD, so no cross-instrument path exists there at all.

title: Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




www.common-metrics.org: a web application to estimate scores from different patient-reported outcome measures on a common scale, 2016 (PMC5069858)
deployed latent-variable and item-response linking of different patient-reported instruments onto a common metric, showing the cross-instrument problem is not unaddressed outside PAIC


Multivariate Higher-Order IRT Model and MCMC Algorithm for Linking Individual Participant Data From Multiple Studies, 2019 (PMC6582193)
establishes a common metric retrospectively across independently conducted studies with different items, which is the measurement-model half of the proposed direction in the individual-participant-data synthesis setting


Standardized Mean Differences: Not So Standard After All (PMC12358740)
documents that the standardizer is a population property, so standardized mean differences vary with within-study standard deviation variability even when the underlying mean difference is fixed


Hopkins 2024, Standardization and other approaches to meta-analyze differences in means, Statistics in Medicine
compares standardization and alternative approaches to meta-analyzing mean differences, supporting the population dependence of the standardized scale


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
its Gaussian individual-patient-data analyses accept mean differences only and explicitly reject SMD, so it offers no cross-instrument path; the code auditor cites this as the concrete state of a population-adjusted implementation

title: Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Bring the existing latent-variable and item-response linking machinery into network and population-adjusted synthesis rather than building it afresh, and state the identifying data it needs, whether anchor items, co-administration or external calibration, with explicit sensitivity to the linking assumptions. Where a standardized scale is unavoidable, make the denominator part of the estimand and report which population’s standard deviation was used, since the choice defines a different quantity rather than a different estimate of the same one. Develop transport theory for that declared standardized estimand, or report target-standardized mean differences on the native scale alongside study-specific residual variances.

title: Different instruments and standardized mean difference transport
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Trials in a network may measure the same continuous construct with different instruments, so the reported means are not on a common metric before any population adjustment. The usual fix, the standardized mean difference, has unclear interpretation and unclear behavior under transport to a different target population.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented latent-variable measurement models as a proposed remedy; the literature auditor found instrument linking to be established methodology in integrative data analysis (PMC5069858, PMC6582193), so what is being proposed is its composition with population adjustment, not the models themselves. The code auditor rejected the framing that SMD transport is unclear in principle and noted that no unique denominator is compelled, since pooled, control-arm, baseline, external-reference and target-population standard deviations define different quantities; the auditors also split on status, with literature judging the entry partially solved and the code auditor judging it open, and that split is left standing.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Two halves with different maturity. The instrument-linking half is not new: I retrieved the common-metrics literature (www.common-metrics.org, PMC5069858, which estimates scores from different patient-reported outcome measures on a common latent scale) and a multi-group multivariate higher-order IRT model for linking individual participant data from multiple studies (PMC6582193). Latent-variable linking of different instruments is therefore an established methodology in integrative data analysis, not merely a ‘proposed remedy’; what is missing is its integration into a network/population-adjusted synthesis, and the co-administration data needed to fit it. The SMD half is better supported: I retrieved ‘Standardized Mean Differences: Not So Standard After All’ (PMC12358740) and Hopkins, ‘Standardization and other approaches to meta-analyze differences in means’ (Stat Med 2024, doi 10.1002/sim.10114), which document that the standardiser is a population property so SMDs vary with within-study SD variability. I found no formal transport theory for the SMD scale, so that specific gap stands. Cites https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5069858/: Shows latent-variable/IRT linking of different PRO instruments onto a common metric is an existing, deployed methodology, so the cross-instrument problem is not unaddressed outside PAIC.. Cites https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6582193/: Retrospectively establishes a common metric across independently conducted studies with different items, i.e. the measurement-model half of the proposed direction, in the IPD-synthesis setting..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C2, C3, and C5 are sound. A simple rescaling is sufficient only when instruments are defensibly affine-equivalent and measurement-invariant. A latent-variable link requires anchor items, co-administration, calibration data, or other identifying restrictions. The SMD’s transport behavior is not mathematically undefined: it is a mean difference divided by a specified reference standard deviation, so changing the population or denominator changes the estimand. The genuine problem is selecting and identifying a scientifically meaningful common scale. C6’s claim about an accepted convention is a literature-consensus claim outside this lens; technically, no unique denominator is compelled, and pooled, control-arm, baseline, external-reference, and target-population SDs define different quantities. The proposed native-scale fallback cannot create a common metric across different instruments without a mapping. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, Gaussian IPD analyses accept MD only and explicitly reject SMD, so no cross-instrument PAIC path exists. High priority is proportionate only for networks that actually mix non-equivalent instruments.

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=1) → R11:caveated(n=2)

text: OUT-06 Overstated Medium-high priority Promising

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Statement
Mixing endpoint and change-score results in a population-adjusted comparison is an estimand and variance-handling choice rather than an unprincipled conversion: the change-score treatment contrast equals the endpoint contrast minus the baseline contrast, and the baseline-endpoint correlation is required for the variance of a change score, not for its mean contrast. Under randomization the baseline contrast is zero in expectation, so endpoint and change analyses can target the same follow-up effect, and meta-epidemiological work across 21 meta-analyses, 189 trials and 41,256 patients found combining them in conventional meta-analysis generally valid, with a mean difference in standardized mean differences of -0.04 (95% CI -0.13 to 0.06) (pmid:23747228). What remains unresolved is the adjustment step: baseline severity is often itself an effect modifier and regression to the mean acts differently in populations with different baseline distributions, and neither target-standardized mean trajectories nor latent-model responder probabilities has an established population-adjusted formulation.

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Why it is open
The unresolved part is the population-adjustment step rather than the combination itself: where baseline severity modifies the effect, change and endpoint analyses can imply different effect-modification structures, so the representation interacts with the adjustment instead of being a fixed offset. Trials measure the outcome repeatedly and on several scales, and joint repeated-measures models need compatible time definitions and within-trial covariances that aggregate publications do not report. Target-standardized trajectories and model-derived responder probabilities are optional estimands with no established formulation under population adjustment, and dichotomizing a reported mean remains invalid without the outcome distribution. cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, models one Gaussian outcome and a raw mean difference with no trajectory or responder path.

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




da Costa et al. 2013, Combining follow-up and change data is valid in meta-analyses of continuous outcomes: a meta-epidemiological study, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology (PMID 23747228)
21 meta-analyses, 189 trials and 41,256 patients; finds no relevant difference between follow-up and change standardized mean differences and concludes that combining them in meta-analysis is generally valid, with the choice prespecified in the protocol; it does not address population adjustment

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Prespecify whether the analysis uses change or endpoint data, following the meta-epidemiological guidance, and handle the variance correctly rather than converting between representations by ad hoc rescaling. Where baseline severity is a plausible effect modifier or more than one timepoint matters, model baseline and follow-up jointly so the adjustment and the estimand stay consistent. Treat target-standardized trajectories and responder probabilities as declared optional estimands, deriving responder probabilities from directly standardized individual-level indicators where individual patient data allow it and from a latent model only where they do not, and keep a prespecified decision-relevant timepoint alongside any trajectory.

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Our study

Change scores and endpoints do not diverge under population adjustment
The question put to it. When baseline severity modifies the treatment effect, do change-score and endpoint analyses give different target-population contrasts after population adjustment, in proportion to the product of the interaction and the baseline shift?
What it found. No. Baseline is pre-treatment, so the target follow-up and change contrasts are one quantity under any adjustment. Across 24 scenarios, MAIC and G-computation never diverged beyond Monte Carlo error, and were identical to machine precision in unanchored comparisons. The only divergence was in naive unanchored comparisons, equal to 1.00 times the baseline shift and independent of the baseline-by-treatment interaction.
Results.

Adjusted estimators: largest mean endpoint-minus-change difference 0.0068, within 3 Monte Carlo SE of zero in every scenario; in unanchored comparisons the per-replicate difference was at most 4e-13.
Naive unanchored comparisons: difference = 1.001 (SE 0.002) x shift + 0.007 (SE 0.007) x interaction x shift. Endpoint bias is (b + beta) shift and change bias (b + beta - 1) shift.
Naive anchored comparisons agree in expectation across representations but are both biased by the unadjusted modification.
The design’s proposed product structure was derived from a misreading: with baseline as a covariate, the treatment and treatment-by-baseline coefficients of a linear model are identical for follow-up and change.

Design.

Estimand

Target-population mean difference in follow-up, B versus A

Methods compared

naive, MAIC on the baseline mean, G-computation with baseline as covariate, each in endpoint and change representation

Data-generating mechanism

Anchored and unanchored comparisons, individual data on A versus C and arm means on B versus C, 24 scenarios crossing baseline shift (0, 0.5, 1 SD), baseline-by-treatment interaction (0, 0.3) and baseline-to-follow-up correlation (0.4, 0.8), 300 per arm.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 24,000 in total


What this does not answer. Continuous outcome with a linear conditional mean only; nonlinear links, threshold-based responder estimands and joint repeated-measures models are not tested. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Change scores, trajectories, and responder-threshold estimands
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. In population-adjusted comparisons the change-versus-endpoint representation is an estimand choice that interacts with baseline severity as an effect modifier, and neither target-standardised mean trajectories nor latent-model responder probabilities have an established formulation; empirical meta-epidemiological work finds that simply combining change and follow-up estimates in conventional meta-analysis is generally valid, so the unresolved part is the adjustment step, not the combination itself.
The source said. “Continuous outcomes in population-adjusted comparisons are reduced to a single-timepoint summary that is sometimes a change from baseline and sometimes an endpoint value, combined without a principled conversion. The report instead calls for target-standardized mean trajectories, multivariate models for repeated measures and multiple scales, and responder probabilities derived from a latent outcome model.”
What was wrong with it. The source treated change-versus-endpoint combination as unresolved and said conversion between them requires the baseline-endpoint correlation; the literature auditor produced da Costa et al. (pmid:23747228, doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2013.03.009), which finds combining them generally valid and recommends prespecifying which is used, and the code auditor showed the correlation claim is mathematically wrong as written, since the correlation governs the variance rather than the mean contrast. The code auditor also rejected the claim that responder probabilities must come from a latent continuous model, because with individual patient data responder indicators can be formed and standardized directly.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

closure-upheld

7 findings from the reading assert this problem is open; the closure was re-examined and stands Put to an independent reviewer with the closing auditors’ reasoning, the work they relied on, and the new findings in view together. The new evidence documents exactly the residual the closure retained: baseline imbalance and effect modification can make change and endpoint representations differ in a population-adjusted analysis, while missing correlations make change-score variances uncertain. The 2025 threshold variation finding also supports the already-conceded absence of an established population-adjusted responder-probability formulation. None of the papers rebuts the algebraic relation between change and endpoint treatment contrasts or the meta-epidemiological evidence that conventional synthesis of the two is generally valid. Examples of unpropagated correlation imputation and inconsistent responder definitions demonstrate poor practice and unresolved extensions, not that the closed universal claim should be restored. (reviewer confidence: high)

Flagged for reopening

9 findings from the reading assert this problem is open while the registry carries overstated Flagged, not applied: reversing an earlier audit’s closure needs the closure’s own evidence re-examined alongside this, which the reading did not do. See documentation/audit/reading/PROPOSED.md.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. Retrieved da Costa et al., ‘Combining follow-up and change data is valid in meta-analyses of continuous outcomes: a meta-epidemiological study’ (J Clin Epidemiol 2013; PMID 23747228; doi 10.1016/j.jclinepi.2013.03.009), 21 meta-analyses, 189 trials, 41,256 patients. It directly addresses the change-versus-endpoint question the entry frames as unresolved and concludes combining them is generally valid, with a mean difference in SMDs of only -0.04 (95% CI -0.13 to 0.06). The entry’s framing that the two are ‘combined without a principled conversion’ therefore overstates the problem for conventional synthesis; the empirically supported guidance is to prespecify which is used. What remains genuinely open is the population-adjustment-specific part: baseline severity as an effect modifier, regression to the mean differing across covariate distributions, and target-standardised mean trajectories or latent-model responder probabilities, none of which da Costa addresses and for which I found no PAIC literature.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C2 is mathematically wrong as written. The treatment contrast in change is the endpoint contrast minus the baseline contrast; baseline-endpoint correlation is required to recover the variance or standard error of a change score, not its mean contrast. Under randomization the baseline contrast is zero in expectation, so endpoint and change analyses can target the same follow-up treatment effect, although finite-sample imbalance, baseline adjustment, and effect modification can matter in PAIC. C3 is therefore possible rather than inevitable. C4 and C6 are reasonable research outputs, but trajectories need not replace a prespecified decision-relevant timepoint and multivariate models require compatible time definitions and covariance information. C5 is right that a reported mean cannot be dichotomized into a responder probability, but a latent continuous model is not the only valid route: with IPD, responder indicators can be formed and standardized directly, while a latent-tail calculation adds distributional assumptions. cpaic currently models one Gaussian outcome and raw MD, with no trajectory or responder path. The unresolved PAIC-specific extensions are real, but the change-versus-endpoint issue and the Medium-high severity are overstated as universal problems.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Statement
The population-adjusted implementations the auditors checked fit Poisson models for counts and offer no negative-binomial, Poisson-lognormal, hurdle, zero-inflated, recurrent-event or frailty family, so those options are unavailable rather than merely uncommon. The consequence is narrower than the source said: where the conditional mean is correctly specified the Poisson estimating score remains unbiased under negative-binomial variance, so residual overdispersion invalidates likelihood-based uncertainty while leaving rate-ratio point estimates consistent, and transport bias instead requires misspecification of the conditional mean, the zero mechanism, the frailty or the exposure weighting. Time to first event and total event burden remain different estimands that can move in different directions, and general count meta-analysis evidence shows pooled effects and precision differ by whether a rate ratio, Poisson, negative-binomial, dichotomized risk ratio or time-to-first-event analysis is used (doi:10.1186/s13643-015-0144-x). The two auditors disagreed about how much of the source’s mechanism survives, and that disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Why it is open
No population-adjusted implementation the auditors checked offers an overdispersed, zero-inflated or recurrent-event likelihood, so an analyst facing exacerbation or relapse counts either accepts Poisson uncertainty or leaves the population-adjusted framework. On the survival side, transporting a recurrent-event effect requires transporting a frailty distribution that is itself population-dependent, and aggregate-data trials report first-event Kaplan-Meier curves or annualized rates rather than the full event history, so the joint and dispersion structure cannot be recovered from what is published. A structural-zero subgroup makes the population a mixture whose mixing proportion can vary across trial populations, which is a transport problem and not only a fitting problem. Whether the closed-form-likelihood barrier that blocks non-standard count likelihoods in ML-NMR has already been removed is an open question the literature auditor flagged but did not check.

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend component ML-NMR to negative-binomial and Poisson-lognormal likelihoods so overdispersion is modeled rather than left to invalidate the reported interval, and add hurdle and zero-inflated formulations whose zero and count components are permitted, not required, to carry different effect-modification structure. Develop recurrent-event and joint frailty models for population-adjusted network synthesis so total burden and time to first event can both be estimated and standardized to the target population, and connect them to the count models for the same underlying process. Check the lead the literature auditor named but did not read, Bayesian synthetic likelihood for multilevel network meta-regression (arxiv:2603.11019), before rebuilding integration machinery, since if it does what its title says it removes the closed-form-likelihood constraint.

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Our study

Overdispersed and zero-inflated counts transported by G-computation
The question put to it. For count outcomes transported to a target, does overdispersion bias the estimate or only its interval, and when the fraction of structural zeros differs between populations, what does a count model transport wrongly and what repairs it?
What it found. Overdispersion leaves the transported rate ratio unbiased and makes the Poisson interval too narrow (coverage down to 0.61); a sandwich or negative binomial restores it. A structural-zero fraction that differs between source and target biases the transported absolute rate in every count model, including zero-inflated Poisson, by up to 0.56 on the log scale; the rate ratio is protected only without effect modification. Recalibrating the zero part to the target’s reported zero proportion repairs the absolute rate when the source has structural zeros to learn from.
Results.

Poisson rate-ratio coverage 0.846 to 0.610 under overdispersion with bias at most 0.010; sandwich 0.926 to 0.948, so the registered rule (0.93 everywhere) was missed by 0.004 in one cell with MCSE 0.012.
Differing structural-zero fractions: absolute log-rate bias 0.40 to 0.56 in absolute value for Poisson, negative binomial and zero-inflated Poisson, coverage 0.000 to 0.028.
Rate ratio with differing zero fractions: bias at most 0.007 without effect modification, up to 0.11 with it.
Zero part recalibrated to the target’s zero proportion: absolute-rate bias at most 0.04 when the source had structural zeros, 0.25 when it had none.

Design.

Estimand

Log rate ratio, A versus C, and log rate under A, in the target population

Methods compared

Poisson, Poisson with sandwich variance, negative binomial, zero-inflated Poisson, zero-inflated Poisson with recalibrated zero part

Data-generating mechanism

G-computation from an individual-data trial with negative-binomial or zero-inflated Poisson counts, 14 cells separating dispersion from structural-zero differences, with and without effect modification; Poisson, sandwich, negative binomial, zero-inflated and recalibrated zero-inflated fits. 500 replicates per cell.

Replicates

500 per scenario, 7,000 in total


What this does not answer. One covariate; frailty, exposure weighting, recurrent events and zero-inflated negative binomial not run. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Overdispersed counts and recurrent events as total disease burden
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source said. “Repeated clinical events such as exacerbations or relapses are analyzed either as Poisson counts, which forces variance to equal the mean and ignores excess zeros, or as time to first event, which discards the recurrent process entirely. Neither negative-binomial and zero-inflated component ML-NMR nor recurrent-event and joint frailty models exist for population-adjusted network synthesis.”
What was wrong with it. The source said a mis-specified count likelihood distorts the transported effect and not only its standard error; the code auditor showed this is false as a general rule, since a correctly specified conditional mean leaves Poisson point estimates consistent under overdispersion. The same auditor narrowed the claim that Poisson is too restrictive to cases with observed residual conditional overdispersion, and rejected the claim that hurdle and zero-inflated formulations require separate effect-modification structure, since those coefficients may be constrained, shared or omitted in one component; the literature auditor judged the entry supported, so the adjudicated verdict is unverifiable with both positions on the record.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): At the requested cpaic revision, cmlnmr() accepts only binomial, Gaussian, Poisson, and survival families. NAMESPACE and the Stan models contain no negative-binomial, Poisson-lognormal, hurdle, zero-inflated, recurrent-event, or frailty path. The core cpaic gap is therefore open, and C6-C7 correctly distinguish first recurrence from total burden. However, C1 needs observed residual conditional overdispersion; Poisson is not universally too restrictive. C3 is false as a general rule: when the conditional mean is correctly specified, the Poisson estimating score can remain unbiased under negative-binomial variance, leaving point effects consistent while model-based uncertainty is wrong. Transport bias requires misspecification of the conditional mean, zero mechanism, frailty, or exposure weighting. C5 also overstates necessity: hurdle and zero-inflated models have two predictors, but their effect-modifier coefficients may be constrained, shared, or omitted in one component. C8-C9 are universal prevalence or absence claims not established by cpaic source inspection.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Verified from the multinma nma() reference that the supported count/rate likelihoods are binomial, bernoulli, poisson and normal plus the survival families, with no negative-binomial, Poisson-lognormal, hurdle or zero-inflated option, so ‘proposed but not yet available’ is accurate for the leading ML-NMR implementation. The general count-meta-analysis literature supports the Poisson-restriction claim: ‘Do alternative methods for analysing count data produce similar estimates? Implications for meta-analyses’ (doi 10.1186/s13643-015-0144-x) shows precision and pooled effects differ by whether rate ratio, Poisson, negative binomial, dichotomised risk ratio or time-to-first-event is used, which also supports the claim that time to first event and total burden are different estimands. I found no recurrent-event or joint-frailty model for population-adjusted network synthesis. One lead worth watching that I did not read: arXiv 2603.11019, ‘Don’t Disregard the Data for Lack of a Likelihood: Bayesian Synthetic Likelihood for Enhanced Multilevel Network Meta-Regression’, which if it does what its title says would remove the closed-form-likelihood barrier for non-standard count likelihoods in ML-NMR.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. At the requested cpaic revision, cmlnmr() accepts only binomial, Gaussian, Poisson, and survival families. NAMESPACE and the Stan models contain no negative-binomial, Poisson-lognormal, hurdle, zero-inflated, recurrent-event, or frailty path. The core cpaic gap is therefore open, and C6-C7 correctly distinguish first recurrence from total burden. However, C1 needs observed residual conditional overdispersion; Poisson is not universally too restrictive. C3 is false as a general rule: when the conditional mean is correctly specified, the Poisson estimating score can remain unbiased under negative-binomial variance, leaving point effects consistent while model-based uncertainty is wrong. Transport bias requires misspecification of the conditional mean, zero mechanism, frailty, or exposure weighting. C5 also overstates necessity: hurdle and zero-inflated models have two predictors, but their effect-modifier coefficients may be constrained, shared, or omitted in one component. C8-C9 are universal prevalence or absence claims not established by cpaic source inspection.
