title: Proportional odds, category probabilities, and ordinal utilities
text:
Statement
Population-adjusted ordinal synthesis already exists and target-standardized category probabilities are already produced: multinma ships ordered multinomial models through the multi() helper, and its predict() method averages over the target population by integrating over the joint covariate distribution or by averaging predictions for a sample of individuals. This is not hypothetical; Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162) fit ordered PASI 75, 90 and 100 outcomes by ML-NMR and report the estimated percentage achieving each endpoint on each treatment in external target populations, under proportional odds. What remains undeveloped is the relaxation half, namely partial proportional odds, adjacent-category and continuation-ratio models in a population-adjusted network, and decision analyses that combine joint category-probability draws with explicitly specified and possibly uncertain utilities.

title: Proportional odds, category probabilities, and ordinal utilities
text:
Why it is open
Proportional odds imposes one treatment coefficient across all cut-points, and a treatment may shift patients out of the worst category without changing the top of the scale; threshold-specific conditional effects can differ, and even a conditional proportional-odds model yields population-dependent marginal odds ratios through non-collapsibility. Aggregate-data publications often report a dichotomized version or a single ordinal odds ratio, so the cut-point-specific pattern needed to test the assumption is unavailable. Utility weights usually come from a preference source outside the trials, though they can also be elicited within a trial, and their uncertainty and cross-population variation add a second transport problem on top of estimation uncertainty. cpaic, the unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, has no ordinal family at all, so non-proportional ordinal component PAIC is unavailable there.

text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build partial proportional odds, adjacent-category and continuation-ratio models for population-adjusted ordinal synthesis on top of the ordered multinomial machinery that already works, rather than rebuilding target-standardized category probabilities. Because joint posterior category probabilities already exist, utility-weighted estimands are largely posterior post-processing, so the work is in specifying and propagating preference uncertainty and in handling preference transport between source and target populations. title: Proportional odds, category probabilities, and ordinal utilities
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Population-adjusted ordinal synthesis exists and target-standardised category probabilities are already produced by multinma and reported in the published plaque-psoriasis ML-NMR application, but that work assumes proportional odds; relaxations that let cut-point-specific and treatment-specific departures be represented, and utility-weighted ordinal estimands with utility uncertainty propagated, remain undeveloped.
The source said. “Ordinal endpoints are common in trials but underdeveloped in population-adjusted comparison: proportional odds can fail differently by treatment and by population, results are reported as a single transported ordinal odds ratio rather than as target-standardized category probabilities, and no framework attaches explicit category utilities to produce a decision-relevant scalar.”
What was wrong with it. The source claimed no established PAIC implementation returns target-standardized ordinal category probabilities; both auditors found this false, citing multinma’s ordered multinomial models with the multi() helper and the published plaque-psoriasis ML-NMR application (doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162, PMID 35997006). The auditors dated the multinma feature differently, the literature auditor to the 0.6.0 release notes and the code auditor to 0.2.0, and that discrepancy is left standing; the code auditor also corrected two side claims, that an ordinal odds ratio plus the target covariate distribution still does not identify absolute category probabilities without comparator cut-points or baseline category probabilities, and that not every scalar summary implies fixed implicit category utilities, since medians, cumulative odds ratios and probabilities of superiority are nonlinear functionals.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The claim ‘No established PAIC implementation currently returns target-standardized ordinal category probabilities’ is false. multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24) added ordered multinomial models via the multi() helper, and predict.stan_nma produces absolute predictions ‘averaged over the target population (i.e. standardised/marginalised), either by (numerical) integration over the joint covariate distribution or by averaging predictions for a sample of individuals’. This capability is not hypothetical: Phillippo et al., ‘Validating the Assumptions of Population Adjustment: Application of Multilevel Network Meta-regression to a Network of Treatments for Plaque Psoriasis’ (Med Decis Making 2023, doi 10.1177/0272989X221117162, PMID 35997006) fits ordered PASI 75/90/100 outcomes by ML-NMR and reports the estimated percentage achieving each PASI endpoint on each treatment in external target populations. What remains genuinely open is the model-relaxation half (partial proportional odds, adjacent-category, continuation-ratio in a population-adjusted network) and utility-weighted ordinal estimands with propagated utility uncertainty; I found nothing on either. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X221117162: Published ML-NMR with an ordered multinomial outcome producing category probabilities standardised to external target populations, contradicting the claim that no established PAIC implementation returns them.. Cites repo:dmphillippo/multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24): Ships ordered multinomial ML-NMR with the multi() helper; predict() marginalises over the target covariate distribution..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C2-C3 are defensible after distinguishing conditional from marginal proportional odds: threshold-specific conditional effects may differ, while even a conditional proportional-odds model can yield population-dependent marginal odds ratios through non-collapsibility. C6 is incomplete because an ordinal odds ratio plus the target covariate distribution still does not identify absolute category probabilities without comparator cut-points or baseline category probabilities. C7 is false: ordered multinomial ML-NMR and target-standardized category predictions already exist in multinma and have been used in the cited psoriasis application. C9 is mathematically sloppy. An expected-utility estimand uses explicit category weights, but medians, cumulative odds ratios, and probabilities of superiority are nonlinear scalar functionals rather than fixed implicit utility weights. C10 is also too categorical because utilities can be elicited within a trial. Once joint posterior category probabilities exist, utility-weighted outcomes are straightforward posterior post-processing, although preference uncertainty and transport may still matter. cpaic itself has no ordinal family, so non-proportional ordinal component PAIC remains open there. title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
Statement
Flexible study-specific baseline hazards for survival ML-NMR are not open where every study supplies sufficiently informative time-to-event data; they are not identified for arms represented only by sparse aggregate counts, where a baseline shape has to be borrowed across studies. The paper this entry cited as prior work develops them, proposing M-splines for the baseline hazard, stratifying the baseline by study to respect randomization, and controlling the resulting nuisance parameters with a weighted random-walk prior on the inverse-softmax transformed spline coefficients so the analyst can choose a large enough number of knots and let the model shrink to appropriate complexity; multinma and cpaic both implement study-stratified flexible baselines with shared smoothing. What is open is that survival beyond the observed support is not identified, so the chosen tail model rather than the data drives extrapolation, and observed-window fit statistics cannot separate models that are observationally equivalent or nearly equivalent on that support. Mixture-cure network meta-analysis exists for the unadjusted case (Chan et al., doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10038, PMID 41626893) and has not been connected to population adjustment or to component treatment models.

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
Why it is open
Beyond the last observed event time the survival function is not identified, so parametric families that fit the observed period equally well diverge afterwards and no fit statistic computed on that window can choose between them; this is assumption management rather than something more data of the same kind can settle. Population adjustment adds a layer because the extrapolation is performed in a target population whose long-term covariate-outcome relationship was never observed, and baseline flexibility, non-proportional hazards and cure structure change the tail interactively. Mixture-cure models split the population into cured and uncured fractions that depend on covariates differently, so the cure fraction and the uncured survival distribution would have to be transported separately, and neither multinma nor cpaic has a cure family or a component-cure path.

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Do not rebuild flexible study-specific baselines; instead assess how the baseline choice that is already available drives extrapolation, and report the data-supported horizon separately from the extrapolated portion with the tail treated as a declared assumption carrying its own sensitivity analysis. Connect mixture-cure network meta-analysis to population adjustment and component models so that both the cure fraction and the uncured survival distribution can be transported and can depend on treatment components. Where follow-up is short, state that the cure fraction rests on parametric assumptions rather than on empirical separation from a long uncured tail.

title: Survival extrapolation is unidentified beyond the observed follow-up
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work and the entry names which part. The source additionally attributed the claim to the wrong work, which is corrected in the entry.
The source titled this. “Baseline hazard flexibility, cure fractions, and extrapolation” The title lists flexible baseline hazards as open, which the entry’s own cited paper develops and which multinma implements.
The source said. “Health technology assessment needs lifetime survival, so population-adjusted survival results are extrapolated far beyond observed follow-up, where the answer comes from the parametric assumption rather than the data. Flexible study-specific baseline hazards remain an open problem for survival ML-NMR even after the 2025 general-likelihood extension, and mixture-cure network meta-analysis has only begun to develop and has not been connected to population adjustment or component models.”
What was wrong with it. The lead claim, that flexible study-specific baseline hazards remain open for survival ML-NMR after the 2025 general-likelihood extension, is contradicted by the paper the entry itself cites: Phillippo et al. (doi:10.1093/jrsssa/qnaf169) stratify the baseline hazard by study and propose M-splines with a shrinkage random-walk prior, which is this entry’s own proposed direction. The code auditor found the same capability implemented in multinma 0.6.0 and at commit 9d150e9 in cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, and narrowed two supporting claims: observed-window fit statistics do discriminate models that fit the observed data differently, and a cure fraction can be estimated under shorter follow-up through strong parametric assumptions, so it is empirical separation of cure from a long uncured tail that needs mature follow-up.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 is directly false at the requested cpaic revision. cmlnmr() offers piecewise-exponential and continuous cubic M-spline baselines, gives every study separate baseline coefficients, and applies shared random-walk smoothing. multinma likewise supplies study-stratified flexible baselines. C2-C5 are otherwise sound: data do not identify survival beyond observed support, so the chosen tail model drives extrapolation. C6 needs its omitted condition. Observed-window fit statistics can distinguish models that fit the observed data differently; they cannot validate different tails when models are observationally equivalent or nearly equivalent on the observed support. cpaic has no cure family or component-cure path, so connecting cure and uncured components to PAIC remains open. C9 is a plausible model, not a necessity. C10 is too categorical: a cure fraction can be estimated under shorter follow-up only through strong parametric assumptions, while empirical separation of cure from a long uncured tail requires sufficiently mature follow-up, not necessarily follow-up longer than most trials. Extrapolation is an assumption-management problem rather than a capability that data alone can solve.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text: OUT-14 Overstated High priority Emerging

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Statement
Population-adjusted survival likelihoods do represent this structure: multinma has supported left, right and interval censoring and left truncation for survival outcomes since 0.6.0, and cpaic’s exact survival likelihood supports observed events, right, left and interval censoring and delayed entry for both individual and aggregate pseudo-patient rows when those fields are supplied. What survives is an information problem rather than a likelihood problem: pseudo individual data reconstructed from a published right-censored Kaplan-Meier curve cannot express delayed entry or interval censoring, because the publication does not report entry times or assessment intervals. Assessment schedules are design features that patient-level covariate balancing cannot correct, though they can be represented in the observation model or, with enough studies, modeled at study level. Once an outcome is dichotomized into an event-by-time proportion the follow-up length and assessment grid disappear from the reported number, and there is no method for placing binary endpoints from trials with different windows on a common time scale.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Why it is open
The capability exists but the inputs often do not, so an analysis built on reconstructed pseudo individual data silently reverts to complete follow-up with exactly observed event times, because reconstruction cannot recover information absent from the publication. Interval censoring induced by different assessment grids coarsens event times differently across trials, and substituting exact times for interval-censored ones can shift progression-type curves in a way that resembles a treatment effect. Different maximum follow-up means trials identify the survival function over different ranges, so any common summary requires either truncation to the shortest window or extrapolation, and each choice changes the estimand. Cross-trial binary event-by-time proportions remain non-comparable when the windows differ, and covariate balancing cannot repair a difference that arises purely from follow-up length.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




multinma (CRAN) 0.6.0, survival models with censoring and truncation support
its release notes list left, right and interval censoring and left truncation as supported, and its set_ipd() reference states that right, left and interval censoring and left truncation, that is delayed entry, are supported for survival outcomes specified with Surv()


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9, exact survival likelihood
supports observed events, right censoring, left censoring, interval censoring and delayed entry in component ML-NMR for individual and aggregate pseudo-patient rows when the required fields are supplied

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Use the censoring and truncation support that already exists by carrying entry times and assessment intervals into the analysis data rather than accepting reconstruction defaults, and say when an analysis has silently reverted to exactly observed event times. Choose a primary horizon supported by all contributing trials and declare anything beyond it as extrapolation. Develop the missing piece, which is treating a binary event-by-time endpoint as a coarsening of a time-to-event process so endpoints from trials with different windows can be placed on a common time scale, and model assessment timing jointly only where that timing is plausibly informative.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Our study

Assessment grids that differ between trials
The question put to it. When two trials assess progression on different visit schedules, how much does treating recorded event times as exact bias a transported RMST difference, and do midpoint imputation or an interval-censored model remove it?
What it found. Treating visit-recorded event times as exact biases a cross-trial RMST difference by half the spacing times the event probability by the horizon, with the sign set by which trial visits less often. A 3-month difference in spacing produced a spurious difference of 1.4 months with no true effect, and removed 1.0 of a true 1.2 months in another scenario. Moving events to the interval midpoint or fitting an interval-censored model reduced the bias below 0.1 month.
Results.

Naive bias on the prediction (d_B/2)F_B(tau) - (d_A/2)F_A(tau): slope 1.014 (SE 0.005) over 32 scenarios.
Where the schedules differed by 2 months or more, naive bias was 0.94 to 1.43 months in absolute value; materiality confirmed in all 16 such scenarios.
Midpoint shift: largest bias 0.081 months; interval-censored Weibull: 0.071 months.
The registered control (equal schedules, zero bias) failed in 2 of 8 cells, both where the arms’ event probabilities differed; there the bias matched the mechanism’s prediction (-0.14 and -0.14 against -0.14 and -0.11).

Design.

Estimand

Difference in restricted mean survival time at 24 months, B minus A

Methods compared

Kaplan-Meier on recorded times, Kaplan-Meier after midpoint shift, interval-censored Weibull

Data-generating mechanism

Unanchored comparison of two single arms with Weibull event times, 32 cells crossing each trial’s assessment spacing (0 to 3 months), the event rate and the true difference; naive, midpoint and interval-censored analyses of RMST at 24 months. 1000 replicates per cell.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 32,000 in total


What this does not answer. Binary event-by-time endpoints, different maximum follow-up, reconstruction error from digitized curves and visit-window jitter were not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Pseudo-IPD cannot express delayed entry or assessment windows
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Delayed entry and interval censoring are supported in population-adjusted survival likelihoods (multinma implements right, left and interval censoring and left truncation), but reconstructed pseudo-IPD from published curves cannot express them, differing assessment grids and follow-up windows are design features that covariate adjustment cannot balance, and there is no method for putting binary endpoints from trials with different windows on a common time scale.
The source titled this. “Delayed entry, interval censoring, and differing follow-up windows” The title lists delayed entry and interval censoring as unrepresented, but population-adjusted survival likelihoods have supported left truncation and interval censoring since multinma 0.6.0.
The source said. “Trials in a network observe patients over different windows and on different assessment grids, with delayed entry and interval-censored endpoints such as radiologically assessed progression; the same heterogeneity is hidden entirely when the endpoint is reported as a binary event-by-time-t proportion. Population-adjusted likelihoods do not represent any of this structure.”
What was wrong with it. The statement that population-adjusted likelihoods do not represent any of this structure is false; the literature auditor cited multinma’s release notes and set_ipd() documentation for left, right and interval censoring and left truncation, and the code auditor found the same support at commit 9d150e9 of cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN. The code auditor also narrowed two claims: differing follow-up under independent censoring is handled by an appropriate survival likelihood, so what remains is unsupported horizons and estimand alignment, and joint modeling of assessment timing is warranted where the timing is informative, whereas a known noninformative grid needs only an interval-censored likelihood.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The claim ‘Population-adjusted likelihoods do not represent any of this structure’ is false. multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24) lists ‘Left/right/interval censoring and left truncation supported’ among the new survival features, and the set_ipd() reference states that right, left and interval censoring and left truncation (delayed entry) are supported for survival outcomes specified with Surv(). So delayed entry and interval censoring are already representable in the leading ML-NMR implementation, for both the individual-level likelihood and, via the general-likelihood integration, the aggregate side. Two claims survive intact and are the defensible core: reconstructed pseudo-IPD from published Kaplan-Meier curves cannot represent left truncation or interval censoring (the Guyot-style algorithm assumes right censoring only), and assessment schedules are design features that no covariate adjustment can balance. I found no work on placing binary endpoints from trials with different follow-up windows on a common time scale by joint modelling of assessment timing and event status, so that part is genuinely open. Cites repo:dmphillippo/multinma NEWS 0.6.0 (2024-01-24): Population-adjusted survival likelihoods that do represent interval censoring and delayed entry..

title: Competing risks and cumulative incidence transport
text: OUT-16 Confirmed open High priority Emerging Tractability 2/5

title: Competing risks and cumulative incidence transport
text:
Statement
A treatment may reduce progression while increasing competing mortality, and where the analysis collapses to a single endpoint that trade-off is not visible; a composite endpoint may still reflect the net first-event effect while obscuring which cause moved. The mathematical core holds: the cumulative incidence for a cause integrates that cause-specific hazard against event-free survival, which depends on the cumulative hazards of every cause, so transporting one cause-specific effect cannot determine target absolute risk without target-standardized baseline hazards for all causes. The converse is the qualification the source omitted, since transporting the complete set of cause-specific hazards does determine the cumulative incidence. Neither auditor found any population-adjusted method for competing risks or cumulative incidence, and the general causal literature makes the same transportability point (doi:10.1002/bimj.70153).

title: Competing risks and cumulative incidence transport
text:
Why it is open
Cause-specific hazards and cumulative incidence functions answer different questions, and population adjustment changes the competing-risk mix because the target population has different background mortality, so the direction of net benefit can flip between populations. Aggregate-data publications typically report a single composite or a single cause without the competing-event information needed to reconstruct cumulative incidence, so the full set of cause-specific hazards is unavailable on the comparator side. A composite, an all-cause first event, a cause-specific hazard and a cumulative incidence are distinct estimands, so collapsing to one endpoint changes the question rather than simplifying the answer. The mechanism is well understood outside evidence synthesis and simply has not been composed with population adjustment.

title: Competing risks and cumulative incidence transport
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Develop transport methods defined for the full set of cause-specific hazards, so that both the cause of interest and the competing causes are standardized to the target population and the cumulative incidence follows from them. Report target-standardized cumulative incidence rather than a single transported cause-specific effect wherever absolute cause-specific risk drives the decision. State what competing-event information the comparator publication actually supplies, since a cumulative-incidence target is unidentified without it.

title: Competing risks and cumulative incidence transport

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “A treatment may reduce progression while increasing competing mortality, but most population-adjusted implementations collapse the disease process to a single endpoint and there is no established way to transport a cause-specific hazard or a cumulative incidence function to a new population.”
What was wrong with it. The source said cause-specific transport does not determine transported cumulative incidence; the code auditor supplied the missing condition, that transporting all cause-specific hazards does determine it, so the obstacle is the incompleteness of what gets transported rather than a property of cause-specific hazards. The same auditor declined to endorse the claim that most PAIC implementations reduce disease processes to a single endpoint, which a technical audit cannot establish, though it confirmed that cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not installable from CRAN, is single-event at commit 9d150e9, with status codes distinguishing censoring types rather than event causes.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): I searched specifically for population-adjusted or indirect-comparison methods for competing risks and cumulative incidence and found none; multinma’s survival likelihoods are single-event, and the maicplus vignettes cover binary and time-to-event endpoints only. The claim that cumulative incidence for one cause depends on all cause-specific hazards is a mathematical identity and needs no source. This entry is one of the cleanest ‘genuinely open’ items in the batch: the mechanism is well understood outside evidence synthesis and simply has not been composed with population adjustment.

title: Component-specific time-varying treatment effects
text: OUT-18 Partially addressed High priority Emerging Tractability 3/5

title: Component-specific time-varying treatment effects
text:
Statement
In component-based survival models each component may have a time-varying effect with a different profile, and no implementation the auditors examined estimates component-specific time-varying effects: cpaic’s survival Stan models use time-invariant component main effects and component-by-covariate interactions and its vignette says so explicitly, multinma handles non-proportionality by stratifying spline coefficients by treatment and study or through aux_regression without decomposing the effect across components, and netmeta’s component machinery is additive on a single contrast scale with no time dimension. The universal form of the claim, that no current method estimates them, is not established, and a time-basis component model is mathematically well defined whenever the component-by-time design is identified. Allowing component-specific time variation does turn additivity into a time-indexed assumption on a specified scale, and additivity of hazard-scale functions does not imply additivity of restricted-mean-survival-time effects.

title: Component-specific time-varying treatment effects
text:
Why it is open
Allowing each component its own time-varying profile multiplies the parameter space by the number of time basis functions, and networks rarely contain the component contrasts over follow-up needed to separate one component’s time profile from another’s, so the coefficients are weakly identified. Aggregate-data trials report survival curves rather than component-resolved hazards, so the information needed to disentangle the profiles is largely absent from the published record. Baseline flexibility does not substitute, since study-specific piecewise or spline baselines change the shape of the baseline hazard rather than the time course of the treatment effect. How much this matters depends on whether component-specific non-proportionality materially affects the target estimand and the decision.

text:
Probable solution or research direction

Pair the estimator with RMST-based reporting and survival-specific quantitative bias analysis, and state the scale on which additivity is being assumed, since hazard-scale additivity does not carry over to RMST.

title: No PAIC workflow carries dependence through transport to net benefit
text: OUT-20 Partially addressed High priority Emerging

title: No PAIC workflow carries dependence through transport to net benefit
text:
Statement
Incremental net monetary benefit in a target population, willingness-to-pay times the expected quality-adjusted outcome minus the expected cost, is a valid decision estimand and can be estimated directly, either by transporting a constructed patient-level net-benefit outcome or by combining target-standardized quality-adjusted-outcome and cost means. Because the expectation is linear, a joint outcome model is not required to identify its mean; covariance is required for the uncertainty, the probability of cost-effectiveness and any nonlinear or patient-level quantity. Defining net monetary benefit as a causal estimand and estimating it directly rather than assembling it downstream already exists in the cost-effectiveness literature (arxiv:2002.04706), so what is unbuilt is the coupling of that idea to evidence synthesis and transport. The open part is a practical PAIC workflow that preserves dependence through synthesis, transport and extrapolation when only marginal aggregate data and external economic or preference inputs are available.

title: No PAIC workflow carries dependence through transport to net benefit
text:
Why it is open
In current practice synthesis and the economic model are separate steps, and the handover typically passes point estimates and marginal uncertainty rather than joint draws, so the correlation between transported outcome estimates and between transport and extrapolation uncertainty is lost. The additional outcome classes, resource use, costs and preferences, are reported in incompatible formats and are frequently absent from publications, so they are supplied by assumption inside economic models rather than estimated. Discontinuation and adherence are post-randomization processes that can act as mediators, intercurrent events, outcomes or time-varying confounders, so linking them requires an explicit choice rather than adding them as further endpoints. Patient preferences come from outside the trial evidence and vary between source and target, adding a preference-transport problem, and the willingness-to-pay parameter makes the estimand decision-rule-dependent rather than purely statistical.

title: No PAIC workflow carries dependence through transport to net benefit
text:

Work

cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9, cmlnmr() Gaussian outcome path
supports binomial, Gaussian, Poisson and survival families, so a precomputed patient-level net-benefit variable is admissible as the numeric outcome in the existing Gaussian component ML-NMR path; it has no built-in net-benefit framework, no quality-adjusted-outcome and cost dependence and no extrapolation framework

title: No PAIC workflow carries dependence through transport to net benefit
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Estimate incremental target net monetary benefit directly, either from a constructed patient-level net-benefit outcome or from transported quality-adjusted-outcome and cost means, and carry the covariance rather than assuming that only a single joint likelihood can deliver it. Keep the workflow modular and pass joint posterior draws across the synthesis, transport and extrapolation steps so dependence survives the handover into the decision quantity. Link efficacy, harms, quality of life, adherence, resource use, costs and preferences coherently, stating for each whether it is an outcome, a mediator, an intercurrent event or an external input, rather than folding all of them into one model.

title: No PAIC workflow carries dependence through transport to net benefit
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “Causal net-benefit estimand with joint uncertainty propagation” The title names the causal net-benefit estimand as the open object, but defining and estimating it directly already exists in the cost-effectiveness literature.
The source said. “Rather than producing separate effect estimates that a downstream economic model recombines, the report proposes targeting a causal net monetary benefit estimand directly in the target population, with uncertainty from synthesis, transport, and extrapolation propagated jointly, and with quality of life, discontinuation and adherence, resource use, costs, and patient preferences modeled inside the same framework.”
What was wrong with it. The source implied that targeting net benefit directly requires a joint outcome model and one monolithic synthesis framework; the code auditor showed the mean is identified from marginal means by linearity and that a modular economic model can preserve covariance by passing joint posterior draws. The literature auditor noted that direct causal net-benefit estimation is not new (arxiv:2002.04706), and both auditors treated the claims that no estimator targets a transported causal net benefit and that no network synthesis models exist for resource use, costs and preferences as absence claims neither could verify from a source.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 and C2 define a valid decision estimand, preferably as incremental target net monetary benefit between treatments. Linearity is crucial: E(lambda Q^a minus C^a) equals lambda E(Q^a) minus E(C^a), so a joint outcome model is not required to identify its mean. A transport estimator can instead use individual net benefit as the outcome or combine transported QALY and cost means. Covariance is needed for correct uncertainty, and C3 is a sound objective, but a modular economic model can preserve it by passing joint posterior draws; one monolithic synthesis model is not required. C4 and C8 are universal absence claims not established by cpaic or by mathematics. C6 is an overextended roadmap: efficacy, harms, costs, adherence, and external preferences need coherent linkage, not necessarily one likelihood. C7 is also too categorical because discontinuation and adherence can be mediators, intercurrent events, outcomes, or time-varying confounders. cpaic@9d150e9 has no built-in net-benefit or extrapolation framework, although its Gaussian path can accept a precomputed numeric net-benefit outcome. The unresolved part is preserving dependence through synthesis, transport, and extrapolation with limited AgD.

title: No consistency test for vector-valued effects in survival NMA
text: OUT-22 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: No consistency test for vector-valued effects in survival NMA
text:
Statement
Where proportional hazards fails, the recommended alternative to a single hazard ratio is a multi-parameter survival synthesis in which each arm is summarized by the parameters of a fitted survival function, such as fractional-polynomial or parametric hazard parameters, and the vector of parameter differences is what the network pools and compares indirectly. Consistency in such a network is a condition on several correlated parameters per contrast, and the standard machinery does not apply: loop inconsistency, node splitting and the design-by-treatment interaction model are all defined for a scalar contrast. Nothing states what it means for a direct and an indirect estimate to agree when each is a curve that may coincide early and diverge late, and nothing calibrates a test of that agreement. Adjacent pieces exist rather than the thing itself. Multivariate network meta-analysis with random inconsistency effects has been built for vectors of contrasts across multiple outcomes, and consistency of direct against indirect evidence has been tested inside a one-step individual participant data Royston-Parmar network carrying a treatment-by-log-time interaction, which needs individual data and covers a single interaction term. What is absent is a definition and a calibrated test for the aggregate-data multi-parameter case, so a network fitted in the model class that non-proportional hazards forces on the analyst returns cross-treatment estimates with no way to detect direct-versus-indirect conflict, which is the check that legitimizes ordinary network meta-analysis.

title: No consistency test for vector-valued effects in survival NMA
text:
Why it is open
A vector test must choose its metric before it can have a size, and the candidates are not equivalent: agreement of the parameter vector, agreement of the survival function over a stated window, and agreement of a decision summary such as restricted mean survival are three different null hypotheses with different power against the same departure, and the field has not chosen among them. Whichever is chosen, the components are strongly correlated within an arm and their covariance has to come from the same fit whose coherence is under test, so the reference distribution is not free of the model being checked. Aggregate networks in this class are small while the parameter vector per contrast is long, so a joint test is close to unidentified: with a handful of trials there are often fewer independent loops than parameters, and the between-study variance for each component is estimated from very little. Tooling reinforces the gap, since the packages that implement inconsistency assessment operate on scalar contrasts, so anyone fitting a multi-parameter survival network leaves that stack behind and has nothing to fall back on.

title: No consistency test for vector-valued effects in survival NMA
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Batson, Greenall & Hudson 2016, PLOS ONE 11(5):e0154870
Reviews survival reporting in randomized trials and its consequences for meta-analysis, and states with a citation that although meta-analysis of survival data based on multi-dimensional treatment effects has been published, a method for evaluating consistency within networks for that methodology has not yet been developed.


Ouwens, Philips & Jansen 2010, Research Synthesis Methods 1(3-4):258-271
Network meta-analysis of parametric survival curves, which defines the multi-parameter treatment effect whose consistency cannot currently be checked.


Jansen 2011, BMC Medical Research Methodology 11:61
Fractional polynomial network meta-analysis of survival data, the most widely used member of the multi-parameter class, in which each contrast is a vector of power-specific coefficients.


Jansen & Cope 2012, BMC Medical Research Methodology 12:152
Extends multidimensional survival network meta-analysis with study-level covariates to explain heterogeneity and reduce inconsistency and confounding bias. It adjusts inconsistency away rather than testing for it, and offers no statistic that would say whether what remains is compatible with consistency.


Dias, Welton, Caldwell & Ades 2010, Statistics in Medicine 29(7-8):932-944
Node splitting for mixed treatment comparison, the standard check that separates direct from indirect evidence for a scalar contrast; it is the method whose vector generalization is missing.


Higgins, Jackson, Barrett, Lu et al. 2012, Research Synthesis Methods 3(2):98-110
The design-by-treatment interaction model, the global inconsistency framework for multi-arm networks, again formulated for scalar contrasts.


Jackson, Bujkiewicz, Law, Riley & White 2018, Biometrics 74(2):548-556
A matrix-based method of moments for multivariate network meta-analysis with multiple outcomes and random inconsistency effects. This is the existing machinery for vector-valued inconsistency; it is developed for vectors indexed by outcome, where the components are separately meaningful, not for vectors of survival-function parameters whose components are only interpretable together.


Freeman & Carpenter 2017, Research Synthesis Methods 8(4):451-464
Bayesian one-step individual participant data network meta-analysis with Royston-Parmar models, which demonstrates a global test for proportional hazards through a treatment-by-log-time interaction and shows how to test consistency of direct and indirect evidence in that model. The nearest existing solution; it requires individual participant data and covers a two-parameter time-varying effect rather than a general parameter vector.

title: No consistency test for vector-valued effects in survival NMA
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define consistency for this class explicitly, preferably on the survival function rather than on the parameters: state the direct and indirect implied survival or hazard curves for a contrast over a declared time window and define the discrepancy as a functional of their difference, so that the null does not depend on the parameterization the analyst happened to choose. Build the test as a vector node split with the contrast covariance taken from the fitted network, and calibrate it by simulation over network size, number of parameters per contrast, correlation between components, degree of non-proportionality and the number of independent loops, reporting type I error and power against departures that appear early, late and only in the extrapolated region. Compare it against the cheaper alternative of testing consistency on a decision summary such as restricted mean survival at a fixed horizon, which reduces the vector to a scalar at a stated cost in power against shape-only conflict. Ship the result in the packages that fit these models, so an analyst who is pushed into a multi-parameter survival model does not simultaneously lose access to the coherence check.

title: No consistency test for vector-valued effects in survival NMA
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this and the reviewer accepted it as specific and well posed, noting that scalar inconsistency diagnostics do not by themselves specify or calibrate a test for correlated vectors of survival-function parameters, and that later literature would need checking before the absence is treated as permanent. The verdict is partially-addressed because vector-valued inconsistency machinery exists for multivariate networks across outcomes and a consistency test has been demonstrated inside an individual-data Royston-Parmar network; neither has been defined or calibrated for aggregate-data multi-parameter survival contrasts.

title: No rule selects the common RMST horizon across unequal follow-up
text: OUT-24 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: No rule selects the common RMST horizon across unequal follow-up
text:
Statement
A synthesis on the restricted mean survival time scale requires one restriction time t* shared by every trial contributing to a contrast, and networks routinely contain trials whose observed follow-up differs by years. Any choice either extrapolates the arms whose last event precedes t, importing model-dependent area under the curve that the hazard-ratio analysis never used, or is pulled back toward the shortest common follow-up, discarding observed events and possibly landing short of the horizon a reimbursement decision needs. The first RMST-based network meta-analysis, 20 nasopharyngeal carcinoma trials and 5144 patients across 26 trial comparisons, set t to 10 years and found that 20 of the 44 trial arms (45.5%) had their last event before the horizon and required extrapolation over a mean of 1.8 years; the 5-year alternative needed no extrapolation but forced the hazard-ratio comparator to be censored at 5 years, an acknowledged loss of information. Under crossing or delayed-effect curves the sign of an RMST difference can itself depend on t, so the horizon is part of the estimand rather than a display setting. No selection rule, admissibility criterion, sensitivity convention or reporting requirement governs t in evidence synthesis, and no method propagates the extrapolation uncertainty the choice creates into the pooled interval or into the treatment ranking.

title: No rule selects the common RMST horizon across unequal follow-up
text:
Why it is open
The tradeoff is structural rather than unexplored: observed information in the longest-followed trials and freedom from extrapolation in the shortest cannot both be had, so no criterion can be optimal on both counts and the choice has to be defended on grounds outside the data. Survival beyond a trial’s last observed event is not identified from that trial, so the imported area is a function of the assumed tail; the resulting uncertainty is model-assumption uncertainty that a within-trial variance does not carry and that current pooling treats as absent. The single-study work on window choice solves a different problem: it establishes how large a t may be given one censoring distribution and how to make inference when t is chosen from the data, whereas a network has as many censoring distributions as trials and needs one t* admissible under all of them simultaneously. The only guidance offered is to prespecify t* by clinical interest, which is a governance answer: it does not say which value is defensible when trials disagree on follow-up and it prices nothing. Because RMST is being promoted as the replacement for the hazard ratio in HTA-facing survival synthesis, the horizon has become a free parameter that can move a reported benefit, including its sign, with no procedure constraining it.

title: No rule selects the common RMST horizon across unequal follow-up
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Petit, Blanchard, Pignon and Lueza 2019, Individual patient data network meta-analysis using either restricted mean survival time difference or hazard ratios: is there a difference? A case study on locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinomas, Systematic Reviews 8:96
first network meta-analysis run on the RMST difference; documents the horizon problem concretely, with 20 of 44 arms extrapolated by a mean of 1.8 years at t* of 10 years, no extrapolation but censored hazard ratios at 5 years, and 5 of 32 league-table comparisons changing interpretation between the two scales; its only guidance is to prespecify t* on clinical grounds


Tian, Jin, Uno, Lu, Huang, Anderson and Wei 2020, On the empirical choice of the time window for restricted mean survival time, Biometrics 76(4):1157-1166
gives the single-study version of the problem a formal treatment: inference for an RMST whose window is itself data-dependent, and a mild condition on the censoring distribution under which t may run to the largest observed or censored follow-up time; it is stated for one comparative study and does not address a horizon common to trials with different censoring distributions


Wei, Royston, Tierney and Parmar 2015, Meta-analysis of time-to-event outcomes from randomized trials using restricted mean survival time: application to individual participant data, Statistics in Medicine 34(21):2881-2898
establishes RMST-based individual participant data meta-analysis as an alternative to the hazard ratio under non-proportional hazards and supplies a diagnostic for the overall proportional-hazards assumption; the restriction time is chosen per application rather than by a stated rule


Lueza, Rotolo, Bonastre, Pignon and Michiels 2016, Bias and precision of methods for estimating the difference in restricted mean survival time from an individual patient data meta-analysis, BMC Medical Research Methodology 16:37
compares estimators of the pooled RMST difference from individual patient data and identifies the pooled Kaplan-Meier approach with random effects as the best bias-variance compromise; it evaluates estimators at a fixed horizon and does not treat the horizon as a quantity to be selected


Hua, Wang and Hong 2025, Network Meta-Analysis of Time-to-Event Endpoints With Individual Participant Data Using Restricted Mean Survival Time Regression, Biometrical Journal 67(1)
extends RMST network meta-analysis beyond two-step aggregation by fitting RMST regression on individual participant data so that covariate moderation and subgroup effects can be estimated; its contribution is the regression structure, and the restriction time is taken as given


Phillippo, Dias, Ades and Welton 2025, Multilevel network meta-regression for general likelihoods: synthesis of individual and aggregate data with applications to survival analysis, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A
delivers restricted means in a target population by integrating a marginal survival function to a horizon, which is the population-adjusted route to the same estimand; the horizon is supplied by the analyst and no admissibility or sensitivity requirement attaches to it

title: No rule selects the common RMST horizon across unequal follow-up
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Start with the estimand: for stated survival families, write the RMST contrast as a function of t* and characterize the horizons at which it changes sign, so that a network reports the leverage of the horizon rather than assuming it away. Define an admissible-horizon set for a network by generalizing the single-study censoring condition, for example the largest t* at which every contributing arm retains a stated minimum at-risk set, and report where the chosen t* sits in that set. Price the extrapolation instead of hiding it: report the extrapolated share of each arm’s restricted mean and propagate tail-model uncertainty into the pooled interval by refitting under alternative tail families or by placing a prior on the tail, rather than passing an extrapolated area forward as observed data. Standardize the reporting minimum: the horizon, which arms were extrapolated to reach it, the mean extrapolation time, and the contrast and ranking at a prespecified set of horizons, so a reader can see whether the conclusion is horizon-stable. Settle the operating characteristics by simulation under crossing and delayed-effect mechanisms with unequal administrative censoring, scoring candidate rules against the truncate-to-shortest and extrapolate-to-clinical-horizon extremes on bias, coverage and rank stability.

title: No rule selects the common RMST horizon across unequal follow-up
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. One reader proposed this from a single paper, the first RMST-based network meta-analysis, and the reviewer accepted it on the ground that a common horizon determines both the information discarded and the extrapolation introduced and can alter the estimand under non-proportional hazards. It is partially addressed rather than untouched because the single-study version of horizon choice has a formal treatment, including an admissibility condition tied to the censoring distribution; the network-level selection rule and the propagation of extrapolation uncertainty do not exist.

title: No criterion says when a network supports surrogate-based prediction
text: OUT-26 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 3/5

title: No criterion says when a network supports surrogate-based prediction
text:
Statement
The strength of a surrogate relationship is contrast-specific and class-specific rather than a property of a whole network, so validating a surrogate across all trials does not establish it for the contrast a decision rests on; in metastatic renal cell cancer the pooled analysis of all trials failed to produce a surrogate threshold effect at all, while the targeted-therapy subset gave a threshold of 3.9 months with R-squared 0.44. The estimator built for this, bivariate network meta-analysis, separates study-level surrogacy within each treatment contrast from treatment-level surrogacy across treatments, and its stated data requirement is a relatively large number of trials per contrast for the first and a relatively large number of treatments for the second. Real networks do not supply that: its own motivating advanced colorectal cancer network drew 15, 24, 4 and 4 trials on its four best-represented contrasts and a single trial on each of the remaining three, and model-comparison statistics could be reported only for contrasts with at least four trials. Where the treatment-level model is used for the case that motivates surrogacy, predicting the effect of a new treatment on a final outcome it has never been measured on, the predictions carry large uncertainty and were found in larger networks to be comparable to or wider than those from an ordinary bivariate meta-analysis that ignores the network entirely, with the properties and assumptions of those models left to future work. Applied networks meanwhile consume surrogate predictions as if they were data: a network meta-analysis of 49 studies from 45 randomized trials and 12 regimens in metastatic colorectal cancer predicted the overall-survival effect for 22 comparisons from tumor response and progression-free survival where survival was unreported, thereby adding three direct comparisons with no survival trial behind them, then ran node-splitting and ranked regimens by SUCRA on the augmented network, from a surrogate relationship whose posterior R-squared was 0.54 with 95 percent credible interval 0.25 to 0.76. What does not exist is a criterion with known operating characteristics: no rule states how many trials per contrast, how many treatments, or what between-study correlation makes contrast-level or treatment-level surrogacy estimable well enough to license prediction; no contrast-specific analog of the surrogate threshold effect has been defined for a network; and no convention requires a network to label which of its contrasts are surrogate-derived or to say whether its inconsistency assessment was computed on measured edges only.

title: No criterion says when a network supports surrogate-based prediction
text:
Why it is open
The quantity a criterion would govern is a between-trial slope and correlation for a single contrast, estimated in practice from one or two trials on that contrast, so within the contrast there is nothing to estimate it from; the only routes are to pool contrasts, which assumes away the contrast-specificity that motivated the model, or to borrow across treatment classes, which imports the same assumption in softer form. Borrowing has been built, with full and partial exchangeability of surrogate relationships across classes, but the amount borrowed is governed by a hierarchical variance the data barely inform and by an analyst’s choice of which classes are exchangeable, so the answer to whether the surrogate holds for this contrast is largely supplied by that choice. Validation by held-out prediction is available only where the final outcome was measured, which is exactly where prediction is not needed; the case that matters, a contrast or treatment with no final-outcome trial, admits no in-sample check, and this is the same structural obstacle that makes cross-outcome borrowing unfalsifiable. The empirical record shows the relationship is not stable across mechanisms of action, so a criterion calibrated on pooled data would not transfer to the contrast it is applied to. Finally the reporting machinery that has been built for surrogate endpoints, the CONSORT extension and its definitional framework, addresses trials, so nothing obliges an evidence synthesis to disclose which of its contrasts were predicted rather than measured, and the incentive to solve the problem is correspondingly weak.

title: No criterion says when a network supports surrogate-based prediction
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Bujkiewicz, Jackson, Thompson, Turner, Stadler, Abrams and White 2019, Statistics in Medicine 38:3322-3341
Introduces bivariate network meta-analysis for surrogate endpoint evaluation, separating study-level surrogacy within a treatment contrast from treatment-level surrogacy across treatments, and states in its discussion that estimating the former needs a relatively large number of trials per contrast and the latter a relatively large number of treatments; reports that new-treatment predictions from the treatment-level models carry large uncertainty and in larger networks are comparable to or more uncertain than those from bivariate meta-analysis, and calls for research on the properties and assumptions of those models.


Papanikos, Thompson, Abrams, Stadler, Ciani, Taylor and Bujkiewicz 2020, Statistics in Medicine 39:1103-1124
Attacks the sparsity directly with two Bayesian hierarchical models that borrow information about the surrogate relationship across treatment classes, one assuming full exchangeability of surrogate relationships and one partial exchangeability to limit borrowing from distinctly different classes, assessed in nine simulated data scenarios against class-by-class subgroup analysis; supplies precision but not a criterion for when the borrowed relationship licenses prediction for a given contrast.


Wheaton, Papanikos, Thomas and Bujkiewicz 2023, Medical Decision Making 43:539-552
Addresses the same sparsity from the data side by supplementing 7 randomized trials with 4 comparative and 2 matched single-arm real-world studies when evaluating progression-free survival as a surrogate for overall survival in metastatic colorectal cancer, reducing uncertainty around the surrogacy parameters and improving predicted treatment effects, at the cost of a selection-of-evidence judgment flagged in the report itself as a bias risk.


Hoang and Kim 2020, Cancers 12:2663
Shows the practice the missing criterion would govern: predicts overall-survival hazard ratios for 22 comparisons from tumor response and progression-free survival using multivariate random-effects surrogacy models, inserts them into a 12-regimen network where they create three new direct comparisons, and then reports node-splitting consistency tests, heterogeneity and SUCRA rankings on the augmented network, from a progression-free survival to overall survival relationship with posterior R-squared 0.54 (95 percent credible interval 0.25 to 0.76).


Poad, Khan, Wheaton, Thomas, Sweeting and Bujkiewicz 2022, Cancers 14:5391
Measures how far surrogacy varies by mechanism of action, evaluating progression-free survival and tumor response as surrogates across 66 randomized trials in metastatic colorectal cancer and finding the tumor response relationships weak overall but stronger within the epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor plus chemotherapy class, with little evidence that KRAS status matters.


Johnson, Liauw and Lassere 2015, Annals of Oncology 26:485-496
Computes the surrogate threshold effect by drug class in metastatic renal cell cancer across 30 qualifying trials, finding that the all-trials and immunotherapy analyses failed to demonstrate a threshold at all while the targeted-therapy trials gave 3.9 months with R-squared 0.44, and concluding that surrogacy is not generalizable across drug classes.


Rotolo, Paoletti and Michiels 2018, Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine 155:189-198
Implements the classical two-step copula method and one-step auxiliary Poisson models for failure-time surrogacy in the surrosurv package, including the option to adjust the second-step regression for measurement error in the estimated treatment effects, so the measurement-error correction at the pairwise level is available software rather than a missing method; supplies no network structure.


Bujkiewicz, Singh, Wheaton, Jenkins, Martina, Hyrich and Abrams 2022, Journal of Clinical Epidemiology 150:171-178
Reuses the bivariate network machinery as an identification device rather than a validation device, bridging disconnected first-line and second-line rheumatoid arthritis networks from 21 trials and 6 emulated target trials so that second-line effects can be predicted where no second-line trial exists; the same construction as surrogate-based prediction, and the same absence of a rule for when the borrowed relationship is trustworthy.


Manyara et al. 2024, BMJ 386:e078524
Gives the CONSORT-Surrogate reporting extension for randomized trials whose primary outcome is a surrogate, nine modified items and two new ones; it is the reporting standard the synthesis setting lacks, since nothing analogous requires a network meta-analysis to report which contrasts were surrogate-predicted or on what surrogacy evidence.


Wheaton and Bujkiewicz 2025, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care 41:e11
Measures the decision exposure: of 47 NICE oncology technology appraisals published between February 2022 and May 2023, 18 used surrogate endpoints and 37 separate surrogate endpoints were discussed, of which 11 were supported by randomized trial evidence, 7 by observational studies, 12 by clinical opinion and 7 by no evidence at all.

title: No criterion says when a network supports surrogate-based prediction
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Turn the stated data requirement into a checkable precondition: derive, for the bivariate network model, the replication and correlation levels at which the contrast-level and treatment-level slopes are estimated with usable precision, and run it before any prediction is issued, in the way contrast estimability is checked before a contrast is reported. Establish operating characteristics by simulating over network topologies rather than single scenarios, varying trials per contrast, number of treatments, and the strength and heterogeneity of the surrogate relationship, and scoring bias, coverage and interval width of predicted final-outcome effects against both the ordinary bivariate model and against issuing no prediction, since the existing evidence is that the network model can be the worse of the two for a new treatment. Define a contrast-specific surrogate threshold effect, the effect on the surrogate needed on that contrast to predict a nonnull effect on the final outcome, and report it per contrast rather than for the pooled network. Validate by deletion where the final outcome was measured: mask final-outcome data one contrast at a time, refit, and report prediction error and coverage indexed by trials per contrast and by whether the masked contrast shares a class with observed ones. Separately, require any network carrying surrogate-predicted contrasts to label them, to report the network with and without them, and to state whether inconsistency was assessed on measured edges only, since an edge that is a deterministic function of other edges cannot supply an independent consistency check.

title: No criterion says when a network supports surrogate-based prediction
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. This rests on weaker provenance than its neighbors. It was not proposed by a reader arguing from a paper; it was reported by 2 of 12 gap labellers as something they looked for and did not find, and the three papers behind it carry unequal weight. One is a pairwise individual-patient-data surrogacy analysis in esophageal cancer whose noted absence, copula estimates unadjusted for measurement error, is an option the package it used already offers, so that strand supports nothing. One is an applied colorectal cancer network whose quoted sentence asks for further individual-patient-data validation, which is a call for more studies; what supports the entry there is what that analysis did rather than what it said, namely feeding 22 predicted survival effects and three manufactured direct comparisons into a ranked network. Only the bivariate network meta-analysis paper states a methodological limit, and it states it in two sentences of its discussion together with a call for research on the properties of its own treatment-level models. The registry was searched for surrogate, surrogacy, bivariate, multivariate, correlated-outcome, trial-level and intermediate-endpoint content and contains no entry on surrogate endpoints; the nearest neighbors, DIS-17 on cross-outcome borrowing as a bridge, OUT-19 on multivariate population adjustment and HET-09 on multivariate inconsistency covariance, concern borrowing between simultaneously measured outcomes rather than the predictive validity of a surrogate for a final outcome, and DEC-08 concerns provenance labeling for connected and disconnected networks rather than surrogate validity. It is filed as partially-addressed because hierarchical borrowing across treatment classes and augmentation with real-world evidence both attack the sparsity that makes contrast-level surrogacy unestimable; neither supplies the criterion with operating characteristics, the contrast-specific threshold, or the labeling requirement, and no work located since 2019 extends the bivariate network model for surrogacy or reports its operating characteristics.
