title: ESS is an insufficient overlap diagnostic and no battery is agreed
text: OVL-02 Partially addressed Very high priority Promising

title: ESS is an insufficient overlap diagnostic and no battery is agreed
text:
Statement
The conventional MAIC effective sample size is a scalar functional of the weight vector: it records only how concentrated the weights are, and carries no information about where in covariate space the weight mass sits, about moments left out of the balancing constraints, about the outcome model, or about the network position of the adjusted edge. Two parts of the proposed eleven-item battery are already built. Glimm and Yau 2022 supply the support-geometry item as a published convex-hull feasibility test with an R package, proving that the MAIC calibration problem has a finite solution only if the target mean lies in the convex hull of the source covariate rows, and demonstrating a real subgroup where a linear program proves infeasibility while optim() silently returns weights with an ESS of 2 percent of n (doi:10.1002/pst.2210); and cpaic, an unreleased development R package on GitHub (commit 9d150e9) that a reader cannot install from CRAN, exports weight_diagnostics(), which already reports ESS, n, entropy efficiency, coefficient of variation, maximum normalized weight, top-5-percent mass and residual balance, and edge_influence(), which reports whether an individual-patient-data edge informs the requested contrast at all. What remains open is standardization rather than invention, plus feasibility for several items: a PAIC reporting and risk-of-bias framework now exists (Ishak et al. 2025, doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1) but does not fix a computed minimum diagnostic set that software must emit, only 3 of 133 reviewed PAIC articles reported all key methodological aspects (doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2023.09.004), and the density-ratio, convex-hull and stratum-specific-ESS items are not generally computable when the target is known only through published marginal moments.

title: ESS is an insufficient overlap diagnostic and no battery is agreed
text:
Why it is open
ESS is a concentration summary of a weight vector, so weight vectors with identical ESS can put their mass in different covariate regions, and nothing in it depends on the outcome model, on excluded moments, or on the network position of the adjusted edge; a nominally healthy ESS can therefore coexist with zero influence of the individual-patient-data edge on the contrast actually reported. Several of the missing items are hard rather than merely unimplemented: when the target is available only as published marginals, a convex-hull check on target means tests calibration feasibility rather than support for the target joint distribution, and stratum-specific ESS measures concentration within observed source strata rather than coverage of the target unless target stratum masses are known. Generalizing the edge-influence diagnostic beyond linear component contrasts to nonlinear and target-standardized contrasts is unsettled, and the existing implementation uses diagonal inverse-edge variances, so it is only an approximation when the fitted network estimator carries within-study covariance. Because ESS is cheap, familiar and reported by default while nothing forces the geometric or analyst-choice items, each analysis can pick the diagnostic that flatters it, and the measured consequence is inconsistent reporting across the applied literature.

title: ESS is an insufficient overlap diagnostic and no battery is agreed
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Glimm and Yau 2022, Geometric approaches to assessing the numerical feasibility for conducting matching-adjusted indirect comparisons
delivers the convex-hull support and feasibility item of the proposed battery, with an R package: proves the MAIC calibration equation has a finite solution only if the target mean lies in the convex hull of the source covariate rows, and shows a real subgroup where a linear program proves infeasibility while optim() silently returns weights with an ESS of 2 percent of n; also states verbatim that ESS measures only the variability of the normalized weights


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9, weight_diagnostics() and edge_influence()
exports weight_diagnostics(), reporting ESS, n, entropy efficiency, coefficient of variation, maximum normalized weight, top-5-percent mass and residual balance, and edge_influence(), reporting whether an individual-patient-data edge informs the requested contrast at all; edge influence uses diagonal inverse-edge variances, so it is approximate for multi-arm studies


Serret-Larmande et al. 2023, A methodological review of population-adjusted indirect comparisons reveals inconsistent reporting and suggests publication bias
documents the part of the problem that is genuinely open: key methodological aspects of PAICs were reported inconsistently, with only three of 133 articles adequately reporting all aspects, and calls for strengthened guidelines


Ishak et al. 2025, PharmacoEconomics
publishes a framework for reliable, transparent and reproducible population-adjusted indirect comparisons, including reporting and risk-of-bias guidance; it does not specify a computed minimum set of overlap and support diagnostics that software must emit by default


Phillippo et al. 2018, Medical Decision Making
notes that the method of moments by definition ensures covariate balance to the level of information published in the aggregate-data trial, which makes standardized differences on balanced moments a convergence check rather than an informative diagnostic; also recommends inspecting the weight distribution directly

title: ESS is an insufficient overlap diagnostic and no battery is agreed
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Demote ESS from a sufficiency certificate to one entry in a standardized battery, and assemble that battery from what exists rather than rebuilding it: adopt the published convex-hull feasibility test and its R package for the support item (doi:10.1002/pst.2210), and take ESS, ESS divided by nominal n, maximum normalized weight, top-share mass, entropy, coefficient of variation and residual balance from weight_diagnostics() in cpaic (https://github.com/choxos/cpaic, commit 9d150e9, unreleased and not installable from CRAN), noting that coefficient of variation adds nothing beyond Kish ESS at fixed n. Drop or demote standardized differences on balanced moments, which are zero by construction under the method of moments and serve only as a convergence check, and state explicitly which items require an assumed target joint distribution rather than published marginals. Generalize edge_influence() so it applies to nonlinear models and target-standardized marginal contrasts rather than only to linear network edges, and make it exact for multi-arm studies by using the fitted within-study covariance. The remaining work is agreement and enforcement: attach the battery to the existing PAIC reporting and risk-of-bias framework (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1) so the items become required outputs rather than optional ones.

title: ESS is an insufficient overlap diagnostic and no battery is agreed
text:
Our study

An infeasible MAIC is signaled by its own balance table, not by its effective sample size
The question put to it. MAIC has no solution when the target mean lies outside the convex hull of the source covariates. Does the optimizer say so, and can ESS, the maximum weight or the residual balance tell infeasible analyses from hard feasible ones?
What it found. The residual imbalance of the returned weights does, almost perfectly: above 0.001 in 99.9% of infeasible and 0.1% of feasible analyses. The optimizer reported convergence on 17% of infeasible problems. ESS ranks analyses well but the conventional rule of ESS below 10% of n flagged 73% of feasible analyses near the hull boundary as well as every infeasible one, so it cannot separate impossible from hard; and hard feasible analyses near the boundary undercovered badly anyway.
Results.

AUROC for infeasibility: residual imbalance 1.000, ESS 0.996, maximum weight 0.993, optimizer non-convergence 0.909.
ESS below 10% of n: flags 100% of infeasible and 73% of feasible analyses in the near-boundary scenarios.
Silent failure: the optimizer reported convergence on 0% to 8% of infeasible problems with 3 covariates and 22% to 34% with 8.
Infeasible analyses had ESS about 1 and no usable estimate; feasible analyses near the boundary had ESS 3 to 14 and coverage 0.62 to 0.85.

Design.

Estimand

Linear-program feasibility of the calibration, and the target marginal log odds ratio

Methods compared

Kish ESS, maximum weight, residual imbalance of the returned weights, optimizer convergence code

Data-generating mechanism

Binary-outcome MAIC with 3 or 8 covariates and a target shifted so 0% to 90% of source samples were infeasible by linear program, with and without effect modification; 24 scenarios; ESS, maximum weight, residual imbalance and convergence code scored as detectors of infeasibility.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 24,000 in total


What this does not answer. Only feasibility of the mean constraint; support for the target joint law cannot be checked from published marginals. Normal covariates, MAIC on means, one sample size; the proposed diagnostics’ computability taxonomy was not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument · Code and data: studies/OVL-02-feasibility-and-what-published-data-can-compute · Protocol: registered before the run

title: ESS is an insufficient overlap diagnostic and no battery is agreed
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “The conventional MAIC effective sample size is a scalar functional of the weight vector that is routinely used as the single summary of overlap, yet it cannot establish support, moment alignment, network relevance, outcome-model stability, or the scientific appropriateness of the target. There is no agreed minimum set of overlap and support diagnostics that PAIC software must report; the report proposes an eleven-item battery.”
What was wrong with it. The source presented all eleven battery items as unbuilt; the literature auditor found the support-geometry item already published with an R package (Glimm and Yau 2022, doi:10.1002/pst.2210) and noted that standardized differences on balanced moments are near-decorative because the method of moments enforces balance by construction (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740), while GPT-5.6 Sol read choxos/cpaic@9d150e9 and confirmed weight_diagnostics() and edge_influence() are exported, adding that coefficient of variation is algebraically one-to-one with Kish ESS at fixed n and that several proposed items are not computable from published marginal moments. The claim that no reporting standard exists also narrows, following a correction established elsewhere in this audit: Ishak et al. 2025 (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1) published a PAIC reporting and risk-of-bias framework, so what is missing is a required computed diagnostic set, not a framework as such.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. I retrieved the full text of Glimm and Yau 2022 (Pharm Stat 21:974-987, arXiv 2108.01896). It supplies verbatim support for claim 2 (‘ESS is in fact only a measure of the variability of the w-tilde-i’s’) and, more importantly, already delivers battery item 7: a published convex-hull support diagnostic with an R package. They prove ‘Equation (2) has a finite solution if and only if x-bar is an element of the set H(Y)={z: z=Yw, 0<=w_i<=1, sum w_i=1}’ and demonstrate a real subgroup where LP-solve shows no solution exists while optim() silently returns weights giving ESS of 2 percent of n. So the support-geometry item is solved, not open. Second caveat: battery item 4 is near-decorative. Phillippo et al. 2018 note ‘the method of moments, by definition, ensures covariate balance,’ so standardized differences on balanced moments are zero by construction and serve only as a convergence check. What remains genuinely open is standardization, not invention: Serret-Larmande et al. 2023 found only 3 of 133 PAIC articles reported all key methodological aspects and called for strengthened guidelines. The cpaic/edge_influence citation checks out against the repository README but is an uncited, unversioned self-citation to an unreleased GitHub package. Cites doi:10.1002/pst.2210: Battery item 7 (convex-hull / support-distance diagnostics) already exists, is published, and ships with an R package; also gives verbatim support for the claim that ESS measures only weight variability.. Cites doi:10.1016/j.jclinepi.2023.09.004: A source that itself asserts the absence of agreed reporting standards, which is the part of OVL-02 that is genuinely open.. Cites https://github.com/choxos/cpaic: Confirms the prior_work attribution: edge_influence() does exist and does report whether IPD inform the contrast..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. C1-C10 capture the central mathematics. ESS equals the inverse squared concentration of normalized weights and contains no covariate locations, outcomes, or network topology. The same weights can be assigned to different covariate regions without changing ESS, and a component contrast can assign zero linear influence to an otherwise well-weighted IPD edge. At cpaic commit 9d150e9, edge_influence() exists, is exported, and implements this contrast-specific diagnostic. Its documented multi-arm limitation matters: it uses diagonal inverse-edge variances, so its influence is only an approximation when the fitted network estimator uses within-study covariance. The proposed battery is useful but heterogeneous: it mixes overlap, achieved balance, model extrapolation, network relevance, and sensitivity analysis. C15 overstates the incremental value of coefficient of variation because, given n, CV and Kish ESS are algebraically one-to-one; entropy and Gini can add different distributional information. C18-C20 are not universally available when the target is known only through marginal moments. A target-moment convex-hull check assesses calibration feasibility, not support for the full target distribution, and stratum-specific ESS measures concentration within observed source strata rather than target coverage unless target stratum masses are known. Thus existing cpaic diagnostics partly resolve the software gap, while a defensible, feasible minimum set remains open. The fieldwide agreement claim is a literature question and is not established by this technical audit. Cites choxos/cpaic@9d150e9cad88f2e6fbcd94dbb92c3dee3b7c2dca: Confirms C10 and partially addresses the proposed battery. NAMESPACE exports edge_influence() and weight_diagnostics(); the former computes contrast-specific linear edge influence, while the latter reports ESS, n, entropy efficiency, CV, maximum normalized weight, top-5-percent mass, and residual balance..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Weight trimming silently changes the estimand
text: OVL-04 Overstated Very high priority Emerging

title: Weight trimming silently changes the estimand
text:
Statement
Ordinary MAIC weight capping or trimming changes the weighting functional, so a trimmed analysis generally no longer identifies the nominal target-population effect: it reduces variance while introducing bias, and the two-stage MAIC simulation states the limitation directly, that truncation ‘shifts the target population or estimand definition’ and ‘requires arbitrary ad hoc decisions on cutoff thresholds’ (doi:10.1186/s12874-022-01692-9). The induced population is not indescribable, however: capping at c defines a tilted distribution proportional to f_source(x) min{w(x), c}, which is data-adaptive and clinically awkward but mathematically statable, so the exact rule and the induced population can and should be reported as a sensitivity or secondary estimand. Estimand-explicit overlap methods also already exist: Fang and He 2026 adopt overlap weights and name the average treatment effect in the overlap population as the target estimand for indirect treatment comparison, with estimators, standard errors and a 1000-replicate simulation in which mean ESS rises from 49.8 and 61.9 under MAIC to 272.5 and 272.7 under overlap weighting at 600 patients per trial, and RMSE falls from 0.432 and 0.485 to 0.208 (doi:10.1007/s43441-026-00976-2). What is still undeveloped is estimand-preserving stabilization that retains the nominal target population, together with adoption, extension beyond the anchored continuous-outcome case, and guidance on when redefining to the overlap population is decision-relevant.

title: Weight trimming silently changes the estimand
text:
Why it is open
Trimming defines the population through a rule on estimated weights, so the induced estimand is data-adaptive and has no clean clinical description even though it has a closed mathematical one, and simple capping does not automatically produce a well-defined overlap population; it may be better described as a biased sensitivity estimate for the original target. Estimand-preserving stabilization is the part with no candidate: weight-only stabilization cannot reduce relative weight dispersion while preserving the full target distribution unless it leaves the normalized weights unchanged, so efficiency gains that keep the nominal target require outcome modeling, augmentation or design information rather than a better cutoff rule. Overlap-weighted estimands solve the naming problem but move the population, and the published version covers the anchored continuous-outcome case, so non-collapsible scales, survival outcomes and network settings are untested. Nothing in current practice forces an analyst to state the cutoff rule or the induced population, which is why the trade stays silent.

title: Weight trimming silently changes the estimand
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Remiro-Azocar 2022 (two-stage MAIC)
shows two-stage MAIC can improve precision in some settings while simulations indicate poor overlap remains a fundamental limitation and truncation induces considerable bias when overlap is poor; states explicitly that truncation shifts the target population or estimand definition and requires arbitrary ad hoc cutoff decisions (also indexed as https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35941551/)


Fang and He 2026, Arbitrated Indirect Treatment Comparisons, Therapeutic Innovation and Regulatory Science
contradicts the claim that estimand-explicit overlap methods for PAIC do not exist: adopts overlap weights, names the average treatment effect in the overlap population as the target estimand, and supplies estimators, standard errors, a 1000-replicate simulation and an arbitration variant for when neither sponsor shares individual patient data; preprint at https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18071 and PMID https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42177327/


Jiang et al. 2025, A critical assessment of matching-adjusted indirect comparisons in relation to target populations
establishes the target-population problem that the overlap estimand answers, including the MAIC paradox in which different entities reach opposing conclusions about which treatment is more effective despite analyzing the same data

title: Weight trimming silently changes the estimand
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Do not build estimand-explicit overlap methods from scratch: extend the published overlap-weight estimand for indirect comparison (doi:10.1007/s43441-026-00976-2) beyond the anchored continuous-outcome case to binary and survival outcomes, non-collapsible scales and network settings, and test whether the overlap population it names is the one decision-makers want, which is the question raised by the target-population critique it answers (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10). Where the nominal target must be retained, the open work is estimand-preserving efficiency through augmentation or outcome modeling rather than through a smarter weight cap, since weight-only stabilization cannot both shrink dispersion and preserve the target distribution. Where trimming is used anyway, require the cutoff rule, the induced tilted population and its effective sample size to be reported, and label the result a secondary or sensitivity estimand rather than the target-population effect.

title: Weight trimming silently changes the estimand
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. Weight truncation trades variance for bias and changes the implicit population without naming it, and estimand-preserving stabilisation that retains the nominal target population is still undeveloped for PAIC. Estimand-explicit overlap methods, by contrast, now exist: Fang and He (2026) propose the average treatment effect in the overlap population (ATO) as an explicitly named target for indirect treatment comparison. What remains open is adoption, extension beyond the anchored continuous-outcome case, and guidance on when redefining to the overlap population is decision-relevant.
The source said. “Weight truncation is applied in practice as a numerical fix for unstable MAIC weights, but it trades variance for bias and usually changes the implicit population, so the reported estimand is no longer the nominal target-population effect. A trimmed analysis should be reported as a secondary effect in an explicitly defined trimmed or overlap population.”
What was wrong with it. The source claimed there is no accepted way to state which population a truncated MAIC estimates and that estimand-explicit overlap methods have not been developed; both auditors judged the entry overstated. The literature auditor found Fang and He 2026 (doi:10.1007/s43441-026-00976-2; preprint https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18071; PMID 42177327), which names the overlap population as the target estimand for indirect comparison with estimators, standard errors and simulation, and GPT-5.6 Sol showed the truncated population is mathematically statable as the tilted density proportional to f_source(x) min{w(x), c} and pointed out that the source’s own cited two-stage MAIC paper already records that truncation shifts the estimand (doi:10.1186/s12874-022-01692-9).

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / overstated. The prior_work citation checks out exactly. Remiro-Azocar 2022 (PMID 35941551) states ‘the simulation study also explores the use of weight truncation in combination with MAIC for the first time’ and ‘It is not as effective when overlap between the trials’ target populations is poor and the extremity of the weights is high. In these scenarios, truncation leads to substantial precision and efficiency gains but induces considerable bias.’ That supports every attributed element. The overstatement is elsewhere: the claim ‘Estimand-explicit overlap methods for PAIC have not yet been developed’ is false as of 2026. Fang and He, Arbitrated Indirect Treatment Comparisons (Ther Innov Regul Sci, DOI 10.1007/s43441-026-00976-2, PMID 42177327; arXiv 2510.18071), propose exactly that: overlap weights targeting a named ATO estimand for indirect comparison, with simulation and an arbitration protocol usable when only AgD is available for the counterpart. They also note ‘because the overlap weights are confined to the interval [0,1], they remain stable’ - i.e. the stability motive for trimming is obtained without trimming. Estimand-preserving stabilisation remains undeveloped; the coverage is anchored and continuous-outcome, so partially-solved. Cites doi:10.1007/s43441-026-00976-2: Directly contradicts ‘Estimand-explicit overlap methods for PAIC have not yet been developed.’ Adopts Li et al. (2018) overlap weights, names the overlap population as the target estimand (ATO), gives estimators plus standard errors, a 1000-replicate simulation, and a variant for when neither sponsor shares IPD (arbitrator simulates covariate IPD from the counterpart’s AgD). Simulation: MAIC mean ESS 49.8 and 61.9 versus overlap-weighted 272.5 and 272.7 at n=600 per trial, with RMSE 0.208 versus 0.432/0.485.. Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10: Establishes the target-population problem that the overlap estimand answers, and is the paper Fang and He respond to..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1, C2, and C4-C6 are correct for ordinary clipping or deletion of high weights, and the cited simulation directly demonstrates the bias-variance trade-off. The report overstates the conceptual gap, however. If the intended target density ratio is w(x), capping at c defines an induced tilted distribution proportional to f_source(x) min{w(x),c}; trimming has an analogous indicator-weighted form. The population may be data-adaptive and clinically awkward, but it can be stated mathematically. Consequently, the assertion that there is no accepted way even to state what population is estimated is too strong. C3 is sensible as reporting advice if the exact rule and resulting target are declared, but simple capping does not automatically produce a clean, clinically defined overlap population and may instead be best described as a biased sensitivity estimate for the original target. C7 and C8 are categorical literature-absence claims outside this audit’s technical lens. Pure weight-only stabilization cannot reduce relative weight dispersion while preserving the complete target distribution unless it leaves normalized weights unchanged; estimand-preserving efficiency gains require additional outcome modeling, augmentation, or design information. The cited work resolves the empirical trade-off, while standardized estimand definition and decision rules remain incomplete. Cites 10.1186/s12874-022-01692-9: The simulation establishes that two-stage MAIC can improve precision and that truncation reduces variance while introducing bias, especially as overlap worsens. The paper also explicitly recognizes that truncation shifts the target population or estimand..

Decision path

R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: No standardized sample-size planning guidance or software for PAIC
text: OVL-06 Confirmed open High priority Emerging

title: No standardized sample-size planning guidance or software for PAIC
text:
Statement
Nominal sample size alone does not determine the precision of a population-adjusted indirect comparison, although it remains an important determinant: information also depends on anticipated overlap, the balancing constraints, the outcome distribution, treatment allocation and the estimator’s own influence function, and for survival outcomes on weighted risk-set and event information rather than on patient counts. No universal effective-sample-size threshold is defensible, and the Kish ESS is not an exact information measure in any case, since Phillippo et al. 2018 note it ‘is likely to be an underestimation of the true ESS’ when the weights are estimated and correlated with the outcome (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740). What is missing is standardized PAIC-specific planning guidance and software, not the possibility of information-based planning: scenario-based planning that posits source and target distributions, derives the anticipated weights and uses influence-function or simulation calculations is already feasible. Simulation design is also not starting from nothing, since the 162-scenario anchored study of Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2021 (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511) and a 2025 study indexed on positivity-violation severity (arxiv:2507.12241) are the de facto templates the field reuses.

title: No standardized sample-size planning guidance or software for PAIC
text:
Why it is open
The information remaining after weighting depends on the mismatch with a target that is not fixed until the comparator population is chosen, so no pre-study calculation expressed in nominal n alone can be binding, and any calculation stated in Kish ESS inherits a quantity that understates the true effective sample size and ignores arm allocation, outcome variance and nuisance-parameter estimation. For survival outcomes the relevant unit is events rather than patients, and even total events and censoring fractions are insufficient without timing, allocation, risk-set composition and the censoring mechanism, so a single grid cannot serve both outcome types. Unanchored designs carry a strictly stronger identification burden, conditional constancy of absolute rather than relative effects, and omitted prognostic structure creates structural bias that a larger sample does not cure, so the harsher grid needed there is about misspecification and confounding scenarios rather than simply larger n. The gap is therefore in standardization and tooling: nothing prevents a design-specific information calculation, but there is no accepted PAIC procedure, no software, and no agreed reporting of what was assumed.

title: No standardized sample-size planning guidance or software for PAIC
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2021, Methods for population adjustment with limited access to individual patient data: a review and simulation study
sources the claim that effective sample size rather than nominal size governs precision in weighting-based PAIC, reporting that the robust sandwich variance estimator underestimates variability where effective sample sizes are small; its 162-scenario survival simulation grid is close to the design grid this entry proposes building


Phillippo et al. 2018, Medical Decision Making
sources the harsher requirements for unanchored comparisons, which assume conditional constancy of absolute effects and require all prognostic variables as well as all effect modifiers; also records that the standard Kish ESS is likely an underestimate of the true ESS, so planning guidance stated in ESS inherits a biased quantity


Serret-Larmande et al. 2025, Assessing the Impact of Covariate Distribution and Positivity Violation on Weighting-Based Indirect Comparisons: a Simulation Study
simulation study explicitly designed around positivity-violation severity and non-normal covariates, supporting the proposal to index design grids on overlap severity rather than on nominal sample size

title: No standardized sample-size planning guidance or software for PAIC
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build scenario-based planning rather than a threshold rule: posit source and target covariate distributions, derive the anticipated weights and their dispersion, and compute precision from the estimator’s influence function or by simulation, reporting weighted event and risk-set information for survival outcomes and stating the assumed overlap explicitly. Extend the existing simulation templates instead of duplicating them, since the 162-scenario anchored study (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511) already varies overlap, imbalance and sample size and the 2025 positivity study (arxiv:2507.12241) already indexes on violation severity; what is added is unanchored scenarios with omitted prognostic variables and misspecification, not merely larger n. Where planning is reported in effective sample size, state that the Kish approximation understates the true ESS and that no threshold on it certifies validity (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740). Package the result as software so that a planning calculation can be reproduced and audited rather than asserted.

title: No standardized sample-size planning guidance or software for PAIC
text:
Our study

Planning a MAIC from the estimator’s influence function, not from n or Kish ESS
The question put to it. Before any data exist, which planning quantity predicts the precision a MAIC will achieve: nominal sample size, Kish effective sample size, or the estimator’s influence-function variance evaluated at posited source and target laws?
What it found. The influence-function variance. It predicted the achieved SD within 10% in 85% of 72 scenarios, missing only at 150 patients with 10% prevalence. Kish ESS was within 10% in 58% and understated the achieved SD in 99% of scenarios, so it is optimistic, not the conservative quantity it is usually taken to be; nominal n was within 10% in 21%.
Results.

Planned SE over achieved SD, median (range): influence function 0.963 (0.827 to 1.023); Kish ESS 0.912 (0.745 to 1.004); nominal n 0.797 (0.541 to 0.985).
Kish ESS understated the achieved SD in 99% of scenarios; its error grew with the target shift.
All 11 influence-function misses were at 150 patients and 10% prevalence; its median ratio was 0.908 at 150 patients and 0.981 at 1000.
The refuting sentence, that nominal n with an overlap adjustment is good enough, fails its registered criterion (58% of scenarios within 10% against the 90% required).

Design.

Estimand

SD of the MAIC estimate of the target marginal log odds ratio

Methods compared

nominal n, Kish ESS, influence-function variance

Data-generating mechanism

Binary-outcome MAIC with 2 or 5 covariates, 72 scenarios crossing total size (150, 400, 1000), target shift, dimension, allocation and prevalence; three planned SEs computed from the posited laws compared with the SD achieved over replicates.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 72,000 in total


What this does not answer. The planner is assumed to know the source and target laws. Binary outcome, anchored-side precision and MAIC on means only; the unanchored bias floor and survival outcomes are not run. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.
Read it: PDF · Markdown · OpenDocument · Code and data: studies/OVL-06-planning-in-information-rather-than-in-n · Protocol: registered before the run

title: No standardized sample-size planning guidance or software for PAIC
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source titled this. “No sample-size or information-planning framework for PAIC” The title says no planning framework exists, which the audit called a non sequitur since scenario-based influence-function and simulation planning is already feasible.
The source said. “Nominal sample size is not the operative information metric for population-adjusted indirect comparisons: information content is driven by effective sample size after reweighting and by event information in the weighted pseudo-population. The report offers proposed design grids while explicitly declining to claim any universal threshold, so there is no framework for planning a PAIC or a PAIC simulation in information terms.”
What was wrong with it. The source moved from ‘no universal threshold’ to ‘no planning framework’, which GPT-5.6 Sol judged a non sequitur, since scenario-based planning conditional on anticipated overlap and estimator-specific influence is already possible and what is missing is standardized guidance and software; it also narrowed ‘nominal n is not the operative metric’ to the weaker claim that nominal n alone is insufficient. The claim was unattributed in the source and is now sourced: the literature auditor supplied Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2021 (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511), whose 162-scenario simulation substantially overlaps the grid the source proposed building, Phillippo et al. 2018 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) for the stronger unanchored assumptions and for the fact that the ESS such guidance would be stated in is itself a biased approximation, and Serret-Larmande et al. 2025 (arxiv:2507.12241) for a simulation already indexed on positivity-violation severity.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict left unchanged

verdict left unchanged Later work reports progress, but on the chronology review the second reviewer judged it ‘no’ at high confidence: The handbook supplies useful IPD meta-analysis simulation planning methods and software, including for interactions, but it does not plan for the defining information losses and assumptions of PAIC. It therefore does not provide the requested standardized PAIC planning framework or tool.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. PubMed searches for sample-size, power or information planning tied to MAIC, PAIC and external-control weighting returned nothing; I found no planning framework, so the entry’s central claim stands and the problem is open. Because the entry is source_unsourced I supply sources below. Two caveats. First, the entry’s own instrument undermines it: Phillippo et al. 2018 state the standard ESS ‘is likely to be an underestimation of the true ESS’ because the weights are estimated and correlated with the outcome, so planning guidance ‘stated in effective sample size’ inherits a known-biased quantity, which the entry does not acknowledge. Second, ‘no framework for planning a PAIC simulation’ is narrower than stated: Remiro-Azocar et al. 2021 already provide a 162-scenario survival-outcome simulation design varying covariate overlap, imbalance and sample size, which is the de facto template the field uses. It is not a planning framework in information terms, but it is not nothing, and the entry’s proposed grid overlaps with it substantially. The harsher-grid-for-unanchored claim is well supported by the assumption hierarchy in Phillippo et al. Cites doi:10.1002/jrsm.1511: Sources the claim that effective sample size, not nominal size, governs precision in weighting-based PAIC, and supplies the existing 162-scenario survival simulation grid the entry proposes to build.. Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740: Sources the harsher-requirements-for-unanchored claim: unanchored comparisons assume conditional constancy of absolute effects and require all prognostic variables as well as all effect modifiers.. Cites arXiv:2507.12241: A recent simulation study explicitly designed around positivity violation severity, supporting the entry’s proposal to index design grids on overlap severity rather than nominal n..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C2 is too absolute: nominal n remains an important information determinant, but it is insufficient by itself. C3 is directionally correct, yet Kish ESS is not an exact information measure for estimated weights, heterogeneous outcomes, treatment contrasts, or survival estimators. Precision is governed by the estimator’s influence function or information matrix, including arm allocation, outcome variance, nuisance-parameter estimation, weighted events, and risk-set composition. C4 faithfully describes the report’s refusal to impose a universal threshold, which is appropriate. C5 is sound because patient counts alone are inadequate for survival designs, although total events and censoring fractions are also insufficient without timing, allocation, risk sets, and censoring mechanisms. C6 correctly recognizes the stronger identification burden of unanchored comparisons, but omitted prognostic structure creates structural bias that a larger sample does not cure; simulations need broader misspecification and confounding scenarios, not necessarily merely larger n values. The logical step from no universal threshold to no planning framework is false. Design-specific planning can posit source and target distributions, derive anticipated weights, and use influence-function calculations or simulation. What remains open is standardized PAIC-specific guidance and software, not the possibility of information-based planning itself. This is primarily a design-roadmap gap rather than a universal validity defect in completed analyses.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: No prospectively blinded calibration program for PAIC and QBA
text:
Statement
The strongest empirical calibration of an unanchored external-control comparison to date is Gupta et al. 2025 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.2152), which replaced the randomized control arms of 14 oncology trials with external control arms built from a nationwide cancer-center network and benchmarked 15 emulated comparisons against the trials’ own randomized results: mean log hazard ratio discrepancy 0.247 unadjusted, 0.139 after adjustment for measured confounders and 0.098 after external adjustment for simulated unmeasured and mismeasured confounders, with per-trial values from -0.229 to 1.205. The bias analysis was prespecified, but the randomized answers were not concealed from the analysts; the trials are named with their published hazard ratios, so this is retrospective benchmarking rather than hidden-truth calibration. No prospectively concealed, analyst-blinded, multi-disease calibration program exists, and concealment is not the only known-truth design, since simulation, open randomized emulation, validation samples and bridge-deletion exercises each quantify specified components of error.

title: No prospectively blinded calibration program for PAIC and QBA
text:
Why it is open
Residual bias is unobservable in the analysis dataset by construction, so calibration requires settings where a randomized answer exists to compare against, and the individual patient data needed are controlled by sponsors rather than available for an independent benchmark. The one substantial exercise is confined to a single disease area and outcome under unusually favorable conditions, verbatim high adherence, few losses to follow-up and no competing events, so it cannot say how QBA behaves under competing events, poor adherence, heavy loss to follow-up or sparse aggregate data. A benchmark discrepancy is a single aggregate number folding every mechanism together, so it can inform a residual-bias distribution only after sampling error, estimand mismatch and outcome-definition differences are separated out, and whether a calibration obtained in one indication, data source and era transports to the submission at hand is itself unverifiable. Retrospective benchmarking also leaves room for analyst adaptation that prospective concealment would remove.

title: No prospectively blinded calibration program for PAIC and QBA
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Gupta et al. 2025, JAMA Network Open
Retrospective benchmarking study: combines experimental arms from 14 randomized oncology trials with external control arms from a nationwide cancer-center network and compares 15 emulated estimates with the original randomized results before and after prespecified QBA. It did not conceal or blind the randomized control arms.

title: No prospectively blinded calibration program for PAIC and QBA
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Extend retrospective randomized-benchmark emulation of the Gupta kind across disease areas, outcomes, data sources and bias mechanisms, and add prospective designs in which the randomized answer is withheld from the analyst so adaptation is removed rather than assumed away, alongside bridge deletion and IPD masking. Publish the exercises as a shared benchmark so competing QBA methods are compared on the same tasks, and pair each calibration with an explicit statement of the setting to which it is claimed to transport. Use the observed discrepancy distributions as priors or stress-test ranges only after random error and estimand mismatch have been separated from systematic discrepancy.

title: No prospectively blinded calibration program for PAIC and QBA
text:
Verification

Verdict. Overstated. 2 independent auditors judged the claim as stated too strong. The strongest such exercise to date replaced the randomized control arms of 14 oncology RCTs with external control arms and benchmarked 15 emulated comparisons against the trials’ own randomized results, with the bias analysis prespecified; no prospectively concealed-truth or analyst-blinded calibration programme exists.
The source titled this. “Empirical calibration of PAIC and QBA against hidden randomized truth” The title asserts calibration against hidden randomized truth, but the audit found the cited study never concealed or blinded the randomized answers from analysts.
The source said. “The only way to measure residual bias in an unanchored comparison is to construct settings where a randomized answer exists but is concealed; the strongest such exercise to date hid the control arms of 14 oncology RCTs and emulated 15 comparisons. No standing programme of hidden-truth calibration, bridge deletion, IPD masking or prospective external-control validation exists, so QBA parameter distributions are elicited with no empirical anchor.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors rejected the hidden-truth framing: Gupta et al. 2025 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.2152) nowhere conceals or blinds the randomized control arms, and describes itself as combining experimental arms from 14 randomized trials with external control arms and then comparing against the original randomized estimates. Its numbers are exact as the entry reported them, but the design property the entry’s premise rested on is not one the study had, and GPT-5.6 Sol added that concealment reduces analyst adaptation without being mathematically required for calibration.

Literature and prior-art check

open / overstated. Retrieved the Gupta et al. 2025 full text (PMID 40136297, PMC11947839). Every number matches exactly: ‘we obtained individual-level patient data from 15 experimental arms in 14 randomized trials’; mean log HR difference 0.247 unadjusted, 0.139 adjusted for measured confounders, 0.098 with external adjustment; Table 3 shows per-trial values from -0.229 to 1.205, confirming material variation; and the setting is verbatim ‘high adherence to the assigned interventions, few losses to follow-up, and no competing events’. The overstatement is the word ‘hid’ and the framing ‘hidden randomized truth’. Nowhere does the paper describe concealing or blinding the randomized control arms from the analysts; the trials are named in Table 1 with their published HRs, and the design is a benchmarking target-trial emulation in which the randomized control arm is replaced by an ECA and then used as the comparison benchmark. The QBA was prespecified, which is not the same as the truth being withheld. The problem’s entire premise (a hidden-truth calibration programme) rests on a design property the cited exercise did not have.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C2-C7 agree with the study details recorded in the repository, but C1 incorrectly calls the Gupta exercise hidden. It was retrospective benchmarking: experimental arms were combined with external controls and compared with the original randomized estimates. The randomized answers were not prospectively concealed or analyst-blinded. More fundamentally, randomized concealed truth is not the only known-truth design. Simulation, openly benchmarked randomized emulations, validation samples, and bridge-deletion exercises can quantify specified components of error, although randomized benchmarks are especially valuable for total causal discrepancy. A collection of benchmark discrepancies can inform a residual-bias distribution only after separating sampling error, estimand mismatch, and outcome-definition differences; it does not identify a transportable bias distribution automatically. Concealment reduces analyst adaptation but is not mathematically required for calibration. The multi-indication standing benchmark remains open and is valuable infrastructure, but it is a roadmap item rather than the only possible validation route. Claims of complete absence in C8 and C13 were not adjudicated as literature-coverage claims.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R8:overstated-majority(n=2)

title: Generic unmeasured confounding collapses distinct bias mechanisms
text:
Statement
The report sets out eleven bias targets for unanchored PAIC and argues they must not be collapsed into one generic unmeasured confounder. The flagship distinction survives scrutiny and now has a source the entry did not cite: Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) state that their sensitivity analysis relies on the important covariates being measured in the company’s own trial and that a covariate unmeasured in both studies would limit what it could achieve, which is exactly the difference between a covariate unreported in the target aggregate data and one absent from the source IPD. The auditors split on how far the taxonomy carries and both brought evidence: the literature auditor judged the distinction supported, while GPT-5.6 Sol held that the categories are neither mutually exclusive nor guaranteed to require different data or causal diagrams, that a binary latent U is a defensible composite net-bias device when labeled as one and misleading only when read as a literal correction for a specific mechanism, and that proxy, negative-control, validation-data and proximal approaches belong alongside the three families the entry names for the unmeasured-in-both case.

title: Generic unmeasured confounding collapses distinct bias mechanisms
text:
Why it is open
When a variable is absent from the source data entirely, its prevalence, outcome association, treatment interaction and correlation with measured covariates must all come from external evidence and none can be checked against the analysis dataset, because an optimizer cannot balance a variable that does not exist. Threats such as differential outcome ascertainment, treatment version or calendar-era care need data (validation substudies, visit-process information, protocol details) and parameters (prevalence, sensitivity and specificity, lag distributions) that a single latent binary confounder does not carry, so a composite device gives the wrong sign and magnitude when it is read as a literal correction. No PAIC tool asks the analyst to declare which mechanism is being modeled: cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) implements a mechanism-specific diagnostic for one of the eleven targets, cross-subnetwork component drift, but nothing combines omitted-variable, selection, measurement, ascertainment and bridge mechanisms, so a balanced-covariate table is still presented as evidence of adjustment for threats it never touched.

title: Generic unmeasured confounding collapses distinct bias mechanisms
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Soutar et al. 2025, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Bayesian data augmentation with a latent variable for subject-level indirect comparisons, imputing an unmeasured confounder under user-specified associations.


Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
States that the proposed QBA relies on the important covariates being measured in the company’s own trial, and that covariates unmeasured in both studies would limit what the sensitivity analysis could achieve. The paper’s own admission that its method covers only the unreported-in-target case.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Implements bridge_fragility(), a mechanism-specific sensitivity diagnostic for one listed target, cross-subnetwork component drift, rather than reducing every threat to a generic latent U. It does not combine omitted-variable, selection, measurement, ascertainment and bridge mechanisms.

title: Generic unmeasured confounding collapses distinct bias mechanisms
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Require analysts to name the specific bias mechanism and its causal diagram, then select matching sensitivity parameters and an analysis family, declaring whether each sensitivity variable is unreported in the target aggregate data, unmeasured in the source IPD, measured with error, or a proxy for design and care differences, while acknowledging that these categories overlap and that a composite latent variable is legitimate when presented as a net-bias device. Build on the mechanism-specific pattern cpaic already demonstrates for bridge drift and extend tooling to support several mechanisms at once rather than only a latent binary confounder. Route the unmeasured-in-both case to bias-function analysis, latent-U data augmentation or partial identification, and consider proxy, negative-control, validation-data and proximal approaches where their additional assumptions are defensible.

title: Generic unmeasured confounding collapses distinct bias mechanisms
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from unverifiable to partially-addressed, on a single finding.
The source said. “The report sets out eleven distinct bias targets for unanchored PAIC, each with its own manifestation, sensitivity parameters and analysis family, and argues they must not be collapsed into one generic unmeasured confounder. The flagship distinction is between a covariate measured in the source IPD but unreported in the target aggregate data and a variable unmeasured in both sources, which no weighting or regression adjustment can address.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed the claim that each mechanism needs its own data and diagram and that a binary latent U is inherently misleading: selection bias can be written as a latent-variable or potential-outcome shift, measurement, ascertainment and missingness can share one observation model, and a composite U is only misleading when read literally. The claim that applied analysts frequently ignore the distinction is an empirical assertion about practice that neither auditor could verify. The flagship distinction itself is now sourced to Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13).
Dissent. codex dissented (supported-with-caveat): The central distinction is correct. A variable measured in source IPD but absent from target summaries can be handled by sensitivity analysis over target moments; a variable absent from source IPD cannot be balanced directly by MAIC. Its association and dependence structure are not nonparametrically identified from the primary data. The eleven-item list is internally accurate. The caveat is that the categories are neither mutually exclusive nor guaranteed to require entirely different data or DAGs: selection bias can be represented through a latent-variable or potential-outcome-shift parameterization, and measurement, ascertainment, and missingness mechanisms may share a joint observation model. A binary latent U is not inherently misleading when explicitly presented as a composite net-bias device; it becomes misleading when interpreted as a literal correction for a specific measurement or care-process mechanism. C9’s three families are reasonable but not exhaustive, since proxy, negative-control, validation-data, and proximal approaches may also apply under additional assumptions. C10 is an unsupported empirical-frequency claim. cpaic 9d150e9 partly addresses the taxonomy through a mechanism-specific bridge_fragility() diagnostic for component-bridge drift, but it does not combine omitted-variable, selection, measurement, ascertainment, and bridge mechanisms.

title: Measurement and misclassification QBA under population adjustment
text:
Statement
Biomarker assays, severity scales, response definitions, cut-points and eligibility criteria can differ between the IPD source and the comparator study, and the matching parameters are mechanism-specific: sensitivity and specificity for binary misclassification, calibration slope and intercept and error variance for continuous proxies, and differential terms only where the error differs by study, treatment or outcome. Nourredine et al. 2025 (doi:10.1002/sim.70236) show what is at stake in an unweighted unanchored external-control design, where sensitivity and specificity of 0.9 still left roughly 67% relative bias and 79.6% interval coverage while a validation-informed likelihood held bias near zero at about 95.5% coverage with wider intervals. A joint latent measurement, outcome, target-distribution and weighting model can be written down in principle, so the gap is the absence of a validated PAIC-specific implementation and of the validation data that would inform it, not the absence of any joint form.

title: Measurement and misclassification QBA under population adjustment
text:
Why it is open
Each study reports its own measured version of the construct and nothing in either dataset identifies the mapping between them, so the error model must come from validation data, external evidence or explicit priors, and any validation-based model carries its own transport assumption into both studies. Misclassification correction modifies the outcome likelihood while MAIC modifies the estimating equation through weights, and no validated implementation combines them; a mismeasured covariate is often also a balancing variable, so the error propagates into the weights as well as the outcome model. Eligibility measurement differences change who is compared while outcome measurement differences change what counts as an event, so the corrections interact wherever the mechanisms co-occur. Internal validation substudies are rarely embedded in sponsor IPD and essentially never exist for a published aggregate comparator, so the most informative parameter source is unavailable exactly where it is needed.

title: Measurement and misclassification QBA under population adjustment
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Nourredine et al. 2025, Statistics in Medicine
Likelihood correction and validation-informed likelihood for misclassified binary outcomes in unanchored external-control comparisons; targets a conditional indirect effect in an unweighted design with no MAIC, propensity weighting or matching.


Gray et al. 2024, Pharmacoepidemiology and Drug Safety
Separately considers a missing confounder, misclassification of exposure and outcome evaluation in external-control studies. Three one-at-a-time scenarios rather than a joint multiple-bias analysis, and disconnected from any population-adjustment step.

title: Measurement and misclassification QBA under population adjustment
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Implement and validate the joint model that is already available on paper, specifying true and observed covariates, eligibility and outcomes together so that validation-study uncertainty propagates into the weights, the target moments and the estimate simultaneously, rather than running measurement correction as a disconnected supplement. Where no validation data exist, define the error model by explicit priors or bounds and report the increase in uncertainty that correction brings rather than only the point correction. Plan validation substudies prospectively in trials and external-control studies, and correct mechanisms jointly where they co-occur or interact rather than as an unconditional rule.

title: Measurement and misclassification QBA under population adjustment
text:
Our study

A misclassified covariate that is both balanced and a modifier
The question put to it. When a binary effect modifier is misclassified in the source, the target or both, which corrections does population adjustment need, and is correcting the outcome model alone enough?
What it found. No. MAIC on a misclassified binary modifier was biased even with identical assays in both studies (-0.03 to -0.13 on the log odds ratio scale), because reweighting recorded categories leaves each category’s true composition at the source’s; correcting the target prevalence alone did not help. Correcting only STC’s outcome model left bias of -0.012 to -0.051. Fully corrected STC and MAIC with weights chosen on the latent prevalence were unbiased (within 0.006).
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: outcome-only correction biased beyond 3 MCSE and 0.03 in some scenarios (to -0.051).
MAIC on the recorded covariate with identical assays: bias beyond 3 MCSE in 4 of 4 scenarios.
Latent-prevalence MAIC and fully corrected STC: bias -0.006 to 0.006.

Design.

Estimand

Marginal log odds ratio, A versus C, in the target’s true covariate law

Methods compared

MAIC on the recorded covariate, MAIC with prevalence correction, MAIC with latent-prevalence weights, STC on the recorded covariate, STC with the outcome model corrected, fully corrected STC

Data-generating mechanism

Anchored transport with a misclassified binary modifier under four assay scenarios and two modification strengths; naive, prevalence-corrected and latent-weight MAIC; naive, outcome-only corrected and fully corrected latent-class STC. 8 cells, 1000 replicates each.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 8,000 in total


What this does not answer. Known assay parameters; one binary covariate; no interval assessment. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Measurement and misclassification QBA under population adjustment
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed, on a single finding.
The source said. “Biomarker assays, severity scales, response definitions, cut-points and eligibility criteria can differ between the IPD source and the comparator study, requiring sensitivity, specificity, calibration slope and intercept and differential-error parameters inside a measurement-error likelihood. Existing demonstrations sit in unweighted external-control designs and run as disconnected supplementary analyses, so no joint form exists for measurement correction and population adjustment, and the internal validation data that would supply the parameters are almost never available.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed three things: the entry required every listed error parameter for every setting, asserted that no joint form of measurement correction and population adjustment exists when one is mathematically available and merely unimplemented, and stated that joint measurement QBA requires validation studies when explicit priors or bounds can also define a sensitivity analysis. It also rejected the entry’s universal ranking of internal validation data above external sources, since a small or selected internal sample with a poor reference standard can be weaker than a well-matched external one. The literature auditor corrected the description of Gray et al. 2024 (doi:10.1002/pds.5796), whose three illustrated biases are missing confounder, misclassification of exposure and outcome evaluation, run one at a time rather than as a joint multiple-bias analysis.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): Measurement non-equivalence is a genuine threat, but C1 wrongly requires every listed parameter. Binary misclassification uses sensitivity and specificity; continuous proxies typically use calibration parameters and error variance; differential-error parameters are needed only when error differs by study, treatment, or outcome. C2 is broadly right after adding structural assumptions as an alternative information source. C3-C6 are technically coherent for binary-outcome misclassification. C7-C8 overstate a universal evidence hierarchy: an internal validation sample is often highly relevant but can be too small, selected, or use a poor reference standard, while a well-matched external validation study can be stronger. C9 misuses multiple-bias analysis; separately running three one-at-a-time scenarios is not a joint multiple-bias analysis. Joint correction is preferable when mechanisms co-occur or interact, not an unconditional requirement. C12 is false because QBA can proceed using explicit priors or bounds without a validation study, although validation data improve identification. A coherent joint latent measurement and outcome model is mathematically available in principle, so the defensible gap is lack of a validated PAIC-specific implementation, not absence of any joint form. At cpaic 9d150e9, NAMESPACE exposes no measurement-error, misclassification, or validation-substudy interface, so that package does not close the implementation gap. Broader no-method claims were not assessed beyond cpaic.

title: Index-date, immortal time and delayed entry in external comparators
text: QBA-08 Partially addressed High priority Promising

title: Index-date, immortal time and delayed entry in external comparators
text:
Statement
When trial and external-comparator eligibility or time zero are causally misaligned, or when cohort classification depends on future survival, index-date error, immortal time and informative left truncation can bias a survival contrast; differing rules alone do not, and delayed entry handled with correct risk sets under conditionally independent truncation is left truncation rather than bias. The alignment half of the problem now has a published method the entry does not cite: Le Coent et al. (arXiv:2509.14183) impute comparable index dates for external controls under delayed treatment initiation with a truncation-aware scheme, combine it with propensity-score weighting or matching rather than leaving alignment as a separate step, and validate it against a randomized benchmark. What remains open is the sensitivity layer: no method indexes the residual time-origin error by a lag or lead distribution and propagates that uncertainty into the transported contrast jointly with the censoring and confounding parameters.

title: Index-date, immortal time and delayed entry in external comparators
text:
Why it is open
An external data source usually has no protocol-defined randomization moment, so time zero must be reconstructed from routine records and the reconstruction error is unobservable; the index-date definition is often unrecoverable from the aggregate publication, so the analyst cannot verify whether a time-origin mismatch exists at all. Alignment methods reduce the misalignment but do not measure the residual error, and the induced bias depends on the joint distribution of that error and the hazard, so it cannot be summarized by a single confounding parameter. It may act in the opposite direction to informative censoring, so it cannot be signed a priori and a one-at-a-time analysis cannot reveal the cancellation.

title: Index-date, immortal time and delayed entry in external comparators
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Gray et al. 2024, Pharmacoepidemiology and Drug Safety
Demonstrates external-control bias scenarios including misclassification of exposure (line of therapy), which misspecifies the index date and survival time. The entry’s description of this as index-date error is loose but defensible.


Le Coent, Rosner, Wang and Hu, Index Date Imputation for Survival Analysis in Externally Controlled Trials with Delayed Treatment Initiation (2025)
Truncation-aware imputation of comparable index dates for external controls under delayed treatment initiation, explicitly combined with propensity-score weighting or matching and benchmarked against a randomized trial. Covers the alignment half; supplies no residual-error sensitivity parameters and does not propagate time-origin uncertainty into the transported contrast.

title: Index-date, immortal time and delayed entry in external comparators
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Define the time origin from an explicit target-trial specification and use the published index-date imputation route where delayed treatment initiation applies, then model the residual misalignment as a sensitivity parameter and propagate its survival impact into the transported contrast. Choose the parameterization the mechanism warrants, whether a continuous lag or lead distribution, a classification error, or a single joint latent-time, entry and event model, rather than requiring a fixed trio of parameters or a separate model per mechanism. Analyze it together with the censoring and confounding parameters because the directions can oppose one another.

title: Index-date, immortal time and delayed entry in external comparators
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “Different eligibility and index-date rules between a trial and an external comparator induce index-date, immortal-time and delayed-entry bias, requiring misclassification-rate, lag or lead distribution and survival-association sensitivity parameters alongside target-trial time-zero emulation.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors found the entry’s premise that population adjustment cannot correct a misaligned time origin, and that time-zero emulation is the only route, materially narrowed by Le Coent et al. (arXiv:2509.14183), which combines truncation-aware index-date imputation with propensity-score weighting or matching. GPT-5.6 Sol also rejected the prescription that index-date QBA requires a misclassification rate, a lag or lead distribution and a survival-association parameter, since continuous index-date error has no misclassification rate and one joint latent-time, entry and event model can cover several mechanisms at once.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 holds only when differing rules misalign causal time zero or condition classification on future survival; different rules alone do not induce bias. Immortal time requires future-survival-dependent classification. Delayed entry is left truncation and is not itself bias when risk sets handle it correctly and truncation is conditionally independent. C2 is too prescriptive: continuous index-date error need not have a misclassification rate, and the three listed parameters are neither necessary nor a canonical minimal set. One joint latent-time, entry, and event model can cover several mechanisms, contrary to C4’s requirement for separate models. Target-trial emulation plus residual-error sensitivity is appropriate, and opposing directions relative to censoring are possible. Index-date imputation now addresses part of the alignment problem, while residual-misalignment QBA remains open.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. Retrieved Le Coent, Rosner, Wang and Hu, ‘Index Date Imputation for Survival Analysis in Externally Controlled Trials with Delayed Treatment Initiation’ (arXiv 2509.14183, Sept 2025, revised June 2026), which the entry does not cite. It targets exactly the mechanism in claims 1 and 4: single-arm follow-up indexed at treatment initiation versus external controls indexed at diagnosis or relapse, inducing immortal time bias and distorted risk sets. It proposes a truncation-aware imputation of comparable index dates for external controls, explicitly integrates that with propensity score weighting or matching rather than leaving it as a separate step, and validates against a randomized benchmark by inducing index-date misalignment in an oncology trial. That materially narrows the entry’s claim that population adjustment ‘cannot correct a misaligned time origin’ and that time-zero emulation is the only route. What remains open is the QBA layer proper: IDI does not index the residual index-date error by lag or lead distribution sensitivity parameters, does not propagate that uncertainty into the transported contrast, (claims 2, 3, 5 stand). Gray et al. 2024 models ‘misclassification of exposure’ (line of therapy) affecting index date and survival time, so the citation is defensible but should be worded that way. Covers the alignment half of the problem; not the sensitivity-parameter half..

title: Target population and joint-distribution uncertainty
text: QBA-10 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Target population and joint-distribution uncertainty
text:
Statement
Aggregate publications report marginal means or proportions, so analysts copy correlations from the IPD source into a single reconstructed target population and treat it as known; Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) do exactly that, taking the marginals from the comparator publication and the correlation structure from their own trial. Published marginal summaries identify a target-standardized effect only when they determine the expectations of every basis function the outcome model uses, which nonlinearity generally defeats; the converse does not hold, since under an identity-link model with a treatment-by-U interaction the target mean of U can suffice despite effect modification, and correlation is irrelevant to a purely additive linear expectation. The target is also commonly the comparator-study population by data availability rather than the reimbursement-relevant population, and Chandler and Ishak (arXiv:2602.17041) show that pairwise PAIC identifies an effect defined in the comparator population, so applying it elsewhere is an additional transport step; because marginal effects are population-dependent on non-collapsible scales, this is not a labeling issue.

title: Target population and joint-distribution uncertainty
text:
Why it is open
Published marginals generally do not identify the target joint distribution, yet the copula and higher moments enter the weights and the standardized arm outcomes, so a step currently treated as data processing is in fact unquantified modeling. Fixing one synthetic population hides that error layer inside what looks like a data-driven target, and nothing in the output records which features of the assumed target law the estimand actually depends on. Producing QBA in the decision-relevant population would require target moments that are usually unavailable, so the bias analysis answers a question about a population no decision maker asked about, and on non-collapsible scales the estimand genuinely changes with the population rather than being relabeled.

title: Target population and joint-distribution uncertainty
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Documents the practice the entry describes: a NORTA construction taking marginals from the comparator publication and the correlation structure from the IPD trial, with the resulting estimand flagged as the marginal treatment effect in the comparator trial population rather than in the RCT population.


Chandler and Ishak 2026, Reframing Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons as a Transportability Problem: An Estimand-Based Perspective and Implications for Health Technology Assessment
Shows that pairwise PAIC approaches typically identify effects defined in the comparator population and that applying these estimates to other populations entails an additional, often implicit, transport step requiring further assumptions. Formalizes the target-population point rather than resolving the joint-distribution problem.

title: Target population and joint-distribution uncertainty
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Replace the single reconstructed target with a set of jointly compatible target laws and run the QBA over the features that materially affect the estimand, rather than mechanically varying every mean, variance, correlation, copula family and higher moment. Disclose the assumed target law explicitly, characterize when the reported summaries are sufficient for the required target expectations and when they are not, and bound or vary the unidentified features in the insufficient case. Require explicit source and target notation for the sensitivity analysis as well as the primary analysis, report results in several explicitly named targets including the decision-relevant population, and use robust standardization where the target law is only partially known.

title: Target population and joint-distribution uncertainty
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 2 findings from 2 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “Aggregate publications report only marginal means or proportions, so analysts copy correlations from the IPD source into a single reconstructed target population and then treat it as known, although the copula family, tail dependence and higher moments are not identified by published marginals. The target is also commonly the comparator-study population by data availability rather than the reimbursement-relevant population, and both the primary analysis and its sensitivity layer inherit that default.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol found the entry’s sufficiency condition stated backwards: target means fail when they do not determine the outcome model’s relevant expectations, not automatically whenever the outcome is nonlinear, the omitted variable interacts with treatment or it correlates with measured covariates. The claim that a joint distribution is unidentified by aggregate data was narrowed to marginal summaries, since sufficiently detailed joint tables or cross-moments can identify dependence features, and a sensitivity analysis should vary jointly compatible target laws in the features that affect the estimand rather than mechanically vary every listed quantity. The entry cited nothing; the literature auditor supplied Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) for current practice and Chandler and Ishak (arXiv:2602.17041) for the target-population point.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Claims 1 to 3 and 6 to 8 are well supported by retrieved literature the entry cites nothing for. Ren et al. 2025 confirms current practice exactly: their NORTA construction takes ‘the marginal distribution of O_i … based on the reported mean for O_j from Study A’ but ‘the correlation structure from Study B’, i.e. correlations are copied from the IPD source into the reconstructed target and then treated as known, and they flag that the resulting estimand is ‘the marginal treatment effect in the comparator trial population, which is different from the marginal treatment effect in the RCT population’. Claim 8 is independently and strongly supported by Chandler and Ishak (arXiv 2602.17041), which shows ‘pairwise PAIC approaches typically identify effects defined in the comparator population and that applying these estimates to other populations entails an additional, often implicit, transport step requiring further assumptions’, and that marginal effects on non-collapsible scales are population-dependent so the labelling is not cosmetic. Claim 4 (QBA should range over copula families and higher moments) is a normative proposal and I found no published PAIC implementation of distributional-uncertainty-set or copula sensitivity, so the problem is open.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).
