Claim 8 is independently and strongly supported by Chandler and Ishak (arXiv 2602.17041), which shows ‘pairwise PAIC approaches typically identify effects defined in the comparator population and that applying these estimates to other populations entails an additional, often implicit, transport step requiring further assumptions’, and that marginal effects on non-collapsible scales are population-dependent so the labelling is not cosmetic. Claim 4 (QBA should range over copula families and higher moments) is a normative proposal and I found no published PAIC implementation of distributional-uncertainty-set or copula sensitivity, so the problem is open. Cites arxiv:2602.17041: Does not solve the problem; formalizes and therefore strengthens claims 7 and 8 with a real citable source, showing the comparator-study population is the identified target and that transporting elsewhere is an extra assumption..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. Let m_a(x)=E(Y^a|X=x). The target mean is E_F[m_a(X)], and published moments identify it only when they identify the expectations of every relevant basis function in m_a. Nonlinearity generally defeats mean-only reconstruction, but C1’s converse is false: under an identity-link model with interaction gammaAU, E(Y1-Y0)=beta_A+gamma*E(U), so the target mean can suffice despite effect modification. Correlation is also irrelevant to a purely additive linear expectation. C3 should refer to marginal summaries, not aggregate data generally, because sufficiently detailed joint tables or cross-moments can identify dependence features. C2 and C8 are correct. Distributional uncertainty sets and copula sensitivity are reasonable options, but C4-C5 should vary compatible target laws and only features affecting the estimand, not mechanically vary every listed quantity. C6-C7 are practice generalizations rather than mathematical universals. The underlying partial-identification problem remains open.

Does the later work answer the earlier work? title: Treatment version, care context and subsequent-therapy drift
text: QBA-12 Confirmed open High priority Emerging

title: Treatment version, care context and subsequent-therapy drift
text:
Statement
Differences in dose, backbone therapy, rescue and subsequent therapy, treatment switching, monitoring intensity and calendar era between the compared studies are a real threat, because with one nominal treatment per study baseline patient balancing cannot separate a study-level implementation shift from the treatment effect and cannot standardize post-baseline therapy. Whether they constitute bias at all depends on the estimand: these differences may define different treatment versions, and post-progression therapy and switching may belong to a treatment-policy estimand rather than being bias in a common treatment effect. Study-level or era-level treatment-shift parameters, hierarchical drift models and commensurate priors can encode assumptions where replicated studies supply the structure, but none is universally required and none identifies perfectly confounded drift on its own; g-methods, intercurrent-event estimands and partial identification are alternatives. The same drift arises in the comparator arm of a connected network, not only in an unanchored comparison: where the care actually delivered under a nominally common control differs across trials, in supervision intensity, monitoring schedule or co-delivered attention, the anchor stops canceling study-level effects, and the analyst’s only options are to keep a contaminated anchor or to discard the comparator arm and accept every unmeasured prognostic difference in an unanchored analysis. No estimator occupies the middle by modeling the control-arm discrepancy explicitly, for instance through a study-level care-intensity or control-response parameter, and no diagnostic states how contaminated an anchor must be before dropping it is the better trade.

title: Treatment version, care context and subsequent-therapy drift
text:
Why it is open
In an unanchored comparison the treatment and the study are the same unit, so any difference in how the treatment was delivered is indistinguishable from a treatment effect, and covariate balancing cannot address drift that is a property of the protocol and care pathway rather than of patients. Switching and subsequent-therapy differences act after baseline, so they operate through a post-randomization pathway that baseline balancing cannot touch, and they change which estimand the comparison targets, because a treatment-policy survival estimate under one set of rescue options is not comparable to one under another. Encoding drift requires study-level design covariates and subsequent-therapy patterns that are seldom extracted, usually only narratively described in the comparator publication and never balanced, and no published PAIC method implements the hierarchical or commensurate structures that would let those assumptions be varied.

title: Treatment version, care context and subsequent-therapy drift
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (the peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18)
States that unanchored comparisons make much stronger assumptions, widely regarded as infeasible, and that the accuracy of an unanchored estimate is unknown because residual bias from unobserved factors cannot be quantified. Supports the structural claims but implements none of the drift parameterizations the entry proposes.


Cooper, Kilvert, Hodgkins, Roskell and Eldar-Lissai 2019, CNS Drugs
A worked case of care-context drift inside a nominally common comparator: the pooled brexanolone trials’ placebo arm delivered 60 hours of medically supervised inpatient infusion care plus regular observation, against outpatient oral placebo elsewhere, and the placebo-arm improvement was substantially larger and faster than in the comparator trials. The response was to judge the arm unsuitable as a common comparator, discard it, and run unanchored matching-adjusted comparisons against other trials’ placebo arms, then rebuild the indirect comparison from those. Anchored and anchor-discarded results are reported side by side, with the stated conclusion that a simple network meta-analysis can give misleading results here, and with the concessions that once the placebo arm is discarded there is no common comparator, that unanchored analyses are more likely to be biased, and that only a small number of relevant characteristics were available for matching. This documents the binary choice the entry describes, keep a contaminated anchor or abandon randomization, and shows nothing measures the trade.


Achana, Cooper, Dias, Lu, Rice, Kendrick and Sutton 2013, Statistics in Medicine
Extends baseline-risk meta-regression from pairwise meta-analysis to networks, giving a study-level control-response structure that a middle-ground estimator could use to absorb comparator-arm discrepancy while retaining the randomized within-study contrast; it is the closest available machinery and has not been connected to the anchored versus unanchored decision.


Dias, Welton, Sutton and Ades 2013, Medical Decision Making (NICE DSU TSD 5)
The baseline natural history model, which synthesizes the control-arm response separately from the relative effects; the existing device for representing a comparator arm whose absolute performance differs across studies, again not linked to the decision of whether an anchor should be kept.

title: Treatment version, care context and subsequent-therapy drift
text:
Probable solution or research direction
State the target intervention and the intercurrent-event strategy first, so it is explicit whether an observed delivery difference is a different treatment version, part of a treatment-policy estimand, or a departure to be modeled. Where it is a departure, introduce study-level or era-level treatment-shift parameters and report results across a range of assumed drift magnitudes rather than assuming exact treatment-version equivalence, using hierarchical drift models or commensurate priors only where replicated studies give their identifying structure some purchase, and g-methods or partial identification otherwise. Analyze these parameters jointly with the confounding and censoring parameters rather than as disconnected scenario analyses.

title: Treatment version, care context and subsequent-therapy drift
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Differences in dose, backbone therapy, rescue and subsequent therapy, treatment switching, monitoring intensity and calendar era between the compared studies form a distinct bias target requiring study-specific or era-specific treatment-shift parameters, handled with design-bias parameters, hierarchical drift models or commensurate priors.”
What was wrong with it. The entry named one class of sensitivity parameters and analysis families as the appropriate response; GPT-5.6 Sol found that too prescriptive, since the differences may define a different treatment version or belong to a treatment-policy estimand, and hierarchical drift models and commensurate priors cannot identify drift that is perfectly confounded with study. The literature auditor could verify none of the entry’s proposals against any published PAIC method and voted unverifiable on support; the entry cited nothing, and the structural point that residual bias from unobserved factors in unanchored comparisons cannot be quantified is in Phillippo et al. 2017 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740), the peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied full-text reading.

merged-in

absorbed a proposal the reading raised separately: No middle-ground model for contaminated anchors 3 citation(s) added. The drafter disagreed with placing it here: The merge is reasonable, since a care-intensity parameter is generally not identified from the affected trials alone and so cannot be a general estimator. Two caveats should be recorded. QBA-12 as published is framed entirely around the unanchored setting, with its statement conditioned on one nominal treatment per study and its why-open opening on the treatment and the study being the same unit, so the anchored case is not covered by the entry as written and the statement addition above is required rather than optional. And QBA-12 prices the bias of keeping a contaminated anchor without pricing the bias of dropping it; the second half of the proposal, a decision rule for when discarding the anchor is the better trade, is a comparison of two bias mechanisms rather than a bias analysis of one, and it should be visible in the merged entry’s proposed direction rather than folded silently into sensitivity analysis.

Citation corrected

normalized a citation year: ‘Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2017, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (the peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18)’ -> ‘Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (the peer-reviewed account of NICE DSU TSD 18)’ 10.1177/0272989X17725740 is cited with two different years across the registry. CrossRef gives 2017 online and 2018 in print; the issue year is used throughout.

Literature and prior-art check

open / unverifiable. This entry has no prior_work and all five claims are normative or definitional. Claims 3 and 5 are logically true given the unanchored design (treatment and study are the same unit; baseline balancing cannot act on post-baseline subsequent therapy) and are consistent with NICE DSU TSD 18 and with Phillippo et al., who note that residual bias from unobserved factors in unanchored comparisons cannot be quantified. Claims 1, 2 and 4 assert that a specific class of sensitivity parameters and analysis families (study- or era-specific treatment-shift parameters, hierarchical drift models, commensurate priors) is the appropriate response; that is a proposal, not a verifiable statement about the literature, and I found no published PAIC method implementing it. Commensurate priors and hierarchical drift models are established devices in historical-borrowing and bias-adjustment literature (bias-adjusted meta-analysis, NICE DSU bias-adjustment TSDs), so the components exist even though the PAIC assembly does not. I vote unverifiable on support rather than guess.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The core concern is real but the proposed remedy is not universal. Dose, backbone, monitoring, and era may define different treatment versions rather than bias in a common treatment effect. Post-progression therapy and switching may likewise be part of a treatment-policy estimand; they become bias problems only relative to a different hypothetical or standardized strategy. With one nominal treatment per study, baseline patient adjustment cannot separate a study-level implementation shift from treatment, and it cannot standardize post-baseline therapies, supporting C3 and the conditional version of C5. C1 and C4 overstate the need for distinct shift parameters or bias models. G-methods, intercurrent-event estimands, or partial identification may be more appropriate. Hierarchical drift models and commensurate priors can encode assumptions when replicated studies provide structure, but they cannot identify perfectly confounded drift and are not automatically appropriate, contrary to C2.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Sensitivity parameters carry their own identification problem
text: QBA-14 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging

title: Sensitivity parameters carry their own identification problem
text:
Statement
Source IPD can identify the omitted variable’s outcome association in the arm it observes, but with one treatment per study the data cannot decompose that slope into a treatment-invariant prognostic component and treatment-specific modification, cannot identify the comparator-arm slope, and cannot establish that either transports to the comparator study or the decision target. A sensitivity analysis that imports such a coefficient, or a prevalence or correlation taken from an external registry or clinical study report, therefore carries a second untestable transport assumption of its own. Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) do exactly this and concede the analysis may be biased if the assumed values for the unmeasured confounders differ from those observed in the IPD study, offering expert elicitation and external-data regression as remedies whose own transport is untested.

title: Sensitivity parameters carry their own identification problem
text:
Why it is open
The observed data do not update a nonidentified bias parameter, so whether a coefficient borrowed from the source IPD or an external registry holds in the comparator study or the decision target is untestable within the analysis, and nothing in current practice flags that the sensitivity parameter has its own identification problem. Non-transportability bites hardest exactly where it matters, when the omitted variable modifies the treatment effect or proxies for care setting, and the standard shortcut of importing one source-arm prognostic coefficient into both potential outcomes quietly assumes that it does not. External sources come from different populations, eras, care pathways and measurement systems, and assessing whether a bias parameter transports would require the same unavailable joint information the QBA was meant to supply, while access to registries, clinical study reports and companion-trial IPD is often restricted.

title: Sensitivity parameters carry their own identification problem
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Fixes the outcome association of the omitted covariate from the IPD source and assumes it applies in the comparator population, conceding the result may be biased if the assumed means for the unmeasured confounders differ from the observed IPD values, and proposing elicitation and external-data regression whose transport is untested.

title: Sensitivity parameters carry their own identification problem
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Report the transport of each sensitivity parameter as an assumption rather than attempting to validate it with a diagnostic built from the same data, and state explicitly which parameters are source-estimated and which are assumed. Parameterize treatment-specific and study-specific associations for the omitted variable with explicit variable-by-treatment interaction terms and report results across a range of assumed modification instead of assuming a purely prognostic omitted variable. Treat externally sourced parameters as estimates carrying their own exchangeability assumption, widening ranges to reflect transport uncertainty or moving to partial identification rather than importing a point value.

title: Sensitivity parameters carry their own identification problem
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed, on a single finding.
The source said. “An omitted-variable outcome association estimated in the source study, or a prevalence or correlation taken from an external registry or clinical study report, is imported into the target as if it transported, so the sensitivity analysis carries a second untestable transport assumption of its own. In an unanchored design with one treatment per study the primary data also cannot separate a study effect, a prognostic effect of the omitted variable and treatment-effect modification by it.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed the identification claim: a study intercept cannot generally mimic a within-source slope for the omitted variable, so a study effect, a prognostic effect and effect modification are not all equally indistinguishable. Importing one coefficient into both potential outcomes is a valid scenario under an explicit no-effect-modification and transport assumption rather than an error, and the entry’s proposal to build transportability diagnostics for bias parameters cannot work as stated, because no diagnostic using the same primary data can test equality of an unobserved target association. The entry cited nothing; the literature auditor supplied Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13).
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 1 surviving finding from: Sensitivity analysis for an unobserved moderator in RCT-to-t. New citations: 10.1214/16-AOAS1001

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. No prior_work is given, but claims 1 to 6 are corroborated by primary sources I retrieved. Ren et al. 2025 fix the outcome association of the omitted covariate from the IPD source and simply assume it applies in the comparator population; they concede the resulting analysis ‘may be biased, particularly when the sample size is small, if the assumed mean values for the unmeasured confounders differ significantly from the observed values in the IPD study’, and their proposed remedies (expert elicitation, external-data regression prediction) are all extrapolations whose transport is untested. Claim 4 is a structural identification fact for the one-treatment-per-study layout and is correct. Claims 7 to 9 are the open part: claim 9 (‘no accepted procedure for assessing whether a bias parameter transports’) is a no-method-exists assertion; my searches found transportability diagnostics for treatment effects but none for bias parameters, so I treat claim 9 as unfalsified rather than positively verified. Note that a structurally untestable transport assumption for a nonidentified parameter cannot be resolved by any paper, so this entry should remain open indefinitely and be framed as a reporting requirement rather than a solvable estimation problem.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1, C5, C7, and C8 are correct. If U is measured and varies in source IPD, that study can estimate its arm-specific U-outcome association. With one treatment per study, the data cannot decompose that source slope into a treatment-invariant prognostic component and treatment-specific modification, identify the comparator-arm slope, or separate treatment and study main effects. C4 is therefore too broad: a study intercept cannot generally mimic a within-source U slope, so all three quantities are not equally indistinguishable. C3 is also conditional rather than mandatory; importing one coefficient is a valid sensitivity scenario under an explicit no-effect-modification and transport assumption, while treatment-specific parameters are needed to relax it. C2 and C6 depend on estimand and scale; on non-collapsible scales even a purely prognostic covariate distribution can change the marginal contrast. External sources can inform but not validate transport. C9 is a literature-exhaustiveness claim outside this lens, and no diagnostic using the same primary data can test equality of an unobserved target association. The open task is honest sensitivity or partial identification, not a diagnostic that creates identification.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Probabilistic QBA needs elicited and validated bias distributions
text: QBA-16 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging

title: Probabilistic QBA needs elicited and validated bias distributions
text:
Statement
Probabilistic QBA needs defensible probability distributions for the bias parameters, and no validated elicitation protocol exists for unanchored PAIC: Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13), having proposed probabilistic QBA as the natural extension of their deterministic method, say that how to obtain such distributions requires further research and offer only initial suggestions. Practice asks experts whether residual confounding is plausible, which produces a scalar with no mapping to any parameter the analysis needs. When bias parameters are not identified by the data their assumed joint distribution dominates the systematic-error component, although the data still determine the observed estimate and its sampling uncertainty, so the output is not simply the input distribution relabeled.

title: Probabilistic QBA needs elicited and validated bias distributions
text:
Why it is open
When bias parameters are nonidentified the likelihood does not update them, so sampling triangular or uniform distributions chosen for convenience propagates that convenience into decision claims with unwarranted apparent precision. Experts are poorly placed to reason about conditional outcome associations on a model scale and about dependence between bias parameters, and general elicitation protocols are not specialized to population-adjusted comparisons or to the non-redundant parameter set a given bias model requires. Nothing in an unanchored design can check elicited values against the data at hand, so the elicitation carries the whole analysis while remaining unvalidated, and the strongest external checks, held-out measured-variable benchmarks and randomized-benchmark emulations, exist in few indications and require a specified data-generating process before coverage can even be defined.

title: Probabilistic QBA needs elicited and validated bias distributions
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Leahy et al. 2023, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
HTA workshop recommendations on transparent sourcing of bias parameters, a-priori specification and sensitivity analysis for QBA inputs. Positions expert elicitation primarily as a way to validate or plausibility-check inputs obtained from other sources, not as the primary parameter source.


Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
Proposes probabilistic QBA as the extension of its deterministic method and states that how to obtain distributions for the marginal means of the unmeasured confounders requires further research, offering only initial suggestions. The strongest available evidence that no validated elicitation protocol exists for unanchored PAIC.

title: Probabilistic QBA needs elicited and validated bias distributions
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Develop PAIC-specific elicitation protocols that target the non-redundant parameters of the chosen bias model, separating prevalence or mean imbalance, outcome association, treatment interaction and, where they apply, measurement error and dependence, expressed on scales clinicians can reason about, and elicit the dependence structure explicitly rather than only marginals. Stress-test elicited distributions using simulation, held-out measured-variable benchmarks and external analogues, and report coverage of the resulting systematic-error and total-error intervals and the correctness of the resulting decisions under a stated data-generating process. Position elicitation as one source in an evidence hierarchy alongside validation and external data, as the Leahy workshop recommends, rather than as the default source.

title: Probabilistic QBA needs elicited and validated bias distributions
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 2 findings from 2 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “Probabilistic QBA requires defensible probability distributions for the bias parameters, but no validated elicitation protocol exists for unanchored PAIC: practice asks experts whether residual confounding is plausible, which produces a scalar with no mapping to any parameter the analysis needs, and elicited distributions have never been checked for interval coverage or decision correctness.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol corrected the claim that a probabilistic QBA output is determined by the bias distributions rather than the data: exact nonidentification means the data do not update the bias parameter, not that the data do not affect the result. The entry’s assertion that validation requires hidden randomized controls or masked IPD is too narrow, since simulation, external validation and held-out measured-variable exercises can assess calibration, and the hidden-truth framing rests on a design property the benchmark study it invokes did not have. The literature auditor also found that Leahy et al. 2023 (doi:10.1017/S0266462323002702) position elicitation primarily as a way to validate or plausibility-check inputs obtained from other sources rather than as the primary parameter source the entry implies.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 2 surviving findings from: A fully Bayesian application of the Copas selection model fo; Evidence synthesis for decision making 3: heterogeneity - su. New citations: 10.1002/sim.5494, 10.1177/0272989x13485157

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. Claim 3 is corroborated by a source asserting the absence: Ren et al. 2025, having proposed probabilistic QBA as the natural extension of their deterministic method, write ‘The area on how to obtain such distributions for the marginal means of the unmeasured confounders requires further research’, then offer only ‘initial suggestions’. That is the strongest available evidence that no validated elicitation protocol exists for unanchored PAIC. Claims 1, 2 and 7 follow. The caveat concerns how Leahy et al. 2023 is used. Retrieved its ten recommendations: elicitation is recommended in a narrower role than the entry implies, ‘Expert elicitation approaches may have a place … primarily as a means to validate or plausibility-check inputs obtained from other sources’, alongside ‘Input parameters should be identified through a systematic and transparent approach and specified a priori in a protocol or analysis plan’ and ‘Sensitivity analyses should account for uncertainty in QBA inputs’. So the workshop supports the entry’s direction but positions elicitation as a validation step rather than a primary parameter source; the citation should say so. Claim 6 (elicited distributions never validated for coverage or decision behaviour) I could not verify by search.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1 incorrectly says the output is determined by bias distributions rather than data. For an adjustment such as theta_adjusted = theta_observed - B, the data determine the observed estimate and sampling uncertainty, while the assumed joint distribution of nonidentified B determines the systematic-error component. Exact nonidentification means the data do not update B, not that the data do not affect the output. C2 and C5 are sound. C4 and C7 should be model-specific: analysts should elicit a nonredundant set of inputs and their joint distribution, but measurement error and dependence are not mandatory when absent, and prognostic and interaction effects need not be elicited twice. C3 and C6 are literature and historical-validation claims outside the permitted lens. Coverage requires a specified repeated-sampling data-generating process and true bias values. Simulation, external validation, and held-out measured-variable exercises can evaluate calibration, although none identifies the actually unmeasured bias from the same unanchored data. The report’s assertion that validation requires hidden randomized controls or masked IPD is too narrow. This is high priority when probabilistic QBA drives a decision, but protocol development is otherwise a roadmap item.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: MAIC sensitivity grids: infeasible calibration and failed fits
text: QBA-18 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging

title: MAIC sensitivity grids: infeasible calibration and failed fits
text:
Statement
With normalized nonnegative weights a matched target moment vector must lie in the convex hull of the source moment vectors, so an assumed moment for an omitted covariate outside that hull cannot be matched exactly, and finite strictly positive exponential tilting generally requires the relative interior, with boundary points needing zero weights or a limiting solution. Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13) give the applied version, restricting their published QBA to STC because a MAIC extension would suffer extreme effective-sample-size loss and might fail to produce feasible weights where overlap on the omitted covariate is limited. What software does with such a point is the open part: infeasibility, failed fits, divergent transitions and extreme weights are worked around or discarded rather than reported, and no implementation returns a feasibility region alongside the effect surface.

title: MAIC sensitivity grids: infeasible calibration and failed fits
text:
Why it is open
An assumed target moment outside the source support means the desired counterfactual cannot be reached by reweighting the observed data, which is scientifically informative, but default software behavior treats it as a numerical nuisance to be worked around, so the surviving output is a selected sample of the sensitivity region rather than the whole of it. Current implementations report one effective sample size and a point estimate, so an unsupported scenario cannot be distinguished from an inconvenient failed run and severe effective-sample-size loss goes unreported. Trimming to rescue a fit silently redefines the target as an overlap population and nothing in the output flags the switch, while ad hoc weight truncation biases estimation of the original target without defining a clean replacement estimand. There is no accepted abstention or bounding rule and no output object that presents a failure map next to the effect surface.

title: MAIC sensitivity grids: infeasible calibration and failed fits
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
States that a sensitivity analysis over the full spectrum of possible values for the omitted covariate includes cases with very limited overlap, where MAIC would suffer an extreme reduction of the effective sample size and may even fail to produce feasible weights. This is why the published QBA covers only STC.

title: MAIC sensitivity grids: infeasible calibration and failed fits
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Develop sensitivity-adjusted calibration for MAIC that returns a feasibility map alongside the effect surface, reporting effective sample size and local effective sample size, weight concentration, residual target-moment imbalance and a support measure such as distance to the support boundary or a depth statistic with its norm and scaling stated, and that distinguishes exact from approximate balance in the output. Specify abstention behavior so software flags or declines an unsupported assumed moment rather than coercing a finite answer, and supply a bound only where the additional outcome and selection assumptions needed for one are stated. Make the feasibility and convergence map a required component of the QBA object and the published report, including the fraction of the sensitivity region in which the analysis could not be computed.

title: MAIC sensitivity grids: infeasible calibration and failed fits
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 3 findings from 3 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “When an omitted covariate’s target moment is unknown, MAIC QBA varies an assumed moment vector and re-solves the calibration; assumed moments outside the convex hull of source support make exact balance infeasible, yet software either coerces a finite answer or errors out. Failed fits, infeasible calibration, divergent transitions and extreme weights are silently discarded rather than reported as results.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol qualified the convex-hull argument and narrowed two claims: an infeasible calibration means exact reweighting of the observed empirical support is impossible rather than that the target counterfactual is logically unsupported, and finite-sample support must be distinguished from optimizer failure. It also found false the claim that approximate balance changes the estimand: trimming to an explicit overlap population changes the estimand, while approximate balance generally changes the estimator and leaves residual imbalance. Returning a bound instead of a coerced answer requires additional outcome and selection assumptions rather than following automatically.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 3 surviving findings from: Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data, S; Can We Trust PAICs in Rare Diseases? Methodological Challeng; Geometric approaches to assessing the numerical feasibility . New citations: 10.1002/pst.2210, 10.1007/978-3-030-82673-4, 10.3390/jmahp14010014

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. The single citation is accurate. Ren et al. 2025 state, as the reason they present QBA only for STC, that ‘the sensitivity analysis should assess the impact of the full spectrum of possible values for U and this would include the cases where there would be very limited overlap on U between the two studies. MAIC approach would suffer an extreme reduction of the effect sample size and may even fail to produce feasible weights’, and again in the discussion that ‘an extension of the MAIC approach would lead to a large reduction of the effective sample size when the overlap in the unmeasured covariates between the studies is small’. That verifies claims 6 and 10 verbatim, and claim 1 follows from the convex-optimization structure of moment balancing. Claims 3, 4, 7, 9 are proposals for software behaviour and reporting, not literature claims. I found no published feasibility-region or support-surface framework for a MAIC sensitivity grid; the closest work assesses positivity violations by simulation rather than returning a feasibility map, so the problem stands open. Claim 5 (trimming or approximate balance changes the estimand) is a correct and uncontroversial consequence of restricting to the overlap population.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The convex-hull claim is correct with an empirical-support qualification. With normalized nonnegative weights, a target moment vector t must satisfy t = sum_i w_i z_i and therefore lie in the convex hull of the source moment vectors. Finite strictly positive exponential tilting generally requires the relative interior; boundary points may require zero weights or a limiting solution. Thus C1, C6, and C10 are sound. C2 and C8 should say that exact reweighting of the observed empirical support is unsupported, not that the target counterfactual itself is logically impossible; finite-sample support and optimizer failure must also be distinguished. C3 is right that software should flag or abstain, but a bound is not automatic and requires additional outcome and selection assumptions. C4 proposes useful diagnostics, although local ESS needs a definition, hull distance depends on scaling and norm, and ordinary outside-hull distance is zero throughout the interior, so distance to the boundary or depth is also needed. C5 is correct when trimming explicitly changes the target to an overlap population. Ad hoc weight truncation may instead bias estimation of the same target without defining a clean replacement estimand. C11 is false for approximate balance alone: approximate balance generally changes the estimator and leaves residual imbalance, but need not change the estimand. C7 and C9 are sound reporting principles when the listed diagnostics apply; divergent transitions are relevant only when a Bayesian component is fitted. Universal claims about software silently discarding failures were not established. This becomes critical when conclusions rely on infeasible or weak-overlap grid points.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Component PAIC needs joint population-and-bridge bias analysis
text: QBA-20 Confirmed open Very high priority Emerging Tractability 4/5

title: Component PAIC needs joint population-and-bridge bias analysis
text:
Statement
In a disconnected component PAIC with no cross-gap evidence, violations of population transportability and of component invariance are both unidentified and should be assessed jointly, since either can offset the other and an analysis that varies only one may report spurious robustness; population or selection bias is not necessarily nonidentified when adequate covariates and transport assumptions are available. Structural bridge bias includes component main-effect drift and component-by-modifier drift across subnetworks, treatment versions, eras or backbones, and can also include component-by-component nonadditivity and backbone interactions. Evaluating a joint sensitivity model means integrating inverse-linked perturbed predictions over the joint target distribution of measured and omitted covariates, with the corresponding marginal survival or RMST functional for time-to-event estimands, and that joint target distribution is what published aggregate data do not supply.

title: Component PAIC needs joint population-and-bridge bias analysis
text:
Why it is open
When no cross-gap evidence exists neither layer is identified, and because they can offset each other a one-at-a-time curve computed with the other layer held at its assumed null cannot reveal the cancellation. The joint parameter space is high-dimensional with correlated drift and no data to inform the correlation, so the dependence structure must be supplied entirely by assumption. The natural-scale integration a joint model requires needs a joint target distribution of measured and omitted covariates that published aggregate data do not provide, and current tooling addresses only bounded component main-effect drift, so the interaction-drift and omitted-variable layers stay unexamined.

title: Component PAIC needs joint population-and-bridge bias analysis
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ackerman et al. 2024, Measurement error and bias in real-world oncology endpoints when constructing external control arms, Frontiers in Drug Safety and Regulation
Empirical demonstration that two bias mechanisms in an external control arm interact non-additively, supporting the non-additivity premise with measurement rather than assertion. Supplied by the literature auditor; the entry cited nothing.

title: Component PAIC needs joint population-and-bridge bias analysis
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Implement a joint sensitivity model placing subnetwork-specific component main-effect drift, component-by-modifier drift, omitted modifiers, measurement bias and decision thresholds in one coherent framework, integrating inverse-linked perturbed predictions over the joint target covariate distribution and using the marginal survival or RMST functional for time-to-event estimands. Report which bias layer dominates under an explicitly stated attribution rule and whether apparent robustness comes from cancellation between the layers. Expose feasibility, effective sample size, edge influence, effect and decision-reversal surfaces and partial-identification bounds as a single object, and state which forms of drift, including component-by-component nonadditivity, the model does and does not cover.

title: Component PAIC needs joint population-and-bridge bias analysis
text:
Our study

One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis of two bias layers reports robustness that the joint analysis does not support
The question put to it. Do one-at-a-time sensitivity analyses of population transportability and component invariance bound their joint effect on a cross-gap contrast, or can the layers offset and report spurious robustness?
What it found. No. With an omitted modifier (population layer) and component drift (bridge layer) acting on one cross-gap log odds ratio of -0.20, each one-at-a-time curve stayed within 0.16 and never reversed the decision, while the joint elicited box reached a bias of -0.41 and 7% of it reversed the decision; 23% to 26% of the box lay outside the one-at-a-time envelope at every scale. Component-by-modifier drift, which current tooling excludes, moved the estimate by 0.04 alone because it acts through its product with the modifier imbalance.
Results.

Scale 1: one-at-a-time envelope -0.156 to 0.157; joint -0.413 to 0.341; 7% of the box reverses the decision.
Masking: in 4% of the box both layers exceed 0.1 in absolute value and the net bias is below 0.05.
Elicited dependence: 32% to 34% of draws outside the one-at-a-time envelope when the layers are positively correlated, 21% to 24% independent, 5% to 12% negatively correlated.

Design.

Estimand

Bias of the reported target marginal log odds ratio of the cross-gap contrast

Methods compared

one-at-a-time sensitivity curves, joint sensitivity region over both layers

Data-generating mechanism

Population-level calculation on a logistic model: omitted-modifier imbalance, component main-effect drift and component-by-modifier drift varied one at a time and jointly over elicited ranges at three scales, with independent and dependent elicitations.

Replicates

Population-level calculation: 21^3 grid and 4000 elicited draws x 3 dependence structures at 3 scales


What this does not answer. Population-level calculation on one logistic model; no sampling, component network fit or survival scale; joint covariate law known, so the cost of eliciting it is not measured; component non-additivity and backbone interactions not included. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Component PAIC needs joint population-and-bridge bias analysis
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “Component PAIC carries at least two distinct nonidentified bias layers, population or selection bias and structural bridge bias comprising component main-effect drift and component-by-modifier interaction drift across subnetworks, treatment versions, eras or backbones, and no existing method quantifies them jointly. Total bias does not decompose additively across the layers, so one-at-a-time curves cannot describe the joint surface.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol corrected the mathematics of the proposed sensitivity model: for a nonlinear link the target arm mean is the expectation of the inverse-linked perturbed predictor over the joint target distribution, so integrating the linear predictor itself is not integration on the natural outcome scale. It also narrowed the non-additivity claim to isolated one-at-a-time effects, since a telescoping additive decomposition can always be constructed with path- and order-dependent contributions and exact additivity does hold under an identity-link model without interactions. The literature auditor could find no published literature on component PAIC as a named method and voted unverifiable, so the entry’s claims that no method or framework exists are true but uninformative.

Literature and prior-art check

open / unverifiable. I could not locate any published literature on ‘component PAIC’ as a named method combining component network meta-analysis with population adjustment, nor any prior_work is offered. Component NMA itself is established (netmeta, and 2026 work on treatment and component hierarchies in CNMA including disconnected networks), and population-adjusted methods are established, but the composite object the entry calls component PAIC, with a ‘bridge’ between subnetworks and component main-effect and component-by-modifier drift, appears to be a construct of this research programme rather than a published method with a literature. That makes claims 4 and 5 (‘no existing method jointly quantifies…’, ‘no current framework combines…’) technically true but uninformative, because there is no established base method to extend. Claim 6 (total bias does not decompose additively across layers) is generically true on non-collapsible scales and is independently supported by Ackerman et al. 2024, who show two measurement mechanisms in external controls interact non-additively. Claims 3 and 7 are design proposals. I vote unverifiable on support because the central objects cannot be checked against any literature.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. The core joint-sensitivity concern is technically valid, but the statement needs conditions. C1 holds in a disconnected analysis with no cross-gap validation and unresolved transport variables; population or selection bias is not necessarily nonidentified when adequate covariates and transport assumptions are available. C2 identifies valid forms of bridge drift, but structural bridge bias can also include component-by-component nonadditivity or backbone interactions, not only main-effect and component-by-modifier drift. C3 is mathematically misstated: for a nonlinear link the target arm mean is E_T[g^{-1}{eta_t(X,U;delta)}], meaning inverse-linked perturbed predictions are integrated over the joint target distribution. Integrating the linear predictor itself is not integration on the natural outcome scale. Survival estimands require the corresponding marginal survival or RMST functional. C4 and C5 are universal method-existence claims that this audit cannot establish. C6 is correct only as a statement about a unique decomposition into isolated one-at-a-time effects. A telescoping additive decomposition can always be constructed, but its contributions are path and order dependent; exact invariant additivity can also hold under an identity-link additive model without interactions. C7 is a sound reporting objective once the attribution rule is defined. The joint problem is decision-critical for disconnected component bridges, while a comprehensive result object remains a roadmap item.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Total bias is non-additive, so one-at-a-time analyses mislead
text:
Statement
Bias mechanisms interact on nonlinear estimand scales, so total bias need not equal the sum of population, bridge and measurement bias, and a set of one-at-a-time curves cannot establish joint robustness, though surviving each curve does not prove that cancellation is what saved the estimate. This now has direct evidence in the external-control setting: Ackerman et al. 2024 (doi:10.3389/fdsfr.2024.1423493) show that misclassified progression events and irregular assessment times occurring together may generate bias greater than the sum of their parts. Joint multiple-bias machinery also already exists outside population adjustment: Brendel, Torres and Arah (doi:10.1093/ije/dyad001) adjust uncontrolled confounding, selection bias and misclassification simultaneously via imputation and regression weighting, with a CRAN implementation, so the PAIC-specific gap is composition of those bias models with the population-adjustment step rather than multiple-bias composition itself. The joint region also has no reportable form. Threshold and tipping-point machinery computes a decision-invariant region in as many dimensions as there are perturbed quantities, but no scalar summary, visualization or reporting convention exists once more than two or three data points, contrasts or bias parameters move at once; the obstruction is stated to be display and interpretation rather than derivation. Candidate low-dimensional functionals such as the minimum-norm violation vector under a stated metric, the region’s inradius, or the fraction of a prespecified plausible bias set that preserves the decision have not been proposed, evaluated or standardized, so the joint robustness statement this entry shows to be necessary is currently one that cannot be printed.

title: Total bias is non-additive, so one-at-a-time analyses mislead
text:
Why it is open
Nonlinear link functions and marginalization make the map from bias parameters to the marginal estimand non-additive, so single-parameter curves do not span the joint bias surface, and cancellation is invisible by construction because each curve is computed with the other mechanisms held at their assumed null. Sequential corrections are order-dependent when mechanisms interact, so the output of one correction is not a valid input to the next, yet sequential correction is what current practice does. A joint bias model composed with the population-adjustment step requires a dependence structure among nonidentified parameters that neither the source IPD nor the aggregate comparator can inform, so that specification lands entirely on elicitation, and computing a joint surface costs far more than one-at-a-time curves. Attribution shares inherit the nonidentification of their inputs and describe a chosen model rather than recovering an underlying quantity.

title: Total bias is non-additive, so one-at-a-time analyses mislead
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Brendel, Torres and Arah 2023, Simultaneous adjustment of uncontrolled confounding, selection bias and misclassification in multiple-bias modelling, International Journal of Epidemiology 52:1220-1230
Provides the joint, non-sequential multiple-bias machinery this entry asks for, adjusting uncontrolled confounding, selection bias and misclassification simultaneously via imputation and regression weighting as an alternative to one-bias-at-a-time adjustment. It has no population-adjustment step.


multibias R package (CRAN)
CRAN implementation of the simultaneous multiple-bias adjustment above, cited by the literature auditor as counter-evidence to the claim that no software composes several bias models jointly.


Ackerman et al. 2024, Measurement error and bias in real-world oncology endpoints when constructing external control arms, Frontiers in Drug Safety and Regulation
Measures non-additive interaction between two bias mechanisms in an external control arm, converting the entry’s non-additivity assertion into evidence.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Varies one common bound on component main-effect drift in bridge_fragility(), explicitly excluding interaction drift, and refits prior scales in prior_sensitivity(). It exports no general joint-bias QBA surface, so the entry’s request for a joint surface in this package is a roadmap feature rather than a defect.


Phillippo, Dias, Ades, Didelez and Welton 2018, Sensitivity of treatment recommendations to bias in network meta-analysis, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 181:843-867
Derives bias-adjustment thresholds and invariant regions for a network meta-analysis recommendation, and states that the obstruction in higher dimensions is not deriving them but visualizing and interpreting them. Its worked outputs are one-dimensional threshold intervals and a two-dimensional polygon, so the joint region a multi-parameter bias analysis produces has no published reporting form.


Phillippo et al. 2019, Threshold Analysis as an Alternative to GRADE for Assessing Confidence in Guideline Recommendations Based on Network Meta-analyses, Annals of Internal Medicine 170:538-546
Puts threshold analysis into guideline practice as a confidence assessment, with the nmathresh package on CRAN. What it delivers to a committee is per-datum invariant intervals, which is the one-dimensional case; it supplies no summary of a joint region over several simultaneously perturbed quantities.

title: Total bias is non-additive, so one-at-a-time analyses mislead
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Compose the existing joint multiple-bias machinery with the population-adjustment step rather than reinventing it: take simultaneous imputation and weighting adjustment for confounding, selection and misclassification and make it operate on a weighted or standardized PAIC estimator, computed from an explicitly defined ideal target trial, a decision estimand and a causal diagram for each departure. Report joint and mechanism-specific results together so reinforcement and cancellation are visible, and state the dependence assumption used, including independence where that is the intended scenario. Present order-robust or Shapley-style summaries as descriptive allocations conditional on the assumed bias model, stating the fixed parameter vector or the joint distribution they average over.

title: Total bias is non-additive, so one-at-a-time analyses mislead
text:
Our study

Do bias mechanisms in an unanchored MAIC combine additively?
This study was designed against DIA-13 and bears on this entry in part. What it does not answer is stated below.
The question put to it. When an omitted confounder, comparator outcome misclassification and covariate measurement error act together on an unanchored MAIC, is their joint bias the sum of their separate biases, and does a one-at-a-time analysis bound it?
What it found. No. An omitted confounder and misclassification of the comparator’s outcome interacted by up to 0.16 on the log odds ratio scale: with both at their largest the joint bias was about half the sum of the separate biases, and with the confounder reversed the joint bias had the opposite sign to that sum. Measurement error in a matched covariate combined nearly additively with either. The joint bias exceeded the largest single-mechanism bias in 22 of 36 combinations, so one-at-a-time analyses neither add up to nor bound it.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: median interaction 30% of the summed separate biases where two or three mechanisms acted.
Confounder by misclassification: interaction up to 0.163; other pairs at most 0.005.
Joint bias beyond the largest single-mechanism bias in 22 of 36 combinations; mechanisms partly cancelled in 16.

Design.

Estimand

Marginal log odds ratio, B versus A, in the target (unanchored)

Methods compared

unanchored MAIC limit under combinations of three bias mechanisms

Data-generating mechanism

Population-level numerical study: exact bias of the MAIC limit over 45 combinations of three mechanisms, with interaction terms by inclusion-exclusion.

Replicates

Population-level calculation, 45 combinations, exact quadrature


What this does not answer. Population-level only; no bias-analysis procedure, false reassurance or tipping sets; three mechanisms; selection and correlated parameters not varied. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Total bias is non-additive, so one-at-a-time analyses mislead
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 1 finding from 1 paper survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed, on a single finding.
The source said. “Total bias does not in general equal the sum of population, bridge and measurement bias: mechanisms interact and can cancel, so an estimate that survives every one-at-a-time sensitivity curve may be robust only by accident. A multiple-bias analysis must specify one joint bias model with preserved parameter dependence rather than independent after-the-fact corrections, and order-robust or Shapley-style attribution of total bias is description, not identification.”
What was wrong with it. The literature auditor found the claim that no software composes several bias models jointly wrong as written: the multibias package on CRAN implements simultaneous adjustment of three bias mechanisms (doi:10.1093/ije/dyad001), and what is missing is composition with the population-adjustment step. GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed three further claims: one-at-a-time analysis cannot establish joint robustness rather than proving cancellation, a multiple-bias analysis should state and explore dependence rather than preserve an unknown dependence (independence is a legitimate scenario and a deterministic grid needs no joint distribution), and Shapley attribution requires a joint parameter distribution only for expected or conditional summaries, not at a fixed bias-parameter vector.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Claims 1, 3, 4, 7 and 8 gain a real empirical citation the entry lacks: Ackerman et al. 2024 show, in exactly the external-control setting, that ‘When misclassified progression events and irregular assessment times occur simultaneously, they may generate bias that is greater than the sum of their parts’. That is a directly measured demonstration of non-additivity between two bias mechanisms in an ECA, and converts the entry’s assertion from theory to evidence. Claim 17 (‘No software composes several bias models jointly with the population-adjustment step’) survives, but should be worded precisely, because software that composes several bias models jointly does exist: the multibias R package on CRAN implements Brendel, Torres and Arah’s simultaneous adjustment of uncontrolled confounding, selection bias and misclassification via imputation and regression weighting (Int J Epidemiol 2023;52:1220-1230), explicitly as an alternative to sequential one-at-a-time correction. What is missing is composition with the population-adjustment step, not multiple-bias composition itself. Claims 15 and 16 (Shapley-style attribution is description, not identification) are correct.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied full-text reading.

merged-in

absorbed a proposal the reading raised separately: High-dimensional decision-invariant regions lack reportable summaries 2 citation(s) added. The drafter disagreed with placing it here: Recorded as a merge, as directed, and the placement is defensible since QBA-22 is where the need for a joint statement is established. The scope is nonetheless wider than QBA-22: the reporting obstruction applies to any multi-parameter invariant region, including threshold analysis over data points and contrasts, which perturbs evidence rather than bias mechanisms, and the component drift surface in CMP-23. If the region-summary question is later worked on in its own right, it will not sit comfortably inside an entry about the non-additivity of bias mechanisms.

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 1 surviving finding from: Applying Quantitative Bias Analysis to Epidemiologic Data, S. New citations: 10.1007/978-3-030-82673-4

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Claims 1, 3, 4, 7 and 8 gain a real empirical citation the entry lacks: Ackerman et al. 2024 show, in exactly the external-control setting, that ‘When misclassified progression events and irregular assessment times occur simultaneously, they may generate bias that is greater than the sum of their parts’. That is a directly measured demonstration of non-additivity between two bias mechanisms in an ECA, and converts the entry’s assertion from theory to evidence. Claim 17 (‘No software composes several bias models jointly with the population-adjustment step’) survives, but should be worded precisely, because software that composes several bias models jointly does exist: the multibias R package on CRAN implements Brendel, Torres and Arah’s simultaneous adjustment of uncontrolled confounding, selection bias and misclassification via imputation and regression weighting (Int J Epidemiol 2023;52:1220-1230), explicitly as an alternative to sequential one-at-a-time correction. What is missing is composition with the population-adjustment step, not multiple-bias composition itself. Claims 15 and 16 (Shapley-style attribution is description, not identification) are correct. Cites 10.1093/ije/dyad001: Provides the joint (non-sequential) multiple-bias machinery and CRAN implementation (multibias) that claim 11 asks for, but without any population-adjustment step, so the PAIC-specific gap in claim 17 stands.. Cites 10.3389/fdsfr.2024.1423493: Empirical demonstration of non-additive interaction between two bias mechanisms in an external control arm; supports claims 1, 3, 4 and 7 with evidence rather than assertion..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / overstated. C1-C4, C6, C8-C11, and C13 are correct as possibility or conditional claims: if B(eta)=T(eta)-T(0), isolated mechanism biases need not sum unless T is additive, while a first-order Taylor expansion gives C2. C7 should say that one-at-a-time analysis cannot establish joint robustness, not that cancellation logically explains survival of each isolated curve. C12 should require stating and exploring dependence, not preserving an unknown dependence: independence can be a legitimate scenario, and a deterministic grid needs no joint distribution. C14 is strong causal-analysis practice, not a mathematical necessity. C15 is correct that Shapley allocation does not identify bias from data, but Shapley values exactly decompose a chosen model-based total. C16 is false in general: at a fixed bias-parameter vector, coalition values and an ordering average suffice; a joint distribution is needed only for expected or conditional Shapley summaries. C17 is a field-wide absence claim that cpaic source cannot establish. At cpaic 9d150e9, bridge_fragility() varies one scalar box bound on component main-effect drift and explicitly excludes interaction drift, while prior_sensitivity() only refits prior scales; there is no general joint-bias QBA export. Thus the cpaic gap is open, but C5 describes a roadmap feature rather than a correctness defect and the overall very-high-priority framing is inflated.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R9:substantiated-single-overstatement:codex

title: Survival QBA beyond the hazard ratio with limited aggregate data
text:
Statement
When proportional hazards is implausible a QBA reporting only a hazard ratio does not answer the decision question, and sensitivity should target the survival functional the decision uses, such as landmark survival, RMST difference, cumulative incidence under competing risks, cure fraction, recurrent-event burden or multistate occupancy; differing follow-up alone does not invalidate a hazard ratio when proportional hazards holds and that ratio is the prespecified estimand. Soutar et al. 2025 (doi:10.1186/s12874-025-02551-z) supply subject-level Bayesian data-augmentation QBA for the difference in RMST under user-specified exposure and outcome associations, recovering the target with minimal bias in the simulated structures studied, but they assume subject-level data for both groups and report that lacking IPD blocked plausibility assessment of their sensitivity scenarios in the applied example. The limited-aggregate-data extension is the open part, and where pseudo-IPD is reconstructed from a published curve its reconstruction error is a distinct uncertainty layer, although landmark survival and in-window RMST can be estimated from a published Kaplan-Meier curve without reconstructing pseudo-IPD at all.

title: Survival QBA beyond the hazard ratio with limited aggregate data
text:
Why it is open
A bias parameter specified on the hazard scale does not induce a fixed distortion of RMST or landmark survival, because RMST is an integral of the survival curve and the mapping depends on the whole baseline hazard and the follow-up window, so a hazard-ratio sensitivity analysis cannot be reinterpreted for the estimand the decision uses; each target needs its own bias model and multistate outcomes need one per transition. Bayesian data augmentation attaches an imputed confounder value to individual records, which the comparator side of an unanchored PAIC does not have, and it depends on correctly specified imputation and outcome models and stable weights that are less checkable when one arm is aggregate. Where reconstruction is used it produces a single deterministic pseudo-dataset, so digitization error, rounding in the numbers at risk and the assumed allocation of censoring times enter as if exact, and the bias model is then built on a dataset that was itself reconstructed.

title: Survival QBA beyond the hazard ratio with limited aggregate data
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Soutar et al. 2025, Flexible quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding in subject-level indirect treatment comparisons with proportional hazards violation, BMC Medical Research Methodology
Treats an unmeasured confounder as missing data and uses Bayesian data augmentation to impute it under user-specified exposure or source and outcome associations, estimating a weighted difference in RMST from subject-level data without relying on proportional hazards. Its applied example could not assess scenario plausibility for lack of IPD, which is the aggregate-data gap.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Treats reconstructed rows as fixed in the likelihood but labels them explicitly as pseudo-IPD and discloses that reconstruction uncertainty is not propagated, which refutes the blanket claim that current practice treats reconstructed data as observed IPD.

title: Survival QBA beyond the hazard ratio with limited aggregate data
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Develop estimand-specific survival QBA that parameterizes bias directly for the quantity the economic model uses and reports the sensitivity surface on that scale rather than the hazard scale, and extend the subject-level RMST data-augmentation route to aggregate or reconstructed comparators with tipping combinations of exposure and survival associations. Where landmark survival or in-window RMST is the target, work from the published Kaplan-Meier curve directly rather than reconstructing pseudo-IPD; where reconstruction is unavoidable, build a distribution over reconstructions consistent with the published curve, numbers at risk and event counts, and propagate that uncertainty together with the confounding parameters. Add censoring QBA when informative censoring is plausible rather than by default.

title: Survival QBA beyond the hazard ratio with limited aggregate data
text:
Our study

Does a hazard-scale bias translate proportionally into RMST?
The question put to it. Can a sensitivity analysis stated as a hazard-ratio bias be reinterpreted as a proportional bias in RMST, the quantity the decision uses?
What it found. No. The RMST change caused by a hazard-scale bias depends on the baseline hazard’s shape and the event level: at the same survival by 24 months the same bias moved RMST up to 1.44 times as much for a decreasing as for an increasing hazard, and the proportional (first-order) reinterpretation understated the change by about 25% with few events and overstated it by up to 8% with many. A hazard-ratio sensitivity analysis must be translated with the baseline curve or stated on the RMST scale.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: ratio of largest to smallest RMST change across shapes 1.20 to 1.44 at matched survival.
Proportional prediction error at a bias hazard ratio of 2: -25% to -26% at 80% survival, -14% to -17% at 50%, -1% to +8% at 20%.

Design.

Estimand

Change in RMST at 24 months induced by a multiplicative hazard bias

Methods compared

exact translation by integration, proportional (first-order) reinterpretation

Data-generating mechanism

Population-level numerical study: four baseline hazard shapes at three survival levels, bias hazard ratios 1.1 to 2, RMST at 24 months against the first-order proportional prediction.

Replicates

Population-level calculation: 4 shapes x 3 survival levels x 4 bias levels


What this does not answer. Only the hazard-to-RMST translation; the PAIC layer, pseudo-IPD and curve-based arms, reconstruction error and tipping sets not run. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Survival QBA beyond the hazard ratio with limited aggregate data
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “A QBA reporting only a hazard ratio is inadequate when hazards are non-proportional or follow-up differs between the compared studies; sensitivity should target landmark survival, RMST differences, cumulative incidence under competing risks, cure fraction, recurrent-event burden and multistate occupancy. The one method that does this properly assumes subject-level data for both groups, while an unanchored PAIC has a published curve, and the pseudo-IPD reconstructed from it is treated downstream as if it were observed data.”
What was wrong with it. GPT-5.6 Sol narrowed several claims: differing follow-up alone does not invalidate a hazard ratio under proportional hazards, the listed survival estimands are a menu rather than a required set, the Soutar recovery result holds for the simulated structures and known associations studied rather than generically, and the claim that current practice treats reconstructed pseudo-IPD as observed data is too broad, since cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) labels reconstructed rows as pseudo-IPD and discloses that their reconstruction uncertainty is not propagated. The absence of an accepted resampling scheme over reconstructions is a matter of consensus rather than mathematical impossibility.
Dissent. codex dissented (overstated): C1 is right under nonproportional hazards when the decision estimand is a survival functional, but differing follow-up alone does not invalidate a hazard ratio if proportional hazards holds and that ratio is the prespecified estimand. C2 is a menu of possible estimands, not a set every analysis must report. C3 is correct: RMST is the integral of the survival curve, so a hazard-scale perturbation has no baseline- and horizon-invariant RMST effect. The censoring distribution affects identification and estimation, not the true RMST mapping under independent censoring. C4, C6, and C7 match the cited Soutar method. C5 is supported only for the simulated structures and known exposure/outcome associations studied, not as a generic recovery theorem. C8 is correct when pseudo-IPD reconstruction is used and its error is material. C9 is too broad: cpaic treats reconstructed rows as fixed in the likelihood but explicitly labels them pseudo-IPD and discloses that reconstruction uncertainty is not propagated. C10 remains open for cpaic and for a limited-aggregate extension of the cited method, but landmark survival and in-window RMST can be estimated directly from a published Kaplan-Meier curve without reconstructing pseudo-IPD. C11 should require censoring QBA only when informative censoring is plausible and reconstruction uncertainty only when reconstruction is used. C12 is a consensus claim, not a mathematical impossibility; multiple-reconstruction and curve-resampling schemes can be defined even if no standard has been adopted.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported. Retrieved Soutar et al. 2025. Claims 4 to 7 verified: it treats the unmeasured confounder as missing data and imputes it under user-specified exposure/source and outcome associations, targets the difference in restricted mean survival time so as to avoid reliance on proportional hazards, reports that ‘imputation-based adjustment was able to recover the true adjusted dRMST with minimal bias across all scenarios’, and is built on combined subject-level covariates and outcomes. Its own applied limitation confirms claim 7: applying the framework to real data, the authors ‘did not have access to IPD, so it was not possible to estimate associations between known confounders’, which blocked plausibility assessment of the sensitivity scenarios. That is the aggregate-data gap the entry names. Claims 8, 9, 12 concern pseudo-IPD reconstruction uncertainty; an active 2025-2026 methods literature on IPD reconstruction from Kaplan-Meier curves and on uncertainty-aware reconstruction now exists and the entry should engage with it, but I did not read those papers closely enough to judge whether any propagates reconstruction uncertainty into a PAIC bias analysis, so I do not credit them.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / overstated. C1 is right under nonproportional hazards when the decision estimand is a survival functional, but differing follow-up alone does not invalidate a hazard ratio if proportional hazards holds and that ratio is the prespecified estimand. C2 is a menu of possible estimands, not a set every analysis must report. C3 is correct: RMST is the integral of the survival curve, so a hazard-scale perturbation has no baseline- and horizon-invariant RMST effect. The censoring distribution affects identification and estimation, not the true RMST mapping under independent censoring. C4, C6, and C7 match the cited Soutar method. C5 is supported only for the simulated structures and known exposure/outcome associations studied, not as a generic recovery theorem. C8 is correct when pseudo-IPD reconstruction is used and its error is material. C9 is too broad: cpaic treats reconstructed rows as fixed in the likelihood but explicitly labels them pseudo-IPD and discloses that reconstruction uncertainty is not propagated. C10 remains open for cpaic and for a limited-aggregate extension of the cited method, but landmark survival and in-window RMST can be estimated directly from a published Kaplan-Meier curve without reconstructing pseudo-IPD. C11 should require censoring QBA only when informative censoring is plausible and reconstruction uncertainty only when reconstruction is used. C12 is a consensus claim, not a mathematical impossibility; multiple-reconstruction and curve-resampling schemes can be defined even if no standard has been adopted. Cites doi:10.1186/s12874-025-02551-z: Provides subject-level Bayesian data-augmentation QBA for difference in RMST under proportional-hazards violation and demonstrates low bias in the studied simulations..
