title: Benchmarking and negative controls as data-based calibration
text:
Statement
Two data-based routes to sensitivity parameters exist, and the first has been implemented for unanchored MAIC: Yi and Jiang 2025 (doi:10.57264/cer-2024-0235) build artificially risk-unbalanced groups with a predetermined hazard ratio of 1.8, reweight on the candidate prognostic factors and check whether the reweighted hazard ratio returns to one, reporting 0.9157 with all covariates included and 1.671 when one critical prognostic factor was omitted. It is a covariate-sufficiency diagnostic: it does not convert an induced bias into a sensitivity-parameter range and does not bound residual bias from unobserved structure. The second route, negative-control outcomes or exposures, needs a control that shares the relevant confounding and selection structure and has no causal relation to the outcome of interest, and it detects rather than quantifies, since a signal may instead reflect failure of the negative-control assumptions and a null signal does not establish absence of bias; converting an association into a bias-parameter range for the primary estimand requires further bridge, completeness or proportional-bias assumptions that have not been developed for population-adjusted comparisons.

title: Benchmarking and negative controls as data-based calibration
text:
Why it is open
A held-out benchmark is limited to what happened to be measured, so it says how strong an observed variable is and never how strong the unobserved structure is; an omitted composite factor can be stronger than any single measured variable, so the familiar argument that no measured covariate produces bias as large as the assumed value establishes nothing without an explicit assumption linking unmeasured structure to the measured covariates, and no procedure scales a single-variable benchmark up to composite or multivariate omitted structure. In an unanchored PAIC the comparator is published aggregate data in which no negative-control outcome is typically reported, so the diagnostic is usually unavailable on the side where it is needed. Converting an observed negative-control association into a bias-parameter range requires bridge or completeness assumptions that have not been worked out for population-adjusted comparisons, so the routine output stays a binary pass or fail.

title: Benchmarking and negative controls as data-based calibration
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Yi and Jiang 2025, A process to validate prognostic factors for unanchored matching-adjusted indirect comparison of single-arm trials in oncology: a proof-of-concept study, Journal of Comparative Effectiveness Research 14:e240235
Implements the held-out prognostic-factor benchmarking route in the unanchored MAIC setting as a covariate-sufficiency diagnostic: with all covariates included the reweighted hazard ratio was 0.9157 (95% CI 0.5629 to 2.493) and with one critical prognostic factor omitted it was 1.671 (95% CI 1.194 to 2.340). It produces no bias-parameter range and no bound on residual bias.

title: Benchmarking and negative controls as data-based calibration
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Treat a held-out benchmark as calibration by analogy that is neither an upper nor a lower bound, rerunning the whole PAIC procedure and accounting for the held-out variable’s scale, prevalence, role and correlation with the retained variables, and extend it so it can address composite and multivariate omitted structure. Use it as one rung of an explicit evidence hierarchy alongside internal validation data, external evidence, randomized-benchmark emulation and formal elicitation rather than as standalone justification. Encourage reporting of candidate negative-control outcomes in trial and external-control publications so the diagnostic becomes usable with aggregate data, and develop the bridge or completeness assumptions under which a negative-control association converts into a bias-parameter range for the primary estimand rather than a pass or fail.

title: Benchmarking and negative controls as data-based calibration
text:
Our study

A single-covariate benchmark against omitted composite structure
The question put to it. Does the bias from dropping the strongest measured covariate bound the residual bias from several omitted variables, and does a scaled benchmark calibrate?
What it found. No. With three or six omitted variables each no stronger than the strongest measured covariate, the leave-one-covariate-out benchmark covered the true residual bias in at most 7% of analyses, the bias being 1.4 to 5.7 times the benchmark. Scaling by the square root of the number of omitted variables did not fix it; scaling by the number itself did when each omitted variable was weaker than the strongest measured one. The benchmark also shrank as omitted structure grew, through odds-ratio non-collapsibility.
Results.

Refuting sentence fails: plain benchmark coverage 0.00 to 0.07 for q of 3 or 6 with each omitted variable at most as strong as the strongest measured.
Scaled by sqrt(q): coverage 0.00 to 0.76; by the oracle correlation-adjusted factor: 0.00 to 0.98; by q: 0.99 to 1.00 at half strength and 0.57 to 0.67 at equal strength.
Median benchmark fell from 0.163 (one weak omitted variable) to 0.067 (six strong correlated ones) while the true bias rose from 0.08 to 0.56 and beyond.

Design.

Estimand

A’s marginal log odds in the target (the unanchored comparison’s A side) and MAIC’s residual bias

Methods compared

leave-one-covariate-out benchmark, benchmark times sqrt(q), benchmark times the oracle correlation-adjusted factor, benchmark times q

Data-generating mechanism

Unanchored binary-outcome MAIC with four measured covariates and one, three or six correlated omitted covariates of varying strength; leave-one-covariate-out benchmark, unscaled and scaled by sqrt(q), by the oracle correlation-adjusted factor and by q; coverage of the true residual bias. 21 cells, 1000 replicates each.

Replicates

1000 per scenario, 21,000 in total


What this does not answer. Omitted variables shifted in the same direction; one overlap level; negative-control route not run. Peer review has not been done.
Peer review. Not yet done. The result stands on the study alone until it is.

title: Benchmarking and negative controls as data-based calibration
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced. Reopened by the full-text reading: 2 findings from 2 papers survived both the reader and an independent second reviewer, so the verdict moves from confirmed-open to partially-addressed.
The source said. “Two data-based routes to sensitivity parameters exist: removing a measured prognostic factor or effect modifier and estimating the bias its omission induces, and using negative-control outcomes or exposures to reveal selection, ascertainment or design differences not removed by adjusting for the measured covariates. Neither converts into a bound on the residual bias affecting the primary estimand.”
What was wrong with it. The entry cited nothing for a benchmarking route that has already been implemented for unanchored MAIC; the literature auditor supplied Yi and Jiang 2025 (doi:10.57264/cer-2024-0235), which does not close the problem but is prior art the entry should carry. GPT-5.6 Sol rejected the entry’s proposal to treat a held-out benchmark as a lower reference point, since it is guaranteed to be neither a lower nor an upper bound, and noted that under explicit additional assumptions negative controls can calibrate an effect on the primary estimand rather than only detect a bias.
Revised by the full-text reading. Applied 2026-07-26 full-text reading of the consolidated library (687 papers).

Verdict changed

confirmed-open -> partially-addressed 2 surviving findings from: A process to validate prognostic factors for unanchored matc; Adjustment for reporting bias in network meta-analysis of an. New citations: 10.1186/1471-2288-12-150, 10.57264/cer-2024-0235

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. The held-out-variable benchmarking route in claim 1 has in fact been implemented for unanchored MAIC and the entry cites nothing for it: Yi and Jiang 2025 (J Comp Eff Res 14:e240235, PMID 40190245) propose a validation framework that builds two artificially risk-unbalanced groups with a predetermined HR of 1.8, reweights on the candidate prognostic factors, and checks whether the reweighted HR returns to one; with all covariates included HR was 0.9157 (95% CI 0.5629-2.493), and omitting one critical prognostic factor moved it to 1.671 (95% CI 1.194-2.340). That is precisely ‘removing a measured prognostic factor and estimating the induced bias’ in the unanchored MAIC setting. Crucially it does not falsify the entry: it is a pass/fail sufficiency diagnostic for covariate selection, it does not convert an induced bias into a sensitivity-parameter range, and it does not bound residual bias from unobserved structure, so claims 2, 3 and the problem itself stand. Claims 4 and 5 on negative controls are correct in substance; negative-control outcomes are essentially never reported in an aggregate comparator publication, which is the binding constraint. Cites 10.57264/cer-2024-0235: Implements the held-out prognostic-factor benchmarking route for unanchored MAIC as a covariate-sufficiency diagnostic. Does not produce a bias-parameter range or a bound on residual bias, so the problem remains open; the entry should cite it as prior art..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 is valid as calibration by analogy, provided the whole PAIC procedure is rerun and the held-out variable’s scale, prevalence, role, and correlation with retained variables are considered. It is a benchmark, not a bound. C2 and C3 are correct absent an explicit assumption linking unmeasured structure to the measured covariates. C4 is correct only for a valid negative control that shares the relevant bias structure and has the required no-causal-effect property; a signal can also reflect failure of the negative-control assumptions, and a null signal does not establish no residual bias. C5 is correct with ‘by itself’: under additional confounding-bridge, completeness, or proportional-bias assumptions, negative controls can identify or calibrate effects on the primary estimand. The proposed direction should not call a held-out benchmark a lower reference point because it is not guaranteed to be either a lower or an upper bound. The limited-aggregate-data calibration problem therefore remains open, but this is a calibration and reporting gap rather than proof that data-based information is impossible.

R5:default-open → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: Reference QBA software and a minimum reporting standard
text:
Statement
QBA for unanchored PAIC is done with bespoke per-submission scripts and no validated reference package with a benchmark suite and model manifest exists; the nearest artefact the literature auditor found is the analysis code accompanying Ren et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.13), a repository with a simulated dataset. Parts of the proposed object are already built: cpaic (choxos/cpaic@9d150e9, an unreleased development package on GitHub, not installable from CRAN) exports estimability labels, effective sample size and weight diagnostics, edge influence, integration-error diagnostics, prior sensitivity and bridge fragility, but no qba(), net-benefit, tipping-surface, partial-identification, benchmark-suite or model-manifest interface. The reporting side is also partly occupied, since Ishak et al. 2025 (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1) publish a PAIC framework covering estimand definition, method and adjustment-variable selection, application, risk-of-bias assessment and comprehensive reporting, and Leahy et al. 2023 (doi:10.1017/S0266462323002702) already require transparent parameter sourcing and code and data sharing, so what no guideline covers is sensitivity-parameter provenance, dependence among bias parameters, feasibility surfaces and failed fits.

title: Reference QBA software and a minimum reporting standard
text:
Why it is open
Bespoke scripting means results cannot be reproduced, compared across submissions or checked by a reviewer, and without a benchmark suite there is no way to establish that an implementation is correct, so software correctness is currently taken on trust. A reference API must expose objects that existing PAIC packages have no representation for, including nonidentified sensitivity parameters, feasibility maps, decision-reversal surfaces and partial-identification bounds, so several checklist items require output that does not yet exist. No reporting guideline covers sensitivity-parameter provenance, dependence assumptions among bias parameters, feasibility surfaces or failed fits, so a reviewer has no standard against which to judge a submitted sensitivity analysis, and the proposed checklist has been neither validated nor adopted by any appraisal body. Economic models consume absolute arm-level survival and event probabilities, so a bias scenario can leave the relative effect plausible while implying arm outcomes no clinician would accept, and reporting only the contrast hides that.

title: Reference QBA software and a minimum reporting standard
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Leahy et al. 2023, International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care
Covers part of the proposed reporting standard: transparent input sourcing, a-priori specification, sharing of all code and data used to inform and conduct QBA analyses with the respective HTA bodies, elicitation and early engagement.


Ishak, Chandler, Liu and Klijn 2025, A Framework for Reliable, Transparent, and Reproducible Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons, PharmacoEconomics 43:691-710
Published PAIC framework covering six elements: estimand definition, PAIC method selection, adjustment-variable selection, application of the adjustment method, risk-of-bias assessment and comprehensive reporting. Occupies part of the reporting-standard space the entry said was empty; does not cover sensitivity-parameter provenance, dependence among bias parameters, feasibility surfaces or failed fits.


cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
Supplies several proposed ingredients: estimability labels, a per-study weight panel (effective sample size, weight-entropy efficiency, coefficient of variation, largest normalized weight, mass in the top 5% of weights), edge influence, integration-error diagnostics, prior sensitivity and bridge fragility. It exports no qba(), net-benefit, tipping-surface, partial-identification, benchmark-suite or model-manifest interface, and its cMAIC returns within-study contrasts rather than bias-adjusted absolute arm outcomes.


Ren et al. 2025, Research Synthesis Methods
The nearest artefact to reference QBA software the literature auditor located: analysis code with a simulated dataset accompanying the paper, rather than a validated package with a benchmark suite or model manifest.

title: Reference QBA software and a minimum reporting standard
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Assemble the reference API from the diagnostics that already exist rather than specifying it from scratch, and release it so a reader can install and check it: make the sensitivity specification, the mode of analysis and the decision threshold explicit arguments, and have the returned object report the estimand and effect scale, identified versus sensitivity-specified quantities, provenance, feasible versus unsupported scenarios and decision-reversal surfaces, invoking effective sample size, partial-identification bounds, dependence, dominance and cancellation only where they are defined for the analysis at hand. Pair it with a benchmark suite and a model manifest, and embed the checklist items in the output so compliance is a by-product of running the analysis. Extend the published PAIC reporting framework with the QBA-specific items it does not cover rather than proposing a rival checklist, and report bias-adjusted absolute arm outcomes wherever the estimator produces them, using clinical implausibility of implied arm outcomes as grounds for excluding scenarios.

title: Reference QBA software and a minimum reporting standard
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source said. “QBA for unanchored PAIC is done with bespoke per-submission scripts and there is no validated reference package, benchmark suite or model manifest. The report proposes a fourteen-item minimum reporting checklist covering target population and exact estimand, causal diagram and bias mechanism, classification of each sensitivity variable, every parameter with scale, range or distribution and evidence source, dependence assumptions, interpretation mode, models used, support and feasibility diagnostics throughout the sensitivity region, all uncertainty layers and failed fits, decision thresholds, the proportion of the region leading to each decision, code, seeds, source data and elicitation materials, bias-adjusted absolute arm outcomes, and a statement of what QBA does not prove.”
What was wrong with it. The literature auditor found the claim that no ITC or PAIC reporting guideline exists overstated, because Ishak et al. 2025 (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1) already publish a PAIC risk-of-bias and reporting framework, so the claim narrows to the QBA-specific items it does not cover, and the requirement to share code and data is already in Leahy et al. 2023 (doi:10.1017/S0266462323002702). GPT-5.6 Sol read cpaic at commit 9d150e9, found several proposed diagnostics already implemented, held that the object’s contents should be required only where they are defined for the analysis at hand, and rejected attributing bias-adjusted absolute arm outcomes to cpaic’s cMAIC, whose README defines cmaic() and cstc() as anchored in the common-comparator sense and whose weighted fit returns within-study contrasts.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): Claim 1 stands: the closest artefact I found is the analysis code accompanying Ren et al. 2025 (a GitHub repository with a simulated dataset), not a validated package with a benchmark suite or model manifest. Claim 7 is already published guidance, not a gap: Leahy et al. 2023 recommend that ‘All code and data used to inform and conduct QBA analyses should be shared with the respective HTA bodies’. Claim 9 is overstated as written, because a PAIC-specific reporting framework the entry does not cite now exists: Ishak, Chandler, Liu and Klijn 2025 (PharmacoEconomics 43:691-710) propose a systematic framework covering six elements of PAIC analyses explicitly including ‘(5) risk-of-bias assessment’ and ‘(6) comprehensive reporting’, motivated by exactly the variability and lack of transparency the entry describes. It does not, as far as I can establish from the abstract, cover sensitivity-parameter provenance, dependence among bias parameters, feasibility surfaces or failed fits, so the narrow version of claim 9 survives, but the sweeping version does not. Claims 2 to 6, 8, 10 and 11 are specifications for a future object and are internally coherent. codex dissented (overstated): C1’s field-wide absence cannot be established from source code or under the instructed non-literature lens. What is source-confirmed is narrower: cpaic 9d150e9 exports bridge_fragility(), prior_sensitivity(), estimability, ESS, edge-influence, weight, and integration diagnostics, but no qba(), net-benefit, tipping-surface, partial-identification, benchmark-suite, or model-manifest API. C2 is a useful design menu, not a universal object contract: ESS is relevant only when weights change, partial-identification bounds only in a bounds mode, and layer dominance or cancellation requires a scale- and model-dependent decomposition. C3 is factually correct only under the report’s grouping of the list into fourteen items. C4’s four categories are neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive. C5 applies to a probabilistic joint specification; a deterministic grid has constraints or allowed combinations but no correlations to report. C6 should require diagnostics where they vary and apply, not mechanically at every point. C7 is a sound transparency aim, but seeds matter only for stochastic computation and source data may require controlled access rather than public release. C8 is correct. C9 is overstated because the cited Leahy guidance already covers transparent parameter sourcing and code/data disclosure, even if it does not supply this PAIC-specific checklist. C10 is usually valuable for unanchored comparisons. C11 is method-dependent and must not be attributed to current cpaic cMAIC: its README defines cmaic() and cstc() as anchored in the common-comparator sense, and its weighted fit returns within-study contrasts rather than an exported bias-adjusted absolute-arm object. The integrated reference API remains open, but several diagnostics and reporting principles are already solved; this is primarily tooling and standards work, not necessarily a very-high-priority methodological defect.

title: Added bias uncertainty can narrow rather than widen a pooled interval
text: QBA-30 Confirmed open High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: Added bias uncertainty can narrow rather than widen a pooled interval
text:
Statement
Propagating an extra study-level uncertainty layer in a random-effects synthesis, whether an assumed departure from missing-at-random, a measurement-error term or a curve-reconstruction term, enters the model as an addition to each study’s within-study variance. Between-study variance is estimated as the excess of observed dispersion over the within-study variances, so raising the latter is arithmetically subtracted from the heterogeneity estimate, and the two movements push the pooled variance in opposite directions with no general rule for which dominates. The pooled interval can therefore narrow as the assumed bias grows: in the pairwise and network models for missing continuous outcomes the summary interval contracts as the missingness-uncertainty parameter increases until the estimated heterogeneity is driven to zero, at roughly a standard deviation of 3 on the informative-missingness difference-of-means scale or 0.2 on the ratio-of-means scale, and only widens beyond that point. No reporting or modeling convention addresses this. Nothing states how to separate genuine heterogeneity from heterogeneity absorbed by the bias layer, which between-study variance estimator to use when a sensitivity parameter is in play, or how to present a sensitivity analysis whose interval moved toward greater apparent precision. The practical consequence is that checking whether the interval widened is not a valid test that uncertainty was propagated, and it is the check most readers apply.

title: Added bias uncertainty can narrow rather than widen a pooled interval
text:
Why it is open
The arithmetic is a property of the standard moment and likelihood estimators of between-study variance rather than a defect of one implementation: any layer that raises within-study variances is subtracted from the heterogeneity estimate, and whether the subtraction or the addition dominates depends on the observed dispersion, the number of studies and the estimator, so there is no single adjustment factor to publish. The direction can differ between contrasts of the same network, so the effect does not cancel across a synthesis and cannot be summarized once for an analysis. The decomposition that would fix it is not identified: genuine between-study heterogeneity and unmodeled study-level bias appear in the same observed dispersion, so separating them requires an external estimate of one of them rather than a better estimator. The effect also inverts the intended reading of a sensitivity analysis, because a decision can move toward greater apparent certainty as the analyst assumes a larger bias, which is exactly the incentive a bias analysis exists to remove; naming the problem therefore means conceding that the field’s informal audit of sensitivity analyses does not work. Nobody has taken it up because the behavior is noticed as a curiosity inside individual papers and treated as a property of one model, rather than as a general feature of adding variance to a random-effects synthesis.

title: Added bias uncertainty can narrow rather than widen a pooled interval
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Mavridis, White, Higgins, Cipriani and Salanti 2015, Allowing for uncertainty due to missing continuous outcome data in pairwise and network meta-analysis, Statistics in Medicine 34(5):721-741
builds informative-missingness difference-of-means and ratio-of-means sensitivity models for pairwise and network meta-analysis and documents the narrowing directly, reporting that the reduction in between-study variance outweighs the increase in within-study variance so the intervals contract as the missingness uncertainty grows; it records the behavior without proposing how to report or estimate around it


White, Higgins and Wood 2008, Allowing for uncertainty due to missing data in meta-analysis, Part 1: Two-stage methods, Statistics in Medicine 27(5):711-727
the two-stage construction in which an informative-missingness parameter and its uncertainty inflate each study’s variance before pooling, which is the mechanism that later subtracts from the heterogeneity estimate


White, Welton, Wood, Ades and Higgins 2008, Allowing for uncertainty due to missing data in meta-analysis, Part 2: Hierarchical models, Statistics in Medicine 27(5):728-745
the hierarchical counterpart, in which the missingness parameter is given a distribution inside the model; it shows the layer can be placed either inside the likelihood or in the variance, a distinction that determines whether the heterogeneity estimate absorbs it


Turner, Spiegelhalter, Smith and Thompson 2009, Bias modelling in evidence synthesis, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 172(1):21-47
the general framework for adding additive and proportional bias terms with elicited variances to studies in a synthesis; it separates a bias shift from a bias variance, which is the distinction a convention would have to enforce, and does not analyze the interaction with the heterogeneity estimate


Welton, Ades, Carlin, Altman and Sterne 2009, Models for potentially biased evidence in meta-analysis using empirically based priors, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 172(1):119-136
supplies empirically grounded priors for bias magnitude and variance from meta-epidemiological data, which is where the size of an added layer would come from in practice


Veroniki et al. 2016, Methods to estimate the between-study variance and its uncertainty in meta-analysis, Research Synthesis Methods 7(1):55-79
catalogs the available between-study variance estimators and their behavior; the estimator determines how much of an added within-study variance is absorbed and how quickly the heterogeneity estimate reaches its lower bound, so the choice is the lever this problem turns on


DerSimonian and Laird 1986, Meta-analysis in clinical trials, Controlled Clinical Trials 7(3):177-188
the moment estimator that defines between-study variance as observed dispersion minus the within-study variances and truncates at zero; it is the source of the subtraction and of the boundary at which the narrowing stops


Riley, Higgins and Deeks 2011, Interpretation of random effects meta-analyses, BMJ 342:d549
argues for reporting a prediction interval alongside the confidence interval for the summary effect; the two respond differently to variance moving between the within-study and between-study components, which makes the pair a candidate reporting fix

title: Added bias uncertainty can narrow rather than widen a pooled interval
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Derive the boundary rather than describing the phenomenon: for each common between-study variance estimator, write the derivative of the pooled variance with respect to an added within-study variance and identify the region in observed dispersion, number of studies and added variance where it is negative, so an analyst can tell in advance which side of the boundary a synthesis sits on. Require any sensitivity analysis that adds an uncertainty layer to report the estimated between-study variance and the within-study variances before and after, next to the pooled interval, so that a narrowing is legible as heterogeneity absorption rather than as gained precision. Report the prediction interval alongside the confidence interval and mark the value of the sensitivity parameter at which the heterogeneity estimate reaches zero, which is a natural landmark and the point past which the interval behaves as expected again. Compare heterogeneity estimators under a sensitivity parameter by simulation, since moment, restricted maximum likelihood, Paule-Mandel and Bayesian estimators with weakly informative priors absorb different amounts of the added variance, and make the estimator choice on that basis rather than by default. Where the layer represents a bias rather than extra noise, model it as a shift with its own variance component outside the within-study variance, so that it cannot be netted off against the heterogeneity estimate at all.

title: Added bias uncertainty can narrow rather than widen a pooled interval
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. One reader proposed this from a single paper, which documents the narrowing explicitly, and the reviewer accepted it on the ground that the reporting and estimation consequences are distinct from the requirement that uncertainty layers be propagated at all. A single-paper basis is weaker than a multi-reader one; what supports the verdict is that the mechanism is a property of standard heterogeneity estimators rather than of that model, and no convention, estimator recommendation or reporting rule for it exists.

title: No criterion selects among design-aware models for a mixed-design network
text: QBA-32 Partially addressed High priority Promising Tractability 4/5

title: No criterion selects among design-aware models for a mixed-design network
text:
Statement
Reviews and protocols that admit non-randomized studies of interventions into a randomized network enumerate the same alternatives to naive pooling: design-adjusted synthesis, non-randomized evidence as informative or power priors, three-level or design-specific hierarchical models, bias-adjusted models, and stratified or sensitivity analysis. All of them are implemented, and crossnma provides four cross-design approaches behind one interface, so availability is not the obstacle. What does not exist is a rule that says which to fit, or evidence that ranks them on anything a decision reads. Where they have been run side by side the point estimates barely separate while the reported uncertainty does: in a type 2 diabetes network of sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists the mean glycated hemoglobin differences at 24 and 52 weeks were similar under every method, naive pooling narrowed the interval relative to randomized evidence alone, a hierarchical model separating designs widened it, and bias-adjustment models moved it in different directions for different treatments. Fit does not arbitrate either: in that network hierarchical and bias-adjustment models all fitted better than naive pooling and nothing in the fit ordered them against each other. Each family also needs a bias magnitude it cannot estimate, since the power-prior exponent runs from 0 to 1 with no data-based value and the mixture-model probability of bias requires informative priors elicited from trained risk-of-bias assessors, with the identifiability of the bias parameters depending on which data happen to be present. The analyst therefore picks the model and, with it, the width of the interval a committee reads.

title: No criterion selects among design-aware models for a mixed-design network
text:
Why it is open
Design-level bias is a study-level offset that enters the same observed dispersion as between-study heterogeneity and the treatment effect, so a mixed network does not separate the three; every family assumes rather than estimates the quantity on which they differ, and data cannot rank assumptions they never see. Fit is the natural tiebreaker and fails structurally, because the families carry similar numbers of free parameters and differ in a shape assumption about bias that a handful of non-randomized studies per contrast cannot resolve, which is why fit separates naive pooling from the rest and then stops. The empirical route that would calibrate the magnitude has been run and returned a near-null average: across 39 systematic reviews and 8 overviews covering 2869 randomized trials and 3924 observational studies the pooled ratio of ratios was 1.08 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.01 to 1.15, rated low certainty, so there is no corpus-level design bias worth plugging in even though individual discrepancies are large. Scoring a criterion needs a randomized answer for the same contrast as ground truth, and that exists only where the non-randomized evidence was not needed, so the validation set systematically excludes the cases the criterion is for. Nothing forces a declaration: the choice is made once, reported as the analysis, and naming it as a choice could only make the result look more fragile than it currently does.

title: No criterion selects among design-aware models for a mixed-design network
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Efthimiou, Mavridis, Debray, Samara, Belger, Siontis, Leucht and Salanti 2017, Combining randomized and non-randomized evidence in network meta-analysis, Statistics in Medicine 36(8):1210-1226
Sets out and compares naive data synthesis, design-adjusted synthesis, non-randomized evidence as prior information and three-level hierarchical models, discussing the advantages and limitations of each in two clinical examples; it supplies the enumeration that later work inherits but no selection rule and no operating characteristics.


Schmitz, Adams and Walsh 2013, Incorporating data from various trial designs into a mixed treatment comparison model, Statistics in Medicine 32(17):2935-2949
Proposes naive pooling, observational data as prior information, and a three-level hierarchical model as the three routes for mixing designs in one network, and notes that the hierarchical form allows bias adjustment while also accounting for between-design heterogeneity.


Hussein, Abrams, Gray, Anwer, Dias and Bujkiewicz 2023, Hierarchical network meta-analysis models for synthesis of evidence from randomised and non-randomised studies, BMC Medical Research Methodology 23:97
Fits naive pooling, hierarchical, class-effect and bias-adjustment models to one type 2 diabetes network and reports that the effect estimates agree while the uncertainty moves differently under each, and that hierarchical and bias-adjustment models all fit better than naive pooling without the fit ordering them among themselves.


Hamza, Schwarzer and Salanti 2024, crossnma: An R package to synthesize cross-design evidence and cross-format data using network meta-analysis and network meta-regression, BMC Medical Research Methodology 24:169
Ships four cross-design approaches behind one interface with default beta priors on the probability of bias keyed to risk-of-bias category and study type, and records that the identifiability of all model parameters, in particular those relating to bias, depends on the available data.


Hamza, Chalkou, Pellegrini, Kuhle, Benkert, Lorscheider, Zecca, Iglesias-Urrutia, Manca, Furukawa, Cipriani and Salanti 2023, Synthesizing cross-design evidence and cross-format data using network meta-regression, Research Synthesis Methods 14(2):283-300
Develops the four approaches that crossnma implements and reports that the relative treatment effects did not change much once design and risk of bias were accounted for, in a multiple sclerosis network and in a network of 431 trials of 21 antidepressants; this is why point estimates cannot separate the model families.


Verde 2021, A bias-corrected meta-analysis model for combining studies of different types and quality, Biometrical Journal 63(2):406-422
Mixture model in which the true effects are a mixture of a component of interest and a hidden bias structure; the source of the probability-of-bias parameter that the network versions require informative priors for.


Jenkins, Hussein, Martina, Dequen-O’Byrne, Abrams and Bujkiewicz 2021, Methods for the inclusion of real-world evidence in network meta-analysis, BMC Medical Research Methodology 21:207
Runs the power-prior down-weighting exponent across its whole range in a relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis network, finds stable point estimates and credible intervals that widen as weight is given to real-world evidence, and concludes that empirical evidence on the biases of individual real-world studies and elicitation methods for their extent are both warranted.


Cameron, Fireman, Hutton, Clifford, Coyle, Wells, Dormuth, Platt and Toh 2015, Network meta-analysis incorporating randomized controlled trials and non-randomized comparative cohort studies for assessing the safety and effectiveness of medical treatments: challenges and opportunities, Systematic Reviews 4:147
States that published research on the prior-based and design-level hierarchical routes is limited and that there is a lack of consensus on what degree of bias adjustment to apply to non-randomized studies.


Toews, Anglemyer, Nyirenda, Alsaid, Balduzzi, Grummich, Schwingshackl and Bero 2024, Healthcare outcomes assessed with observational study designs compared with those assessed in randomized trials: a meta-epidemiological study, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 1:MR000034
Pools 39 systematic reviews and 8 overviews covering 2869 randomized trials and 3924 observational studies and reports a ratio of ratios of 1.08 (95 percent confidence interval 1.01 to 1.15) at low certainty; the corpus-level anchor a design-bias prior would be calibrated against, and it is close to null.


Zhao, Song, Wang, Li and Kang 2026, Naive pooling of randomized and non-randomized evidence in network meta-analyses: a meta-epidemiological study protocol, Frontiers in Medicine 13:1868332
Protocol to measure how often published networks published from 2020 to 2025 pool randomized and non-randomized evidence without any design-specific adjustment; it lists the design-aware alternatives as a menu and offers no criterion for choosing among them.

title: No criterion selects among design-aware models for a mixed-design network
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Score the families rather than enumerate them again: simulate networks in which the design-level bias is known, crossing its size, its sign, whether it varies by treatment class, the number of non-randomized studies per contrast and their relative precision, and report coverage of the decision-relevant contrast, interval width, and how often the recommendation changes under each family, with naive pooling and randomized-only synthesis as the two reference behaviors. Score each family when it is wrong as well as when it is right, since the operational question is which degrades least under a bias structure it did not assume. Add an empirical arm over networks carrying both randomized and non-randomized evidence on the same contrast, using the randomized subnetwork as the reference and recording the discrepancy each family leaves; that is the only calibration data the problem admits, and it also yields a distribution of realized design bias by indication that could replace the near-null corpus average. Require the bias magnitude to carry a declared provenance in the output, stating whether it was elicited, taken from a corpus or set by convention, and report the value of the down-weighting exponent or bias prior at which the recommendation flips, which is a tipping point rather than a choice. Where nothing selects a family, report the envelope over all of them, since the spread across models is the quantity a committee actually needs.

title: No criterion selects among design-aware models for a mixed-design network
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. This came from labeller-reported absence rather than from a paper arguing for it: 3 of 12 gap labellers named it independently while working on other gaps, and the eight future-research sentences behind it span eight distinct papers from 2013 to 2026. The absence as reported, that nothing models the bias when randomized and non-randomized studies enter one network, is false, and the entry has been narrowed to the claim the sources actually support. Two of the eight sentences, Dias et al. 2013 and Wei et al. 2015 on separating true between-trial variation from bias-induced variation, are already registered as QBA-30 and were dropped; a third, the call in Hussein et al. 2023 for a network extension of the mixture model with class-varying bias, has since been supplied by crossnma. Registry search found DEC-22, which rates confidence in a mixed-design network and explicitly sets the synthesis side aside as solved, DIS-07, which states the same calibration problem for external-control bridges across a disconnected gap, and DEC-24, which asks for a common scale for borrowing intensity rather than a rule for choosing a model; none states the selection problem. The verdict is partially-addressed because the model families, their implementations and risk-of-bias-keyed default priors exist and a corpus-level empirical anchor now exists in Toews et al. 2024; what is missing is a criterion with operating characteristics and any per-study calibration of the bias magnitude.

title: No machine-readable specification standard for ITC analyses
text: SFW-02 Confirmed open Very high priority Emerging

title: No machine-readable specification standard for ITC analyses
text:
Statement
The report proposes a cross-package machine-readable object, illustrated as a YAML specification, recording the estimand (population, outcome, contrast, intercurrent-event strategy), the evidence structure, the bridge, the adjustment, the quantitative bias analysis configuration and the requested output, and the literature auditor confirmed every field verbatim in the source at section 16.6. No such schema was found, but that is an exhaustive software-landscape negative neither auditor could verify rather than an established fact. Prose-level reporting structure for PAIC does exist: Ishak et al. 2025 (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1) publishes a framework for reliable, transparent and reproducible population-adjusted indirect comparisons, but it governs what an analyst reports and does not define a machine-readable object that packages read and emit. A schema would also make analyses portable and auditable only if it carried controlled definitions, versioning, validation rules, provenance and explicit mappings to package-specific estimands, so serializing labels into YAML is necessary rather than sufficient.

title: No machine-readable specification standard for ITC analyses
text:
Why it is open
Every package encodes these choices implicitly in its own arguments and defaults, so moving an analysis between tools means re-deriving the specification from code, and the published reporting framework is a prose checklist a reviewer reads rather than an artifact a program can validate. Standardizing function names would not help, because the packages implement genuinely different models; what is shared is the scientific specification, not the API. Current packages lead with the estimate and keep assumptions in model code and prior specifications, so there is nothing to serialize without new work. Adoption further requires controlled vocabularies and estimand mappings agreed among independently maintained packages that have no incentive structure for that coordination.

title: No machine-readable specification standard for ITC analyses
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




Ishak et al. 2025, A Framework for Reliable, Transparent, and Reproducible Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons, PharmacoEconomics
publishes a reporting and risk-of-bias framework for population-adjusted indirect comparisons, the closest existing thing to a PAIC reporting standard; it is prose for analysts rather than a machine-readable specification that packages can read, emit or validate

title: No machine-readable specification standard for ITC analyses
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Build the schema on top of the reporting framework that already exists rather than beside it: take the elements Ishak et al. 2025 asks analysts to report and give them controlled definitions, a version, validation rules, provenance fields and explicit mappings to each package’s estimand conventions. Have synthesis packages read and emit it, and generate the assumptions map, bridge ledger and bias ledger from it, printed before the estimate rather than after. Make round-tripping the acceptance test: the same specification loaded into two packages should yield the same declared estimand and target, not merely the same field names.

title: No machine-readable specification standard for ITC analyses
text:
Verification

Verdict. Confirmed open. Auditors agreed the problem is open and no counterevidence surfaced.
The source said. “The report proposes a cross-package machine-readable object, illustrated as a YAML specification, recording the estimand (population, outcome, contrast, intercurrent-event strategy), the evidence structure (connectedness, number of randomized subnetworks, which studies have IPD), the bridge (type, components, drift sensitivity), the adjustment (modifiers, prognostics, target distribution), the QBA configuration and the output requested, and argues the bridge ledger itself should be machine-readable so that assumption and sensitivity summaries can be generated automatically. No such schema or package-generated ledger exists.”
What was wrong with it. The source stated as fact that no machine-readable bridge-ledger schema exists and that no package generates assumption and sensitivity summaries automatically; both auditors classed these as exhaustive negatives they could not confirm, and GPT-5.6 Sol added that a schema is enabling infrastructure rather than a condition for a valid analysis. The reporting side is not empty either: Ishak et al. 2025 (doi:10.1007/s40273-025-01503-1) already publishes a PAIC reporting and risk-of-bias framework in prose.

Literature and prior-art check

open / supported-with-caveat. I retrieved the source document (documentation/open_problems_itc_paic_cpaic_qba_2026.md, section 16.6, lines 2324-2359) and every self-referential claim checks out verbatim: the YAML block contains estimand (population, outcome, contrast, strategy: ‘treatment policy’), evidence (connected, randomized_subnetworks, ipd_studies), bridge (type, components, drift_sensitivity), adjustment (modifiers, prognostics, target_distribution), qba (mode, omitted_variables, selection_bias, outcome_misclassification, component_drift, parameter_sources) and output (marginal, conditional, partial_identification), followed by ‘This is more valuable than forcing all packages to share the same function names. It makes the scientific specification portable and auditable.’ The two existence claims (‘no machine-readable schema for a disconnected-network bridge ledger currently exists’; ‘no current package automatically generates assumption and sensitivity summaries’) are negatives I searched for and could not confirm from any source that itself asserts the absence; per calibration they are unverifiable, not supported. Adjacent prior art exists on machine-readable evidence-synthesis databases but it concerns extraction databases, not estimand/bridge specification.

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

open / supported-with-caveat. C1 and C4-C8 describe a technically feasible schema, and scientific semantics are more important than standardized function names as claimed in C2. C3 holds only if the schema also has controlled definitions, versioning, validation rules, provenance, and explicit mappings to package-specific estimands; serializing labels into YAML alone does not make analyses portable or auditable. The illustrated fields are proposed requirements, not an implemented or enforced standard. C9-C10 are exhaustive software-landscape claims that cannot be established from technical reasoning alone, while C11 is an unquantified sociological generalization. The interoperability and auditability problem is real, but a machine-readable schema is enabling infrastructure rather than an identification condition or a universal prerequisite for a valid decision-grade analysis.

Decision path

R5:default-open → R11:caveated(n=2)

title: No neutral cross-package benchmark suite for PAIC implementations
text: SFW-04 Partially addressed Very high priority Emerging Tractability 5/5

title: No neutral cross-package benchmark suite for PAIC implementations
text:
Statement
No neutral field-wide benchmark exists that compares baseline connection, CNMA, component PAIC, reference prediction, dose-response models, class effects and partial identification under shared disconnected-network data-generating mechanisms, with public seeds, versioned expected outputs and analytic-truth unit tests. Package-local infrastructure of that kind does exist: at commit 9d150e9 cpaic, an unreleased development package on GitHub that is not on CRAN, ships seeded disconnected-network fixtures with known truth, analytic estimability and likelihood tests, deliberate non-estimability tests, multi-arm tests and cross-package equivalence checks against maicplus. Independent comparative simulation also exists for parts of the field: Chandler and Proskorovsky (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1759) compared four families of MAIC variance estimator across 108 scenarios, and Liu et al. (doi:10.1007/s40258-025-00952-1) ran a 729-scenario full-factorial comparison of unanchored MAIC against naive indirect comparison, neither promoting a method of its own. What is missing is the neutral, maintained, cross-package suite that any implementation can be run against.

title: No neutral cross-package benchmark suite for PAIC implementations
text:
Why it is open
Cross-package validation needs an agreed estimand and input format, neither of which exists, so outside a single package’s own fixtures there is nothing for expected outputs to be expected against. The independent simulation studies that do exist each answer one question and were not built to be re-run by others, so they are evidence rather than infrastructure: no seeds, manifests or reference implementations survive for the next comparison. The mechanisms that would actually discriminate between bridges, namely bridge violation, component drift, unmeasured modifiers and design differences, are still rarely simulated by anyone. Benchmarks are maintenance work with no publication reward and need cross-group coordination nobody owns, so discrepancies surface only in appraisals, where they are attributed to analyst choice rather than to software behavior.

title: No neutral cross-package benchmark suite for PAIC implementations
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




cpaic, unreleased development package on GitHub (not on CRAN), commit 9d150e9
provides seeded disconnected-network data with known truth, analytic estimability and likelihood tests, deliberate non-estimability tests, multi-arm tests and cross-package equivalence tests against maicplus; package-local validation infrastructure that partially resolves the analytic-truth half of the claim but does not replace an independent benchmark


Chandler and Proskorovsky 2024, Uncertain about uncertainty in matching-adjusted indirect comparisons? A simulation study to compare methods for variance estimation, Res Synth Methods 15(6):1094-1110
compares four families of MAIC variance estimator across 108 anchored and unanchored scenarios for binary and time-to-event outcomes, with no method of its own to promote; author-neutral comparative evidence for one part of the field, but not re-runnable infrastructure


Liu et al. 2025, Is the Use of Unanchored Matching-Adjusted Indirect Comparison Always Superior to Naive Indirect Comparison on Survival Outcomes? A Simulation Study
runs a 729-scenario three-level full factorial over IPD and aggregate sample size, covariate strength, correlation, overlap and effect size, identifying where unanchored MAIC is more biased than naive indirect comparison; again author-neutral evidence rather than a maintained benchmark

title: No neutral cross-package benchmark suite for PAIC implementations
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Generalize what already exists rather than starting over: promote cpaic’s seeded known-truth fixtures and cross-package equivalence tests into a package-independent repository, and re-express the published author-neutral simulations as re-runnable scenarios with seeds and manifests. Add the adversarial data-generating mechanisms nobody currently simulates, including bridge violation, component drift, unmeasured modifiers and design difference, and declare an estimand and decision-relevant performance measures for each. Ship versioned expected outputs, analytic-truth unit tests and reference implementations with containerized workflows so any ITC or PAIC package can be run against them and discrepancies are attributable to software rather than to analyst choice.

title: No neutral cross-package benchmark suite for PAIC implementations
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “No neutral benchmark suite or analytic-truth tests for PAIC code” The title says analytic-truth tests do not exist, but seeded known-truth fixtures, analytic and non-estimability tests and cross-package equivalence checks were found.
The source said. “There is no open benchmark suite for ITC, PAIC, disconnected-network, component and QBA methods with synthetic and real exemplars, public seeds, expected outputs, analytic-truth unit tests and cross-package validation, and no shared set of disconnected-network data-generating mechanisms under which baseline connection, CNMA, cpaic, reference prediction, dose-response models, class effects and partial identification can be compared. The report argues such a neutral comparison is a publication in its own right and may have more practical influence than another estimator paper.”
What was wrong with it. The source claimed PAIC software is not routinely unit tested against analytic truth and that no benchmark datasets or cross-package tests exist; GPT-5.6 Sol found seeded known-truth fixtures, analytic and deliberate non-estimability tests and cross-package equivalence checks already in cpaic at commit 9d150e9, and the literature auditor rejected the premise that comparative evidence comes mostly from the authors of the method being promoted, naming two author-neutral simulation studies (doi:10.1002/jrsm.1759, doi:10.1007/s40258-025-00952-1). The claim was unattributed in the source and is now sourced; the field-wide benchmark gap survives.
Dissent. literature dissented (open): Source-document checks pass exactly: line 2147 rates ‘Public adversarial benchmark and empirical bridge-deletion suite’ Impact 5, Novelty 3, Tractability 5, so the ‘tractability 5 out of 5’ figure is right; line 2233 states verbatim that the paper ‘may have more practical influence than another estimator paper because the field lacks trusted comparative benchmarks and has almost no reference-grade QBA software for limited-AgD unanchored PAIC’; line 1165 matches the disconnected-network benchmark claim. No maintained neutral suite with public seeds, versioned expected outputs and analytic-truth unit tests exists, so the core claim stands. The caveat is the why_open assertion that comparative evidence ‘comes mostly from simulations run by the authors of the method being promoted’. Two counterexamples: Chandler & Proskorovsky (2024) ran 108 scenarios comparing four MAIC variance families with no method to promote, and Liu et al. (2025) ran a 729-scenario full-factorial MAIC versus naive comparison. Wigle & Beliveau (2022) likewise report the first simulation comparison of CNMA models. codex dissented (overstated): The inspected sources do not contain a neutral field-wide suite comparing every named method under common disconnected-network data-generating mechanisms, so the central benchmark problem remains. However, C2, C4, and C6 are too categorical: cpaic already contains a seeded disconnected-network fixture with known truth, analytic estimability and likelihood tests, deliberate non-estimability tests, multi-arm tests, and cross-package equivalence checks. C5 is technically correct. C8 is defensible only for the full all-method comparison. C7 is a QBA software-coverage claim rather than a mathematical result. C9 is a prediction, C10 merely reports the agenda’s own rating, and C11 is an unquantified ecosystem judgment. Existing package-local tests partially solve implementation verification but do not replace an independent benchmark.

title: ML-NMR runtime can constrain repeated sensitivity analyses at scale
text:
Statement
multinma ML-NMR can become computationally expensive as aggregate-data integration rows and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo gradient evaluations grow, which can constrain repeated sensitivity analyses in large models. Open issue #66 (raised 17 March 2026) reports 24 hours or more for 16000 iterations with 200-plus integration points in a random-effects model over many studies, and open issue #29 (14 January 2024) requests a cmdstanr backend, which may improve compilation and execution but does not remove the model’s integration arithmetic. The auditors disagreed on how far this generalizes and both readings stand: the literature auditor verified every claim as stated and read the tracker as evidence that users hit prohibitive runtimes, while GPT-5.6 Sol found that release 0.9.1 already reduced the default integration burden and added integration checking, so the evidence supports a material caution at larger scales rather than a general block on routine sensitivity analysis.

title: ML-NMR runtime can constrain repeated sensitivity analyses at scale
text:
Why it is open
ML-NMR requires numerical integration over the covariate distribution inside every likelihood and gradient evaluation, and while integration nodes and design data can be reused, the parameter-dependent likelihood terms cannot, so cost grows with total integration rows and is not amortizable across iterations. At large scale that turns computation into a methodological constraint, because the sensitivity analyses, prior checks and simulation studies the rest of the agenda demands multiply the cost. How large is large enough to matter has never been characterized, which is exactly why two auditors read the same tracker differently. The backend request reflects the same pressure but addresses compilation and execution rather than the integration arithmetic itself.

title: ML-NMR runtime can constrain repeated sensitivity analyses at scale
text:
Verification

Verdict. Unverifiable. Auditors disagreed and the disagreement was evidence-bearing on both sides.
The source titled this. “multinma ML-NMR runtime blocks routine sensitivity analysis” The audit explicitly did not sustain the title’s claim that runtime blocks routine sensitivity analysis, since release 0.9.1 lowered the default integration burden.
The source said. “multinma, described as the most mature open Bayesian NMA/NMR/ML-NMR platform, carries a runtime and numerical-integration burden, with an open issue on high runtime in ML-NMR when there are many studies and many integration points, and an open request for a cmdstanr backend.”
What was wrong with it. The title claim that runtime blocks routine sensitivity analysis was not sustained: GPT-5.6 Sol found in the 0.9.1 release source that ML-NMR models are now much faster to run by default (dmphillippo/multinma@4fe8a6e) and that cost depends on total integration rows, outcome model, parameter dimension and gradient evaluations rather than simply studies times points times iterations, and also called the most mature platform label an unsupported superlative. The literature auditor verified issues #66 and #29 and the 0.9.1 release date exactly as stated, so the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved.
Dissent. literature dissented (supported): Retrieved the multinma issue tracker directly. Issue #66 ‘High runtime for ML-NMR’ is open (raised 2026-03-17) and its body confirms the exact conditions claimed: many studies and many integration points. Issue #29 ‘Option to use cmdstanr as the backend’ is open (2024-01-14). CRAN release history confirms 0.9.1 published 2026-04-16. Every claim in this entry is accurate as stated. One framing note the entry itself pre-empts elsewhere: #66 is a user question rather than a maintainer-acknowledged defect, and no maintainer statement in the thread concedes a runtime bug; the evidence supports ‘users hit prohibitive runtimes’, not ‘the package is inefficient’. codex dissented (overstated): ML-NMR does incur a real integration burden because aggregate-data likelihood contributions must be evaluated across integration rows during repeated HMC log-density and gradient evaluations, supporting C2. The cost is not literally just studies multiplied by points and MCMC iterations: it depends on total integration rows, outcome model, parameter dimension, leapfrog and gradient evaluations, and parallelization. Parameter-independent nodes and design data can be reused, while parameter-dependent likelihood terms generally cannot. Version 0.9.1 already reduced the default integration burden and added integration checking, so the evidence supports a material caution at larger scales, not the general title claim that routine sensitivity analysis is blocked. A cmdstanr backend may improve compilation, execution, and workflow, but it does not remove the model’s integration arithmetic; the backend request therefore does not prove that the current backend determines achievable model size. C1 is an unsupported superlative. C3-C5 concern issue and release metadata rather than statistical correctness, and their current online state cannot be refreshed under the no-web constraint.

title: No agreed leave-one-out unit for mixed IPD and aggregate likelihoods
text: SFW-08 Partially addressed High priority Established

title: No agreed leave-one-out unit for mixed IPD and aggregate likelihoods
text:
Statement
Open multinma issues record poor Pareto-k behavior together with ambiguity over the unit of leave-one-out prediction (#60), absent prior-sensitivity tooling (#32) and uncertainty around rankings and SUCRA (#17). Two of these are implementation gaps with published prescriptions rather than missing methods: #32 asks multinma to expose log-prior evaluations so the existing power-scaling method in priorsense can be used, and #17 asks for SUCRA credible intervals following Trinquart et al., which is arithmetic on the mean-rank posterior. multinma 0.9.1 already reports posterior rank distributions with credible intervals through posterior_ranks() and shows prior-to-posterior movement through plot_prior_posterior(), so the ranking and prior-dependence gaps are narrower than stated. What is genuinely unsettled is the held-out unit: loo.stan_nma delegates to rstan::loo while the log-likelihood mixes patient-level IPD, arm-level aggregate and study-level contrast contributions, so the unit is heterogeneous, no unit selection or exact-refit fallback is exposed, and no field convention fixes which unit answers which predictive question.

title: No agreed leave-one-out unit for mixed IPD and aggregate likelihoods
text:
Why it is open
In a hierarchical evidence-synthesis model there is no single natural held-out unit, and multinma’s log-likelihood mixes patients, arms and study-level contrasts, so a reported leave-one-out number aggregates over units that answer different predictive questions and is not comparable across analyses. No convention fixes the unit and no exact-refit or grouped fallback is exposed for when the importance-sampling approximation degrades, which is precisely when the model is complex enough for the comparison to matter. Prior dependence in sparse or partially disconnected networks is visible only if the analyst chooses to look, since power-scaling needs a log-prior the package does not expose and the prior-versus-posterior plot is qualitative. Rankings compound this because SUCRA is a nonlinear functional of the posterior reported without an interval, even though the mean-rank interval it would be derived from is already available.

title: No agreed leave-one-out unit for mixed IPD and aggregate likelihoods
text:
What has been tried




Work
What it contributes




multinma 0.9.1 (CRAN, published 16 Apr 2026)
implements Bayesian ML-NMR whose leave-one-out predictive validation, prior-sensitivity and ranking tooling are at issue; loo.stan_nma delegates to rstan::loo over a log-likelihood that mixes patient, arm and study-level contributions

quotes the published prescription of Trinquart et al. for translating the mean-rank credible interval into a SUCRA credible interval; the gap is implementation, not derivation

title: No agreed leave-one-out unit for mixed IPD and aggregate likelihoods
text:
Probable solution or research direction
Settle the held-out unit first, because it is the only item with no published answer: define what leaving out a patient, an arm, a study or a treatment means in hierarchical NMA and ML-NMR, implement a diagnostic for each, and provide an exact-refit or grouped fallback when Pareto-k diagnostics fail. The other three are plumbing against known prescriptions: expose log-prior evaluations so priorsense power-scaling works, derive SUCRA intervals from the mean-rank posterior as Trinquart et al. specify, and surface both by default rather than as optional extra analysis. Report Pareto-k failure as a statement about the approximation rather than about the model, so users do not discard a valid fit.

title: No agreed leave-one-out unit for mixed IPD and aggregate likelihoods
text:
Verification

Verdict. Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.
The source titled this. “No agreed leave-one-out unit or prior-sensitivity tooling for ML-NMR” The title says prior-sensitivity tooling is absent, but the power-scaling prescription is off the shelf and prior-posterior plotting already ships in multinma 0.9.1.
The source said. “Open multinma issues record poor Pareto-k behavior, ambiguity over the unit of leave-one-out prediction, absent prior-sensitivity tooling and unquantified uncertainty around rankings and SUCRA, alongside a table caution that predictive validation for this class of model is complex. These are model-validation and decision-uncertainty problems for hierarchical evidence synthesis, not only diagnostic warnings in one package.”
What was wrong with it. Both auditors narrowed the entry: the literature auditor found that prior-sensitivity and SUCRA uncertainty have off-the-shelf prescriptions named in the issues themselves (priorsense power-scaling in #32, Trinquart et al. in #17), so no tooling exists overstates them, and GPT-5.6 Sol found posterior_ranks() and plot_prior_posterior() already shipping in 0.9.1. GPT-5.6 Sol also corrected the reading of Pareto-k, which signals that the importance-sampling approximation is unreliable rather than that the fitted model has failed.

Literature and prior-art check

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. All five issue claims verify against open multinma issues. #60 ‘DIC/LOO bad pareto k and general interpretation’ contains both the Pareto-k failure and, explicitly, the leave-one-out unit ambiguity: the reporter asks whether LOO is mixing leave-one-patient-out error for IPD studies with leave-one-study-out error for aggregate studies. #17 ‘Uncertainty around SUCRA’ is open since 2022. #32 requests logprior evaluations. The caveat is that two of the four sub-problems have off-the-shelf published solutions awaiting only package plumbing, so ‘no tooling exists’ overstates them: #32 asks multinma to expose lprior so the existing priorsense power-scaling method (Kallioinen et al. 2024, cited in the issue) can be used, and #17 asks for SUCRA credible intervals following Trinquart et al., a fix that is arithmetic on the mean-rank posterior. The genuinely open item is the field convention for the held-out unit in hierarchical NMA/ML-NMR, which no source resolves. Cites https://github.com/dmphillippo/multinma/issues/32: Shows prior-sensitivity methodology already exists (power-scaling, priorsense); the multinma gap is exposing lprior, not the absence of a method.. Cites https://github.com/dmphillippo/multinma/issues/17: SUCRA uncertainty has a published prescription (Trinquart et al.) quoted in the issue; the gap is implementation..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens

partially-solved / supported-with-caveat. In multinma 0.9.1, loo.stan_nma delegates to rstan::loo while log_lik combines patient-level IPD, arm-level aggregate-data, and study-level contrast contributions. The held-out unit is therefore heterogeneous, and no unit-selection or exact-refit fallback is exposed. Formal prior-sensitivity and SUCRA-uncertainty tooling remain gaps. However, posterior_ranks already reports posterior rank distributions with credible intervals, and plot_prior_posterior exposes prior-to-posterior movement. Poor Pareto-k indicates unreliable PSIS approximation, not failure of the fitted model itself. Cites dmphillippo/multinma@4fe8a6e9977b7ba6ef93822dda43b617b256587a: Provides posterior uncertainty for treatment rankings and qualitative inspection of prior dependence, although it does not provide formal power-scaling sensitivity or SUCRA intervals..

Decision path

section: How the evidence falls in time
text:
How the evidence falls in time
8 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2014 to 2022. The most recent paper to touch this reports progress on it, and every paper calling it open is older.
It is also being closed in pieces: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.
Does the later work answer the earlier work? Put to an independent reviewer with the older and newer claims side by side, it judged that the later work answers a component of it, leaving a named part (medium confidence). The later work establishes general principles for choosing grouped LOO units and provides a trial-level solution for pure aggregate-data meta-analysis. Neither resolves how mixed-granularity likelihood contributions should be grouped or compared in an ITC/PAIC implementation such as multinma. What remains: An agreed held-out unit and predictive estimand for likelihoods combining patient-level IPD, aggregate-arm, and study-level contrast contributions, with suitable diagnostics and exact-refit fallback.
